title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Preface
Welcome to Data Science and Macroeconomic Models! This is an interactive, AI-powered Python book on intermediate macroeconomics. It brings real economic data and macroeconomic models together, with Python code you can run and change and an AI assistant to help you along the way. Its aim is that you do macroeconomics, not only read about it: you find the big facts in the data yourself, and then you build, operate and question the models behind them.
Macroeconomics begins with facts. How fast have living standards risen? Why are some countries so much richer than others? How do output, unemployment and inflation move when the economy turns down? We need answers from the data before we can build a model. Models are our best attempt to explain the facts, and the facts tell us which models deserve our attention. My hope is simple: by the end of this book, you will be as comfortable asking the data a question as you are drawing a diagram, and you will enjoy doing both.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Why this book
The book rests on three pillars:

Data science: find the facts. You download, plot and explore real macroeconomic data, and you decide for yourself what pattern the data show.
Macroeconomic models: explain the facts. You move sliders, change parameters and edit the Python code of each model, and you check how well it accounts for the facts you found.
AI-powered learning: learn faster, and check everything. An AI assistant helps you write and understand the code, and AI-drawn mind maps and lecture slides give you the big picture of every chapter.

Each chapter is an interactive notebook. You can read it on this website or run it in Google Colab, with nothing to install.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Stylized facts: where models begin
A stylized fact is a broad pattern in the data that holds across many countries or over long periods. It is “stylized” because it leaves out details and exceptions. Not every year or every country fits it exactly, but the pattern is strong enough that a good theory should explain it.
The term comes from the economist Nicholas Kaldor. In Kaldor (1961), he argued that theory should start from a summary of the facts, not from convenient assumptions. He then listed six stylized facts of economic growth:

Output per worker grows at a roughly constant rate over long periods.
Capital per worker also grows over time.
The rate of return on capital is roughly constant.
The ratio of capital to output is roughly constant.
The shares of labor and capital in national income are roughly constant.
The growth rate of output per worker differs widely across countries.

These six facts set the agenda for growth theory. With technological progress, the Solow model (Chapters 5 and 6) reproduces the first five. The sixth raised a new question, why countries differ so much, which Chapters 3 to 6 take up.
Stylized facts are not carved in stone. They summarize the data, so new data can revise them. Take labor’s share of income, long described as “about two-thirds.” Jones (2024, Chapter 2) notes that it has drifted down since around 1970. In the Chapter 2 notebook, you check this yourself with the latest U.S. national accounts. Labor earned 0.65 of income on average from 1950 to 2025, close to two-thirds, but its share has been below 0.60 since 2022. Is the old fact still a fact? The data alone do not settle it, but they tell you exactly which question to ask.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Pillar 1: From data to facts
Jones (2024) gives data a central role. Its chapters are full of figures of real economies, and its models are judged by how well they explain what those figures show. This book takes one more step. Instead of reading the facts from a printed figure, you derive them yourself.
Every data figure in this book is interactive. Each one is built from public data, usually updated to the latest available year. You can:

Explore the figures. Hover over any point to read its value, zoom into a period, or press play to watch countries move over time.
Change the question. Switch countries, years and variables with simple widgets or a one-line change in the code. Does the fact you see for the United States also hold for Japan, Brazil or Nigeria? Does it survive if the sample starts in 1990 instead of 1960?
Get fresh data. Appendix B shows how to download data directly from FRED, the World Bank, the IMF, the ECB, Eurostat, the OECD, the Penn World Table, the Maddison Project and Our World in Data. Your facts can be as current as the data.

The aim is not to replace the facts in Jones (2024). It is to make you comfortable asking the data a question and judging the answer, which is what macroeconomists do every day.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Pillar 2: From facts to models
Once you have a fact, you want to know why it holds. That is the job of a model. The models in this book follow those in Jones (2024):

The long run: the production model, the Solow model and the Romer model of ideas. Appendix D takes them to the Penn World Table: growth accounting splits each economy’s GDP growth into capital, labor and TFP, and development accounting splits its income gap with the United States the same way, for any economies you choose. Appendix E asks whether poor countries catch up: it derives the speed of convergence from the Solow model and measures β- and σ-convergence across 84 countries since 1960. Appendix F adds human capital to the Solow model and replicates Mankiw, Romer and Weil (1992): saving, schooling and population growth explain most of the income differences across countries, then and with the Penn World Table 11.0. Appendix G asks where the productivity gaps come from: it replicates Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001), who use the mortality of early European settlers as an instrument to estimate the effect of institutions on income, with pyfixest and linearmodels.
The short run: the IS curve, monetary policy, the Phillips curve and the AS/AD framework.
Applications: consumption, investment, government budgets, trade and exchange rates.
The frontier: the dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models of Chapter 15, which central banks use for policy analysis and forecasting. Appendix H shows how to write them, solve them with rational expectations and estimate them, with Snowdrop, a free Python package developed at the IMF. Appendix I is the advanced version of Chapter 15: it solves the estimated Smets–Wouters model and recomputes the chapter’s impulse responses.

Here, however, you can operate every model:

On this website, each model figure of the chapters has a slider. Move it to see how the outcome changes with a parameter.
In Colab, each model figure has live sliders and buttons that solve the model again as you move them.
In the code, each model is a few lines of plain Python, right next to its figure. Change a parameter, add a shock or replace an equation, and see what happens. This is where you can go beyond the textbook.

Then you close the loop by putting the model next to the data. Which facts does the model explain? Which does it miss? A model that misses an important fact is not a failure; it is the reason for the next chapter. For example, the Solow model explains much of why some countries are rich and others poor. On its own, however, it cannot explain why growth continues decade after decade. The economics of ideas in Chapter 6 fills that gap.
The chapters compare models with data by eye. Appendix H takes the last step that research takes: it estimates a model. The data choose the parameter values that make them most likely, by maximum likelihood or by Bayesian methods, and the estimation shows which parameters the data can pin down and which they cannot. There you estimate Ireland’s (2004) New Keynesian model on U.S. data from 1948 to 2002 and reproduce its published estimates.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Pillar 3: AI-powered learning
AI tools are changing how we learn, write code and do research. This book puts them to work for you in three ways:

An AI assistant at your side. Colab includes Gemini, an AI assistant that can explain a line of code, fix an error or write a new plot from a plain-language request. Other assistants, such as Claude or ChatGPT, work just as well. Ask one to explain a model’s equations in plain words, to suggest another country to compare, or to turn your own idea into code. Section A.5 of Appendix A shows how to use Colab’s AI tools, how to write good prompts and how to check the answers.
AI-drawn mind maps. Every chapter and appendix opens with a mind map: a hand-drawn visual summary of its questions, its facts and its models. The maps were drawn with AI image generation, and I checked every label, equation and number on them against the chapter. Look at the map before you start a chapter, and come back to it when you finish.
Lecture slides. Every chapter and appendix has a lecture deck, made with AI assistance from the chapter itself, with live charts you can hover over and play with. The Open Lecture Slides badge at the top of each chapter opens it.

Use AI, but check it. An AI assistant can write code that runs and still answers the wrong question. Read what it writes, run it, and compare the result with what you know. Treat it as a fast and tireless study partner, not as an oracle.
How AI helped build this book. I wrote this book with the help of AI tools, and I want to be open about it. Claude (Anthropic) helped me write the code, the text and the lecture slides. Codex (OpenAI) drew the mind maps. Gemini (Google) is the assistant built into Colab, where every notebook runs. I checked every result: the code is run and tested, the numbers are computed from the data, and every figure names its sources.

Key resources for learning
This book

The website, https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/: every chapter, with its interactive figures and model sliders.
The GitHub repository, quarcs-lab/macro102-site: the notebooks, their sources and the data files behind every figure.

The badges at the top of each chapter

Open AI Notebook: run the chapter’s notebook in Google Colab, with live sliders and buttons, and ask Gemini, Colab’s AI assistant, for help with the code.
Open Lecture Slides: the chapter’s lecture deck, with live charts.
Open Data Apps: a code-free page that collects the chapter’s interactive data charts, in the chapters that have one.
Model Apps (coming soon): code-free pages with the chapter’s interactive models.

section: A companion to Jones (2024), not a substitute
text:
A companion to Jones (2024), not a substitute
This book is an interactive data-science companion to Jones (2024). Its 21 chapters have the same titles and follow the same order, so you can work through the two books side by side. I recommend reading a chapter of Jones (2024) first, for the economic reasoning and the full discussion. Then open the matching notebook to work with the data and the models. The notebooks do not repeat the textbook’s explanations, and they do not replace it.
This book is independent. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or the publisher of the textbook. Every figure is an original adaptation, drawn with this book’s own code:

Data figures are inspired by figures in Jones (2024). They are rebuilt from public data, usually updated to the latest year and extended to other countries.
Model figures are adapted from its diagrams, with their own parameter values, layout and interactive controls.

A Sources note below every figure names the figure in Jones (2024) that inspired it and links to the data sources, so you can open them and explore the data yourself.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
Who this book is for
I wrote this book for anyone who wants to see macroeconomics at work in real data:

Undergraduate students in intermediate macroeconomics, who want to see the ideas of the course at work in real data and learn practical Python along the way.
Master’s students in business, public policy and development programs, who need a hands-on, data-driven understanding of the macroeconomy for analysis and policy work.
Self-learners, who want a hands-on path through macroeconomics at their own pace, with no software to install.
Data-science learners, who know some Python and want meaningful economic questions to apply it to.
Macroeconomists, who know the theory and want to learn Python for data science with models they already know, and who want a free Python alternative to Dynare and IRIS for solving and estimating DSGE models (Appendices H and I).

No programming experience is assumed. Appendix A is a guided tour of Colab, Python, Colab’s AI tools for coding and learning, and the data-science libraries used in the book. Appendix C reviews the math, with Python code for each calculation.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
How the book is organized
Like Jones (2024), this book is built around one famous graph: U.S. GDP per person since 1870. The graph shows a long-run upward trend and short-run fluctuations around it, and it raises the question of what the future holds. The chapters are grouped into four parts, as in the sidebar:

Preliminaries (Chapters 1–2): what macroeconomics studies and how we measure the macroeconomy.
The Long Run (Chapters 3–8): economic growth, production, the Solow model, ideas, the labor market and inflation.
The Short Run (Chapters 9–15): economic fluctuations, the Great Recession and the Covid-19 pandemic, the IS curve, monetary policy and the Phillips curve, the AS/AD framework, financial crises and DSGE models.
Applications (Chapters 16–21): consumption, investment, the government, international trade and exchange rates, and parting thoughts on what macroeconomics has learned and what remains open.
Appendices A–I: first the tools (A–C): Colab and Python, live access to macroeconomic data and a math review. Then economic growth (D–G): growth and development accounting, growth and convergence across countries, the augmented Solow growth model, and growth and institutions. Last, DSGE models (H–I): DSGE modeling with Python, and the Smets–Wouters model of Chapter 15 solved in Python.

Every chapter has the same structure:

A mind map and the chapter’s badges (Colab, lecture slides and, where available, data apps) open the chapter.
A Model overview builds the chapter’s main model step by step, from assumptions to solution and predictions, and ends with the model in code.
Thematic sections work through the chapter’s figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, …). Each figure comes with a goal, the code that draws it, and a “What to notice” summary.
Your turn tasks, with hints, ask you to change the data or the model and interpret the result.
Concluding remarks sum up what the data showed and what the models explained.
Practice problems (conceptual, data-based and modeling), with hints and full solutions, close Chapters 1–20.

title: Data Science and Macroeconomic Models
text:
How to use this book

Getting started

On this website you can read every chapter, see all the figures, hover over the data points and move the precomputed sliders under each model figure.
In Google Colab you can run the code yourself. Click the Open AI Notebook badge at the top of a chapter, then choose Runtime → Run all. Every model figure gets live sliders and buttons, and you can try every “Your turn” task in an empty code cell.
No installation is needed. Colab already has numpy, pandas, plotly and ipywidgets, and the data are read directly from this book’s GitHub repository. The appendices that need extra packages install them in their first code cell: Appendix B its data libraries, and Appendices H and I the Snowdrop package (about 20 seconds).
New to Python or Colab? Start with Appendix A.



For each chapter
Read the chapter in Jones (2024) first. The textbook gives you the economic reasoning and the full discussion. The notebook then lets you work with the data and the models behind it.
Look at the mind map. The map at the top of the chapter shows its questions, its facts and its models at a glance. Click it to open the full-size image.
Open the notebook. Read it on this website, or click Open AI Notebook and choose Runtime → Run all to bring every chart and slider to life.
Explore the data figures. Hover, zoom, press play and switch countries. Ask yourself whether the fact holds for other countries and other years.
Operate the models. Before you move a slider, predict what will happen. Then move it and check your prediction against the chart.
Do the “Your turn” tasks. Each one asks you to change the data or the model and to interpret the result. Try it yourself before you open the hint.
Ask an AI assistant when you are stuck. Ask Gemini in Colab to explain a line of code or an equation, or to help you with a “Your turn” task. Then check its answer.
Study the lecture slides. The Open Lecture Slides badge opens the chapter’s deck, a compact review of its facts and models with live charts.
Open the Data Apps. When the chapter has them, the Open Data Apps badge opens a code-free page with all its interactive data charts in one place.
Try the practice problems. Conceptual, data-based and modeling problems close the chapter. Work on each one before you look at the hints and the full solution.

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Learning goals
Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: income, employment, inflation, unemployment and deficits. It works in four steps: document the facts, build a model, compare the model with the facts, and use the model for experiments. By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
1.1 Model overview
Meet Islandia, a small imaginary island country that we follow through the whole book. Before we can explain anything about Islandia, we must measure it: how fast its prices rise, how many islanders have jobs, how fast its income grows. Then we need a way to explain what we measured: a model, a small economy written as a few equations. This section builds both kits step by step, and every later chapter reuses them.






NoteThe big idea



The question. How do we turn an economy’s raw numbers into facts we can compare, and how does a model explain those facts?
The answer in one sentence. Rates, ratios and growth rates make the facts comparable across countries and decades, and a model turns inputs we choose into the outcomes we want to explain.
What goes in and what comes out. The two measurement blocks take data (prices, jobs, output) and give back inflation, the labor-market ratios, the output gap, growth rates and doubling times. The labor-market model takes three parameters and a minimum wage, and gives back the wage, employment and unemployment.
Road map.

Measuring the facts: rates, ratios and the output gap: inflation, the key relations between the labor-market ratios, and the output gap.
Growth rates and compound growth: compound growth, the average growth rate and the rule of 70.
How a model works: the labor market: the assumptions, solving the model, and what the model predicts.
Extension: a minimum wage: what happens when a law puts a floor under the wage.
Model in code: the key results as Python functions, checked with numbers. Every later section reuses these functions.

Notation. A bar over a letter marks a parameter: a number the model builder chooses, such as \(\bar{a}\) or \(\bar{f}\). Letters without a bar are endogenous variables: the model determines them (in the measurement blocks, the data record them). A subscript \(t\) marks the year, as in \(y_t\). In the code we simply write a, l and f.

Meaning

1.1.1 Measuring the facts: rates, ratios and the output gap

Definitions
Islandia keeps statistics like any real country. Almost every number in this chapter is a rate or a ratio, not a total. Dividing by the right total makes a small country comparable with a large one, and 1960 comparable with 2025.

Inflation. Let \(P_t\) be the price level in year \(t\), for example a consumer price index. The inflation rate is the percentage change of prices over one year (Fig. 3): \[\pi_t = 100\times\frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}}.\]
Jobs. Each adult is employed (\(E\)), unemployed (\(U\): has no job but is looking for one), or out of the labor force. The labor force is \(LF = E + U\), and \(Pop\) is the adult population. Three ratios describe the labor market: \[u = \frac{U}{LF}\ \ \text{(unemployment rate, Fig. 4)}, \qquad e = \frac{E}{Pop}\ \ \text{(employment-population ratio, Fig. 2)}, \qquad p = \frac{LF}{Pop}\ \ \text{(participation rate)}.\]
Deficits. With \(Y\) for GDP, both deficits of Fig. 5 are measured as shares of GDP: \[\text{budget deficit} = \frac{\text{government spending} - \text{government revenue}}{Y}, \qquad \text{trade deficit} = \frac{\text{imports} - \text{exports}}{Y}.\] A negative deficit is a surplus.
Potential output. \(Y^{pot}_t\) is what the economy would produce if all prices could adjust freely and all workers and machines were fully used. Actual output \(Y_t\) moves around it (Fig. 7).



Deriving the key relations
Step 1: from inflation back to prices. Multiply the definition of \(\pi_t\) by \(P_{t-1}/100\), then add \(P_{t-1}\) to both sides:
\[P_t = P_{t-1}\left(1 + \frac{\pi_t}{100}\right).\]
Each year multiplies the price level by a factor \(1 + \pi_t/100\). Inflation of 3,080 percent, as in Argentina in 1989 (Fig. 3), multiplies prices by \(1 + 30.8 = 31.8\) in a single year. For prices to rise a thousandfold within one year we need \(1 + \pi/100 = 1000\), that is \(\pi = 99{,}900\) percent. Over several years the yearly factors multiply:
\[\frac{P_T}{P_0} = \left(1 + \frac{\pi_1}{100}\right)\left(1 + \frac{\pi_2}{100}\right)\cdots\left(1 + \frac{\pi_T}{100}\right).\]
Two years of 10 percent inflation raise prices by \(1.1 \times 1.1 = 1.21\), that is by 21 percent and not 20: the second year’s inflation also applies to the first year’s increase.
Step 2: employment, participation and unemployment. Start from \(E = LF - U\) and divide both sides by \(Pop\). Then take \(LF/Pop\) out as a common factor:
\[e = \frac{E}{Pop} = \frac{LF - U}{Pop} = \frac{LF}{Pop}\left(1 - \frac{U}{LF}\right).\]
The first fraction on the right is \(p\) and the one in brackets is \(u\), which gives the first key result.






ImportantKey result: employment, participation and unemployment



\[e = p\,(1 - u) \tag{1}\]
The share of adults with a job is the share in the labor force times the share of the labor force that has a job.
In the data. In February 2020 about 63.3 percent of U.S. adults were in the labor force and 3.5 percent of them were unemployed, so \(e = 63.3 \times (1 - 0.035) \approx 61.1\) percent, the value in Fig. 2.








TipIn words



Islandia’s employment ratio can fall for two quite different reasons. Some islanders lose their jobs and keep looking for new ones, so unemployment rises. Or some islanders give up looking and leave the labor force, so participation falls. Equation (1) keeps the two stories apart, which no single headline number can do.


Step 3: the output gap. The gap measures how far actual output is from potential, in percent of potential:






ImportantKey result: the output gap



\[\text{gap}_t = 100\times\left(\frac{Y_t}{Y^{pot}_t} - 1\right) \tag{2}\]
It is negative when the economy makes less than it could.
Islandia in numbers. In a bad year when Islandia produces 95.3 percent of its potential output, its gap is \(100\times(0.953-1) = -4.7\) percent.


Multiplying out gives the gap in dollars, \(Y_t - Y^{pot}_t = (\text{gap}_t/100)\times Y^{pot}_t\). The same formula works per person: dividing both outputs by the population leaves the ratio \(Y_t/Y^{pot}_t\) unchanged, so the gap in percent is the same, and the gap in dollars per person is \((\text{gap}_t/100)\times Y^{pot}_t/Pop_t\). For small gaps, \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) (Appendix C.6) gives the log form \(\text{gap}_t \approx 100\,(\ln Y_t - \ln Y^{pot}_t)\). The short-run chapters measure fluctuations in this way.
Step 4: why divide by GDP. The growth rate of a ratio is the growth rate of its numerator minus that of its denominator (Appendix C.5). For a deficit \(D\),
\[g_{D/Y} \approx g_D - g_Y.\]
A deficit that grows as fast as GDP keeps the same weight in the economy, even though in dollars it is many times larger than in 1960. That is why Fig. 5 compares shares of GDP and not dollars.

Dividing by the right total turns raw counts into rates that we can compare across countries and decades.



What the numbers tell us
The two labor-market ratios. The table reads equation (1) one input at a time, at the February 2020 values \(p = 63.3\%\) and \(u = 3.5\%\):








A change of …
changes \(e = p(1-u)\) by
Why




\(+1\) point in the unemployment rate \(u\)
\(-p \approx -0.63\) points
a point of \(u\) is a point of the labor force, not of all adults


\(+1\) point in the participation rate \(p\)
\(+(1-u) \approx +0.97\) points
most new participants find a job



In logs, \(\ln e = \ln p + \ln(1-u)\) (Appendix C.4), so the percentage change of \(e\) splits exactly into a participation part and an unemployment part. By April 2020 participation had dropped to about 60.1 percent and unemployment had jumped to about 14.8 percent. Check 5 in Model in code shows that roughly 70 percent of the fall in \(e\) came from higher unemployment and 30 percent from people leaving the labor force.
The output gap is negative in a recession and positive in a boom. Its log form is accurate only for small gaps: for a gap as deep as the Great Depression’s, the two versions differ by about 2 points (Check 6 in the code).






NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia’s prices rise by 10 percent this year and by 10 percent again next year. By how much do they rise over the two years, and why is the answer not 20 percent?


Answer

By 21 percent. Step 1 says that each year multiplies the price level by \(1 + \pi_t/100\), so the two years give \(1.1 \times 1.1 = 1.21\). The second year’s 10 percent also applies to the first year’s increase.

2. Islandia’s employment-population ratio falls, but its unemployment rate stays the same. What must have happened?


Answer

By equation (1), \(e = p(1-u)\). With \(u\) unchanged, the fall in \(e\) can only come from a fall in the participation rate \(p\): some islanders stopped looking for work and left the labor force.






1.1.2 Growth rates and compound growth

Definitions
The growth rate of a variable \(y_t\), such as Islandia’s GDP per person, from year \(t\) to year \(t+1\) is its percentage change, written as a decimal:
\[g_t = \frac{y_{t+1} - y_t}{y_t} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad y_{t+1} = y_t\,(1 + g_t).\]
The inflation rate of the block above is the growth rate of the price level, times 100. The average annual growth rate between year 0 and year \(T\) is the one constant rate \(g\) that would carry \(y_0\) to \(y_T\) in \(T\) years.


Solving: compound growth
Step 1: growth at a constant rate. If \(y\) grows at the same rate \(g\) every year, apply the rule year after year and substitute each line into the next:
\[y_1 = y_0(1+g), \qquad y_2 = y_1(1+g) = y_0(1+g)^2, \qquad y_3 = y_2(1+g) = y_0(1+g)^3, \qquad \dots\]
The exponent simply counts the years, so after \(t\) years we reach the box below.






ImportantKey result: compound growth



\[y_t = y_0\,(1+g)^t \tag{3}\]
This is compound growth (Appendix C.3): each year’s growth applies to a level that already includes the growth of all the years before.
Islandia in numbers. If Islandia’s income per person grows 2 percent a year, after 100 years it is \((1.02)^{100} \approx 7.2\) times its starting level.








TipIn words: growth feeds on itself



When Islandia’s income grows 2 percent this year, next year’s 2 percent is taken from a larger base. So the yearly gains themselves keep getting bigger. Over a century this multiplies income about seven times.


Step 2: the average growth rate. Solve equation (3) for \(g\), with \(T\) years. Divide by \(y_0\), raise both sides to the power \(1/T\) (because \(\left((1+g)^T\right)^{1/T} = 1+g\)), and subtract 1:
\[\frac{y_T}{y_0} = (1+g)^T \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left(\frac{y_T}{y_0}\right)^{1/T} = 1 + g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g = \left(\frac{y_T}{y_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1.\]
Fig. 7 applies this formula to U.S. GDP per person from 1870 to 2025, with \(T = 155\): the answer is about 1.9 percent a year. Read backwards, the same formula tells us the growth rate a target needs: a tenfold rise in a century needs \(g = 10^{1/100} - 1 \approx 2.3\) percent a year.
Step 3: logs and the ratio scale. Take the natural log of equation (3), using \(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\) and \(\ln(x^t) = t\ln x\) (Appendix C.4):
\[\ln y_t = \ln y_0 + t\,\ln(1+g).\]
The log of \(y\) is a straight line in time, with slope \(\ln(1+g)\). A ratio scale draws exactly this, so a series that grows at a constant rate is a straight line in Figs. 1 and 7, and a steeper line means faster growth. Every doubling covers the same vertical distance, because \(\ln(2y) - \ln y = \ln 2\) whatever the level of \(y\). For small \(g\), \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\) (Appendix C.6), which gives a second way to compute an average growth rate: \(g \approx (\ln y_T - \ln y_0)/T\).
Step 4: the rule of 70. How many years does it take for \(y\) to double? Put \(y_T/y_0 = 2\) into equation (3) and take logs: \(T\ln(1+g) = \ln 2\), so \(T = \ln 2/\ln(1+g)\). Now use \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\) and \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\), which gives \(T \approx 0.70/g\). At 1.9 percent a year, U.S. income per person doubles about every \(70/1.9 \approx 37\) years, a little over four doublings between 1870 and 2025.






ImportantKey result: the average growth rate and the rule of 70



\[g = \left(\frac{y_T}{y_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1 \tag{4}\]
\[T_{\text{double}} \approx \frac{0.70}{g} = \frac{70}{100\,g} \tag{5}\]
Equation (4) finds the one constant rate that links two levels \(T\) years apart. Equation (5) turns a growth rate into a doubling time: divide 70 by the growth rate in percent.
Islandia in numbers. At 2 percent a year, Islandia’s income per person doubles about every \(70/2 = 35\) years; the exact answer, \(\ln 2/\ln 1.02\), is 35.0 years.



Growth compounds: a steady rate adds the same percentage each year, not the same amount, so the level climbs ever faster.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia’s income per person grows 3 percent a year. Use the rule of 70 to find how long it takes to double, and compare with the exact answer.


Answer

Equation (5) gives \(70/3 \approx 23.3\) years. The exact doubling time is \(\ln 2/\ln 1.03 \approx 23.4\) years.

2. Islandia’s income per person rose tenfold in a century. What average growth rate does equation (4) give?


Answer

With \(y_T/y_0 = 10\) and \(T = 100\), equation (4) gives \(g = 10^{1/100} - 1 \approx 0.023\), about 2.3 percent a year.





What the model predicts
Small differences in growth rates add up. Write equation (3) for two countries and divide one by the other. Relative income changes by the factor \(\left((1+g_1)/(1+g_2)\right)^t\), and in logs
\[\ln\frac{y_{1,t}}{y_{2,t}} = \ln\frac{y_{1,0}}{y_{2,0}} + t\left[\ln(1+g_1) - \ln(1+g_2)\right] \approx \ln\frac{y_{1,0}}{y_{2,0}} + t\,(g_1 - g_2).\]
A gap of only half a percentage point, kept up for 150 years, changes relative income by \(0.005 \times 150 = 0.75\) in logs, a factor of \(e^{0.75} \approx 2.1\). That is about what happened between the United States and Argentina (Fig. 7).
How the growth rate moves the outcomes. The log form gives the effect of the growth rate on the level after \(T\) years: \(d\ln y_T/dg = T/(1+g) \approx T\). One extra point of growth for 100 years adds about \(100 \times 0.01 = 1\) to \(\ln y_{100}\), which multiplies the final level by about \(e \approx 2.7\). The table shows the same effect exactly, from equations (3) and (5):

The rule of 70 is very close for the growth rates of rich countries, and it only begins to drift for fast growth such as 10 percent a year.

Small differences in growth rates, kept up for generations, become large differences in living standards.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia and a neighboring island start out equally rich. Islandia then grows 2 percent a year and its neighbor 1 percent. About how many times richer is Islandia after 100 years?


Answer

By equation (3), the ratio of the two incomes after 100 years is \((1.02/1.01)^{100} \approx 2.7\). The log form gives the same answer: a gap of \(0.01 \times 100 = 1\) in logs is a factor of \(e \approx 2.72\).






1.1.3 How a model works: the labor market

Assumptions
Every model in this book has the same structure. The model builder chooses the inputs, and the model’s equations determine the outcomes:

parameters are inputs that stay fixed, unless the model builder changes them in an experiment;
exogenous variables are inputs that may change over time, along a path the model builder sets in advance (for example a population that grows by 1 percent a year);
endogenous variables are the outcomes, the unknowns that the equations solve for.

The smallest example on Islandia is a single market for hours of work. The islanders offer hours, Harbor Boatworks, the island’s firm, hires them, and a single wage \(w\) is paid for every hour. Three equations describe the market:
\[L^s = \bar{a}\,w + \bar{\ell} \quad\text{(labor supply)}, \qquad L^d = \bar{f} - w \quad\text{(labor demand)}, \qquad L^s = L^d \quad\text{(the market clears)}.\]
The parameters are \(\bar{a} > 0\), the extra hours offered per extra dollar of wage, and the zero-wage hours \(\bar{\ell}\) and \(\bar{f}\). \(\bar{f}\) measures the boatworks’ capacity, and \(\bar{\ell}\) could also be an exogenous variable that grows with the population. The wage \(w\) and the hours \(L^s\) and \(L^d\) are endogenous.
Labor supply slopes up: a higher wage draws out more hours. Labor demand slopes down: each extra dollar of wage makes one hour less worth hiring. The model has three equations and three unknowns. Once the market clears, \(L^s\) and \(L^d\) are the same number, employment \(L\), so the outcomes are just \(w\) and \(L\). We assume \(\bar{f} > \bar{\ell}\): otherwise islanders would offer more hours at a zero wage than the boatworks wants, and the wage could not be positive.

A model is a small machine: parameters go in, the equations do the work, and endogenous variables come out.



Solving the model
Step 1: one equation in one unknown. Put the supply and demand equations into the market-clearing condition. Only the wage is left:
\[\bar{a}\,w + \bar{\ell} = \bar{f} - w.\]
Step 2: solve for the wage. Add \(w\) to both sides and subtract \(\bar{\ell}\), so that all the terms with \(w\) are on the left: \(\bar{a}w + w = \bar{f} - \bar{\ell}\), or \((1+\bar{a})\,w = \bar{f} - \bar{\ell}\). Dividing both sides by \(1+\bar{a}\) gives the equilibrium wage, equation (6) in the box below.
Step 3: solve for employment. Put \(w^*\) into the demand equation and write everything over the common denominator \(1+\bar{a}\):
\[L^* = \bar{f} - w^* = \frac{(1+\bar{a})\bar{f} - (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})}{1+\bar{a}}.\]
In the numerator, \((1+\bar{a})\bar{f} - \bar{f} = \bar{a}\bar{f}\), which leaves equation (7).






ImportantKey result: the equilibrium wage and employment



\[w^* = \frac{\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}}{1 + \bar{a}} \tag{6}\]
\[L^* = \frac{\bar{a}\bar{f} + \bar{\ell}}{1 + \bar{a}} \tag{7}\]
The wage is high when Harbor Boatworks wants many hours compared with the hours islanders offer anyway.
Islandia in numbers. Every slider of Figs. 6 and 8 starts from the values of the textbook’s worked exercise, \(\bar{a} = 2\), \(\bar{\ell} = 30\) and \(\bar{f} = 60\). Then \(w^* = (60 - 30)/3 = 10\) and \(L^* = (2\times60 + 30)/3 = 50\).


The supply equation gives the same answer: \(\bar{a}w^* + \bar{\ell} = \left(\bar{a}\bar{f} - \bar{a}\bar{\ell} + \bar{\ell} + \bar{a}\bar{\ell}\right)/(1+\bar{a}) = (\bar{a}\bar{f} + \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\). At \(w^*\) the hours offered equal the hours wanted. Splitting the fraction in (7) shows that employment is a weighted average of the two zero-wage numbers, \(L^* = \frac{\bar{a}}{1+\bar{a}}\bar{f} + \frac{1}{1+\bar{a}}\bar{\ell}\).






TipIn words



Islanders would like a high wage, and Harbor Boatworks would like a low one. The wage settles where the hours the islanders offer just match the hours the boatworks wants. The more strongly islanders respond to the wage, the closer employment gets to what the boatworks would like to hire.








NoteCheck your understanding



1. Harbor Boatworks wins a large order and would now hire \(\bar{f} = 63\) hours at a zero wage. With \(\bar{a} = 2\) and \(\bar{\ell} = 30\), what are the new \(w^*\) and \(L^*\)?


Answer

Equation (6) gives \(w^* = (63 - 30)/3 = 11\), and equation (7) gives \(L^* = (2\times63 + 30)/3 = 52\). The wage rises by 1 dollar and employment by 2 hours.





What the model predicts
The fourth step of the method is to run experiments: change one input and compare the new outcomes with the old ones. Equations (6) and (7) are straight lines in \(\bar{f}\) and \(\bar{\ell}\), so their coefficients are the effects. For \(\bar{a}\) we differentiate (Appendix C.7): \(w^* = (\bar{f}-\bar{\ell})(1+\bar{a})^{-1}\) gives \(dw^*/d\bar{a} = -(\bar{f}-\bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})^2 = -w^*/(1+\bar{a})\), and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\) moves by the same amount in the opposite direction.

A shift of demand is shared between the wage and employment. The wage takes the share \(1/(1+\bar{a})\) and employment the rest: the more responsive islanders are, the more a rise in demand shows up as extra hours and the less as higher pay. A shift of supply moves the wage and employment in opposite directions.
Elasticities. Taking logs of equations (6) and (7), \(\ln w^* = \ln(\bar{f}-\bar{\ell}) - \ln(1+\bar{a})\) and \(\ln L^* = \ln(\bar{a}\bar{f}+\bar{\ell}) - \ln(1+\bar{a})\), gives the percentage effects:

\(-0.67\%\) and \(+0.13\%\)



Because the model is made of straight lines rather than powers, these elasticities change with the starting point. The model is far simpler than any real labor market, with one wage and no schooling, training or distance, but it already shows the logic of every later model: write the equations, solve them for the endogenous variables, and read off how each input moves each outcome.

A shift in labor demand moves the wage and employment together; a shift in labor supply moves them apart.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. More islanders reach working age, so \(\bar{\ell}\) rises from 30 to 33 hours. Which curve shifts, and what happens to \(w^*\) and \(L^*\) at the baseline?


Answer

Labor supply shifts right. By the first table, each extra hour of \(\bar{\ell}\) lowers \(w^*\) by \(1/(1+\bar{a}) = 1/3\) of a dollar and raises \(L^*\) by \(1/3\) of an hour. So the wage falls from 10 to 9 and employment rises from 50 to 51.






1.1.4 Extension: a minimum wage

Assumptions
The textbook’s example of a parameter is a minimum wage set by law, \(\bar{w}_{\min}\). Suppose Islandia passes such a law. Keep the three equations above, but forbid any wage below the floor. When the floor is above \(w^*\), the wage equals the floor, and nobody can make Harbor Boatworks hire more hours than it wants at that wage. Employment is then read off the demand curve, and the extra hours that islanders offer are unemployment:
\[w = \max(w^*, \bar{w}_{\min}), \qquad L = L^d(w) = \bar{f} - w, \qquad U = L^s(w) - L^d(w).\]


Solving the model
Case 1: the floor does not bind, \(\bar{w}_{\min} \le w^*\). Nothing changes: \(w = w^*\), \(L = L^*\) and \(U = 0\).
Case 2: the floor binds, \(\bar{w}_{\min} > w^*\). Then \(w = \bar{w}_{\min}\). Subtract demand from supply at that wage:
\[U = (\bar{a}\,\bar{w}_{\min} + \bar{\ell}) - (\bar{f} - \bar{w}_{\min}) = (1+\bar{a})\,\bar{w}_{\min} - (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}).\]
Equation (6) says that \(\bar{f} - \bar{\ell} = (1+\bar{a})\,w^*\). Substituting it and taking \(1+\bar{a}\) out as a common factor gives the box below.






ImportantKey result: unemployment under a binding minimum wage



\[U = (1+\bar{a})\,(\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*) \tag{8}\]
Employment falls to \(L = \bar{f} - \bar{w}_{\min} = L^* - (\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*)\). Unemployment is the hours islanders offer at the floor that Harbor Boatworks does not hire.
Islandia in numbers. With the baseline values, a floor of 12 is 2 dollars above \(w^* = 10\), so employment falls to \(50 - 2 = 48\) hours and unemployment is \(3 \times 2 = 6\) hours, the numbers Fig. 6 shows.








TipIn words



Each dollar of the floor above the market wage pulls two ways at once. Harbor Boatworks hires one hour less, and islanders offer \(\bar{a}\) hours more. So the gap between hours offered and hours hired widens by \(1+\bar{a}\) hours for every dollar.




What the model predicts




Floor at or below \(w^*\)
Floor above \(w^*\)

No curve moves: the floor is a horizontal line in the diagram, and the market slides up the demand curve. Above \(w^*\), each extra dollar of the floor cuts employment by 1 hour and raises unemployment by \(1+\bar{a} = 3\) hours. A floor below the market wage has no effect at all.

A minimum wage above the market wage buys higher pay with fewer hours hired and more unemployment.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia raises its minimum wage to 14, with the baseline values. What are the wage, employment and unemployment?


Answer

The floor binds, because 14 is above \(w^* = 10\). The wage is 14, employment is \(60 - 14 = 46\) hours, and by equation (8) unemployment is \(3\times(14-10) = 12\) hours.









NoteRecap




Rates and ratios make the facts comparable: inflation, unemployment and deficits are percentages, not totals (Fig. 3).
The labor-market ratios are linked: \(e = p(1-u)\), so the employment ratio falls when unemployment rises or when people leave the labor force (Fig. 2).
The output gap measures how far output is from potential, \(100(Y_t/Y^{pot}_t - 1)\).
Growth compounds: \(y_t = y_0(1+g)^t\) is a straight line on a ratio scale, and the rule of 70 turns a growth rate into a doubling time (Fig. 1, Fig. 7).
A model turns inputs into outcomes: in the labor market, \(w^* = (\bar{f}-\bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\) and \(L^* = (\bar{a}\bar{f}+\bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\) (Fig. 8).
A binding minimum wage creates unemployment of \((1+\bar{a})(\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*)\) hours (Fig. 6).

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
1.2 Model in code
Now we turn the Key results into Python. The section has three parts: the setup (folded, because it is the same in every chapter), the model as functions, and numerical checks of the Key results. Run its cells once, in order. Every later section of the notebook reuses them.

1.2.1 Setup
Run the setup cells once, before anything else. They load the Python libraries, give every chart the same look, store the address of the chapter’s data and define the helpers that only the book website needs. You can use the notebook without reading them; open the box if you are curious.






NoteShow the setup code





The first cell loads the libraries and sets the look of the charts. Its comments explain each step.

# @title Setup: libraries, chart colors and the data location
# Text after a "#" is a comment: Python ignores it, it is there for human readers.

# Step 1: load the libraries. `import` loads a library, a toolbox written by
# other people, and `as np` gives it a short nickname, so the code stays short.
import numpy as np                    # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                   # data tables
import plotly.express as px           # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go     # charts built piece by piece (model figures)
import plotly.io as pio               # settings shared by every chart
# sliders, buttons and menus for the interactive figures
from ipywidgets import (interact, fixed, FloatSlider, IntSlider, IntRangeSlider, ToggleButtons, Dropdown,
                        SelectMultiple)

# Step 2: one light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
# the same chart size in Colab and on the website
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47", "#e0a33b"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full slider labels

# Step 3, Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets.
# `try` runs the indented lines; if the import fails (we are not in Colab),
# `except` skips them.
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# Step 4: the data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch01/"

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with precomputed sliders or menus. The next three cells build those versions. Run them and move on.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. labor_market
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "f"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

The data figures of this chapter let you add other countries. On the website, a menu above each of these figures adds a group of countries (the G7, a world region, …); the next cell builds those menus.

# @title Helpers for the website's country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_traces(data, y, skip, x="year", fmt=".1f", markers=False):
    """One line per country of a long table (country, x, y), leaving out the countries in skip.

    Arguments
        data    : a long table with a "country" column, the x column and the y column
        y       : the name of the column to draw
        skip    : the countries to leave out (the ones the figure already draws)
        x       : the name of the column on the horizontal axis
        fmt     : the number format of the hover label, e.g. ".1f"
        markers : True to draw a dot at every point as well
    Returns
        a dictionary that maps each country to a list with its one trace
    """
    # one trace per country that is not in `skip`, in its own color from COLORS
    extra = {}
    for name, part in data.groupby("country"):
        if name not in skip:
            extra[name] = [go.Scatter(x=part[x], y=part[y], name=name,
                                      mode="lines+markers" if markers else "lines",
                                      line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=2),
                                      hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: %{{y:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>")]
    return extra


def country_menu(fig, extra, countries):
    """Add the extra countries' traces hidden, and a menu that shows one group of them (G7, a region, ...).

    The traces already in fig (the textbook's) stay as they are, and slider steps only switch those.

    Arguments
        fig       : a Plotly figure with the textbook's traces (and maybe a slider)
        extra     : the extra countries' traces, from country_traces
        countries : the country table, with the columns country, region, g7, g20 and oecd
    Returns
        the same figure, with the extra traces hidden and the menu of groups above the plot
    """
    # Step 1: add every extra trace, hidden, and remember its country
    n = len(fig.data)
    owner = []
    for name, traces in extra.items():
        for trace in traces:
            trace.visible = False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(name)
    # Step 2: the groups of the menu: G7, G20, OECD, then each region, A to Z
    groups = {"G7": countries.country[countries.g7], "G20": countries.country[countries.g20],
              "OECD": countries.country[countries.oecd]}
    for region in sorted(countries.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = countries.country[countries.region == region]
    # Step 3: one button per group. A button switches only the extra traces (`rest`)
    # and rescales the y-axis to the lines that are shown.
    rest, autoscale = list(range(n, len(fig.data))), {"yaxis.autorange": True}
    # the first button hides every extra country
    buttons = [dict(label="Textbook only", method="update",
                    args=[{"visible": [False] * len(owner)}, autoscale, rest])]
    for label, members in groups.items():
        # True for the extra traces whose country is in this group
        visible = [o in set(members) for o in owner]
        # leave out the groups without any extra country
        if any(visible):
            buttons.append(dict(label=f"+ {label} ({sum(visible)})", method="update",
                                args=[{"visible": visible}, autoscale, rest]))
    # the menu sits above the plot, at the right, with room for it in the top margin
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=0, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    # Step 4: the slider steps (if any) switch only the first n traces, the textbook's
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        for step in slider.steps:
            step.args = [{"visible": list(step.args[0]["visible"])}, step.args[1], list(range(n))]
    return fig

The last helper builds the website version of a figure that shows one country at a time, chosen from a menu.

# @title Helper for the website's one-country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Like slider_figure, but with a dropdown menu: one precomputed figure per value (e.g. per country).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure
        name        : the argument the menu sets, e.g. "country"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a menu that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[values.index(start)].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (values[i] == start)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one menu entry per value: its curves, title, labels, shapes and axes
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes],
                  "yaxis": f.layout.yaxis.to_plotly_json(),
                  "xaxis": f.layout.xaxis.to_plotly_json()}
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    # Step 4: put the menu above the plot, at the right, starting at the start value
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start), x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02,
                yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig






1.2.2 The model as functions
The labor-market model has two curves, supply and demand, and one Key result: the equilibrium wage and employment, equations (6) and (7). We write each one as a Python function: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives back a result. Every later section of the notebook reuses labor_supply, labor_demand and equilibrium.

# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses.
# `a=2.0` gives a a default value, used whenever we do not pass one.
# The text in triple quotes describes the function.
def labor_supply(w, a=2.0, l=30.0):
    """Hours of work the islanders offer at the wage w.

    The labor-supply curve of Fig. 8:  L^s = a-bar w + l-bar

    Arguments
        w : the wage
        a : the slope of labor supply, a-bar (extra hours per extra dollar)
        l : the hours offered at a zero wage, l-bar
    Returns
        the hours supplied, L^s
    """
    # `return` gives back the result
    return a * w + l


def labor_demand(w, f=60.0):
    """Hours of work Harbor Boatworks wants to hire at the wage w.

    The labor-demand curve of Fig. 8:  L^d = f-bar - w

    Arguments
        w : the wage
        f : the hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, f-bar
    Returns
        the hours demanded, L^d
    """
    # each extra dollar of wage makes one hour less worth hiring
    return f - w


def equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """The wage and employment at which supply equals demand.

    Equations (6) and (7):  w* = (f-bar - l-bar) / (1 + a-bar),  L* = (a-bar f-bar + l-bar) / (1 + a-bar)

    Arguments
        a : the slope of labor supply, a-bar
        l : the hours offered at a zero wage, l-bar
        f : the hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, f-bar
    Returns
        the equilibrium wage w* and employment L*, as two numbers
    """
    w_star = (f - l) / (1 + a)                  # equation (6)
    L_star = labor_demand(w_star, f)            # put w* into demand: equation (7)
    # a function can return two results at once, separated by a comma
    return w_star, L_star

The growth block gives two more formulas: the average growth rate that links two levels, equation (4), and the exact doubling time behind the rule of 70, equation (5).

def average_growth(start, end, years):
    """The constant yearly growth rate that turns `start` into `end` in `years` years.

    Equation (4):  g = (y_T / y_0)^(1/T) - 1

    Arguments
        start : the first level, y_0
        end   : the last level, y_T
        years : the number of years between them, T
    Returns
        the average growth rate g, as a decimal (0.02 = 2 percent)
    """
    # `**` means "to the power of"
    return (end / start) ** (1 / years) - 1


def doubling_time(g):
    """Exact number of years it takes to double at the growth rate g.

    Equation (5) is its approximation:  T = ln 2 / ln(1 + g), close to 70 / (100 g)

    Arguments
        g : the growth rate, as a decimal
    Returns
        the doubling time in years
    """
    # `np.log` is the natural logarithm, ln
    return np.log(2) / np.log(1 + g)



1.2.3 Checking the key results
The formulas came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, one Key result at a time. First Islandia’s baseline, \(\bar{a} = 2\), \(\bar{\ell} = 30\) and \(\bar{f} = 60\): the wage from equation (6), put into either curve, must give the employment of equation (7).

# Islandia's equilibrium; the two results of the function go into two variables
w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
# An f-string, f"... {w_star:.1f}", puts a value into the text;
# ":.1f" means "one decimal".
print(f"Equilibrium wage       w* = {w_star:.1f}")
print(f"Equilibrium employment L* = {L_star:.1f}   (equation 7: {(2 * 60 + 30) / (1 + 2):.1f})")
# at w* the hours offered equal the hours wanted
print(
    f"At w*, supply = {labor_supply(w_star):.1f} and demand = {labor_demand(w_star):.1f}: the market clears")

Equilibrium wage       w* = 10.0
Equilibrium employment L* = 50.0   (equation 7: 50.0)
At w*, supply = 50.0 and demand = 50.0: the market clears


Check 1: the elasticities. We raise each parameter by 1 percent and see by what percentage \(w^*\) and \(L^*\) change. The table above predicts \(+2\%\) and \(+0.8\%\) for \(\bar{f}\), \(-1\%\) and \(+0.2\%\) for \(\bar{\ell}\), and \(-0.67\%\) and \(+0.13\%\) for \(\bar{a}\).

# Step 1: the baseline equilibrium
w0, L0 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0)
# Step 2: one parameter 1% higher at a time; ":+.2f" shows the sign and two decimals
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0 * 1.01)
print(f"1% higher f: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0 * 1.01, f=60.0)
print(f"1% higher l: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0 * 1.01, l=30.0, f=60.0)
print(f"1% higher a: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")

1% higher f: w* +2.00%,  L* +0.80%
1% higher l: w* -1.00%,  L* +0.20%
1% higher a: w* -0.66%,  L* +0.13%


The answers for \(\bar{f}\) and \(\bar{\ell}\) are exact, because \(w^*\) and \(L^*\) are straight lines in those two parameters. For \(\bar{a}\) they are close but not exact, because an elasticity describes very small changes.
Check 2: the minimum wage. For several floors, we compute unemployment directly, as hours supplied minus hours demanded at the wage that holds, and compare the result with equation (8).

# the market wage, w* = 10, without a floor
w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
# `for w_min in (8, 11, 12, 14):` runs the indented lines once for each floor.
# `max(a, b)` is the larger of two numbers.
for w_min in (8, 11, 12, 14):
    w = max(w_star, w_min)                                   # the wage that holds
    # unemployment, directly: hours offered minus hours hired
    direct = labor_supply(w) - labor_demand(w)
    # equation (8); `max(..., 0)` gives zero when the floor does not bind
    formula = max((1 + 2.0) * (w_min - w_star), 0)
    print(f"floor {w_min:2d}: wage {w:4.1f}, employment {labor_demand(w):4.1f}, "
          f"unemployment {direct:4.1f} (direct) and {formula:4.1f} (equation 8)")

floor  8: wage 10.0, employment 50.0, unemployment  0.0 (direct) and  0.0 (equation 8)
floor 11: wage 11.0, employment 49.0, unemployment  3.0 (direct) and  3.0 (equation 8)
floor 12: wage 12.0, employment 48.0, unemployment  6.0 (direct) and  6.0 (equation 8)
floor 14: wage 14.0, employment 46.0, unemployment 12.0 (direct) and 12.0 (equation 8)


Check 3: compound growth. We let GDP per person grow by 1.9 percent a year for 155 years, one year at a time, and compare the result with equation (3). Then equation (4) must recover the growth rate, and the log formula must come close.

# Step 1: grow a level of 1 by 1.9% a year. `range(155)` counts 0, 1, ..., 154, so
# the loop runs 155 times; `_` names a loop counter we do not need.
level = 1.0
for _ in range(155):
    # one year of growth: the new value replaces the old one
    level = level * (1 + 0.019)
# Step 2: compare with equations (3) and (4) and with the log formula
print(f"Year by year: level after 155 years = {level:.3f}")
print(f"Equation (3): (1.019)^155           = {(1 + 0.019) ** 155:.3f}")
print(f"Equation (4) recovers g             = {100 * average_growth(1.0, level, 155):.3f}%")
print(f"Log formula (ln y_T - ln y_0) / T   = {100 * (np.log(level) - np.log(1.0)) / 155:.3f}%")
# Step 3: the growth rate that makes income ten times larger in a century
print(f"Tenfold in 100 years needs g        = {100 * average_growth(1, 10, 100):.2f}%")

Year by year: level after 155 years = 18.493
Equation (3): (1.019)^155           = 18.493
Equation (4) recovers g             = 1.900%
Log formula (ln y_T - ln y_0) / T   = 1.882%
Tenfold in 100 years needs g        = 2.33%


Check 4: the rule of 70. We compare equation (5) with the exact doubling time, and add the factor after 100 years, as in the table above.

# for each growth rate: the exact doubling time, the rule of 70 and (1 + g)^100
for g in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10):
    print(f"g = {100 * g:4.1f}%: doubles in {doubling_time(g):5.1f} years "
          f"(rule of 70: {70 / (100 * g):5.1f}); "
          f"factor after 100 years {(1 + g) ** 100:7.1f}")

g =  1.0%: doubles in  69.7 years (rule of 70:  70.0); factor after 100 years     2.7
g =  2.0%: doubles in  35.0 years (rule of 70:  35.0); factor after 100 years     7.2
g =  3.0%: doubles in  23.4 years (rule of 70:  23.3); factor after 100 years    19.2
g =  5.0%: doubles in  14.2 years (rule of 70:  14.0); factor after 100 years   131.5
g = 10.0%: doubles in   7.3 years (rule of 70:   7.0); factor after 100 years 13780.6


Check 5: two labor-market ratios. We plug the February and April 2020 values into both sides of equation (1). Then we split the fall of \(e\) into its two parts with logs.

# Step 1: February 2020, per 100 adults; both sides of equation (1)
# 63.3 of 100 adults are in the labor force
Pop, LF = 100.0, 63.3
# 3.5 percent of the labor force is unemployed
U = 0.035 * LF
# left side of equation (1): E / Pop, in percent
e_feb = 100 * (LF - U) / Pop
print(f"February 2020: E/Pop = {e_feb:.2f}%,   p(1 - u) = {63.3 * (1 - 0.035):.2f}%")
# Step 2: April 2020 from equation (1), and the fall of ln e split into its two parts
e_apr = 60.1 * (1 - 0.148)                       # equation (1) for April 2020
fall = np.log(e_apr) - np.log(e_feb)
part_p = np.log(60.1) - np.log(63.3)             # participation part
part_u = np.log(1 - 0.148) - np.log(1 - 0.035)   # unemployment part
# Step 3: the shares of the two parts; ":.0%" shows a share as a percentage
print(f"April 2020:    e = {e_apr:.1f}%, a fall of {e_feb - e_apr:.1f} points")
print(
    f"Share of the log fall due to participation: {part_p / fall:.0%}, to unemployment: {part_u / fall:.0%}")
print(f"The two parts add up: {part_p + part_u:.4f} = {fall:.4f}")

February 2020: E/Pop = 61.08%,   p(1 - u) = 61.08%
April 2020:    e = 51.2%, a fall of 9.9 points
Share of the log fall due to participation: 29%, to unemployment: 71%
The two parts add up: -0.1764 = -0.1764


Check 6: compounding prices and the log form of the gap. A year of 3,080 percent inflation, two years of 10 percent, and equation (2) against its log form for small and large gaps.

# Step 1: inflation compounds: prices are multiplied by (1 + inflation) each year
print(f"3,080% inflation multiplies prices by {1 + 3080 / 100:.1f}")
print(f"Two years of 10% raise prices by {100 * ((1 + 0.10) * (1 + 0.10) - 1):.0f}%")
# Step 2: the output gap for 2009, the Great Depression and 1944, exactly and in logs
for ratio_to_potential in (0.953, 0.83, 1.23):
    exact = 100 * (ratio_to_potential - 1)                   # equation (2)
    approx = 100 * np.log(ratio_to_potential)                # log form
    print(
        f"Y / Y_pot = {ratio_to_potential:.3f}: gap {exact:+6.1f}% (equation 2), {approx:+6.1f}% (log form)")

3,080% inflation multiplies prices by 31.8
Two years of 10% raise prices by 21%
Y / Y_pot = 0.953: gap   -4.7% (equation 2),   -4.8% (log form)
Y / Y_pot = 0.830: gap  -17.0% (equation 2),  -18.6% (log form)
Y / Y_pot = 1.230: gap  +23.0% (equation 2),  +20.7% (log form)


The log form is within a tenth of a point for a gap like 2009’s, but it is off by almost 2 points for the Great Depression’s 17 percent, and by more than 2 for the wartime boom of 1944.

1.3 Income over time and across countries
The first big fact of macroeconomics is how unequal incomes are, both across countries and across time. We compare GDP per person for six economies and for many more.

Fig. 1: GDP per person in six countries
Goal. Document the first big fact of macroeconomics: income differs enormously across countries and over time.
The data come from the Maddison Project, which estimates GDP per person for every country over long periods. GDP (gross domestic product) is the overall income of a country; Chapter 2 explains how it is measured. All values are in 2022 dollars, so they can be compared across years.

Beyond the textbook’s six countries
The Maddison Project covers far more than six countries. The file maddison_world.csv holds all of them, already in long form and in the same 2022 dollars, for every year with an estimate. A second file, countries.csv, lists every economy with its world region and its membership of the G7, the G20 and the OECD. Every data figure of this notebook uses it.

Before we use a new file, we check that it agrees with the one we trust. For the six countries at the benchmark years, the two files should hold exactly the same numbers.

# Compare the two files at the textbook's benchmark years
BENCHMARKS = list(six.year)                          # the textbook's benchmark years
# `.isin(list)` is True for the rows whose value is in the list
on_benchmarks = world[world.year.isin(BENCHMARKS)]
# `.merge(other, on=[...])` joins two tables, matching rows with the same year and
# country; columns with the same name get the endings _x (long) and _y (world)
check = long.merge(on_benchmarks, on=["year", "country"])
print(
    f"{len(check)} matching rows, largest difference: "
    f"{(check.gdppc_x - check.gdppc_y).abs().max()} dollars"
)

78 matching rows, largest difference: 0 dollars


Every country keeps the same color in every figure. The textbook’s countries get fixed colors of our palette, and each of the other countries one of 24 distinct colors.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, one color per country (for every data figure)
# Step 1: the textbook's countries get fixed colors of our palette
COLORS = {
    "United States": BLUE,
    "United Kingdom": TEAL,
    "Japan": GREEN,
    "Argentina": "#5aa0d8",
    "South Africa": "#0b4f47",
    "China": "#e0a33b",
    "Euro area": "#7b5ea7",
    "Europe": "#7b5ea7",
}
# Step 2: 24 distinct colors for the other countries
OTHER = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24
# `for i, name in enumerate(...)` hands over each name together with its position
# i (0, 1, 2, ...). `i % 24` is the remainder after dividing by 24, so the 24
# colors repeat in turn. `if name not in COLORS:` skips the names with a color.
for i, name in enumerate(countries.country):
    if name not in COLORS:
        COLORS[name] = OTHER[i % len(OTHER)]


The textbook draws this figure on a ratio scale: each step up the vertical axis doubles the value (1,000, 2,000, 4,000, …). Equal distances then mean equal percentage changes, so a country growing at a steady rate draws a straight line (the log form of equation 3). Chapter 3 explains ratio scales in detail.
The function gdp_per_person draws the chosen countries at the benchmark years, on a ratio or a linear scale. It is only drawing code, so it is folded: open it to see how it works.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, GDP per person at the benchmark years
# the textbook's six countries, and the numbers printed on the ratio-scale axis
BOOK = (
    "United States",
    "United Kingdom",
    "Japan",
    "Argentina",
    "South Africa",
    "China",
)
TICKS = [500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000]


def gdp_per_person(scale="ratio", chosen=BOOK):
    """GDP per person of the chosen countries at the textbook's benchmark years.

    Draws Fig. 1 (inspired by Fig. 1.1 in Jones): 1870-2022, in 2022 dollars.

    Arguments
        scale  : "ratio" or "linear", the vertical scale
        chosen : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen countries. `set(chosen) - set(data.country)`
    # keeps the chosen names that have no data
    data = on_benchmarks[on_benchmarks.country.isin(chosen)]
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    title = (
        "2022: U.S. income per person 5× South Africa's; "
        "China's up 24-fold since 1950"
    )
    # `", ".join(missing)` writes the names in one line, separated by commas
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)

    # Step 2: one line per country (`color=`). `color_discrete_map=COLORS` fixes
    # each country's color, and `log_y=True` gives a ratio scale
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="year",
        y="gdppc",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        markers=True,
        log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
        title=title,
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )

    # Step 3: the vertical axis. `x if condition else y` picks x when the condition
    # is true: one step lower for a very poor country, higher for a very rich one
    low = 800 if data.gdppc.min() >= 800 else 400
    high = 90000 if data.gdppc.max() <= 90000 else 250000
    # `tickvals` sets the numbers printed on the axis (Plotly's own labels are hard
    # to read on a ratio scale). On a ratio scale the range is given in powers of
    # ten: `np.log10(800)`
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=TICKS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high - 10000])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1865, 2027])
    return fig



# Fig. 1 with controls. `interact` calls gdp_per_person and redraws its figure
# every time you change a control. `ToggleButtons` gives one button per option.
# `SelectMultiple` is a list from which you can pick several entries: hold Ctrl
# (Cmd on a Mac) and click to add or remove a country. The `;` at the end only
# hides an extra line of text.
interact(
    gdp_per_person,
    scale=ToggleButtons(options=["ratio", "linear"], value="ratio",
                        description="vertical scale"),
    chosen=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value=BOOK, rows=8,
                          description="countries"),
);



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with buttons for the scale and a menu of countries
# Step 1: the figure with the textbook's six countries
fig = gdp_per_person()
# Step 2: two buttons switch the vertical axis between a ratio and a linear scale
fig.update_layout(
    updatemenus=[
        dict(
            type="buttons",
            direction="right",
            x=0.01,
            y=0.98,
            xanchor="left",
            yanchor="top",
            buttons=[
                dict(
                    label="ratio scale",
                    method="relayout",
                    args=[{"yaxis.type": "log", "yaxis.autorange": True,
                           "yaxis.tickvals": TICKS}],
                ),
                dict(
                    label="linear scale",
                    method="relayout",
                    args=[{"yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.autorange": True,
                           "yaxis.tickvals": None}],

)

Sources. Data: Maddison Project Database 2023, GDP per capita (gdppc), Groningen Growth and Development Centre (Bolt and van Zanden 2024, doi:10.34894/INZBF2), converted from 2011 to 2022 dollars with the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis GDP deflator (A191RD3A086NBEA), via FRED. Country groups: World Bank country classifications. Prepared files: data/ch01/fig1-1.csv, data/ch01/maddison_world.csv and data/ch01/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
On the website, the menu above the chart adds a group of countries; click a country in the legend to hide it, or double-click to show it alone.
What to notice.

In every year, the richest of the six countries has several times the income of the poorest. In 2022 the United States leads and South Africa is last.
The U.K. was richer than the United States in 1870 and 1890; by 1900 the United States was ahead.
Japan’s income fell between 1929 and 1950 (World War II) and then rose very fast: it passed South Africa in the 1950s and Argentina in the 1960s. China was almost flat until 1950 and has grown fast since, passing Argentina by 2020.
Switch to the linear scale: the lines for poorer countries are squeezed near zero, and the early growth of every country becomes invisible. That is why the textbook uses a ratio scale.
Add South Korea: with 1,288 dollars per person in 1950 it was poorer than Japan was in 1870. It grew so fast that by 2020 it had passed Japan. Many countries have no estimate before 1950, so their lines start there.



Key numbers: how much richer?
The textbook asks why the typical American is “more than 10 times richer” than a century ago and “25 times richer” than the typical Ethiopian. A wider file holds every available year for the six countries and for Ethiopia, so we can check both numbers.

What to notice.

The ratio rose from about 56 percent in the early 1960s to a peak of 64.7 percent in April 2000.
It falls in every recession (the shaded bands), but the last two falls are far deeper than the others: the 2007–09 recession and the Covid-19 collapse of spring 2020.
After 2009 the recovery was slow. After the Covid drop the ratio bounced back within two years, but it has not returned to its February 2020 level of 61.1 percent.


Key numbers: how deep was each fall?
The textbook says that the two latest recessions brought the sharpest declines in employment in more than 50 years. For each recession, we compare the ratio in the peak month with its lowest value up to two years after the trough (employment often keeps falling after a recession ends).

# The fall of the ratio in each recession. `set_index("date")` uses the dates as
# row labels, so `ratio[:peak]` keeps every month up to the peak
ratio = emp.set_index("date").emp_pop_ratio
falls = []
for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
    # `.iloc[-1]` takes the last of those months: the ratio at the peak
    at_peak = ratio[:peak].iloc[-1]
    # the lowest value up to two years after the trough;
    # `pd.DateOffset(years=2)` adds two years to a date
    lowest = ratio[peak:trough + pd.DateOffset(years=2)].min()
    # each pass of the loop adds one row to the list `falls`
    falls.append([peak.strftime("%Y-%m"), at_peak, lowest, at_peak - lowest])
# the list becomes a DataFrame at the end
pd.DataFrame(
    falls,
    columns=["Recession peak", "Ratio at peak", "Lowest after", "Fall (points)"],
).round(1)

Beyond the United States: employment around the world
The International Labour Organization (ILO) estimates the employment-population ratio for almost every country, once a year since 1991, and the World Bank publishes these estimates. Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2 for other countries, the ILO estimates
def employment_chart(chosen=("United States",)):
    """The employment-population ratio, ages 15 and over, of the chosen countries.

    Draws Fig. 2 for many countries (inspired by Fig. 1.2 in Jones): 1991-2025,
    ILO estimates.

    Arguments
        chosen : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen countries, and the names without data
    data = employment[employment.country.isin(chosen)]
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    title = "Employment-population ratio, ages 15 and over (ILO estimates)"
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    # Step 2: one line per country, each in its own color
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="year",
        y="emp_pop_ratio",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
        title=title,
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "emp_pop_ratio": "Employment-population ratio (percent)",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )
    # Step 3: the axes; the vertical one is widened in one step if needed
    low = 40 if data.emp_pop_ratio.min() >= 40 else 10
    high = 70 if data.emp_pop_ratio.max() <= 70 else 90
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1990, 2026])
    return fig

Add Germany and Japan. In 2020 the U.S. ratio (ILO, yearly) fell by 3.9 points, Germany’s by only 1.2 and Japan’s by 0.3. Both countries paid firms to keep workers on reduced hours instead of laying them off, so the Covid-19 recession cost far fewer jobs there.
Germany’s ratio rose from 53.9 percent in 2007 to 59.4 percent in 2019, while the U.S. ratio fell from 62.0 to 60.5 percent: a recession is not the only thing that moves employment.
Ratios differ a lot across countries, from below 30 percent (e.g. Yemen) to above 80 percent (e.g. Tanzania, Qatar). Low ratios often mean that few women work for pay; very high ones often mean that people cannot afford not to work. These numbers are model-based ILO estimates, so read single years for poor countries with care.
