# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, inflation in the chosen economies
# the textbook's four economies
BOOK_INFLATION = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Euro area", "Japan")


def inflation_chart(chosen=BOOK_INFLATION):
    """CPI inflation, 1960-2025, of the chosen economies.

    Draws Fig. 3 (inspired by Fig. 1.3 in Jones), with a dashed zero line.

    Arguments
        chosen : the economies to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    data = world_inflation[world_inflation.country.isin(chosen)]
    # Step 1: the top of the axis. `for top in [...]:` tries the steps in order,
    # and `break` leaves the loop at the first step that is high enough
    for top in [25, 50, 100, 250, 1000, 5000, 25000, 100000]:
        if data.inflation.max() <= top:
            break
    # Step 2: the title. `data.inflation.idxmax()` is the row label of the highest
    # inflation, and `data.loc[row]` reads that row
    title = (
        "Inflation peaked in the 1970s (24% in the U.K.) "
        "and surged again in 2021–22"
    )
    if set(chosen) != set(BOOK_INFLATION) and len(data) > 0:
        row = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
        title = (
            f"Highest inflation shown: {row.country}, "
            f"{row.inflation:,.1f}% in {row.year}"
        )
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    # Step 3: one line per economy
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="year",
        y="inflation",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        title=title,
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)",
            "country": "Economy",
        },
    )
    # Step 4: a dashed zero line (below it, prices fall), and the axes
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[min(-5, data.inflation.min() - 2), top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    # hover over a year to see every economy's rate in one box
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig

The vertical axis runs to 14 percent, and to 30 or 40 percent when a chosen country had higher unemployment.
First the number in the title: europe_us_ratio divides Europe’s rate by the U.S. rate in every year of the period, and averages the result.

def europe_us_ratio(period):
    """The average ratio of Europe's unemployment rate to the U.S. rate (Fig. 4).

    The mean, over the years of the period, of  u(Europe) / u(United States)

    Arguments
        period : the first and the last year, (start, end)
    Returns
        the average ratio (2: Europe's rate is twice the U.S. rate)
    """
    # `start, end = period` unpacks a pair of numbers into two variables
    start, end = period
    # the years of the period: `&` means "and", and each condition needs its own
    # brackets
    chosen_years = unemp[(unemp.year >= start) & (unemp.year <= end)]
    # the ratio in each year, then its average
    return (chosen_years["Europe"] / chosen_years["United States"]).mean()



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, unemployment rates and a shaded period
# the textbook's three economies
BOOK_UNEMP = ("United States", "Europe", "Japan")


def unemployment_chart(period=(2006, 2025), chosen=BOOK_UNEMP):
    """Unemployment rates of the chosen economies, with a shaded period.

    Draws Fig. 4 (inspired by Fig. 1.4 in Jones); the title reports the average
    Europe/U.S. ratio over the shaded period.

    Arguments
        period : the shaded period, (start, end)
        chosen : the economies to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the ratio of the title (europe_us_ratio), and the chosen rows
    start, end = period
    ratio = europe_us_ratio(period)
    data = world_unemp[world_unemp.country.isin(chosen)]
    title = (
        f"{start}–{end}: Europe's rate was {ratio:.2f} times the U.S. rate "
        "on average"
    )
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    # Step 2: one line per economy
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="year",
        y="unrate",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        title=title,
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "unrate": "Unemployment rate (percent)",
            "country": "Economy",
        },
    )
    # Step 3: the gray band: the chosen period
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    # Step 4: the axes; the vertical one is widened in steps if needed
    top = 14 if data.unrate.max() <= 14 else (30 if data.unrate.max() <= 30 else 40)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1954, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig



# Fig. 4 with controls. An `IntRangeSlider` has two handles, so it chooses a whole
# period at once
interact(

1.5 Budget and trade deficits
Two deficits often make the news: the government spending more than it collects, and a country buying more from abroad than it sells. Here we look at both for the United States.

Fig. 5: Budget and trade deficits in the United States

The budget deficit is what the federal government spends beyond its revenue, and the trade deficit is what the country imports beyond its exports. Both are measured as a percentage of GDP, so that years with very different GDP can be compared. A negative deficit is a surplus.

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, budget and trade deficits of one country
def deficits_chart(country="United States"):
    """The budget and trade deficits of one country, in percent of GDP.

    Draws Fig. 5 (inspired by Fig. 1.5 in Jones); a negative deficit is a surplus.

    Arguments
        country : the country to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the country's rows, with readable column names
    data = world_deficits[world_deficits.country == country]
    data = data.rename(
        columns={"budget_deficit": "Budget deficit", "trade_deficit": "Trade deficit"}
    )
    title = f"{country}: budget deficit (general government) and trade deficit"
    if country == "United States":
        title = (
            "U.S. budget deficit near 14% of GDP in 2020; "
            "trade deficit peaked in 2006"
        )
    # Step 2: one line per deficit
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="year",
        y=["Budget deficit", "Trade deficit"],
        color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
        labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP", "variable": "Deficit"},
        title=title,
    )
    # Step 3: a dashed zero line: below it, a surplus
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    # Step 4: the vertical axis. `np.floor` and `np.ceil` round down and up, so
    # `5 * np.ceil(x / 5)` is the next multiple of 5 above x: the axis grows in
    # steps of 5 points when a country's deficits are large
    values = data[["Budget deficit", "Trade deficit"]]
    low = min(-5, 5 * np.floor(values.min().min() / 5))
    high = max(15, 5 * np.ceil(values.max().max() / 5))
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
1.6 What a model does
With the facts in hand, we turn to the tool that explains them. A small live model shows how inputs go in and outcomes come out.

Fig. 6: The structure of economic models
Goal. See what a model does: it takes inputs and determines outcomes.
Every economic model has the same structure. The model builder picks the inputs:

parameters, fixed numbers such as \(\bar{a}\), \(\bar{\ell}\), \(\bar{f}\), or a minimum wage set by law;
exogenous variables, inputs that may change over time in a way the model builder decides in advance, such as the number of people in the economy.

The model, a set of equations, then determines the endogenous variables, here the wage and employment. The textbook draws this as three boxes: inputs → MODEL → outcomes. Below, the boxes are live: every slider is an input, and the right box shows the outcomes the model computes.
We add one input the textbook mentions as an example of a parameter: a minimum wage. If it is below \(w^*\), it has no effect. If it is above \(w^*\), the wage equals the minimum wage, firms hire only the hours they demand at that wage, and the hours that workers offer but cannot sell are unemployment, \(L^s - L^d\), which is equation (8) of the Model overview. (Think of \(\bar{\ell}\) as growing with the number of people in the economy: more people offer more hours at any wage.)
First we compute the outcomes. labor_outcomes puts the inputs into the model: it finds \(w^*\), applies the minimum wage, and returns the wage, employment and unemployment.

def labor_outcomes(a, l, f, w_min):
    """The outcomes of the labor-market model with a minimum wage (Fig. 6).

    Equations (6) to (8):  w = max(w*, minimum wage),  L = L^d(w) = f-bar - w,
    unemployment = L^s(w) - L^d(w), zero when the minimum wage does not bind

    Arguments
        a     : the slope of labor supply, a-bar
        l     : the hours offered at a zero wage, l-bar
        f     : the hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, f-bar
        w_min : the minimum wage (0: none)
    Returns
        w          : the wage that holds
        L          : employment, the hours hired
        unemployed : the hours offered but not hired
    """
    # Step 1: the market equilibrium, equations (6) and (7)
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    # Step 2: a minimum wage above w* sets the wage
    w = max(w_star, w_min)
    # firms hire the hours they demand at that wage
    L = labor_demand(w, f)
    # Step 3: hours offered but not hired, equation (8); `max(..., 0.0)` gives
    # zero, not -0.00, when w = w*
    unemployed = max(labor_supply(w, a, l) - L, 0.0)
    return w, L, unemployed



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 6, the three boxes and the two arrows
def add_boxes(fig, inputs, model, outcomes):
    """Draw the three boxes of Fig. 6 with their text, and the arrows between them.

    Arguments
        fig      : the figure to draw in
        inputs   : the text of the left box
        model    : the text of the middle box
        outcomes : the text of the right box
    """
    # Step 1: one pass of the loop per box. `fig.add_shape(type="rect", ...)` draws
    # a rectangle, and `fig.add_annotation(...)` writes the text in its middle
    boxes = [[0.0, 0.33, inputs], [0.39, 0.61, model], [0.67, 1.0, outcomes]]
    for x0, x1, text in boxes:
        fig.add_shape(
            type="rect",
            x0=x0,
            x1=x1,
            y0=0.12,
            y1=0.88,
            fillcolor="#ecf3fa",
            line=dict(color=BLUE),
        )
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=(x0 + x1) / 2,
            y=0.5,
            text=text,
            showarrow=False,
            font=dict(size=13),
        )
    # Step 2: one pass per green arrow, from a box to the next. An annotation with
    # `showarrow=True` draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y)
    for x_from, x_to in [[0.33, 0.39], [0.61, 0.67]]:
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=x_to,
            y=0.5,
            ax=x_from,
            ay=0.5,
            xref="x",
            yref="y",
            axref="x",
            ayref="y",
            text="",
            showarrow=True,
            arrowhead=3,
            arrowwidth=4,
            arrowcolor=GREEN,
        )




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 6, the structure of economic models
def structure_of_models(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0, w_min=0.0):
    """A live model: inputs (parameters) -> MODEL -> outcomes (endogenous variables).

    Draws Fig. 6 (adapted from Fig. 1.6 in Jones) as three boxes; the right box
    shows the outcomes the model computes.

    Arguments
        a     : the slope of labor supply, a-bar
        l     : the hours offered at a zero wage, l-bar
        f     : the hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, f-bar
        w_min : the minimum wage (0: none)
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the outcomes (labor_outcomes)
    w, L, unemployed = labor_outcomes(a, l, f, w_min)

    # Step 2: the text of the boxes; `<br>` starts a new line, `<b>...</b>` makes
    # text bold and `<i>...</i>` italic
    inputs = (
        f"<b>INPUTS</b><br><i>parameters and exogenous<br>variables</i><br><br>"
        f"supply slope a = {a:.1f}"
        f"<br>hours at zero wage l = {l:.0f}<br>demand at zero wage f = {f:.0f}"
        f"<br>minimum wage = {w_min:.0f}"
    )
    model = (
        "<b>MODEL</b><br><br>Lˢ = a·w + l<br>Lᵈ = f − w<br>Lˢ = Lᵈ, unless<br>"
        "a minimum wage<br>is above w*"
    )
    outcomes = (
        f"<b>OUTCOMES</b><br><i>endogenous variables</i><br><br>wage w = {w:.2f}"
        f"<br>employment L = {L:.2f}<br>unemployment = {unemployed:.2f}"
    )

    # Step 3: `go.Figure()` starts an empty chart; the boxes and arrows (add_boxes)
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_boxes(fig, inputs, model, outcomes)
    # Step 4: no axes, only the boxes; the title reports the outcomes
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Inputs → model → outcomes: wage w = {w:.2f}, employment L = {L:.2f}"
    )
    return fig



# Fig. 6 with sliders. A `FloatSlider` chooses a number between `min` and `max` in
# steps of `step`; `value` is where it starts: the textbook's numbers
interact(
    structure_of_models,
    a=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=4.0, step=0.5,
                  description="supply slope a", style=WIDE),
    l=FloatSlider(value=30, min=20, max=40, step=5,
                  description="hours at zero wage l", style=WIDE),
    f=FloatSlider(value=60, min=50, max=70, step=5,
                  description="demand at zero wage f", style=WIDE),
    w_min=FloatSlider(value=0, min=0, max=20, step=1,
                      description="minimum wage", style=WIDE),
);



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Fig. 6 with a precomputed slider for the minimum wage
# one picture of Fig. 6 per minimum wage; 12 is just above w* = 10
slider_figure(
    structure_of_models,
    "w_min",
    [0, 5, 10, 12, 15, 20],     # the minimum wages
    start=0,
    label="minimum wage",
)





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 1.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With the textbook’s inputs, the outcomes are \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\), and nobody who wants to work at that wage is left out.
A minimum wage of 5 or 10 changes nothing, because it is not above the market wage. A minimum wage of 12 raises the wage to 12, cuts employment to 48, and leaves 6 hours of unemployment.
You never set the wage or employment directly: they are endogenous. You only change inputs, and the model works out the outcomes. That is what the textbook means by running an experiment with a model.

text:
1.7 The long run and the short run
One chart organizes the whole textbook: the steady rise of U.S. income per person over 150 years, and the swings around that trend.

Fig. 7: Per capita GDP in the United States
Goal. See the three features of the graph that organizes the whole textbook: long-run growth, short-run fluctuations, and the question of what comes next.
The file has two columns. gdppc_actual is real GDP per person. gdppc_potential is potential output: what GDP per person would be if prices were fully flexible and all resources were fully employed. From 1949 on, potential output comes from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO); before 1949 it is a smooth statistical trend of the actual series, so the early years should be read with care.

# Load Fig. 7's data: actual and potential GDP per person, year by year
usgdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-7.csv")

The average annual growth rate \(g\) between 1870 and 2025 is the constant rate that turns the 1870 value into the 2025 value in 155 years: \(y_{2025} = y_{1870}(1+g)^{155}\) (equation 3), so \(g = (y_{2025}/y_{1870})^{1/155} - 1\) (equation 4).

# Average annual growth, equation (4). `usgdp.set_index("year").gdppc_actual`
# gives a column whose rows are labeled by year, so `y[2025]` is the 2025 value
y = usgdp.set_index("year").gdppc_actual
g = (y[2025] / y[1870]) ** (1 / 155) - 1
print(f"Average annual growth, 1870-2025: {100 * g:.2f}%")

Average annual growth, 1870-2025: 1.88%


The same chart can be drawn for any country in the Maddison file of Fig. 1. Only the United States has an official estimate of potential output (from the CBO), so other countries show actual GDP per person only.
long_run_growth picks the data of one country and computes its average growth rate, equation (4), between its first and its last year.

def long_run_growth(country):
    """GDP per person of one country, and its average annual growth rate (Fig. 7).

    Equation (4), from the first year 0 to the last year T:  g = (y_T / y_0)^(1/T) - 1

    Arguments
        country : the country's name
    Returns
        data        : the country's rows; GDP per person is the column "Actual"
                      (and, for the United States, "Potential")
        series      : the names of the columns to draw
        first, last : the first and the last row
        growth      : the average annual growth rate g, as a decimal
    """
    # Step 1: the country's rows; only the United States has potential output
    if country == "United States":
        data = usgdp.rename(
            columns={"gdppc_actual": "Actual", "gdppc_potential": "Potential"}
        )
        series = ["Actual", "Potential"]
    else:
        data = world[world.country == country].rename(columns={"gdppc": "Actual"})
        series = ["Actual"]
    # Step 2: `data.iloc[0]` is the first row and `data.iloc[-1]` the last, so the
    # growth rate uses each country's own first and last year
    first, last = data.iloc[0], data.iloc[-1]
    growth = (last.Actual / first.Actual) ** (1 / (last.year - first.year)) - 1
    return data, series, first, last, growth



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 7, per capita GDP on a ratio scale
def per_capita_chart(country="United States"):
    """Per capita GDP on a ratio scale, with its average growth rate in the title.

    Draws Fig. 7 (inspired by Fig. 1.7 in Jones); for the United States, potential
    output too (dashed).

    Arguments
        country : the country to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (long_run_growth)
    data, series, first, last, growth = long_run_growth(country)
    # in percent, rounded for the title; + 0.0 turns "-0.0" into "0.0"
    growth_pct = round(100 * growth, 1) + 0.0

    # Step 2: one line per series, on a ratio scale; potential output dashed
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="year",
        y=series,
        log_y=True,
        color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "value": "Per capita GDP (2022 dollars, ratio scale)",
            "variable": "Series",
        },
        title=(
            f"{country}: GDP per person grew {growth_pct:.1f}% a year, "
            f"{first.year:.0f}–{last.year:.0f}"
        ),
    )
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Potential"), line_dash="dash")

    # Step 3: the axes; the vertical one goes lower for a poor country and higher
    # for a very rich one
    smallest = data.Actual.min()
    low = 3500 if smallest >= 3500 else (1000 if smallest >= 1000 else 400)
    high = 100000 if data.Actual.max() <= 100000 else 250000
    fig.update_yaxes(
        tickvals=[500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000],
        range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)],
    )
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1865, 2030])

    # Step 4: the factor of growth, top left. On a ratio-scale axis an
    # annotation's height is also given in powers of ten: `y=np.log10(30000)`
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=1870,
        y=np.log10(0.8 * high),
        showarrow=False,
        xanchor="left",
        font=dict(size=14),
        text=(
            f"Income in {last.year:.0f}: {last.Actual / first.Actual:.1f} times"
            f"<br>its {first.year:.0f} level"
        ),
    )
    return fig



# Fig. 7 with a menu of countries
interact(
    per_capita_chart,
    country=Dropdown(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value="United States",
                     description="country"),
);



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Fig. 7 with a menu of countries (the G20 and OECD members)
# Step 1: the menu's countries: the United States first, then the other G20 and

members = countries[countries.g20 | countries.oecd].country
options = ["United States"] + sorted(

# Step 2: one precomputed figure per country, and the menu that shows one
dropdown_figure(per_capita_chart, "country", options, start="United States")





                                
                                            




Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis via FRED: real GDP (GDPCA), population (B230RC0A052NBEA) and GDP deflator (A191RD3A086NBEA); Congressional Budget Office, Real Potential GDP (GDPPOT), via FRED; before 1929 and for other countries: Maddison Project Database 2023, GDP per capita (gdppc), Groningen Growth and Development Centre (Bolt and van Zanden 2024, doi:10.34894/INZBF2) (the textbook uses the Barro-Ursúa data before 1929). Prepared files: data/ch01/fig1-7.csv and data/ch01/maddison_world.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
The website’s menu lists the G20 and OECD members; in Colab you can choose any of the countries.
What to notice.

The long run. Income per person rose enormously, and on a ratio scale the line is close to straight: growth of almost 2 percent a year, sustained for over 150 years.
The short run. Actual GDP (solid) moves around potential output (dashed). The Great Depression of the 1930s and the World War II boom of the 1940s are the only deviations you can see easily.
The future. The line raises an obvious question: will growth continue at the same rate?
Choose Japan: 2.1 percent a year from 1870 to 2022, faster than the United States. Choose Argentina: only 1.4 percent, so its income fell from about half of the U.S. level in 1870 to less than a third in

Small differences in growth rates add up to large differences in income.



Key numbers: the long run

# The long run in numbers: the levels, two factors of growth and the growth rate
print(f"1870: ${y[1870]:,}    2022: ${y[2022]:,}    2025: ${y[2025]:,}")
print(f"Rise from 1870 to 2022: a factor of {y[2022] / y[1870]:.1f}")
print(f"Rise from 1922 to 2022: a factor of {y[2022] / y[1922]:.1f}")
print(f"Average growth, 1870-2025: {100 * g:.2f}% a year")

1870: $4,634    2022: $77,942    2025: $82,643
Rise from 1870 to 2022: a factor of 16.8
Rise from 1922 to 2022: a factor of 8.1
Average growth, 1870-2025: 1.88% a year


The textbook reports $4,200 in 1870 and $76,000 in 2022, “more than a factor of 15”. Our 2022 value is close ($77,942). Our 1870 value is about 10 percent higher, because we use newer historical estimates (the Maddison Project) for the years before 1929. The rise is a factor of almost 17, and average growth is 1.9 percent a year, which the textbook rounds to 2 percent.
This series also lets us revisit the claim of Fig. 1. Here, U.S. income in 2022 is about 8.1 times its 1922 level: more than the 5.8 of the Maddison data, but still short of “more than 10 times”. The two sources disagree because estimating income a century ago is hard, and they measure prices differently. When sources disagree, report the range.


The short run: the output gap
This part stays U.S.-only: potential output comes from the CBO, which estimates it only for the United States. (The IMF and the OECD publish output-gap estimates for rich countries, but only since about 1980 and from models that differ from the CBO’s.)
The gap between actual and potential output, in percent, is \(100 \times (\text{actual} / \text{potential} - 1)\) (equation 2). It is negative in recessions. The chart below plots it for every year, and the title converts the gap of the chosen year into dollars per person and for a family of four.
First the numbers. A new column holds the gap of every year, and gap_in_year reads the gap of one year, in percent and in dollars per person.

# the output gap of every year, equation (2). `usgdp["gap"] = ...` adds a new
# column, computed row by row from two other columns
usgdp["gap"] = 100 * (usgdp.gdppc_actual / usgdp.gdppc_potential - 1)


def gap_in_year(year):
    """The output gap of one year, in percent and in dollars per person (Fig. 7).

    Equation (2):  gap = 100 (actual / potential - 1); in dollars: actual - potential

    Arguments
        year : the year
    Returns
        row     : that year's row of usgdp; row.gap is the gap in percent
        dollars : actual minus potential GDP per person, in dollars
    """
    # `usgdp[usgdp.year == year].iloc[0]` picks the one row of the chosen year
    row = usgdp[usgdp.year == year].iloc[0]
    # negative in a recession: output below potential
    dollars = row.gdppc_actual - row.gdppc_potential
    return row, dollars



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 7, the U.S. output gap
def output_gap_chart(year=2009):
    """Actual GDP per person relative to potential, in percent, year by year.

    Draws the second feature of Fig. 7 (inspired by Fig. 1.7 in Jones), with a dot
    on the chosen year.

    Arguments
        year : the year marked and reported in the title
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the title (gap_in_year)
    row, dollars = gap_in_year(year)
    # Step 2: one bar per year; `px.bar` draws a bar chart
    fig = px.bar(
        usgdp,
        x="year",
        y="gap",
        color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL],
        labels={"year": "Year", "gap": "Actual relative to potential (percent)"},
    )
    # Step 3: a black dot on the chosen year; `add_trace` adds one curve or set of
    # points to a figure
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[year],
            y=[row.gap],
            mode="markers",
            name=str(year),
            marker=dict(color="black", size=11),
        )
    )
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-20, 25])
    # Step 4: the title; `:+,.0f` in an f-string shows a sign, thousands separators
    # and no decimals
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"{year}: gap {row.gap:+.1f}%, or {dollars:+,.0f} dollars per person "
            f"({4 * dollars:+,.0f} for a family of four)"
        )
    )
    return fig



# The output gap with a slider for the year
interact(
    output_gap_chart,
    year=IntSlider(value=2009, min=1870, max=2025, step=1,
                   description="year", style=WIDE),
);



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Fig. 7's output gap with a precomputed slider for the year
# the Great Depression, World War II, 1982, 2009, Covid-19 and the latest year
slider_figure(
    output_gap_chart,
    "year",
    [1933, 1944, 1982, 2009, 2020, 2025],
    start=2009,
    label="year",
)





                                
                                            




Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis via FRED: real GDP (GDPCA) and population (B230RC0A052NBEA); Congressional Budget Office, Real Potential GDP (GDPPOT), via FRED, from 1949 (before 1949 a smooth statistical trend); before 1929: Maddison Project Database 2023, GDP per capita (gdppc), Groningen Growth and Development Centre (Bolt and van Zanden 2024, doi:10.34894/INZBF2). Prepared files: data/ch01/fig1-7.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The Great Depression is by far the deepest gap: 17 percent below potential in 1933. The World War II boom put output 23 percent above potential in 1944.
Since 1949 (the CBO years), no gap has been larger than about 6 percent. The largest is 1982 (6.2 percent below potential).
The textbook says output in 2009 was about 6 percent below potential, a loss of about $4,000 per person. With today’s revised data the 2009 gap is 4.7 percent, or about $3,100 per person and $12,300 for a family of four. Statistical agencies revise their estimates of the past as new information arrives.



Key numbers: issues for the future
The textbook asks whether the next century will bring another tenfold rise in income. We compute what a tenfold rise would mean and what growth rate it would need.

# A tenfold rise in a century: the level it means, where the historical growth
# rate leads, and the rate it needs (equation 4 with a factor of 10)
print(f"Ten times the 2022 level: ${10 * y[2022]:,}")
print(
    "Income after 100 more years at the historical rate: "
    f"${y[2025] * (1 + g) ** 100:,.0f}"
)
print(
    "Growth rate needed for a tenfold rise in 100 years: "
    f"{100 * (10 ** (1 / 100) - 1):.2f}% a year"
)

Ten times the 2022 level: $779,420
Income after 100 more years at the historical rate: $530,230
Growth rate needed for a tenfold rise in 100 years: 2.33% a year


Ten times today’s income is about $780,000 per person, close to the textbook’s $750,000. At the historical growth rate of 1.9 percent, income would rise by a factor of about 6.4 in a century; a tenfold rise needs about 2.3 percent a year (equation 4 with a factor of 10). Small differences in growth rates add up over long periods.

section: 1.8 Solving a model: the labor market
text:
1.8 Solving a model: the labor market
Finally, we draw the labor-market model from the Model overview and use it for experiments, changing one input at a time.

Fig. 8: The labor market
Goal. Draw the supply-and-demand diagram of the labor market and see how the equilibrium moves when a parameter changes.
The diagram puts employment \(L\) on the horizontal axis and the wage \(w\) on the vertical axis. Labor supply \(L^s = \bar{a}w + \bar{\ell}\) slopes up, and labor demand \(L^d = \bar{f} - w\) slopes down. They cross at the equilibrium \((L^*, w^*)\). When you move a slider away from the textbook’s values, the textbook’s curves stay on the chart as dashed gray lines, so you can see the shift.
The function labor_market draws the two curves and the equilibrium that equilibrium computes. It is only drawing code, in three folded parts: the curves, their labels and the equilibrium, then the figure.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 8, the supply and demand curves
def add_labor_curves(fig, w, a, l, f):
    """Draw labor supply and demand of Fig. 8, and the textbook's curves for comparison.

    Arguments
        fig     : the figure to draw in
        w       : the wages at which we draw the curves
        a, l, f : the parameters a-bar, l-bar and f-bar
    """
    # Step 1: away from the textbook's values, keep its curves as dashed gray lines
    if (a, l, f) != (2.0, 30.0, 60.0):
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=labor_supply(w),
                y=w,
                name="Textbook curves (a=2, l=30, f=60)",
                line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash"),
            )
        )
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=labor_demand(w),
                y=w,
                showlegend=False,
                line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash"),
            )
        )
    # Step 2: the wage is on the vertical axis, so the hours supplied and demanded
    # at each wage are the x values: supply in teal, demand in blue
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=labor_supply(w, a, l),
            y=w,
            name="Lˢ",
            showlegend=False,
            line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3),
        )
    )
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=labor_demand(w, f),
            y=w,
            name="Lᵈ",
            showlegend=False,
            line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
        )
    )




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 8, the curve labels and the equilibrium
def add_labels_and_equilibrium(fig, a, l, f, w_star, L_star):
    """Write the names of the curves of Fig. 8, and mark the equilibrium (L*, w*).

    Arguments
        fig            : the figure to draw in
        a, l, f        : the parameters a-bar, l-bar and f-bar
        w_star, L_star : the equilibrium wage and employment, w* and L*
    """
    # Step 1: as in the textbook, the curves are named on the chart, at their ends.
    # `xanchor`/`yanchor` say which corner of the label touches that point.
    # Supply leaves the chart at the top or at the right edge
    w_end = min(30, (100 - l) / a)
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=labor_supply(w_end, a, l),
        y=w_end,
        text="Lˢ",
        showarrow=False,
        xanchor="right",
        yanchor="bottom",
        font=dict(size=18, color=TEAL),
    )
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=labor_demand(30, f),
        y=30,
        text="Lᵈ",
        showarrow=False,
        xshift=-4,
        xanchor="right",
        yanchor="top",
        font=dict(size=18, color=BLUE),
    )
    # Step 2: dotted lines from the equilibrium to both axes, and a black dot on it
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[0, L_star, L_star],
            y=[w_star, w_star, 0],
            mode="lines",
            showlegend=False,
            line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dot"),
        )
    )
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[L_star],
            y=[w_star],
            mode="markers",
            name="Equilibrium (L*, w*)",
            marker=dict(color="black", size=12),
        )
    )




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 8, the labor market
def labor_market(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """Labor supply and demand, and the equilibrium (L*, w*).

    Draws Fig. 8 (adapted from Fig. 1.8 in Jones). Away from the textbook's values,
    the textbook's curves stay on the chart as dashed gray lines.

    Arguments
        a : the slope of labor supply, a-bar
        l : the hours offered at a zero wage, l-bar
        f : the hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, f-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: `np.linspace(0, 30, 100)` creates 100 evenly spaced wages from 0 to
    # 30; and the equilibrium, equations (6) and (7)
    w = np.linspace(0, 30, 100)
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    # Step 2: `go.Figure()` starts an empty chart; then the curves, their labels
    # and the equilibrium
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_labor_curves(fig, w, a, l, f)
    add_labels_and_equilibrium(fig, a, l, f, w_star, L_star)
    # Step 3: the title reports the equilibrium; fixed axes, so the curves move
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Equilibrium: wage w* = {w_star:.2f}, employment L* = {L_star:.2f}",
        showlegend=True,
        xaxis=dict(
            title="Employment, L",
            range=[0, 100],
            tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100],
        ),
        yaxis=dict(title="Wage, w", range=[0, 30]),
    )
    return fig



# Fig. 8 with sliders for the three parameters
interact(
    labor_market,
    a=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=4.0, step=0.5,
                  description="supply slope a", style=WIDE),
    l=FloatSlider(value=30, min=20, max=40, step=5,
                  description="hours at zero wage l", style=WIDE),
    f=FloatSlider(value=60, min=50, max=70, step=5,
                  description="demand at zero wage f", style=WIDE),
);



Show the code of the website version
# @title Website version: Fig. 8 with a precomputed slider for demand at a zero wage
# one picture of Fig. 8 per value of f-bar
slider_figure(
    labor_market,
    "f",
    [50, 55, 60, 65, 70],     # the values of f
    start=60,
    label="demand at zero wage f",
)





                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 1.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With the textbook’s parameters the curves cross at \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\), the answer to the textbook’s worked exercise.
A higher \(\bar{f}\) shifts labor demand to the right: the wage and employment both rise.
A higher \(\bar{\ell}\) shifts labor supply to the right: employment rises but the wage falls.
A larger \(\bar{a}\) makes supply respond more to the wage. The supply curve gets flatter in this diagram, and it pivots around the point where the wage is zero.


Key numbers: three experiments
Equations (6) and (7), \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\) and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\), show how much each parameter moves the outcomes. With \(\bar{a} = 2\), raising \(\bar{f}\) by 3 raises \(w^*\) by \(3/3 = 1\); raising \(\bar{\ell}\) by 3 lowers \(w^*\) by 1.

# Three experiments: the textbook's inputs, then l-bar or f-bar 3 higher. The loop
# goes through a list of lists: each inner list holds a name and three parameter
# values, which the line `for name, a, l, f in ...` unpacks
for name, a, l, f in [
    ["textbook", 2, 30, 60],
    ["l up by 3", 2, 33, 60],
    ["f up by 3", 2, 30, 63],
]:
    w_new, L_new = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    print(f"{name:10}  w* = {w_new:5.2f}   L* = {L_new:5.2f}")

textbook    w* = 10.00   L* = 50.00
l up by 3   w* =  9.00   L* = 51.00
f up by 3   w* = 11.00   L* = 52.00


Your turn. Find values of \(\bar{\ell}\) and \(\bar{f}\) that keep the wage at \(w^* = 10\) but raise employment to \(L^* = 60\) (keep \(\bar{a} = 2\)). Check your answer with equilibrium.


Hint

\(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\), so \(L^* = 60\) with \(w^* = 10\) needs \(\bar{f} = 70\). Then choose \(\bar{\ell}\) so that \((\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/3 = 10\). Try it with the sliders too.

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
1.9 Concluding remarks

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole. Its big questions start from facts like these: huge income gaps across countries, deep recessions such as 2008–09 and 2020, the inflation of the 1970s and of 2021–22, high unemployment in Europe, and large U.S. budget and trade deficits. It answers them in four steps: document the facts, build a model, compare the model with the facts, and use the model for experiments.
A model takes parameters and exogenous variables as inputs and determines the endogenous variables. In the labor-market model, equations (6) and (7) give \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1 + \bar{a})\) and \(L^* = (\bar{a}\bar{f} + \bar{\ell})/(1 + \bar{a})\). A demand shift moves both in the same direction, a supply shift moves them in opposite directions, and a binding minimum wage creates the unemployment of equation (8).
Growth compounds, equation (3). The average growth rate is equation (4), and the rule of 70, equation (5), turns a growth rate into a doubling time. U.S. GDP per person has grown at almost 2 percent a year since 1870 (the long run), doubling about every 37 years, with output gaps, equation (2), that are small except in the Great Depression and World War II (the short run).
The employment-population ratio is the participation rate times the employed share of the labor force, equation (1). Checking claims against the data matters: some textbook numbers hold exactly, others change with newer data.
The next chapter shows how GDP, the measure behind most of these figures, is defined and measured.

title: 1. Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Practice problems
These problems practise the chapter in three ways: conceptual problems apply its equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to its data files, and modeling problems use the labor-market model to answer policy questions. Each one is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it in the answer cell first, and only then open the Hint and the Solution. The sliders of the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website versions of Figs. 6 and 8 above.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): How much did U.S. prices rise in 2021–23? In the data of Fig. 3 (the consumer price index of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (CPIAUCNS), via FRED), U.S. inflation was 4.7 percent in 2021, 8.0 percent in 2022 and 4.1 percent in 2023.

By what percentage was the price level of 2023 higher than that of 2020?
Suppose a news report adds up the three rates and says that prices rose 16.8 percent. Why is that too low?
The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2 percent a year over the longer run. It measures inflation with a different price index, but take the target at face value: how many years of 2 percent inflation would raise prices as much as these three years did?



Hint

Step 1 of the Model overview: each year multiplies the price level by \(1 + \pi_t/100\). For (c), set \(1.02^T\) equal to your factor from (a) and take logs, as in the derivation of the rule of 70.

Your answer:


Solution


The yearly factors multiply:

\[\frac{P_{2023}}{P_{2020}} = 1.047 \times 1.080 \times 1.041 = 1.1771,\]
so the 2023 price level was 17.7 percent above that of 2020. By equation (4), that is an average of \(1.1771^{1/3} - 1 = 5.6\) percent a year.

Adding the rates ignores compounding. Multiply out the product:

\[(1 + 0.047)(1 + 0.080)(1 + 0.041) = 1 + \underbrace{0.047 + 0.080 + 0.041}_{0.168} + \underbrace{0.047 \times 0.080 + 0.047 \times 0.041 + 0.080 \times 0.041 + 0.047 \times 0.080 \times 0.041}_{0.0091}.\]
The sum, 16.8 percent, is only the first part. The cross terms, 0.9 points, are there because the 8.0 percent of 2022 applied to prices that were already 4.7 percent higher, and so on. The longer and higher the inflation, the bigger the error from adding.

Set \(1.02^T = 1.1771\) and take logs:

\[T = \frac{\ln 1.1771}{\ln 1.02} = \frac{0.1631}{0.0198} = 8.2 \text{ years}.\]
In three years, prices rose as much as they would in about eight years at the Fed’s target. Prices do not go back down when inflation falls: in 2023 the price level was 10.9 percent above the path of 2 percent inflation (\(1.1771/1.02^3 = 1.109\)).

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Spain and the United States in the Great Recession: lost jobs or lost workers? The table holds two ratios from this chapter’s data: the employment-population ratio \(e\) (ages 15 and over, ILO modelled estimates via the World Bank) and the unemployment rate \(u\) (Spain: European Commission, AMECO; United States: Bureau of Labor Statistics (UNRATE), via FRED).

\(u\), percent

Use equation (1) to compute the participation rate \(p\) of each country in both years. (The ratios come from different sources, so treat \(p\) as an approximation.)
Split the change of \(\ln e\) from 2007 to 2013 into a participation part and an unemployment part, as in Check 5 of “Model in code”. What share of the fall does each part explain, in each country?
In which country did the crisis show up partly as people leaving the labor force? Suggest one reason why participation could even rise in a deep recession.



Hint

Solve equation (1) for \(p\), with \(u\) written as a decimal. Taking logs of equation (1) turns the product into a sum, so the change of \(\ln e\) is the change of \(\ln p\) plus the change of \(\ln(1-u)\).

Your answer:


Solution


Equation (1), \(e = p(1-u)\), gives \(p = e/(1-u)\):





\(p = e/(1-u)\)




Spain, 2007
\(53.5/0.918 = 58.3\)


Spain, 2013
\(43.7/0.739 = 59.1\)


United States, 2007
\(62.0/0.954 = 65.0\)


United States, 2013
\(58.1/0.926 = 62.7\)




In logs, \(\ln e = \ln p + \ln(1-u)\), so \(\Delta\ln e = \Delta\ln p + \Delta\ln(1-u)\).


Spain: \(\Delta\ln e = \ln(43.7/53.5) = -0.202\). The participation part is \(\ln(59.13/58.28) = +0.015\), and the unemployment part is \(\ln(0.739/0.918) = -0.217\). Higher unemployment explains 107 percent of the fall; participation explains \(-7\) percent, because it rose and so softened the fall.
United States: \(\Delta\ln e = \ln(58.1/62.0) = -0.065\). The participation part is \(-0.035\) (54 percent of the fall), and the unemployment part is \(-0.030\) (46 percent).


In the United States, about half of the drop in the share of adults with a job came from people who stopped looking for work. Spain lost far more jobs (its ratio fell by 9.8 points, against 3.9 in the United States), but almost all of the loss shows up in its 26 percent unemployment rate. One reason participation can rise in a slump is the added-worker effect: when one earner of a family loses a job, others start to look for work to keep up the family’s income. The lesson for reading Figs. 2 and 4 is that the same fall of \(e\) can mean very different things for \(u\), so look at both.


Problem 3 (Challenge): When could China catch up with the United States? In the Maddison data of Fig. 1 (Maddison Project Database 2023), GDP per person in 2022 was 75,459 dollars in the United States and 24,821 dollars in China, a ratio of 3.04. In these data, China’s income per person grew 7.4 percent a year from 2000 to 2010 and 5.9 percent a year from 2010 to 2022. The IMF’s World Economic Outlook of October 2026 projects that China’s real GDP growth will slow from 5.0 percent in 2025 to 3.3 percent in 2030.

Suppose both countries grow at constant rates, \(g_C\) and \(g_U\), from 2022 on. Use equation (3) to derive the number of years \(T\) until China’s income per person reaches the U.S. level. Give the approximate version for small growth rates too.
Compute \(T\) for \(g_C = 5\) percent and \(g_U = 1.5\) percent (a scenario, not a forecast).
Compute \(T\) again for \(g_C = 3.3\) percent, using the IMF’s projection for 2030 as a rough stand-in for growth per person.
What constant growth rate would China need to catch up by 2050, if U.S. income per person grows 1.5 percent a year? Why might any constant-growth answer be too optimistic for a country that is catching up?



Hint

Write equation (3) once for each country, set the two incomes equal in year \(T\), and move both growth factors to one side. Taking logs turns the powers into products. For (d), solve the same equation for \(g_C\), with \(T = 28\).

Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution


Catch-up happens when \(y_{C,0}(1+g_C)^T = y_{U,0}(1+g_U)^T\). Divide both sides by \(y_{C,0}(1+g_U)^T\):

\[\left(\frac{1+g_C}{1+g_U}\right)^T = \frac{y_{U,0}}{y_{C,0}}.\]
Take logs, using \(\ln(x^T) = T\ln x\) and \(\ln(a/b) = \ln a - \ln b\):
\[T\left[\ln(1+g_C) - \ln(1+g_U)\right] = \ln\frac{y_{U,0}}{y_{C,0}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T = \frac{\ln(y_{U,0}/y_{C,0})}{\ln(1+g_C) - \ln(1+g_U)} \approx \frac{\ln(y_{U,0}/y_{C,0})}{g_C - g_U},\]
where the last step uses \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\). China has to close a log gap of \(\ln 3.04 = 1.112\), and it closes it at a speed equal to the difference of the growth rates. This is the “small differences add up” result of the Model overview, read backwards.

\(T = 1.112/(\ln 1.05 - \ln 1.015) = 1.112/(0.0488 - 0.0149) = 1.112/0.0339 = 32.8\) years, so around 2055. The approximation gives \(1.112/0.035 = 31.8\) years.
\(T = 1.112/(\ln 1.033 - \ln 1.015) = 1.112/0.0176 = 63.3\) years, so around 2085. Growth of 3.3 instead of 5 percent cuts the speed of catch-up from 3.5 to 1.8 points a year, and so almost doubles the time.
With \(T = 28\), solve for \(g_C\): \(1 + g_C = 1.015 \times 3.04^{1/28} = 1.015 \times 1.0405 = 1.0561\), so China would need 5.6 percent a year in every year until 2050. That is faster than the 5.0 percent of 2025 and far above the projected 3.3 percent. A constant rate is optimistic because catch-up growth tends to slow down as a country gets richer: it can no longer grow fast just by building machines from a low base and copying technologies that already exist. Chapters 5 and 6 explain why.

ratio = 75459 / 24821
for g_C in (0.05, 0.033):
    T = np.log(ratio) / (np.log(1 + g_C) - np.log(1 + 0.015))
    print(f"China at {100 * g_C:.1f}%: catches up after {T:.1f} years (approximation {np.log(ratio) / (g_C - 0.015):.1f})")
print(f"Growth needed to catch up by 2050: {100 * (1.015 * ratio ** (1 / 28) - 1):.2f}% a year")



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): The misery index. Adding the inflation rate and the unemployment rate gives a rough measure of economic hardship, often called the misery index. Use the U.S. columns of fig1-3.csv (consumer prices from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (CPIAUCNS)) and fig1-4.csv (the Bureau of Labor Statistics unemployment rate (UNRATE)), both via FRED.

Compute the U.S. misery index for every year in both files.
Which five years had the highest index? What do they have in common?
Inflation reached 8.0 percent in 2022. Where does 2022 rank, and why was it a less miserable year than 1980?



Hint

.merge(other, on="year") keeps the years that are in both tables. Add the columns inflation_us and unrate_us, then use .sort_values(..., ascending=False). To find the rank of 2022, count the years with a higher index.


# Your answer here



Solution

Merge the two files on the year (1960–2025), add the two U.S. columns, and sort.
prices = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-3.csv")
jobs = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-4.csv")
misery = prices.merge(jobs, on="year")
misery["misery"] = misery.inflation_us + misery.unrate_us
ranked = misery.sort_values("misery", ascending=False)
print(ranked[["year", "inflation_us", "unrate_us", "misery"]].head(5).round(1))
value_2022 = misery[misery.year == 2022].misery.iloc[0]
higher = misery[misery.misery > value_2022]
print(f"2022: index {value_2022:.1f}, rank {len(higher) + 1} of {len(misery)} years")
print("Years with a higher index:", higher.year.tolist())
The five worst years are 1980 with an index of 20.7 (inflation 13.5 percent plus unemployment 7.2 percent), then 1981 with 18.0, 1975 with 17.6, 1979 with 17.1 and 1974 with 16.7. All of them fall in the high-inflation decade of Fig. 3, and each has inflation above 9 percent. The 2022 index is 11.7, only 13th of the 66 years: every year from 1974 to 1984 was worse, and so was 2011 (low inflation, but unemployment near 9 percent). In 2022 high inflation came with very low unemployment, 3.65 percent, while in 1980 it came with a recession. The index treats a point of inflation and a point of unemployment as equally painful, which is a strong assumption, so read it as a rough summary.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Growth miracles and growth disasters since 1950. Use maddison_world.csv, GDP per person from the Maddison Project Database 2023 (Bolt and van Zanden 2024).

For every country with an estimate in both 1950 and 2022, compute the average annual growth rate of GDP per person with equation (4).
Which five countries grew fastest, and which five slowest?
How many countries were poorer in 2022 than in 1950? Which ones?
What is the median growth rate, and how often does income double at that rate (equation (5))?



Hint

Keep the rows of one year with maddison[maddison.year == 1950], and use .set_index("country").gdppc to get a column labeled by country; do the same for 2022. Dividing the two columns matches the countries, and .dropna() drops the countries that miss one of the years. The period is 72 years long.


# Your answer here



Solution

Take each country’s 1950 and 2022 values, apply equation (4) with \(T = 72\), and sort.
maddison = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
start = maddison[maddison.year == 1950].set_index("country").gdppc
end = maddison[maddison.year == 2022].set_index("country").gdppc
growth = 100 * ((end / start) ** (1 / 72) - 1)               # equation (4), in percent a year
growth = growth.dropna().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"{len(growth)} countries with estimates for 1950 and 2022")
print(growth.head(5).round(2))
print(growth.tail(5).round(2))
print("Poorer in 2022 than in 1950:", sorted(growth[growth < 0].index))
print(f"Median: {growth.median():.2f}% a year, doubling every {70 / growth.median():.0f} years")
146 countries have both estimates. The fastest growers are Oman with 5.53 percent a year, South Korea with 5.31, Taiwan with 5.12, Botswana with 5.00 and Equatorial Guinea with 4.76; China is sixth, with 4.52. At 5.3 percent a year, South Korea’s income doubled about every 13 years, so it rose about 41-fold. The slowest are Liberia (\(-1.87\) percent a year), the Central African Republic (\(-1.08\)), Mozambique (\(-0.70\)), Venezuela (\(-0.66\)) and Syria (\(-0.60\)).
Eight countries were poorer in 2022 than in 1950: the Central African Republic, DR Congo, Haiti, Liberia, Madagascar, Mozambique, Syria and Venezuela. The median country grew 2.08 percent a year, so its income doubled about every 34 years. The United States grew 1.89 percent a year in the same data (growth["United States"]), so the median country grew a little faster than the United States. Estimates for poor countries in 1950 are rough (Liberia’s 4,065 dollars is more than three times South Korea’s 1,288), so check the extremes before you build a story on them.

Problem 6 (Challenge): Output gaps and unemployment. When output falls below potential, firms need fewer workers, so the output gap of Fig. 7 and the unemployment rate of Fig. 4 should move together. Use fig1-7.csv (real GDP from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (GDPCA) and potential output from the Congressional Budget Office (GDPPOT), both via FRED) and the U.S. column of fig1-4.csv.

Compute the output gap with equation (2) and merge it with the unemployment rate. Which years do both files cover?
Compute the correlation of the gap and the unemployment rate. Then fit a straight line \(u = \alpha + \beta \times \text{gap}\). What do \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) mean?
Which two years lie furthest above the line, and which two furthest below? Suggest a reason for one of them.



Hint

.corr() gives the correlation of two columns. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits the best straight line through the points and returns its slope first and its intercept second. The distance of a year from the line is its actual unemployment rate minus the rate that the line predicts.


# Your answer here



Solution

The merged table covers 1955–2025, the years of the unemployment file. The fitted line gives each year’s predicted rate, and the “miss” is the actual rate minus the prediction.
okun = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-7.csv").merge(pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-4.csv"), on="year")
okun["gap"] = 100 * (okun.gdppc_actual / okun.gdppc_potential - 1)        # equation (2)
print(f"{len(okun)} years, {okun.year.min()}-{okun.year.max()}")
print(f"Correlation: {okun.gap.corr(okun.unrate_us):.2f}")
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(okun.gap, okun.unrate_us, 1)
print(f"Fitted line: u = {intercept:.2f} + ({slope:.2f}) x gap")
okun["miss"] = okun.unrate_us - (intercept + slope * okun.gap)
print(okun.sort_values("miss")[["year", "gap", "unrate_us", "miss"]].round(2).iloc[[0, 1, -2, -1]])

71 years, 1955–2025.
The correlation is \(-0.86\): years with output below potential are years of high unemployment. The line is \(u = 5.71 - 0.64 \times \text{gap}\). The slope \(\beta = -0.64\) says that each point of output below potential comes with about 0.64 points more unemployment. The intercept \(\alpha = 5.71\) is the unemployment rate the line predicts when output equals potential, a rough estimate of the rate that does not come from the business cycle. This relation is known as Okun’s law. Ball, Leigh and Loungani (2013) test it on U.S. data since 1948 and on twenty advanced economies, and find a strong and stable relationship in most countries. Chapter 9 returns to it.
Furthest above the line: 2010 (unemployment 9.61 percent, 1.76 points above the line) and 1966 (1.47 above). Furthest below: 2017 (1.75 below) and 2018 (1.65 below). In 2010 the gap was closing, but unemployment had not yet come down: a possible reason is that firms waited to see whether the recovery after the financial crisis would last before they hired again. In 2016–2019 unemployment fell to rates that the line would only predict for a boom: the rate that does not come from the business cycle may have fallen, or the CBO’s estimate of potential output may be too high for those years. Either way, a fitted line summarizes the average year, and the exceptions are where the interesting questions are.




Modeling problems
Problem 7 (Basic): A city council’s minimum-wage menu. The labor market of a hypothetical city is the model of Fig. 6, with the baseline values \(\bar{a} = 2\), \(\bar{\ell} = 30\) and \(\bar{f} = 60\). The council considers minimum wages of 11, 12, 13 and 14 dollars. It wants to raise the total pay of employed workers, \(w \times L\), by at least 20 percent over its value without a minimum wage, and to keep unemployment below 10 hours.

Use the slider to read employment and unemployment at each floor, and compute total pay.
Which floors meet both goals?
Under the floor you would choose, who gains and who loses?



Hint

Without a minimum wage, total pay is \(w^* L^* = 10 \times 50\). Raising it by 20 percent sets the target. Read employment and unemployment off the OUTCOMES box at each floor.


interact(structure_of_models, a=fixed(2.0), l=fixed(30.0), f=fixed(60.0),
         w_min=FloatSlider(value=10, min=10, max=20, step=1, description="minimum wage", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 6 above, adapted from Fig. 1.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution


Without a floor, total pay is \(10 \times 50 = 500\), so the target is \(1.2 \times 500 = 600\). Above \(w^* = 10\), employment is read off the demand curve, \(L = 60 - \bar{w}_{\min}\), and unemployment is equation (8), \(U = 3(\bar{w}_{\min} - 10)\):










Floor
Employment \(L\)
Unemployment \(U\)
Total pay \(\bar{w}_{\min} \times L\)




11
49
3
539


12
48
6
576


13
47
9
611


14
46
12
644




Only a floor of 13 meets both goals: total pay of 611 is above 600, and unemployment of 9 hours is below 10. A floor of 12 does not raise pay enough, and a floor of 14 creates too much unemployment.
Workers who keep their hours gain: their pay rises 30 percent, from 10 to 13 an hour, so total pay rises although 3 fewer hours are worked. Workers who lose those 3 hours lose, and 6 more hours are offered by people drawn in by the higher wage who find no job, which makes 9 hours of unemployment. Firms pay more and hire less. The U.S. Congressional Budget Office’s 2019 study of a $15 federal minimum wage weighs the same trade-off for the whole country: higher pay for many low-wage workers and fewer jobs for some, with a lot of uncertainty about how many.

w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
print(f"No floor: total pay {w_star * L_star:.0f}")
for w_min in (11, 12, 13, 14):
    L = labor_demand(w_min)                                  # firms hire on their demand curve
    U = labor_supply(w_min) - L                              # equation (8)
    print(f"floor {w_min}: employment {L:.0f}, unemployment {U:.0f}, total pay {w_min * L:.0f}")

Problem 8 (Intermediate): A hiring subsidy. Instead of a minimum wage, the government pays firms \(s\) dollars for every hour of work they hire. Real wage subsidies are close to this: the U.S. Work Opportunity Tax Credit, for example, gave employers a tax credit on the first-year wages of job seekers from certain groups whom they hired (generally up to $2,400 per worker, for hires who started by the end of 2025). Start from the baseline of Fig. 8.

Show that with the subsidy, labor demand becomes \(L^d = (\bar{f} + s) - w\), where \(w\) is the wage workers receive. Which curve moves?
The government wants employment of 54 hours. Use the sliders to find the subsidy. By how much do the wage of workers and the net cost of an hour to firms change, and what does the subsidy cost the government?
In Problem 7, a minimum wage of 12 also raised the wage to 12. Compare the two policies: employment, unemployment, and who pays.
Set \(\bar{a} = 4\), so that workers respond more to pay, and keep the subsidy from (b). What share of the subsidy do workers get now?



Hint

With the subsidy, an hour of work costs the firm \(w - s\). Use that cost in place of \(w\) in the demand equation. For (b), equation (7) with \(\bar{f} + s\) in place of \(\bar{f}\) gives employment as a function of \(s\).


def subsidy_market(s=0.0, a=2.0):
    """Fig. 8 with a hiring subsidy of s dollars an hour: labor demand becomes (f + s) - w."""
    fig = labor_market(a, 30.0, 60.0 + s)
    w_sub, L_sub = equilibrium(a, 30.0, 60.0 + s)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Subsidy {s:.0f}: workers get w* = {w_sub:.2f}, firms pay {w_sub - s:.2f}, L* = {L_sub:.2f}")
    return fig


interact(subsidy_market,
         s=FloatSlider(value=0, min=0, max=7, step=1, description="subsidy per hour s", style=WIDE),
         a=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="supply slope a", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 8 above with a hiring subsidy added, adapted from Fig. 1.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution


Without a subsidy, the firm hires \(\bar{f} - w\) hours when an hour costs it \(w\). With the subsidy, an hour costs only \(w - s\), so it hires \(\bar{f} - (w - s) = (\bar{f} + s) - w\) hours. At any wage, the firm wants \(s\) more hours: the demand curve shifts right by \(s\), exactly like a rise of \(\bar{f}\) by \(s\). The supply curve does not move.
Equation (7) with \(\bar{f} + s\): \(L^* = \left(2(60 + s) + 30\right)/3 = 50 + 2s/3\). Employment of 54 needs \(2s/3 = 4\), so \(s = 6\). Equation (6) gives the wage workers receive, \(w^* = (66 - 30)/3 = 12\): it rises by 2. Firms pay \(12 - 6 = 6\) an hour, 4 less than before. The subsidy costs \(6 \times 54 = 324\) dollars. Workers get a third of the subsidy, \(1/(1+\bar{a})\), and firms two thirds, \(\bar{a}/(1+\bar{a})\).
Both policies raise the wage to 12. The minimum wage of 12 cuts employment to 48 hours and leaves 6 hours of unemployment, but it costs the government nothing: firms and the workers who lose hours pay for it. The subsidy raises employment to 54 hours with no unemployment, but taxpayers pay 324 dollars. The choice is between a cost that falls on some workers and firms and a cost that falls on taxpayers.
With \(\bar{a} = 4\), the market starts at \(w^* = 30/5 = 6\) and \(L^* = 54\). With \(s = 6\), \(w^* = 36/5 = 7.2\) and \(L^* = 58.8\). Workers get \(1.2\) of the 6 dollars, a fifth, which is \(1/(1+\bar{a})\). When workers respond strongly to pay, a small rise in the wage draws out many hours, so the wage needs to rise less and firms keep most of the subsidy.

for a in (2.0, 4.0):
    w0, L0 = equilibrium(a, 30.0, 60.0)
    w1, L1 = equilibrium(a, 30.0, 60.0 + 6)                 # the subsidy s = 6 shifts demand
    print(f"a = {a}: wage {w0:.2f} -> {w1:.2f}, firms pay {w1 - 6:.2f}, employment {L0:.2f} -> {L1:.2f}, "
          f"workers' share {(w1 - w0) / 6:.2f}, cost {6 * L1:.1f}")

Problem 9 (Challenge): A wave of new workers, with and without a minimum wage. In 1980, the Mariel boatlift brought Cuban immigrants to Miami and raised the city’s labor force by about 7 percent. Yet Card (1990) found almost no effect on the wages or the unemployment of the less-skilled workers who already lived there. Use the model of Fig. 6 to think about such an inflow, which shifts labor supply to the right by raising \(\bar{\ell}\).

Without a minimum wage, how large an inflow would cut the market wage by a tenth, from 10 to 9 dollars? Find the new \(\bar{\ell}\) with the slider and check it with equation (6). Before the inflow, the city’s workers offer 50 hours at \(w^* = 10\). What wage cut, in percent, does the model predict for an inflow of Miami’s size, 7 percent of those hours?
Now let the inflow raise \(\bar{\ell}\) from 30 to 35, with a minimum wage of 12 in place before and after it. Show that employment does not change and that unemployment rises by the full 5 hours. Then derive the general result: when the floor binds, how do \(L\) and \(U\) change with \(\bar{\ell}\)?
The newcomers also spend their income, so firms may want more workers. Without a floor, which rise of \(\bar{f}\) would keep the market wage at 10 after the inflow of (b)? What then happens to employment, and to unemployment under the floor of 12?
Policy question: does a minimum wage protect the workers already in a city from an inflow of new workers? Use your results, and say what Card’s finding suggests about the model.



Hint

For (a), equation (6) tells you by how much \(w^*\) falls for each extra hour of \(\bar{\ell}\); turn it around. An inflow of 7 percent adds the same number of hours at every wage. When the floor binds, employment is read off the demand curve at the floor: which parameters appear in \(L = \bar{f} - \bar{w}_{\min}\)? For (c), equation (6) shows that \(w^*\) depends on \(\bar{f}\) and \(\bar{\ell}\) only through their difference.


interact(structure_of_models, a=fixed(2.0),
         l=FloatSlider(value=30, min=30, max=40, step=1, description="hours at zero wage l", style=WIDE),
         f=FloatSlider(value=60, min=60, max=70, step=1, description="demand at zero wage f", style=WIDE),
         w_min=FloatSlider(value=0, min=0, max=15, step=1, description="minimum wage", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 6 above, adapted from Fig. 1.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution


By equation (6), \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\) falls by \(1/(1+\bar{a}) = 1/3\) of a dollar for each extra hour of \(\bar{\ell}\). A cut of 1 dollar therefore needs \(\bar{\ell}\) to rise by \(1 + \bar{a} = 3\) hours, to 33: the slider shows \(w^* = (60 - 33)/3 = 9\). An inflow of 7 percent of the 50 hours adds \(0.07 \times 50 = 3.5\) hours at every wage, so \(\bar{\ell}\) rises to 33.5 and \(w^* = (60 - 33.5)/3 = 8.83\): a cut of 1.17 dollars, or 11.7 percent. In the model, the wage falls by a larger percentage than the labor force rises. Employment rises by only 1.17 hours, to 51.17, a third of the 3.5 extra hours offered, because the lower wage makes everyone offer fewer hours. Card found almost no wage cut at all.
Before the inflow, the floor of 12 gives \(w = 12\), \(L = 60 - 12 = 48\) and \(U = 3(12 - 10) = 6\). After it, equation (6) gives \(w^* = (60 - 35)/3 = 8.33\), still below 12, so the floor binds again: \(w = 12\) and \(L = 48\), but \(U = (2 \times 12 + 35) - 48 = 11\). In general, when the floor binds,

\[L = \bar{f} - \bar{w}_{\min}, \qquad U = (1 + \bar{a})\,\bar{w}_{\min} - (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}),\]
(the second is equation (8) with \(w^*\) written out), so \(\partial L/\partial\bar{\ell} = 0\) and \(\partial U/\partial\bar{\ell} = 1\): every extra hour offered becomes an hour of unemployment.

By equation (6), \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\) stays at 10 if \(\bar{f}\) rises by as much as \(\bar{\ell}\), to 65. Then \(L^* = 65 - 10 = 55\): employment rises by the full 5 hours, and nobody’s wage falls. Under the floor of 12, \(L = 65 - 12 = 53\), also 5 more hours, and \(U = (24 + 35) - 53 = 6\), the same as before the inflow.
A binding minimum wage protects the wage of those who work, but if demand does not grow, it does not protect jobs: the same 48 hours are shared among more people offering work, and unemployment absorbs the whole inflow. Without a floor, the wage falls instead, by almost 12 percent for an inflow of Miami’s size (a). Card’s finding of almost no effect on wages or unemployment fits neither case on its own; it fits case (c), in which demand grows with the newcomers. The model is too simple to say how much demand grows. That is a question for data, and a good example of the fourth step of the method: compare the model’s predictions with the facts.

cases = [(30, 60, 0), (33, 60, 0), (33.5, 60, 0), (35, 60, 0), (30, 60, 12), (35, 60, 12), (35, 65, 0), (35, 65, 12)]
for l, f, w_min in cases:
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(2.0, l, f)
    w = max(w_star, w_min)                                   # the wage that holds
    L = labor_demand(w, f)
    U = max(labor_supply(w, 2.0, l) - L, 0.0)                # equation (8); zero if the floor does not bind
    print(f"l = {l}, f = {f}, floor {w_min:2d}: wage {w:5.2f}, employment {L:5.2f}, unemployment {U:5.2f}")

title: 2. Measuring the Macroeconomy
text:
Learning goals
This chapter is about measurement: how economists turn millions of transactions into a few numbers that describe a whole economy. By the end of it you will be able to:

title: 2. Measuring the Macroeconomy
2. Measuring the Macroeconomy
text:
2.1 Model overview
Back on Islandia, the island country we met in Chapter 1, a small statistics office has a job to do every year: put one number on everything the island produced. Farms grow grain, mills grind it, bakeries sell bread, Harbor Boatworks builds boats, the Islandia Treasury hires teachers, and some goods arrive by ship from Mainland. How do the statisticians add all of that up without counting anything twice? How do they tell a richer year from a year in which only prices went up? And how can Islandia compare itself with Mainland, which pays in another currency? This section builds the accounting tools that answer these three questions, following Islandia’s statisticians step by step.






NoteThe big idea



The question. How do we turn millions of purchases and paychecks into a few numbers that describe a whole economy, and compare them across years and across countries?
The answer in one sentence. Gross domestic product (GDP), the market value of all final goods and services produced in a period, gives the same total whether we add up production, spending or income, and dividing it by the right price level turns it into real output that can be compared over time and between countries.
What goes in and what comes out. This chapter has no behavior to model and no parameters to choose. In go data: prices and quantities, producers’ sales and purchases, incomes, exchange rates and price levels. Out come is GDP and its shares, labor’s share of income, real GDP, the price level and inflation, and GDP at common prices.

2.1.1 Production, expenditure and income

Definitions

A final good ends up with its last user: a household, a firm that keeps it as capital, the government, or a buyer abroad. An intermediate good disappears into some other good made in the same period, like the grain in Islandia’s bread or the electricity that runs a mill.
Producer \(j\) earns revenue \(R_j\) from its sales and pays \(M_j\) for the intermediate inputs it buys. The difference is its value added, the part of the value of its output that it created itself: \[VA_j \equiv R_j - M_j.\]
Capital (buildings, machines, boats, software) helps to make output but is not used up within the period. Its wear and tear is called depreciation. GDP is gross because depreciation is not taken out; subtracting it gives net domestic product.
Value added is paid out as income: compensation of employees (wages, salaries and benefits), taxes on production less subsidies, depreciation, and the net operating surplus, which goes to the owners. The operating surplus is whatever is left, so the four pieces always add up to value added.
Spending on final goods comes in four parts: consumption \(C\); investment \(I\) (business structures, equipment, intellectual property products such as software and R&D, new housing, and the change in inventories); government purchases \(G\); and net exports \(NX\), exports \(X\) minus imports \(IM\). When the Islandia Treasury hires a teacher or buys a ferry, that is part of \(G\). When it pays a pension, or interest on its debt, it only moves income from some islanders to others and buys nothing, so that payment is not part of \(G\).
Only new production counts. Selling a used boat a second time produces nothing new, but the dealer’s margin does count: it pays for the service of finding a buyer.



Deriving the results
Step 1: value added adds up to final sales. Picture a chain of \(J\) producers. The first buys no inputs, each one sells all of its output to the next, and the last one sells to final users. So \(M_1 = 0\) and \(M_j = R_{j-1}\), and
\[VA_1 = R_1, \qquad VA_2 = R_2 - R_1, \qquad \dots, \qquad VA_J = R_J - R_{J-1}.\]
Now add them up. Each revenue except the last shows up twice: with a plus sign as the seller’s revenue, and with a minus sign as the buyer’s cost. So the sum telescopes:
\[\sum_{j=1}^{J} VA_j = R_1 + (R_2 - R_1) + \dots + (R_J - R_{J-1}) = R_J.\]
The same cancellation works in any web of sales between firms, because each sale of an intermediate good is revenue for one firm and a cost for another. Counting production and counting final sales therefore give the same GDP:
\[\text{GDP} = \sum_j VA_j = \text{value of the final goods and services}.\]






TipIn words: count each stage once



If Islandia’s statisticians simply added up every firm’s sales, the grain inside a loaf of bread would be counted twice: once when the farm sells it to the mill, and again inside the price of the bread. Subtracting what each firm bought from other firms keeps only its own contribution, so every stage of the chain is counted exactly once.


Step 2: production = income. Add up the income split of value added over all producers:
\[\text{GDP} = \text{compensation} + \text{taxes on production less subsidies} + \text{net operating surplus} + \text{depreciation}.\]
Since the operating surplus is the leftover, every dollar of value added ends up as somebody’s income. In practice, though, statisticians measure income from other records (tax returns, payrolls) than the ones they use for spending. The income total is called gross domestic income (GDI), and the small gap between GDI and GDP is the statistical discrepancy.
Step 3: production = expenditure. Final goods are bought by households, firms, the government and foreigners. So buyers at home spend \(C + I + G\), and buyers abroad spend \(X\). Some of what \(C\), \(I\) and \(G\) buy, though, was made abroad and is not domestic production. Taking those imports out leaves the domestic output that went to final users: \(C + I + G + X - IM\). And goods that were made this year but not sold? They count as inventory investment, part of \(I\), as if the producer had bought its own output. So every unit produced has a buyer somewhere in the accounts:
\[Y = C + I + G + NX, \qquad NX \equiv X - IM.\]
This is the national income identity: GDP \(Y\) seen from the spending side.






ImportantKey result: GDP counted three ways



\[\text{GDP} = \sum_j VA_j = \text{value of the final goods and services} \tag{1}\]
\[Y = C + I + G + NX, \qquad NX \equiv X - IM \tag{2}\]
Equation (1): value added and final sales give the same total, which Step 2 shows is also paid out as income. Equation (2) splits it by buyer.
Islandia in numbers. An Islandia farm sells grain worth $40 to a mill, the mill sells flour worth $70 to a bakery, and the bakery sells bread worth $120 to islanders. The value added is \(40 + 30 + 50 = 120\), exactly the value of the bread. Adding up all sales would give \(230\).


Step 4: shares of GDP. Divide both sides of (2) by \(Y\) (Appendix C.2):
\[1 = \frac{C}{Y} + \frac{I}{Y} + \frac{G}{Y} + \frac{NX}{Y}.\]
The four shares sum to 100 percent in every year. Now compare two years. The left side is 1 in both, so its change is zero:
\[\Delta\frac{C}{Y} + \Delta\frac{I}{Y} + \Delta\frac{G}{Y} + \Delta\frac{NX}{Y} = 0.\]
If one share goes up, others must come down (Fig. 2). We compute shares from nominal values; the second block explains why.
Step 5: labor’s share of income. We want the part of income that pays for work. Two items belong neither clearly to labor nor clearly to capital. Taxes on production \(T\) (such as sales taxes) are nobody’s labor or capital income. Proprietors’ income \(\mathit{Prop}\), what the self-employed earn, pays both for their own work and for their own equipment, like an islander who fishes from a boat she owns. Income net of these taxes is
\[\text{GDI} - T = \text{compensation} + \mathit{Prop} + \text{other capital income}.\]
Assume that labor gets the same fraction of proprietors’ income as it gets of all other income, and call that fraction \(\theta\):
\[\theta = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \text{compensation} = \theta\,(\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}).\]
Labor’s total income is then compensation plus the fraction \(\theta\) of proprietors’ income. As a share of income net of taxes, it is
\[\frac{\text{compensation} + \theta\,\mathit{Prop}}{\text{GDI} - T} = \frac{\theta\,(\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}) + \theta\,\mathit{Prop}}{\text{GDI} - T} = \frac{\theta\,(\text{GDI} - T)}{\text{GDI} - T} = \theta.\]
So the labor share is \(\theta\):






ImportantKey result: labor’s share of income



\[\text{labor share} = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - \text{taxes on production} - \text{proprietors' income}} \tag{3}\]
The capital share is one minus the labor share. Fig. 3 uses equation (3).
Islandia in numbers. Take round numbers for one year: GDI of 100, taxes on production of 7, proprietors’ income of 9 and compensation of 54 (in billions). Equation (3) gives a labor share of \(54/84 \approx 0.643\), while the simple ratio compensation/GDI is only \(0.54\).








TipIn words: the self-employed



We cannot tell which part of the fisher’s income pays for her work and which part pays for her boat. So we leave proprietors out of both the top and the bottom of the fraction. That gives the same answer as splitting their income in the same proportions as everybody else’s.

GDP measures market production, not welfare. It leaves out work done at home (cooking, caring for one’s own children), the value of longer and healthier lives, leisure, and the using up of natural resources and harm to the environment.
