1. In Islandia’s chain, the mill now buys grain worth $40 and sells flour worth $80, and the bakery still sells bread worth $120. What is each producer’s value added, and what is GDP?


Answer

The farm adds 40, the mill \(80 - 40 = 40\) and the bakery \(120 - 80 = 40\). By equation (1), GDP is \(40 + 40 + 40 = 120\), the value of the bread. A higher price for flour moves value added from the bakery to the mill but leaves GDP unchanged.

2. An islander buys a new boat built on Mainland. Why does Islandia’s GDP not change?


Answer

The boat raises consumption \(C\) by its price, but it is also an import, so it lowers \(NX = X - IM\) by the same amount. In equation (2) the two changes cancel. The boat was produced on Mainland, so it is part of Mainland’s GDP, not Islandia’s.






2.1.2 Real GDP: quantity indexes and chain weighting

Definitions
Islandia produces goods \(i = 1, \dots, n\). Good \(i\) has price \(p_{i,t}\) and quantity \(q_{i,t}\) in year \(t\).

Nominal GDP values each year’s goods at that same year’s prices: \(\text{nominal GDP}_t = \sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}\).
Real GDP at the prices of a base year \(b\) values each year’s goods at one fixed set of prices: \(\sum_i p_{i,b}\,q_{i,t}\). Since the prices never change, it moves only when the quantities move. It is measured in “year-\(b\) dollars”.
The expenditure share of good \(i\) is \(s_{i,t} \equiv p_{i,t}q_{i,t}\big/\sum_k p_{k,t}q_{k,t}\). In every year the shares add up to one.
The growth rate of the quantity of good \(i\) is \(g_i\), so \(q_{i,t+1} = (1+g_i)\,q_{i,t}\).

The price level, also called the GDP deflator, is defined as nominal GDP divided by real GDP, \(P_t \equiv \text{nominal GDP}_t/\text{real GDP}_t\). Multiply both sides by real GDP:






ImportantKey result: the price level links nominal and real GDP



\[\text{nominal GDP}_t = P_t \times \text{real GDP}_t \tag{4}\]
Real GDP tracks only quantities, and the price level \(P_t\) picks up the rest. If Islandia made just one good, \(P_t\) would be its price and real GDP its quantity. In the base year real and nominal GDP coincide, so \(P_b = 1\) (or 100, as an index).




Deriving the results
Step 1: two ways to hold prices fixed. To measure real growth from year \(t\) to year \(t+1\), we can value the quantities of both years at the starting prices (the Laspeyres index), or at the ending prices (the Paasche index):
\[1 + g^L = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}}, \qquad 1 + g^P = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t}}.\]
Step 2: Laspeyres growth is an average of the goods’ growth rates. In the top of the fraction, write \((1+g_i)\,q_{i,t}\) for \(q_{i,t+1}\), and split the fraction into one term per good:
\[1 + g^L = \sum_i \frac{p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}}{\sum_k p_{k,t}\,q_{k,t}}\,(1+g_i) = \sum_i s_{i,t}\,(1+g_i) = \sum_i s_{i,t} + \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i = 1 + \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i.\]
The last step uses the fact that the shares sum to one.
Step 3: Paasche growth is an average too, with other weights. Flip the Paasche fraction upside down and write \(q_{i,t+1}/(1+g_i)\) for \(q_{i,t}\):
\[\frac{1}{1+g^P} = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t}}{\sum_k p_{k,t+1}\,q_{k,t+1}} = \sum_i \frac{p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_k p_{k,t+1}\,q_{k,t+1}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+g_i} = \sum_i \frac{s_{i,t+1}}{1+g_i}.\]






ImportantKey result: the two indexes as weighted averages



\[g^L = \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i, \qquad \frac{1}{1+g^P} = \sum_i \frac{s_{i,t+1}}{1+g_i} \tag{5}\]
Both indexes average the growth rates of the individual goods. Laspeyres weights each good by its share of spending in the first year. Paasche uses the shares of the last year, in the form of a weighted harmonic mean of the growth factors.
Islandia in numbers. Suppose Islandia makes only apples and computers, as in the textbook’s example. From 2026 to 2027 apples grow 10 percent and computers 20 percent. In 2026 computers take a share of about 0.833 of spending, so \(g^L = 0.167\times 10\% + 0.833 \times 20\% \approx 18.3\%\). At the 2027 prices the Paasche rate is about 17.7%.








TipIn words: why the two indexes disagree



The weights depend on prices. On Islandia, computers got cheaper relative to apples while their quantity grew faster. At the old prices computers were still expensive, so the Laspeyres index gives the fast-growing good a big weight and reports more growth. At the new prices computers weigh less, and the Paasche index reports less.


When do the two agree? (a) If every quantity grows at the same rate \(g\), both formulas in (5) give exactly \(g\), since the shares sum to one. (b) If every price changes by the same factor \(\lambda\), so that \(p_{i,t+1} = \lambda p_{i,t}\), then \(\lambda\) cancels from the top and the bottom of the Paasche fraction, and it turns into the Laspeyres fraction. So the two indexes can differ only when relative prices change. Usually the goods whose relative price falls, like computers, are also the goods whose quantity grows fastest. At the starting prices those goods are still expensive and carry a large weight, so \(g^L > g^P\). The longer the period, the more relative prices change, and the wider the gap.
Step 4: chain weighting. The chain-weighted index splits the difference and averages the two growth rates:
\[g^{\text{chain}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(g^L + g^P\right).\]






ImportantKey result: chain-weighted growth



\[g^{\text{chain}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(g^L + g^P\right) \tag{6}\]
Statistical agencies use the Fisher index, the geometric mean of the two growth factors, \(1 + g^F = \sqrt{(1+g^L)(1+g^P)}\). When the two rates are close, the two kinds of average are practically the same (Appendix C.6); the code below compares them.
Islandia in numbers. Averaging 18.3% and 17.7% gives chain-weighted growth of about 18.0% from 2026 to 2027.


Step 5: linking the years into a chain. Equation (6) is applied to each pair of neighboring years, so the weights are always the prices of those two years. To get levels from the growth rates, choose a benchmark year \(b\) in which real GDP is set equal to nominal GDP. Then step forward and backward one year at a time:
\[X_{t+1} = X_t\,(1 + g^{\text{chain}}_{t,t+1}), \qquad X_t = \frac{X_{t+1}}{1 + g^{\text{chain}}_{t,t+1}},\]
where \(X_t\) is chained real GDP. Across several years the growth factors multiply, \(X_T = X_b\,(1+g_{b,b+1})(1+g_{b+1,b+2})\cdots(1+g_{T-1,T})\). The levels are reported in “chained year-\(b\) dollars”.

Real GDP ignores pure price changes. When only prices move, every index reports zero real growth, and the whole change in nominal GDP lands in the price level.
Fixed base years go out of date. Over long spans the Laspeyres index overstates growth and the Paasche index understates it. The U.S. national accounts moved to chain weighting in the 1990s, a time of fast-falling computer prices.
Chained components do not add up. Each chained component has its own weights, so chained \(C + I + G + NX\) is generally not equal to chained GDP. For shares, use nominal values, which do add up (equation 2). For real growth rates, use chained real values.


Real GDP holds prices fixed so that only quantities move, and chain weighting keeps those prices up to date.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. One year every price on Islandia doubles, and every quantity stays the same. What happens to nominal GDP, to real growth by each index, and to the price level?


Answer

Nominal GDP doubles. Relative prices do not change, so the Laspeyres, Paasche and chained indexes all report zero real growth (the first row of the table). By equation (4), the price level doubles: the whole change in nominal GDP is a change in prices.

2. Islandia’s computers grew 20 percent and its apples 10 percent. Without computing anything, why must every index of real growth lie between these two numbers?


Answer

By equation (5), the Laspeyres and Paasche rates are weighted averages of the goods’ growth rates, with weights that are positive and sum to one. An average can never be larger than the largest item or smaller than the smallest. The chained rate of equation (6) averages the two again, so it lies in the same range.






2.1.3 Price indexes and inflation

Definitions

The GDP deflator is the price level of equation (4), \(P_t = \text{nominal GDP}_t/\text{real GDP}_t\), usually multiplied by 100 so that it equals 100 in the base year.
The inflation rate is the growth rate of the price level, \(\pi_{t+1} \equiv P_{t+1}/P_t - 1\).
Each quantity index has a twin price index. The Laspeyres price index prices the starting quantities at both years’ prices, \(\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t}\big/\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}\). The Paasche price index uses the ending quantities, \(\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}\big/\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}\).



Deriving the results
Step 1: nominal growth splits exactly into a price part and a quantity part. Multiply and divide the growth factor of nominal GDP by \(\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}\):
\[\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}} = \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}}}_{\text{Paasche price index}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}}}_{\text{Laspeyres quantity index}}.\]
Multiplying and dividing by \(\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t}\) instead gives the Laspeyres price index times the Paasche quantity index. Multiply the two splits together and take the square root: the Fisher price index times the Fisher quantity index is also exactly the growth factor of nominal GDP. That is why a chained price index and chained real GDP always satisfy equation (4).
Step 2: the growth rate of a product. Write equation (4) for two neighboring years and divide one by the other. The growth factor of a product is the product of the growth factors:
\[1 + g_{\text{nominal}} = (1+\pi)(1+g_{\text{real}}) = 1 + \pi + g_{\text{real}} + \pi\,g_{\text{real}}.\]
Take 1 away from both sides: \(g_{\text{nominal}} = \pi + g_{\text{real}} + \pi\,g_{\text{real}}\). The last term multiplies two small numbers, so it is much smaller than the others. Dropping it (Appendix C.5) leaves
\[g_{\text{nominal GDP}} \approx \pi + g_{\text{real GDP}}.\]






ImportantKey result: nominal growth = inflation + real growth



\[g_{\text{nominal GDP}} \approx \pi + g_{\text{real GDP}} \tag{7}\]
To get inflation from the other two, solve the exact form for \(\pi\): \(\pi = (1+g_{\text{nominal}})/(1+g_{\text{real}}) - 1 \approx g_{\text{nominal}} - g_{\text{real}}\). In natural logs the split is exact: \(\ln(\text{nominal GDP}) = \ln P + \ln(\text{real GDP})\), so the changes in logs add up with no error (Appendix C.4).
Islandia in numbers. From 2026 to 2027 Islandia’s nominal GDP grows 27.5% and chained real GDP 18.0%. The rule of thumb puts inflation at \(27.5 - 18.0 = 9.5\) percent, but the exact formula gives about 8.0%.








TipIn words: more expensive goods, or more goods



Islandia’s nominal GDP can grow because each apple and each computer costs more, or because there are more apples and computers. Equation (7) simply adds the two sources. The small cross term it leaves out is the price increase on the extra goods.


Step 3: rates over different periods. With quarterly data, the change from a year ago compares a quarter with the same quarter one year before, \(P_t/P_{t-4} - 1\). A one-quarter change becomes an annual rate by compounding it four times, \((P_t/P_{t-1})^4 - 1\), which is close to four times the quarterly rate when that rate is small (Appendix C.3). Over \(T\) years, the average annual growth rate \(\bar{g}\) is the constant rate that carries the first value to the last: \(P_T = P_0(1+\bar{g})^T\). Raise both sides of \(P_T/P_0 = (1+\bar{g})^T\) to the power \(1/T\) and subtract 1:
\[\bar{g} = \left(\frac{P_T}{P_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1.\]
(Here the bar marks an average over the years, not a parameter.)
Step 4: changing the base year. Rebasing an index to year \(b\) means \(P'_t = 100 \times P_t/P_b\). The constant \(100/P_b\) cancels in every ratio, \(P'_{t+1}/P'_t = P_{t+1}/P_t\), so rebasing shifts the level of the index but leaves every growth rate and inflation rate as it was.


What the framework predicts
Take the change in logs of equation (4), \(\Delta\ln(\text{nominal GDP}) = \Delta\ln P + \Delta\ln(\text{real GDP})\): the elasticity of nominal GDP with respect to the price level is 1, and with respect to real GDP it is also 1.

The rule of thumb in equation (7) works well when rates are small. With 2 percent inflation and 2 percent real growth, the cross term is only \(0.02 \times 0.02 = 0.0004\), or 0.04 percentage points. In Islandia’s apples-and-computers example, with prices up 8 percent and quantities up 18 percent, it is about 1.5 points (see the checks below). Nominal growth is roughly inflation plus real growth; the small cross term matters only when rates are large.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia’s nominal GDP grows 5 percent in a year and its real GDP 3 percent. What is inflation by the rule of thumb, and what is it exactly?


Answer

By equation (7), \(\pi \approx 5 - 3 = 2\) percent. The exact form gives \(\pi = 1.05/1.03 - 1 \approx 1.94\%\). With rates this small the cross term is tiny, so the rule of thumb is close.

2. Islandia’s price level doubles over 10 years. What is the average annual inflation rate, and why is it not simply 10 percent?


Answer

By Step 3, \(\bar{g} = 2^{1/10} - 1 \approx 7.18\%\) a year. Ten years at 10 percent would multiply prices by \(1.1^{10} \approx 2.59\), not by 2, because each year’s increase builds on the higher prices of the year before.






2.1.4 Comparing countries: exchange rates and purchasing power parity

Definitions
Islandia’s statisticians will also ask whether their island is richer or poorer than Mainland, which uses a different currency. The tools are the same for any pair of countries. We write them for the textbook’s pair, China and the United States, and use its numbers.

The exchange rate \(e\) is the number of yuan that buy one dollar in the currency market.
China’s GDP in its own currency is \(Y^{\text{yuan}}\). Converted at the exchange rate, it is \(\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} = Y^{\text{yuan}}/e\).
\(\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}\) and \(\text{price level}_{\text{China}}\) are the cost of the same basket of goods in each country, both in dollars at the exchange rate. Their ratio, the relative price level, says how expensive China is compared with the United States.
The PPP conversion factor is the number of yuan that buy in China what one dollar buys in the United States: \(\text{PPP} = e \times \text{price level}_{\text{China}}/\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}\).



Deriving the results
Step 1: China’s real output. Equation (4) holds in China too, with every value in dollars. Solve it for real GDP:
\[\text{real GDP}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}}.\]
Step 2: value China’s goods at U.S. prices. To compare like with like, we price China’s quantities at the prices that hold in the United States:
\[\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}} \times \text{real GDP}_{\text{China}}.\]
Step 3: substitute Step 1 into Step 2.
\[\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}} \times \text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}.\]






ImportantKey result: GDP at common prices



\[\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}} \times \text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} \tag{8}\]
Dollar GDP is divided by China’s relative price level. Where goods are cheap, the same dollars stand for more goods.
In numbers. With the textbook’s 2019 data, 95.1 trillion yuan at 6.91 yuan per dollar is about $13.8 trillion, 67 percent of U.S. GDP of $20.6 trillion. Chinese prices are 68.4 percent of U.S. prices, so at U.S. prices China’s GDP is about $20.1 trillion, 98 percent of U.S. GDP.








TipIn words: cheap haircuts



Suppose a haircut on Islandia costs half of what it costs on Mainland. Converting Islandia’s GDP at the exchange rate counts each Islandia haircut as half a Mainland haircut, even though it is the same service. Valuing both islands’ goods at the same prices fixes this, and it raises the measured output of the cheaper place.


Step 4: the shortcut through the PPP factor. Put \(\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} = Y^{\text{yuan}}/e\) into (8) and gather the terms in the denominator:
\[\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{Y^{\text{yuan}}}{e \times \text{price level}_{\text{China}}/\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}} = \frac{Y^{\text{yuan}}}{\text{PPP}}.\]
So we can bypass the exchange rate entirely: GDP in yuan divided by the PPP conversion factor is GDP at U.S. prices.
Step 5: how much of the gap is due to prices? Divide (8) by U.S. GDP and take logs (Appendix C.4):
\[\ln\frac{\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{GDP}_{\text{U.S.}}} = \ln\frac{\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{GDP}_{\text{U.S.}}} - \ln\frac{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}.\]
The log gap at common prices is the log gap at the exchange rate minus the log of the relative price level. When China is cheaper, that log is negative, and the gap at common prices is smaller. Dividing both GDPs by population gives the same split for GDP per person.
Pricing China’s goods at U.S. prices is the cross-country cousin of a Laspeyres index; pricing U.S. goods at Chinese prices would be the Paasche version. In practice, the World Bank’s International Comparison Program and the Penn World Table use average world prices (“international dollars”), much as chain weighting averages the two indexes over time.


What the framework predicts









A 1% rise in …
GDP at the exchange rate
GDP at common prices

\(-1\%\)

\(+1\%\)

\(+1\%\)

\(+1\%\)
\(+1\%\)
0




Common prices do not react to the currency market. A swing in the exchange rate moves GDP in dollars one for one, but leaves the comparison at common prices where it was, because China’s goods get cheaper in dollars by the same 1 percent (the elasticity of dollar GDP with respect to \(e\) is \(-1\)).
Rich countries look less far ahead at common prices. Services that cannot be traded, such as haircuts or restaurant meals, take a lot of labor, so they are cheap where wages are low. Poor countries therefore have low price levels, and comparisons at exchange rates exaggerate the income gaps between rich and poor countries.


To compare countries, value their goods at the same prices; exchange rates alone make cheap countries look poorer than they are.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Suppose that at the exchange rate Islandia’s GDP is 40 percent of Mainland’s, and that goods on Islandia cost 80 percent of what they cost on Mainland. How large is Islandia’s GDP at Mainland’s prices, as a share of Mainland’s GDP?


Answer

By equation (8), divide the share at the exchange rate by the relative price level: \(40/0.8 = 50\) percent. Because Islandia is cheaper, the gap shrinks from 60 to 50 percentage points.

2. Islandia’s currency loses value against Mainland’s, while nothing else changes on either island. What happens to Islandia’s GDP at the exchange rate and at common prices?


Answer

At the exchange rate, Islandia’s GDP falls in Mainland’s currency, one for one with the currency (the first row of the table). At common prices nothing changes: the same goods are produced, and Islandia’s relative price level falls by exactly as much, so the two effects cancel in equation (8).









NoteRecap




One total, three ways: value added, final spending and income all add up to GDP, equations (1) and (2); the spending shares move together (Fig. 2).
Labor’s share leaves taxes and proprietors’ income out of the denominator, equation (3) (Fig. 3).
Real GDP values quantities at fixed prices; Laspeyres and Paasche are weighted averages of the goods’ growth rates, and chain weighting averages the two, equations (5) and (6).
Prices and inflation: nominal GDP is the price level times real GDP, equation (4), and nominal growth is about inflation plus real growth, equation (7) (Fig. 4; Fig. 5 plots the inflation rate).
Comparing countries needs common prices, equation (8): at exchange rates, poor countries look poorer than they are (Comparing countries).

title: 2. Measuring the Macroeconomy
text:
2.2 Model in code
Now we turn the measurement rules into Python. The section has three parts: the setup (folded, because it is nearly the same in every chapter), the rules as functions, and numerical checks of the Key results, from Islandia’s bakery to China at common prices. Run its cells once, in order. Every later section of the notebook reuses them.

2.2.1 Setup
Run the setup cells once, before anything else. They load the Python libraries, give every chart the same look, store the address of the chapter’s data and define four helpers that only the book website needs. You can use the notebook without reading them; open the box if you are curious.






NoteShow the setup code





The first cell loads the libraries and sets the look of the charts. Its comments explain each step.

# @title Setup: libraries, chart colors and the data location
# Text after a "#" is a comment: Python ignores it, it is there for human readers.

# Step 1: load the libraries. `import` loads a library, a toolbox written by
# other people, and `as pd` gives pandas the short nickname pd, so the code stays short.
import numpy as np                    # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                   # data tables
import plotly.express as px           # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go     # charts built piece by piece
import plotly.io as pio               # settings shared by every chart
# menus, buttons and sliders for the interactive figures
from ipywidgets import interact, ToggleButtons, Dropdown, SelectMultiple, FloatSlider, IntSlider

# Step 2: one light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
# the same chart size in Colab and on the website
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47", "#e0a33b"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full widget labels

# Step 3, Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets.
# `try` runs the indented lines; if the import fails (we are not in Colab),
# `except` skips them.

    import google.colab

except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# Step 4: the data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch02/"

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider or menu. The next helpers build those versions. Run them and move on.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. changes_chart
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "base_year"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

The data figures of this chapter let you add other countries. On the website, a menu above each of these figures adds a group of countries (the G7, a world region, …); the next cell builds those menus.

# @title Helpers for the website's country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_traces(data, y, skip, x="year", fmt=".1f", markers=False):
    """One line per country of a long table, leaving out the countries in `skip`.

    Arguments
        data    : a long table with one row per country and year (columns country, x, y)
        y       : the column to draw
        skip    : the countries to leave out
        x       : the column on the horizontal axis
        fmt     : the number format of the hover text, e.g. ".1f"
        markers : True to draw a dot at every point of the line
    Returns
        a dictionary: each country's name and its list of traces (one line in its color)
    """
    # Step 1: go through the table one country at a time
    extra = {}
    for name, part in data.groupby("country"):
        if name not in skip:
            # Step 2: one line for this country, in its COLORS color, with hover text
            extra[name] = [go.Scatter(x=part[x], y=part[y], name=name,
                                      mode="lines+markers" if markers else "lines",
                                      line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=2),
                                      hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: %{{y:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>")]
    return extra


def country_menu(fig, extra, countries):
    """Add the extra countries' lines hidden, and a menu that shows one group of them.

    The groups are the G7, the G20, the OECD and each world region. The traces already in
    fig (the textbook's) stay as they are, and the slider steps only switch those.

    Arguments
        fig       : a Plotly figure with the textbook's countries
        extra     : the other countries' lines, from country_traces
        countries : a table with one row per country (columns country, region, g7, g20, oecd)
    Returns
        the same figure, with the extra lines hidden and the group menu above the plot
    """
    # Step 1: add every extra line, hidden, and remember whose line it is
    n = len(fig.data)                           # the number of textbook traces
    owner = []
    for name, traces in extra.items():
        for trace in traces:
            trace.visible = False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(name)
    # Step 2: the groups of the menu: G7, G20, OECD, then each region, A to Z
    groups = {"G7": countries.country[countries.g7], "G20": countries.country[countries.g20],
              "OECD": countries.country[countries.oecd]}
    for region in sorted(countries.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = countries.country[countries.region == region]
    # Step 3: one button per group; each switches only the extra lines, `rest`
    rest, autoscale = list(range(n, len(fig.data))), {"yaxis.autorange": True}
    buttons = [dict(label="Textbook only", method="update",
                    args=[{"visible": [False] * len(owner)}, autoscale, rest])]
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in set(members) for o in owner]
        # leave out a group with no country in the data
        if any(visible):
            buttons.append(dict(label=f"+ {label} ({sum(visible)})", method="update",
                                args=[{"visible": visible}, autoscale, rest]))
    # Step 4: put the menu above the plot, at the right
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=0, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    # Step 5: make every slider step switch only the textbook traces, the first n
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        for step in slider.steps:
            step.args = [{"visible": list(step.args[0]["visible"])}, step.args[1], list(range(n))]
    return fig

The last helper is like slider_figure, but with a dropdown menu, for the figures that show one country at a time.

# @title Helper for the website's one-country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Like slider_figure, but with a dropdown menu: one precomputed figure per value.

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. composition_chart
        name        : the argument the menu sets, e.g. "country"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute (e.g. the countries)
        start       : the value shown first
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a menu that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[values.index(start)].layout)
    # Step 2: copy every trace into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (values[i] == start)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one menu entry per value: its traces, title, labels, shapes and axes
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes],
                  "yaxis": f.layout.yaxis.to_plotly_json(),
                  "xaxis": f.layout.xaxis.to_plotly_json()}
        # a second vertical axis (Fig. 2)
        if "yaxis2" in f.layout.to_plotly_json():
            layout["yaxis2"] = f.layout.yaxis2.to_plotly_json()
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    # Step 4: put the menu above the plot, at the right
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start), x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02,
                yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig






2.2.2 The model as functions
This chapter has no behavior to model, but its measurement rules are formulas, and we write each one as a Python function: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives back a result. The first three are shares, the value of production, and chain-weighted growth, equation (6).

# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses, and
# `return` gives back the result. The text in triple quotes describes the function.
def share(part, total):
    """Share of a part in a total, in percent.

    Tables 2.1 and 2.2, and the shares of equation (2):  share = 100 * part / total

    Arguments
        part  : the part, e.g. consumption or compensation
        total : the total, e.g. GDP
    Returns
        the share of the part in the total, in percent
    """
    return 100 * part / total


def gdp_value(prices, quantities):
    """Value of production: price times quantity, added over all goods.

    Equation (4) and the indexes of equation (5) use it:  value = sum over i of p_i * q_i
    With each year's own prices it is nominal GDP; with fixed prices, real GDP.

    Arguments
        prices     : the price of each good, p_i
        quantities : the quantity of each good, q_i
    Returns
        the value of production, in dollars
    """
    # multiply good by good; `.sum()` adds up all the values of a column or a row
    return (prices * quantities).sum()


def chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche):
    """Chain-weighted growth of real GDP.

    Equation (6):  g_chain = (g_L + g_P) / 2

    Arguments
        g_laspeyres : the Laspeyres growth rate, g_L (at the starting prices)
        g_paasche   : the Paasche growth rate, g_P (at the ending prices)
    Returns
        the chain-weighted growth rate, g_chain
    """
    # the simple average of the two growth rates
    return (g_laspeyres + g_paasche) / 2

The last two functions compare countries. One converts GDP into dollars at the market exchange rate, and the other values it at U.S. prices, equation (8).

def to_dollars(gdp_local, exchange_rate):
    """GDP in dollars at the market exchange rate.

    The first step of equation (8):  GDP in dollars = GDP in local currency / e

    Arguments
        gdp_local     : GDP in the local currency, e.g. trillions of yuan
        exchange_rate : the exchange rate e, units of local currency per dollar
    Returns
        GDP in dollars
    """
    return gdp_local / exchange_rate


def at_common_prices(gdp_dollars, relative_price_level):
    """Real GDP at U.S. prices.

    Equation (8):  real GDP at U.S. prices = GDP in dollars / (price level / U.S. price level)

    Arguments
        gdp_dollars          : GDP in dollars, from to_dollars
        relative_price_level : the country's price level relative to the U.S. (U.S. = 1)
    Returns
        real GDP at U.S. prices, in dollars
    """
    # where goods are cheap (a relative price level below 1), the same dollars buy more
    return gdp_dollars / relative_price_level



2.2.3 Checking the key results
The rules came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, one Key result at a time, mostly with small made-up examples from Islandia.
Check 1: value added adds up to final sales (equation 1). Islandia’s chain of three producers: a farm grows grain worth $40 and sells it to a mill; the mill turns it into flour worth $70 and sells it to a bakery; the bakery sells bread worth $120 to islanders.

# Step 1: each producer's sales and purchases. `pd.Series({...})` builds one
# labeled column from a dictionary: the keys become the labels.
revenue = pd.Series({"farm": 40, "mill": 70, "bakery": 120})
# each buys the output of the one before
inputs = pd.Series({"farm": 0, "mill": 40, "bakery": 70})
# Step 2: value added; subtracting two Series subtracts the values with the same label
value_added = revenue - inputs
print(value_added)
# Step 3: equation (1): the sum of value added equals the final sales
print(f"Sum of value added:   ${value_added.sum()}")
print(f"Final sales (bread):  ${revenue['bakery']}")
print(f"Sum of all revenues:  ${revenue.sum()}   (counts the grain three times and the flour twice)")

farm      40
mill      30
bakery    50
dtype: int64
Sum of value added:   $120
Final sales (bread):  $120
Sum of all revenues:  $230   (counts the grain three times and the flour twice)


Check 2: the labor share (equation 3). We take made-up round numbers for one year’s income on Islandia (in billions) and check the algebra of Step 5: splitting proprietors’ income in the economy-wide proportion gives the same labor share as leaving it out of the fraction.

# Step 1: Islandia's income in one year, in billions
gdi, taxes, proprietors, compensation = 100.0, 7.0, 9.0, 54.0
# Step 2: the labor share in two ways
theta = compensation / (gdi - taxes - proprietors)                  # equation (3)
# proprietors' income split by theta
split = (compensation + theta * proprietors) / (gdi - taxes)
# Step 3: both give the same share; compensation / GDI alone is too low
print(f"Labor share, equation (3):                 {theta:.4f}")
print(f"Labor share with proprietors split:        {split:.4f}")
print(f"Simple share, compensation / GDI:          {compensation / gdi:.4f}   (lower)")

Labor share, equation (3):                 0.6429
Labor share with proprietors split:        0.6429
Simple share, compensation / GDI:          0.5400   (lower)


Check 3: real GDP in the economy of Table 2.4. In this example Islandia produces only apples and computers, as in the textbook’s Table 2.4. We store its prices and quantities in two small tables, one row per year.

# Prices and quantities of the two goods, one row per year.
# `pd.DataFrame({...}, index=[...])` builds a table from a dictionary: each key
# becomes a column, and the `index` gives the row labels.
prices = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [1, 2, 3], "computers": [900, 1000, 1000]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
quantities = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [500, 500, 550], "computers": [5, 5, 6]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
prices

Nominal GDP uses each year’s own prices. Real GDP holds the prices fixed. The Laspeyres index measures the change from 2026 to 2027 with the initial (2026) prices, and the Paasche index with the final (2027) prices. Chain weighting averages the two growth rates (equation 6).

# Step 1: nominal GDP, each year at its own prices. `prices.loc[2026]` picks the
# row for 2026. An f-string, f"... {x:,.0f}", puts a value into the text: ","
# adds thousands separators, ".0f" shows no decimals, ".1%" a percentage.
for year in [2025, 2026, 2027]:
    print(f"Nominal GDP in {year}: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[year], quantities.loc[year]):,.0f}")

# Step 2: growth 2026-2027, nominal and at fixed prices; multiplying two rows,
# `prices.loc[2026] * quantities.loc[2027]`, multiplies the matching columns
g_nominal = gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
# Laspeyres: at the 2026 prices; Paasche: at the 2027 prices
g_laspeyres = gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_paasche = gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_chain = chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche)              # equation (6)
# Step 3: the numbers of Table 2.4
print(f"Real GDP in 2027 at 2026 prices: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]):,.0f}")
print(f"Real GDP in 2026 at 2027 prices: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2026]):,.0f}")
print(f"Growth 2026-2027: nominal {g_nominal:.1%}, Laspeyres {g_laspeyres:.1%}, "
      f"Paasche {g_paasche:.1%}, chain-weighted {g_chain:.1%}")
# Step 4: chained real GDP in 2026, going back one year from 2027 (nominal GDP $7,650)
print(f"Chained real GDP in 2026, benchmarked to 2027: ${7650 / (1 + g_chain):,.0f}")
# the rule of thumb of equation (7)
print(f"Inflation (nominal growth minus real growth):  {g_nominal - g_chain:.1%}")

Nominal GDP in 2025: $5,000
Nominal GDP in 2026: $6,000
Nominal GDP in 2027: $7,650
Real GDP in 2027 at 2026 prices: $7,100
Real GDP in 2026 at 2027 prices: $6,500
Growth 2026-2027: nominal 27.5%, Laspeyres 18.3%, Paasche 17.7%, chain-weighted 18.0%
Chained real GDP in 2026, benchmarked to 2027: $6,482
Inflation (nominal growth minus real growth):  9.5%


These are the numbers of Table 2.4: real growth is 18.3 percent at 2026 prices, 17.7 percent at 2027 prices, and 18.0 percent chain-weighted. Nominal GDP grew 27.5 percent, so by the rule of thumb in equation (7) prices rose by about \(27.5 - 18.0 = 9.5\) percent. (The textbook gets $6,483 for chained real GDP in 2026, because it rounds the growth rate to 18.0 percent first; with the unrounded rate we get $6,482.)
Check 4: the two indexes as weighted averages (equation 5). Apples grew 10 percent and computers 20 percent. Weighting these rates with the 2026 spending shares must give the Laspeyres rate, and the harmonic form with the 2027 shares must give the Paasche rate. If every price rises by the same factor, the two indexes must agree.

# Step 1: prices and quantities of the two years, and the spending shares
p0, p1 = prices.loc[2026], prices.loc[2027]
q0, q1 = quantities.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]
s0 = p0 * q0 / gdp_value(p0, q0)                 # spending shares in 2026
s1 = p1 * q1 / gdp_value(p1, q1)                 # spending shares in 2027
growth_i = q1 / q0 - 1                           # growth of each good's quantity
# Step 2: equation (5), both sides for each index
print(f"Shares of computers: {s0['computers']:.3f} in 2026, {s1['computers']:.3f} in 2027")
print(f"Laspeyres: direct {g_laspeyres:.4%}   share-weighted average {(s0 * growth_i).sum():.4%}")
print(f"Paasche:   direct {g_paasche:.4%}   harmonic form          {1 / (s1 / (1 + growth_i)).sum() - 1:.4%}")
# Step 3: every price 50% higher, so relative prices are unchanged
p_scaled = 1.5 * p0
g_scaled = gdp_value(p_scaled, q1) / gdp_value(p_scaled, q0) - 1
print(f"Paasche when all prices rise by the same factor: {g_scaled:.4%} (= Laspeyres)")

Shares of computers: 0.833 in 2026, 0.784 in 2027
Laspeyres: direct 18.3333%   share-weighted average 18.3333%
Paasche:   direct 17.6923%   harmonic form          17.6923%
Paasche when all prices rise by the same factor: 18.3333% (= Laspeyres)


The price of apples rose by half while computers kept their price, so computers became relatively cheaper, and their quantity grew faster. At the 2026 prices computers carry more weight, which is why the Laspeyres rate is the higher one.
Check 5: the exact split of nominal growth, and the Fisher index. Step 1 of the price block says that a price index times the matching quantity index gives the growth factor of nominal GDP exactly. Step 2 says that the rule of thumb in equation (7) misses the cross term \(\pi\,g\).

# Step 1: the price indexes; `x ** 0.5` is the square root of x (Fisher)
price_laspeyres = gdp_value(p1, q0) / gdp_value(p0, q0)
price_paasche = gdp_value(p1, q1) / gdp_value(p0, q1)
price_fisher = (price_laspeyres * price_paasche) ** 0.5
g_fisher = ((1 + g_laspeyres) * (1 + g_paasche)) ** 0.5 - 1
# Step 2: each price index times the matching quantity index gives nominal growth
print(f"Nominal growth factor:                     {1 + g_nominal:.5f}")
print(f"Paasche price x Laspeyres quantity:        {price_paasche * (1 + g_laspeyres):.5f}")
print(f"Laspeyres price x Paasche quantity:        {price_laspeyres * (1 + g_paasche):.5f}")
print(f"Fisher price x Fisher quantity:            {price_fisher * (1 + g_fisher):.5f}")
print(f"Real growth: chain-weighted {g_chain:.4%}, Fisher {g_fisher:.4%}")
# Step 3: exact inflation, (1 + pi) = (1 + nominal growth) / (1 + real growth)
exact = (1 + g_nominal) / (1 + g_chain) - 1
print(f"Inflation: rule of thumb {g_nominal - g_chain:.2%}, exact {exact:.2%}, "
      f"Fisher price index {price_fisher - 1:.2%}")
# Step 4: the cross term pi * g that equation (7) leaves out
print(f"Cross term pi x g: {exact * g_chain:.2%}  ->  {exact:.2%} + {g_chain:.2%} + {exact * g_chain:.2%} "
      f"= {exact + g_chain + exact * g_chain:.2%}")

Nominal growth factor:                     1.27500
Paasche price x Laspeyres quantity:        1.27500
Laspeyres price x Paasche quantity:        1.27500
Fisher price x Fisher quantity:            1.27500
Real growth: chain-weighted 18.0128%, Fisher 18.0124%
Inflation: rule of thumb 9.49%, exact 8.04%, Fisher price index 8.04%
Cross term pi x g: 1.45%  ->  8.04% + 18.01% + 1.45% = 27.50%


The four products agree to the last digit, and the arithmetic and geometric averages of the two growth rates differ only in the third decimal. But with rates this large, the rule of thumb is off: prices in this economy rose by about 8.0 percent, not 9.5. The missing 1.5 points are the cross term.
Check 6: rates over different periods. A price level that rises 1 percent every quarter rises by more than 4 percent a year, because the increases compound. And a price level that doubles in 10 years grows at an average annual rate of \(2^{1/10} - 1\).

# Step 1: 1% a quarter, compounded over four quarters
quarterly = 0.01
print(f"1% a quarter, compounded: {(1 + quarterly) ** 4 - 1:.4%} a year (simple rule: {4 * quarterly:.0%})")
# Step 2: the average annual growth rate when prices double in 10 years
g_bar = 2 ** (1 / 10) - 1
print(f"Prices double in 10 years: average growth {g_bar:.3%} a year")
print(f"Check: (1 + {g_bar:.5f})^10 = {(1 + g_bar) ** 10:.4f}")

1% a quarter, compounded: 4.0604% a year (simple rule: 4%)
Prices double in 10 years: average growth 7.177% a year
Check: (1 + 0.07177)^10 = 2.0000


Check 7: China and the United States at common prices (equation 8). We use the textbook’s 2019 numbers: U.S. GDP of $20.6 trillion, China’s GDP of 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar, and Chinese prices at 68.4 percent of U.S. prices.

# China's GDP in dollars, then at U.S. prices, equation (8)
# 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar (2019)
china_dollars = to_dollars(95.1, 6.91)
# goods in China cost 68.4% of U.S. prices
china_ppp = at_common_prices(china_dollars, 0.684)
# both as a share of U.S. GDP, $20.6 trillion
print(f"China at the exchange rate: ${china_dollars:.1f} trillion, {china_dollars / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")
print(f"China at common prices:     ${china_ppp:.1f} trillion, {china_ppp / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")

China at the exchange rate: $13.8 trillion, 67% of U.S. GDP
China at common prices:     $20.1 trillion, 98% of U.S. GDP


With these numbers, China’s economy looks like two-thirds of the U.S. economy at the exchange rate, but almost exactly as large at common prices. The next cell checks Steps 4 and 5 and the first row of the table of predictions: the PPP shortcut, the log split of the gap, and a 1 percent weaker yuan.

# Step 1: the PPP shortcut, yuan that buy what one dollar buys in the U.S.
ppp = 6.91 * 0.684
print(f"PPP factor: {ppp:.3f} yuan per dollar; 95.1 / PPP = ${95.1 / ppp:.2f} trillion (= {china_ppp:.2f})")
# Step 2: the log split of the gap; `np.log` is the natural logarithm
gap_exchange, gap_prices = np.log(china_dollars / 20.6), np.log(0.684)
print(f"Log gap at the exchange rate {gap_exchange:.4f} - log relative price level {gap_prices:.4f} "
      f"= {gap_exchange - gap_prices:.4f};  log gap at common prices {np.log(china_ppp / 20.6):.4f}")
# Step 3: the yuan weakens by 1 percent
e_new = 6.91 * 1.01
dollars_new = to_dollars(95.1, e_new)
# China's relative price level falls with e
ppp_new = at_common_prices(dollars_new, ppp / e_new)
print(f"1% weaker yuan: GDP in dollars {dollars_new / china_dollars - 1:+.2%}, "
      f"at common prices {ppp_new / china_ppp - 1:+.2%}")

PPP factor: 4.726 yuan per dollar; 95.1 / PPP = $20.12 trillion (= 20.12)
Log gap at the exchange rate -0.4033 - log relative price level -0.3798 = -0.0235;  log gap at common prices -0.0235
1% weaker yuan: GDP in dollars -0.99%, at common prices +0.00%


The log gap at common prices is close to zero, so China and the United States had almost the same GDP. A weaker yuan makes China’s GDP look about 1 percent smaller in dollars, while the comparison at common prices does not move at all.

We first split GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports, and follow the shares of the four parts over time.

Fig. 1: Composition of U.S. GDP

The file has one row per year and one column per share of GDP, in percent.

The World Bank’s investment share is about 4 points higher and its government share about 4 points lower: the same spending sits in a different box. Consumption and net exports agree. Before you compare countries, check that the numbers use the same definitions.
The textbook stacks the shares on top of each other: net exports at the bottom, then consumption, investment, and government purchases up to 100 percent. Because net exports are negative in recent decades, consumption starts below zero in those years. First the data: composition_data picks the BEA’s U.S. shares, or the World Bank’s shares of any other country, made long in the same way.

# The World Bank's column names, and the readable names we give them
WB_NAMES = {
    "consumption": "Consumption",
    "investment": "Investment",
    "government": "Government purchases",
    "net_exports": "Net exports",
}
BEA = "United States (BEA)"            # the menu entry for the BEA's U.S. data


def composition_data(country=BEA):
    """The expenditure shares of one country, as a long table (Fig. 1).

    The four shares of equation (2): C, I, G and NX as a percent of GDP, one row per
    component and year.

    Arguments
        country : BEA for the BEA's U.S. data, or a country of the World Bank file
    Returns
        a table with the columns year, share and component
    """
    # the BEA's U.S. data: the long table built above
    if country == BEA:
        return long
    # another country: its World Bank shares, made long in the same way
    data = world[world.country == country].melt(
        id_vars="year",
        value_vars=list(WB_NAMES),
        value_name="share",
    )
    data["component"] = data.variable.map(WB_NAMES)
    return data



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, the composition of GDP
# the order of the stack, from the bottom up, and a fixed color for each component
ORDER = ["Net exports", "Consumption", "Investment", "Government purchases"]
COLORS_GDP = {
    "Net exports": "#e0a33b",
    "Consumption": "#5aa0d8",
    "Investment": GREEN,
    "Government purchases": TEAL,
}
LABELS = {"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "component": "Component"}


def composition_chart(style="stacked areas", country=BEA):
    """The expenditure shares of GDP, stacked or as separate lines.

    Draws Fig. 1 (inspired by Fig. 2.1 in Jones): the BEA's U.S. data, or the World
    Bank's data for any other country.

    Arguments
        style   : "stacked areas" or "separate lines"
        country : BEA for the BEA's U.S. data, or a country of the World Bank file
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (composition_data) and the title
    data = composition_data(country)
    title = (
        "Since 1950: consumption ≈ 64%, government ≈ 20%, "
        "investment ≈ 17% of U.S. GDP"
    )
    if country != BEA:
        title = f"Composition of GDP in {country} (World Bank definitions)"

    # Step 2: `px.area` stacks the areas in the order of `category_orders`, and
    # `px.line` draws one line per component instead
    if style == "stacked areas":
        draw = px.area
    else:
        draw = px.line
    fig = draw(
        data,
        x="year",
        y="share",
        color="component",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS_GDP,         # a fixed color for each component
        category_orders={"component": ORDER},
        labels=LABELS,
        title=title,
    )
    # a dashed line at zero: below it, net exports are negative
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)

    # Step 3: the axes grow in steps of 10 points for countries with unusual shares.
    # `data.groupby("year").share.sum()` adds up the four shares within each year
    # (the top of the stack), and `max(a, b)` is the larger of two numbers
    top = max(data.groupby("year").share.sum().max(), data.share.max())
    # `np.floor` and `np.ceil` round down and up, so `10 * np.ceil(x / 10)` is the
    # next multiple of 10 above x
    low = min(-10, 10 * np.floor(data.share.min() / 10))
    high = max(100, 10 * np.ceil(top / 10))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.year.min(), 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high])
    return fig



# Fig. 1 with buttons and a menu. `interact` draws the figure again whenever you
# change a widget. `ToggleButtons` is a row of buttons, one per option, and a
# `Dropdown` is a menu from which you choose one entry. The `;` at the end only
# hides an extra line of text.
interact(
    composition_chart,
    style=ToggleButtons(options=["stacked areas", "separate lines"],
                        description="chart", style=WIDE),
    country=Dropdown(options=[BEA] + sorted(world.country.unique()), value=BEA,
                     description="country"),
);

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, national accounts (NIPA Table 1.1.5), via FRED: GDP (GDPA), personal consumption expenditures (PCECA), gross private domestic investment (GPDIA), government consumption expenditures and gross investment (GCEA) and net exports (A019RC1A027NBEA); other countries: World Bank, World Development Indicators, shares of GDP: household consumption (NE.CON.PRVT.ZS), gross capital formation (NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS), government consumption (NE.CON.GOVT.ZS) and external balance on goods and services (NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS). Country groups: World Bank country classifications. Prepared files: data/ch02/fig2-1.csv, data/ch02/expenditure_world.csv and data/ch02/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 2.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
The website’s menu lists the G20 and OECD members; in Colab you can choose any of the countries.
What to notice.

From 1950 on, the shares hardly move: consumption averages about 64 percent, government purchases about 20 percent and investment about 17 percent (see the numbers below).
World War II stands out. In 1943–1944 government purchases took 48 percent of GDP, and consumption and investment were squeezed.
During the Great Depression, investment collapsed to 3 percent of GDP in 1932, while the consumption share peaked at 82 percent.
Net exports were zero or slightly positive for most years before 1976, and negative in every year since. The deficit was deepest in 2006. Hover over the lines to read the values, and click a component in the legend to hide it.
Choose China: in 2024 consumption was only 40 percent of GDP and investment also 40 percent, about twice the U.S. investment share. Choose Ireland: in 2025 its net exports were 40 percent of GDP, because multinational firms book large exports there.


# Averages and extremes of the four shares.
# `by_year.loc[1950:]` keeps the rows from 1950 on
by_year = shares.set_index("year")

# `.idxmin()` that of the smallest
print(
    f"Government purchases peaked at {by_year.government_share.max():.1f}% "
    f"in {by_year.government_share.idxmax()}"
)
print(

    f"in {by_year.investment_share.idxmin()}"
)
print(
    f"Deepest trade deficit: {by_year.net_exports_share.min():.1f}% "
    f"in {by_year.net_exports_share.idxmin()}"
)
# the latest year with positive net exports
print(
    "Last year with a trade surplus: "
    f"{by_year[by_year.net_exports_share > 0].index.max()}"
)

# The lines of Table 2.1: each column of nipa and its label in the table
EXPENDITURE = {
    "gdp": "Gross domestic product",

    "exports": "   Exports",
    "imports": "   Imports",

The function below builds the table for any year. Population is in thousands, so GDP per person in dollars is billions × 1,000,000 / population.

def expenditure_table(year):
    """Table 2.1: the expenditure approach to U.S. GDP in one year.

    Each line in trillions of dollars, as a share of GDP (equation 2), and per person.

    Arguments
        year : the year of the table, e.g. 2022
    Returns
        a table with one row per line of EXPENDITURE, rounded to one decimal
    """
    # Step 1: the lines of that year, in billions of dollars
    row = nipa.loc[year, list(EXPENDITURE)]
    # Step 2: three columns; population is in thousands
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Trillions of dollars": row / 1000,
            "Share of GDP (percent)": share(row, row["gdp"]),
            "Per person (dollars)": row * 1_000_000 / nipa.loc[year, "population"],
        }
    )
    # Step 3: the readable labels as row labels
    table.index = list(EXPENDITURE.values())
    return table.round(1)

def shares_data(country=BEA):
    """The expenditure shares of one country since 1970 (Fig. 2).

    The shares of equation (2), C, I, G and NX as a percent of GDP, one row per year.

    Arguments
        country : BEA for the BEA's U.S. data, or a country of the World Bank file
    Returns
        data        : one row per year, one column per component
        first, last : the first and the last row of data
    """
    # Step 1: the BEA's U.S. data, or the World Bank's data from 1970 on;
    # `.rename(columns=WB_NAMES)` gives the World Bank's columns our names
    data = recent
    if country != BEA:
        data = world[(world.country == country) & (world.year >= 1970)].rename(
            columns=WB_NAMES
        )
    # Step 2: `data.iloc[0]` is the first row and `data.iloc[-1]` the last
    first, last = data.iloc[0], data.iloc[-1]
    return data, first, last

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, the two vertical axes
def shares_layout(fig, data):
    """The two vertical axes of Fig. 2, the legend and the years.

    The left axis (I, G, NX) and the right axis (consumption) widen in steps of 10
    points when a country's shares do not fit.

    Arguments
        fig  : the figure of Fig. 2
        data : the shares drawn (shares_data)
    """
    # Step 1: the ranges, in steps of 10 points (`np.floor` and `np.ceil`, Fig. 1)
    others = data[["Government purchases", "Investment", "Net exports"]]
    low = min(-6, 10 * np.floor(others.min().min() / 10))
    high = max(46, 10 * np.ceil(others.max().max() / 10) + 20)
    c_low = min(36, 10 * np.floor(data.Consumption.min() / 10) - 30)
    c_high = max(70, 10 * np.ceil(data.Consumption.max() / 10))
    # Step 2: `a if condition else b` picks a when the condition is true: the
    # textbook's ticks for the U.S. ranges, Plotly's own otherwise.
    # `overlaying="y"` puts the second axis on top of the first one, and
    # `side="right"` puts its labels on the right; `fig.update_layout` sets them all
    fig.update_layout(
        yaxis=dict(
            range=[low, high],
            tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25] if high == 46 else None,
        ),
        yaxis2=dict(
            title="Consumption (percent of GDP)",
            overlaying="y",
            side="right",
            range=[c_low, c_high],
            tickvals=[60, 64, 68] if c_low == 36 else None,
            showgrid=False,
        ),
        legend=dict(x=1.1),            # the legend clear of the right axis
        xaxis=dict(range=[1969, 2026]),
    )

def shares_chart(country=BEA):
    """The expenditure shares since 1970, with consumption on the right axis.

    Draws Fig. 2 (inspired by Fig. 2.2 in Jones): the BEA's U.S. data, or the World
    Bank's data for any other country.

    Arguments
        country : BEA for the BEA's U.S. data, or a country of the World Bank file
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (shares_data); did the consumption share rise or fall?
    data, first, last = shares_data(country)
    verb = "rose" if last.Consumption > first.Consumption else "fell"

    # Step 2: `px.line` with a list of columns as `y` draws one line per column
    fig = px.line(

        y=["Government purchases", "Investment", "Net exports"],
        color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, GREEN, "#e0a33b"],
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "value": "Share of GDP (percent)",
            "variable": "Component",
        },
        title=(
            f"{country}: consumption {verb} from {first.Consumption:.0f}% "
            f"to {last.Consumption:.0f}% of GDP, {first.year:.0f}–{last.year:.0f}"
        ),
    )
    # Step 3: `fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(...))` adds one more line, consumption, and
    # `yaxis="y2"` attaches it to a second vertical axis
    fig.add_trace(

            x=data.year,

        )
    )
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    # Step 4: the two vertical axes (shares_layout)

The consumption share rose from 60.3 percent in 1970 to 67.6 percent in 2025, and since 2010 it has stayed between about 66.6 and 68.6 percent. The government share fell from 23.5 to 17.4 percent, and net exports went from a small surplus to a deficit of 3.0 percent. Because the four shares always add up to 100, the four changes must add up to zero: a rise in one share is always matched by falls in others. The chart below shows the changes directly.
share_changes subtracts the base year’s shares from every later year, and computes the four changes to 2025 that the title reports.

def share_changes(base_year=1970):
    """The change in each expenditure share since a base year (Fig. 2, changes).

    change = share in year t - share in base_year, in percentage points. The four
    changes add up to zero, because the four shares always add up to 100.

    Arguments
        base_year : the year the changes are measured from
    Returns
        long_changes : one row per component and year, with its change since base_year
        change_2025  : the change of each share from base_year to 2025
    """
    # Step 1: `wide.loc[base_year:] - wide.loc[base_year]` subtracts one row from
    # every row, column by column. `.reset_index()` turns the year labels back into
    # an ordinary column, which `melt` and Plotly need
    changes = (wide.loc[base_year:] - wide.loc[base_year]).reset_index()
    # Step 2: from wide to long, one row per component and year
    long_changes = changes.melt(
        id_vars="year",
        var_name="component",
        value_name="change",
    )
    # Step 3: the four changes from base_year to 2025, for the title
    change_2025 = wide.loc[2025] - wide.loc[base_year]
    return long_changes, change_2025

2.4 Who earns GDP: labor’s share
The same GDP is also income. Here we ask how much of it goes to workers, and whether that share has really stayed constant.

Fig. 3: Labor’s share of GDP
Goal. Check one of the classic “stylized facts” of macroeconomics: that labor earns about two-thirds of GDP, year after year.
The income approach splits GDP into the income earned by workers (compensation: wages, salaries and benefits) and the income earned by the owners of capital. Two parts need care. Taxes on production (such as sales taxes) are income of neither, so they are left out. And the income of the self-employed (proprietors’ income) mixes both, so it is split between labor and capital in the same proportion as in the rest of the economy. The result is
\[\text{labor share} = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - \text{taxes on production} - \text{proprietors' income}}\]
where GDI is gross domestic income, the income-side measure of GDP.

The textbook points to a downward trend since about 1970. Our chart adds a straight trend line fitted to the data: pick the year where the line starts, and see how steep the decline is. You can also add other countries from the Penn World Table (including the United States, to compare the two measures).
labor_trend fits that line: it keeps the years from the starting year on, and returns the slope and the intercept of the best straight line through them.

def labor_trend(start=1970):
    """The straight trend line through the U.S. labor share since start (Fig. 3).

    Least squares:  labor share = a + b * year, fitted to the years from start on.

    Arguments
        start : the first year of the trend
    Returns
        after     : the rows of the labor share from start on
        slope     : b, the change of the share per year (as a fraction)
        intercept : a
    """
    after = labor[labor.year >= start]
    # `np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` fits the best straight line y = a + b x through the
    # points (by least squares), and returns the slope b first, the intercept a second
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(after.year, after.labor_share, 1)
    return after, slope, intercept

    """
    # `for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):` hands over each country's name
    # and rows in turn, so each gets its own line
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, labor's share of GDP
def labor_share_chart(start=1970, chosen=()):
    """Labor's share of GDP, 1950-2025, with a trend line from start.

    Draws Fig. 3 (inspired by Fig. 2.3 in Jones); other countries from the Penn World
    Table.

    Arguments
        start  : the first year of the trend line
        chosen : the countries to add, from the Penn World Table
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the trend (labor_trend)
    after, slope, intercept = labor_trend(start)

    # Step 2: the U.S. labor share, a blue line with the area below it shaded
    fig = px.line(
        labor,
        x="year",
        y="labor_share",
        labels={"year": "Year", "labor_share": "Labor share of GDP"},
    )
    fig.update_traces(
        line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
        fill="tozeroy",
        fillcolor="rgba(22, 82, 140, 0.12)",
        name="Labor share (textbook)",
        showlegend=True,
    )
    # the trend line a + b * year, green and dashed
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=after.year,
            y=intercept + slope * after.year,
            name=f"Trend since {start}",
            line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash"),
        )
    )
    # Step 3: the chosen countries; `.isin(chosen)` keeps their rows
    extra = pwt[pwt.country.isin(chosen)]
    add_pwt_lines(fig, extra)

    # Step 4: the vertical axis widens in steps of 0.05 until every value fits.
    # `pd.concat([a, b])` stacks two columns into one: every value on the chart
    shown = pd.concat([labor.labor_share, extra.labor_share])
    low = 0.55 if shown.min() >= 0.55 else 0.05 * np.floor(shown.min() / 0.05)
    high = 0.75 if shown.max() <= 0.75 else 0.05 * np.ceil(shown.max() / 0.05)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1950, 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(
        range=[low, high],
        tickvals=[0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75] if low == 0.55 else None,  # no corner label
    )
    # Step 5: the title. The slope is per year, as a fraction: x 100 for
    # percentage points, x 10 for a decade
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"Labor share: trend since {start} is {1000 * slope:+.1f} "
            "percentage points per decade"
        )
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

On average, labor earned 0.65 of income from 1950 to 2025, close to the two-thirds of the stylized fact. Until 2021 the share stayed between 0.60 and 0.70.
But the share is not constant. It peaked at 0.69 in 1970 and has drifted down since: from 1970 the trend falls by about 1.3 percentage points per decade. Move the starting year to 1990 or 2000 and the decline looks even steeper.
Since 2022 the share has been below 0.60 for the first time in these data (0.586 in 2025). Our values for the last years in the textbook are slightly lower than the book’s, because of the 2023 data revision. Part of the decline reflects how the national accounts treat software and R&D, which is still debated by researchers.
Add other countries. The labor share fell in Germany too (0.69 in 1970, 0.64 in 2023), but it rose in Japan (0.51 to 0.59) and South Korea (0.42 to 0.55). Two-thirds is a rough rule for rich countries, not a law of nature. Oil exporters such as Qatar (0.18) and Kuwait (0.25) have very low shares, because most of their income is oil revenue. Some values are doubtful: the Penn World Table puts Venezuela at exactly 0.0844 in every year from 2019 to 2023, a value carried forward, not measured. Look at the extremes before you trust a cross-country file.


Key numbers: Table 2.2, the income approach

# Table 2.2 for 2022. The lines of the income approach: each column of nipa and
# its label in the table
INCOME = {
    "gdp": "Gross domestic product",
    "compensation": "Compensation of employees",
    "wages": "   Wages and salaries",
    "benefits": "   Benefits",
    "taxes_less_subsidies": "Taxes less subsidies on businesses",
    "net_operating_surplus": "Net operating surplus of businesses",
    "depreciation": "Depreciation of fixed capital",
}


def income_table(year):
    """Table 2.2: the income approach to U.S. GDP in one year.

    Each line in trillions of dollars, as a share of GDP, and per person.

    Arguments
        year : the year of the table, e.g. 2022
    Returns
        a table with one row per line of INCOME, rounded to one decimal
    """
    # Step 1: the lines of that year, in billions of dollars
    row = nipa.loc[year, list(INCOME)]
    # Step 2: three columns, as in Table 2.1; population is in thousands
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Trillions of dollars": row / 1000,
            "Share of GDP (percent)": share(row, row["gdp"]),
            "Per person (dollars)": row * 1_000_000 / nipa.loc[year, "population"],
        }
    )
    table.index = list(INCOME.values())
    return table.round(1)


# the table for 2022, with the textbook's shares in a last column

income_2022["Textbook share"] = [100.0, 53.2, 43.9, 9.3, 6.5, 23.5, 16.8]

# @title Drawing code: Figs. 4 and 5, the recession bands
def shade_recessions(fig):
    """Add a gray band for every NBER recession, as FRED does.

    Used by Figs. 4 and 5 (inspired by Figs. 2.4 and 2.5 in Jones).

    Arguments
        fig : a figure with dates on the horizontal axis
    Returns
        the same figure, with the bands
    """
    # `range(len(recessions))` gives the row numbers 0, 1, 2, ..., so the `for`
    # loop visits every recession once
    for i in range(len(recessions)):
        # `fig.add_vrect` draws a vertical band between two dates
        fig.add_vrect(
            x0=recessions.start[i],
            x1=recessions.end[i],
            fillcolor=GRAY,
            opacity=0.25,
            line_width=0,
        )
    return fig


The World Bank publishes the GDP deflator of about 200 countries, once a year. Each country publishes its index with its own base year, so deflator_world.csv has been rebased: every country’s deflator is divided by its 2012 value and multiplied by 100, like the U.S. series. The file also holds the yearly inflation rate of each deflator, which Fig. 5 uses. We place each yearly value in the middle of its year.

The chart draws the U.S. quarterly series and, if you choose them, other countries’ yearly series. When a chosen country’s prices were far lower or higher, the axis widens tenfold until every value fits.
deflator_data picks the yearly deflators of the chosen countries, and computes how many times the U.S. price level rose since 1947, the number in the title.

def deflator_data(chosen=()):
    """The chosen countries' deflators, and the rise of the U.S. price level (Fig. 4).

    The U.S. price level rose by the factor P(latest quarter) / P(1947 Q1), with P the
    GDP deflator of equation (4).

    Arguments
        chosen : the countries to add, e.g. ("Japan", "Turkey")
    Returns
        extra  : the rows of deflators for those countries, where a deflator exists
        factor : how many times the U.S. price level rose since 1947
    """
    # Step 1: the chosen countries' rows; `.dropna(subset=[...])` drops the rows
    # with no value in that column
    extra = deflators[deflators.country.isin(chosen)].dropna(
        subset=["deflator_2012_100"]
    )
    # Step 2: the latest U.S. value over the first one
    us_level = deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100
    factor = us_level.iloc[-1] / us_level.iloc[0]
    return extra, factor



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, the vertical axis
def deflator_axis(fig, scale, extra):
    """The vertical axis of Fig. 4, wide enough for every value on the chart.

    It starts at 9 to 150 (linear) or 9 to 170 (ratio scale), and widens tenfold
    at a time until every value fits.

    Arguments
        fig   : the figure of Fig. 4
        scale : "linear" or "ratio"
        extra : the rows of the chosen countries (deflator_data)
    """
    # Step 1: every value on the chart, U.S. and chosen countries
    shown = pd.concat([deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100, extra.deflator_2012_100])
    low, high = 9, (170 if scale == "ratio" else 150)
    # Step 2: a `while` loop repeats its indented lines as long as its condition is
    # true: the bottom shrinks tenfold until the smallest value fits above it, and
    # the top grows tenfold until the largest value fits below it
    while low > shown.min():
        low = low / 10
    while high < shown.max():
        high = high * 10
    # Step 3: on a log axis Plotly wants the limits as powers of ten (`np.log10`)
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(
            tickvals=[10, 20, 40, 80, 160] if (low, high) == (9, 170) else None,
            range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)],
        )
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, the level of the GDP deflator
def deflator_chart(scale="linear", chosen=()):
    """The GDP deflator (2012 = 100): U.S. quarterly since 1947, other countries yearly.

    Draws Fig. 4 (inspired by Fig. 2.4 in Jones), with the recession bands.

    Arguments
        scale  : "linear" or "ratio", the vertical scale
        chosen : the countries to add, from the World Bank file
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (deflator_data)
    extra, factor = deflator_data(chosen)

    # Step 2: the U.S. line; `log_y=True` draws a ratio scale
    fig = px.line(
        deflator,
        x="date",
        y="gdp_deflator_2012_100",
        log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
        labels={
            "date": "Quarter",
            "gdp_deflator_2012_100": "GDP deflator (index, 2012 = 100)",
        },
    )
    fig.update_traces(
        line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
        name="United States (quarterly)",
        showlegend=True,
    )
    # Step 3: one yearly line per chosen country, in its color
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=part.date,
                y=part.deflator_2012_100,
                name=name,
                line=dict(color=COLORS[name]),
            )
        )
    # Step 4: the recession bands, the axis and the title
    shade_recessions(fig)
    deflator_axis(fig, scale, extra)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"The U.S. price level rose about {factor:.0f}-fold from 1947 to 2026"
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

Prices rose slowly until the mid-1960s, much faster in the 1970s and early 1980s, and then at a steadier pace, until the jump of 2021–2022.
On the linear scale the line rises about as steeply in the 2000s as in the 1970s, because the same percentage increase adds more index points when prices are already high. Switch to the ratio scale: there the slope is the percentage rate of change, and the 1970s clearly stand out.
Add Japan: its deflator fell from 119 in 1994 to 100 in 2013, two decades of deflation. Add Turkey on the ratio scale: its price level in 2025 was more than 30,000 times its 1990 level.


# Average annual inflation in four periods. With dates as row labels,
# `level["1965"]` picks the four quarters of 1965, and `.mean()` averages them
level = deflator.set_index("date").gdp_deflator_2012_100
for start, end in [(1947, 1965), (1965, 1983), (1983, 2019), (2019, 2025)]:
    # the average annual growth rate: (end / start)^(1 / years) - 1
    yearly = (
        level[str(end)].mean() / level[str(start)].mean()
    ) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1
    print(f"{start}-{end}: prices rose {yearly:.1%} a year on average")

1983-2019: prices rose 2.2% a year on average

Key numbers: nominal GDP = price level × real GDP
The textbook asks how much more real GDP the United States produced in 2022 than in 1995. Real GDP in our national accounts file is measured in chained 2017 dollars.

    f"${nipa.loc[2022, 'gdp'] / 1000:.1f} trillion (2022)"

print(f"Real GDP grew by a factor of    {real_ratio:.2f}")

Taking growth rates of equation (4) gives a handy approximation (equation 7): the growth of nominal GDP is about the growth of the price level plus the growth of real GDP.

# Growth rates in percent: nominal GDP, real GDP and the price level.

# the price level, nominal GDP / real GDP, equation (4)

# equation (7): nominal growth is about price growth plus real growth
growth["prices + real"] = growth.prices + growth.real_gdp

Fig. 5: The annual inflation rate using the GDP deflator
Goal. Turn the price level into an inflation rate, the percentage change of the price level.
FRED’s “Percent Change from Year Ago” compares each quarter with the same quarter one year earlier:
\[\pi_t = 100 \times \left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-4}} - 1\right)\]
where \(P_t\) is the GDP deflator in quarter \(t\). A second common measure compares each quarter with the quarter before and turns the change into an annual rate: \(100 \times \left[(P_t/P_{t-1})^4 - 1\right]\).

# the change from the quarter before, turned into an annual rate
quarterly = 100 * ((level / level.shift(1)) ** 4 - 1)

    {"change from a year ago": year_ago, "quarterly change, annual rate": quarterly}
