text:
3.2 Model in code
Now we turn the tools of the Model overview into Python. The section has three parts: the setup (folded, because it is the same in every chapter), the tools as functions, and numerical checks of the Key results. Run its cells once, in order. Every later section of the notebook reuses them.

3.2.1 Setup
Run the setup cells once, before anything else. They load the Python libraries, give every chart the same look, store the address of the chapter’s data and define two helpers that only the book website needs. You can use the notebook without reading them; open the box if you are curious.






NoteShow the setup code





The first cell loads the libraries and sets the look of the charts. Its comments explain each step.

# @title Setup: libraries, chart colors and the data location
# Text after a "#" is a comment: Python ignores it, it is there for human readers.

# Step 1: load the libraries. `import` loads a library, a toolbox written by
# other people, and `as np` gives it a short nickname, so the code stays short.
import numpy as np                              # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                             # data tables
import plotly.express as px                     # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go               # charts built piece by piece
import plotly.io as pio                         # settings shared by every chart
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots       # several panels in one figure
# sliders, buttons and menus for the interactive figures
from ipywidgets import interact, FloatSlider, IntRangeSlider, ToggleButtons, Dropdown, SelectMultiple

# Step 2: one light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
# the same chart size in Colab and on the website
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)
# the colors of the lines, in order
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47", "#e0a33b", "#b04a5a"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full slider labels

# Step 3, Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets.
# `try` runs the indented lines; if the import fails (we are not in Colab),
# `except` skips them.
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# Step 4: the data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch03/"

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider or menu. The next two helpers build those versions. Run them and move on.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. population_path
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "n"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


# @title Helper for the website versions with many countries (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_menu(fig, shown, regions, label="Textbook countries"):
    """Draw the countries in `shown` and put every other country one click away in the legend.

    With more than 40 countries, a menu above the plot chooses the region whose countries the legend lists.
    Traces that are not countries stay as they are.

    Arguments
        fig     : a Plotly figure with one trace per country
        shown   : the countries drawn at the start
        regions : maps each country to its region
        label   : the name of the first menu entry
    Returns
        the same figure, with the visibility set and, for many countries, the region menu
    """
    # Step 1: the menu entries, the textbook countries and then one entry per region
    # the traces that are countries, and each of their regions once, A to Z
    countries = [trace.name for trace in fig.data if trace.name in regions]
    groups = [label] + sorted(set(regions[name] for name in countries))
    if len(countries) <= 40:
        groups = [None]                     # a short legend lists every country at once
    # Step 2: for each entry, which traces are drawn, in the legend only, or hidden
    buttons = []
    for group in groups:
        visible = []
        for trace in fig.data:
            if trace.name in shown:
                visible.append(True)                    # a textbook country: drawn
            elif trace.name not in regions:
                # not a country: as it was
                visible.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)
            elif group is None or regions[trace.name] == group:
                visible.append("legendonly")            # in this region: a click away
            else:
                visible.append(False)                   # another region: hidden
        buttons.append(dict(label=group, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    # Step 3: start with the first entry, and add the menu when there is more than one
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    if len(groups) > 1:
        menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
        fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig






3.2.2 The model as functions
Three Key results do most of the work in this chapter: the constant growth rule, equation (2), the exact doubling time, equation (4), and the average annual growth rate, equation (6). We write each one as a Python function: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives back a result. The later sections use all three.

# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses.
# The text in triple quotes describes the function.
def constant_growth(y0, g, t):
    """Value after t years of constant growth.

    Equation (2):  y_t = y0 (1 + g)^t

    Arguments
        y0 : the starting value, y_0
        g  : the constant growth rate, g-bar (0.02 for 2 percent)
        t  : the number of years (a number or an array of years)
    Returns
        the value after t years, y_t
    """
    # `return` gives back the result; `**` means "to the power of"
    return y0 * (1 + g) ** t


def growth_rate(y0, yt, t):
    """Average annual growth rate between two values t years apart.

    Equation (6):  g = (y_t / y_0)^(1/t) - 1

    Arguments
        y0, yt : the values at the start and t years later, y_0 and y_t
        t      : the number of years between them
    Returns
        the average annual growth rate, g (0.02 for 2 percent)
    """
    # equation (2) solved for g
    return (yt / y0) ** (1 / t) - 1


def doubling_time(g):
    """Exact number of years it takes a value to double.

    Equation (4):  t = ln 2 / ln(1 + g)

    Arguments
        g : the constant growth rate, g-bar
    Returns
        the doubling time in years
    """
    # `np.log` is the natural logarithm, ln
    return np.log(2) / np.log(1 + g)



3.2.3 Checking the key results
The formulas came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, one Key result at a time.
Check 1: compounding. We follow the population of Fig. 3, 6 billion people growing at 2 percent, and compare compound growth, equation (2), with simple growth, which adds the same 2 percent of the starting value every year.

# Compound and simple growth of 6 billion people at 2%, after 1, 35, 70 and 100 years
print("Years   compound growth, eq. (2)   simple growth")
# A `for` loop runs its indented lines once for each value after `in`
for t in (1, 35, 70, 100):
    compound = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, t)       # equation (2)
    simple = 6.0 * (1 + 0.02 * t)                  # 2% of the start, added t times
    # An f-string, f"... {value:.2f}", puts a value into the text; ":.2f" means
    # "two decimals", and ":8.2f" also pads the number to 8 characters
    print(f"{t:5d}   {compound:15.2f} billion   {simple:8.2f} billion")

Years   compound growth, eq. (2)   simple growth
    1              6.12 billion       6.12 billion
   35             12.00 billion      10.20 billion
   70             24.00 billion      14.40 billion
  100             43.47 billion      18.00 billion


After 35 years compound growth has doubled the population, and after 70 years quadrupled it. Simple growth gets only to 1.7 and 2.4 times the start.
Check 2: a straight line in logs. Equation (3) says that the log of a constantly growing variable rises by the same amount, \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\), every year.

# Step 1: the population in years 0 to 5. `np.arange(0, 6)` gives 0, 1, ..., 5,
# and `constant_growth` works on all of them at once
years = np.arange(0, 6)
L = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, years)
# Step 2: the yearly change in ln L. `np.diff` subtracts each value from the
# next one, and `.round(4)` keeps four decimals
print("Population (billions):    ", L.round(4))
print("Yearly change in ln L:    ", np.diff(np.log(L)).round(5))
# Step 3: the slope that equation (3) predicts
print(f"Slope of eq. (3), ln(1.02): {np.log(1.02):.5f}   (close to g = 0.02)")

Population (billions):     [6.     6.12   6.2424 6.3672 6.4946 6.6245]
Yearly change in ln L:     [0.0198 0.0198 0.0198 0.0198 0.0198]
Slope of eq. (3), ln(1.02): 0.01980   (close to g = 0.02)


Check 3: the Rule of 70. We compare the exact doubling time, equation (4), with the approximations of equation (5), and confirm that the population really is twice as large after one exact doubling time.

# Step 1: the doubling time at four growth rates, exact and approximate
print("Growth rate   exact, eq. (4)   69.3 / g   Rule of 70, eq. (5)")
for g in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.07):
    G = 100 * g                                     # the growth rate in percent
    print(f"{G:9.0f}%   {doubling_time(g):14.2f}   {69.3 / G:8.2f}   {70 / G:19.2f}")
# Step 2: 6 billion at 2% for one exact doubling time should give 12 billion
print(f"At 2%, after {doubling_time(0.02):.2f} years: {constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, doubling_time(0.02)):.3f} billion")

Growth rate   exact, eq. (4)   69.3 / g   Rule of 70, eq. (5)
        1%            69.66      69.30                 70.00
        2%            35.00      34.65                 35.00
        3%            23.45      23.10                 23.33
        7%            10.24       9.90                 10.00
At 2%, after 35.00 years: 12.000 billion


The Rule of 70 is within half a year of the exact answer at these growth rates. In relative terms its error grows once growth rates go well beyond a few percent: at 7 percent it is off by more than 2 percent.
Check 4: the average annual growth rate. Equation (6) must undo equation (2), the log version of step 4 must agree with it, and the geometric mean of step 5 must give the right answer where the plain average does not.

# Step 1: grow 6 billion at 2% for 100 years, then recover the 2% with equation (6)
end = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, 100)
print(f"6 billion at 2% for 100 years:          {end:.2f} billion")
print(f"Equation (6) gives back:                {growth_rate(6.0, end, 100):.4f}")
# Step 2: the log version, the slope of ln y turned back into a growth rate
print(f"Log version, exp(slope) - 1:            {np.exp((np.log(end) - np.log(6.0)) / 100) - 1:.4f}")
# Step 3: over one year the formula is a plain percentage change
print(f"One year, t = 1 (a percentage change):  {growth_rate(6.0, 6.3, 1):.4f}")
# Step 4: the geometric mean of +10% and -10% is below 0
print(f"Up 10% then down 10%, two years:        {growth_rate(1.0, 1.10 * 0.90, 2):+.4f}   (not 0)")
# Step 5: a 1% higher end point after 100 years barely moves the growth rate
higher = growth_rate(6.0, 1.01 * end, 100)
print(f"Final value 1% higher: the growth rate rises by {100 * (higher - 0.02):.4f} percentage points")

6 billion at 2% for 100 years:          43.47 billion
Equation (6) gives back:                0.0200
Log version, exp(slope) - 1:            0.0200
One year, t = 1 (a percentage change):  0.0500
Up 10% then down 10%, two years:        -0.0050   (not 0)
Final value 1% higher: the growth rate rises by 0.0101 percentage points


Check 5: the growth rules. We take the U.S. growth rates of Fig. 9, 1.9 percent for GDP per person and 1.4 percent for the population, and compare each rule with the exact growth over one year.

# Step 1: GDP per person and population, U.S. since 1870 (Fig. 9), and the values
# one year later
gy, gL = 0.019, 0.014
y0, L0 = 1.0, 1.0
y1, L1 = y0 * (1 + gy), L0 * (1 + gL)
# Step 2: each rule, equations (7) to (9), against the exact growth over the year
print(f"Product  y x L:    rule (7) {gy + gL:.5f}   exact {(y1 * L1) / (y0 * L0) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Ratio    y / L:    rule (8) {gy - gL:.5f}   exact {(y1 / L1) / (y0 / L0) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Power    y^(1/3):  rule (9) {gy / 3:.5f}   exact {y1 ** (1 / 3) / y0 ** (1 / 3) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Power    L^(-2):   rule (9) {-2 * gL:.5f}   exact {L1 ** -2 / L0 ** -2 - 1:.5f}")
# Step 3: in logs, ln(yL) = ln y + ln L, so the product rule holds exactly
change_logs = np.log(y1 * L1) - np.log(y0 * L0)
print(f"In logs the product rule is exact: {change_logs:.5f} = {np.log(1 + gy) + np.log(1 + gL):.5f}")

Product  y x L:    rule (7) 0.03300   exact 0.03327
Ratio    y / L:    rule (8) 0.00500   exact 0.00493
Power    y^(1/3):  rule (9) 0.00633   exact 0.00629
Power    L^(-2):   rule (9) -0.02800   exact -0.02742
In logs the product rule is exact: 0.03272 = 0.03272


Each rule misses the exact answer by less than a tenth of a percentage point (the cross term, here \(0.019 \times 0.014 \approx 0.0003\) for the product), and in logs the product rule holds exactly. The Your turn after Fig. 9 checks equation (10) in the same way.

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, a color for every country
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses.

    As far as the palette allows: when every color is taken, the country gets the one
    that its groups use least.

    Arguments
        names  : the countries to color, one at a time
        groups : the lists of countries shown together (the website's menu views)
        fixed  : {country: color} for the book's countries, or None
    Returns
        a dictionary {country: color}
    """
    # start from a copy of the fixed colors (or an empty dictionary)
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue                    # `continue` skips to the next country
        # Step 1: the list `used` collects the colors of the countries shown with it
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            for other in group:
                if name in group and other in colors:
                    used.append(colors[other])
        # Step 2: the palette colors not in `used`; best of all, one no country has yet
        free, unused = [], []
        for c in PALETTE:
            if c not in used:
                free.append(c)
                if c not in colors.values():
                    unused.append(c)
        # Step 3: no free color: the one `used` counts least often (`.count`),
        # searching from the end of the palette (`reversed`)
        least = PALETTE[-1]
        for c in reversed(PALETTE):
            if used.count(c) < used.count(least):
                least = c
        # the first of: an unused color, a free one, the least used one
        colors[name] = (unused + free + [least])[0]
    return colors

The title of the chart reports how many times GDP per person grew in one of the chosen countries: the United Kingdom when it is chosen, otherwise the first country in your list. long_run_growth picks the rows to draw and computes that growth factor.

def long_run_growth(start, countries):
    """The data of Fig. 1, and how many times GDP per person grew in one country.

    The growth factor:  y_last / y_first, GDP per person in the last year with an
    estimate over GDP per person in the first one

    Arguments
        start     : the first year to show
        countries : the countries to show
    Returns
        chosen : the rows of `everyone` for those countries, from `start` on
        name   : the country of the title: the U.K. when it is chosen, otherwise
                 the first country (None when there are no data)
        one    : the rows of that country
        factor : its growth factor, y_last / y_first
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen countries from the year `start` on. `&` means
    # "and", and `.isin(countries)` keeps the rows whose country is in the list
    chosen = everyone[(everyone.year >= start) & everyone.country.isin(countries)]
    if chosen.empty:
        return chosen, None, None, None          # no data: nothing to compare
    # Step 2: the country of the title. `a if condition else b` gives a when the
    # condition is true and b otherwise
    name = (
        "United Kingdom"
        if "United Kingdom" in set(chosen.country)
        else chosen.country.iloc[0]
    )
    # Step 3: its growth factor: the last estimate over the first one
    one = chosen[chosen.country == name]
    factor = one.gdp.iloc[-1] / one.gdp.iloc[0]
    return chosen, name, one, factor

The function short turns a long official name into the usual short one, so that titles stay on one line.

def short(name):
    """A short country name for titles.

    For example 'Bolivia (Plurinational State of)' -> 'Bolivia'.

    Arguments
        name : the country's name in the data
    Returns
        the short name
    """
    # `name.split(" (")[0]` cuts the text at " (" and keeps the first piece:
    # this drops '(...)' and ': Mainland'
    name = name.split(" (")[0].split(":")[0]
    # `SHORT_NAMES.get(name, name)` looks the name up in the dictionary, and
    # returns it unchanged when it is not there
    return SHORT_NAMES.get(name, name)




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, economic growth over the very long run
def very_long_run(start=1, scale="linear", countries=tuple(BOOK_SIX)):
    """GDP per person over the very long run, one line per country.

    Draws Fig. 1 (inspired by Fig. 3.1 in Jones): GDP per person in multiples of
    500 dollars, from the year `start` to 2022.

    Arguments
        start     : the first year
        scale     : "linear" or "ratio", the vertical scale
        countries : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data and the growth factor of the title (long_run_growth)
    chosen, name, one, factor = long_run_growth(start, countries)

    # Step 2: `px.line` draws one line per value of `color=`, here one per country
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y="gdp",
        color="country",
        markers=True,                    # `markers=True`: a dot for each estimate
        log_y=(scale == "ratio"),        # `log_y=True` gives a ratio scale (Fig. 4)
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,       # `color_discrete_map`: one color per country
        category_orders={"country": list(countries)},
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "gdp": "GDP per person (multiple of 500 dollars)",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )
    if chosen.empty:
        fig.update_layout(
            title=f"No data for the chosen countries since the year {start}"
        )
        return fig

    # Step 3: the title reports the growth factor of one country
    label = "U.K." if name == "United Kingdom" else short(name)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"{label} GDP per person in {one.year.iloc[-1]} was {factor:.0f} times "
            f"its level in the year {one.year.iloc[0]}"
        )
    )
    # Step 4: on the ratio scale, tick values that are easy to read
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500])
    return fig



# Fig. 1 with menus. `interact` calls very_long_run and draws the figure again

What to notice.

For almost all of history, GDP per person stayed between 1 and 3 times the subsistence level, in every country (only the United Kingdom had pulled a little higher by 1500–1700). Then, in the last two or three centuries, it shot up: the curve looks like a hockey stick.
Growth started at different times: first in the United Kingdom and the United States, later in Japan and Argentina, and only in the last few decades in China. Ghana’s rise is much smaller.
Choose a first year of 1820 or 1900 to stretch out the modern era, and switch to the ratio scale to separate the lines.
Add Italy and Egypt, two of the few countries with an estimate for the year 1. Italy, the center of the Roman Empire, was then richer than any of the textbook’s six countries, and Egypt was about as rich as China. Today Italy has about 62 percent of U.S. GDP per person and Egypt about 23 percent.

The function draws the U.S. alone from the official series, as the textbook does. As soon as you add a country, every line, the U.S. one included, comes from the Maddison Project, so that all countries are measured in the same way. The title then compares the richest and the poorest country you chose. income_data picks the rows and computes the number in the title.

def income_data(countries):
    """The data of Fig. 2, and the comparison its title reports.

    One country: its growth factor, y_last / y_first. Several countries: the income
    ratio of the richest to the poorest in their latest year, y_rich / y_poor.

    Arguments
        countries : the countries to show
    Returns
        chosen : their rows (the official series when the U.S. is alone)
        latest : the last row of each country
        factor : the growth factor or the income ratio (None when there are no data)
    """
    # Step 1: the U.S. alone uses the official series. `tuple(countries) ==
    # ("United States",)` checks whether it is the only country chosen, and
    # `.assign(country="United States")` adds a column with that name in every row
    if tuple(countries) == ("United States",):
        chosen = us.assign(country="United States")
    else:
        chosen = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    # Step 2: `.groupby("country").last()` keeps the last row of each country,
    # here its latest year
    latest = chosen.groupby("country").last()
    # Step 3: the number of the title
    if chosen.empty:
        factor = None                                    # no data
    elif len(latest) == 1:
        # one country: how many times its GDP per person grew
        factor = chosen.iloc[-1].gdppc / chosen.iloc[0].gdppc
    else:
        # several: the richest over the poorest, in their latest year
        factor = latest.gdppc.max() / latest.gdppc.min()
    return chosen, latest, factor

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, per capita GDP
def income_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """GDP per person (2022 dollars), one line per country.

    Draws Fig. 2 (inspired by Fig. 3.2 in Jones). The U.S. alone uses the official
    series to 2025; with other countries, every line comes from the Maddison Project.

    Arguments
        countries : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data and the number of the title (income_data)
    chosen, latest, factor = income_data(countries)

    # Step 2: one thick line per country, in its own color
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y="gdppc",
        color="country",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)

    # Step 3: the title: growth in one country, or the richest against the poorest
    if chosen.empty:
        fig.update_layout(title="Choose at least one country")
    elif len(latest) == 1:
        first, last = chosen.iloc[0], chosen.iloc[-1]
        label = "U.S." if first.country == "United States" else short(first.country)
        fig.update_layout(
            title=(
                f"{label} GDP per person grew about {factor:.0f}-fold "
                f"from {first.year} to {last.year}"
            )
        )
    else:
        # `.idxmax()` gives the label of the largest value: the richest country
        rich, poor = latest.gdppc.idxmax(), latest.gdppc.idxmin()
        fig.update_layout(
            title=(
                f"{latest.year.max()}: GDP per person {factor:.0f} "
                f"times higher in {short(rich)} than in {short(poor)}"
            )
        )
    return fig

title: 3. An Overview of Long-Run Economic Growth
text:
3.4 The mathematics of growth
Constant growth produces a curve that bends upward, which is hard to read. These figures show why, and how a ratio scale turns that curve into a straight line.

Fig. 3: Population over time
Goal. See what constant growth looks like when we plot it.
Suppose the world population starts at \(L_0 = 6\) billion and grows at a constant rate \(\bar{n} = 2\%\) a year. Each year the population is multiplied by \((1+\bar{n})\):
\[L_{t+1} = L_t\,(1+\bar{n})\]
This is equation (1) written for the population. Applying it year after year gives \(L_t = L_0(1+\bar{n})^t\) (equation 2). The cell below checks this with a loop: it multiplies by \(1.02\) one hundred times and compares the result with the formula.

# Equation (1) applied 100 times, against formula (2). `range(100)` gives the
# numbers 0, 1, ..., 99, so the loop runs exactly 100 times
L = 6.0
for year in range(100):
    L = L * (1 + 0.02)                     # equation (1), applied once per year
print(f"Year by year:  L_100 = {L:.2f} billion")
print(f"Formula (2):   L_100 = {constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, 100):.2f} billion")

Year by year:  L_100 = 43.47 billion
Formula (2):   L_100 = 43.47 billion


The function below draws the path of equation (2) for 100 years. It only needs constant_growth, so all of its code is drawing code.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, population over time
def population_path(L0=6.0, n=0.02):
    """The population path L_t = L0 (1 + n)^t over 100 years.

    Draws Fig. 3 (adapted from Fig. 3.3 in Jones), with equation (2).

    Arguments
        L0 : the starting population in billions, L_0
        n  : the constant growth rate, n-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the path, equation (2), in the years 0 to 100
    t = np.arange(0, 101)
    L = constant_growth(L0, n, t)

    # Step 2: `go.Figure()` starts an empty chart, and `add_trace` adds a curve to it
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Population", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4))
    )

    # Step 3: the title reports the population after 100 years; `L[-1]` is the
    # last value of the array
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"L0 = {L0:.0f} billion growing at {100 * n:.1f}% a year: "
            f"after 100 years, L = {L[-1]:.1f} billion"
        ),
        xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[0, 102], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100]),
        # `max(100, 1.05 * L[-1])` is the larger of the two numbers: the vertical
        # axis stays at 0 to 100 unless the curve would leave it
        yaxis=dict(
            title="Population L (billions)",
            range=[0, max(100, 1.05 * L[-1])],
        ),
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

At 2 percent a year, 6 billion people become 43.5 billion after a century, more than seven times as many. (This is only an illustration: demographers expect population growth to fall toward zero.)
The curve bends upward, just like U.S. GDP per person in Fig. 2. A constant growth rate adds a larger amount each year, because it applies to a larger base.
From this picture alone, it is hard to tell whether the growth rate is constant. Fig. 4 fixes that.

Fig. 4: Population over time, revisited
Goal. Learn to read a ratio scale, on which constant growth is a straight line.
At 2 percent a year, the population doubles about every 35 years (Rule of 70: \(70/2 = 35\)). It goes from 6 to 12, 24 and 48 billion. On a ratio scale, the vertical axis is labeled 6, 12, 24, 48: each step doubles the one before. Equal distances then mean equal percentage changes, so a constant growth rate draws a straight line.
The function below draws the same path on both scales, with a dot at every doubling time. It only needs constant_growth and doubling_time, so all of its code is drawing code.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, the paths and the dots in both panels
def add_two_scale_paths(fig, t, L, dots, L_dots):
    """The curves of Fig. 4: the path in each panel, and the dots at each doubling.

    Arguments
        fig       : the two-panel figure
        t, L      : the years and the population in each of them
        dots      : the years of each doubling
        L_dots    : the population in those years
    """
    # the path: blue in panel (a), green in panel (b)
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Standard scale", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4)),
        row=1,
        col=1,
    )
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Ratio scale", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4)),
        row=1,
        col=2,
    )
    # the black dots in both panels, with one entry in the legend
    for col in [1, 2]:
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=dots,
                y=L_dots,
                name="Each doubling",
                mode="markers",
                showlegend=(col == 1),
                marker=dict(color="black", size=10),
            ),
            row=1,
            col=col,
        )




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, population on a standard and a ratio scale
def population_two_scales(n=0.02):
    """The same population path on (a) a standard scale and (b) a ratio scale.

    Draws Fig. 4 (adapted from Fig. 3.4 in Jones): 6 billion people growing at rate n,
    equation (2), with a dot at every doubling time, equation (4).

    Arguments
        n : the constant growth rate, n-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the path, and its value at every doubling time T.
    # `np.linspace(0, 105, 200)` gives 200 evenly spaced years from 0 to 105, and
    # `np.arange(0, 106, T)` gives 0, T, 2T, ... up to 105
    T = doubling_time(n)
    t = np.linspace(0, 105, 200)
    dots = np.arange(0, 106, T)
    L, L_dots = constant_growth(6, n, t), constant_growth(6, n, dots)

    # Step 2: `make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, ...)` makes two panels side by side,
    # and `row=1, col=2` sends a trace to the second one (add_two_scale_paths)
    fig = make_subplots(
        rows=1,
        cols=2,
        subplot_titles=(
            "(a) Standard scale: the curve bends upward",
            "(b) Ratio scale: a straight line",
        ),
    )
    add_two_scale_paths(fig, t, L, dots, L_dots)

    # Step 3: the axes. No label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Year", range=[-3, 108], tickvals=[25, 50, 75, 100])
    # panel (a): fixed, with room for n = 2.5%
    fig.update_yaxes(
        title_text="Population L (billions)",
        range=[0, 85],
        row=1,
        col=1,
    )
    # panel (b): a ratio scale. On a log axis the range is given in powers of ten,
    # with `np.log10`
    fig.update_yaxes(
        type="log",
        range=[np.log10(4.5), np.log10(150)],
        tickvals=[6, 12, 24, 48, 96],
        row=1,
        col=2,
    )
    # Step 4: the title reports the doubling time and the Rule of 70
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"n = {100 * n:.1f}%: doubles every {T:.1f} years "
            f"(Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n):.1f})"
        )
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

In panel (a), the dots are equally spaced in time (one every 35 years), but the jumps between them get bigger. In panel (b), the dots are equally spaced in both directions, and the curve is a straight line.

Fig. 5: U.S. per capita GDP on a ratio scale
Goal. Use the ratio scale to read the growth rate of real data.
Here are the data of Fig. 2 again, now on a ratio scale, with a dashed line that grows at a constant rate. The line’s level is chosen to fit the data as closely as possible (by least squares, in logarithms). You can also choose another country; its data then come from the Maddison Project, and the vertical axis adapts.
fitted_line picks the data and computes the dashed line: the starting level that fits the data best, then growth at the rate \(g\) from there.

def fitted_line(g, country):
    """The data of Fig. 5, and the constant-growth line that fits them best.

    The line y_t = y_0 (1 + g)^t of equation (2), with the starting level y_0 chosen
    by least squares in logs: ln y_0 is the average of ln y_t - t ln(1 + g)

    Arguments
        g       : the growth rate of the line, g-bar
        country : the country (the U.S. uses the official series)
    Returns
        data : the country's rows, with GDP per person `gdppc` by year
        line : the value of the line in each year of the data
    """
    # Step 1: the official U.S. series, or the country's Maddison data
    data = us if country == "United States" else world[world.country == country]
    years = data.year - data.year.iloc[0]          # years since the first one
    # Step 2: the best-fitting starting level. `np.log(data.gdppc)` takes the log
    # of every value at once, and `.mean()` averages them. On a ratio scale a
    # constant growth line is a straight line in logs, which is why we fit it there
    level = (np.log(data.gdppc) - years * np.log(1 + g)).mean()
    # Step 3: the line, equation (2) from that level
    line = np.exp(level) * (1 + g) ** years
    return data, line



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, per capita GDP on a ratio scale
# tick values that double each time, for the ratio scales of Figs. 5 and 6
DOUBLINGS = [250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000, 256000]


def ratio_scale_chart(g=0.02, country="United States"):
    """GDP per person on a ratio scale, with a constant-growth line at rate g.

    Draws Fig. 5 (inspired by Fig. 3.5 in Jones).

    Arguments
        g       : the growth rate of the dashed line, g-bar
        country : the country
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data and the line (fitted_line)
    data, line = fitted_line(g, country)
    label = "U.S." if country == "United States" else short(country)

    # Step 2: the data in blue, on a ratio scale (`log_y=True`)
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="year",
        y="gdppc",
        log_y=True,
        labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)"},
    )
    fig.update_traces(
        line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
        name=f"{label} data",
        showlegend=True,
    )
    # Step 3: the dashed green line
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=data.year,
            y=line,
            name=f"Constant growth at {100 * g:.2f}%",
            line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash"),
        )
    )

    # Step 4: the vertical range: the textbook's for the U.S.; for another country,
    # from a little below the lowest value to a little above the highest one, in
    # powers of ten (`np.log10`), because the axis is a ratio scale
    low, high = 2500, 140000
    if country != "United States":
        low = min(data.gdppc.min(), line.min()) / 1.3
        high = max(data.gdppc.max(), line.max()) * 1.3
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=DOUBLINGS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])

    # Step 5: the title reports the growth rate of the line and its doubling time
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"{label}: dashed line at {100 * g:.2f}% a year, doubling every "
            f"{doubling_time(g):.0f} years"
        )
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

The data stay close to a straight line with a slope of about 2 percent a year for more than 150 years. This is one of the most remarkable facts in macroeconomics.
Look closely: before 1929 the data rise a little more slowly than the line, and from 1950 to 2005 a little faster. The Great Depression (early 1930s) and World War II (early 1940s) are the big wiggles.

South Korea’s line is steep from the 1960s on, Argentina’s flattens after 1975, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s falls for decades. The textbook applies the rule for computing growth rates, equation (6), to $4,200 in 1870 and $76,000 in 2022. We do the same with our data, and for two shorter periods.

text:
3.5 Growth across countries
Now we compare countries: their growth paths since 1870, and the link between how rich a country was and how fast it grew afterward.

Fig. 6: Per capita GDP since 1870
Goal. Compare the growth paths of several countries on a ratio scale.
The textbook plots one value per decade, to smooth out short-run ups and downs. We also have every available year, from a wider data file, so you can see what the smoothing hides. We add India, which the textbook discusses but does not draw, and you can add any other country of the Maddison Project (the world table of Fig. 2).

The title compares one country with the United States: Japan when it is chosen, otherwise the first country in your list. The helper versus_us finds the first and the last year in which both have data.

def versus_us(name):
    """The first and the last year in which a country and the U.S. both have data.

    In each, the country's GDP per person relative to the U.S.: y / y_US

    Arguments
        name : the country
    Returns
        first, share_first : the first such year, and the country's GDP per person
                             relative to the U.S. in it
        last, share_last   : the same for the last such year
    """
    # Step 1: the two countries side by side, one column each (`.pivot`)
    pair = world[world.country.isin([name, "United States"])].pivot(
        index="year",
        columns="country",
        values="gdppc",
    )
    # Step 2: the ratio; `.dropna()` keeps the years in which both have data
    ratio = (pair[name] / pair["United States"]).dropna()
    return ratio.index[0], ratio.iloc[0], ratio.index[-1], ratio.iloc[-1]

def countries_since_1870(frequency="every decade", countries=tuple(SEVEN)):
    """GDP per person on a ratio scale (2022 dollars), by decade or every year.

    Draws Fig. 6 (inspired by Fig. 3.6 in Jones). The title compares one country with
    the U.S. (versus_us).

    Arguments
        frequency : "every decade" (the textbook's years) or "every year"
        countries : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen countries; by decade, the textbook's years only
    chosen = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    if frequency == "every decade":
        chosen = chosen[chosen.year.isin(BENCHMARKS)]

    # Step 2: one line per country, on a ratio scale
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y="gdppc",
        color="country",
        log_y=True,
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        # `category_orders` fixes the order of the countries in the legend
        category_orders={"country": list(countries)},
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )

    # Step 3: the title compares one country with the U.S.: Japan when it is chosen.
    # `list(countries)` makes a list we can change, and `.remove(...)` deletes one
    # entry from it
    others = list(countries)
    if "United States" in others:
        others.remove("United States")
    title = "Choose a country to compare with the United States"
    if others:
        name = "Japan" if "Japan" in others else others[0]
        first, share_first, last, share_last = versus_us(name)
        title = (
            f"{short(name)} went from {share_first:.0%} of U.S. GDP per person in "
            f"{first} to {share_last:.0%} in {last}"
        )

    # Step 4: the textbook's vertical range, or one fixed wider range when a chosen
    # country lies outside it
    low, high = 700, 90000
    if not chosen.empty and (chosen.gdppc.min() < low or chosen.gdppc.max() > high):
        low, high = 250, 300000
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=DOUBLINGS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    fig.update_layout(title=title)
    return fig

3.6 Counting people, not countries
Weighting each country by its population changes the picture. This figure shows how many of the world’s people live at each level of income.

Fig. 8: The world’s population by per capita GDP
Goal. Count people instead of countries.
In Fig. 7 China and Luxembourg each count as one dot. Here every person counts equally. For a given year, we sort countries from poorest to richest and add up their populations. The chart shows the percentage of the world’s population that lives in countries with GDP per person at or below each level. Income is measured relative to the U.S. level in 2019 for every year, so that the curves can be compared.
cumulative_shares sorts the countries of one year and adds up their populations. share_below gives the share of the world’s people below the dashed line of the chart, 5 percent of the 2019 U.S. level.

def cumulative_shares(year):
    """The countries sorted from poorest to richest, with cumulative population shares.

    share = 100 (population of this country and all poorer ones) / world population

    Arguments
        year : the year
    Returns
        the rows of `sample` for that year, from poorest to richest, with a new
        column `share` (percent of world population)
    """
    # Step 1: sort from poorest to richest. `.copy()` makes a separate table, so that
    # adding a column does not touch `sample`
    table = sample[sample.year == year].sort_values("y_rel_us_2019").copy()
    # Step 2: `.cumsum()` gives running totals: the first value, then the sum of the
    # first two, and so on. Dividing by the total turns them into percentages
    table["share"] = 100 * table.pop_millions.cumsum() / table.pop_millions.sum()
    return table


def share_below(year):
    """The share of world population below the dashed line of Fig. 8.

    share = population of the countries below 5% of the 2019 U.S. level / world
    population

    Arguments
        year : the year
    Returns
        the share (0.69 for 69 percent)
    """
    below = cumulative_shares(year)
    # the population of the countries below 5% of the 2019 U.S. level
    poor = below[below.y_rel_us_2019 < 0.05].pop_millions.sum()
    return poor / below.pop_millions.sum()



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 8, the world's population by per capita GDP
def population_distribution(year=2019):
    """The cumulative share of world population by GDP per person, `year` and 1960.

    Draws Fig. 8 (inspired by Fig. 3.8 in Jones): GDP per person relative to the
    U.S. level in 2019, with a dashed line at 5 percent of it.

    Arguments
        year : the year drawn next to 1960
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the two years in one long table, and the share below the dashed line
    # (cumulative_shares, share_below)
    both = pd.concat([cumulative_shares(1960), cumulative_shares(year)])
    poor = share_below(year)

    # Step 2: one line per year; `line_shape="hv"` draws it as steps, one per country
    fig = px.line(
        both,
        x="y_rel_us_2019",
        y="share",
        color="year",
        line_shape="hv",
        hover_name="country",
        log_x=True,
        range_x=[1 / 200, 2],
        range_y=[0, 102],
        color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN, BLUE],
        labels={
            "y_rel_us_2019": "Per capita GDP (U.S. = 1 in 2019, ratio scale)",
            "share": "Share of world population (percent)",
            "year": "Year",
        },
    )
    # Step 3: `add_vline` draws the dashed vertical line at 5% of the U.S. level
    fig.add_vline(x=0.05, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=FRACTIONS, ticktext=FRACTION_NAMES)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"{year}: {poor:.0%} of people live below 5% of the 2019 U.S. level "
            "(dashed line)"
        )
    )
    return fig

text:
3.7 Rules for growth rates
Last, three handy rules: the growth rate of a product is a sum, of a ratio a difference, and of a power a multiple. We check them with U.S. data.

Fig. 9: U.S. population, GDP and per capita GDP
Goal. See the rules for growth rates at work.
Three rules make growth rates easy to work with (equations 7 to 9). If \(x\) grows at rate \(g_x\) and \(y\) at rate \(g_y\), then

the product \(z = x \times y\) grows at \(g_x + g_y\);
the ratio \(z = x / y\) grows at \(g_x - g_y\);
the power \(z = x^a\) grows at \(a \times g_x\).

Total GDP is GDP per person times population, so its growth rate is the sum of the two growth rates. To see this, the chart divides each series by its value in the first year, so all three lines start at 1. For the United States we use the official series of the textbook figure. For any other country we compute total GDP from the Maddison Project’s GDP per person and population.

# Load the data of Fig. 9: the official U.S. series, with the years as row labels
usa = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-9.csv").set_index("year")


def country_table(country):
    """Population, GDP per person and total GDP by year, as in `usa`.

    Total GDP is GDP per person times population: Y = y L

    Arguments
        country : the country (the U.S. uses the official series)
    Returns
        a table by year: population (thousands), GDP per person and total GDP
        (billions of 2022 dollars)
    """
    if country == "United States":
        return usa                              # the official series of the textbook
    # Step 1: the country's Maddison data. `.astype(float)` turns whole numbers with
    # gaps into ordinary numbers
    one = world[world.country == country].set_index("year")
    table = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "population_thousands": one.pop_thousands.astype(float),
            "gdppc": one.gdppc,
        }
    )
    # Step 2: total GDP in billions: y times L (in thousands), divided by a million
    table["gdp_billions"] = table.gdppc * table.population_thousands / 1e6
    return table.dropna()

If the period starts before a country’s data do, the chart starts in the country’s first year, and the title says which years it uses.

def growth_rules(period, country):
    """The three series of Fig. 9 relative to the first year, and their growth rates.

    Equation (6) for each series. Rule (7): g_Y = g_y + g_L, approximately

    Arguments
        period  : (first year, last year)
        country : the country
    Returns
        start, end : the first and the last year with data
        chosen     : the three series, each divided by its first-year value
                     (None when the period has no data)
        rates      : the average annual growth rate of each series, in percent
    """
    table = country_table(country)
    # Step 1: `start, end = period` unpacks the pair of years into two variables
    start, end = period
    if end == start:                    # both handles on one year: use one year
        end = min(start + 1, 2025)
        start = end - 1
    chosen = table.loc[start:end]
    if len(chosen) < 2:
        return start, end, None, None   # no data in the period
    # Step 2: the first and the last year with data
    start, end = chosen.index[0], chosen.index[-1]
    # Step 3: the growth rates, equation (6), in percent; + 0.0 avoids "-0.00"
    rates = (
        100 * growth_rate(chosen.iloc[0], chosen.iloc[-1], end - start)
    ).round(2) + 0.0
    # Step 4: dividing the table by its first row divides every column by its own
    # first value, so all three series start at 1
    chosen = (chosen / chosen.iloc[0]).reset_index().rename(
        columns={
            "gdp_billions": "Total GDP",
            "gdppc": "Per capita GDP",
            "population_thousands": "Population",
        }
    )
    return start, end, chosen, rates



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 9, population, GDP and per capita GDP
def growth_rules_chart(period=(1870, 2025), country="United States"):
    """Total GDP, GDP per person and population, each relative to its first year.

    Draws Fig. 9 (inspired by Fig. 3.9 in Jones), on a ratio scale.

    Arguments
        period  : (first year, last year)
        country : the country
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the series and their growth rates (growth_rules)
    start, end, chosen, rates = growth_rules(period, country)
    if chosen is None:                          # no data in the period
        return go.Figure().update_layout(
            title=f"No data for {short(country)} in {start}–{end}"
        )

    # Step 2: one line per series, on a ratio scale
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y=["Total GDP", "Per capita GDP", "Population"],
        log_y=True,
        color_discrete_sequence=["#e0a33b", GREEN, BLUE],
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "value": "Relative to the first year (ratio scale)",
            "variable": "Series",
        },
    )
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000])
    # a little room on the left: no label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[start - (end - start) / 20, end])

    # Step 3: the title: GDP growth is about per capita growth plus population growth
    label = "" if country == "United States" else f"{short(country)}, "
    sign = "+" if rates.population_thousands >= 0 else "−"
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"{label}{start}–{end}: GDP {rates.gdp_billions:.2f}% ≈ per capita "
            f"{rates.gdppc:.2f}% {sign} population "
            f"{abs(rates.population_thousands):.2f}% a year"
        )
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

From 1870 to 2025, total GDP grew 3.3 percent a year, per capita GDP 1.9 percent and population 1.4 percent. The first number is (almost exactly) the sum of the other two.
The sum is not exact because growth over a whole year compounds: \((1+g_Y) = (1+g_y)(1+g_L)\). For small rates the extra term \(g_y \times g_L\) is tiny.
Population growth has slowed to less than 1 percent a year since 1980, so growth in GDP per person now accounts for a larger part of GDP growth. Choose a later starting year to see it.
Choose Niger: from 1950 to 2022 its GDP grew 2.9 percent a year, but its population grew 2.8 percent, so GDP per person barely changed. Fast GDP growth can hide stagnant living standards. Choose Japan and a period that starts in 2010: its population has been shrinking since then.

title: 3. An Overview of Long-Run Economic Growth
text:
3.8 Concluding remarks

Sustained growth in living standards is very recent. It began about 200 years ago and spread unevenly, which produced the Great Divergence in incomes across countries.
A growth rate is a percentage change. Growing at a constant rate, a variable is multiplied by \(1+\bar{g}\) each year, equation (1), so after \(t\) years it equals \(y_t = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t\), the constant growth rule, equation (2). Compounding makes the yearly increase grow, and small differences in growth rates become large gaps in levels.
In logs, constant growth is a straight line, equation (3), so on a ratio scale the slope is the growth rate. A variable doubles in exactly \(\ln 2/\ln(1+\bar{g})\) years, equation (4), or in about \(70/g\) years, the Rule of 70, equation (5). U.S. GDP per person has grown at close to 2 percent a year for more than 150 years.
The average annual growth rate between two years, equation (6), is the one constant rate that links the two end points: a geometric mean of the yearly growth factors.
Growth rates differ a lot across countries, and small differences compound into huge income gaps. Counting people rather than countries, poverty has fallen dramatically, mainly because of growth in China and India.
Growth rates of products are sums, of ratios are differences, and of powers are multiples, equations (7) to (9). Applied to the production function, they split output growth into productivity growth plus weighted input growth, equation (10).
The next chapter builds a first model to explain why some countries are so much richer than others.

title: 3. An Overview of Long-Run Economic Growth
text:
Practice problems
These problems put the chapter’s tools to work in three ways: conceptual problems apply the growth-rate math to real cases, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data to find patterns and facts, and modeling problems use the chapter’s interactive charts to answer policy questions. Each problem is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it first, then open the Hint, and only then the Solution. The sliders in the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): China’s plan to double its economy. China’s 13th Five-Year Plan (2016–2020) set out to “ensure that China’s 2010 GDP and per capita personal income double by 2020”. Its table of targets has GDP rising from 67.7 trillion yuan in 2015 to more than 92.7 trillion yuan in 2020 (13th Five-Year Plan, official English translation, Chapter 3 and Box 2).

What average annual growth rate does doubling GDP in the ten years from 2010 to 2020 require?
What average annual growth rate do the plan’s GDP numbers for 2015 and 2020 imply? If the goal was to be met, what does that say about growth from 2010 to 2015?
The goal also named income per person. In this chapter’s Maddison data, China’s population grew about 0.5 percent a year from 2010 to 2020. How fast must total GDP grow for GDP per person to double in ten years?



Hint

Doubling means \(y_t/y_0 = 2\) with \(t = 10\) in equation (6). In (b), the two five-year periods must together multiply GDP by 2. In (c), GDP per person is GDP divided by the population, so the ratio rule, equation (8), applies.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Put \(y_{2020}/y_{2010} = 2\) and \(t = 10\) into equation (6):
\[\bar{g} = 2^{1/10} - 1 = 1.0718 - 1 = 0.0718.\]
Doubling in ten years takes growth of about 7.2 percent a year. The Rule of 70, equation (5), agrees: at 7.2 percent a variable doubles in about \(70/7.2 \approx 9.7\) years.
(b) Equation (6) with \(t = 5\):
\[\bar{g} = \left(\frac{92.7}{67.7}\right)^{1/5} - 1 = 1.3693^{1/5} - 1 = 0.0649,\]
about 6.5 percent a year, the “more than 6.5 percent” of the plan’s table. That is slower than the 7.2 percent of (a), so the first five years had to be faster. Call \(g_1\) the growth rate of 2010–2015. The two periods together must double GDP. Taking the fifth root of both sides of that condition, and then dividing by 1.0649:
\[(1+g_1)^5 \times 1.0649^5 = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1+g_1) \times 1.0649 = 2^{1/5}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1+g_1 = \frac{1.1487}{1.0649} = 1.0787.\]
The plan’s 6.5 percent was enough only if GDP had grown about 7.9 percent a year from 2010 to 2015.
(c) GDP per person is \(y = Y/L\), so the ratio rule, equation (8), gives \(g_y = g_Y - g_L\), or \(g_Y = g_y + g_L\). With \(g_y = 7.18\) percent from (a) and \(g_L = 0.5\) percent:
\[g_Y \approx 7.18 + 0.5 = 7.68 \text{ percent}, \qquad \text{or exactly} \quad (1.0718)(1.005) - 1 = 0.0772.\]
Total GDP must grow about 7.7 percent a year: over ten years it must rise by a factor of \(2 \times 1.005^{10} = 2.10\), not 2. A goal for income per person is harder to reach than the same goal for GDP whenever the population grows.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Greece’s slump, or why a fall needs a bigger rise. Greece’s debt crisis led to a joint rescue by the European Union and the IMF in May 2010 (IMF press release, 9 May 2010). In this chapter’s data (maddison_world.csv, from the Maddison Project Database 2023), Greek GDP per person peaked in 2008 and then fell every year until 2013:



Year
2008
2013
2022




GDP per person (2022 dollars)
37,296
28,816
32,621




By what percentage did GDP per person fall from 2008 to 2013? By what percentage must it rise from its 2013 level to get back to the 2008 level? Show that after a fall by a fraction \(x\), the rise needed is \(x/(1-x)\).
Use equation (6) to compute the average annual growth rate from 2008 to 2013, and from 2013 to 2022.
If Greece kept growing at its 2013–2022 rate after 2022, in what year would GDP per person be back at its 2008 level? How many years of that growth did the slump of 2008–2013 undo?



Hint


Write the 2013 level as \((1-x)\) times the 2008 level, and ask which factor takes it back. (c) The Model overview shows that a variable growing at the rate \(\bar{g}\) takes \(t = \ln m/\ln(1+\bar{g})\) years to grow by a factor \(m\).


Your answer:


Solution

(a) The ratio of the two levels is \(28{,}816/37{,}296 = 0.7726\), so GDP per person fell by \(1 - 0.7726 = 0.2274\), about 22.7 percent. To get back, it must be multiplied by \(37{,}296/28{,}816 = 1.2943\): a rise of 29.4 percent. In general, if \(y_{2013} = (1-x)\,y_{2008}\), the factor back is \(1/(1-x)\), and the rise is
\[\frac{1}{1-x} - 1 = \frac{1 - (1-x)}{1-x} = \frac{x}{1-x} = \frac{0.2274}{0.7726} = 0.294.\]
The rise is larger than the fall because it starts from a lower base.
(b) From 2008 to 2013, \(0.7726^{1/5} - 1 = -0.0503\): GDP per person fell about 5.0 percent a year. From 2013 to 2022, \((32{,}621/28{,}816)^{1/9} - 1 = 1.1320^{1/9} - 1 = 0.0139\), about 1.4 percent a year.
(c) In 2022 Greece was still \(1 - 32{,}621/37{,}296 = 12.5\) percent below its 2008 level. The factor still to go is \(m = 37{,}296/32{,}621 = 1.1433\), so
\[t = \frac{\ln 1.1433}{\ln 1.0139} = \frac{0.1339}{0.0138} = 9.7 \text{ years}.\]
At 1.4 percent a year, Greece gets back to its 2008 level around 2032, 24 years after the peak. The slump undid \(\ln 1.2943/\ln 1.0139 = 18.7\) years of growth at that rate. Over 2008–2022 as a whole, equation (6) gives \((32{,}621/37{,}296)^{1/14} - 1 = -0.95\) percent a year. A deep slump costs living standards for a long time, because the recovery has to climb back from a lower base.

Problem 3 (Challenge): How long until India catches up? The World Bank estimates that India’s real GDP must grow 7.8 percent a year on average for 22 years to reach the country’s goal of high-income status by 2047; from 2000 to 2024, growth averaged 6.3 percent (World Bank press release, 28 February 2025).

Suppose India’s population grows 1.05 percent a year, its rate from 2012 to 2022 in this chapter’s Maddison data. What growth rate of GDP per person does GDP growth of 7.8 percent give? By what factor do GDP and GDP per person rise in 22 years?
A poorer country P starts with the fraction \(r_0 = y^P_0/y^R_0\) of the income per person of a richer country R. P grows at the constant rate \(\bar{g}_P\) and R at \(\bar{g}_R\), with \(\bar{g}_P > \bar{g}_R\). Derive the number of years \(t\) until P reaches the fraction \(r^*\) of R’s income. Then show that the income gap halves about every \(70/(g_P - g_R)\) years, with the growth rates in percent.
In the Maddison data, India’s GDP per person was 13.28 percent of the U.S. level in 2022, and U.S. GDP per person grew 1.11 percent a year from 2000 to 2022. If the U.S. kept that pace, how many years would India need to reach half the U.S. level with the growth rate of (a)? And with its own 2000–2022 rate of 4.83 percent? (Half the U.S. level is our yardstick, not the World Bank’s definition of high income.)



Hint


Write equation (2) for both countries and divide the first by the second, so the starting levels become the ratio \(r_0\). Then take logs, as in the derivation of the doubling time, equation (4), and use \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\).
Start from \(r_0 = 0.1328\) and aim for \(r^* = 0.5\).


Your answer:

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) The ratio rule, equation (8), gives \(g_y \approx 7.8 - 1.05 = 6.75\) percent, or exactly \(1.078/1.0105 - 1 = 0.0668\), about 6.7 percent a year. In 22 years GDP rises by a factor of \(1.078^{22} = 5.22\) and GDP per person by \(1.0668^{22} = 4.15\).
(b) Equation (2) for each country gives \(y^P_t = y^P_0(1+\bar{g}_P)^t\) and \(y^R_t = y^R_0(1+\bar{g}_R)^t\). Dividing the first by the second:
\[\frac{y^P_t}{y^R_t} = r_0\left(\frac{1+\bar{g}_P}{1+\bar{g}_R}\right)^t.\]
Set the left-hand side equal to \(r^*\), divide both sides by \(r_0\), and take logs:
\[\ln\frac{r^*}{r_0} = t\left[\ln(1+\bar{g}_P) - \ln(1+\bar{g}_R)\right]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
t = \frac{\ln(r^*/r_0)}{\ln(1+\bar{g}_P) - \ln(1+\bar{g}_R)} \approx \frac{\ln(r^*/r_0)}{\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R}.\]
This is the ratio rule at work: relative income \(y^P/y^R\) grows at about \(\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R\), so it behaves like any variable growing at that rate. Halving the gap means doubling the ratio, \(r^*/r_0 = 2\), so \(t \approx \ln 2/(\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R) \approx 0.70/(\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R) = 70/(g_P - g_R)\) with the rates in percent. If \(\bar{g}_P \le \bar{g}_R\), the gap never closes.
(c) The ratio must rise by the factor \(r^*/r_0 = 0.5/0.1328 = 3.77\), and \(\ln 3.77 = 1.33\).
r0 = 0.1328                                    # India relative to the U.S. in 2022 (Maddison)
for g_india in [1.078 / 1.0105 - 1, 0.0483]:
    years = np.log(0.5 / r0) / (np.log(1 + g_india) - np.log(1 + 0.0111))
    print(f"India growing {100 * g_india:.2f}% a year: half the U.S. level after {years:.1f} years, around {2022 + years:.0f}")
At 6.68 percent a year India reaches half the U.S. level after 24.7 years, around 2047; at its 2000–2022 pace of 4.83 percent it takes 36.7 years, until about 2059. The Rule-of-70 view gives the same picture: at a growth gap of \(6.68 - 1.11 = 5.57\) points the gap halves every \(70/5.57 = 12.6\) years, and it must halve \(\log_2 3.77 = 1.9\) times. Faster growth by 1.85 points a year brings the date forward by 12 years.



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): The Great Divergence in one number. The file maddison_world.csv holds GDP per person (2022 dollars) for 169 countries from the Maddison Project Database 2023. Find the richest and the poorest country in 1870 and in 2022, and the ratio of their GDP per person. How many countries have an estimate in each year, and how does that affect the comparison?


Hint

maddison[maddison.year == 1870] keeps one year. .idxmax() gives the row label of the largest value, and .loc[...] then picks that row. len(...) counts the countries. To compare like with like, you can keep in 2022 only the countries that also appear in 1870.


# Your answer here



Solution

For each year, keep its rows, find the rows of the largest and the smallest GDP per person, and divide. Then repeat 2022 with the 1870 countries only.
maddison = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
for year in [1870, 2022]:
    one_year = maddison[maddison.year == year]
    richest = one_year.loc[one_year.gdppc.idxmax()]
    poorest = one_year.loc[one_year.gdppc.idxmin()]
    print(f"{year}: {len(one_year)} countries; {richest.country} {richest.gdppc:,} / "
          f"{poorest.country} {poorest.gdppc:,} = {richest.gdppc / poorest.gdppc:.1f}")
in_1870 = maddison[maddison.year == 1870].country
same = maddison[(maddison.year == 2022) & maddison.country.isin(in_1870)]
print(f"2022, the same {len(same)} countries: {same.gdppc.max() / same.gdppc.min():.1f}")
In 1870 the richest country, the United Kingdom (7,520 dollars), was 9.1 times as rich as the poorest, Nepal (827 dollars). In 2022 Qatar (192,456 dollars) was 250 times as rich as the Central African Republic (769 dollars). But only 70 countries have an estimate for 1870, against 169 in 2022: in Sub-Saharan Africa only Liberia and South Africa have one, and Qatar is an oil exporter with fewer than 3 million people. Among the same 70 countries, the ratio in 2022 is 108.9 (Norway against Liberia). Either way, the gap between the richest and the poorest grew more than tenfold: that is the Great Divergence.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Booms, busts and the average growth rate. The file fig3-2.csv holds U.S. GDP per person (2022 dollars) from 1870 to 2025: from 1929 it comes from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, real GDP (GDPCA), via FRED and the BEA’s population, and before 1929 from the Maddison Project Database 2023.

Compute the growth rate of every year. Which five years saw the largest falls? Match them with the U.S. recessions dated by the NBER.
For 1870–2025, 1870–1949 and 1950–2025, compare the plain average of the yearly growth rates with the average annual growth rate of equation (6).
In which period is the gap between the two averages larger? Compare the standard deviations of the yearly growth rates, and explain.



Hint

.pct_change() gives the growth rate from each year to the next, and .sort_values().head(5) lists the five smallest. For (c), recall step 5 of the derivation of equation (6): a rise of 10 percent followed by a fall of 10 percent.


# Your answer here



Solution

Compute the yearly growth rates once, list the smallest, and then, for each period, compare their mean with growth_rate applied to the first and the last year.
us_gdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-2.csv").set_index("year").gdppc
yearly = us_gdp.pct_change().dropna()                 # the growth rate of each year, from 1871
print((100 * yearly.sort_values().head(5)).round(1))
for first, last in [(1870, 2025), (1870, 1949), (1950, 2025)]:
    rates = yearly.loc[first + 1:last]
    plain = 100 * rates.mean()
    eq6 = 100 * growth_rate(us_gdp[first], us_gdp[last], last - first)
    print(f"{first}-{last}: plain average {plain:.2f}%, equation (6) {eq6:.2f}%, "
          f"standard deviation {100 * rates.std():.1f}%")
(a) The five largest falls are 1932 (−13.5 percent), 1946 (−12.5), 1914 (−10.0), 1908 (−9.8) and 1930 (−9.5). 1930 and 1932 fall in the NBER’s contraction of August 1929 to March 1933: the Great Depression. 1908 and 1914 fall in the contractions of May 1907 to June 1908 and January 1913 to December 1914 (before 1929 these are estimates). 1946 is the first year after World War II, when war production was cut back.
(b) From 1870 to 2025 the plain average is 1.99 percent and equation (6) gives 1.88 percent. For 1870–1949 the two are 1.92 and 1.72 percent; for 1950–2025, 1.99 and 1.97 percent.
(c) The gap is about 0.2 points before 1950 and only 0.02 points after. The standard deviation of the yearly growth rates was 6.3 percent before 1950 and 2.2 percent after: the early economy swung far more. A fall hurts more than an equal rise helps (\(1.10 \times 0.90 = 0.99\)), so the plain average overstates growth, and more so the bigger the swings. A handy rule is that the gap is about half the variance: \(0.063^2/2 = 0.0020\), or 0.2 points. Use equation (6) for growth over a period.

Problem 6 (Intermediate): Argentina’s century of relative decline. Alan Taylor describes Argentina’s economic history as one of the most dramatic cases of divergence in modern times (Taylor 2014, NBER Working Paper 19924). Compare it in maddison_world.csv with two other countries rich in land and settled by immigrants, Australia and Canada.

Compute the GDP per person of Argentina, Australia and Canada relative to the United States in 1913 and in 2022.
Compute the average annual growth rate of the four countries from 1913 to 2022.
How rich would Argentina have been in 2022 if it had grown as fast as Australia since 1913? Compare this with its actual level.



Hint

Turn the four countries into a wide table, one column per country, with .pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc"), as in the Key numbers of Fig. 6. Then growth_rate gives (b), and constant_growth gives (c).


# Your answer here



Solution

Make the wide table, divide each year’s row by the U.S. value, then apply equation (6) and equation (2).
maddison = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
four_names = ["Argentina", "Australia", "Canada", "United States"]
four = maddison[maddison.country.isin(four_names)].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
for year in [1913, 2022]:
    print(year, (four.loc[year] / four.loc[year, "United States"]).round(2).to_dict())
for name in four_names:
    print(f"{name}: {growth_rate(four.loc[1913, name], four.loc[2022, name], 109):.2%} a year")
g_aus = growth_rate(four.loc[1913, "Australia"], four.loc[2022, "Australia"], 109)
what_if = constant_growth(four.loc[1913, "Argentina"], g_aus, 109)
print(f"Argentina at Australia's rate: {what_if:,.0f} dollars, {what_if / four.loc[2022, 'Argentina']:.1f} times its actual level")
(a) In 1913 Argentina had 60 percent of U.S. GDP per person, Canada 70 percent and Australia 81 percent. In 2022 Argentina had 31 percent, while Canada had risen to 78 percent and Australia to 89 percent.
(b) From 1913 to 2022, GDP per person grew 1.02 percent a year in Argentina, 1.71 percent in Australia, 1.72 percent in Canada and 1.62 percent in the United States.
(c) At Australia’s 1.71 percent, Argentina’s 7,808 dollars of 1913 would have become about 49,400 dollars in 2022, 2.1 times its actual 23,600 dollars. A gap of 0.7 points a year looks small, but by the ratio rule it makes Argentina’s income relative to Australia’s fall about 0.7 percent a year, which halves it in about \(70/0.7 = 100\) years. That is what happened: Argentina had 74 percent of Australia’s GDP per person in 1913 and 35 percent in 2022.

Problem 7 (Challenge): A fairer test of catch-up. Fig. 7 plots each country’s growth against its income in 2023, and the chapter warns that its upward tilt is partly built in. Patel, Sandefur and Subramanian (2021) find that poorer countries have been catching up with richer ones, slowly, since the mid-1990s (Journal of Development Economics, doi:10.1016/j.jdeveco.2021.102687). Check this with pwt_income.csv from the Penn World Table 11.0, for the 110 countries of Fig. 7 (those with in_sample true, without Venezuela).

Compute each country’s average annual growth rate of GDP per person from 1960 to 2023, and from 2000 to 2023.
For each period, compute the correlation of growth with the log of GDP per person relative to the United States in the starting year, and with the log of relative GDP per person in 2023.
What do the four correlations say about convergence? How many countries grew faster than the United States in each period?



Hint

Build one table per starting year with merge, as the code of Fig. 7 does, and add a column with np.log(...) of relative income. table.growth.corr(table.log_start) gives a correlation. For (c), ask why a country that grew fast must end up rich, whatever its start.


# Your answer here



Solution

For each starting year, merge the start-year and 2023 values, compute growth with equation (6), divide by the U.S. value of the same year, take logs and correlate.
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_income.csv")
panel = panel[panel.in_sample & (panel.country != "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)")]
last_year = panel[panel.year == 2023][["iso3", "gdp_pc"]]
for start_year in [1960, 2000]:
    pair = panel[panel.year == start_year][["iso3", "country", "gdp_pc"]].merge(last_year, on="iso3",
                                                                                suffixes=("_start", "_2023"))
    pair["growth"] = 100 * growth_rate(pair.gdp_pc_start, pair.gdp_pc_2023, 2023 - start_year)
    usa_row = pair[pair.country == "United States"].iloc[0]
    pair["log_start"] = np.log(pair.gdp_pc_start / usa_row.gdp_pc_start)
    pair["log_2023"] = np.log(pair.gdp_pc_2023 / usa_row.gdp_pc_2023)
    print(f"{start_year}-2023, {len(pair)} countries: correlation with the start level "
          f"{pair.growth.corr(pair.log_start):.2f}, with the 2023 level {pair.growth.corr(pair.log_2023):.2f}; "
          f"{(pair.growth > usa_row.growth).sum()} grew faster than the U.S. ({usa_row.growth:.2f}%)")
(a)–(b) For 1960–2023 the correlation of growth with the starting level is −0.05, and with the 2023 level +0.66. For 2000–2023 it is −0.34 with the starting level and −0.05 with the 2023 level.
(c) The +0.66 of Fig. 7’s view is mostly built in: a country that grew fast became rich by 2023, whatever its start. Against the starting level, 1960–2023 shows almost no relation: on average, poor countries in 1960 did not grow faster than rich ones, so there was no catch-up across the world as a whole. Since 2000 the correlation is negative, −0.34: poorer countries grew faster on average, as Patel, Sandefur and Subramanian find. It is still weak, so catch-up is slow and many poor countries lag. From 1960, 64 of the 110 countries grew faster than the United States (2.03 percent a year); from 2000, 85 did (the U.S. grew 1.32 percent a year).



Modeling problems
Problem 8 (Basic): Will the world’s population double again? The United Nations reports that the world population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022, twelve years after it passed 7 billion. It expects 9 billion in about 15 years, around 2037, and a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s (United Nations, Global Issues: Population). Food and energy planners want to know how soon the world will need twice as much as today. The widget is the doubling chart of Fig. 4 with a finer slider for the growth rate. It starts at 6 billion, but the doubling time does not depend on the starting level.

What was the average annual growth rate of the world population from 7 to 8 billion? Set the slider close to it: how many years would a doubling take at that rate?
Do the same for the UN’s path from 8 to 9 billion.
What average growth rate takes the world from 8 billion in 2022 to 10.3 billion around 2085? Why can a constant growth rate never produce a peak? What population in 2085 would a planner predict by extending the growth rate of (a)?

Use equation (6) with the two population levels and the number of years between them. The chart’s title then gives the exact doubling time, equation (4), and the Rule of 70. For (c), equation (1) says how much a population growing at a constant \(\bar{n}\) adds in a year.


def world_doubling(n=0.015):
    """Fig. 3.4 with a finer slider: the doubling time of equation (4) for the growth rate n."""
    fig = population_two_scales(n)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"n = {100 * n:.2f}%: doubles every {doubling_time(n):.1f} years "
                            f"(Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n):.1f})")
    return fig


interact(world_doubling,
         n=FloatSlider(value=0.015, min=0.003, max=0.025, step=0.0005, description="growth rate n", style=WIDE,
                       readout_format=".4f"));

Source. The model of Fig. 4 above, adapted from Fig. 3.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

for name, low, high, years in paths:

print(f"8 billion at the 7-to-8 rate for 63 years: {constant_growth(8, growth_rate(7, 8, 12), 63):.1f} billion")
(a) Equation (6) gives \(\bar{n} = (8/7)^{1/12} - 1 = 0.0112\), or 1.12 percent a year. On the slider, 1.10 percent gives a doubling time of 63.4 years and 1.15 percent gives 60.6 years. The exact doubling time is \(\ln 2/\ln(1+\bar{n}) = 12\ln 2/\ln(8/7) = 62.3\) years (Rule of 70: 62.6).
(b) From 8 to 9 billion in 15 years, \(\bar{n} = (9/8)^{1/15} - 1 = 0.0079\), or 0.79 percent a year. The slider at 0.80 percent shows 87.0 years; the exact doubling time is \(15\ln 2/\ln(9/8) = 88.3\) years (Rule of 70: 88.8).
(c) From 8 to 10.3 billion in 63 years, \(\bar{n} = (10.3/8)^{1/63} - 1 = 0.0040\), only 0.40 percent a year, with a doubling time of 172.8 years. But a constant growth rate can never produce a peak. By equation (1), a population growing at a constant \(\bar{n} > 0\) adds \(\bar{n}L_t\) people every year, a positive amount that grows with \(L_t\), so the population rises forever. A peak needs a growth rate that falls to zero and then turns negative, which is what the UN expects as birth rates keep falling. A planner who extended the 1.12 percent of 2010–2022 would predict 16.1 billion people in 2085, almost 6 billion more than the UN’s peak. On the UN’s projections, the world population will not double again from 8 billion, so plans built on a constant growth rate would greatly overstate future needs.

Problem 9 (Intermediate): Fewer births, faster growth? In 2022 a woman in Niger had about 6.1 children on average, against 2.2 in Bangladesh, where the fertility rate has fallen from 6.8 in 1970 (World Bank, World Development Indicators, Fertility rate, total (SP.DYN.TFRT.IN)). Bangladesh’s GDP grew 6.57 percent and its population 1.41 percent, so GDP per person grew 5.09 percent and doubles in about 14 years.
(b) With \(g_Y = 4.10\) and \(g_L = 1.41\) percent, the ratio rule gives \(g_y = 4.10 - 1.41 = 2.69\) percent, which doubles GDP per person in about 26 years. On this arithmetic the adviser is right.
(c) But GDP growth would not stay the same. Problem 10 (Challenge): Can poverty fall to 3 percent by 2030?     poor_share[year] = below.pop_millions.sum() / shares_year.pop_millions.sum()
