5.2 Model in code
Now we turn the Key results into Python. The section has four parts: the setup (folded, because it is the same in every chapter), the model as functions, numerical checks of the Key results, and the drawing tools that the figures use (folded too). Run its cells once, in order. Every later section of the notebook reuses them.

5.2.1 Setup
Run the setup cells once, before anything else. They load the Python libraries, give every chart the same look, store the address of the chapter’s data and define two helpers that only the book website needs. You can use the notebook without reading them; open the box if you are curious.






NoteShow the setup code





The first cell loads the libraries and sets the look of the charts. Its comments explain each step.

# @title Setup: libraries, chart colors and the data location
# Text after a "#" is a comment: Python ignores it, it is there for human readers.

# Step 1: load the libraries. `import` loads a library, a toolbox written by
# other people, and `as np` gives it a short nickname, so the code stays short.
import numpy as np                              # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                             # data tables
import plotly.express as px                     # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go               # charts built piece by piece
import plotly.io as pio                         # settings shared by every chart
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots       # several panels in one figure
# sliders and buttons for the interactive figures
from ipywidgets import interact, interact_manual, FloatSlider, ToggleButtons, Dropdown, fixed

# Step 2: one light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
# the same chart size in Colab and on the website
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full slider labels

# Step 3, Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets.
# `try` runs the indented lines; if the import fails (we are not in Colab),
# `except` skips them.
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# Step 4: the data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch05/"

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider. The next two helpers build those versions. Run them and move on.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. solow_diagram
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "s"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


# @title Helper for the website versions with many countries (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_menu(fig, shown, regions, label="Textbook countries"):
    """Draw the countries in `shown` and put every other country one click away in the legend.

    With more than 40 countries, a menu above the plot chooses the region whose countries the legend lists.
    Traces that are not countries stay as they are.

    Arguments
        fig     : a Plotly figure with one trace per country
        shown   : the countries drawn at the start
        regions : maps each country to its region
        label   : the name of the first menu entry
    Returns
        the same figure, with the visibility set and, for many countries, the region menu
    """
    # Step 1: the menu entries, the textbook countries and then one entry per region
    # the traces that are countries, and each of their regions once, A to Z
    countries = [trace.name for trace in fig.data if trace.name in regions]
    groups = [label] + sorted(set(regions[name] for name in countries))
    if len(countries) <= 40:
        groups = [None]                     # a short legend lists every country at once
    # Step 2: for each entry, which traces are drawn, in the legend only, or hidden
    buttons = []
    for group in groups:
        visible = []
        for trace in fig.data:
            if trace.name in shown:
                visible.append(True)                    # a textbook country: drawn
            elif trace.name not in regions:
                visible.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)   # not a country: as it was
            elif group is None or regions[trace.name] == group:
                visible.append("legendonly")    # in this region: a click away
            else:
                visible.append(False)                   # another region: hidden
        buttons.append(dict(label=group, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    # Step 3: start with the first entry, and add the menu when there is more than one
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    if len(groups) > 1:
        menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
        fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig






5.2.2 The model as functions
Two Key results hold the whole model: the production function, equation (1), and the steady state, equations (3), (4) and (9). We write each one as a Python function: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives back a result. The first function is output per person.

# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses.
# `A=1.0` gives A a default value, used whenever we do not pass one.
# The text in triple quotes describes the function.
def output(k, A=1.0):
    """Output per person, from the production function.

    Equation (1):  y = A k^(1/3)

    Arguments
        k : capital per person
        A : productivity, A-bar (1 unless we pass another value)
    Returns
        output per person, y
    """
    # `return` gives back the result; `**` means "to the power of"
    return A * k ** (1 / 3)

The steady state is where investment just covers depreciation. Solving equation (2) for that point gives \(k^*\), and putting \(k^*\) into the production function gives \(y^*\). The argument n is population growth, which adds to depreciation (equation 9). It is 0 unless we pass another value, so the same functions serve the basic model and the model with population growth in Fig. 11.

def steady_state_k(s, d, A=1.0, n=0.0):
    """Steady-state capital per person, k*.

    Equation (3), or (9) with population growth:  k* = (s A / (n + d))^(3/2)

    Arguments
        s : investment rate, s-bar
        d : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A : productivity, A-bar
        n : population growth rate, n-bar (0 in the basic model)
    Returns
        steady-state capital per person, k*
    """
    # investment s A k^(1/3) equals (n + d) k exactly at k*; solving for k gives:
    return (s * A / (n + d)) ** (3 / 2)


def steady_state_y(s, d, A=1.0, n=0.0):
    """Steady-state output per person, y*.

    Equation (4), or (9) with population growth:  y* = A^(3/2) (s / (n + d))^(1/2)

    Arguments
        s : investment rate, s-bar
        d : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A : productivity, A-bar
        n : population growth rate, n-bar (0 in the basic model)
    Returns
        steady-state output per person, y*
    """
    # the same as output(steady_state_k(s, d, A, n), A), written as one formula
    return A ** (3 / 2) * (s / (n + d)) ** (1 / 2)



5.2.3 Checking the key results
The formulas came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, one Key result at a time, using Islandia’s values \(\bar{s}=0.4\), \(\bar{d}=0.1\) and \(\bar{A}=1\). First the steady state itself: the formula for \(y^*\) and the production function applied to \(k^*\) must give the same number, and so must both sides of equation (5).

# Islandia's steady state, from equation (3) and then equation (1)
k_star = steady_state_k(s=0.4, d=0.1)
y_star = output(k_star)

# An f-string, f"... {value:.2f}", puts a value into the text;
# ":.2f" means "two decimals".
print(f"Steady-state capital per person k* = {k_star:.2f}")
print(f"Steady-state output per person  y* = {y_star:.2f}")
# equation (4) must give the same y* as the line above
print(f"Check with equation (4):        y* = {steady_state_y(s=0.4, d=0.1):.2f}")
# consumption is what is not invested, c* = (1 - s) y*
print(f"Consumption per person          c* = {(1 - 0.4) * y_star:.2f}")
# both sides of equation (5), K/Y = s/d
print(f"Capital-output ratio, eq. (5): k*/y* = {k_star / y_star:.2f}   and s/d = {0.4 / 0.1:.2f}")
print(f"Real interest rate (1/3)(d/s):   r* = {100 * 0.1 / (3 * 0.4):.1f}%")

Steady-state capital per person k* = 8.00
Steady-state output per person  y* = 2.00
Check with equation (4):        y* = 2.00
Consumption per person          c* = 1.20
Capital-output ratio, eq. (5): k*/y* = 4.00   and s/d = 4.00
Real interest rate (1/3)(d/s):   r* = 8.3%


Check 1: Islandia really converges to \(k^*\). We start Islandia with very few tools and apply equation (2) for 300 years, one year at a time. Capital should approach the \(k^*\) of the formula.

# Step 1: start far below the steady state
k = 1.0

# Step 2: apply equation (2) once a year. `range(300)` counts 0, 1, ..., 299,
# so the `for` loop runs its indented lines 300 times.
# `if year in (10, 50, 100)` is true only in those years.
for year in range(300):
    if year in (10, 50, 100):
        print(f"Year {year:3d}: k = {k:.3f}")
    # new k = old k + investment - depreciation
    k = k + 0.4 * output(k) - 0.1 * k

# Step 3: compare the end point with the formula
print(f"Year 300: k = {k:.3f}   (formula: k* = {steady_state_k(s=0.4, d=0.1):.3f})")

Year  10: k = 3.883
Year  50: k = 7.709
Year 100: k = 7.991
Year 300: k = 8.000   (formula: k* = 8.000)


Check 2: the elasticities. We raise each parameter by 1 percent and see by what percentage \(y^*\) changes. The comparative-statics table predicts \(+0.5\%\) for \(\bar{s}\), \(+1.5\%\) for \(\bar{A}\) and \(-0.5\%\) for \(\bar{d}\).

# Step 1: y* at Islandia's values
base = steady_state_y(s=0.4, d=0.1, A=1.0)

# Step 2: y* with one parameter 1% higher, relative to the base (0.005 = 0.5%)
change_s = steady_state_y(s=0.4 * 1.01, d=0.1, A=1.0) / base - 1
change_A = steady_state_y(s=0.4, d=0.1, A=1.0 * 1.01) / base - 1
change_d = steady_state_y(s=0.4, d=0.1 * 1.01, A=1.0) / base - 1

# Step 3: show them in percent; ":+.3f" shows the sign and three decimals
print(f"1% higher s: y* changes by {100 * change_s:+.3f}%")
print(f"1% higher A: y* changes by {100 * change_A:+.3f}%")
print(f"1% higher d: y* changes by {100 * change_d:+.3f}%")

1% higher s: y* changes by +0.499%
1% higher A: y* changes by +1.504%
1% higher d: y* changes by -0.496%


The answers are close to 0.5, 1.5 and −0.5 but not exact. An elasticity describes very small changes, and 1 percent is small but not zero.
Check 3: the speed of transition. Equation (6) says that the growth rate of capital depends only on how far \(k_t\) is from \(k^*\). We compare it with the growth rate computed directly from equation (2). The 50 percent row is Islandia right after the storm in What the model predicts.

# Islandia's steady state, the benchmark for "how far from k*"
k_star = steady_state_k(s=0.4, d=0.1)

# For capital at 50%, 95% and 150% of the steady state, compute the growth
# rate of k in two ways; ":.0%" shows a share as a percentage
for share in (0.5, 0.95, 1.5):
    k = share * k_star
    direct = (0.4 * output(k) - 0.1 * k) / k        # equation (2): net investment / k
    formula = 0.1 * ((k_star / k) ** (2 / 3) - 1)   # equation (6)
    print(f"k = {share:.0%} of k*: growth of k = {100 * direct:+.2f}% (direct), {100 * formula:+.2f}% (eq. 6)")

k = 50% of k*: growth of k = +5.87% (direct), +5.87% (eq. 6)
k = 95% of k*: growth of k = +0.35% (direct), +0.35% (eq. 6)
k = 150% of k*: growth of k = -2.37% (direct), -2.37% (eq. 6)


Check 4: population growth. With \(\bar{n} = 0.02\) and \(\bar{d} = 0.08\), equation (9) gives the same steady state as \(\bar{n} = 0\) and \(\bar{d} = 0.1\), because only \(\bar{n}+\bar{d}\) matters. Faster population growth, 3 percent, should lower \(y^*\) by about 5 percent.

# y* with 2% and with 3% population growth (equation 9); n + d is 0.10 and then 0.11
y_n2 = steady_state_y(s=0.4, d=0.08, n=0.02)
y_n3 = steady_state_y(s=0.4, d=0.08, n=0.03)
print(f"n = 2%: y* = {y_n2:.3f}")
print(f"n = 3%: y* = {y_n3:.3f}   ({100 * (y_n3 / y_n2 - 1):+.1f}%)")

n = 2%: y* = 2.000
n = 3%: y* = 1.907   (-4.7%)




5.2.4 Drawing tools
The Solow diagrams of the figures share four small tools: one draws a curve and writes its name on the plot, one draws an arrow along the capital axis, and two set up the axes. Run them and move on, or open the box to see how they work.






NoteShow the drawing tools





As in the textbook, every curve of a Solow diagram carries its name on the plot, right after its last point inside the axes, so the diagrams need no legend. add_curve draws one curve and writes its name. If the name of another curve already sits close by, it leaves the name out, so that two names never overlap.

# @title Drawing tool: a curve with its name on the plot
def add_curve(fig, k, y, label, color, y_max, dash="solid", row=None, col=None):
    """Draw one curve of a Solow diagram and write its name at its last point inside the axes.

    Arguments
        fig      : the figure to draw on
        k, y     : the points of the curve (arrays)
        label    : the curve's name, e.g. "Investment, s·y"
        color    : its color, e.g. TEAL
        y_max    : the top of the vertical axis
        dash     : "solid" or "dash"
        row, col : the panel to draw in (only for figures with two panels, Figs. 5 and 7)
    """
    # Step 1: keep the part of the curve below the top of the axes. `y <= y_max`
    # gives True or False for each point; `k[inside]` keeps the points where it is True.
    inside = y <= y_max
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k[inside], y=y[inside], name=label, mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)), row=row, col=col)
    # [-1] is the last element: the last point inside the axes
    k_end, y_end = k[inside][-1], y[inside][-1]

    # Step 2: is another name already close by? (`abs` is the absolute value)
    for old in fig.layout.annotations:
        if old.showarrow is False and old.xref != "paper":
            if abs(old.y - y_end) < y_max / 12 and abs(old.x - k_end) < k[-1] / 3:
                # yes: a bare `return` leaves the function early, without a name
                return

    # Step 3: write the name right after the curve's last point: level with it when
    # the curve reaches the right edge, just below the top if it leaves through the top
    if inside[-1]:
        anchor = "middle"
    else:
        anchor = "top"
    fig.add_annotation(x=k_end, y=y_end, text=label, showarrow=False, xanchor="left", yanchor=anchor,
                       xshift=5, font=dict(color=color, size=13), row=row, col=col)

add_arrow shows where capital moves: from a starting point toward the steady state.

# @title Drawing tool: an arrow along the capital axis
def add_arrow(fig, k_from, k_to, height):
    """Draw an arrow along the k-axis from k_from to k_to (none if the two are the same).

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        k_from : where capital starts
        k_to   : where capital goes
        height : the height of the arrow on the vertical axis
    """
    # draw it only if the two points are visibly apart
    if abs(k_to - k_from) > 0.1:
        fig.add_annotation(x=k_to, y=height, ax=k_from, ay=height, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor=GREEN)

The axes of each diagram are fixed, so that you can see the curves move. Only when an extreme slider setting would push a steady state off the chart does axis_end widen an axis, by doubling it until the point fits.

# @title Drawing tools: fixed axes that widen only when needed
def axis_end(top, end):
    """The end of a fixed axis, doubled until the highest point fits on the chart.

    Arguments
        top : the highest point to show, e.g. k*
        end : the usual end of the axis
    Returns
        the end of the axis: `end`, or a doubled value if `top` would fall off
    """
    # a `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is true: here, as long as
    # the point would fall off the chart, double the axis
    while top > 0.95 * end:
        end = 2 * end
    return end


def k_axis(k_end):
    """The k-axis of a Solow diagram, from 0 to k_end, with round ticks and none at 0 (the corner).

    Arguments
        k_end : the end of the axis (from axis_end)
    Returns
        the axis settings, for fig.update_layout(xaxis=...)
    """
    # `//` divides and drops the remainder; ticks 5 apart on the usual axis, 0 to 20
    step = 5 * (k_end // 20)
    # list(range(5, 21, 5)) is [5, 10, 15, 20], the ticks of the usual axis
    return dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, k_end], tickvals=list(range(step, k_end + 1, step)))

title: 5. The Solow Growth Model
section: 5.3 The Solow diagram and the steady state
text:
5.3 The Solow diagram and the steady state
We start with the diagram that solves the model: investment and depreciation against capital per person. Where the two curves cross, the economy is in its steady state.

Fig. 1: The Solow diagram
Goal. See why the economy moves toward the steady state \(k^*\) from any starting point \(k_0\).
The Solow diagram plots the two parts of equation (2) against capital per person \(k\):

investment \(\bar{s}y = \bar{s}\bar{A}k^{1/3}\), which is a curve because of diminishing returns;
depreciation \(\bar{d}k\), which is a straight line.

When investment is above depreciation, net investment is positive, so capital grows. When it is below, capital shrinks. Where the two cross, capital stops changing: that point is the steady state \(k^*\). In the figure, the green bar at a starting point \(k_0\) is net investment, the gap between the two curves, and the green arrow on the horizontal axis shows where capital moves.
First we compute the two numbers the figure reports. solow_point finds the steady state \(k^*\) and the net investment at the starting point \(k_0\): the height of the green bar.

def solow_point(s, d, A, k0):
    """The steady state, and net investment at a starting point (Fig. 1).

    Equations (3) and (2):  k* = (s A / d)^(3/2),  net investment = s A k0^(1/3) - d k0

    Arguments
        s  : investment rate, s-bar
        d  : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A  : productivity, A-bar
        k0 : starting capital per person, k0
    Returns
        k_star : steady-state capital per person, k*
        net    : net investment at k0 (positive: capital grows; negative: it shrinks)
    """
    k_star = steady_state_k(s, d, A)
    # investment minus depreciation at k0: the change in capital, equation (2)
    net = s * output(k0, A) - d * k0
    return k_star, net



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, the Solow diagram
def solow_diagram(s=0.4, d=0.1, A=1.0, k0=2.7):
    """The Solow diagram: investment s*y and depreciation d*k against k.

    Draws Fig. 1 (adapted from Fig. 5.1 in Jones), with the net investment bar at k0
    and an arrow that shows where capital moves.

    Arguments
        s  : investment rate, s-bar
        d  : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A  : productivity, A-bar
        k0 : starting capital per person, k0
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (solow_point)
    k_star, net = solow_point(s, d, A, k0)
    # rounded for the title; + 0.0 turns "-0.000" into "0.000"
    net = round(net, 3) + 0.0

    # Step 2: fixed axes, so that you can see the curves move when a parameter
    # changes. 0 to 20, wider only when k* would fall off the chart
    k_end = axis_end(k_star, 20)
    # `np.linspace(0, k_end, 200)`: 200 evenly spaced values of k from 0 to k_end,
    # the points at which we draw the curves
    k = np.linspace(0, k_end, 200)
    # the top of the vertical axis, higher only when needed
    y_max = axis_end(d * max(k0, k_star), 2.2)

    # Step 3: `go.Figure()` starts an empty chart, and each `add_trace` adds one
    # curve or set of points (`add_curve` calls it and writes the curve's name)
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, k, s * output(k, A), "Investment, s·y", TEAL, y_max)
    add_curve(fig, k, d * k, "Depreciation, d·k", BLUE, y_max)
    # the green bar: net investment at k0, from d*k0 up to s*y0
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[k0, k0],
            y=[d * k0, s * output(k0, A)],
            name="Net investment at k0",
            mode="lines",
            line=dict(color=GREEN, width=5),
        )
    )
    # the steady state: a black dot labeled k*
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[k_star],
            y=[d * k_star],
            name="Steady state",
            mode="markers+text",
            text=["k*"],
            textposition="top left",
            marker=dict(color="black", size=11),
        )
    )
    # an arrow on the k-axis (`add_arrow` draws it with `add_annotation`, which
    # writes a piece of text or an arrow on the chart): from k0 toward k*
    add_arrow(fig, k0, k_star, 0.05)

    # Step 4: the title reports k* and net investment at k0
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"k* = {k_star:.2f}   |   net investment at k0 = {k0:.1f}: {net:+.3f}",
        xaxis=k_axis(k_end),
        yaxis=dict(title="Investment and depreciation", range=[0, y_max]),
        showlegend=False,
        margin=dict(r=150),            # room on the right for the curve names
    )
    return fig

# Your turn: try it here



Fig. 2: The Solow diagram with output
Goal. Add the production function to the diagram and read off output, investment and consumption in the steady state.
Every unit of output is either consumed or invested. So consumption per person is the gap between the output curve and the investment curve: \(c = y - \bar{s}y = (1-\bar{s})\,y\).
Again we compute first. steady_state_uses gives the steady state and splits \(y^*\) into its two uses: investment \(\bar{s}y^*\) and consumption \(c^* = (1-\bar{s})\,y^*\).

def steady_state_uses(s, d, A):
    """The steady state, and the two uses of its output (Fig. 2).

    Equations (3) and (1), then y* = s y* + c*:  consumption c* = (1 - s) y*

    Arguments
        s : investment rate, s-bar
        d : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A : productivity, A-bar
    Returns
        k_star, y_star : steady-state capital and output per person, k* and y*
        i_star, c_star : steady-state investment and consumption per person
    """
    # the steady state, equations (3) and (1)
    k_star = steady_state_k(s, d, A)
    y_star = output(k_star, A)
    # every unit of output is either invested or consumed
    i_star = s * y_star
    c_star = (1 - s) * y_star
    return k_star, y_star, i_star, c_star



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, the Solow diagram with output
def solow_with_output(s=0.4, d=0.1, A=1.0):
    """The Solow diagram with output: y, s*y and d*k, with consumption at k*.

    Draws Fig. 2 (adapted from Fig. 5.2 in Jones).

    Arguments
        s : investment rate, s-bar
        d : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A : productivity, A-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (steady_state_uses)
    k_star, y_star, i_star, c_star = steady_state_uses(s, d, A)

    # Step 2: fixed axes. 0 to 20, wider only when k* would fall off the chart
    k_end = axis_end(k_star, 20)
    k = np.linspace(0, k_end, 200)
    # 0 to 3, higher only when y* would fall off the chart
    y_max = axis_end(y_star, 3.0)

    # Step 3: the three curves
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, k, output(k, A), "Output, y", GREEN, y_max)
    add_curve(fig, k, s * output(k, A), "Investment, s·y", TEAL, y_max)
    add_curve(fig, k, d * k, "Depreciation, d·k", BLUE, y_max)

    # Step 4: consumption in the steady state: the black bar from s*y* up to y*
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[k_star, k_star],
            y=[s * y_star, y_star],
            name="Consumption, c*",
            mode="lines+markers",
            line=dict(color="black", width=4),
        )
    )
    # its label, halfway up the bar
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=k_star,
        y=(1 + s) / 2 * y_star,
        text="c*",
        showarrow=False,
        xanchor="left",
        xshift=6,
    )

    # Step 5: the title reports y* and its two uses
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"y* = {y_star:.2f}   investment = {i_star:.2f}   "
            f"consumption c* = {c_star:.2f}"
        ),
        xaxis=k_axis(k_end),
        yaxis=dict(title="Output, investment, depreciation", range=[0, y_max]),
        showlegend=False,
        margin=dict(r=150),            # room on the right for the curve names
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

The black bar \(c^*\) is steady-state consumption. A higher \(\bar{s}\) raises \(y^*\), but it also means a larger share of output is invested rather than consumed.
Productivity \(\bar{A}\) moves both the output curve and the investment curve. That is why it has such a large effect on \(y^*\): the exponent on \(\bar{A}\) in equation (4) is \(3/2\).

5.4 Does the model fit the data?
The steady state makes a simple prediction about capital and investment across countries. Here we check it with the Penn World Table.

Fig. 3: Explaining capital across countries
Goal. Test a prediction of the Solow model with real data.
In the steady state \(\bar{s}y^* = \bar{d}k^*\), so the capital-output ratio is simply (equation 5)
\[\frac{K^*}{Y^*} = \frac{k^*}{y^*} = \frac{\bar{s}}{\bar{d}}\]
If depreciation rates are similar across countries, countries that invest a larger share of their output should have more capital relative to output. Let us check this with the Penn World Table.

Each row is a country. inv_rate_avg_1990_2023 is the average investment rate (percent of GDP) and ky_2023 is the capital-output ratio in 2023. The model’s prediction is equation (5), \(K/Y = s/d\), and predicted_ky computes it. The investment rate in the data is in percent, so the function divides it by 100 first. The drawing code then plots the countries and adds the model’s line with add_curve.

def predicted_ky(s_percent, d):
    """The capital-output ratio that the Solow model predicts (Fig. 3).

    Equation (5):  K*/Y* = s / d

    Arguments
        s_percent : investment rate, s-bar, in percent (as in the data)
        d         : depreciation rate, d-bar
    Returns
        the steady-state capital-output ratio, K*/Y*
    """
    # the data give s in percent: divide by 100 first
    return (s_percent / 100) / d



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, the data and the model line K/Y = s/d
def capital_output_chart(d=0.07):
    """The capital-output ratio against the investment rate, with the model line.

    Draws Fig. 3 (inspired by Fig. 5.3 in Jones): one point per country, and the line
    K/Y = s/d of equation (5).

    Arguments
        d : depreciation rate of the model line, d-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: one point per country; hover over a point to see its name
    fig = px.scatter(
        capital,
        x="inv_rate_avg_1990_2023",
        y="ky_2023",
        hover_name="country",
        labels={
            "inv_rate_avg_1990_2023":
                "Investment rate, s (percent, 1990–2023 average)",
            "ky_2023": "Capital-output ratio, K/Y (2023)",
        },
    )
    # Step 2: the model line, for investment rates from 0 to 55 percent
    s = np.linspace(0, 55, 100)
    add_curve(fig, s, predicted_ky(s, d), "Solow: K/Y = s/d", TEAL, 7)
    # Step 3: fixed axes, so that the line visibly turns when d changes
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Data and the Solow prediction with d = {d:.2f}",
        xaxis=dict(range=[0, 55], tickvals=[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]),
        yaxis_range=[0, 7],
        margin=dict(r=150),            # room on the right for the line's name
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

The points slope upward, as the model predicts: countries that invest more have more capital relative to output.

# Your turn: try it here


Key numbers: how much of the rich–poor gap is due to investment?
With equal depreciation rates, equation (7) splits the income ratio between rich and poor countries into a productivity part and an investment part:
\[\frac{y^*_{rich}}{y^*_{poor}} = \left(\frac{\bar{A}_{rich}}{\bar{A}_{poor}}\right)^{3/2} \times \left(\frac{\bar{s}_{rich}}{\bar{s}_{poor}}\right)^{1/2}\]
In the textbook, the five richest countries are 75 times richer than the five poorest, and investment rates differ by a factor of about 4. Investment therefore explains a factor of \(\sqrt{4}=2\), which leaves \(75/2 = 37.5\) for productivity. Let us redo the calculation with the latest data. title: 5. The Solow Growth Model
text:
5.5 Experiments: more investment, faster depreciation
Now we change one parameter at a time and watch the economy move to a new steady state, first in the diagram and then year by year.

Fig. 4: An increase in the investment rate
Goal. Run the first experiment. The economy sits in its steady state, and then the investment rate rises permanently from \(\bar{s}\) to \(\bar{s}'\).
The investment curve \(\bar{s}y\) rotates upward, and the depreciation line does not move. At the old \(k^*\), investment now exceeds depreciation, so capital accumulates until the new steady state \(k^{**}\).
The function below draws the diagram. It needs only the two steady states of equation (3), from steady_state_k, so all of its code is drawing code: open it to see how the curves and the dots are placed.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, an increase in the investment rate
def increase_in_s(s=0.4, s_new=0.6, d=0.1, A=1.0):
    """The Solow diagram when the investment rate rises from s to s_new.

    Draws Fig. 4 (adapted from Fig. 5.4 in Jones): the investment curve shifts up, and
    capital moves from the old steady state k* to the new one, k**.

    Arguments
        s     : old investment rate, s-bar
        s_new : new investment rate, s-bar'
        d     : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A     : productivity, A-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the old and the new steady state, equation (3)
    k_old, k_new = steady_state_k(s, d, A), steady_state_k(s_new, d, A)

    # Step 2: fixed axes. 0 to 25, wider only when a steady state would fall off
    k_end = axis_end(max(k_old, k_new), 25)
    k = np.linspace(0, k_end, 200)
    y_max = axis_end(d * max(k_old, k_new), 2.75)

    # Step 3: the curves; the new ones first, so that their names win a tight spot
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, k, s_new * output(k, A), "s′·y (new)", TEAL, y_max)
    add_curve(fig, k, d * k, "Depreciation, d·k", BLUE, y_max)
    add_curve(fig, k, s * output(k, A), "s·y (old)", GRAY, y_max, dash="dash")

    # Step 4: the two steady states, labeled where no curve passes
    if k_new > k_old:
        places = ["bottom right", "top left"]
    else:
        places = ["top left", "bottom right"]
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[k_old, k_new],
            y=[d * k_old, d * k_new],
            name="k* (old) and k** (new)",
            mode="markers+text",
            text=["k*", "k**"],
            textposition=places,
            marker=dict(color="black", size=11),
        )
    )
    # an arrow on the k-axis, from k* to k**
    add_arrow(fig, k_old, k_new, 0.08)

    # Step 5: the title reports both steady states and their ratio
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"k* = {k_old:.2f}  →  k** = {k_new:.2f}   "
            f"(k**/k* = {k_new / k_old:.2f})"
        ),
        xaxis=k_axis(k_end),
        yaxis=dict(title="Investment and depreciation", range=[0, y_max]),
        showlegend=False,
        margin=dict(r=150),            # room on the right for the curve names
    )
    return fig



# Fig. 4 with sliders for the old and the new investment rate
interact(
    increase_in_s,

);

What to notice.

With \(\bar{s}\) going from 0.4 to 0.6, steady-state capital rises by a factor of \((0.6/0.4)^{3/2} \approx 1.84\).
Set \(\bar{s}' < \bar{s}\) and the experiment runs in reverse: capital falls to a lower steady state.

Fig. 5: Output after an increase in the investment rate
Goal. Follow output per person year by year after the investment rate rises in 2030.
The Solow model cannot be solved with a formula for every year, but a computer can simply apply equation (2) one year at a time. This is called a simulation. The function below starts the economy in its old steady state and changes the parameters in change_year. We will reuse it in Figs. 7 and 13.

def simulate(s_old=0.4, s_new=0.4, d_old=0.1, d_new=0.1, destroyed=0.0,
             A=1.0, change_year=2030, first_year=2015, last_year=2115):
    """Output per person, year by year, when something changes in change_year.

    Equation (2) applied once a year. The economy starts in its old steady state.
    From change_year on, the investment rate is s_new and the depreciation rate is
    d_new; in change_year a share `destroyed` of the capital stock is lost.

    Arguments
        s_old, s_new : investment rate before and from change_year, s-bar and s-bar'
        d_old, d_new : depreciation rate before and from change_year, d-bar and d-bar'
        destroyed    : the share of capital lost in change_year (0: none)
        A            : productivity, A-bar
        change_year  : the year of the change
        first_year, last_year : the first and the last year of the simulation
    Returns
        years  : the years, first_year to last_year
        y_path : output per person in each of those years (an array)
    """
    # Step 1: the years; `np.arange(2015, 2116)` gives the whole years 2015 to 2115
    years = np.arange(first_year, last_year + 1)
    # start in the old steady state
    k = steady_state_k(s_old, d_old, A)

    # Step 2: one pass of the `for` loop per year. `y_path = []` starts an empty
    # list, and `y_path.append(...)` adds one more number to its end
    y_path = []
    for year in years:
        # this year's parameters: the old ones before the change, the new ones from it
        if year < change_year:
            s, d = s_old, d_old
        else:
            s, d = s_new, d_new
        if year == change_year:
            k = k * (1 - destroyed)            # an earthquake or a war destroys capital
        y_path.append(output(k, A))
        # capital accumulation, equation (2): next year's k
        k = k + s * output(k, A) - d * k
    return years, np.array(y_path)

The figure has two panels: (a) the Solow diagram with output, and (b) output per person over time. Panel (a) is small, so its curves carry short names: output \(y\), the old investment curve \(\bar{s}y\) (dashed), the new one \(\bar{s}'y\), and depreciation \(\bar{d}k\).
On a ratio scale (a logarithmic axis), equal distances mean equal percentage changes. The slope of the line is then the growth rate.
Two numbers come out of the experiment: the new steady state \(k^{**}\), and the growth rate of output in 2031, the first year after the change. rise_in_s runs the simulation and computes both.

def rise_in_s(s_new=0.6, s=0.4, d=0.1):
    """The experiment of Fig. 5: the investment rate rises from s to s_new in 2030.

    Equation (2) year by year (simulate), and the new steady state, equation (3).

    Arguments
        s_new : new investment rate, s-bar'
        s     : old investment rate, s-bar
        d     : depreciation rate, d-bar
    Returns
        years, y    : the years 2015-2115 and output per person in each
        k_new       : the new steady-state capital per person, k**
        growth_2031 : the growth rate of output per person in 2031, in percent
    """
    years, y = simulate(s_old=s, s_new=s_new, d_old=d, d_new=d)
    # the new steady state; the simulation approaches it
    k_new = steady_state_k(s_new, d)
    # y[15] is 2030 and y[16] is 2031
    growth_2031 = 100 * (y[16] / y[15] - 1)
    return years, y, k_new, growth_2031

    """The Solow diagram when the depreciation rate rises from d to d_new.

    and capital falls from the old steady state k* to the new one, k**.

    Arguments

        A     : productivity, A-bar
    Returns

    # Step 1: the old and the new steady state, equation (3)
    k_old, k_new = steady_state_k(s, d, A), steady_state_k(s, d_new, A)

    # Step 2: fixed axes. 0 to 20, wider only when a steady state would fall off
    k_end = axis_end(max(k_old, k_new), 20)

    # Step 4: the two steady states, labeled where no curve passes
    if k_new < k_old:

    else:

    fig.add_trace(

            text=["k*", "k**"],
            textposition=places,
            marker=dict(color="black", size=11),
        )
    )
    # an arrow on the k-axis, from k* to k**
    add_arrow(fig, k_old, k_new, 0.06)

    # Step 5: the title reports both steady states and their ratio
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(

5.6 Transition dynamics in the data
The model says that an economy grows faster the farther it is below its steady state. These figures look for that pattern in real growth rates and investment rates.

Fig. 8: Growth rates in the OECD
Goal. Use the principle of transition dynamics to read real growth data.
If rich countries share similar steady states, those that were poorer at the start should be further below their steady state, and so they should grow faster. We check this for the 24 OECD countries that the textbook uses, measuring growth from a starting year up to 2023.

def growth_since(start, end=2023):
    """One row per country: GDP per person in `start`, and its growth up to `end`.

    Average annual growth, in percent:  100 ((end value / start value)^(1 / years) - 1)

    Arguments
        start : the starting year
        end   : the last year
    Returns
        a table: the country, its OECD flag, GDP per person in both years, the
        average annual growth rate and the starting year
    """
    # Step 1: GDP per person in the first and in the last year
    first = panel[panel.year == start][["iso3", "country", "oecd", "gdp_pc"]]
    last = panel[panel.year == end][["iso3", "gdp_pc"]]
    # Step 2: `merge` joins the two tables on the country code `iso3`, much like
    # matching rows by ID in a spreadsheet; the suffixes name the two GDP columns
    table = first.merge(last, on="iso3", suffixes=("_start", "_end")).dropna()
    # Step 3: the average annual growth rate, in percent
    table["growth"] = 100 * (
        (table.gdp_pc_end / table.gdp_pc_start) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1
    )
    table["start_year"] = start
    return table

def short(name):
    """A short country name for titles.

    For example 'Bolivia (Plurinational State of)' -> 'Bolivia'.

    Arguments
        name : the country's name in the data
    Returns
        the short name
    """
    # `name.split(" (")[0]` cuts the text at " (" and keeps the first piece:
    # this drops '(...)' and ': Mainland'
    name = name.split(" (")[0].split(":")[0]
    # `SHORT_NAMES.get(name, name)` looks the name up in the dictionary, and
    # returns it unchanged when it is not there
    return SHORT_NAMES.get(name, name)

# 44 colors from two of Plotly's palettes

for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:

        PALETTE.append(c)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")              # too close to the book's U.S. blue: used last

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 10, a color for every country
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses.

    As far as the palette allows: when every color is taken, the country gets the one
    that its groups use least.

    Arguments
        names  : the countries to color, one at a time
        groups : the lists of countries shown together (the website's menu views)
        fixed  : {country: color} for the book's countries, or None
    Returns
        a dictionary {country: color}
    """
    # start from a copy of the fixed colors (or an empty dictionary)
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue                    # `continue` skips to the next country
        # Step 1: the list `used` collects the colors of the countries shown with it
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            for other in group:
                if name in group and other in colors:
                    used.append(colors[other])
        # Step 2: the palette colors not in `used`; best of all, one no country has yet
        free, unused = [], []
        for c in PALETTE:
            if c not in used:
                free.append(c)
                if c not in colors.values():
                    unused.append(c)
        # Step 3: no free color: the one `used` counts least often (`.count`),
        # searching from the end of the palette (`reversed`)
        least = PALETTE[-1]
        for c in reversed(PALETTE):
            if used.count(c) < used.count(least):
                least = c
        # the first of: an unused color, a free one, the least used one
        colors[name] = (unused + free + [least])[0]
    return colors

The economics of Fig. 10 is one number per country: its average investment rate since 1990. investment_data picks the rows of the chosen countries and computes it.

def investment_data(country_a, country_b):
    """The investment rates of Fig. 10: two countries and the United States.

    Arguments
        country_a, country_b : the two countries to compare (names as in `panel`)
    Returns
        names    : the chosen countries, each once, without the United States
        chosen   : their rows of `panel` with data, and those of the United States
        averages : each country's average investment rate since 1990, in percent
        missing  : the countries with no investment data
    """
    # Step 1: each country once (you might pick the same country twice, or the
    # United States, which is always drawn)
    names, missing = [], []
    for name in [country_a, country_b]:
        if name != "United States" and name not in names:
            names.append(name)
    # Step 2: their rows; `panel.country.isin([...])` keeps the rows whose country
    # is in the list
    chosen = panel[panel.country.isin(names + ["United States"])]
    chosen = chosen.dropna(subset=["inv_rate"])
    # Step 3: each country's average investment rate since 1990, and the countries
    # that have no data at all
    averages = {}
    for name in names + ["United States"]:
        recent = chosen[(chosen.country == name) & (chosen.year >= 1990)].inv_rate
        averages[name] = recent.mean()
        if name not in set(chosen.country):
            missing.append(name)
    return names, chosen, averages, missing

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 10, investment in two countries and the U.S.
def investment_chart(country_a="Republic of Korea", country_b="Philippines"):
    """The investment rates of two countries and the United States, 1950-2023.

    Draws Fig. 10 (inspired by Fig. 5.10 in Jones).

    Arguments
        country_a, country_b : the two countries drawn next to the United States
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (investment_data), and a title with each average since 1990
    names, chosen, averages, missing = investment_data(country_a, country_b)
    title = "Average investment rate since 1990:"
    for name in names + ["United States"]:
        title = title + f" {short(name)} {averages[name]:.0f}%,"
    # `.rstrip(",")` removes the last comma
    title = title.rstrip(",")
    if missing:
        short_missing = []
        for name in missing:
            short_missing.append(short(name))
        title = f"No investment data for {' and '.join(short_missing)}"

    # Step 2: one line per country, each in its own color
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y="inv_rate",
        color="country",
        category_orders={"country": names + ["United States"]},
        color_discrete_map=INV_COLORS,
        labels={"inv_rate": "Investment rate (percent of GDP)", "year": "Year"},
    )

    # Step 3: the textbook's 0-60 percent, widened in steps for the few countries
    # that invest more. `a if condition else b` gives a when the condition is true
    # and b otherwise; `np.ceil` rounds up
    top = 60
    biggest = chosen.inv_rate.max()
    if biggest > 57:

    fig.update_layout(
        title=title,
        yaxis_range=[min(0, chosen.inv_rate.min() - 2), top],
        xaxis=dict(range=[1950, 2023], tickvals=[1960, 1980, 2000, 2020]),
        legend_title_text="",
    )

What to notice.

Korea’s investment rate rose from about 13 percent in the 1950s to more than 40 percent in the 1990s. Investment in the United States and the Philippines stayed much flatter.
Choose Singapore and Botswana, two other fast growers of Fig. 9. Singapore already invested about 40 percent of GDP around 1960 and peaked at 68 percent in 1982 (the vertical axis widens to show it). Botswana’s rate jumped from below 10 percent in 1965 to about 60 percent in the early 1970s, when its first diamond mines were built. In small economies one large project can move the rate by 10 points or more in a year.
A permanently higher investment rate means a higher steady state, and Korea grew fast during its transition toward it.


Key numbers: Korea relative to the United States
With equal depreciation rates, equation (7) gives the ratio of steady-state incomes:
\[\frac{y^*_{Korea}}{y^*_{US}} = \left(\frac{\bar{A}_{Korea}}{\bar{A}_{US}}\right)^{3/2} \times \left(\frac{\bar{s}_{Korea}}{\bar{s}_{US}}\right)^{1/2}\]
We take the investment rates from the data, and then ask what productivity ratio would explain the actual income ratio in 2023.

# Step 1: the investment rates since 1990 (computed for Fig. 3's Key numbers) and
# GDP per person in 2023; `.iloc[0]` takes the value of the first (only) row
s_kor, s_usa = investment["Republic of Korea"], investment["United States"]
y_kor = latest[latest.country == "Republic of Korea"].gdp_pc.iloc[0]
y_usa = latest[latest.country == "United States"].gdp_pc.iloc[0]

# Step 2: equation (7) with equal depreciation rates: the investment part, and
# then the productivity ratio that explains the rest
investment_part = (s_kor / s_usa) ** 0.5
# solve equation (7) for A_Korea / A_US
A_ratio = ((y_kor / y_usa) / investment_part) ** (2 / 3)
print(f"Investment rates since 1990: Korea {s_kor:.1f}%, United States {s_usa:.1f}%")
print(f"Investment part of eq. (7):  {investment_part:.2f}")
print(f"Actual income ratio, 2023:   {y_kor / y_usa:.2f}")
print(f"Implied productivity ratio:  {A_ratio:.2f}")

title: 5. The Solow Growth Model
text:
5.7 Population growth
Adding population growth gives a second reason why capital per person can fall, and it lowers the steady state.

Fig. 11: The Solow diagram with population growth
Goal. Add population growth at rate \(\bar{n}\) and see what changes.
Every year new workers arrive, and they must be equipped with capital too. Part of investment is therefore used up just to keep capital per person constant. The capital accumulation equation becomes equation (8):
\[\Delta k_{t+1} = \bar{s}y_t - (\bar{n}+\bar{d})\,k_t\]
so population growth works like extra depreciation. The steady state is \(y^* = \bar{A}^{3/2}\left(\frac{\bar{s}}{\bar{n}+\bar{d}}\right)^{1/2}\) (equation 9). In the figure, the dashed gray line \(\bar{d}k\) shows the case without population growth. We keep \(\bar{n}+\bar{d}=0.10\) at the start, so the baseline is the same as in Fig. 1.
The function below draws the diagram from the steady state of equation (9), so all of its code is drawing code.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 11, the Solow diagram with population growth
def solow_with_population(s=0.4, n=0.02, d=0.08, A=1.0):
    """The Solow diagram with population growth: s*y against the line (n + d)*k.

    Draws Fig. 11 (adapted from Fig. 5.11 in Jones).

    Arguments
        s : investment rate, s-bar
        n : population growth rate, n-bar
        d : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A : productivity, A-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the steady state with population growth, equation (9)
    k_star = steady_state_k(s, d, A, n=n)
    y_star = output(k_star, A)

    # Step 2: fixed axes. 0 to 20, wider only when k* would fall off the chart
    k_end = axis_end(k_star, 20)
    k = np.linspace(0, k_end, 200)
    y_max = axis_end(s * y_star, 2.2)

    # Step 3: the curves; the dashed gray line is the case without population growth
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, k, s * output(k, A), "Investment, s·y", TEAL, y_max)
    add_curve(fig, k, (n + d) * k, "(n + d)·k", BLUE, y_max)
    add_curve(fig, k, d * k, "d·k", GRAY, y_max, dash="dash")
    # the steady state: a black dot labeled k*
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[k_star],
            y=[(n + d) * k_star],
            name="Steady state",
            mode="markers+text",
            text=["k*"],
            textposition="top left",
            marker=dict(color="black", size=11),
        )
    )

    # Step 4: the title reports k*, y* and the growth rate of total GDP, n

text:
5.8 A disaster: the earthquake
Finally, a shock that destroys capital but leaves every parameter unchanged. The model predicts a fast recovery back to the old steady state.

Fig. 12: The Solow diagram after an earthquake
Goal. See what happens when a disaster destroys part of the capital stock but leaves the population and the parameters unchanged.
An earthquake does not shift any curve, because \(\bar{s}\), \(\bar{d}\) and \(\bar{A}\) are all the same. The economy just jumps to the left along the \(k\)-axis. Below the steady state, investment exceeds depreciation, so capital grows back toward the same \(k^*\).
The earthquake changes one number: capital per person falls from \(k^*\) to \(k_0\). earthquake_capital computes both.

def earthquake_capital(destroyed, s=0.4, d=0.1, A=1.0):
    """Capital per person before and right after an earthquake (Fig. 12).

    Equation (3) for k*, then k0 = (1 - destroyed) k*; no parameter changes.

    Arguments
        destroyed : the share of the capital stock destroyed
        s         : investment rate, s-bar
        d         : depreciation rate, d-bar
        A         : productivity, A-bar
    Returns
        k_star : capital per person before the earthquake, the steady state k*
        k0     : capital per person right after it
    """
    k_star = steady_state_k(s, d, A)
    # the earthquake destroys a share of the capital stock
    k0 = (1 - destroyed) * k_star
    return k_star, k0



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 12, the jump from k* to k0
def mark_earthquake(fig, k_star, k0, A):
    """Mark the earthquake on the Solow diagram of Fig. 12.

    Two dots on the output curve, y* before and y0 after, and a red arrow along the
    k-axis from k* to k0.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        k_star : capital per person before the earthquake, k*
        k0     : capital per person right after it
        A      : productivity, A-bar
    """
    # output before and after: two dots on the output curve
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[k_star, k0],
            y=[output(k_star, A), output(k0, A)],
            name="Output before and after",
            mode="markers+text",
            text=["y*", "y0"],
            textposition="top left",
            marker=dict(color="black", size=11),
        )
    )
    # the red arrow: the jump from k* to k0, drawn in the units of the axes
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=k0,
        y=0.15,
        ax=k_star,
        ay=0.15,
        xref="x",
        yref="y",
        axref="x",
        ayref="y",
        showarrow=True,
        arrowhead=3,
        arrowwidth=2,
        arrowcolor="crimson",
        text="earthquake",
    )




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 12, the Solow diagram after an earthquake
def earthquake_diagram(destroyed=0.5):
    """The Solow diagram when an earthquake moves the economy from k* to k0.

    Draws Fig. 12 (adapted from Fig. 5.12 in Jones); no curve shifts.

    Arguments
        destroyed : the share of the capital stock destroyed
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the parameters do not change; capital before and after
    s, d, A = 0.4, 0.1, 1.0
    k_star, k0 = earthquake_capital(destroyed, s, d, A)
    k = np.linspace(0, 14, 200)

    # Step 2: the three curves; 2.7 is the top of the vertical axis
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, k, output(k, A), "Output, y", GREEN, 2.7)
    add_curve(fig, k, s * output(k, A), "Investment, s·y", TEAL, 2.7)
    add_curve(fig, k, d * k, "Depreciation, d·k", BLUE, 2.7)
    # Step 3: output before and after, and the jump from k* to k0
    mark_earthquake(fig, k_star, k0, A)

    # Step 4: the title reports the fall in capital and in output
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"k falls from {k_star:.1f} to {k0:.1f};  "
            f"output falls to {output(k0) / output(k_star):.0%} of y*"
        ),
        xaxis=dict(
            title="Capital per person, k",
            range=[0, 14],
            tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14],
        ),
        yaxis=dict(title="Output, investment, depreciation", range=[0, 2.7]),
        showlegend=False,
        margin=dict(r=150),            # room on the right for the curve names
    )
    return fig

The steady state does not change, so the economy eventually returns to exactly where it started.

# Your turn: try it here



Fig. 13: Output per person after an earthquake
Goal. Follow the recovery year by year. We reuse simulate, now with a destroyed share of capital in 2030.
The recovery has two numbers: how much output falls in 2030, and the first year in which it is back within 1 percent of \(y^*\). earthquake_recovery simulates the economy and computes both.

def earthquake_recovery(destroyed):
    """Output per person when an earthquake destroys capital in 2030 (Fig. 13).

    Equation (2) year by year (simulate), from the steady state.

    Arguments
        destroyed : the share of the capital stock destroyed in 2030
    Returns
        years, y : the years 2015-2115 and output per person in each
        fall     : the fall in output in 2030, in percent of y*
        back     : the years after 2030 in which output is back within 1% of y*
    """
    years, y = simulate(destroyed=destroyed)
    # y[0] is the steady state y* (2015) and y[15] is output in 2030
    fall = 100 * (1 - y[15] / y[0])
    # a boolean array is True where both conditions hold; `years[...]` keeps those
    back = years[(years > 2030) & (y >= 0.99 * y[0])]
    return years, y, fall, back



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 13, output per person after an earthquake
def output_after_earthquake(destroyed=0.5, scale="ratio"):
    """Output per person over time when an earthquake destroys capital in 2030.

    Draws Fig. 13 (adapted from Fig. 5.13 in Jones).

    Arguments
        destroyed : the share of the capital stock destroyed in 2030
        scale     : "ratio" or "linear", the vertical scale
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the recovery (earthquake_recovery)
    years, y, fall, back = earthquake_recovery(destroyed)

    # Step 2: output over time, and the steady state as a dashed line
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=years,
            y=y,
            name="Output per person",
            line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3),
        )
    )
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[2015, 2115],
            y=[y[0], y[0]],
            name="Steady state y*",
            mode="lines",
            line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash"),
        )
    )

    # Step 3: a ratio or a linear vertical scale
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(
            type="log",
            range=[np.log10(0.8), np.log10(2.2)],
            tickvals=[1, 1.5, 2],
        )
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0.8, 2.2])

    # Step 4: the title reports the fall and the first year back near y*
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"Output falls by {fall:.0f}% in 2030 and is back "
            f"within 1% of y* in {back[0]}"
        ),
        xaxis=dict(
            title="Year",
            range=[2015, 2115],
            tickvals=[2030, 2050, 2070, 2090, 2110],
        ),
        yaxis_title="Output per person, y",
    )
    return fig

title: 5. The Solow Growth Model
text:
5.9 Concluding remarks

The Solow model makes capital endogenous. Its two key equations, the production function (1) and capital accumulation (2), say that capital grows when investment \(\bar{s}y\) exceeds depreciation \(\bar{d}k\). It stops growing at the steady state, equations (3) and (4): \(k^* = (\bar{s}\bar{A}/\bar{d})^{3/2}\) and \(y^* = (\bar{s}/\bar{d})^{1/2}\bar{A}^{3/2}\).
The elasticities of \(y^*\) are \(3/2\) for productivity and only \(1/2\) for the investment rate, so productivity differences explain most income gaps between countries (equation 7).
Because of diminishing returns to capital, capital accumulation cannot be the engine of long-run growth: output per person settles at a constant \(y^*\).
Changes in \(\bar{s}\), \(\bar{d}\) or \(\bar{n}\) change the level of the steady state. The economy then grows or shrinks for a while, and fastest when it is farthest from the steady state (the principle of transition dynamics, equation 6). Population growth works like extra depreciation, equations (8) and (9).
The data agree with the model on capital-output ratios (equation 5) and on catch-up within the OECD. But for the world as a whole, productivity differences, not investment, explain most of the gap between rich and poor countries.
The next chapter looks for the engine of long-run growth: new ideas.

title: 5. The Solow Growth Model
text:
Practice problems
These problems put the Solow model to work in three ways, at three levels (Basic, Intermediate and Challenge): conceptual problems apply its equations to real growth stories, data-based problems send you back to this chapter’s Penn World Table files, and modeling problems answer policy questions with the chapter’s interactive diagrams. Try each problem on your own first, and only then open its Hint and its Solution. The sliders of the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of the matching figure above.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): Can investment alone keep growth going? In the 1950s and 1960s the Soviet Union grew fast, largely by investing massively in factories and machines. Krugman (1994) argued that growth driven by more inputs, rather than by higher productivity, runs into diminishing returns and must slow down. Easterly and Fischer (1995) found that Soviet growth slowed from 1950 to 1987 because the returns to capital fell, while productivity growth stayed roughly constant. Use equation (4), and hold \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{d}\) fixed.

A planner raises the investment rate in steps of 10 points: from 0.2 to 0.3, then to 0.4, then to 0.5. By what percentage does steady-state output per person \(y^*\) rise at each step?
Start from \(\bar{s} = 0.4\). What is the largest rise in \(y^*\) that any investment rate could deliver, and how much would people consume at that rate?
In two or three sentences, use the model to explain why growth that relies on investment alone slows down.



Hint

With \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{d}\) fixed, equation (4) makes \(y^*\) proportional to \(\bar{s}^{1/2}\). So the ratio of two steady states is the square root of the ratio of the two investment rates. For (b), ask how large \(\bar{s}\) can possibly be.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Write equation (4) for the old and the new investment rate and divide. \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{d}\) cancel:
\[\frac{y^*_{new}}{y^*_{old}} = \left(\frac{\bar{s}_{new}}{\bar{s}_{old}}\right)^{1/2}.\]

From 0.2 to 0.3: \(1.5^{1/2} \approx 1.225\), so \(y^*\) rises by 22.5 percent.
From 0.3 to 0.4: \((4/3)^{1/2} \approx 1.155\), a rise of 15.5 percent.
From 0.4 to 0.5: \(1.25^{1/2} \approx 1.118\), a rise of 11.8 percent.

Each step moves another 10 percent of output from consumption to investment, but it buys a smaller and smaller gain.
(b) The investment rate cannot be larger than 1. At \(\bar{s} = 1\), output per person would be \((1/0.4)^{1/2} = 2.5^{1/2} \approx 1.581\) times its level at \(\bar{s} = 0.4\): at most 58 percent more. But consumption, \(c^* = (1-\bar{s})y^*\), would be zero. All of output would go into replacing the capital that wears out.
(c) Because of diminishing returns, each new machine adds less output than the one before (the exponent \(1/3\) on capital), but it adds the same \(\bar{d}\) to depreciation. So a higher investment rate raises the steady state by less and less, and once the economy reaches its new steady state, growth stops. Investment alone gives a burst of growth during the transition, not growth that lasts. To keep growing, an economy must keep raising its productivity \(\bar{A}\), which is the point of Krugman’s argument and of the Soviet record. Chapter 6 shows where lasting productivity growth comes from.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Ethiopia’s investment boom. The World Bank credits Ethiopia’s state-led development model with improving infrastructure and living standards (World Bank). In our Penn World Table data, Ethiopia’s investment rate averaged 4.9 percent of GDP in 1990–1999 and 24.9 percent in 2010–2019. GDP per person rose from 666 dollars in 1999 to 2,439 dollars in 2019 (in 2021 dollars).

Hold \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{d}\) fixed. By what factor would the rise in the investment rate alone raise Ethiopia’s steady-state output per person?
Suppose that Ethiopia was close to its steady state both in 1999 and in 2019. By what factor must productivity \(\bar{A}\) have risen to explain the actual rise in GDP per person?
Take logs of equation (4). What share of the rise in \(\ln y\) does investment account for, and what share does productivity?
Is the assumption of (b) plausible? If Ethiopia was still below its new steady state in 2019, is the true rise in \(\bar{A}\) larger or smaller than your answer to (b)?



Hint

For (a), equation (4) makes \(y^*\) proportional to \(\bar{s}^{1/2}\). For (b), write equation (4) for both years and divide: \(y^*_{2019}/y^*_{1999} = (\bar{A}_{2019}/\bar{A}_{1999})^{3/2}\times(\bar{s}_{2019}/\bar{s}_{1999})^{1/2}\). Then solve for the productivity ratio. For (c), the log of a product is the sum of the logs.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) With \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{d}\) fixed, \(y^*\) changes with the square root of the investment rate: \((24.9/4.9)^{1/2} = 5.08^{1/2} \approx 2.25\). A fivefold rise in the investment rate would, on its own, a bit more than double steady-state output per person.
(b) The actual rise is \(2{,}439/666 \approx 3.66\). If both years are steady states, equation (4) gives
\[3.66 = \left(\frac{\bar{A}_{2019}}{\bar{A}_{1999}}\right)^{3/2}\times 2.25
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\bar{A}_{2019}}{\bar{A}_{1999}} = \left(\frac{3.66}{2.25}\right)^{2/3} \approx 1.38.\]
Productivity would have risen by about 38 percent in 20 years, or 1.6 percent a year.
(c) In logs, equation (4) for the two years gives
\[\ln\frac{y_{2019}}{y_{1999}} = \frac{3}{2}\ln\frac{\bar{A}_{2019}}{\bar{A}_{1999}} + \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{\bar{s}_{2019}}{\bar{s}_{1999}}.\]
The investment term is \(\ln 2.25 \approx 0.81\) and the total is \(\ln 3.66 \approx 1.30\), so investment accounts for \(\ln 2.25/\ln 3.66 \approx 0.63\) of the rise, and productivity for the remaining 0.37. This is unusual. Across countries, investment explains only a small part of income gaps (Key numbers under Fig. 3). Ethiopia is an exception because its investment rate rose fivefold.
(d) Probably not. Equation (6) says that capital moves only gradually toward a new steady state, so after only a decade or so of high investment Ethiopia was most likely still catching up in 2019, with \(y_{2019}\) below its new steady state. The steady-state rise would then be larger than 3.66, and the rise in \(\bar{A}\) needed to explain it larger than 38 percent. Our 38 percent is a lower bound. The same World Bank page adds that the model did not raise productivity enough to transform the economy, and in our data Ethiopia’s investment rate fell back to 12.7 percent by 2023.
The numbers, as a check:
inv_factor = (24.9 / 4.9) ** 0.5                    # (a) equation (4) with A and d fixed
income_factor = 2439 / 666                           # (b) the actual rise in y
A_factor = (income_factor / inv_factor) ** (2 / 3)
print(f"(a) investment factor: {inv_factor:.2f}")
print(f"(b) income factor: {income_factor:.2f}, implied productivity factor: {A_factor:.2f}")
print(f"(c) investment share of the rise in ln y: {np.log(inv_factor) / np.log(income_factor):.2f}")
It prints 2.25, then 3.66 and 1.38, then 0.63.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Why doesn’t capital flow to poor countries? With diminishing returns, capital should earn much more where it is scarce, so savers in rich countries should be eager to invest in poor ones. Lucas (1990) pointed out that a simple production model predicts a return to capital in India many times the return in the United States, and yet capital does not flow that way. In our data, GDP per person in the United States was 8.1 times that of India in 2023, and the average investment rates since 1990 were 23.8 percent (United States) and 25.0 percent (India).

With \(y = \bar{A}k^{1/3}\), the marginal product of capital is \(MPK = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}k^{-2/3}\). Show that \(MPK = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}^{3}y^{-2}\). If India and the United States had the same \(\bar{A}\), how many times larger would India’s MPK be in 2023?
Lucas used a capital exponent of 0.4 and a U.S.–India income ratio of 15. Redo (a) for \(y = \bar{A}k^{\alpha}\), and find his answer.
Now let each country have its own \(\bar{A}\), and suppose that both are in their steady states, with the same \(\bar{d}\). Use equation (5) to find the ratio of their MPKs. What solves the puzzle?



Hint

Solve the production function for capital, \(k = (y/\bar{A})^3\), and substitute it into the MPK. For (c), equation (5) gives \(y^*/k^*\), and \(MPK = \frac{1}{3}\,y/k\) (step 7 of the Model overview).

Your answer:


Solution

(a) From \(y = \bar{A}k^{1/3}\) we get \(k^{1/3} = y/\bar{A}\), so \(k = (y/\bar{A})^3\) and
\[k^{-2/3} = \left(\frac{y}{\bar{A}}\right)^{-2} = \bar{A}^{2}y^{-2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
MPK = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\cdot\bar{A}^{2}y^{-2} = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}^{3}y^{-2}.\]
With the same \(\bar{A}\), only \(y\) differs, so \(MPK_{India}/MPK_{US} = (y_{US}/y_{India})^{2} = 8.1^2 \approx 66\). A machine in India would earn about 66 times as much as the same machine in the United States.
(b) Now \(MPK = \alpha\bar{A}k^{\alpha-1}\) and \(k = (y/\bar{A})^{1/\alpha}\), so \(k^{\alpha-1} = (y/\bar{A})^{(\alpha-1)/\alpha}\) and
\[MPK = \alpha\bar{A}^{1/\alpha}y^{(\alpha-1)/\alpha}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{MPK_{India}}{MPK_{US}} = \left(\frac{y_{US}}{y_{India}}\right)^{(1-\alpha)/\alpha}.\]
With \(\alpha = 0.4\) the exponent is \(0.6/0.4 = 1.5\), and \(15^{1.5} \approx 58.1\): Lucas’s famous factor of 58.
(c) In the steady state \(k^*/y^* = \bar{s}/\bar{d}\) (equation 5), so
\[MPK^* = \frac{1}{3}\,\frac{y^*}{k^*} = \frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\bar{d}}{\bar{s}}.\]
Productivity has dropped out. With the same \(\bar{d}\), \(MPK_{India}/MPK_{US} = \bar{s}_{US}/\bar{s}_{India} = 23.8/25.0 \approx 0.95\): India’s return would be about 5 percent lower, not 66 times higher. The puzzle came from assuming the same \(\bar{A}\). India is poorer mainly because its productivity is lower (equation 7), and lower productivity also lowers what each machine earns. By the formula of (a), the two MPKs are equal when \(\bar{A}_{India}/\bar{A}_{US} = (1/8.1)^{2/3} \approx 0.25\). When Caselli and Feyrer (2007) measured MPKs across countries, they found them “remarkably similar”. The policy lesson: more capital alone does not earn high returns in a poor country unless its productivity rises too.



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): Do rich countries invest more? Equation (4) says that countries that invest more should be richer. Check this with the Penn World Table 11.0 (pwt_panel.csv) and the World Bank income groups in regions.csv. Compute each country’s average investment rate since 1990, after dropping the implausible rows above 100 percent (see the warning under Fig. 3), and then the median of these averages in each income group. Do the medians rise with income?


Hint

Keep the rows with (pwt.year >= 1990) & (pwt.inv_rate <= 100), average inv_rate by iso3 with groupby, and attach the averages to the regions.csv table with .map on its iso3 column. Then use groupby("income_group") and .median().


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(c) Divide the accumulation equation by \(K_t\):

(a) By equation (4), \(c^* = (1-\bar{s})(\bar{s}/\bar{d})^{1/2}\bar{A}^{3/2}\). In logs,
\[\ln c^* = \ln(1-\bar{s}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\bar{s} - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\bar{d} + \tfrac{3}{2}\ln\bar{A}.\]
Setting the derivative with respect to \(\bar{s}\) to zero:
\[-\frac{1}{1-\bar{s}} + \frac{1}{2\bar{s}} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2\bar{s} = 1-\bar{s} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{s} = \frac{1}{3}.\]
For a general \(\alpha\), \(\ln c^* = \ln(1-\bar{s}) + \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\ln\bar{s}\) plus terms without \(\bar{s}\), so
\[-\frac{1}{1-\bar{s}} + \frac{\alpha}{(1-\alpha)\bar{s}} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1-\alpha)\bar{s} = \alpha(1-\bar{s}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{s} = \alpha.\]
Neither \(\bar{d}\) nor \(\bar{A}\) matters. A higher \(\bar{s}\) raises output but lowers the share of it that people consume, and at \(\bar{s} = \alpha\) the two effects just balance. At that point the return on capital equals depreciation: with the formula of step 7, \(\frac{1}{3}\,\bar{d}/\bar{s} = \bar{d}\) when \(\bar{s} = 1/3\).
(b) The title shows \(c^* = 1.19\) at \(\bar{s} = 0.42\) and \(1.22\) at \(0.33\). With the functions, \(c^* = 0.58 \times 2.049 \approx 1.189\) at 0.42 and \(\frac{2}{3}\times 1.826 \approx 1.217\) at \(1/3\): a gain of 2.4 percent. The gain is small because \(c^*\) is flat near its peak.
(c)
years, y_path = simulate(s_old=0.42, s_new=1 / 3)
c_path = []
for i in range(len(years)):
    if years[i] < 2030:
        c_path.append((1 - 0.42) * y_path[i])
    else:
        c_path.append((1 - 1 / 3) * y_path[i])
c_path = np.array(c_path)
print(f"Before the cut: c = {c_path[0]:.3f}")
print(f"2030: c = {c_path[15]:.3f}   2050: c = {c_path[35]:.3f}   2115: c = {c_path[-1]:.3f}")
print(f"Lowest c from 2030 on: {c_path[15:].min():.3f}")
Consumption jumps from 1.189 to 1.366 in 2030, 14.9 percent more, because people now consume two thirds of an output that has not changed yet, instead of 58 percent. Then it slowly declines, to 1.256 in 2050 and 1.218 in 2115, as capital falls toward the new steady state, where \(c^* = 1.217\). It never drops below its old level: no year is worse. An economy that invests more than the golden-rule rate can consume more in every year by investing less. Economists call such an economy dynamically inefficient.
(d) Inside the model, the IMF’s advice is right: for an economy that invests 42 percent of output with a capital exponent of \(1/3\), investing less raises consumption now and later. Two reasons for caution. First, by (a), the golden-rule rate equals the capital exponent; if capital’s share of income in China were well above one third, the golden-rule rate would be higher too and the case for a cut would be weaker. Second, the Solow model is a long-run model in which whatever is not invested is consumed. It says nothing about the short-run risk that a sudden fall in investment lowers demand and output, the question that Chapters 9 to 13 take up.

title: 6. Growth and Ideas
6. Growth and Ideas
text:
6.1 Model overview
In Chapter 5, Islandia got richer by building tools, but each extra boat added less than the one before, so tool building alone ran out of steam. Now an islander draws a better hull design. Harbor Boatworks can use that one drawing in every yard on the island at the same time, and the drawing never wears out. Can a steady stream of new ideas like this one keep Islandia getting richer year after year? This section answers with Paul Romer’s model of ideas, and we follow Islandia through every step.






NoteThe big idea



The question. Capital alone cannot sustain growth. What can keep income per person rising decade after decade?
The answer in one sentence. New ideas: because an idea is nonrival, it raises the output of every worker at once, so a research workforce that keeps growing keeps income per person growing.
What goes in and what comes out. We choose how productive research is, the share of people who do research, population growth, how much ideas matter in production and, once capital is back, the investment and depreciation rates. The model gives back the stock of ideas, the level of income per person on its balanced growth path, its long-run growth rate, and the path from any starting point.
Road map.

The economics of ideas: what makes ideas special, and why solving the model leads to increasing returns and prices above marginal cost.
The Romer model: the assumptions, the solution for the stock of ideas and long-run growth, and what the model predicts when research changes.
Combining Solow and Romer: capital comes back and amplifies the growth that ideas create.
Growth accounting: splitting measured growth into capital, labor composition and productivity.
Model in code: the key results as Python functions, checked with numbers.

Notation. A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number we choose from outside the model; the exponent \(\gamma\) (gamma) is a parameter too, written without a bar. Letters without a bar are endogenous variables, which the model determines. In the code we write z, l, n, gamma, s and d.
