Islandia’s baseline. The textbook’s Figs. 9.1 and 9.6 print no numbers. So every model figure and every worked example below uses one illustrative baseline for Islandia:

potential output starts at \(\bar{Y}_0 = 100\) and grows by \(\bar{g} = 2\) percent a year;
short-run output follows a wave between \(+2\) and \(-2\) percent (the \(\pm 2\%\) marked in Fig. 9.1) that repeats every 8 years, \(\tilde{Y}_t = 2\sin(2\pi t/8)\) percent. In whole years it takes the values \(0, +1.41, +2, +1.41, 0, -1.41, -2, -1.41, 0\);
the slope of the Phillips curve is \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), close to the textbook’s estimate of about 1/3 for U.S. data;
long-run inflation is \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, and Okun’s slope is \(-1/2\).

Fig. 9 works through a textbook exercise that comes with its own numbers (\(\bar{\nu} = 1\), \(\tilde{Y} = +3\%\)), and there we use those.

9.1.1 Trend and cycle: potential output and short-run output

Definitions
Two models with two jobs. The book works with two models at the same time:



Model
What it determines
Built in




long-run model
potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) and long-run inflation \(\bar{\pi}\)
Chapters 3–8 (the combined Solow–Romer model of Chapter 6, the quantity theory of Chapter 8)


short-run model
actual output \(Y_t\) and actual inflation \(\pi_t\), year by year or quarter by quarter
Chapters 9–15



Inside the short-run model, \(\bar{Y}_t\) and \(\bar{\pi}\) are exogenous. The long-run model hands them over, and that is why they carry bars. The endogenous variables are \(Y_t\) and \(\pi_t\). Long-run inflation has no time subscript: in the end it is a steady target that policymakers choose (Chapter 13).
Potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) is what Islandia produces when its tools, workers and ideas are used at a pace it can keep up year after year. Think of it as a cruising speed, not a top speed. For a while Harbor Boatworks can produce more than potential, by running overtime shifts and putting off repairs to its slipways. In a bad year it produces less.
Shocks push actual output away from potential. On Islandia they come in many forms:

a jump in the price of imported fuel, or a sudden freeze in lending;
a tax cut, or a new technology that delivers more (or less) than hoped;
a storm, or a boom or a slump in Mainland, Islandia’s trading partner.

The short run is the stretch of time over which such deviations last, usually around two years.
Short-run output. We can always write output as its trend plus the distance from it, \(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t + (Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)\). But a shortfall of 100 boats is a disaster for a tiny economy and a rounding error for a giant one. So we measure the distance relative to potential output:






ImportantKey result: short-run output



\[\tilde{Y}_t \equiv \frac{Y_t - \bar{Y}_t}{\bar{Y}_t}. \tag{1}\]
It is positive in a boom (\(Y_t > \bar{Y}_t\)), negative in a slump (\(Y_t < \bar{Y}_t\)), and zero when the economy runs exactly at potential.


\(\tilde{Y}_t\) goes by several names. It is the percentage gap between actual and potential output, the output gap, or detrended output: what remains of output after the trend has been removed.
Recessions. A recession begins when short-run output turns negative. It is usually counted as over once short-run output hits its lowest point and starts to rise, even though output is still below potential at that moment. In the United States, the dates of each peak and trough are set by a dating committee of the NBER, the National Bureau of Economic Research. It looks at employment, sales and industrial production, not just at GDP.

Short-run output measures how far Islandia runs above or below its sustainable pace, as a percentage of potential output.



Working with the definitions
Step 1: actual output as potential output times a factor. Multiply both sides of equation (1) by \(\bar{Y}_t\), then add \(\bar{Y}_t\) to both sides:
\[\tilde{Y}_t\bar{Y}_t = Y_t - \bar{Y}_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_t = \bar{Y}_t + \tilde{Y}_t\bar{Y}_t.\]
Factoring out \(\bar{Y}_t\) gives equation (2) in the box below.






ImportantKey result: actual output = trend × cycle



\[Y_t = \bar{Y}_t\,(1 + \tilde{Y}_t). \tag{2}\]
The cycle factor is a little above 1 in a boom and a little below 1 in a slump.
Islandia in numbers. In year 2, at the top of the boom, potential output is \(100\times1.02^2 = 104.04\) and \(\tilde{Y}_2 = +2\%\), so actual output is \(104.04\times1.02 = 106.12\). In year 6, at the bottom of the slump, potential is \(100\times1.02^6 = 112.62\) and actual output is \(112.62\times0.98 = 110.36\). Going back with equation (1), \((110.36 - 112.62)/112.62 = -0.02\): a gap of \(-2\) percent.


The function actual_output builds the baseline in exactly this way. It multiplies the trend \(\bar{Y}_t = 100\times(1.02)^t\) (compound growth, Appendix C.3) by the cycle factor \(1 + 0.02\sin(2\pi t/8)\).
Step 2: the trend drops out. The trend sits in both the numerator and the denominator of equation (1). In the baseline, \(Y_t - \bar{Y}_t = \bar{Y}_t\times0.02\sin(2\pi t/8)\). Dividing by \(\bar{Y}_t\) cancels the growth factor \((1.02)^t\) and leaves \(\tilde{Y}_t = 2\sin(2\pi t/8)\) percent, whatever the growth rate of potential output. When the trend is steep, the cycle is harder to spot in a chart of \(Y_t\), but \(\tilde{Y}_t\) does not change at all (Fig. 1).
Step 3: short-run output as a log difference. Take the natural log of equation (2). The log of a product is the sum of the logs (Appendix C.4):
\[\ln Y_t = \ln\bar{Y}_t + \ln(1 + \tilde{Y}_t).\]
When \(x\) is small, \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) (Appendix C.6). Apply it with \(x = \tilde{Y}_t\) and move \(\ln\bar{Y}_t\) to the left-hand side. The result is equation (3) in the box after step 4: to a close approximation, the gap in percent is the log of actual output minus the log of potential output.
The approximation works very well for ordinary gaps: \(\ln(1.02) = 0.0198\) and \(\ln(0.98) = -0.0202\), both within 0.03 points of \(\pm 2\%\). It is less accurate in very deep slumps: a gap of \(-10\%\) has a log difference of \(\ln(0.90) = -0.105\), half a point away. Many statistical agencies report gaps in logs for this very reason, since logs turn ratios into differences.
Step 4: growth rates. Write equation (3) for year \(t\) and for year \(t-1\), and subtract the second from the first:
\[\ln Y_t - \ln Y_{t-1} \approx \left(\ln\bar{Y}_t - \ln\bar{Y}_{t-1}\right) + \left(\tilde{Y}_t - \tilde{Y}_{t-1}\right).\]
The change in the log of a variable is approximately its growth rate (Appendix C.5). Potential output grows at the rate \(\bar{g}\), so the first bracket is \(\bar{g}\) and the second is \(\Delta\tilde{Y}_t\):






ImportantKey result: the gap in logs and in growth rates



\[\tilde{Y}_t \approx \ln Y_t - \ln\bar{Y}_t \tag{3}\]
\[g_{Y,t} \approx \bar{g} + \Delta\tilde{Y}_t \tag{4}\]
Islandia in numbers. From year 1 to year 2 the gap rises from \(+1.41\) to \(+2\), so output grows by about \(2 + 0.59 = 2.59\) percent. From year 4 to year 5 the gap falls from \(0\) to \(-1.41\), so output grows by only about \(2 - 1.41 = 0.59\) percent.


The exact version of equation (4) comes from dividing equation (2) for year \(t\) by equation (2) for year \(t-1\): \(Y_t/Y_{t-1} = (1+\bar{g})\times(1+\tilde{Y}_t)/(1+\tilde{Y}_{t-1})\).






TipIn words: growing, yet sliding into a slump



Islandia’s output has two engines: the trend, which always pushes forward at \(\bar{g}\), and the cycle, which adds speed while the gap widens upward and takes speed away while it shrinks. Between years 4 and 5 Harbor Boatworks still builds a few more boats than the year before, so output still grows. But it grows more slowly than potential, so the gap opens below zero: Islandia is sliding into a slump while its output rises.


Step 5: quarterly and annualized rates. GDP is published every quarter, and quarterly growth is usually reported as an annualized rate: the growth we would get if the quarter’s pace lasted a full year. Compounding over four quarters gives \((1+g_q)^4 - 1\), which is close to \(4g_q\) when \(g_q\) is small. A quarter with 1 percent growth is reported as \(1.01^4 - 1 = 4.06\%\), roughly 4 percent. In the other direction, potential output that grows by 2 percent a year grows by \(1.02^{1/4} - 1 = 0.496\%\) per quarter, just under a quarter of 2 percent.

Actual growth is trend growth plus the change in the gap, so Islandia can keep growing and still slide into a slump.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. In year 1 of the baseline, potential output is \(100\times1.02 = 102\) and short-run output is \(+1.41\) percent. What is Islandia’s actual output?


Answer

By equation (2), \(Y_1 = \bar{Y}_1(1+\tilde{Y}_1) = 102\times1.0141 \approx 103.44\).

2. In a deep slump, Islandia’s actual output is 95 percent of potential. What is the gap by equation (1), and what is the log difference of equation (3)? Why do we rarely worry about the difference between them?


Answer

Equation (1) gives \((95 - 100)/100 = -5\) percent. The log difference is \(100\ln(0.95) \approx -5.13\) percent, a little larger in size. They differ by only about \(0.13\) points, because \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) is accurate for small \(x\).





What the framework predicts
Growth alone does not tell us where the economy stands. Equation (4) has one number we can observe, \(g_{Y,t}\), and two we cannot, \(\bar{g}\) and \(\Delta\tilde{Y}_t\). Suppose GDP grows at an annualized 5 percent. That fits potential growth of 5 percent with an unchanged gap. It fits just as well potential growth of 2 percent with a gap that widened by 3 points. Potential output is never observed, so it has to be estimated. Three methods are common:

draw a smooth trend through real GDP;
average the actual GDP of the quarters around each date;
like the U.S. Congressional Budget Office (CBO), compute what a Solow-style production function delivers when labor and capital are at sustainable levels.

Each estimate can be revised as new data come in, and the measured gaps shift with it (Fig. 3).
A slump does not need falling output. In the baseline, Islandia’s output never shrinks: its slowest growth is about 0.6 percent a year. Still, Islandia spends four years out of every eight below potential. A recession is defined by the gap, not by the sign of growth.
What a slump costs. Add up short-run output over the years below potential. The total is the output lost, measured as a percent of one year’s potential output. In the baseline, the slump years 5, 6 and 7 give \(-1.41 - 2 - 1.41 = -4.83\) percent of a year’s potential output. Over the whole cycle, though, the boom years add \(+4.83\), and the total is exactly zero. So smoothing out the cycle completely would gain far less than the cost of one recession, because the booms would disappear too.
Comparative statics.









Change
Path of \(\bar{Y}_t\)
Short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\)
Growth of actual output \(g_Y\)




faster potential growth \(\bar{g}\)
steeper trend
unchanged (step 2)
rises one for one, equation (4)


bigger swings of the cycle
unchanged
larger booms and slumps
larger swings around \(\bar{g}\)


larger economy, higher \(\bar{Y}_0\)
scaled up
unchanged
unchanged



In logs, equation (3) reads \(\ln Y_t \approx \ln\bar{Y}_t + \tilde{Y}_t\). So the elasticity of actual output with respect to potential output is 1, and each point of short-run output adds about one percent to actual output.

A slump is about the gap, not about falling output, and over a full cycle the booms and slumps cancel out.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia’s potential output now grows by 4 percent a year instead of 2, while the cycle stays the same. What is short-run output in year 6? About how fast does actual output grow from year 4 to year 5?


Answer

Short-run output in year 6 is still \(-2\) percent: the trend cancels out of equation (1) (step 2). By equation (4), output grows by about \(4 - 1.41 = 2.59\) percent from year 4 to year 5.

2. Islandia’s GDP grows by 3 percent this year, and potential output grows by 2 percent. Is Islandia in a boom?


Answer

We cannot tell yet. By equation (4), the gap rose by about \(3 - 2 = 1\) point, so it is closing from below or widening from above. If the gap started at \(-2\) percent, it is now about \(-1\) percent: Islandia is recovering, but it is still in a slump. Growth tells us how the gap changes, not where it is.






9.1.2 The Phillips curve

Assumptions
The short-run model stands on three premises. In our own words, and for Islandia:

Shocks never stop. Something is always hitting Islandia, pushing \(Y_t\) away from \(\bar{Y}_t\) or inflation away from \(\bar{\pi}\).
Policy can move output in the short run. The Bank of Islandia and the Islandia Treasury can raise or lower spending, and with it output, for a while. In this chapter we go one step further and let policymakers pick \(\tilde{Y}_t\) directly. Chapters 11 and 12 show how they do it.
Output and inflation trade off over time. A hot economy makes inflation speed up, and a cold one makes it slow down. This premise is the Phillips curve, in the box below.







ImportantKey result: the Phillips curve



\[\Delta\pi_t \equiv \pi_t - \pi_{t-1} = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t, \qquad \bar{\nu} > 0. \tag{5}\]
The slope \(\bar{\nu}\) is the number of points by which inflation rises in a year for each percent that output runs above potential.
Islandia in numbers. With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), a boom of \(\tilde{Y}_t = +2\%\) raises inflation by \(0.33\times2 = 0.66\) points in a year, and a slump of \(-2\%\) lowers it by \(0.66\) points.








TipIn words: why prices speed up in a boom



When demand runs hot, Harbor Boatworks is working beyond its sustainable pace. It pays overtime at premium wages, its machines run without a break, and its boats are scarce. So it raises its prices by more than the inflation everyone expected. When every firm on the island does the same at once, inflation itself goes up. In a slump the yards have idle capacity, firms hold back their price increases to win customers, and inflation comes down.


The curve is about the change in inflation, not its level. Chapter 12 builds a fuller version that adds a term for price shocks, such as a jump in the price of oil.

A hot economy speeds inflation up and a cold one slows it down: the gap moves the change in inflation, not its level.



Solving the model
Step 1: a rule that carries inflation forward. Add \(\pi_{t-1}\) to both sides of equation (5):
\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t.\]
This is a difference equation (Appendix C.10). Feed it last year’s inflation and this year’s short-run output, and it returns this year’s inflation.
Step 2: apply it year after year. Start from inflation \(\pi_0\) in year 0:
\[\pi_1 = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_1,\] \[\pi_2 = \pi_1 + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_2 = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\left(\tilde{Y}_1 + \tilde{Y}_2\right),\] \[\pi_3 = \pi_2 + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_3 = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\left(\tilde{Y}_1 + \tilde{Y}_2 + \tilde{Y}_3\right).\]
Carrying on for \(t\) years gives equation (6) in the box.






ImportantKey result: inflation as a running total



\[\pi_t = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\tilde{Y}_s. \tag{6}\]
Islandia in numbers. Over the baseline cycle, inflation goes \(2 \to 2.47 \to 3.13 \to 3.59\) percent in years 1 to 3, stays at \(3.59\) in year 4, and is back at 2 percent in year 8, because the gaps of a full cycle add up to zero.








TipIn words: inflation keeps a tally



Think of inflation as a tally that Islandia keeps of all its past booms and slumps. A boom that has ended still leaves inflation higher than before. Only a slump of the same total size wipes the tally back to where it started.


Step 3: steady inflation. Inflation stays constant, \(\Delta\pi_t = 0\), exactly when \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\). Any inflation rate can last as long as output sits at potential. That is why the Phillips curve cannot pin down long-run inflation \(\bar{\pi}\): it comes from the long run and from policy.
Step 4: a boom that lasts. Suppose policymakers hold output at the same gap \(\tilde{Y}\) every year. Then the sum in equation (6) is \(t\) copies of \(\tilde{Y}\), and \(\pi_t = \pi_0 + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\,t\). Inflation climbs in a straight line, by \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) points every year, and it never stops. With the baseline slope \(0.33\) and a gap held at \(+2\) percent, inflation rises by \(0.66\) points a year: \(2 \to 2.66 \to 3.32 \to 3.98\) percent. Fig. 9 runs this experiment.
Step 5: the output cost of lowering inflation. Set \(t = T\) in equation (6), subtract \(\pi_0\) from both sides and divide by \(\bar{\nu}\). The result is equation (7):






ImportantKey result: the cost of a disinflation



\[\sum_{s=1}^{T}\tilde{Y}_s = \frac{\pi_T - \pi_0}{\bar{\nu}}. \tag{7}\]
To bring inflation down, the gaps must add up to a negative number, and the slope alone fixes how large that total is. The ratio \(1/\bar{\nu}\), the output lost per point of disinflation, is often called the sacrifice ratio.
Islandia in numbers. With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), lowering inflation by one point takes a cumulative gap of \(-1/0.33 = -3.03\) percent-years: for example, \(-3.03\) percent for a single year, or \(-1.01\) percent in each of three years.


Policy decides how to spread the pain over the years. It does not decide how much pain there is in total.

Inflation remembers every past gap, so bringing it down takes a slump whose total size the slope alone decides.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia’s inflation has drifted up to 4 percent, and the Bank of Islandia wants it back at 2 percent. With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), what cumulative gap does that take? If the Bank spreads it evenly over four years, how deep is the slump each year?


Answer

By equation (7), the gaps must add up to \((2 - 4)/0.33 \approx -6.06\) percent-years. Spread over four years, that is about \(-1.52\) percent of output in each year.

2. Starting from inflation of 2 percent, policymakers hold Islandia’s output 1 percent above potential for three years, then bring it back to potential. Where does inflation end up, and does it drift back to 2 percent on its own?


Answer

By equation (6), inflation ends at \(2 + 0.33\times3 = 2.99\) percent, about 3 percent. It stays there: at potential, \(\Delta\pi_t = 0\) (step 3). Getting back to 2 percent needs a slump that adds up to \(-0.99/0.33 = -3\) percent-years (equation 7).





What the model predicts








Short-run output
Change in inflation
Path of inflation




\(\tilde{Y}_t > 0\) (boom)
\(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t > 0\)
rising


\(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\) (at potential)
\(\Delta\pi_t = 0\)
steady at any level


\(\tilde{Y}_t < 0\) (slump)
\(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t < 0\)
falling



Comparative statics. One more percent of short-run output changes the change in inflation by the slope, \(\partial\Delta\pi_t/\partial\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{\nu}\). Both variables are already in percent, so the slope works like an elasticity.

A steeper curve (higher \(\bar{\nu}\)) turns the line counterclockwise around the origin. A boom then pushes inflation up faster, and a disinflation gets cheaper: its output cost \(1/\bar{\nu}\) in equation (7) falls.
A price shock (Chapter 12) shifts the whole line up: inflation rises even with output at potential.
A different long-run inflation rate \(\bar{\pi}\) leaves the line where it is, because the curve is about changes in inflation.

Inflation peaks as the slump begins. By equation (6), inflation rises while \(\tilde{Y}_t > 0\) and falls while \(\tilde{Y}_t < 0\). Its highest point is therefore the moment the gap crosses zero from above: the start of a recession. In Islandia’s baseline cycle, inflation peaks at \(3.59\) percent in years 3 and 4 and then falls back to 2 percent. Fig. 5 shows the same pattern in U.S. data: inflation tends to peak close to the start of each recession and to fall during it.
No free lunch from a permanent boom. Keeping output above potential buys inflation that rises year after year (step 4). And inflation that is too high comes down only after a stretch of output below potential (equation 7). That is how the Volcker disinflation of the early 1980s worked (Fig. 6).

Inflation peaks just as a slump begins, and no policy can hold output above potential without ever-rising inflation.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Suppose Islandia’s Phillips curve were steeper, with \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\) instead of \(0.33\). How many percent-years of output would it cost to lower inflation by one point?


Answer

By equation (7), the sacrifice ratio is \(1/\bar{\nu} = 1/0.5 = 2\) percent-years, down from \(3.03\).

2. In the baseline cycle, the boom peaks in year 2, yet inflation is highest in years 3 and 4. Why the delay?


Answer

Equation (5) ties the gap to the change in inflation. In year 3 the gap is smaller than in year 2, but still positive, so inflation keeps rising. In year 4 the gap is zero and inflation holds still. Only from year 5, when the gap turns negative, does inflation fall.






9.1.3 Okun’s law

Definitions
The unemployment rate is \(u_t\). The natural rate of unemployment \(\bar{u}\) is the rate the economy settles at in the long run (Chapter 7): the labor-market partner of potential output. The difference \(u_t - \bar{u}\) is cyclical unemployment. Okun’s law is a rule of thumb fitted to U.S. data (Fig. 8):






ImportantKey result: Okun’s law



\[u_t - \bar{u} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\tilde{Y}_t. \tag{8}\]
For each percent that output falls short of potential, unemployment sits half a point above its natural rate.
Islandia in numbers. At the bottom of the baseline slump, \(\tilde{Y} = -2\%\), so Islandia’s unemployment is \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\times(-2) = 1\) point above its natural rate.








TipIn words: why jobs move less than output



When orders dry up, Harbor Boatworks does not only let workers go. It also cuts hours, and it keeps some workers on the payroll even when it does not quite need them, to have them ready for the recovery. And some islanders who lose their jobs stop looking for work for a while, so they are not counted as unemployed. That is why the slope of Okun’s law is smaller than 1 in size.




Working with the law
Step 1: from unemployment back to output. Multiply both sides of equation (8) by \(-2\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = -2\,(u_t - \bar{u}).\]
In the baseline slump, \(\tilde{Y} = -2\%\) goes with unemployment 1 point above its natural rate. The other way round, unemployment 1 point below the natural rate signals output 2 percent above potential.
Step 2: changes in unemployment. Write equation (8) for years \(t\) and \(t-1\) and subtract. The natural rate is constant, so it drops out:
\[\Delta u_t = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Delta\tilde{Y}_t.\]
Equation (4) says that \(\Delta\tilde{Y}_t \approx g_{Y,t} - \bar{g}\). Putting it in place of \(\Delta\tilde{Y}_t\) gives the growth form of Okun’s law:






ImportantKey result: Okun’s law in growth rates



\[\Delta u_t \approx -\tfrac{1}{2}\left(g_{Y,t} - \bar{g}\right). \tag{9}\]
Islandia in numbers. From year 4 to year 5 of the baseline, output grows by only about 0.6 percent, so unemployment rises by about \(-\tfrac{1}{2}(0.6 - 2) = +0.7\) point.


Step 3: the Phillips curve in terms of unemployment. Put \(\tilde{Y}_t = -2(u_t - \bar{u})\) from step 1 into the Phillips curve, equation (5):
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\times\left[-2\,(u_t - \bar{u})\right] = -2\bar{\nu}\,(u_t - \bar{u}).\]
Inflation rises when unemployment is below its natural rate and falls when it is above it. With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), each point of unemployment above the natural rate lowers inflation by \(0.66\) points a year. This is the form in which the trade-off was first spotted in the data, with unemployment on the horizontal axis (Chapter 12 tells that story).

Islandia loses jobs whenever its output grows more slowly than potential, even while output is still growing.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia’s unemployment rate is 1.5 points above its natural rate. What is the output gap? With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), how fast is inflation changing?


Answer

By step 1, \(\tilde{Y} = -2\times1.5 = -3\) percent. By equation (5), \(\Delta\pi = 0.33\times(-3) = -0.99\) points a year. The unemployment form of step 3 gives the same answer: \(-2\times0.33\times1.5 = -0.99\).

2. Islandia’s output grows by 2 percent, exactly as fast as potential, but unemployment stays 1 point above its natural rate. Does this contradict Okun’s law?


Answer

No. Equation (9) says \(\Delta u_t \approx 0\) when output grows at \(\bar{g}\): unemployment stays put, whatever its level. Growth at the trend rate never closes a gap. To bring unemployment down, Islandia’s output must grow faster than potential for a while.





What the law predicts










Short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\)
\(+2\%\)
\(0\)
\(-2\%\)
\(-4\%\)




Cyclical unemployment \(u_t - \bar{u}\) (points)
\(-1\)
\(0\)
\(+1\)
\(+2\)




Booms pull unemployment below the natural rate and slumps push it above. The two gaps move together closely, as the tight cloud of points in Fig. 8 shows.
A steeper Okun slope (larger in size) would mean bigger swings in unemployment for the same output gap.
Together with equation (7): with \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), cutting inflation by one point costs \(3.03\) percent-years of output, or about \(\tfrac{1}{2}\times 3.03 \approx 1.5\) point-years of extra unemployment.
Because the two gaps move in step, the later short-run chapters can follow output alone, and translate it into unemployment with equation (8) whenever they need to.




9.1.4 A preview of the full short-run model

Assumptions
The full model still takes the long run as given: \(\bar{Y}_t\), \(\bar{\pi}\) and \(\bar{u}\) come from outside. It keeps the three premises above, and fills Islandia with more actors: islanders who consume, Harbor Boatworks deciding how much to invest, the Islandia Treasury spending, trade with Mainland, and the Bank of Islandia running monetary policy.


How the pieces fit together
The next chapters build a chain of cause and effect. It runs from the interest rate to output, and from output to inflation and unemployment:






ImportantKey result: the short-run chain



\[\underbrace{R_t}_{\text{real interest rate}} \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{IS curve}\ }\; \tilde{Y}_t \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{Phillips curve}\ }\; \Delta\pi_t, \qquad \tilde{Y}_t \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{Okun's law}\ }\; u_t - \bar{u}.\]
The signs run all the way through: a higher \(R_t\) means a lower \(\tilde{Y}_t\), then falling inflation and higher unemployment.



The IS curve (Chapter 11) says that a higher real interest rate \(R_t\) cuts investment and other spending financed by borrowing, and so lowers short-run output.
The MP curve (Chapter 12) shows how a central bank, by choosing a short-term nominal rate (the federal funds rate, for the Fed), sets the real interest rate in the short run.
The Phillips curve, equation (5), then turns short-run output into a change in inflation, and Okun’s law, equation (8), turns it into unemployment.

This chapter skips the first link: it lets policymakers choose \(\tilde{Y}_t\) directly.






TipIn words: from the Bank’s rate to islanders’ jobs



Suppose the Bank of Islandia raises its interest rate. Borrowing gets dearer, so Harbor Boatworks puts off its new slipway and islanders buy fewer boats on credit. Spending falls, output drops below potential, and the yards hire fewer workers. With idle capacity, firms raise their prices more slowly, and inflation eases.




What the model predicts

Policy can lean against shocks and keep \(\tilde{Y}_t\) close to zero, which keeps inflation steady (equation 5).
It cannot hold output above potential year after year without inflation climbing without limit (equation 6).
High inflation comes down only through a period of output below potential, at a total cost set by the slope (equation 7).
In practice the job is harder than in the model, because potential output is not observed (equation 4) and new shocks keep arriving.


Policy can keep inflation steady by keeping output near potential, but it can never buy a lasting boom.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. A shock pushes Islandia’s output 2 percent below potential for one year, and policy does nothing. By how much do inflation and unemployment move that year?


Answer

By equation (5), inflation falls by \(0.33\times2 = 0.66\) points. By equation (8), unemployment rises to \(\tfrac{1}{2}\times2 = 1\) point above its natural rate.

2. The Bank of Islandia lowers the real interest rate to fight that slump. Trace the signs through the chain.


Answer

A lower \(R_t\) raises spending, so \(\tilde{Y}_t\) rises toward zero (the IS curve). A smaller slump means inflation falls less (equation 5) and unemployment comes closer to its natural rate (equation 8).









NoteRecap




Trend and cycle: actual output is the trend times a cycle factor, \(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t(1+\tilde{Y}_t)\), and short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\) is the percentage gap (Fig. 1).
Growth is not the gap: \(g_{Y,t} \approx \bar{g} + \Delta\tilde{Y}_t\), so output can grow during a slump, and the gap depends on an estimate of potential (Fig. 3).
The Phillips curve: \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\), so a boom raises inflation and a slump lowers it (Fig. 6); inflation peaks as a recession begins (Fig. 5).
Inflation is a running total: a lasting boom raises inflation without end (Fig. 9), and each point of disinflation costs \(1/\bar{\nu}\) percent-years of output.
Okun’s law: \(u_t - \bar{u} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\tilde{Y}_t\), so each percent of output below potential adds half a point of unemployment (Fig. 8).
The road ahead: the next chapters add the links from the interest rate to output, \(R_t \to \tilde{Y}_t \to \Delta\pi_t\) and \(u_t\).

9.2 Model in code
Now we turn the Key results into Python. The section has four parts: the setup (folded, because it is the same in every chapter), the model as functions, numerical checks of the Key results, and the drawing and data tools that the figures use (folded too). Run its cells once, in order. Every later section of the notebook reuses them.

9.2.1 Setup
Run the setup cells once, before anything else. They load the Python libraries, give every chart the same look, store the address of the chapter’s data and define two helpers that only the book website needs. You can use the notebook without reading them; open the box if you are curious.






NoteShow the setup code





The first cell loads the libraries and sets the look of the charts. Its comments explain each step.

# @title Setup: libraries, chart colors and the data location
# Text after a "#" is a comment: Python ignores it, it is there for human readers.

# Step 1: load the libraries. `import` loads a library, a toolbox written by
# other people, and `as np` gives it a short nickname, so the code stays short.
import numpy as np                              # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                             # data tables
import plotly.express as px                     # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go               # charts built piece by piece
import plotly.io as pio                         # settings shared by every chart
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots       # several panels in one figure
# sliders, buttons and menus for the interactive figures
from ipywidgets import interact, interact_manual, FloatSlider, ToggleButtons, Dropdown, SelectMultiple, fixed

# Step 2: one light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
# the same chart size in Colab and on the website
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full slider labels

# Step 3, Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets.
# `try` runs the indented lines; if the import fails (we are not in Colab),
# `except` skips them.
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# Step 4: the data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch09/"

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider. The next two helpers build those versions and keep the other countries one click away in the legend. Run them and move on.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. phillips_diagram
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "nu"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


# @title Helper for the website's country legends (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def add_legend_traces(fig, traces, keep=()):
    """Add traces that start hidden but stay in the legend (click to show them).

    If the figure has a slider, its steps only switch the figure's own traces, so the countries you
    clicked on stay on the chart when you move the slider.

    Arguments
        fig    : a Plotly figure, with or without a slider
        traces : the extra traces, e.g. one per other country
        keep   : the names of the traces that are drawn from the start
    Returns
        the same figure, with the extra traces added
    """
    # Step 1: add the traces; all but those in `keep` show only in the legend.
    # `len` counts the items of a list: here the figure's own traces.
    n = len(fig.data)
    for t in traces:
        if t.name not in keep:
            t.visible = "legendonly"
        fig.add_trace(t)
    # Step 2: make every slider step switch only the first n traces (the figure's own)
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        steps = []
        for step in slider.steps:
            steps.append(dict(method=step.method, label=step.label,
                              args=[step.args[0], step.args[1], list(range(n))]))
        slider.steps = steps
    return fig






9.2.2 The model as functions
The frameworks of this chapter are three short formulas: the definition of short-run output, equations (1) and (2), the Phillips curve, equation (5), and Okun’s law, equation (8). We write each one as a Python function: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives back a result. Islandia’s baseline gives the default values. The first cell builds Islandia’s output: the trend, the cycle around it, and the gap between the two.

# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses.
# `g=2.0` gives g a default value, used whenever we do not pass one.
# The text in triple quotes describes the function.
def potential_output(t, g=2.0, Y0=100.0):
    """Potential output Ybar_t: a smooth trend that grows g percent a year.

    Islandia's trend, as in Fig. 1:  Ybar_t = Y0 (1 + g/100)^t

    Arguments
        t  : the year (a number or an array of years)
        g  : growth rate of potential output, g-bar, in percent
        Y0 : potential output in year 0, Ybar_0
    Returns
        potential output in year t, Ybar_t
    """
    # `return` gives back the result; `**` means "to the power of"
    return Y0 * (1 + g / 100) ** t


def actual_output(t, A=2.0, g=2.0, cycle=8):
    """Actual output Y_t: potential output times a cycle factor.

    Equation (2):  Y_t = Ybar_t (1 + Y~_t),  with Y~_t = A sin(2 pi t / cycle) percent

    Arguments
        t     : the year (a number or an array of years)
        A     : the size of the swings, in percent (+A at the top, -A at the bottom)
        g     : growth rate of potential output, g-bar, in percent
        cycle : the length of one cycle, in years
    Returns
        actual output in year t, Y_t
    """
    # `np.sin` is the sine function, a smooth wave between -1 and 1 (`np.pi` is
    # the number pi), so the wave repeats every `cycle` years
    return potential_output(t, g) * (1 + A / 100 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / cycle))


def short_run_output(Y, Ybar):
    """Short-run output Y~: the percentage gap between actual and potential output.

    Equation (1):  Y~ = 100 (Y - Ybar) / Ybar

    Arguments
        Y    : actual output (a number or a column of data)
        Ybar : potential output, Ybar
    Returns
        short-run output, in percent
    """
    # positive in a boom, negative in a slump
    return 100 * (Y - Ybar) / Ybar

The next two functions link the gap to inflation and to unemployment. Each one is a straight line through zero: with no gap, inflation is steady and unemployment is at its natural rate.

def phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu=0.33):
    """The Phillips curve: the change in inflation caused by short-run output.

    Equation (5):  delta pi = nu-bar * Y~

    Arguments
        Y_tilde : short-run output Y~, in percent
        nu      : slope of the Phillips curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        the change in inflation, in percentage points
    """
    # a boom (Y~ > 0) raises inflation, a slump (Y~ < 0) lowers it
    return nu * Y_tilde


def okun_law(Y_tilde, slope=-0.5):
    """Okun's law: cyclical unemployment from short-run output.

    Equation (8):  u - u-bar = slope * Y~, with a slope of -1/2

    Arguments
        Y_tilde : short-run output Y~, in percent
        slope   : Okun's slope (-1/2 in the textbook)
    Returns
        cyclical unemployment u - u-bar, in percentage points
    """
    # each percent of output below potential adds half a point of unemployment
    return slope * Y_tilde



9.2.3 Checking the key results
The formulas came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, one Key result at a time, using Islandia’s baseline: potential output grows 2 percent a year, short-run output swings between \(+2\) and \(-2\) percent, and \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\).
Check 1: equations (1) and (2), and the trend drops out. At the top of the boom (year 2) and the bottom of the slump (year 6), we compute short-run output from the baseline and rebuild actual output from it. Then we change the growth of potential output and recompute short-run output in year 6.

# Step 1: the top of the boom (year 2) and the bottom of the slump (year 6).
# A `for` loop repeats its indented lines once for each value after `in`.
for t in (2, 6):
    # `Ybar, Y = a, b` gives two variables their values in one line
    Ybar, Y = potential_output(t), actual_output(t)
    Y_tilde = short_run_output(Y, Ybar)
    # An f-string, f"... {value:+.2f}", puts a value into the text;
    # ":.2f" means "two decimals", and the "+" adds a sign
    print(f"Year {t}: potential {Ybar:.2f}, actual {Y:.2f}, Y~ = {Y_tilde:+.2f}% (equation 1)")
    # equation (2): rebuild actual output from the trend and the gap
    print(f"        equation (2): Ybar x (1 + Y~) = {Ybar * (1 + Y_tilde / 100):.2f}")

# Step 2: Y~ in year 6 for three growth rates of potential output
for g in (0.0, 2.0, 4.0):
    Y_tilde = short_run_output(actual_output(6, g=g), potential_output(6, g=g))
    print(f"Potential grows {g:.0f}% a year: Y~ in year 6 = {Y_tilde:+.2f}%")

Year 2: potential 104.04, actual 106.12, Y~ = +2.00% (equation 1)
        equation (2): Ybar x (1 + Y~) = 106.12
Year 6: potential 112.62, actual 110.36, Y~ = -2.00% (equation 1)
        equation (2): Ybar x (1 + Y~) = 110.36
Potential grows 0% a year: Y~ in year 6 = -2.00%
Potential grows 2% a year: Y~ in year 6 = -2.00%
Potential grows 4% a year: Y~ in year 6 = -2.00%


Check 2: the log difference, equation (3). For gaps of different sizes we compare the exact gap with \(100\times(\ln Y - \ln\bar{Y}) = 100\ln(1+\tilde{Y})\).

# For gaps from +2 to -10 percent, compare Y~ with the log difference of equation (3).
# `np.log` is the natural logarithm; ":+6.1f" reserves 6 characters for the
# number, so that the columns line up.
for gap in (2.0, -2.0, -5.0, -10.0):
    log_gap = 100 * np.log(1 + gap / 100)  # ln Y - ln Ybar, in percent
    print(f"Y~ = {gap:+6.1f}%   log difference = {log_gap:+7.2f}%   error {log_gap - gap:+.2f} points")

Y~ =   +2.0%   log difference =   +1.98%   error -0.02 points
Y~ =   -2.0%   log difference =   -2.02%   error -0.02 points
Y~ =   -5.0%   log difference =   -5.13%   error -0.13 points
Y~ =  -10.0%   log difference =  -10.54%   error -0.54 points


Check 3: growth rates, equation (4). Year by year over one cycle, we compare the exact growth rate of actual output with potential growth (2 percent) plus the change in short-run output.

# `range(1, 9)` counts 1, 2, ..., 8, so the loop visits every year of one cycle
for t in range(1, 9):
    # Step 1: the exact growth rate of Y, from this year's and last year's levels
    exact = 100 * (actual_output(t) / actual_output(t - 1) - 1)
    # Step 2: Y~ this year and last year
    gap_now = short_run_output(actual_output(t), potential_output(t))
    gap_before = short_run_output(actual_output(t - 1), potential_output(t - 1))
    # Step 3: equation (4) with g = 2: potential growth plus the change in Y~
    approx = 2.0 + (gap_now - gap_before)
    print(f"Year {t}: Y~ = {gap_now:+5.2f}%   growth of Y = "
          f"{exact:4.2f}% (exact), {approx:4.2f}% (equation 4)")

Year 1: Y~ = +1.41%   growth of Y = 3.44% (exact), 3.41% (equation 4)
Year 2: Y~ = +2.00%   growth of Y = 2.59% (exact), 2.59% (equation 4)
Year 3: Y~ = +1.41%   growth of Y = 1.41% (exact), 1.41% (equation 4)
Year 4: Y~ = +0.00%   growth of Y = 0.58% (exact), 0.59% (equation 4)
Year 5: Y~ = -1.41%   growth of Y = 0.56% (exact), 0.59% (equation 4)
Year 6: Y~ = -2.00%   growth of Y = 1.39% (exact), 1.41% (equation 4)
Year 7: Y~ = -1.41%   growth of Y = 2.61% (exact), 2.59% (equation 4)
Year 8: Y~ = +0.00%   growth of Y = 3.46% (exact), 3.41% (equation 4)


Check 4: the Phillips curve over one cycle, equations (5) and (6). We move inflation forward one year at a time with equation (5), and compare it with the running-total formula, equation (6). Inflation should peak in years 3 and 4 and be back at 2 percent by the end of the cycle.

# Step 1: year 0, inflation at its long-run rate
pi = 2.0
# `total_gap` is a running total: it starts at zero and adds one year's gap
# each time round the loop
total_gap = 0.0

# Step 2: move inflation forward one year at a time
for t in range(1, 9):
    Y_tilde = short_run_output(actual_output(t), potential_output(t))
    # one year of equation (5): `pi = pi + ...` replaces last year's inflation
    # with this year's
    pi = pi + phillips_curve(Y_tilde)
    total_gap = total_gap + Y_tilde
    # equation (6): long-run inflation plus nu-bar times the running total
    formula = 2.0 + 0.33 * total_gap
    print(f"Year {t}: Y~ = {Y_tilde:+5.2f}%   inflation "
          f"{pi:.3f}% (year by year), {formula:.3f}% (equation 6)")

Year 1: Y~ = +1.41%   inflation 2.467% (year by year), 2.467% (equation 6)
Year 2: Y~ = +2.00%   inflation 3.127% (year by year), 3.127% (equation 6)
Year 3: Y~ = +1.41%   inflation 3.593% (year by year), 3.593% (equation 6)
Year 4: Y~ = +0.00%   inflation 3.593% (year by year), 3.593% (equation 6)
Year 5: Y~ = -1.41%   inflation 3.127% (year by year), 3.127% (equation 6)
Year 6: Y~ = -2.00%   inflation 2.467% (year by year), 2.467% (equation 6)
Year 7: Y~ = -1.41%   inflation 2.000% (year by year), 2.000% (equation 6)
Year 8: Y~ = +0.00%   inflation 2.000% (year by year), 2.000% (equation 6)


The same running total measures the cost of the slump: the gaps of years 5 to 7 add up to the output lost, and the whole cycle adds up to zero.

# Step 1: add up the gaps of the slump, years 5 to 7
lost = 0.0
for t in (5, 6, 7):
    lost = lost + short_run_output(actual_output(t), potential_output(t))
print(f"Output lost in years 5-7: {lost:.2f} percent of a year's potential output")

# Step 2: the whole cycle adds up to zero. `abs` is the absolute value: it drops
# the meaningless minus sign of a tiny rounding error such as -0.0000000000000004
print(f"Sum of Y~ over the whole cycle (years 1-8): {abs(total_gap):.2f}")

Output lost in years 5-7: -4.83 percent of a year's potential output
Sum of Y~ over the whole cycle (years 1-8): 0.00


Check 5: the cost of a disinflation, equation (7). To lower inflation from 2 to 1 percent with \(\bar{\nu} = 0.33\), equation (7) asks for a cumulative gap of \(-3.03\) percent-years. We try it all in one year and spread over three years: both must end at 1 percent.

# Step 1: equation (7), the cumulative Y~ that lowers inflation from 2 to 1 percent
needed = (1.0 - 2.0) / 0.33
print(f"Cumulative Y~ needed: {needed:.2f} percent-years")

# Step 2: two paths for Y~. `[a, b, c]` is a list, here one Y~ per year.
fast = [needed]                                               # all of it in one year
slow = [needed / 3, needed / 3, needed / 3]                   # spread over three years

# Step 3: a loop inside a loop. The outer one picks a path, the inner one runs
# through its years with equation (5); `len(path)` is the number of years.
for path in (fast, slow):
    pi = 2.0
    for Y_tilde in path:
        pi = pi + phillips_curve(Y_tilde)
    print(f"{len(path)} year(s) at Y~ = {path[0]:+.2f}%: inflation ends at {pi:.2f}%")

# Step 4: Okun's law, equation (8), turns the lost output into extra unemployment
print(f"Okun's law: extra unemployment, summed over the years = {okun_law(needed):+.2f} point-years")

Cumulative Y~ needed: -3.03 percent-years
1 year(s) at Y~ = -3.03%: inflation ends at 1.00%
3 year(s) at Y~ = -1.01%: inflation ends at 1.00%
Okun's law: extra unemployment, summed over the years = +1.52 point-years


Check 6: Okun’s law, equations (8) and (9). From year 4 to year 5 of the baseline, output still grows. We compute the change in unemployment from equation (8) and from the growth form, equation (9). Then we check that the Phillips curve in unemployment terms, \(\Delta\pi = -2\bar{\nu}(u - \bar{u})\), gives the same answer as equation (5).

# Step 1: Y~ in years 4 and 5, and the growth of output in between
gap_4 = short_run_output(actual_output(4), potential_output(4))
gap_5 = short_run_output(actual_output(5), potential_output(5))
growth = 100 * (actual_output(5) / actual_output(4) - 1)

# Step 2: the change in unemployment from equation (8), then from equation (9)
change_u = okun_law(gap_5) - okun_law(gap_4)
print(f"Year 4 to 5: output grows {growth:.2f}%, unemployment changes by {change_u:+.2f} points (equation 8)")
print(f"Equation (9): -1/2 x ({growth:.2f} - 2) = {-0.5 * (growth - 2.0):+.2f} points")

# Step 3: cyclical unemployment at the bottom of the baseline slump, Y~ = -2%
u_gap = okun_law(-2.0)
print(f"Y~ = -2%: u - u_bar = {u_gap:+.2f} points")

# Step 4: the Phillips curve in unemployment terms must match equation (5)
print(f"Phillips curve with unemployment: -2 x 0.33 x ({u_gap:+.2f}) = {-2 * 0.33 * u_gap:+.2f}; "
      f"with output: {phillips_curve(-2.0):+.2f}")

Year 4 to 5: output grows 0.56%, unemployment changes by +0.71 points (equation 8)
Equation (9): -1/2 x (0.56 - 2) = +0.72 points
Y~ = -2%: u - u_bar = +1.00 points
Phillips curve with unemployment: -2 x 0.33 x (+1.00) = -0.66; with output: -0.66


The two ways of computing the change in unemployment differ a little (0.71 against 0.72 points), because equation (4) is an approximation.


9.2.4 Drawing and data tools
The figures share a few tools: one writes a curve’s name next to the curve, one shades the U.S. recessions, and the others load the data for other countries and give every country its own color. Run them and move on, or open the box to see how they work.

The textbook writes the name of each curve next to it, so our model figures do the same instead of using a legend. side says whether the name sits above ("bottom"), beside ("middle") or below ("top") the end point.

# @title Drawing tool: a curve's name next to its end point
def add_end_label(fig, x, y, text, color, side="middle", row=None, col=None, xanchor="left"):
    """Write a curve's name next to its end point (x, y), in the curve's color.

    Arguments
        fig      : the figure to draw on
        x, y     : the end point of the curve
        text     : the curve's name, e.g. "Phillips curve"
        color    : its color, e.g. TEAL
        side     : "bottom" puts the name above the point, "middle" beside it,
                   "top" below it
        row, col : the panel to draw in (only for figures with two panels, Figs. 1 and 9)
        xanchor  : "left" writes the name to the right of the point, "right" to its left
    """
    # `a if condition else b` is a one-line choice: it gives a when the condition is
    # true and b otherwise. Here it moves the name 4 pixels to the right or the left.
    fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor=xanchor, yanchor=side,
                       xshift=4 if xanchor == "left" else -4, font=dict(color=color, size=15),
                       row=row, col=col)

Several data figures shade the U.S. recessions, so we write the shading once, here. A small file lists the start (peak) and end (trough) month of every U.S. recession since 1960, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER).

# @title Data tool: shading the U.S. recessions
# Step 1: read the recession dates. `pd.read_csv` reads a data file into a
# DataFrame, a table with named columns, and `parse_dates=[...]` turns text
# such as "2020-02-01" into real dates.
recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start="1960-01-01"):
    """Shade every NBER recession, from peak to trough, that ends after the date start.

    Used in Figs. 3 and 5.

    Arguments
        fig   : the figure to draw on, with dates on the horizontal axis
        start : a date such as "1970-01-01"; recessions that end earlier are left out
    """
    # Step 2: `zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough)` hands over one (peak, trough)
    # pair at a time, and the `if` skips recessions that end before `start`
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            # `fig.add_vrect` shades the band between the two dates
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)

# @title Color tool: a palette of 44 colors, and the color for one country
# Step 1: the colors that are too pale on white
LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]
# Step 2: build the palette. `PALETTE = []` starts an empty list, and `.append`
# adds one color at a time.
PALETTE = []
# Plotly's 24 dark colors, all but one medium blue ...
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24:
    if c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
# ... and the 20 "Alphabet" colors that are not too pale: 44 in all
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(c)
# the medium blue is too close to the U.S. navy, so it comes last
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")


def first_free(used, taken):
    """The palette color least used by a country's group-mates.

    It prefers a color that no country has taken yet.

    Arguments
        used  : the colors of the countries shown together with this one (a list)
        taken : the colors that any country already has
    Returns
        one color of PALETTE
    """
    # Step 1: the first color that neither the group-mates nor any other country uses.
    # `return` inside a loop stops the function at the first color that fits.
    for c in PALETTE:
        if c not in used and c not in taken:
            return c
    # Step 2: none is free, so take the color the group-mates use least.
    # `used.count(c)` counts how often c appears in the list `used`, and
    # `reversed(PALETTE)` walks through the palette from its last color,
    # far from the colors always on show.
    best = PALETTE[-1]
    for c in reversed(PALETTE):
        if used.count(c) < used.count(best):
            best = c                    # a big group shares out the colors evenly
    return best

group_colors walks through the countries one by one and gives each the best free color.

# @title Color tool: a color for every country
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, if possible.

    Arguments
        names  : every country, in the order they get their colors
        groups : the lists of countries shown together (the menu's views)
        fixed  : {country: color} for the textbook's countries, so the default view
                 keeps the book's colors (None for no fixed colors)
    Returns
        a dictionary {country: color}
    """
    # Step 1: `dict(fixed or {})` starts from a copy of the fixed colors
    # (an empty dictionary when there are none)
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        # `continue` skips a country that already has a color
        if name in colors:
            continue
        # Step 2: `used` collects the colors of the countries shown with this one
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    if other in colors:
                        used.append(colors[other])
        # Step 3: the best free color for this country
        colors[name] = first_free(used, list(colors.values()))
    return colors

9.3 Trend and cycle
We start with a made-up economy to see the key idea of the chapter: actual output equals potential output plus short-run fluctuations around it.

Fig. 1: Economic fluctuations and short-run output
Goal. See how removing the trend from actual output leaves the ups and downs of the business cycle.
Panel (a) draws actual output \(Y_t\) around a smooth potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\). Panel (b) draws short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\) from equation (1): the same wiggle, with the trend taken out. The gray bars in panel (a) are the gaps \(Y - \bar{Y}\) at the top of the boom and at the bottom of the slump.
The function below draws both panels. It only calls the output functions of “Model in code”, so all of its code is drawing code: open it to see how the two panels are built.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, panel (b), short-run output
def fluctuations_panel_b(fig, t, Y, Ybar, A):
    """Panel (b) of Fig. 1: short-run output over one cycle, with a boom and a slump.

    The teal curve is Y~ from equation (1), and the dashed line Y~ = 0 is output at
    potential.

    Arguments
        fig  : the two-panel figure; panel (b) is row 1, column 2
        t    : the times, in years
        Y    : actual output at those times, Y
        Ybar : potential output at those times, Ybar
        A    : the size of the swings, in percent
    """
    # Step 1: the curve of short-run output, equation (1)
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=t,
            y=short_run_output(Y, Ybar),
            name="Short-run output, Ỹ",
            line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3),
        ),
        row=1,
        col=2,
    )
    # Step 2: `fig.add_hline` draws a horizontal line, here at Y~ = 0: output at
    # potential
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color=GREEN, width=2, dash="dash"), row=1, col=2)
    add_end_label(fig, 8, 0, "Ỹ", TEAL, "bottom", 1, 2)
    # Step 3: the labels of the boom (year 2) and the slump (year 6); xref="x2"
    # and yref="y2" place them in panel (b)
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=2,
        y=A,
        xref="x2",
        yref="y2",
        text="Boom: Ỹ > 0",
        showarrow=False,
        yshift=14,
    )
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=6,
        y=-A,
        xref="x2",
        yref="y2",
        text="Slump: Ỹ < 0",
        showarrow=False,
        yshift=-14,
    )
    # the vertical axis of panel (b), fixed
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5.2, 5.2], row=1, col=2)




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, actual, potential and short-run output
def fluctuations(A=2.0, g=2.0):
    """Actual and potential output (a) and short-run output (b), over one 8-year cycle.

    Draws Fig. 1 (adapted from Fig. 9.1 in Jones). The gray bars in panel (a) are the
    gaps Y - Ybar at the top of the boom (year 2) and the bottom of the slump (year 6).

    Arguments
        A : the size of the swings, in percent
        g : growth rate of potential output, g-bar, in percent
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the curves, equation (2). `np.linspace(0, 8, 201)` gives 201 evenly
    # spaced times from 0 to 8 years: t[50] = 2 and t[150] = 6
    t = np.linspace(0, 8, 201)
    Y, Ybar = actual_output(t, A, g), potential_output(t, g)

    # Step 2: `make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2)` makes two panels side by side, and
    # `row=..., col=...` tells `add_trace` which panel to draw in
    titles = ("(a) Actual and potential output", "(b) Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)")
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=titles)

    # Step 3: panel (a). `go.Scatter` is one curve, and `add_trace` adds it
    actual = go.Scatter(
        x=t,
        y=Y,
        name="Actual output, Y",
        line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
    )
    fig.add_trace(actual, row=1, col=1)
    trend = go.Scatter(
        x=t,
        y=Ybar,
        name="Potential output, Ȳ",
        line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash"),
    )
    fig.add_trace(trend, row=1, col=1)
    # the gray bars: the gaps at the boom and the slump; `None` breaks the line
    gaps = go.Scatter(
        x=[2, 2, None, 6, 6],
        y=[Ybar[50], Y[50], None, Ybar[150], Y[150]],
        name="Gap, Y − Ȳ",
        mode="lines",
        line=dict(color=GRAY, width=4),
    )
    fig.add_trace(gaps, row=1, col=1)
    # Y and Ybar meet at t = 8: one name above, one below
    add_end_label(fig, 8, Y[-1], "Y", BLUE, "bottom", 1, 1)
    add_end_label(fig, 8, Ybar[-1], "Ȳ", GREEN, "top", 1, 1)

    # Step 4: panel (b), with the function above
    fluctuations_panel_b(fig, t, Y, Ybar, A)

    # Step 5: fixed axes, so that you can see the curves move when a parameter
    # changes; the title reports the swings and the growth of potential output
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Time (years)", range=[0, 8])
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Output", range=[94, 145], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"Boom: Ỹ = +{A:.1f}%   Slump: Ỹ = −{A:.1f}%   |   "
            f"potential grows {g:.1f}% a year"
        ),
        showlegend=False,
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

Panel (b) looks just like actual output in panel (a), without the upward trend. That is why economists also call \(\tilde{Y}\) detrended output.
Raise the growth of potential output to 4 percent. In panel (a) the slump almost disappears: even at the bottom of the cycle, actual output still grows by more than 2 percent a year. In panel (b) nothing changes. Strong growth hides the cycle, which is exactly what happens with real GDP in Fig. 2.
Set \(\bar{g} = 0\) and the two panels look the same: potential output is then a constant 100, so \(Y - \bar{Y}\) and \(\tilde{Y}\) are the same numbers.

def gdp_levels(country):
    """Actual and potential GDP of one country (Fig. 2).

    The United States: the CBO's data, in trillions of 2022 dollars. Other
    countries: the OECD's, in trillions of 2021 dollars at PPP.

    Arguments
        country : the country's name, e.g. "Greece"
    Returns
        a table with the columns year, "Actual GDP" and "Potential GDP"
    """
    if country == "United States":
        return us_levels
    # the country's years with real GDP, with the same column names as the U.S.
    data = others[others.country == country].dropna(subset=["gdp_real"])
    return data.rename(
        columns={"gdp_real": "Actual GDP", "gdp_potential": "Potential GDP"}
    )

The title of the chart states a finding. gdp_title finds the deepest slump below potential output, with equation (1).

def gdp_title(country, data):
    """A title with the finding of Fig. 2: the deepest slump below potential output.

    Short-run output Y~ of every year, equation (1); the title reports its lowest
    value and the year.

    Arguments
        country : the country's name
        data    : its table, from gdp_levels
    Returns
        the title, a line of text
    """
    # Step 1: short-run output Y~ of every year, equation (1)
    gaps = short_run_output(data["Actual GDP"], data["Potential GDP"])
    if country == "United States":
        return (
            "Actual and potential GDP move together, "
            "except in the 1930s and 1940s"
        )
    # Step 2: `.notna().any()` is True when a column has at least one number, and
    # `.idxmin()` gives the row label of the smallest value
    if gaps.notna().any():
        return (
            f"{country}: the deepest slump was {-gaps.min():.1f}% below potential, "
            f"in {data.year[gaps.idxmin()]}"
        )
    return f"{country}: actual GDP only (the OECD estimates no potential output)"

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, the tick values of the ratio scale
# the U.S. ticks: each one doubles the one before
TICKS = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]


def ratio_ticks(low, high):
    """Tick values 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, ... from low to high, for a ratio scale.

    A narrow range gets more ticks, so that the axis always shows a few numbers.

    Arguments
        low, high : the bottom and the top of the axis
    Returns
        a list of tick values
    """
    # Step 1: the steps within each power of ten (`a if c else b` picks one)
    steps = [1, 2, 5] if high / low > 8 else [1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 7]
    # a narrow range needs more ticks
    if high / low < 3:
        steps = [1, 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
    # Step 2: every step times every power of ten from 0.001 to 100 that lies
    # between low and high
    ticks = []
    for power in range(-3, 3):
        for step in steps:
            if low <= step * 10 ** power <= high:
                ticks.append(round(step * 10 ** power, 3))
    return ticks

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, real GDP, actual and potential
def gdp_chart(scale="ratio", country="United States"):
    """Real GDP, actual and potential, of one country, on a ratio or a linear scale.

    Draws Fig. 2 (inspired by Fig. 9.2 in Jones).

    Arguments
        scale   : "ratio" or "linear", the vertical scale
        country : the country's name
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data, the unit of the vertical axis and the title
    data = gdp_levels(country)
    unit = (
        "Trillions of 2022 dollars"
        if country == "United States"
        else "Trillions of 2021 dollars (PPP)"
    )
    title = gdp_title(country, data)

    # Step 2: `px.line` with a list `y=[...]` draws one line per column, and
    # `log_y=True` gives a ratio scale
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="year",
        y=["Actual GDP", "Potential GDP"],
        log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
        title=title,
        color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
        labels={"year": "Year", "value": unit, "variable": "Series"},
    )
    # potential GDP dashed, actual GDP thick
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Potential GDP"), line_dash="dash")
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Actual GDP"), line_width=3)

    # Step 3: the vertical axis. `tickvals` sets the numbers printed on the axis,
    # and on a ratio scale the axis `range` is given in powers of ten:
    # `np.log10(0.9)`
    if country == "United States":
        ticks, ratio_range, linear_top = TICKS, [np.log10(0.9), np.log10(32)], 30
    else:
        # from 10 percent below the lowest GDP to 10 percent above the highest
        low, high = 0.9 * data["Actual GDP"].min(), 1.1 * data["Actual GDP"].max()
        ticks = ratio_ticks(low, high)
        ratio_range = [np.log10(low), np.log10(high)]
        linear_top = 1.05 * high
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=ticks, range=ratio_range)
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, linear_top])
    # Step 4: the horizontal axis, from the year before the first one to 2026
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.year.min() - 1, 2026])
    return fig

def potential_growth(start, end):
    """Average annual growth of potential output from year start to year end.

    The growth rate that turns Ybar_start into Ybar_end in (end - start) years:
    (Ybar_end / Ybar_start)^(1 / (end - start)) - 1, in percent.

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year
    Returns
        the average annual growth rate, in percent
    """
    return 100 * ((potential[end] / potential[start]) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1)

Key numbers: what does a recession cost?
The textbook adds up the output lost in a slump: about 6 percent of a year’s GDP in a typical recession. We can measure it. We walk through the quarters, and each time \(\tilde{Y}\) turns negative we start adding up the shortfall until output is back at potential. A quarter is a quarter of a year, so each quarter adds \(-\tilde{Y}/4\) percent of a year’s GDP.

# The output lost in each slump, from the quarter Y~ turns negative until output
# is back at potential.
# Step 1: walk through the quarters. `.items()` hands over one (date, value) pair
# at a time. `None` means "no value yet": `start is None` is true while we are not
# inside a slump. `total += x` is short for `total = total + x`.
slumps = []
start, total = None, 0.0
for date, value in series.short_run_output.items():
    if value < 0:
        if start is None:                      # a new slump begins
            start, total = date, 0.0
        total += -value / 4                    # lost output, percent of a year's GDP
    # output is back at potential: the slump is over
    elif start is not None:
        # its length in years: `.days` counts the days between two dates
        years = (date - start).days / 365.25
        slumps.append([start.strftime("%Y-%m"), date.strftime("%Y-%m"), years, total])
        start = None
# Step 2: the table of the slumps that lasted a year or more
slumps = pd.DataFrame(
    slumps,
    columns=["Slump starts", "Back at potential", "Years", "Lost output (% of GDP)"],
)
slumps[slumps.Years >= 1].round(1)

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, changes in employment
def employment_chart(view="full range", country="United States"):
    """The percent change in employment from the month (or quarter) before.

    Draws Fig. 4 (inspired by Fig. 9.4 in Jones), with the largest fall labeled.

    Arguments
        view    : "full range" or "zoom on normal months"
        country : the country's name
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data, and the month (or quarter) with the largest fall.
    # `f"{date:%B %Y}"` writes a date as "April 2020", and `date.quarter` is its
    # quarter of the year (1 to 4).
    data, freq = employment_data(country)
    low = data.loc[data.emp_change_pct.idxmin()]
    # the date of the largest fall, and the title
    if country == "United States":
        when = f"{low.date:%B %Y}"
        title = "Employment grows in most months; 2008–09 and April 2020 stand out"
    else:
        when = f"{low.date.year} Q{low.date.quarter}"
        title = (
            f"{country}: employment fell most in {when}, "
            f"by {-low.emp_change_pct:.1f}% in one quarter"
        )

    # Step 2: `px.bar` draws one bar per row
    fig = px.bar(
        data,
        x="date",
        y="emp_change_pct",
        title=title,
        labels={
            "date": "Year",
            "emp_change_pct": f"{freq} change in employment (percent)",
        },
    )
    fig.update_traces(marker_color=BLUE, marker_line_width=0)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)

    # Step 3: the full range labels the largest fall. `add_annotation` writes a
    # label with an arrow that points at a data point; `ax` and `ay` set where the
    # label sits, in pixels from that point.
    if view == "full range":
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=low.date,
            y=low.emp_change_pct,
            text=f"{when}: {low.emp_change_pct:.1f}%",
            showarrow=True,
            arrowhead=2,
            ax=-110,
            ay=0,
        )
        if country == "United States":
            fig.update_yaxes(
                range=[-15, 4.5],
                tickvals=[-14, -12, -10, -8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4],
            )
    else:
        # the zoom; no label in the bottom-left corner
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[-1, 2], tickvals=[-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5])

    # Step 4: half a year of space at both ends of the horizontal axis
    pad = pd.DateOffset(months=6)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.date.min() - pad, data.date.max() + pad])
    return fig

INFLATION_RANGES = [[-2.5, 15.5], [-5, 31], [-10, 62], [-20, 124], [-50, 310]]


def inflation_range(low, high):
    """The first range in INFLATION_RANGES that contains low and high.

    The axis widens in steps, so that it only moves when a country needs more room.

    Arguments
        low, high : the lowest and the highest value to show
    Returns
        [bottom, top] (the widest range if none contains both)
    """
    # the first range that holds both values
    for bottom, top in INFLATION_RANGES:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    return INFLATION_RANGES[-1]


def add_inflation_countries(fig, data):

    One line with markers per country, a title that names the highest inflation
    shown, and a vertical axis wide enough for every point.

        color="country",
        markers=True,
        hover_name="year",

    # Step 3: the vertical axis holds every point, and zero
    low, high = min(data.inflation.min(), 0), max(data.inflation.max(), 0)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=inflation_range(low, high))

title: 9. An Introduction to the Short Run
text:
9.5 The Phillips curve
When output is above potential, inflation tends to rise. We draw this relationship in the model and then measure it in U.S. data.

Fig. 6: The Phillips curve
Goal. Draw the Phillips curve and see how short-run output moves inflation.
Think of a hot holiday toy. When demand is high, the firm that makes it runs overtime and pays its workers more, and the toy is scarce. So its price rises faster than usual. In a booming economy, it is as if every firm made the hot toy: all of them raise prices faster than the current inflation rate, so inflation goes up. In a slump the opposite happens. The Phillips curve, equation (5), puts this in one line:
\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t\]
When output is at potential (\(\tilde{Y} = 0\)), inflation is steady. Our function phillips_curve from “Model in code” draws the line. The black dot is the economy, at the short-run output you choose.
The function below draws the figure. It only calls phillips_curve, so all of its code is drawing code: open it to see how the line, the dot and the dashed guides are placed.


Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 6, the economy on the Phillips curve
def mark_economy(fig, Y_tilde, dpi):
    """Mark the economy on the Phillips curve of Fig. 6: a dot and two guides.

    Also writes which side of the chart is a slump and which a boom.

    Arguments
        fig     : the figure of Fig. 6
        Y_tilde : short-run output Y~, in percent
        dpi     : the change in inflation at Y~, delta pi
    """
    # Step 1: the economy, a black dot
    dot = go.Scatter(
        x=[Y_tilde],
        y=[dpi],
        name="The economy",
        mode="markers",
        marker=dict(color="black", size=13),
    )
    fig.add_trace(dot)
    # Step 2: dashed guides from the dot to the axes; `add_shape(type="line", ...)`
    # draws a straight segment
    guide = dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=Y_tilde, y0=-3.2, x1=Y_tilde, y1=dpi, line=guide)
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=-6.5, y0=dpi, x1=Y_tilde, y1=dpi, line=guide)
    # Step 3: the two sides of the chart
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=-3.2,
        y=2.8,
        text="← Ỹ < 0: output below potential",
        showarrow=False,
    )
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=3.2,
        y=-2.8,
        text="Ỹ > 0: output above potential →",
        showarrow=False,
    )




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 6, the Phillips curve
def phillips_diagram(nu=0.33, Y_tilde=0.0):
    """The Phillips curve delta pi = nu-bar * Y~, with the economy at Y_tilde.

    Draws Fig. 6 (adapted from Fig. 9.6 in Jones).

    Arguments
        nu      : slope of the Phillips curve, nu-bar
        Y_tilde : short-run output Y~, in percent
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the line, stopped where its name still fits below the top
    Y_end = min(6.0, 2.6 / nu)
    Y = np.linspace(-Y_end, Y_end, 100)
    # Step 2: the change in inflation at Y~, equation (5). An `if ... elif ...
    # else` block picks one of three cases.
    dpi = phillips_curve(Y_tilde, nu)
    if dpi > 0:
        verdict = "inflation rises"
    elif dpi < 0:
        verdict = "inflation falls"
    else:
        verdict = "inflation is steady"

    # Step 3: the Phillips curve and its name, then the economy
    fig = go.Figure()
    curve = go.Scatter(
        x=Y,
        y=phillips_curve(Y, nu),
        name="Phillips curve",
        line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4),
    )
    fig.add_trace(curve)
    add_end_label(fig, Y_end, phillips_curve(Y_end, nu), "Phillips curve", TEAL,
                  "bottom", xanchor="right")
    mark_economy(fig, Y_tilde, dpi)

    # Step 4: the title does the arithmetic of equation (5); the tick values leave
    # no labels in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"Ỹ = {Y_tilde:+.2f}%  →  Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_tilde:+.2f}) = "
            f"{dpi:+.2f} points: {verdict}"
        ),
        xaxis=dict(
            title="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)",
            range=[-6.5, 6.5],
            tickvals=[-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6],
        ),
        yaxis=dict(
            title="Change in inflation, Δπ (points)",
            range=[-3.2, 3.2],
            tickvals=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3],
        ),
        showlegend=False,
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

To the right of zero (a boom), \(\Delta\pi > 0\): inflation rises. To the left (a slump), \(\Delta\pi < 0\): inflation falls.
The line always goes through the origin: only output at potential keeps inflation steady.
A steeper curve (a larger \(\bar{\nu}\)) means a boom raises inflation faster, but also that a slump brings it down faster.


How the short-run model works: the Volcker disinflation
In 1979 U.S. inflation was above 11 percent (Fig. 5), and the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker set out to bring it down. The Phillips curve says that the only way to lower inflation is to push output below potential. Tight monetary policy did exactly that: short-run output averaged about \(-6\) percent in 1982 (Fig. 3 shows the quarters). The model then predicts falling inflation, and inflation did fall to about 3 percent by 1983.
Let us check the model’s prediction for 1981–1983 with the annual short-run output of Fig. 7 below.

# `np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` fits the best straight line y = a + b x through the
# points (by least squares, also called OLS) and returns the slope b first and
# the intercept a second

The fitted slope is about 0.35, close to the textbook’s “about 1/3”. Now we draw the data with our model line \(\Delta\pi = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\), and you choose \(\bar{\nu}\). The title adds up the squared misses, the squared vertical distances between the points and the line. The smaller that number, the better the line fits.

# Step 1: the years that get a text label on the chart. `.where(condition, "")`
# keeps a value where the condition is true and puts "" elsewhere, so only a few
# years get a label (hover over any point to see its year).

phillips["label"] = phillips.year.astype(str).where(phillips.year.isin(LABELS), "")
# Step 2: two periods, two colors. `np.where(condition, a, b)` picks a or b row
# by row.
phillips["period"] = np.where(
    phillips.year <= 2022, "1961–2022 (in the textbook)", "2023–2025 (new data)"
