text:
Practice problems
These problems apply the chapter’s tools in three ways: conceptual problems use the equations of the Model overview on real episodes, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data files, and modeling problems answer policy questions with small calculators built on the chapter’s frameworks. Each problem is marked Basic, Intermediate or Challenge; try it on your own before you open the Hint, and then the Solution. The calculators run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, the interactive figures above still work.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): Japan’s 34-year climb back. Japan’s main stock index, the Nikkei 225, closed at a record of 38,915.87 on 29 December 1989, at the top of a bubble; Japan’s real house prices in the BIS data of Fig. 1 peaked a year later, in 1991Q1. After the bubble burst, the stock index fell on and off for two decades, to a low of 7,054.98 on 10 March 2009. It closed above its 1989 record for the first time on 22 February 2024, at 39,098.68. All three values are from Nikkei Inc., Nikkei Stock Average (NIKKEI225), via FRED.


By how many percent did the index fall from the record to the 2009 low, equation (1)? By how many percent did it then have to rise to get back to the record, equation (3)?


The climb from the low to February 2024 took 14.95 years. What average growth rate per year does equation (2) give? Compare it with the log shortcut \(\ln(X_T/X_0)/T\).


Suppose the index had grown by 5 percent a year from its 2009 low. How many years would the climb back to the record have taken?




Hint

In (a) the fraction that was lost is \(f = 1 - 7{,}054.98/38{,}915.87\). In (b) the factor is \(39{,}098.68/7{,}054.98\). In (c), write \(1.05^T\) = record / low and take logs of both sides to solve for \(T\). The functions rise_needed and annual_growth of “Model in code” do the arithmetic of (a) and (b).


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The fraction lost is \(f = 1 - 7{,}054.98/38{,}915.87 = 0.8187\), so the index fell by 81.9 percent. Equation (3) gives the rise needed:
\[100\times\frac{f}{1-f} = 100\times\frac{0.8187}{0.1813} = 451.6 \text{ percent}.\]
This is the same as \(100\times(38{,}915.87/7{,}054.98 - 1)\), because \(1/(1-f)\) is the record divided by the low. After losing four fifths of its value, the index had to multiply by about 5.5 to recover.
(b) The factor is \(39{,}098.68/7{,}054.98 = 5.542\). Equation (2) gives
\[g = 5.542^{1/14.95} - 1 = 0.121,\]
or 12.1 percent a year, for 15 years. The log shortcut gives \(\ln 5.542/14.95 = 11.5\) percent. It is lower because \(\ln(1+g) < g\), and the gap grows with \(g\): the shortcut works best for slow growth.
(c) Solve \(1.05^T = 38{,}915.87/7{,}054.98 = 5.516\). Taking logs of both sides, \(T\ln 1.05 = \ln 5.516\), so
\[T = \frac{\ln 5.516}{\ln 1.05} = \frac{1.708}{0.0488} = 35.0 \text{ years}.\]
Even with fast growth of 12 percent a year, the climb took 15 years; at a more normal 5 percent it would have taken 35. That is the lesson of equation (3): the rise needed grows much faster than the fall, so a deep crash is undone only slowly. The real S&P 500 of Fig. 4 lost 51.7 percent in 2007–09 and needed a rise of 107 percent; the Nikkei needed more than four times that.
record, low, back = 38915.87, 7054.98, 39098.68
fall = 1 - low / record
print(f"(a) fall {100 * fall:.1f}%, rise needed {rise_needed(fall):.1f}%")
factor = back / low
print(f"(b) factor {factor:.3f}: g = {100 * annual_growth(factor, 14.95):.1f}% a year, "
      f"shortcut {100 * np.log(factor) / 14.95:.1f}%")
print(f"(c) years at 5% a year: {np.log(record / low) / np.log(1.05):.1f}")

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Long-Term Capital Management, 1998. LTCM was a hedge fund that bet on small price differences between similar securities, such as government bonds. Each bet earned little, so the fund borrowed a lot: at the end of 1997 it held about 30 dollars of debt for every dollar of its own capital. In August 1998, after Russia stopped paying its debts, LTCM lost 44 percent of its value in that one month. In September the Federal Reserve Bank of New York brought its creditors together, and 14 banks and brokers put 3.6 billion dollars of new capital into the fund, so that it did not have to sell its assets in a hurry. All facts are from Federal Reserve History, “Near Failure of Long-Term Capital Management”.


With a leverage ratio \(\ell = 30\), what fall in the value of LTCM’s assets would have wiped out its owners, equation (7)?


The fund’s debts did not change in August. By how many percent did the value of its assets fall, if the loss cost the owners 44 percent of their equity, equation (6)?


After that loss, and before selling anything, what was LTCM’s leverage ratio?


Suppose LTCM had tried to bring its leverage back to 30 without new capital. How many dollars of assets would it have had to sell per dollar of its equity before the loss, equation (8)? What share of the assets it still held is that? Use the answer to explain why the New York Fed preferred new capital to a sale of the fund’s assets.




Hint

Work per dollar of equity: set \(E = 1\), so that \(D = 30\) and \(A = D + E = 31\). The August loss is \(x = 0.44\). In (c) the new leverage is \(D/(E - x)\). In (d), equation (8) gives the sales, and the assets still held are \(A - x\).

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Equation (7): \(f^* = 1/(1+\ell) = 1/31 = 3.2\) percent. A fall of only 3.2 percent in the value of everything LTCM owned would have left its owners with nothing.
(b) Equation (6) says \(\Delta E/E = (1+\ell)\,\Delta A/A\). Solving for the return on the assets,
\[\frac{\Delta A}{A} = \frac{\Delta E/E}{1+\ell} = \frac{-44}{31} = -1.42 \text{ percent}.\]
A loss of less than one and a half percent on its assets cost the owners 44 percent of their money.
(c) Per dollar of equity, the fund had \(E = 1\), \(D = 30\) and \(A = 31\). After the loss \(x = 0.44\), equity is \(E - x = 0.56\) and assets are \(A - x = 30.56\), while the debt is still 30. Leverage jumps to
\[\frac{D}{E - x} = \frac{30}{0.56} = 53.6.\]
The fund was now much closer to the edge: its new cushion, equation (7), was \(0.56/30.56 = 1.8\) percent of its assets.
(d) Equation (8): the sales needed are \(\ell\,x = 30\times0.44 = 13.2\) dollars per dollar of the original equity. That is \(13.2/30.56 = 43.2\) percent of the assets the fund still held. Check: after the sales, assets are \(30.56 - 13.2 = 17.36\) and debt is \(30 - 13.2 = 16.8\), so leverage is \(16.8/0.56 = 30\) again.
Interpretation. Selling more than two fifths of a huge portfolio of hard-to-trade securities in a few weeks would have pushed their prices down. Other leveraged banks and funds that held similar securities would then have lost equity, and equation (8) would have forced them to sell as well: the loop of losses and sales of the Model overview. The Fed feared exactly such a fire sale, which could have harmed the whole economy (same source). New capital raised \(E\) without any sales, so leverage came down without a fire sale.

Problem 3 (Challenge): What did lenders fear in Greece? Before the euro crisis, lenders treated Greek government bonds almost like German ones. In 2007 the 10-year yield averaged 4.50 percent in Greece and 4.22 percent in Germany. In February 2012 it averaged 29.24 percent in Greece and 1.85 percent in Germany (OECD long-term government bond yields, monthly averages, via FRED: Greece, IRLTLT01GRM156N; Germany, IRLTLT01DEM156N). Treat each bond as a one-year loan that is renewed every year: the Greek yield is the risky rate \(i\), the German yield is the safe rate \(i^f\), and \(p\) is the probability that Greece defaults within the year.


Use the approximation in equation (10) to read the default probability that lenders saw in 2007.


Solve \((1-p)(1+i) = 1+i^f\) exactly for \(p\), and compute \(p\) for February 2012. Why is the approximation poor now?


Equation (10) assumes that lenders get nothing back after a default. Suppose they recover a fraction \(R\) of what they were owed. Write the lender’s new indifference condition, solve it for \(p\), and show that the spread is then approximately \(p(1-R)\), the expected loss per year.


In March 2012 Greece did restructure the bonds held by private lenders, who lost about 65 percent of the present value of their claims (Zettelmeyer, Trebesch and Gulati 2013). With \(R = 0.35\), what default probability does the February 2012 spread imply? Give two reasons why a spread can overstate the true probability of default.




Hint

In (b), divide by \(1+i\) and isolate \(p\). In (c), a default now pays the lender \(R(1+i)\) instead of 0: add that case, with its probability, to the expected payoff, set the sum equal to \(1+i^f\) and factor out \(1+i\). For (d), the Model overview names two things besides default risk that move a spread.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The spread was \(4.50 - 4.22 = 0.28\) points, so \(p \approx 0.28\) percent a year. Lenders saw almost no risk of a Greek default.
(b) Divide \((1-p)(1+i) = 1+i^f\) by \(1+i\), then solve for \(p\):
\[1 - p = \frac{1+i^f}{1+i} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p = 1 - \frac{1+i^f}{1+i} = \frac{i - i^f}{1+i}.\]
For February 2012, \(p = (0.2924 - 0.0185)/1.2924 = 0.2739/1.2924 = 21.2\) percent a year. The approximation \(p \approx
i - i^f\) would say 27.4 percent. It is poor because it needs \(p\) and \(i^f\) to be small, so that \(1+i \approx 1\); here \(1 + i = 1.29\).
(c) With recovery, the expected payoff of the loan must still equal the safe payoff:
\[(1-p)(1+i) + pR(1+i) = 1+i^f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1+i)\,\big[1 - p(1-R)\big] = 1+i^f.\]
Solving as in (b), \(p(1-R) = 1 - (1+i^f)/(1+i) = (i - i^f)/(1+i)\), so
\[p = \frac{i - i^f}{(1+i)(1-R)}.\]
With \(R = 0\) this is the result of (b). To see the spread, solve the same condition for \(1+i = (1+i^f)/[1 - p(1-R)]\) and subtract \(1+i^f\):
\[i - i^f = \frac{(1+i^f)\,p(1-R)}{1 - p(1-R)} \approx p(1-R)\]
when \(p\) and \(i^f\) are small. The spread prices the expected loss: the chance of a default times the share of the money lost in it. For the same \(p\), a higher recovery means a smaller spread, which the Model overview stated in words.
(d) \(p = 0.2119/0.65 = 32.6\) percent a year. Lenders priced Greek bonds as if there were about a one-in-three chance of a default within the year, and a month later the restructuring came. The spread can overstate the true probability because (1) lenders dislike risk and ask for more than the expected loss, and (2) in a crisis the bonds are hard to sell, so lenders also ask for a liquidity premium. In 2012 lenders also worried that Greece might leave the euro and repay in a new, weaker currency, a risk that a default probability does not capture.
i, i_safe = 0.2924, 0.0185
p = (i - i_safe) / (1 + i)
print(f"(b) p = {100 * p:.1f}% a year; approximation {100 * (i - i_safe):.1f}%")
R = 0.35
p_R = (i - i_safe) / ((1 + i) * (1 - R))
payoff = (1 - p_R) * (1 + i) + p_R * R * (1 + i)
print(f"(d) p = {100 * p_R:.1f}% a year; expected payoff {payoff:.4f} = safe payoff {1 + i_safe:.4f}")



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): Inflation at its most extreme. The file inflation_panel.csv of Fig. 10 holds 12-month inflation, measured as a log change, for 61 economies. Besides the textbook’s three series, it uses Eurostat’s harmonised index of consumer prices and the IMF’s Consumer Price Index dataset.


Find the highest value in the whole file: which country, and which month?


Turn it into a percent change with equation (4), using the function percent_from_log of Fig. 10. Compare the result with the approximation \(\pi^{\log} + (\pi^{\log})^2/200\) of the Model overview.


Why does the choice between the two measures matter so much here, and so little for the U.S. in 2022?




Hint

Read the file into a table, say world. Then world.inflation.idxmax() gives the row label of the largest value, and world.loc[...] gives that whole row, with its country and date. For (c), look at the size of the second-order term in the approximation.


# Your answer here



Solution

Read the file, find the row with the largest log change, and convert it with equation (4).
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_panel.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
top = world.loc[world.inflation.idxmax()]
print(f"Highest: {top.country}, {top.date:%b %Y}, log change {top.inflation:.1f}")
print(f"Percent change, equation (4): {percent_from_log(top.inflation):.1f}%")
print(f"Approximation pi + pi^2 / 200: {top.inflation + top.inflation ** 2 / 200:.1f}%")
us = world[world.country == "United States"]
us_top = us.loc[us.inflation.idxmax()]
print(f"U.S. peak: {us_top.date:%b %Y}, log change {us_top.inflation:.2f}, percent change "
      f"{percent_from_log(us_top.inflation):.2f}%")
(a) The highest value is Argentina’s in April 2024: a log change of 135.9.
(b) Equation (4) turns it into a percent change of 289.4 percent: prices were almost four times as high as a year earlier. The two-term approximation gives only 228.4 percent, 61 points too little.
(c) The gap between the two measures grows with the square of inflation, and faster still at very high rates, where the terms left out of the approximation (\(x^3/6\), \(x^4/24\), …) are large too. At the U.S. peak of June 2022 the log change was 8.67 and the percent change 9.06, a gap of 0.4 points. At Argentina’s peak the gap is more than 150 points. With high inflation, always check which of the two measures a table reports.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Investment, the engine of recessions? Equation (13) splits the change in GDP into the contributions of its components. Apply it to every U.S. recession since 1953, from the NBER peak quarter to the trough quarter, with the files us_quarterly.csv (real GDP and its components from the BEA’s national accounts, via FRED, e.g. GDPC1) and recessions.csv (NBER recession dates, via FRED, USREC).


In how many of the 11 recessions did investment subtract from GDP growth? In how many was investment’s contribution alone larger than the whole change in GDP?


Average the contributions over the nine recessions before 2007. Which component accounts for the fall in GDP in a typical recession?


In which two recessions was investment not the largest negative contribution? Suggest a reason for each.




Hint

Check 7 of “Model in code” computes the contributions for two recessions. Read recessions.csv into a table, say nber, put Check 7’s inner loop inside a loop over zip(nber.peak_quarter, nber.trough_quarter), and store one dictionary per recession in a list; then pd.DataFrame(rows) makes the table. For (c), contrib[list(SIGN)].idxmin(axis=1) names the most negative contribution in each row.


# Your answer here



Solution

For each recession, take the rows of the peak and trough quarters, compute each component’s share of GDP at the peak times its percent change (imports with a minus sign), and collect the results in a table.
quarterly = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_quarterly.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")
nber = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough", "peak_quarter", "trough_quarter"])
SIGN = {"consumption": 1, "investment": 1, "government": 1, "exports": 1, "imports": -1}
rows = []
for peak, trough in zip(nber.peak_quarter, nber.trough_quarter):
    before, after = quarterly.loc[peak], quarterly.loc[trough]
    row = {"peak": peak.year, "GDP (%)": percent_change(after.gdp, before.gdp)}
    for part, sign in SIGN.items():
        row[part] = sign * 100 * (after[part] - before[part]) / before.gdp     # share x change, equation (13)
    rows.append(row)
contrib = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("peak")
print(contrib.round(2))
print("Investment negative in", (contrib.investment < 0).sum(), "of", len(contrib), "recessions")
print("Investment alone below the GDP change in", (contrib.investment < contrib["GDP (%)"]).sum(), "recessions")
print(contrib.iloc[:9].mean().round(2))
print(contrib[list(SIGN)].idxmin(axis=1))
(a) Investment subtracted from GDP growth in all 11 recessions. In 6 of them, those of 1960, 1969, 1973, 1981, 2001 and 2007, its contribution alone was larger than the whole change in GDP. In 2001, GDP even rose by 0.50 percent between the NBER quarters, while investment subtracted 1.15 points.
(b) In the nine recessions before 2007, GDP fell by 1.60 percent on average and investment contributed \(-1.62\) points: investment accounts for all of the typical fall. Consumption (+0.24), government purchases (+0.25) and imports (+0.27) added a little on average, and exports subtracted 0.13. Investment is only about a sixth of GDP, but it swings so much that it drives the typical recession.
(c) In 1953, government purchases subtracted 2.83 points, more than the whole fall in GDP of 2.43 percent. The Korean War ended with an armistice in July 1953 (National Archives), and U.S. defense spending fell by 10.9 percent from 1953Q2 to 1954Q2 (BEA, national defense consumption expenditures and gross investment, FDEFX, via FRED). In 2020, consumption subtracted 6.86 points, because people stayed away from shops, restaurants and travel during the pandemic, as the Model overview explained.

Problem 6 (Intermediate): Fewer jobs or fewer hours? Fig. 7 noted that some countries paid firms to keep their workers on reduced hours in 2020. Test the idea across countries with two OECD files (OECD Data Explorer): real GDP from the quarterly national accounts in gdp_quarterly_panel.csv (index, 2019Q4 = 100) and employment from labour force surveys in employment_panel.csv (thousands of people).


For each economy, compute the percent change in real GDP and in employment from 2019Q4 to 2020Q2. How many economies have both? What is the correlation between the two changes?


Compute the ratio of the employment change to the GDP change: the percent of jobs lost per percent of output lost. What is its median? Which economies have the lowest and the highest ratios, and where are the U.S., Canada, Germany, Japan and the U.K.?


Data hygiene. Which economy’s ratio says more about its GDP data than about its jobs?




Hint

Make two Series with the countries as labels, for example gdp[gdp.date == "2020-04-01"].set_index("country").gdp_index - 100. pd.DataFrame({"gdp": ..., "jobs": ...}) lines them up by country, and .dropna() keeps the economies with both. For (c), look at the top of the ranking, and reread the data-hygiene note under Fig. 6.


# Your answer here



Solution

Compute both changes as Series labeled by country, put them side by side and divide.
gdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gdp_quarterly_panel.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
workers = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "employment_panel.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
gdp_change = gdp[gdp.date == "2020-04-01"].set_index("country").gdp_index - 100       # index 2019Q4 = 100
before = workers[workers.date == "2019-10-01"].set_index("country").employment
after = workers[workers.date == "2020-04-01"].set_index("country").employment
q2 = pd.DataFrame({"gdp": gdp_change, "jobs": percent_change(after, before)}).dropna()
q2["ratio"] = q2.jobs / q2.gdp
print(len(q2), "economies; correlation", round(q2.gdp.corr(q2.jobs), 2))
print("median ratio", round(q2.ratio.median(), 2))
print(q2.sort_values("ratio").round(2).iloc[[0, 1, 2, 3, -4, -3, -2, -1]])
print(q2.loc[["United States", "Canada", "Germany", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "Spain"]].round(2))
(a) 43 economies have both changes, and their correlation is only 0.21. In 2020 the size of the fall in output said little about the size of the fall in jobs.
(b) The median ratio is 0.24: in the typical economy, employment fell by about a quarter of a percent for each percent of lost output. The lowest ratios are New Zealand’s, \(-0.07\) (its employment even rose by 0.70 percent while GDP fell by 10.54 percent), Luxembourg’s, 0.02, and the U.K.’s and Slovenia’s, 0.06. The U.K. lost 22.19 percent of its output but only 1.30 percent of its jobs. Germany, 0.19, is below the median, and Japan, 0.24, is the median economy. At the other end are Ireland, 3.07, Costa Rica, 2.42, Chile, 1.91, and the United States, 1.46, where GDP fell by 9.09 percent and employment by 13.30 percent; Canada’s ratio is close to one, 1.02. Where firms were paid to keep their workers, the fall in output showed up as fewer hours per worker; in the U.S. and Canada, firms laid workers off.
(c) Ireland. Its GDP fell by only 1.67 percent, because much of Irish GDP is the profits of multinational firms (Fig. 6), which hardly fell. Its ratio of 3.07 says more about how Irish GDP is measured than about Irish jobs.

Problem 7 (Challenge): Bigger bubbles, deeper slumps? Did the countries with the largest house-price busts after 2005 also have the largest rises in unemployment? Use the file house_prices_panel.csv of Fig. 1 (BIS real residential property prices) and the file unemployment_panel.csv of Fig. 9 (OECD harmonised unemployment rates).


For each economy, compute the largest fall in real house prices between 2005 and 2014 with peak_to_trough, and the largest rise in the unemployment rate between 2007 and 2014 with low_to_high. Keep only economies with all 40 quarters (house prices) and all 96 months (unemployment) of data, and drop the euro area, which is an average of its members.


Compute the correlation, and fit a straight line with np.polyfit. On average, by how many points more did unemployment rise for each 10 points of extra fall in house prices?


Which economies lie furthest above and below the line? Does the correlation show that falling house prices caused the rise in unemployment?




Hint

Read the house-price file into a table, say house_data, and loop over house_data.groupby("country"), as largest_fall does. Store each result in a dictionary under the country’s name; peak_to_trough(...)[2] is the change in percent. Do the same for unemployment. pd.DataFrame({"house_fall": falls, "unemp_rise": rises}).dropna() lines the two up. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and the intercept.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

Measure the bust and the slump country by country, keep the economies with complete data, and compare.
house_data = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "house_prices_panel.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
unemp_data = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "unemployment_panel.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
falls = {}
for name, rows in house_data.groupby("country"):
    series = rows.set_index("date").real_house_price
    if len(series["2005":"2014"]) == 40:                 # all 40 quarters of 2005-2014
        falls[name] = peak_to_trough(series, "2005-01-01", "2014-12-31")[2]
rises = {}
for name, rows in unemp_data.groupby("country"):
    series = rows.set_index("date").unemployment_rate
    if len(series["2007":"2014"]) == 96:                 # all 96 months of 2007-2014
        rises[name] = low_to_high(series, "2007-01-01", "2014-12-31")[2]
crisis = pd.DataFrame({"house_fall": falls, "unemp_rise": rises}).dropna().drop("Euro area")
print(len(crisis), "economies; correlation", round(crisis.house_fall.corr(crisis.unemp_rise), 2))
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(crisis.house_fall, crisis.unemp_rise, 1)
crisis["above_line"] = crisis.unemp_rise - (intercept + slope * crisis.house_fall)
print(f"slope {slope:.3f}, intercept {intercept:.2f}")
print(crisis.sort_values("above_line").round(1))
(a) 29 economies have complete data in both files. A fall of 0.0 means that real house prices were at their highest in the last quarter of the window, 2014Q4 (Australia, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Sweden). peak_to_trough looks for a trough only after the peak, so it finds none, and earlier dips do not count: Sweden’s real house prices fell by 10.2 percent to 2008Q4, and Canada’s by 9.3 percent to 2009Q1. Germany’s rise of 0.0 has the same cause: its unemployment rate was highest in January 2007, at the start of the window.
(b) The correlation is \(-0.79\): the larger the fall in house prices, the larger the rise in unemployment. The slope is \(-0.224\), so each 10 points of extra fall in real house prices go with about 2.2 points more of a rise in unemployment.
(c) Greece (9.6 points above the line) and Spain (7.0) had far larger rises in unemployment than their house-price busts predict: in both, the euro crisis of 2010–13 followed the financial crisis. Hungary (\(-5.1\)), the United States (\(-4.6\)) and the United Kingdom (\(-4.0\)) lie furthest below the line. The correlation does not prove causation. Busts and slumps had common causes, such as the banking crises behind both, and causation also runs the other way: people who lose their jobs cannot pay their mortgages, which pushes house prices down further. The data are consistent with the chapter’s story, in which lost housing wealth and damaged banks cut spending, but they cannot prove it.



Modeling problems
Problem 8 (Basic): Short and sharp, or long and mild? A hypothetical government must choose between two ways to fight an epidemic. A strict lockdown makes real GDP fall by 15 percent at once, and GDP then climbs back to its old level in a straight line over 4 quarters. Milder rules make GDP fall by only 5 percent, but the climb back takes 16 quarters. The calculator below draws such a slump and adds up its cost with equation (12).


Find the cumulative GDP loss of each strategy. Which one costs more output?


Compare each loss with the triangle rule \(\tfrac12\,d\,T\) of the Model overview, with \(T\) in years.


Keep the 4 quarters. How deep could the strict lockdown’s fall be before it costs as much output as the mild rules?




Hint

Set the two sliders to each strategy in turn and read the title. For (c), raise the fall one point at a time and compare the loss with the one you found for the mild rules.


def slump_calculator(depth=15, quarters=4):
    """The cumulative GDP loss of a slump that climbs back in a straight line (equation 12)."""
    climb = np.linspace(100 - depth, 100, quarters + 1)          # from the trough back to the old level
    index = np.concatenate([[100.0], climb, np.full(28 - quarters, 100.0)])
    quarter = np.arange(len(index))                              # quarter 0 is the old peak
    unit = "quarters"
    if quarters == 1:
        unit = "quarter"
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=quarter, y=np.full(len(index), 100.0), mode="lines", name="Old level",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=quarter, y=index, mode="lines+markers", fill="tonexty", name="Real GDP",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), fillcolor="rgba(0, 128, 112, 0.25)"))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Fall {depth}%, back in {quarters} {unit}: loss {gdp_loss(index):.1f}% of a year's GDP "
                            f"(triangle {0.5 * depth * quarters / 4:.1f})",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Quarters after the old peak", range=[-0.5, 29.5]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Real GDP (old peak = 100)", range=[72, 103]))
    return fig


interact(slump_calculator,
         depth=IntSlider(value=15, min=1, max=25, step=1, description="fall in GDP (percent)", style=WIDE),
         quarters=IntSlider(value=4, min=1, max=24, step=1, description="quarters to climb back", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the cumulative GDP loss of the Model overview, equation (12), adapted from the discussion of the pandemic’s lost GDP in Chapter 10 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The strict lockdown costs 9.4 percent of a year’s GDP and the mild rules 10.6 percent. The mild rules cost more output, although their fall is only a third as deep.
(b) The triangle rule gives \(\tfrac12\times15\times1 = 7.5\) for the strict lockdown and \(\tfrac12\times5\times4 = 10.0\) for the mild rules, so it ranks them the same way. Both sums are larger than the triangles. With quarterly steps the shortfalls are \(d,\ d(T_q-1)/T_q,\ \dots,\ d/T_q,\ 0\) over the \(T_q\) quarters of the climb. Their sum is \(d(T_q+1)/2\), so equation (12) gives
\[\text{GDP loss} = \frac{d\,(T_q+1)}{8},\]
which is the triangle \(\tfrac12 d\,(T_q/4)\) plus \(d/8\): the trough quarter counts in full. That adds 1.9 points for the strict lockdown and 0.6 for the mild rules.
(c) A fall of 17 percent: then \(17\times5/8 = 10.6\), the cost of the mild rules. A fall of 16 percent costs 10.0. Duration matters as much as depth: a slump twice as long costs about twice as much. A lockdown also saves lives, which Problem 10 adds to the comparison.
strict = np.linspace(85, 100, 5)       # a 15 percent fall, back in 4 quarters
mild = np.linspace(95, 100, 17)        # a 5 percent fall, back in 16 quarters
print(f"strict {gdp_loss(strict):.3f}, mild {gdp_loss(mild):.3f}")
for depth in [16, 17]:
    print(f"strict with a {depth}% fall: {gdp_loss(np.linspace(100 - depth, 100, 5)):.3f}")

Problem 9 (Intermediate): Silicon Valley Bank, March 2023. At the end of 2022, SVB Financial Group, the parent of Silicon Valley Bank, reported total assets of 211.79 billion dollars, cash of 13.80 billion, deposits of 173.11 billion and equity of 16.00 billion. Its assets included bonds to be held to maturity, carried on its balance sheet at a book value of 91.32 billion but with a market value of only 76.17 billion, because interest rates had risen since it bought them (SVB Financial Group, 2022 annual report on Form 10-K, SEC EDGAR). Almost all deposits, 94 percent, were uninsured. On 9 March 2023 depositors withdrew more than 40 billion dollars and asked for about 100 billion more for the next day, and the bank was closed on 10 March (Federal Reserve, review of the supervision of SVB).


If SVB had had to sell those bonds, what fire-sale discount \(\delta\) would it have faced? What was its net worth at market prices?


The calculator starts at SVB’s numbers, in billions: cash 13.8, equity 16.0, \(\delta = 0.17\). Could the bank survive the first day’s run of 40? The two days’ run of 140? What is the largest run \(W^*\) it could survive?


On 12 March the Federal Reserve began to lend to banks against such bonds valued at par, their face value, so that banks would not have to sell them (Federal Reserve, 12 March 2023). What does that do to \(\delta\) in the model, and to the loss from a run of 140? Alternatively, how much cash would SVB have needed to survive a run of 140 at \(\delta = 0.17\)?


The same day, the authorities guaranteed all of SVB’s deposits, insured or not (joint statement, 12 March 2023). Use the model’s idea of a self-fulfilling run to explain why.




Hint

In (a), the discount is the share of the book value that a sale at market prices would lose; at market prices, net worth falls by that same loss, in dollars. In (b), move the withdrawals slider and watch the black dot and the title; \(W^*\) is equation (9) set equal to the equity. In (c), set the discount to 0, then put it back and raise the cash.


def run_calculator(withdrawals=140, cash=13.8, discount=0.17, equity=16.0):
    """A bank run with fire sales (equation 9): the net worth left after runs of every size."""
    runs = np.arange(0, 181, 1)
    left = []
    for W in runs:
        left.append(equity - run_loss(W, cash, discount))
    now = round(equity - run_loss(withdrawals, cash, discount), 1) + 0.0     # + 0.0: never print -0.0
    limit = "no run can sink it"
    if discount > 0:
        limit = f"it survives runs up to {cash + equity * (1 - discount) / discount:.1f}"
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=runs, y=left, mode="lines", name="Net worth left", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[withdrawals], y=[now], mode="markers", name="This run",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Run of {withdrawals}: net worth left {now:.1f} billion; {limit}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Withdrawals W (billions of dollars)", range=[0, 180]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Net worth left (billions)", range=[-100, 45]))
    return fig


interact(run_calculator,
         withdrawals=IntSlider(value=140, min=0, max=175, step=5, description="withdrawals W", style=WIDE),
         cash=FloatSlider(value=13.8, min=0, max=80, step=0.2, description="cash and reserves R", style=WIDE),
         discount=FloatSlider(value=0.17, min=0, max=0.3, step=0.01, description="fire-sale discount δ", style=WIDE),
         equity=FloatSlider(value=16.0, min=2, max=40, step=0.5, description="equity E", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the bank-run model of the Model overview, equation (9), adapted from the discussion of bank runs in Chapter 10 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) \(\delta = 1 - 76.17/91.32 = 16.6\) percent. At market prices the bonds were worth \(91.32 - 76.17 = 15.15\) billion less than on the books, almost all of the 16.00 billion of equity: net worth at market prices was only 0.85 billion. On paper SVB was solvent; at market prices it had almost no cushion left.
(b) With \(\delta = 0.17\), a run of 40 costs \(0.17\times(40-13.8)/0.83 = 5.4\) billion, equation (9), and leaves a net worth of 10.6: the bank survives the first day. A run of 140 costs 25.8 billion and leaves \(-9.8\): the bank is insolvent. Setting the loss equal to \(E\) gives
\[W^* = R + E\,\frac{1-\delta}{\delta} = 13.8 + 16.0\times\frac{0.83}{0.17} = 91.9 \text{ billion},\]
about 53 percent of the deposits. With the unrounded discount of 16.6 percent, \(W^* = 94.2\). The run that came was far larger than that.
(c) Lending against the bonds at par means the bank can raise cash on their full face value without selling them, so in the model \(\delta = 0\). Then equation (9) gives a loss of 0 for any run, and the title says that no run can sink the bank. (In the model every asset can be turned into cash this way; in reality SVB’s cash, its bonds held to maturity and its other bonds, 26.07 billion in the same 10-K, came to 131.2 billion on its balance sheet, less than 140, so it would also have needed loans against its other assets.) Without such lending, the cash it needed solves \(W - R = E(1-\delta)/\delta\): \(R = 140 - 78.1 = 61.9\) billion, about 4.5 times what it had. Set the cash slider to 62: the net worth left is 0.0, just enough.
(d) Uninsured depositors run when they expect the others to run, because those who come late may lose their money. Each run forces fire sales that make the bank insolvent, so the expectation fulfills itself. A guarantee of all deposits removes the reason to run, as deposit insurance does in the Model overview. The authorities also feared that depositors at other banks with many uninsured deposits would run next: the same statement guaranteed all the deposits of Signature Bank in New York, which was closed that day.
book, market, R, E = 91.32, 76.17, 13.80, 16.00          # SVB Financial Group, end of 2022, billions
print(f"(a) discount {100 * (1 - market / book):.1f}%; net worth at market prices {E - (book - market):.2f}")
for W in [40, 140]:
    print(f"(b) run {W}: loss {run_loss(W, 13.8, 0.17):.1f}, net worth left {16.0 - run_loss(W, 13.8, 0.17):.1f}")
print(f"(b) W* = {13.8 + 16.0 * 0.83 / 0.17:.1f}; with the exact discount {R + E * market / (book - market):.1f}")
print(f"(c) cash needed {140 - 16.0 * 0.83 / 0.17:.1f}; net worth left with cash of 62: {16.0 - run_loss(140, 62, 0.17):.2f}")
print(f"(c) run of 140 at zero discount: loss {run_loss(140, 13.8, 0):.1f}; cash and bonds {R + book + 26.07:.1f}")

Problem 10 (Challenge): Was the lockdown worth it? A hypothetical country has an income of 60,000 dollars per person. Health experts expect a strict lockdown to avert 500 deaths per million people, each saving on average 10 years of life, at a cost of 4 percent of a year’s GDP in lost output. Value a life as the chapter does, at \(V = 10\) million dollars spread over \(T = 40\) years; the calculator computes the value of a year of life \(v\) with or without discounting.


Without discounting (\(r = 0\)), compare the cost and the benefit per person. Is the lockdown worth it? And with \(r = 3\) percent?


Find the break-even number of deaths averted, first with the sliders and then with a formula that you derive. How does it change with the cost, the years of life saved and the discount rate?


In the real pandemic, many people stayed home on their own. In U.S. phone data, visits to businesses fell by 60 percentage points, and legal restrictions explain only 7 of them (Goolsbee and Syverson 2021). How should this change the cost and the benefit you count for a lockdown? Name one more thing the calculator leaves out.




Hint

The cost per person is the lost share of income times 60,000. The benefit is the life-years saved per person, \(m/10^6\) times the years per death, times \(v\). Set the two equal and solve for \(m\). For (c), ask what would have happened without the lockdown.


def lockdown_calculator(cost=4.0, deaths_averted=500, years_saved=10, r=0.0):
    """Lost output against the value of the life-years a lockdown saves (lives lost and their value)."""
    V, T, income = 10e6, 40, 60_000               # value of a life, years left, income per person (hypothetical)
    v = V / T                                     # value of a year of life, without discounting
    if r > 0:
        v = r * V / (1 - (1 + r) ** -T)           # with discounting
    lost, saved = cost / 100 * income, deaths_averted / 1e6 * years_saved * v      # dollars per person
    verdict = "break-even"
    if round(saved) > round(lost):
        verdict = "worth it"
    if round(saved) < round(lost):
        verdict = "not worth it"
    top = 7500
    if max(lost, saved) > 7000:
        top = 30000                               # a wider axis only when a bar needs it
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["Lost output", "Value of life-years saved"], y=[lost, saved], marker_color=[GRAY, TEAL],
                           text=[f"{lost:,.0f}", f"{saved:,.0f}"], textposition="outside", cliponaxis=False))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Per person: lost output {lost:,.0f}, life-years saved {saved:,.0f} dollars: {verdict}",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Dollars per person", range=[0, top]))
    return fig


interact(lockdown_calculator,
         cost=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.5, max=10, step=0.5, description="lost output (% of GDP)", style=WIDE),
         deaths_averted=IntSlider(value=500, min=0, max=2000, step=5, description="deaths averted (per million)", style=WIDE),
         years_saved=IntSlider(value=10, min=1, max=20, step=1, description="years of life per death", style=WIDE),
         r=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0, max=0.06, step=0.01, description="discount rate r", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the value of a statistical life in the Model overview, adapted from the discussion of lives lost in the pandemic in Chapter 10 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The cost is \(0.04\times60{,}000 = 2{,}400\) dollars per person. The lockdown saves \(500/10^6\times10 = 0.005\) years of life per person. Without discounting a year of life is worth \(v = V/T = 250{,}000\) dollars, so the benefit is \(0.005\times250{,}000 = 1{,}250\) dollars: not worth it at these numbers. With \(r = 3\) percent, \(v = 0.03\times10^7/(1-1.03^{-40}) = 432{,}624\) dollars and the benefit is 2,163 dollars, still a little below the cost: 90 percent of it.
(b) Write \(c\) for the cost in percent of income \(y\), \(m\) for the deaths averted per million and \(\Delta L\) for the years of life per death. Break-even means
\[\frac{c}{100}\,y = \frac{m}{10^6}\,\Delta L\,v \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m^* = \frac{10^6\,c\,y}{100\,\Delta L\,v}.\]
Without discounting, \(m^* = 10^6\times2{,}400/(10\times250{,}000) = 960\) deaths averted per million; with \(r = 3\) percent, \(m^* = 555\). On the sliders, the title reads “break-even” at 960 when \(r = 0\), and it turns from “not worth it” to “worth it” between 550 and 555 when \(r = 0.03\). The break-even rises in proportion to the cost \(c\) (and to income \(y\)), falls in proportion to the years saved \(\Delta L\), and falls with \(r\), because discounting raises the value of each year, \(v\).
(c) Only what the lockdown itself changes should count. If people would have stayed home anyway, much of the lost output would have been lost without the lockdown, so its own cost is smaller than the whole fall in GDP. For the same reason, staying home on one’s own would have averted some deaths, so the deaths averted by the lockdown itself are fewer. Both sides of the comparison shrink, and the answer depends on which shrinks more. The calculator also leaves out illness that does not kill, lost schooling, who pays the cost and who gains the life-years, and the uncertainty about \(m\) and \(\Delta L\) when the decision has to be made. If most of the deaths averted are of older people, who have fewer years ahead, try 5 years of life per death: the break-even doubles.
V, T, r, income = 10e6, 40, 0.03, 60_000
cost = 4 / 100 * income
for v in [V / T, r * V / (1 - (1 + r) ** -T)]:
    benefit = 500 / 1e6 * 10 * v
    print(f"v = {v:,.0f}: benefit {benefit:,.0f} vs cost {cost:,.0f}; break-even {1e6 * cost / (10 * v):.1f} per million")

title: 11. The IS Curve

Learning goals
Chapter 9 measured the ups and downs of the economy. This chapter builds the first piece of the model that explains them: the IS curve, which links the real interest rate to short-run output. By the end of it you will be able to:

title: 11. The IS Curve
11. The IS Curve
text:
11.1 Model overview
Back on Islandia, the island country whose tools we counted in Chapter 5, Harbor Boatworks is thinking about a new boat shed. The firm would pay for it with a loan, so it compares two numbers: what the shed would earn each year, and the interest on the loan. This year the Bank of Islandia has pushed the real interest rate up, fewer sheds pay for themselves, and Islandia spends less on new tools. How far below its potential level does Islandia’s output then fall? This section answers with the IS curve, the first building block of the short-run model, and follows Islandia through every step.






NoteThe big idea



The question. When the real interest rate rises, how far does output fall below its potential level, and why?
The answer in one sentence. A real interest rate above the return on new capital cuts investment, and with less spending, output falls below potential; the downward-sloping line that links the interest rate to short-run output is the IS curve.
What goes in and what comes out. We choose the normal share of each kind of spending, how strongly investment reacts to the interest rate, the marginal product of capital and, for now, the real interest rate itself. The model gives back short-run output, the percentage gap between actual and potential output, together with every use of output. The second block adds the size of the multiplier, and the third gives the spending plan of a household that smooths its consumption over a lifetime.
Road map.

The IS curve: the assumptions, solving the model step by step, and what the model predicts: moving along the curve versus shifting it.
The multiplier: what changes when islanders’ consumption reacts to booms and slumps.
Permanent income and consumption smoothing: the household decision behind the consumption equation, and why the timing of taxes may not matter.
Model in code: the Key results as Python functions, checked with numbers, plus the drawing tools that every figure reuses.

Notation. As everywhere in the book, a bar over a letter marks something the short-run model takes as given: a parameter such as \(\bar{b}\), or a value handed over by the long-run model, such as potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) and the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\). Letters without a bar are endogenous variables. The real interest rate \(R_t\) has no bar because Chapter 12 will make it endogenous; in this chapter we simply take it as given. In the code we write a, b and r_bar.

11.1.1 The IS curve

Assumptions
Time runs in periods \(t\) (think of quarters or years). Six equations describe Islandia’s short run, and each of them holds in every period.
1. Where output goes. Everything Islandia produces ends up in one of four places. Islanders consume it, Harbor Boatworks invests it in new tools, the Islandia Treasury buys it, or Mainland buys it as exports. Goods that Islandia buys from Mainland are subtracted, because they were made abroad (Chapter 2):
\[Y_t = C_t + I_t + G_t + EX_t - IM_t. \tag{1}\]
This is the national income identity. Add \(IM_t\) to both sides and it reads the other way round: what Islandia produces plus what it brings in from Mainland is everything it has to work with, and it uses all of it in exactly four ways.
2 to 5. Four uses of output that track potential output. Consumption, government purchases, exports and imports are each a fixed share of potential output:
\[C_t = \bar{a}_c\bar{Y}_t, \qquad G_t = \bar{a}_g\bar{Y}_t, \qquad EX_t = \bar{a}_{ex}\bar{Y}_t, \qquad IM_t = \bar{a}_{im}\bar{Y}_t.\]
Potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\) is what Islandia would make with all its workers and tools fully employed. The long-run model of Chapters 5 and 6 pins it down, so here it is given. Tying consumption to \(\bar{Y}_t\), and not to actual output \(Y_t\), is a real assumption about behavior:

potential output moves slowly, so when a slump pulls \(Y_t\) down, \(\bar{Y}_t\) barely changes;
so islanders keep spending much as before, for instance by drawing on their savings.

The third block explains why households behave this way. As rough benchmarks for the United States, consumption is close to two thirds of GDP and government purchases close to one fifth.
6. Investment reacts to the interest rate. The investment share has a normal level \(\bar{a}_i\). It rises above that level or falls below it depending on how the real interest rate \(R_t\) compares with the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\):
\[\frac{I_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_i - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}). \tag{2}\]
Why does the gap matter? Take one unit of output that Harbor Boatworks could turn into a new tool. Installed, the tool yields \(\bar{r}\) extra units of output a period later. Put in the bank instead, or used to pay off a loan, the same unit earns \(R_t\). Say \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent and \(R_t = 3\) percent. If the firm borrows 100 units and builds a shed with them, the shed adds 5 units of output, the loan costs 3 units of interest, and 2 units are left over. Projects like this pay, so investment rises above normal. When \(R_t\) is above \(\bar{r}\), the bank wins, and the firm builds less than usual. The parameter \(\bar{b} > 0\) measures how strongly firms respond: each percentage point of gap moves investment by \(\bar{b}\) percentage points of potential output.
In the long run the two rates are equal, \(R_t = \bar{r}\). Firms keep adding capital until its marginal product falls to the interest rate, as in the Solow model of Chapter 5, and investment rests at its normal share \(\bar{a}_i\). In the short run the two rates can differ. The Bank of Islandia can move \(R_t\) within a day, while the marginal product of capital changes only as new sheds and boats are built and put to work. \(\bar{r}\) has no time subscript because it is constant along a balanced growth path; \(\bar{Y}_t\) keeps its subscript because potential output grows.
Here is the whole model: six equations for six endogenous variables, \(Y_t\), \(C_t\), \(I_t\), \(G_t\), \(EX_t\) and \(IM_t\).

Islandia’s baseline: the numbers used in this notebook. Every IS diagram starts from one set of values, the ones the textbook uses in its own diagrams: no aggregate demand shock, \(\bar{a} = 0\); a sensitivity of investment \(\bar{b} = 2\); and a marginal product of capital \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent. For the demand shares we pick illustrative values, in percent of potential output, that add up to 100: consumption \(\bar{a}_c = 65\), investment \(\bar{a}_i = 17\), government purchases \(\bar{a}_g = 20\), exports \(\bar{a}_{ex} = 12\) and imports \(\bar{a}_{im} = 14\). We measure \(\tilde{Y}\), \(R\), \(\bar{r}\) and \(\bar{a}\) in percent (or percentage points), so every number below is a percentage.

Harbor Boatworks invests more when a new tool earns more than a loan costs, and less when it earns less.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. In the baseline, \(\bar{a}_i = 17\), \(\bar{b} = 2\) and \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent. The Bank of Islandia lowers the real interest rate to 3 percent. What share of potential output does Harbor Boatworks now invest?


Answer

By equation (2), \(I_t/\bar{Y}_t = 17 - 2\times(3 - 5) = 17 + 4 = 21\) percent of potential output: 4 points above normal, because each new tool now earns 2 points more than the loan costs.

2. The Bank raises the real interest rate to 8 percent. At the same time, a new hull design raises the marginal product of capital to 8 percent too. Does investment change?


Answer

No. Equation (2) depends only on the gap \(R_t - \bar{r}\), which is still zero, so investment stays at its normal share, \(\bar{a}_i = 17\) percent of potential output. A high interest rate does not hold investment back when new tools earn just as much.





Solving the model
Step 1: write every use of output as a share of potential output. Divide both sides of the identity (1) by \(\bar{Y}_t\). Each term becomes a share:
\[\frac{Y_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \frac{C_t}{\bar{Y}_t} + \frac{I_t}{\bar{Y}_t} + \frac{G_t}{\bar{Y}_t} + \frac{EX_t}{\bar{Y}_t} - \frac{IM_t}{\bar{Y}_t}.\]
Step 2: substitute the demand equations. Divide each of assumptions 2 to 5 by \(\bar{Y}_t\): \(C_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_c\), \(G_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_g\), \(EX_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_{ex}\) and \(IM_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_{im}\). Equation (2) already gives the investment share. Put all five on the right-hand side:
\[\frac{Y_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_c + \big[\bar{a}_i - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r})\big] + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{ex} - \bar{a}_{im}.\]
Five of the six unknowns are gone. Only \(Y_t\) is left, and it depends on the interest rate and on parameters.
Step 3: from the output ratio to short-run output. Short-run output, defined in Chapter 9, is the percentage gap between actual and potential output. Split the fraction in two to see how it relates to the ratio on the left of step 2:
\[\tilde{Y}_t \equiv \frac{Y_t - \bar{Y}_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \frac{Y_t}{\bar{Y}_t} - \frac{\bar{Y}_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \frac{Y_t}{\bar{Y}_t} - 1.\]
For small gaps, \(\tilde{Y}_t \approx \ln Y_t - \ln\bar{Y}_t\) (Appendix C.6). So \(\tilde{Y}_t = -0.02\), or \(-2\) percent, means that Islandia produces 2 percent less than its potential.
Step 4: subtract 1 from both sides. The left side of step 2 becomes \(\tilde{Y}_t\). On the right, gather the constant terms into one group:
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \underbrace{\bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{ex} - \bar{a}_{im} - 1}_{\text{call it } \bar{a}} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}).\]
Give the group a name, \(\bar{a}\), and six equations have shrunk to one straight line:






ImportantKey result: the IS curve



\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}), \qquad \bar{a} \equiv \bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{ex} - \bar{a}_{im} - 1. \tag{3}\]
Short-run output falls as the real interest rate rises above the marginal product of capital, by \(\bar{b}\) points for each point of gap. The aggregate demand shock \(\bar{a}\) sets where the line sits.
Islandia in numbers. In the baseline, \(\bar{a} = 0\), \(\bar{b} = 2\) and \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent. A real interest rate of 4 percent gives \(\tilde{Y} = 0 - 2\times(4 - 5) = +2\) percent, and one of 7 percent gives \(\tilde{Y} = 0 - 2\times(7 - 5) = -4\) percent.








TipIn words



Islandia’s output can leave its potential for two reasons. The first is \(\bar{a}\), the aggregate demand shock: it packs the five spending shares into one number, which says how far total spending at normal interest rates sits from potential output. The second is the interest-rate term, and there only the gap \(R_t - \bar{r}\) counts, not the level of \(R_t\). A high interest rate does not stop Harbor Boatworks from building if each new shed earns just as much.


Step 5: the long-run value of \(\bar{a}\). In the long run Islandia produces at potential, \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0\), and the interest rate equals the marginal product of capital, \(R_t = \bar{r}\). Put both into equation (3): \(0 = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\times 0\), so \(\bar{a} = 0\). Through the definition of \(\bar{a}\), this means that at potential the five spending shares add up to exactly one: \(\bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{ex} - \bar{a}_{im} = 1\). Islandia’s baseline shares pass this test, since \(65 + 17 + 20 + 12 - 14 = 100\) percent. So \(\bar{a} = 0\) is the normal case, and shocks to spending push \(\bar{a}\) away from zero for a while.
Step 6: the curve on a graph. The textbook draws the curve with output across and the interest rate up, so we solve equation (3) for \(R_t\). Move the interest-rate term to the left and \(\tilde{Y}_t\) to the right, then divide by \(\bar{b}\) (Appendix C.9):
\[\bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}) = \bar{a} - \tilde{Y}_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R_t = \bar{r} + \frac{\bar{a} - \tilde{Y}_t}{\bar{b}}.\]
In this form the IS curve is a line with slope \(-1/\bar{b}\) through the point \((\tilde{Y}, R) = (\bar{a}, \bar{r})\). With \(\bar{b} = 2\) the slope is \(-0.5\): to raise output by one point, the interest rate must fall by half a point. A larger \(\bar{b}\) gives a flatter line.
The same numbers, share by share. The Key result gave Islandia’s output at two interest rates in one step. Building it up from the six equations gives the same answers:

at \(R = 4\) percent, investment is \(17 - 2\times(4 - 5) = 19\) percent of potential output, so \(Y/\bar{Y} = 65 + 19 + 20 + 12 - 14 = 102\) percent and \(\tilde{Y} = +2\) percent;
at \(R = 7\) percent, investment is \(17 - 2\times 2 = 13\) percent, \(Y/\bar{Y} = 96\) percent and \(\tilde{Y} = -4\) percent.

Step 7: why the curve is called “IS”. The letters stand for investment equals saving, and the identity (1) shows why. Keep investment on the right and move every other term to the left:
\[Y_t - C_t - G_t + (IM_t - EX_t) = I_t.\]
Now add and subtract tax revenue \(T_t\) on the left. Since \(-T_t + T_t = 0\), only the grouping changes:






ImportantKey result: investment equals saving



\[\underbrace{(Y_t - T_t - C_t)}_{\text{private saving}} + \underbrace{(T_t - G_t)}_{\text{government saving}} + \underbrace{(IM_t - EX_t)}_{\text{foreign saving}} = I_t. \tag{4}\]
Three kinds of saving together pay for investment: what islanders keep from their after-tax income, the Treasury’s surplus, and what Mainland lends Islandia when it ships more goods than it buys.
Islandia in numbers. At potential, with the baseline shares and taxes of, say, 18 percent of potential output, private saving is \(100 - 18 - 65 = 17\), government saving is \(18 - 20 = -2\) (a deficit) and foreign saving is \(14 - 12 = 2\). Total saving is 17 percent of potential output, exactly the investment share.


Each piece has a plain meaning. Households save the part of their after-tax income that they do not consume. The Islandia Treasury saves when its tax revenue exceeds its purchases, that is, when it runs a surplus. Mainland saves in Islandia when it ships Islandia more goods than it buys from it, because it is lending Islandia the difference. John Hicks introduced the curve in 1937, as a compact algebraic version of Keynes’s General Theory. Equation (4) returns when the book studies budget deficits and the trade balance.

Six equations shrink to one downward-sloping line: an interest rate above the return on capital means output below potential.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. In the baseline, the Bank of Islandia sets the real interest rate at 6 percent. What share of potential output is invested, and what is short-run output?


Answer

By equation (2), investment is \(17 - 2\times(6 - 5) = 15\) percent of potential output. Adding up the uses, \(Y/\bar{Y} = 65 + 15 + 20 + 12 - 14 = 98\) percent, so output is 2 percent below potential. Equation (3) gives the same answer in one step: \(\tilde{Y} = 0 - 2\times(6 - 5) = -2\).

2. At potential, with \(R = \bar{r}\), the Islandia Treasury raises taxes from 18 to 20 percent of potential output and keeps its purchases unchanged. Which kinds of saving in equation (4) change, and does total saving still equal investment?


Answer

In this block consumption follows potential output, so it stays at its share of 65. Private saving falls to \(100 - 20 - 65 = 15\) percent, government saving rises to \(20 - 20 = 0\), and foreign saving stays at \(14 - 12 = 2\) percent. Total saving is still 17 percent, the investment share: equation (4) is an identity, so it holds whatever the Treasury does.





What the model predicts
Comparative statics. Equation (3) is linear, so each effect is a constant: the derivative of \(\tilde{Y}_t\) with respect to that parameter (Appendix C.7). Because \(\tilde{Y}\) is already a percentage, each number reads as “percent of potential output per percentage point”.

What the signs mean for Islandia:

Along or shift. The IS curve plots output against the interest rate, so a change in \(R_t\) is read off the curve itself: a movement along it. A change in anything else in equation (3) changes the output that goes with each interest rate: a shift of the whole curve.
Demand shocks pass into output one for one. Suppose Harbor Boatworks grows optimistic about a new boat design and raises \(\bar{a}_i\) by 1 point. Then \(\bar{a}\) goes from 0 to 1 and, at an unchanged interest rate, output ends up 1 percent above potential. It works the same way in reverse for gloomy islanders (\(\bar{a}_c\) falls), cuts in Treasury purchases (\(\bar{a}_g\) falls) or a slump on Mainland that lowers the demand for Islandia’s exports (\(\bar{a}_{ex}\) falls). The last case is how recessions travel from one country to another.
The slope comes from investment. The more strongly investment reacts to the interest rate (a larger \(\bar{b}\)), the more output moves when the interest rate moves.
Potential output does not shift the curve. When a new technology lifts potential output, actual output rises in the same proportion, so the gap \(\tilde{Y}_t\) stays the same. A storm that wrecks part of Islandia’s tools works the same way: actual and potential output fall together.
But the return on capital does. The same technology, or the same storm, can also raise the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\): the tools that survive, or the tools that use the new ideas, earn more. At an unchanged \(R_t\) investment rises, and output goes up by \(\bar{b}\) points for every point of \(\bar{r}\).


A change in the interest rate moves Islandia along its IS curve; a change in anything else shifts the whole curve.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. A slump on Mainland cuts Islandia’s export share from 12 to 10 percent of potential output, and the Bank keeps the real interest rate at \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent. What is the new \(\bar{a}\), where is output, and how does the IS curve move?


Answer

By the definition in equation (3), \(\bar{a} = 65 + 17 + 20 + 10 - 14 - 100 = -2\). At \(R = \bar{r}\), output is 2 percent below potential. The whole curve shifts left by 2 points, the same kind of shift as for the pessimistic consumers of Fig. 8.

2. A better hull design raises the marginal product of capital from 5 to 6 percent, while the Bank keeps the real interest rate at 5 percent. Why does output rise, and by how much?


Answer

A new tool now earns 1 point more than a loan costs, so Harbor Boatworks builds more. By equation (3), \(\tilde{Y} = 0 - 2\times(5 - 6) = +2\) percent: \(\bar{b}\) points of output for each point of \(\bar{r}\). The IS curve shifts up by 1 point, as in Fig. 9.






11.1.2 The multiplier

Assumptions
Keep every assumption of the IS curve except the consumption equation. Consumption now also reacts to booms and slumps:
\[\frac{C_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_c + \bar{x}\,\tilde{Y}_t, \qquad 0 < \bar{x} < 1.\]
When Islandia’s output is 1 percent above potential, islanders consume \(\bar{x}\) percent of potential output more than their normal share. The parameter \(\bar{x}\) stands for households that spend part of a short-lived rise in income instead of smoothing it away. The third block shows why such households show up in the data.


Solving the model
Step 1: redo the derivation with the new consumption share. Steps 1 to 4 of the IS curve go through as before, with one extra term on the right, because \(C_t/\bar{Y}_t\) now equals \(\bar{a}_c + \bar{x}\tilde{Y}_t\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} + \bar{x}\,\tilde{Y}_t - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}),\]
with \(\bar{a}\) defined exactly as in equation (3). Short-run output now appears on both sides.
Step 2: solve for \(\tilde{Y}_t\). Subtract \(\bar{x}\tilde{Y}_t\) from both sides, factor out \(\tilde{Y}_t\), and divide by \(1 - \bar{x}\), which is positive because \(\bar{x} < 1\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t - \bar{x}\,\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1 - \bar{x})\,\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}).\]






ImportantKey result: the IS curve with a multiplier



\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{1}{1 - \bar{x}}\times\big[\bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r})\big] \tag{5}\]
The factor \(1/(1 - \bar{x})\) is the multiplier. Since \(\bar{x}\) lies between 0 and 1, it is larger than 1: every effect of equation (3) is scaled up.
Islandia in numbers. With \(\bar{x} = 1/3\) the multiplier is \(1/(2/3) = 1.5\), and with \(\bar{x} = 1/2\) it is 2. In the baseline with \(\bar{x} = 1/3\), a 1-point rise in the interest rate lowers output by \(2\times 1.5 = 3\) percent instead of 2 percent.


Step 3: the same result, round by round. Where does the extra output come from? Let the interest rate rise by 1 point in the baseline. Investment falls by \(\bar{b} = 2\) points of potential output, so in the first round output falls by 2 percent. Lower output means lower incomes, and consumption falls by \(\bar{x}\) times that, \(\frac{1}{3}\times 2 = \frac{2}{3}\) of a point: a second round. That cut in spending lowers other incomes and trims consumption again, by \(\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{2}{3} = \frac{2}{9}\) of a point, and so on. Adding up all the rounds:
\[\Delta\tilde{Y} = -2\,\big(1 + \bar{x} + \bar{x}^2 + \bar{x}^3 + \cdots\big).\]
The bracket is a geometric series (Appendix C.12). Call it \(S\). Multiplying by \(\bar{x}\) moves every term one place along, \(\bar{x}S = \bar{x} + \bar{x}^2 + \bar{x}^3 + \cdots\), and subtracting this from \(S\) leaves only the first term: \(S - \bar{x}S = 1\), so \(S = 1/(1 - \bar{x})\). The total is \(-2\times 1.5 = -3\) percent, exactly what equation (5) gives. The series adds up to a finite number only when \(\bar{x} < 1\), which is why the model needs that assumption: if every lost unit of income cut spending by a unit or more, the rounds would never die out.






TipIn words: the rounds of spending



Harbor Boatworks builds fewer sheds, so its boatbuilders earn less. They spend less at the island’s market, so the stallholders earn less, and they in turn spend a little less too. Each round is a third the size of the one before, so the echoes fade, but together they make the first fall half as large again.


Step 4: a second route to a multiplier, through investment. Multiply equation (2) by \(\bar{Y}_t\) to write investment in levels:
\[I_t = \bar{a}_i\bar{Y}_t - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r})\,\bar{Y}_t.\]
Investment grows in step with potential output. One reason is cash flow, the funds firms have left after paying their costs. Harbor Boatworks can pay for a shed more cheaply out of its own funds than with a loan, and the cash flow of all firms together moves roughly with potential output. If cash flow also rises in a boom, investment gets an extra term in \(\tilde{Y}_t\). Write it, with a label of our own, as \(+\bar{z}\tilde{Y}_t\) in the investment share. Then steps 1 and 2 give a multiplier of \(1/(1 - \bar{x} - \bar{z})\), as long as \(\bar{x} + \bar{z} < 1\). The curve keeps the same form; only the size of the multiplier changes.
