0.00



Yes: the model says that households with little liquid wealth spend the rebate and those with more save it, as Johnson, Parker and Souleles find. In the band between 3.8 and 4 the MPC is \((2 - f_{\text{today}}/2)/0.1 = 20 - 5f_{\text{today}}\), so an MPC of 0.3 needs \(f_{\text{today}} = (20 - 0.3)/5 = 3.94\): a household so close to its constraint that the rebate just lifts it off. Such households are rare, since the band is only 0.2 wide. An average MPC of 20 to 40 percent must therefore come mainly from a mix of households that spend all and households that spend nothing.
(c) The average MPC is
\[\text{MPC} = \lambda \times 1 + (1 - \lambda) \times 0 = \lambda .\]
So the share of households with little liquid wealth equals the average MPC. Estimates of 20 to 40 percent within three months point to \(\lambda\) between 0.2 and 0.4, and about two-thirds within six months to \(\lambda \approx\) 0.67. The estimates cover only nondurable goods, so counting all spending could give a larger share. Either way, a sizable share of households behaved as if they had little liquid wealth and could not borrow.
(d) In the permanent-income view, consumption depends on total wealth, and total wealth changes when the household learns about the rebate, in June. From then on the rebate is already part of \(\bar{X}\), so the arrival of the check is no news and should not move spending: this is the random-walk logic, where only surprises change consumption. A household that waits for the check before it spends is one that could not borrow against a payment it knew was coming. The random mailing dates let the researchers compare households that had their check with households that were still waiting, so the jump at arrival is not a seasonal or business-cycle effect.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Aging Japan and life-cycle saving. Japan’s population has aged fast. Its old-age dependency ratio, the number of people aged 65 and over per 100 people aged 15 to 64, rose from 20.2 in 1994 to 50.7 in 2024 (World Bank, Age dependency ratio, old). Over the same years, Japan’s household saving rate fell from 12.8 to 0.7 percent in the OECD data of Fig. 4. Use the life-cycle worker of the Model overview: \(T = 60\) periods of life, of which the first \(W = 40\) are working periods at income \(y\), with \(R = 0\), \(\beta = 1\) and no bequests.

Suppose the same number of people is born every period, so that every age group has the same size. Show that the total saving of all households is exactly zero, although every worker saves.
Now let there be \(N\) workers and \(dN\) retirees, so that \(d\) is the number of retirees per worker. Show that total saving as a share of total labor income is \[s = 1 - \frac{W}{T}\,(1 + d).\] Which value of \(d\) makes \(s = 0\), and how does it relate to part (a)?
Treat the dependency ratio as \(d\), so \(d = 0.202\) in 1994 and \(d = 0.507\) in 2024. Compute \(s\) for both years and compare with the data.
Name two features of the real world that the model leaves out and that could explain why it predicts more saving in 1994 than the data show.



Hint


At any moment there are \(W\) workers, each saving \(y - c\), and \(T - W\) retirees, each spending \(c\) out of their wealth. Use \(c = Wy/T\) from equation (8). (b) Add up what the \(N\) workers save and what the \(dN\) retirees spend out of their wealth, then divide by total labor income.



# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) By equation (8), every person consumes \(c = Wy/T\) in every period. With one person born per period, at any moment \(W\) people are working and \(T - W\) are retired. Workers save \(y - c\) each, and retirees dissave \(c\) each, so total saving is
\[W(y - c) - (T - W)\,c = Wy - Tc = Wy - T\cdot\frac{Wy}{T} = 0.\]
The saving of the workers exactly pays for the consumption of the retirees, so total household wealth stays constant, although each worker builds up wealth for his own retirement.
(b) Total saving is \(N(y - c) - dN c\) and total labor income is \(Ny\). Divide, then use \(c/y = W/T\):
\[s = \frac{N(y - c) - dNc}{Ny} = 1 - \frac{c}{y} - d\,\frac{c}{y} = 1 - \frac{c}{y}(1+d) = 1 - \frac{W}{T}(1 + d).\]
Setting \(s = 0\) gives \(1 + d = T/W\), so \(d = (T - W)/W = 20/40 = 0.5\). That is the ratio of retirees to workers of part (a): with equal age groups there are \(T - W = 20\) retirees for every \(W = 40\) workers. A younger population (\(d < 0.5\)) saves; an older one (\(d > 0.5\)) dissaves.
(c) With \(W/T = 2/3\):

1994: \(s = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1.202) = 0.199\), about 19.9 percent;
2024: \(s = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1.507) = -0.005\), about −0.5 percent.

T, W = 60, 40
for year, d in [(1994, 0.202), (2024, 0.507)]:
    s = 1 - (W / T) * (1 + d)                       # part (b)
    print(f"{year}: d = {d}, model saving rate = {100 * s:.1f}%")
print(f"No saving when d = (T - W)/W = {(T - W) / W:.2f}")
The model gets the direction right: as Japan’s ratio passed the threshold of 0.5, household saving should have fallen to about zero, and in the data it did, to 0.7 percent. But the model’s fall, 20.3 points, is larger than the fall in the data, 12.1 points, because it starts too high in 1994.
(d) Some possibilities:

Public pensions. When the state pays part of retirement income out of the contributions of current workers, workers need less private saving and retirees run down less of their own wealth. The model, with no pensions, overstates both.
Bequests and precautionary saving in old age. Retirees who want to leave wealth to their children, or who keep a buffer against a long life and health costs, dissave less than \(c\).
A rough match of \(d\). The dependency ratio counts everyone over 64, but people do not all stop working on their 65th birthday. The model also has no income growth and no interest rate, both of which change how much each generation saves.




Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): Did debt and saving move together? Figs. 3 and 4 suggest that U.S. households borrowed more as they saved less. Merge fig16-3.csv, household debt in percent of GDP (from the Federal Reserve’s Financial Accounts, CMDEBT, via FRED), and fig16-4.csv, the personal saving rate (from the BEA, PSAVERT, via FRED), on date. Compute the correlation between the debt ratio and the saving rate for 1970–2007 and for 2008 to the end of the data. Did the link survive the financial crisis?


Hint

Read the two files into two new tables, say us_debt and us_saving. Then us_debt.merge(us_saving, on="date") puts the two series side by side, one row per quarter. Keep the rows with .date.dt.year <= 2007 for the first period and >= 2008 for the second, and apply .corr to the two columns of each part.


# Your answer here



Solution

Merge the two files, split the quarters at the start of 2008, and compute one correlation for each part. New names such as us_debt keep the tables of Figs. 3 and 4 unchanged, so their widgets still work.
us_debt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig16-3.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
us_saving = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig16-4.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
us_both = us_debt.merge(us_saving, on="date")
us_before = us_both[us_both.date.dt.year <= 2007]
us_after = us_both[us_both.date.dt.year >= 2008]
for name, part in [("1970-2007", us_before), ("2008-2026", us_after)]:
    link = part.debt_gdp_pct.corr(part.saving_rate)
    print(f"{name}: {len(part)} quarters, correlation {link:.2f}")
print(us_before.iloc[[0, -1]])
print(us_after.iloc[[0, -1]])

1970–2007 (152 quarters): the correlation is −0.93, close to a perfect negative line. Debt rose from 42.9 to 96.8 percent of GDP while the saving rate fell from 12.0 to 2.2 percent.
2008–2026 (74 quarters): the correlation is only −0.09. Debt fell, to 65.7 percent of GDP in the last quarter, apart from the jump of 2020 when GDP collapsed, but saving first rose, then jumped in the pandemic and came back down, to 4.4 percent.

So the tight inverse link did not survive the crisis. Before 2008 both series followed one long trend in opposite directions, and two series with strong trends tend to show a strong correlation, whatever causes them. A correlation alone does not show that one series drives the other.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): After the 2008 crisis, who saved more? If households fear for their future, precautionary saving says they should save more, and perhaps most where they had borrowed most. Use the household debt of the Bank for International Settlements (household_debt.csv, quarterly) and the household saving rates of the OECD (saving_rates.csv, annual).

For each country, compute the rise of household debt, in percent of GDP, from 2000 to 2007 (use the yearly averages of the quarterly data), and the change of the saving rate from 2007 to 2009.
In how many of the countries with both numbers did saving rise from 2007 to 2009? What is the correlation between the two changes?
Name two countries that fit the pattern well and two clear exceptions, and suggest a reason for one exception.



Hint

Add a year column with .date.dt.year; then .groupby(["country", "year"]).debt_gdp.mean() gives yearly averages. pivot_table(index="country", columns="year", values=...) puts the years in columns, so wide[2007] - wide[2000] is one change per country. Put the two changes in one table with pd.DataFrame({...}) and drop the countries that miss one of them with .dropna().


# Your answer here



Solution

Average the quarterly debt data by year, put the years side by side for both files, and take the two differences. pd.DataFrame lines the countries up by name, and .dropna() keeps only the countries with both numbers.
debt_q = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "household_debt.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
debt_q["year"] = debt_q.date.dt.year
debt_y = debt_q.groupby(["country", "year"]).debt_gdp.mean().reset_index()     # yearly averages
debt_wide = debt_y.pivot_table(index="country", columns="year", values="debt_gdp")
save_y = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "saving_rates.csv")
save_wide = save_y.pivot_table(index="country", columns="year", values="saving_rate")
crisis = pd.DataFrame({"debt rise 2000-07": debt_wide[2007] - debt_wide[2000],
                       "saving change 2007-09": save_wide[2009] - save_wide[2007]}).dropna()
rose = (crisis["saving change 2007-09"] > 0).sum()
crisis_corr = crisis["debt rise 2000-07"].corr(crisis["saving change 2007-09"])
print(f"{len(crisis)} countries; saving rose in {rose}; correlation {crisis_corr:.2f}")
crisis.sort_values("debt rise 2000-07").round(1)
(a)–(b) The two files share 25 countries. Saving rose from 2007 to 2009 in 20 of them, and the correlation between the debt build-up and the rise in saving is 0.54: households saved more where they had borrowed more.
(c) Spain (debt up 36.5 points of GDP, saving up 6.0 points) and Denmark (36.3 and 5.1) fit the pattern well: a large build-up of debt, then a sharp turn to saving. At the other end, Germany and Japan, where household debt fell before the crisis, barely changed their saving (−0.3 and +1.4). The two clearest exceptions, the countries farthest from a straight line through the cloud, are Mexico, where saving jumped by 6.1 points with little debt build-up (+4.2), and Italy, whose households added 15.2 points of debt but saved less in 2009 (−1.3). Greece is a milder exception: its households borrowed as much as Spain’s (+36.4) but raised saving by only 2.3 points. A possible reason for Greece: its debt crisis turned into a deep recession, with real GDP 27 percent lower in 2013 than in 2008 (World Bank, GDP, constant 2015 US$), so many households could not save more. From 2010 on its saving rate is negative in every year of our data. The correlation of 0.54 leaves much of the variation unexplained, and two numbers per country are a short story: treat the pattern as suggestive, not as proof.



Modeling problems
Problem 6 (Intermediate): A student loan or a tax rebate? Take the baseline Irving with \(R = 0\) and \(\beta = 1\): no financial wealth, income 1 today and 5 in the future. He cannot borrow, so he consumes 1 today and 5 later. A government considers two hypothetical policies: (i) a student-loan program that lets him borrow up to \(L\) today and repay it in the future; (ii) a rebate \(\Delta\) today, paid for by a tax of \(\Delta\) on Irving in the future (with \(R = 0\) no interest is due). The sliders below redraw Fig. 2 with his consumption today as \(c_1\) and in the future as \(c_2\).

With the rebate at 0, find the smallest loan limit at which Irving consumes his unconstrained plan. By how much does lifetime utility rise?
Set the loan limit back to 0 and move the rebate. Show that a rebate \(\Delta\) has the same effect as a loan limit \(L = \Delta\), and explain why.
What is the MPC out of the rebate for rebates up to 2, and above 2? What does this say about the claim that debt-financed tax cuts cannot raise consumption?
Confirm your numbers with constrained_today and lifetime_utility.



Hint

The unconstrained plan is \(\bar{X}/2\). With a loan, the constraint of equation (9) becomes \(c_{\text{today}} \le y_{\text{today}} + L\). For (b), write Irving’s two budgets with the rebate and compare them with his budgets under a loan.


def loan_or_rebate(limit=0.0, rebate=0.0):
    """Fig. 2 for the baseline Irving (R = 0) who may borrow up to `limit` and gets a rebate repaid by a later tax."""
    y_now, y_later = 1.0 + rebate, 5.0 - rebate             # the later tax repays the rebate (R = 0)
    wanted = consumption_plan(0.0, y_now, y_later, 0.0)[0]  # equation (6): half of total wealth
    c1 = min(wanted, y_now + limit)                         # equation (9), with a loan of at most `limit`
    c2 = y_now + y_later - c1                               # the rest is spent in the future
    fig = smoothing_diagram(c1, c2, "log")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"c₁ = {c1:.2f} today, c₂ = {c2:.2f} later:  lifetime utility "
                            f"{lifetime_utility(c1, c2):.3f}  (free borrowing {2 * np.log(3):.3f})")
    return fig


interact(loan_or_rebate,
         limit=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=3.0, step=0.25, description="loan limit L", style=WIDE),
         rebate=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=3.0, step=0.25, description="rebate Δ", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 2 above, with the borrowing constraint of equation (9), adapted from Fig. 16.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) Total wealth is \(\bar{X} = 0 + 1 + 5 = 6\), so the unconstrained plan is \(c_{\text{today}} = c_{\text{future}} = 3\). With a loan limit \(L\), Irving consumes \(c_{\text{today}} = \min\{3,\ 1 + L\}\). The sliders show \(c_1\) rising one for one with \(L\) until \(L = 2\), where \(c_1 = c_2 = 3\) and the two dots meet: the smallest limit is \(L = 2\), and a larger limit changes nothing. Lifetime utility rises from \(\log 1 + \log 5 = 1.609\) to \(2\log 3 = 2.197\), by 0.588. Another way to see the size of this gain: the uneven path \((1, 5)\) gives the same lifetime utility as a smooth path of \(\sqrt{1 \times 5} = 2.236\) in each period, so the constraint hurts Irving as much as losing about 25 percent of his smooth consumption of 3.
(b) With the rebate, Irving’s budgets are \(c_{\text{today}} + f_{\text{future}} = 1 + \Delta\) and \(c_{\text{future}} = 5 - \Delta + f_{\text{future}}\), with \(f_{\text{future}} \ge 0\). Write \(b = \Delta - f_{\text{future}}\) for the part of the rebate he spends today. Then \(c_{\text{today}} = 1 + b\) and \(c_{\text{future}} = 5 - b\) with \(b \le \Delta\). With a loan of at most \(L\) and no rebate, the budgets are \(c_{\text{today}} = 1 + b\) and \(c_{\text{future}} = 5 - b\) with \(b \le L\). The two sets of choices are the same when \(\Delta = L\), and the sliders show identical dots and titles for, say, \(L = 1, \Delta = 0\) and \(L = 0, \Delta = 1\). A rebate that the same person repays through later taxes is a loan from the government.
(c) For \(\Delta \le 2\) the constraint binds, so \(c_{\text{today}} = 1 + \Delta\): the MPC is 1. Above 2 Irving can already afford his plan of 3, so he saves the rest of the rebate to pay the later tax: the MPC is 0, and Ricardian equivalence holds. So a debt-financed tax cut does raise consumption today when it reaches households that cannot borrow, but it gives them nothing extra over their lifetime: consumption later falls by the same amount. The policy works by lending to them, and a student-loan program would do the same.
(d)
for size in [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0]:
    c1 = constrained_today(0.0, 1.0 + size, 5.0 - size, 0.0)    # rebate `size`, repaid by a later tax
    c2 = 6.0 - c1                                               # total resources are 6 with R = 0
    print(f"rebate {size}: c_today = {c1:.2f}, c_future = {c2:.2f}, lifetime utility {lifetime_utility(c1, c2):.3f}")
print(f"Smooth path with the utility of (1, 5): {np.sqrt(5):.3f} per period")
The rebates 0, 1, 2 and 3 give consumption today of 1.00, 2.00, 3.00 and 3.00, and lifetime utility of 1.609, 2.079, 2.197 and 2.197.

Problem 7 (Challenge): Unemployment insurance and precautionary saving. Irving’s future income is now risky: \(5 - s\) or \(5 + s\) with equal chances, where \(s\) is the spread (the Model overview used \(s = 2\)). A hypothetical unemployment-insurance program narrows the spread but keeps average future income at 5. Keep \(R = 0\), \(\beta = 1\), log utility, \(f_{\text{today}} = 0\) and \(y_{\text{today}} = 1\). The slider below finds Irving’s best consumption today by a grid search, and redraws Fig. 2 with his two possible levels of future consumption as \(c_1\) and \(c_2\).

Read consumption today for \(s = 2\), \(1\) and \(0\). How much does an insurance that halves the spread from 2 to 1 raise consumption today?
Derive a formula for consumption today from the expected Euler equation. Show that \[c_{\text{today}} = \frac{18 - \sqrt{36 + 8s^2}}{4}.\]
Show that for small spreads precautionary saving, \(3 - c_{\text{today}}\), is about \(s^2/6\). Does it grow with the spread or with its square? What does that mean for the first and the last steps of a program that removes the risk step by step?



Hint

Future consumption is \(6 - s - c\) or \(6 + s - c\), where \(c = c_{\text{today}}\). Write \(a = 6 - c\): the average of \(1/(a - s)\) and \(1/(a + s)\) simplifies to \(a/(a^2 - s^2)\). Solve the quadratic and keep the root that leaves positive consumption in the bad case. For (c), use \(\sqrt{1 + x} \approx 1 + x/2\) for small \(x\) (Appendix C.6).


def insurance(spread=2.0):
    """Fig. 2 for risky future income 5 - spread or 5 + spread (R = 0, beta = 1); c_today from a grid search."""
    grid = np.linspace(0.01, 5.99 - spread, 20001)              # c_today that keeps consumption positive
    low, high = 6.0 - spread - grid, 6.0 + spread - grid        # future income + saving (1 - c_today)
    U = np.log(grid) + 0.5 * np.log(low) + 0.5 * np.log(high)   # expected lifetime utility
    best = np.argmax(U)
    extra = round(3.0 - grid[best], 2) + 0.0                     # precautionary saving; + 0.0 avoids -0.0
    fig = smoothing_diagram(low[best], high[best], "log")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"spread {spread:.2f}: c_today = {grid[best]:.2f}, precautionary saving {extra:.2f}; "
                            f"future c {low[best]:.2f} or {high[best]:.2f}")
    return fig


interact(insurance,
         spread=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=4.0, step=0.25, description="income spread s", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 2 above, with the risky future income of the precautionary-saving block of the Model overview, adapted from Fig. 16.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) The title reads \(c_{\text{today}} = 2.44\) for \(s = 2\) (precautionary saving 0.56), \(2.84\) for \(s = 1\) (0.16) and \(3.00\) for \(s = 0\). Halving the spread raises consumption today by 0.40, or 17 percent, although average future income does not change. The chart shows the risk itself: the narrower the spread, the closer the average utility (the open circle) moves to the utility of the average (the dot on the curve). As the Model overview explains, it is the curvature of marginal utility \(1/c\) that turns this risk into extra saving.
(b) Irving saves \(1 - c\) today, so future consumption is \(6 - s - c\) or \(6 + s - c\). The expected Euler equation with \(\beta(1+R) = 1\) is
\[\frac{1}{c} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{6 - s - c} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{6 + s - c}.\]
With \(a = 6 - c\), the right side is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{(a + s) + (a - s)}{(a - s)(a + s)} = \dfrac{a}{a^2 - s^2}\). Cross-multiplying, \(a^2 - s^2 = ac\). Put \(a = 6 - c\) back:
\[(6 - c)^2 - s^2 = (6 - c)\,c \;\Longrightarrow\; 36 - 12c + c^2 - s^2 = 6c - c^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; 2c^2 - 18c + (36 - s^2) = 0.\]
The quadratic formula gives \(c = \big[18 \pm \sqrt{324 - 8(36 - s^2)}\big]/4 = \big[18 \pm \sqrt{36 + 8s^2}\big]/4\). The plus root is at least 6, so it would leave consumption of \(6 - s - c \le -s\), zero or less, in the bad case. The minus root is the answer:
\[c_{\text{today}} = \frac{18 - \sqrt{36 + 8s^2}}{4}.\]
With \(s = 0\) it gives \((18 - 6)/4 = 3\), and with \(s = 2\) it gives \((18 - \sqrt{68})/4 = 2.44\), the \((9 - \sqrt{17})/2\) of the Model overview.
(c) Factor out 36: \(\sqrt{36 + 8s^2} = 6\sqrt{1 + 2s^2/9} \approx 6\,(1 + s^2/9) = 6 + 2s^2/3\). Then \(c_{\text{today}} \approx (12 - 2s^2/3)/4 = 3 - s^2/6\), so precautionary saving is about \(s^2/6\): it grows with the square of the spread, that is, with the variance of income.
for s in [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]:
    c = (18 - np.sqrt(36 + 8 * s ** 2)) / 4                  # the formula of part (b)
    low, high = 6 - s - c, 6 + s - c                          # future consumption, bad and good case
    print(f"s = {s}: c_today = {c:.3f}, precautionary saving {3 - c:.3f} (approx. {s ** 2 / 6:.3f}); "
          f"1/c = {1 / c:.4f}, average of 1/c_future = {0.5 / low + 0.5 / high:.4f}")
The two sides of the expected Euler equation agree for every spread. The approximation is close for small spreads (0.167 against 0.158 for \(s = 1\)) and too large for big ones. Because saving grows with the square of the risk, the first steps of an insurance program do the most: cutting the spread from 4 to 3 raises consumption today by 0.60 (from 1.30 to 1.90), while removing the last unit of spread, from 1 to 0, adds only 0.16. Insurance against large losses, such as a long spell of unemployment, frees up the most consumption today.

title: 17. Investment
text:
Learning goals
Investment links the present to the future: a firm that buys a machine today gives up money now for output later. One tool, the arbitrage equation, explains investment in machines, in stocks and in houses. By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

title: 17. Investment
17. Investment
text:
17.1 Model overview
Back on Islandia, Harbor Boatworks builds the island’s fishing boats. This year it has some cash to spare, and it faces a plain choice: leave the money in a savings account at a bank in town, or buy one more machine for its workshop, say a power saw that cuts planks. How many machines should the firm own, and how much should it spend on new ones each year? One idea answers both questions, and it also prices a share of Harbor Boatworks and an islander’s seaside cottage.






NoteThe big idea



The question. How much capital does a firm want to own, and how does that wish turn into a yearly flow of investment?
The answer in one sentence. By the arbitrage equation, a firm adds capital until the last unit earns its user cost: the bank’s interest plus wear and tear, minus any rise in its price.
What goes in and what comes out. We choose the interest rate, depreciation, the expected price change of capital, taxes and productivity. The model gives back the user cost, desired capital, the investment rate, and the prices of a share and a house.
Road map.

Investment and the user cost of capital: the assumptions, the arbitrage equation and the user cost in solving the model, and what the model predicts.
Taxes and the user cost: what a tax on Harbor Boatworks’ profits does to the cost of capital.
From desired capital to investment: how many machines the firm wants, and what share of output it invests.
The stock market: pricing a share: what a share of Harbor Boatworks is worth.
Tobin’s q: the stock market and investment: how the share price tells the firm whether to invest.
Housing: the arbitrage equation for a house: the price of a cottage bought with a mortgage.
Model in code: every key result as a Python function, checked with numbers.

Notation. A bar over a letter marks a parameter that comes from outside the model, such as \(\bar{d}\) or \(\bar{A}\); Jones writes some given numbers, such as \(R\), \(\tau\) and \(L\), without a bar. All rates are decimals: \(R = 0.02\) means 2 percent a year.

17.1.1 Investment and the user cost of capital

Assumptions

Two uses of cash. Harbor Boatworks has money to spare. It can leave it in the bank for a year at the interest rate \(R\). Or it can buy one unit of capital, a power saw, at the price \(p_k\), use it in the workshop for a year, and sell it at the end of the year for \(p_{k,t+1} = p_k + \Delta p_k\).
No risk. The firm knows in advance what each option pays, so only the size of the payoff matters.
Diminishing returns. One more saw raises output by the marginal product of capital, \(MPK\). With the other inputs held fixed, \(MPK\) falls as the firm owns more capital (Chapter 4).
Wear and tear. Like Islandia’s tools in Chapter 5, the saws wear out: a fraction \(\bar{d}\) of the capital is used up during the year.
Profit maximization. The firm shifts money between the bank and the workshop until no shift can raise its profits.

The production model of Chapter 4 gave a first answer: add capital until \(MPK = R\). The argument below extends that rule to capital that wears out and changes in price.


Solving the model
Step 1: the arbitrage equation. Imagine the firm puts the same \(p_k\) dollars into each option for one year, and compare the payoffs. The bank pays interest on the whole sum. The saw pays its marginal product, plus whatever its price did during the year: a capital gain if the price went up, a capital loss if it went down. When the firm has chosen its capital stock well, neither option pays more than the other.






ImportantKey result: the arbitrage equation



\[\underbrace{R\cdot p_k}_{\text{deposit } p_k \text{ in the bank}} = \underbrace{MPK + \Delta p_k}_{\text{buy the machine, sell it after a year}} \tag{1}\]
Two safe uses of the same money must pay the same.








TipIn words: why the two sides end up equal



Suppose a new saw paid Harbor Boatworks more than the bank. Then the firm would buy another one. But each extra saw has less work to do than the one before, so \(MPK\) falls, and the firm keeps buying until the saw’s payoff has come down to the bank’s. If it paid less, the firm would hold fewer, busier saws. Either way it settles where equation (1) holds.


Step 2: returns per dollar. Choose the unit of capital so that one unit costs one dollar today, \(p_k = 1\), and divide both sides of (1) by \(p_k\). The left side is now just \(R\), and \(\Delta p_k/p_k\) is the capital gain in percent. Solve for \(MPK\):
\[R = MPK + \frac{\Delta p_k}{p_k} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad MPK = R - \frac{\Delta p_k}{p_k}.\]
If the price of capital never changes, \(\Delta p_k = 0\), we are back at the Chapter 4 rule, \(MPK = R\).
Step 3: depreciation. Wear and tear is a capital loss of its own kind: after a year in the workshop, only a share \(1-\bar{d}\) of the saw is left to sell. So we let \(p_k\) be the price of a new unit and write depreciation as its own term. One dollar of capital then returns \(MPK - \bar{d} + \Delta p_k/p_k\). Set this equal to \(R\), and move \(\bar{d}\) and the capital gain to the other side:
\[R = MPK - \bar{d} + \frac{\Delta p_k}{p_k} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad MPK = R + \bar{d} - \frac{\Delta p_k}{p_k}.\]






ImportantKey result: the user cost



\[MPK = \underbrace{R + \bar{d} - \frac{\Delta p_k}{p_k}}_{\text{user cost of capital, } uc} \tag{2}\]
We call \(uc\) the user cost of capital: what one more unit of capital costs to use for a year. It has three parts: the interest given up by not leaving the money in the bank (\(R\)), the part of the machine that wears out (\(\bar{d}\)), and, with a minus sign, any rise in the machine’s price, which the firm gets back when it sells.
Islandia in numbers. With this notebook’s baseline, \(R = 0.02\), \(\bar{d} = 0.08\) and a constant price of capital, \(uc = 0.02 + 0.08 - 0 = 0.10\). A saw must add at least 10 cents of output a year for every dollar it costs.



A machine is worth buying only if it earns the bank’s interest plus its own wear and tear, minus any rise in its price.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Harbor Boatworks also uses design computers, whose price falls by 4 percent a year. With \(R = 0.02\) and \(\bar{d} = 0.08\), what is their user cost?


Answer

A falling price is a capital loss, \(\Delta p_k/p_k = -0.04\). Equation (2) gives \(uc = 0.02 + 0.08 + 0.04 = 0.14\), or 14 percent. Each dollar of computers must add 14 cents of output a year, not 10.

2. Suppose the last saw the firm bought adds more output than its user cost. Has the firm chosen its capital stock well?


Answer

No. One more saw would pay more than the same money in the bank, so the firm should buy it. Diminishing returns then bring \(MPK\) down to the user cost of equation (2).





What the model predicts
In Fig. 1, \(MPK\) is a curve that falls as capital rises, and the user cost is a flat line, because it does not depend on how many saws the firm owns. The firm buys capital up to the point where the two meet. Anything that raises the user cost lifts the flat line and moves that point to the left:

Equipment whose price keeps falling, such as computers, loses value every year on top of wearing out, so it is expensive to hold. A building on land that tends to gain value brings a capital gain, which lowers its user cost. So, for the same \(MPK\) curve, a firm holds fewer computers and more buildings.

Higher interest rates, faster wear and expected price falls all raise the user cost, and the firm wants fewer machines.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. The interest rate on Islandia rises from 2 to 3 percent, with \(\bar{d} = 0.08\) and no price change. What is the new user cost, and which way does Harbor Boatworks’ desired capital stock move?


Answer

By equation (2), \(uc = 0.03 + 0.08 = 0.11\). The flat line in Fig. 1 moves up, so it meets the falling \(MPK\) curve at a smaller capital stock: the firm wants fewer saws.






17.1.2 Taxes and the user cost

Assumptions
Keep every assumption above, and add a corporate income tax. The Islandia Treasury takes a share \(\tau\) of the extra income that each unit of capital produces, so Harbor Boatworks keeps \((1-\tau)MPK\). As in the textbook’s version, depreciation and capital gains are not taxed. One unit of new capital still costs one dollar, \(p_k = 1\).


Solving the model
Step 1: the arbitrage equation after tax. The money still costs \(R\). What a dollar of capital returns is now the marginal product after tax, minus depreciation, plus the capital gain:
\[\underbrace{R}_{\text{cost of the funds}} = \underbrace{(1-\tau)MPK - \bar{d} + \frac{\Delta p_k}{p_k}}_{\text{return on a dollar of capital}}.\]
Step 2: solve for the marginal product. Add \(\bar{d}\) to both sides and subtract the capital gain, so that only the taxed term is left on the right: \(R + \bar{d} - \Delta p_k/p_k = (1-\tau)MPK\). Divide both sides by \(1-\tau\):
\[MPK = \frac{R + \bar{d} - \Delta p_k/p_k}{1-\tau}.\]






ImportantKey result: the user cost with a corporate tax



\[MPK = \underbrace{\frac{R + \bar{d} - \Delta p_k/p_k}{1-\tau}}_{\text{user cost with the tax}} \tag{3}\]
The tax divides the user cost by \(1-\tau\).
Islandia in numbers. A tax of \(\tau = 0.35\) raises the baseline user cost from \(0.10\) to \(0.10/0.65 \approx 0.154\), about 15.4 percent.








TipIn words



The Islandia Treasury takes a slice of what every saw produces, but it pays no part of the saw’s costs. The interest, the wear and tear and the price change are just as before. So a saw must produce more before tax, by the factor \(1/(1-\tau)\), to leave Harbor Boatworks the same return after tax as the bank.



A tax on the profits of capital works like a higher price of using it: the bar each machine must clear goes up.



What the model predicts

Direction. A higher tax rate always raises the user cost, so the firm wants less capital. In Fig. 2 the user-cost line shifts up and the firm climbs its \(MPK\) curve to a smaller capital stock.
Size. Take logs of equation (3) (Appendix C.4): \(\ln uc = \ln(R + \bar{d} - \Delta p_k/p_k) - \ln(1-\tau)\). When the share the firm keeps, \(1-\tau\), falls by 1 percent, the user cost rises by 1 percent.
The tax magnifies everything else. With the tax, each extra point of \(R\) or \(\bar{d}\) raises the user cost by \(1/(1-\tau)\) points: 1.54 points when \(\tau = 0.35\).
Comparing countries. Suppose the user cost before tax is the same in every country. Then equation (3) gives each country’s user cost from a single known one: \(uc_i = uc_{\text{US}}\times(1-\tau_{\text{US}})/(1-\tau_i)\). With \(uc_{\text{US}} = 0.10\) and \(\tau_{\text{US}} = 0.21\), the user cost before tax is \(0.10\times0.79 = 0.079\). This is how we rebuild Table 17.1 in the key numbers after Fig. 2.


Corporate taxes raise the cost of capital, and they make it more sensitive to interest rates and depreciation.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Use the before-tax user cost of 0.079 from Table 17.1. What is the user cost in a country whose corporate tax rate is 30 percent?


Answer

By equation (3), \(uc = 0.079/(1-0.30) = 0.079/0.70 \approx 0.113\), about 11.3 percent.

2. Why does a tax make the user cost react more strongly to a change in the interest rate?


Answer

In equation (3), the interest rate sits in the numerator, which is divided by \(1-\tau\). So each point of \(R\) adds \(1/(1-\tau)\) points to the user cost, more than one point whenever \(\tau > 0\).






17.1.3 From desired capital to investment

Assumptions

Production. Harbor Boatworks (or Islandia as a whole) produces with the Cobb-Douglas function of Chapter 4, \(Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}\), with labor fixed at \(L\).
Desired capital. The firm holds the capital stock at which \(MPK = uc\), with the user cost of equation (2), or of equation (3) when there is a tax.
Capital accumulation. As in the Solow model, next year’s capital is this year’s investment plus the capital that has not worn out: \[K_{t+1} = I_t + (1-\bar{d})K_t.\]
Growth. In the long run the capital stock grows at a rate \(g_K \equiv \Delta K_{t+1}/K_t\), which the growth models of Chapters 5 and 6 determine. Here we take it as given.

Our baseline. Besides \(R = 0.02\) and \(\bar{d} = 0.08\), we set \(\bar{A} = 0.3\) and \(L = 1\). These two values are our own choice. They make the desired capital stock exactly \(K = 1\) and output \(Y = 0.3\), so that Figs. 1 and 2 start from round numbers. For the investment rate we use an illustrative \(g_K = 0.02\).


Solving the model
Step 1: the marginal product of capital. \(MPK\) is the derivative of output with respect to capital, with labor held fixed (Appendix C.7). By the power rule, the exponent \(1/3\) moves to the front and drops by one, to \(1/3 - 1 = -2/3\):
\[MPK = \frac{\partial Y}{\partial K} = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}K^{-2/3}L^{2/3}.\]
Two other ways of writing this are useful. First, \(\bar{A}K^{-2/3}L^{2/3} = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}/K = Y/K\), since dividing by \(K\) lowers its exponent by one. Second, \(K^{-2/3}L^{2/3} = (L/K)^{2/3}\), since two powers with the same exponent combine into one power of their ratio (Appendix C.3). Hence
\[MPK = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{K} = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\bar{A}\left(\frac{L}{K}\right)^{2/3}.\]
The exponent on \(K\) is negative, so \(MPK\) falls as capital rises: diminishing returns. (In the textbook’s statement of this production function the exponent on labor is printed as \(1/2\). Constant returns to scale require \(2/3\), which is also the value the \(MPK\) formula uses.)
Step 2: the desired capital stock. Set the second form equal to the user cost and solve for \(K\). First multiply both sides by \(3/\bar{A}\):
\[\frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\left(\frac{L}{K}\right)^{2/3} = uc \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left(\frac{L}{K}\right)^{2/3} = \frac{3\,uc}{\bar{A}}.\]
Then raise both sides to the power \(3/2\), because \(\left((L/K)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2} = L/K\), and flip both sides:
\[\frac{L}{K} = \left(\frac{3\,uc}{\bar{A}}\right)^{3/2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K = L\left(\frac{\bar{A}}{3\,uc}\right)^{3/2}.\]
Step 3: the capital-output ratio. Now set the first form equal to the user cost, \(\frac{1}{3}\,Y/K = uc\), and multiply both sides by 3 to get \(Y/K = 3\cdot uc\).






ImportantKey result: the marginal product and the desired capital stock



\[MPK = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{K} = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\bar{A}\left(\frac{L}{K}\right)^{2/3} \tag{4}\]
\[K^{\text{desired}} = L\left(\frac{\bar{A}}{3\,uc}\right)^{3/2} \tag{5}\]
\[\frac{Y}{K} = 3\cdot uc \tag{6}\]
Islandia in numbers. In the baseline, \(\bar{A}/(3\,uc) = 0.3/0.3 = 1\), so \(K^{\text{desired}} = 1\). Output is \(3\times0.10 = 0.30\) per unit of capital, so the firm holds capital worth \(1/0.3 \approx 3.3\) years of output.








TipIn words: what productivity does and does not change



If Harbor Boatworks’ workers became more productive, every saw would earn more, and the firm would want more saws (equation 5). But equation (6) holds for any \(\bar{A}\) and \(L\). Output and capital rise together, so the ratio of output to capital stays where the user cost puts it.


Step 4: the investment that reaches the desired stock. In the accumulation equation, put the firm’s current capital \(K_t\) on the right and its desired capital in place of \(K_{t+1}\), then solve for investment:
\[I_t = K^{\text{desired}} - (1-\bar{d})K_t.\]
A firm with \(K_t = 0.5\) that wants \(K = 1\) next year must invest \(1 - 0.92\times0.5 = 0.54\): 0.50 to grow and 0.04 to replace the capital that wears out. If \(K^{\text{desired}}\) is below \((1-\bar{d})K_t\), the formula gives a negative number. The firm then stops investing and lets depreciation shrink its capital, or sells some of it.
Step 5: the investment rate. Subtract \(K_t\) from both sides of the accumulation equation to write it as a change, and divide by \(K_t\):
\[\Delta K_{t+1} = I_t - \bar{d}K_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\Delta K_{t+1}}{K_t} = \frac{I_t}{K_t} - \bar{d}.\]
Write \(I_t/K_t\) as the product \((I_t/Y_t)\cdot(Y_t/K_t)\). The \(Y_t\) cancels, so the value does not change, but the investment rate \(I_t/Y_t\) now shows up:
\[g_K = \frac{I_t}{Y_t}\cdot\frac{Y_t}{K_t} - \bar{d}.\]
Replace \(Y_t/K_t\) by \(3\cdot uc\) from equation (6), add \(\bar{d}\) to both sides, and divide by \(3\cdot uc\).






ImportantKey result: the investment rate



\[\frac{I_t}{Y_t} = \frac{g_K + \bar{d}}{3\cdot uc} \tag{7}\]
Islandia in numbers. With \(g_K = 0.02\), \(\bar{d} = 0.08\) and \(uc = 0.10\), the investment rate is \(0.10/0.30 \approx 33\) percent. With the 35 percent tax, \(uc \approx 0.154\) and the rate falls to about 21.7 percent.








TipIn words



The numerator is the new capital needed for each unit Harbor Boatworks already owns: enough to grow by \(g_K\) and to replace what wore out. The denominator turns “per unit of capital” into “per unit of output”. When the user cost is high, the firm holds little capital for each boat it builds (equation 6), so keeping that small stock growing takes only a small share of output.



The user cost sets how much capital a firm wants, and the investment rate is what it takes to keep that capital growing.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. The interest rate rises to \(R = 0.03\), so \(uc = 0.11\), with \(\bar{A} = 0.3\), \(L = 1\) and \(g_K = 0.02\). What are Harbor Boatworks’ desired capital and Islandia’s investment rate?


Answer

Now \(3\,uc = 0.33\). Equation (5) gives \(K^{\text{desired}} = (0.3/0.33)^{3/2} \approx 0.87\), down from 1. Equation (7) gives \(I/Y = 0.10/0.33 \approx 0.303\), about 30.3 percent instead of 33 percent.

2. After the 35 percent tax, the firm wants \(K \approx 0.52\) but owns \(K = 1\). If it stops investing, how many years does depreciation take to bring its capital below the new target?


Answer

With \(I_t = 0\), the accumulation equation gives \(K_{t+1} = 0.92\,K_t\). After \(n\) years capital is \(0.92^n\), and \(0.92^n < 0.52\) first holds at \(n = 8\) (since \(0.92^8 \approx 0.513\)). So it takes 8 years without any investment, as the key numbers after Fig. 2 confirm.





What the model predicts
Take logs of equations (5) and (7) (Appendix C.4):
\[\ln K^{\text{desired}} = \ln L + \tfrac{3}{2}\ln\bar{A} - \tfrac{3}{2}\ln 3 - \tfrac{3}{2}\ln uc, \qquad
\ln\frac{I}{Y} = \ln(g_K + \bar{d}) - \ln 3 - \ln uc.\]
Each coefficient is an elasticity:









A 1% rise in …
changes \(K^{\text{desired}}\) by
changes \(I/Y\) by
Which curve moves




user cost \(uc\) (from \(R\), \(\bar{d}\), a capital loss or \(\tau\))
\(-1.5\%\)
\(-1\%\)
user-cost line up


productivity \(\bar{A}\)
\(+1.5\%\)
\(0\)
\(MPK\) curve up


labor \(L\)
\(+1\%\)
\(0\)
\(MPK\) curve up


the after-tax share \(1-\tau\)
\(+1.5\%\)
\(+1\%\)
user-cost line down




Capital reacts more than one for one. Desired capital is proportional to \(uc^{-3/2}\), so the 35 percent tax shrinks it by the factor \(0.65^{3/2} \approx 0.52\), nearly in half. The reason is the long, flat tail of the \(MPK\) curve: when returns fall off slowly, a small rise in the return the firm demands removes a lot of capital.
Productivity and labor raise capital, not the investment rate. They push the \(MPK\) curve up, so the firm wants more capital. But they do not appear in equation (7): output grows in proportion, and \(I/Y\) stays put.
Depreciation pulls two ways. A higher \(\bar{d}\) adds replacement investment to the numerator of (7), and it also raises the user cost in the denominator. Write \(uc = R + \bar{d} - \Delta p_k/p_k\) and take the derivative: the net effect on \(I/Y\) has the sign of \(R - \Delta p_k/p_k - g_K\). In our baseline \(R = g_K = 0.02\) and there is no capital gain, so the two effects cancel exactly and \(I/Y = 1/3\), capital’s exponent, for any \(\bar{d}\).
A theory of the saving rate. The Solow model of Chapter 5 took the investment rate \(\bar{s}\) as given. Equation (7) explains it: taxes, interest rates and depreciation move it through the user cost. Add the growth models (which set \(g_K\)) and the Euler equation of Chapter 16 (which sets the long-run interest rate), and equations (6) and (7) close a long-run model of a closed economy: its capital-output ratio, its investment rate, and so the share of GDP that is consumed.
Reaching the target takes time. Installing new capital is costly and disrupts production, so real firms approach \(K^{\text{desired}}\) over several years, not in one jump.


Desired capital is very sensitive to the user cost, while the investment rate depends only on the user cost, growth and depreciation.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Keep \(R = g_K = 0.02\) and no capital gain, but let depreciation rise from 0.08 to 0.12. What is the new investment rate?


Answer

The user cost becomes \(0.02 + 0.12 = 0.14\), and equation (7) gives \(I/Y = (0.02 + 0.12)/(3\times0.14) = 0.14/0.42 \approx 0.333\). The rate does not move: more replacement investment is exactly offset by a smaller capital stock per unit of output.






17.1.4 The stock market: pricing a share

Assumptions

Two uses of savings. An islander can deposit savings in the bank at the interest rate \(R\), or buy one share of Harbor Boatworks at the price \(p_s\), hold it for a year and sell it.
Two payoffs from a share. During the year the firm pays each shareholder a dividend, part of its profits. At the end of the year the share sells at its new price, \(p_s + \Delta p_s\).
No risk. The islander knows the dividend and next year’s price. Real shares are risky; we leave risk out.
Steady growth. In the last steps the dividend grows at a constant rate \(g\) each year, with \(g < R\).



Solving the model
Step 1: the arbitrage equation for a stock. Put \(p_s\) dollars into each option. The bank pays \(R\cdot p_s\). The share pays its dividend plus its capital gain. With no risk, the two must be equal; otherwise everyone would want only the better one, and its price would move:
\[\underbrace{R\cdot p_s}_{\text{bank}} = \underbrace{\text{dividend} + \Delta p_s}_{\text{share}}.\]
The dividend plays the part that \(MPK\) played for the saw: it is what the asset pays even if its price stays the same.
Step 2: returns in percent. Divide both sides by \(p_s\).






ImportantKey result: the arbitrage equation for a stock



\[R = \underbrace{\frac{\text{dividend}}{p_s}}_{\text{dividend yield}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Delta p_s}{p_s}}_{\text{capital gain, in percent}} \tag{8}\]
The interest rate equals the stock’s total return: its dividend yield plus its percentage capital gain.


If the share paid more than the bank, islanders would rush to buy it. Its price would rise today, and both terms on the right would shrink until the gap was gone.
Step 3: solve for the price. Subtract the capital gain from both sides of (8), so that \(R - \Delta p_s/p_s = \text{dividend}/p_s\). Then flip both sides and multiply by the dividend:
\[p_s = \frac{\text{dividend}}{R - \Delta p_s/p_s}.\]
Step 4: steady dividend growth. Let the dividend grow at \(g\), and guess that the price is always the same multiple of this year’s dividend. Then the price grows as fast as the dividend, \(\Delta p_s/p_s = g\), and step 3 becomes \(p_s = \text{dividend}/(R - g)\).
The guess holds up. Rearranged, the arbitrage equation of step 1 says \(p_{s,t+1} = (1+R)\,p_{s,t} - \text{dividend}_t\). If \(p_{s,t} = \text{dividend}_t/(R-g)\), then
\[p_{s,t+1} = \text{dividend}_t\left[\frac{1+R}{R-g} - \frac{R-g}{R-g}\right] = \text{dividend}_t\,\frac{1+g}{R-g} = \frac{\text{dividend}_{t+1}}{R-g},\]
so the same formula holds next year, and every year after.






ImportantKey result: the price of a share



\[p_s = \frac{\text{dividend}}{R - g} \tag{9}\]
Islandia in numbers. With \(R = 0.05\), a share of Harbor Boatworks that pays 3 dollars a year forever is worth \(3/0.05 = 60\) dollars. If the dividend grows at \(g = 0.02\), the share is worth \(3/0.03 = 100\) dollars.








TipIn words: a share is worth its future dividends



Equation (9) is the present discounted value of every dividend the share will ever pay (Appendix C.12). A dividend that stays the same is discounted at \(R\). A dividend that grows is discounted at the smaller rate \(R - g\), which is why growth makes a share so much more valuable.


The algebra: a dividend \(D\) paid one year from now, growing at \(g\) after that, is worth today
\[\frac{D}{1+R} + \frac{D(1+g)}{(1+R)^2} + \frac{D(1+g)^2}{(1+R)^3} + \dots = \frac{D}{1+R}\cdot\frac{1}{1 - \frac{1+g}{1+R}} = \frac{D}{1+R}\cdot\frac{1+R}{R-g} = \frac{D}{R-g},\]
by the sum of a geometric series, \(1 + x + x^2 + \dots = 1/(1-x)\), with \(x = (1+g)/(1+R) < 1\).
Step 5: the price-earnings ratio. Divide both sides of (9) by the firm’s earnings, its accounting profit per share. The share of earnings paid out as dividends is the payout ratio.






ImportantKey result: the price-earnings ratio



\[\frac{p_s}{\text{earnings}} = \frac{\text{dividend}/\text{earnings}}{R - g} \tag{10}\]
Islandia in numbers. With a payout ratio of one half, \(R = 0.05\) and \(g = 0.02\) (the starting values of Fig. 3), the model’s P/E ratio is \(0.5/0.03 \approx 16.7\).



A share is worth the present value of its dividends, discounted at the interest rate minus their growth rate.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islanders come to expect Harbor Boatworks’ dividend of 3 dollars to grow at 3 percent instead of 2, with \(R = 0.05\). What is the share worth now, and what is the P/E ratio with a payout of one half?


Answer

By equation (9), \(p_s = 3/(0.05 - 0.03) = 3/0.02 = 150\) dollars, up 50 percent from 100. By equation (10), the P/E ratio rises to \(0.5/0.02 = 25\).





What the model predicts

Signs. The price and the P/E ratio rise with the dividend (or the payout ratio) and with expected growth \(g\). They fall when the interest rate \(R\) rises.
Sensitivity. In logs, \(\ln p_s = \ln(\text{dividend}) - \ln(R-g)\): the price has an elasticity of \(-1\) with respect to the gap \(R - g\). A small gap makes small changes large in percentage terms. Cutting \(R - g\) from 3 to 2 percentage points, a cut of one third, raises the price by half (\(0.03/0.02 = 1.5\)). A P/E ratio of 40 with a payout of one half needs a gap of only \(0.5/40 = 1.25\) points.
Bubbles are hard to spot. Turn (10) around to read the gap that the market’s price implies: \(R - g = \text{payout}/(P/E)\). A high P/E ratio may be a bubble, or it may mean that savers expect faster growth or lower interest rates. The data have a hard time telling the two apart (Fig. 3).
Efficient markets. If prices already reflect all that is known about future dividends, only news that nobody expected can move them. Good surprises are as likely as bad ones, so today’s information cannot predict tomorrow’s price change: the price follows a random walk. Real markets come close to this benchmark, since most actively managed mutual funds fail to beat a simple index fund for long. Still, prices swing more than dividends seem to justify, and bubbles appear from time to time.


Because the gap between interest and growth is small, small shifts in beliefs can move share prices a lot.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia’s stock market trades at a P/E ratio of 40, and firms pay out half their earnings. What gap \(R - g\) does that price imply, and does it prove there is a bubble?


Answer

Turning equation (10) around, \(R - g = 0.5/40 = 0.0125\), or 1.25 percentage points. It does not prove a bubble: the same price fits savers who expect faster dividend growth or lower interest rates, and the price alone cannot tell these stories apart.






17.1.5 Tobin’s q: the stock market and investment

Definitions
James Tobin compared two values of the same firm. One is what the stock market says the firm is worth, \(V\): the present value of all its future profits. The other is what it would cost to buy all of its capital new, \(p_kK\).






ImportantKey result: Tobin’s q



\[q = \frac{V}{p_kK} = \frac{\text{stock market value of the firm}}{\text{replacement cost of its capital}} \tag{11}\]
Tobin’s \(q\) compares what the market pays for Harbor Boatworks with the cost of rebuilding its workshop.




Solving the model
Step 1: the value of a firm that owns only capital. Take a firm with the Cobb-Douglas technology above, \(p_k = 1\), no taxes and a constant price of capital. Capital is paid its marginal product, so the firm’s capital income is \(MPK\cdot K\), exactly a third of output with the exponent \(1/3\). Each year it spends \(\bar{d}K\) to replace the capital that wore out, which keeps \(K\) constant, and it pays the rest to its shareholders. So its dividend is constant, \((MPK - \bar{d})K\), and equation (9) with \(g = 0\) gives the firm’s value:
\[V = \frac{(MPK - \bar{d})K}{R}.\]
Step 2: divide by the value of capital. With \(p_k = 1\), the denominator of equation (11) is just \(K\), which cancels.






ImportantKey result: q for a firm that owns only capital



\[q = \frac{MPK - \bar{d}}{R} \tag{12}\]
Islandia in numbers. At its desired capital, \(K = 1\), Harbor Boatworks has \(MPK = 0.10\) and \(q = (0.10 - 0.08)/0.02 = 1\). With only \(K = 0.5\), it has \(MPK \approx 0.159\) and \(q \approx 3.9\).


Step 3: the link to the user cost. \(q = 1\) exactly when \(MPK - \bar{d} = R\), that is, when \(MPK = R + \bar{d}\): the user cost of equation (2) without a capital gain. So a \(q\) above 1 is the stock market’s way of saying that \(MPK\) is above the user cost:
\[q > 1 \iff MPK > uc \iff \text{the firm should invest}.\]






TipIn words



When \(q > 1\), Harbor Boatworks could sell new shares, spend the money on saws, and be worth more than the saws cost: investing creates value for its owners. When \(q < 1\), the firm is worth less than its machines, and its owners would gain by selling some of them.



Tobin’s q reads the firm’s investment signal off the stock market: above one, buy capital; below one, shrink.



What the model predicts

\(q\) near 1. If adjusting the capital stock cost nothing, firms would keep \(MPK = uc\) at every moment, so \(q\) would always be 1. When installing capital is slow and costly (a production line must stop, a new plant must be built), firms close the gap gradually, and \(q\) can stay above or below 1 for a while.
\(q\) predicts investment. Firms with a high \(q\) should invest, and firms with a low \(q\) should shrink.
In the data, \(q\) is often well above 1, because firms own assets that are not counted in \(K\): brand names, patents and know-how, which the stock market values too.
Financial frictions. Studies of many firms find that tax changes move investment through \(q\) and the user cost, as the theory predicts. But a firm’s own cash flow, and how easily it can borrow from banks or raise money in financial markets, also matter, and the simple model leaves them out.


In practice q drifts away from one, because capital takes time to install and markets value more than machines.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Harbor Boatworks has overbuilt and owns \(K = 1.2\). With the baseline \(\bar{A} = 0.3\), \(L = 1\), \(R = 0.02\) and \(\bar{d} = 0.08\), what are its \(MPK\) and its \(q\)? What should it do?


Answer

Equation (4) gives \(MPK = 0.1\times(1/1.2)^{2/3} \approx 0.089\). Equation (12) gives \(q = (0.089 - 0.08)/0.02 \approx 0.43\). Since \(q < 1\), its \(MPK\) is below the user cost of 0.10: it should stop investing and let its capital shrink toward \(K = 1\).






17.1.6 Housing: the arbitrage equation for a house

Assumptions

The investor. An islander can keep her down payment in the bank at the interest rate \(R\), or use it to buy a seaside cottage at the price \(P^{\text{house}}\), rent it out for a year, and sell it.
Leverage. The down payment is a share \(\bar{x}\) of the price. She borrows the rest, \((1-\bar{x})P^{\text{house}}\), with a mortgage at the rate \(R\). The leverage ratio, the price of the house per dollar of her own money, is \(1/\bar{x}\).
Taxes. Mortgage interest is deductible at the tax rate \(\tau\), so each dollar of interest costs her only \(1-\tau\) dollars.
The house. It earns a rent, wears out at the rate \(\bar{d}\) of its value, and its price changes by \(\Delta P^{\text{house}}\) during the year. There is no risk, and buying or selling costs nothing.



Solving the model
Step 1: the arbitrage equation. The bank pays \(R\) on the down payment. The cottage pays the rent, minus depreciation, plus the capital gain, minus the interest on the mortgage after tax:
\[R\cdot\bar{x}P^{\text{house}} = \text{rent} - \bar{d}P^{\text{house}} + \Delta P^{\text{house}} - R(1-\tau)(1-\bar{x})P^{\text{house}}.\]
Step 2: divide by the price. Every term except the rent contains \(P^{\text{house}}\):
\[R\bar{x} = \frac{\text{rent}}{P^{\text{house}}} - \bar{d} + \frac{\Delta P^{\text{house}}}{P^{\text{house}}} - (1-\tau)R(1-\bar{x}).\]
Step 3: collect the interest terms. Move every term except the rent ratio to the left. Expand \((1-\tau)R(1-\bar{x}) = (1-\tau)R - (1-\tau)R\bar{x}\). The two terms in \(R\bar{x}\) then combine into \(R\bar{x} - (1-\tau)R\bar{x} = \tau\bar{x}R\):
\[\frac{\text{rent}}{P^{\text{house}}} = \tau\bar{x}R + (1-\tau)R + \bar{d} - \frac{\Delta P^{\text{house}}}{P^{\text{house}}}.\]
Step 4: solve for the price. Flip both sides and multiply by the rent.






ImportantKey result: the price of a house



\[P^{\text{house}} = \frac{\text{rent}}{\tau\bar{x}R + (1-\tau)R + \bar{d} - \Delta P^{\text{house}}/P^{\text{house}}} \tag{13}\]
The denominator is the user cost of a house.
Islandia in numbers. With the values of the house price key numbers, a rent of 6,000 dollars a year, \(R = 0.04\), \(\bar{d} = 0.02\), \(\tau = 0.3\), \(\bar{x} = 0.2\) and expected price growth of 0.02, the denominator is \(0.0024 + 0.028 + 0.02 - 0.02 = 0.0304\), and the cottage is worth \(6000/0.0304\), about 197,000 dollars.








TipIn words



The cottage’s user cost works like the saw’s in equation (2): the interest on the down payment and on the loan (made cheaper by the tax deduction), plus depreciation, minus the price gain she expects. The price is the present value of the rents, discounted at that user cost. Without the tax, \(\tau = 0\), the denominator is just \(R + \bar{d} - \Delta P^{\text{house}}/P^{\text{house}}\), the user cost of any capital good.



A house is priced like any capital good: its rent divided by its user cost.



What the model predicts
The price rises when the denominator of (13) falls. The derivative of the denominator with respect to each parameter gives:



A rise in …
changes the denominator by
House price




rent

rises in proportion


interest rate \(R\)
\(\tau\bar{x} + 1 - \tau\) per point
falls

\(+1\) per point

\(-1\) per point
rises

\(+\tau R\) per unit
falls
