title: 18. The Government and the Macroeconomy
text:
Practice problems
The problems come in three types: conceptual problems apply the accounting relations of the Model overview to real cases, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data, and modeling problems use small calculators built on those relations to answer policy questions. Each one is labeled Basic, Intermediate or Challenge; try it on your own first, then open the Hint and the Solution. The calculators run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, the website version of Fig. 6 above shows the debt projection.

Conceptual problems
Problem 1 (Basic): Who lends to the German government? In 2025 Germany reformed its constitutional debt brake, the rule that limits government borrowing. The IMF’s 2025 Article IV press release on Germany projects a general government balance of −2.4 percent of GDP for 2025 and −3.4 percent for 2026, while the current account surplus shrinks from 4.5 to 4.0 percent of GDP. Foreign saving is minus the current account balance: a country with a surplus lends to the rest of the world.

In our data (gov_finance.csv, from the OECD national accounts via the OECD Data Explorer, the file behind the country menus of Figs. 1 and 5), Germany’s private investment was 17.6 percent of GDP in 2024 and its budget balance −2.6 percent. The same IMF release puts the 2024 current account surplus at 5.8 percent of GDP. Use equation (9) to compute German private saving in 2024.
Suppose the 2026 projections come true and private saving stays at the same share of GDP. By how much does private investment change from 2025 to 2026? Which values of \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) in equation (10) describe this case?
What would private saving have to do for investment not to fall at all?



Hint

In equation (9), government saving is the budget balance \(T - G\) and foreign saving is \(IM - EX\), which is minus the current account. For (b), take the change of every term of equation (9) from 2025 to 2026, and watch the signs: a larger deficit is a fall in government saving, and a smaller current account surplus is a rise in foreign saving.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Solve equation (9) for private saving:
\[Y - T - C = I - (T - G) - (IM - EX) = 17.6 - (-2.6) - (-5.8) = 26.0 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
German households and firms saved 26.0 percent of GDP. Only 17.6 points financed private investment at home: 2.6 points went to the government’s deficit and 5.8 points were lent abroad. (The budget balance in our file is net lending, which already subtracts the government’s own investment. That is why it pairs with private investment in the identity.)
(b) Take changes of equation (9). Private saving does not change, government saving falls by 1.0 point (\(-3.4 - (-2.4)\)) and foreign saving rises by 0.5 point (the surplus falls from 4.5 to 4.0):
\[\Delta I = 0 + (-1.0) + 0.5 = -0.5 \text{ point of GDP}.\]
This is equation (10) with \(\Delta = 1\), \(\theta = 0\) and \(\phi = 0.5\): \(\Delta I = -(1 - 0 - 0.5) \times 1 = -0.5\). Half of the extra deficit is financed by lending less abroad, and the other half crowds out private investment.
(c) Investment does not fall when \(\theta + \phi = 1\), so with \(\phi = 0.5\) private saving must rise by \(\theta\Delta = 0.5\) point of GDP. That happens if households save part of their higher incomes, or save for the higher taxes they expect later (Ricardian equivalence).
Interpretation. Because Germany starts with a large current account surplus, much of its new borrowing can come from saving that now goes abroad, so crowding out can be small. Equation (9) is an identity, though: it says how the deficit must be financed, not why. The projected fall in the surplus could also come from higher investment rather than from the deficit.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Greece in 2011: could any surplus have stopped the debt? At the end of 2010, Greece’s gross government debt was 147.85 percent of GDP (gross_debt.csv, from the IMF’s Public Finances in Modern History database, as in Fig. 2). In 2011 investors lost confidence: the yield on 10-year Greek government bonds averaged 15.75 percent (OECD, via FRED, series IRLTLT01GRM156N), and nominal GDP fell by 9.0 percent (World Bank, GDP in current local currency, NY.GDP.MKTP.CN).

Suppose the whole debt paid the 2011 market yield. Use equation (7) to compute the primary surplus that would have held the debt ratio at 147.85 percent of GDP in 2011. Compare it with Greek government revenue, which was 44.6 percent of GDP in 2011 (gov_finance.csv).
Now suppose the interest rate were zero. What primary surplus would still have been needed? What does this say about the role of growth?
In our data, the ratio rose to 175.1 percent of GDP in 2011, and fell to 164.3 percent in 2012, the year in which Greece restructured its privately held bonds (Zettelmeyer, Trebesch and Gulati 2013). Use the “confidence and default” argument of the Model overview to explain why a high debt can become impossible to stabilize, and why lowering the interest rate on the debt had to be part of the solution.



Hint

Write both rates as decimals: \(i = 0.1575\) and \(g = -0.090\). A falling GDP makes \(i - g\) larger than \(i\). For (c), follow a rise in \(i\) through equation (7), and ask what a larger required surplus does to the lenders’ belief that they will be repaid.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Equation (7) with \(i = 0.1575\), \(g = -0.090\) and \(b = 147.85\):
\[-d = \frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.1575 - (-0.090)}{1 - 0.090} \times 147.85 = \frac{0.2475}{0.910} \times 147.85 = 0.272 \times 147.85 = 40.2 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
With revenue of 44.6 percent of GDP, a primary surplus of 40.2 percent would have left only 4.4 percent of GDP for all spending other than interest: no schools, no pensions, no police. No government can do that.
(b) With \(i = 0\):
\[-d = \frac{0 - (-0.090)}{1 - 0.090} \times 147.85 = \frac{0.090}{0.910} \times 147.85 = 14.6 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
Even free borrowing would have required a surplus of 14.6 percent of GDP, because a shrinking GDP raises the ratio by itself: the denominator falls. In equation (7), a fall in \(g\) weighs as much as a rise in \(i\). Growth is the “magic elixir” of Fig. 2 in reverse.
(c) When lenders start to doubt repayment, they ask for a higher \(i\). By equation (7), a higher \(i\) raises the surplus needed to stop the ratio from rising. Raising that surplus means tax increases and spending cuts, which lower GDP in the short run, so \(g\) falls as well. The required surplus grows again, repayment looks even less likely, and lenders ask for a still higher rate. The fear fulfills itself: at a yield of 15.75 percent and a shrinking GDP, no feasible primary surplus could stabilize the ratio. The way out is to lower \(i\) or the debt itself, by a restructuring (a partial default, as in 2012) or by borrowing from official lenders instead of the market. The ratio fell from 175.1 to 164.3 percent in 2012 even though GDP kept falling, because the restructuring cut the face value of the debt.
One detail: only new bonds pay the market yield, while old bonds keep the rate at which they were sold. The average rate on the whole debt was therefore much lower than 15.75 percent, and (a) is an upper bound. That is also why the ratio rose by 27.2 points in 2011, primary deficit included, and not by the 40.2 points that interest minus growth alone would have added at the market yield.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Norway’s oil fund and the generations to come. Norway’s government owns far more than it owes: in our data (net_debt.csv, the OECD’s government balance sheets via the OECD Data Explorer, as in Fig. 4), its net debt was −413.8 percent of GDP in 2024, most of it the oil fund. Norway’s fiscal rule says that, over time, the budget may spend only the fund’s expected real return, now estimated at 3 percent a year, and never the fund itself. Work in real terms: by the inflation argument of the Model overview, replace \(i\) by the real return \(r = 3\%\) and \(g\) by real GDP growth, which we assume is 1.5 percent a year (an illustrative value, not a forecast). Treat all net assets as one fund, and leave out new oil revenue.

Rewrite equation (4) for a government that starts with assets, \(B_1 < 0\). What does it allow the government to do?
Under the 3 percent rule, how large is the primary deficit (spending above non-oil taxes) in the first year, 2025? Give it in percent of that year’s GDP, as \(d_t\) in equation (5); the fund’s 413.8 percent is measured against the GDP of 2024. What happens to the real value of the fund, and to its ratio to GDP after 30 years?
Use equation (7) to find the primary deficit that would keep the fund at 413.8 percent of GDP forever.
The deficit allowed by the 3 percent rule shrinks as a share of GDP. After how many years does it fall below the deficit of (c)? Which rule treats future generations better? (This last question has no single right answer: argue for one.)



Hint

For (a), look at the sign of the right side of equation (4) when \(B_1 < 0\). For (b), spending exactly the real return leaves the fund’s real value unchanged, while real GDP grows 1.5 percent a year, already in the first year. For (c), put \(b = -413.8\) into equation (7) and read the sign of \(d\). For (d), compare the two deficits in the first year, then ask how long it takes GDP to grow by that factor; the rule of 70 gives a quick answer.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) With \(B_1 < 0\), equation (4) reads
\[(T_1 - G_1) + \frac{T_2 - G_2}{1+i} = (1+i)B_1 < 0.\]
The present value of the budget balances is negative: the government may run primary deficits, as long as their present value equals its assets plus the interest on them, \((1+i)\lvert B_1\rvert\). With many periods it can do so forever: a deficit equal to the return on the fund leaves the fund intact.
(b) The first-year deficit is the real return on the fund, \(0.03 \times 413.8 = 12.4\) percent of 2024 GDP. Equation (5) divides it by the GDP of 2025, which is 1.5 percent larger:
\[d_{2025} = \frac{0.03 \times 413.8}{1.015} = \frac{12.4}{1.015} = 12.2 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
The fund’s real value does not change, but real GDP grows, so the ratio shrinks by the growth rule for a ratio, \(g_b = 0 - 1.5\%\):
\[\frac{413.8}{1.015^{30}} = 264.7 \text{ percent of GDP after 30 years},\]
and the deficit the rule allows in that thirtieth year is \(0.03 \times 264.7 = 7.9\) percent of that year’s GDP.
(c) Equation (7) in real terms, with \(b = -413.8\):
\[-d = \frac{r - g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.03 - 0.015}{1.015} \times (-413.8) = -6.1, \qquad\text{so } d = 6.1 \text{ percent of GDP}.\]
A permanent primary deficit of 6.1 percent of GDP keeps the assets at 413.8 percent of GDP. Check with the steady state: \(b^* = \frac{1+g}{g-r}\,d = \frac{1.015}{-0.015} \times 6.115 = -413.8\).
(d) The 3 percent rule’s first deficit, 12.2 percent of GDP from (b), is exactly twice the 6.1 percent of (c), since \(r/(r-g) = 0.03/0.015 = 2\). Its deficit shrinks with the ratio, at the rate of real growth, so it falls to the level of (c) once GDP has doubled from its level in the first year. By the rule of 70 that takes about \(70/1.5 \approx 47\) years (\(\ln 2 / \ln 1.015 = 46.6\) exactly): the rule’s deficit is larger than that of (c) in each of the first 47 years and smaller from the 48th year on.

The 3 percent rule gives every generation the same real amount (in kroner of today’s value). The generations living in the next half century get more than under the rule of (c), and those after them less, as a share of their (larger) incomes.
The constant-ratio rule gives every generation the same share of GDP. It spends less today and lets the fund grow with the economy.

Future generations will be richer, which is an argument for spending more now (the 3 percent rule). Expected returns are uncertain, which is an argument for spending less (if the real return turns out lower than 3 percent, the 3 percent rule eats into the fund). The arithmetic of equations (4) and (7) shows the trade-off; choosing between the two rules is a value judgment. In reality the fund has kept growing: Norway’s net debt was −154.9 percent of GDP in 2011 and −413.8 percent in 2024 in our data. According to the page linked above, the state’s net oil revenue is paid into the fund every year (this problem leaves it out), and the fund’s investments have earned large returns.



Data-based problems
Problem 4 (Basic): How much of each tax dollar goes to interest? The file federal_budget.csv, which we built from the Office of Management and Budget’s Historical Tables, has the lines of Table 18.1 for every fiscal year from 1940 to 2025, in percent of GDP.

In FY2025, how many cents of each dollar of federal revenue went to net interest?
Is that a record since FY1940? Which earlier years came close, and why was interest so high then? (Fig. 2 helps.)
In which fiscal years was net interest larger than defense spending?



Hint

Keep the rows with release == "actual (FY2027 Budget)", so that each year appears once, and make year the index. Both net_interest and total_revenue are in percent of GDP, so 100 * net_interest / total_revenue is the number of cents per dollar of revenue. .sort_values(ascending=False).head() lists the largest values.


# Your answer here



Solution

We keep the actual numbers, divide net interest by revenue, rank the years, and compare interest with defense.
fed = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "federal_budget.csv")
fed = fed[fed.release == "actual (FY2027 Budget)"].set_index("year")
cents = 100 * fed.net_interest / fed.total_revenue      # cents of interest per dollar of revenue
print(f"FY2025: {cents[2025]:.1f} cents of each dollar of revenue went to net interest")
print("The five highest years:")
print(cents.sort_values(ascending=False).head().round(1))
print(f"Lowest since 1980: {cents.loc[1980:].min():.1f} cents in FY{cents.loc[1980:].idxmin()}")
print("Net interest above defense in:", fed.index[fed.net_interest > fed.defense].tolist())

(a) In FY2025, 18.5 cents of each dollar of federal revenue paid the interest on the debt.
(b) It is the highest share since FY1940, but only just: FY1991 had 18.4 cents, FY1992 18.3 cents and FY1990 17.9 cents, and FY2024 also had 17.9 cents. Around 1990 the debt had grown fast (from 25.5 percent of GDP in FY1980 to 47.9 percent in FY1993, Fig. 2) while interest rates were high. The lowest share since 1980 was 6.9 cents in FY2015: the debt was large (72.2 percent of GDP), but interest rates were very low. The interest bill depends on the debt and on the interest rate.
(c) Only in FY2024 and FY2025. In our data, which start in FY1940, the federal government had never before paid more in interest than for its military.


Problem 5 (Intermediate): Big government, big debt? Is it true that countries with large governments also have large debts? Use the 2024 general government spending of gov_spending.csv (from the OECD’s Government at a Glance, via the OECD Data Explorer), the 2024 gross debt of gross_debt.csv (from the IMF’s Public Finances in Modern History database) and the budget balances of gov_finance.csv (OECD national accounts).

Put each country’s 2024 spending and gross debt side by side. How many countries have both, and what is the correlation between the two?
List the countries that spend more than 47 percent of GDP but owe less than 60 percent of GDP, and those that spend less than 40 percent of GDP but owe more than 100 percent.
Now average each country’s budget balance over 2000–2024 and correlate it with the 2024 gross debt. Explain the difference between (a) and (c) with the flow budget constraint, equation (2).



Hint

The files spell some countries differently (“U.S.” in one, “United States” in the other), so match them on the three-letter code iso3. For (c), groupby("iso3").balance.mean() gives one average per country, and pd.concat([first, second], axis=1).dropna() lines up two Series by their country code.


# Your answer here



Solution

We merge the two 2024 tables on iso3, then filter the corners of the scatter, then repeat with the average balance.
spend = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gov_spending.csv")
debt_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gross_debt.csv")
both = spend[spend.year == 2024].merge(debt_all[debt_all.year == 2024][["iso3", "gross_debt"]], on="iso3")
print(f"(a) {len(both)} countries, correlation {both.gov_spending.corr(both.gross_debt):.2f}")
big_low = both[(both.gov_spending > 47) & (both.gross_debt < 60)]
small_high = both[(both.gov_spending < 40) & (both.gross_debt > 100)]
print(big_low[["country", "gov_spending", "gross_debt"]].round(2).to_string(index=False))
print(small_high[["country", "gov_spending", "gross_debt"]].round(2).to_string(index=False))

fin_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gov_finance.csv")
recent = fin_all[(fin_all.year >= 2000) & (fin_all.year <= 2024)]
average_balance = recent.groupby("iso3").balance.mean()
debt_2024 = debt_all[debt_all.year == 2024].set_index("iso3").gross_debt
pair = pd.concat([average_balance, debt_2024], axis=1).dropna()
print(f"(c) {len(pair)} countries, correlation {pair.balance.corr(pair.gross_debt):.2f}")

(a) 36 countries have both numbers, and the correlation is only 0.19: the size of government says little about its debt.
(b) Six countries spend more than 47 percent of GDP but owe less than 60 percent: Denmark (47.33 and 31.45 percent), Iceland, Norway, Poland, Slovakia and Sweden (50.47 and 32.99). Two spend less than 40 percent but owe more than 100 percent: Japan (38.73 and 236.66) and the United States (39.57 and 122.32).
(c) Across 39 countries, the correlation between the average balance of 2000–2024 and the 2024 debt is −0.52: countries with larger deficits (more negative balances) owe more. By equation (2), the debt grows by the primary deficit \(G_t - T_t\) plus interest. What builds up debt is the gap between spending and taxes, not the level of spending. Sweden and Denmark spend a lot, but they also tax a lot; Japan and the United States spend less but have taxed even less, year after year.


Problem 6 (Intermediate): Do countries with bigger deficits invest less? If deficits crowd out investment, equation (10), countries with larger deficits over many years should have lower investment rates. Use the general government balance and private investment of gov_finance.csv (OECD national accounts, via the OECD Data Explorer).

For each country, average the budget balance and private investment over 2000–2019, the twenty years before the pandemic. What is the correlation across countries? Does its sign fit the crowding-out story?
Name one country that fits the story well and two that clearly do not.
Why is this comparison across countries a weak test of equation (10)? Name two reasons.



Hint

First drop the rows where either column is missing with .dropna(subset=["balance", "private_investment"]), then use groupby("country")[["balance", "private_investment"]].mean(). Crowding out means that a lower balance (a bigger deficit) comes with lower investment, so it predicts a positive correlation.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

We average each country over 2000–2019, then correlate the averages and look at the extremes. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits a straight line and returns its slope first.
fin_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gov_finance.csv")
pre_covid = fin_all[(fin_all.year >= 2000) & (fin_all.year <= 2019)]
pre_covid = pre_covid.dropna(subset=["balance", "private_investment"])
means = pre_covid.groupby("country")[["balance", "private_investment"]].mean()
slope = np.polyfit(means.balance, means.private_investment, 1)[0]
print(f"{len(means)} countries: correlation {means.balance.corr(means.private_investment):.2f}, slope {slope:.2f}")
print("Largest deficits:")
print(means.sort_values("balance").head().round(1))
print("Highest investment rates:")
print(means.sort_values("private_investment", ascending=False).head(3).round(1))

(a) Across 36 countries the correlation is 0.14, and the fitted slope is 0.26: one point of GDP more in average deficit comes with only 0.26 point less investment. The sign fits crowding out, but the relation is weak; most of the differences in investment have nothing to do with the budget.
(b) Greece fits the story: the largest average deficit (−6.5 percent of GDP) and the lowest investment rate (14.3 percent). South Korea fits it too, with an average surplus of 1.5 percent of GDP and high investment, 26.8 percent. The United States does not: it has the second-largest deficit, −6.1 percent of GDP, but an average investment rate of 17.7 percent. Nor does China, which invests by far the most, 36.6 percent of GDP, with an average deficit of 2.0 percent of GDP.
(c) First, equation (10) allows private and foreign saving to fill the gap: in open economies, foreigners can finance a deficit (\(\phi > 0\)), as Fig. 5 suggests they did for the United States. Second, many other things differ across countries: households’ saving habits (very high in China), demography, the stage of development, and the business cycle, which moves deficits and investment at the same time. A correlation across countries cannot separate these forces from the effect of the deficit.


Problem 7 (Challenge): Interest rates, growth and the U.S. debt, FY1950–2025. Equation (5) says that the debt ratio grows by the factor \((1+i)/(1+g)\), plus the primary deficit. Here you measure \(i\) and \(g\) for the United States, year by year. Use federal_budget.csv (fiscal-year GDP in billions of dollars, net interest and the budget balance in percent of GDP) and the debt held by the public at the end of each fiscal year in fig18-2.csv (both from the OMB Historical Tables).

Compute the effective interest rate of each year, net interest divided by the debt at the start of the year, and the growth rate of nominal GDP. In how many years from FY1950 to FY2025 was \(i\) below \(g\), and what was the average gap \(i - g\)?
Average \(i\) and \(g\) by decade. In which decades was \(i\) above \(g\)? How does that fit the path of the debt ratio in Fig. 2?
What were \(i\), \(g\) and \(i - g\) in FY2022? Explain the number with the inflation argument of the Model overview.
Use equation (5), with your \(i\), \(g\) and the primary deficit, to predict each year’s debt ratio from the year before, and compare with the actual ratio for FY2019–2025. Which years does equation (5) miss by more than 2 points?



Hint

The debt at the start of year \(t\) is the debt at the end of year \(t-1\): in dollars, debt_ratio / 100 * GDP, then .shift(1). Net interest in dollars is net_interest / 100 * GDP. The primary deficit, in percent of GDP, is the total deficit minus interest: -balance - net_interest. Compute every column before you keep the years 1950–2025, so that FY1950 has a previous year.


# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

We line up the two files by year, compute the debt in dollars, the effective rate, growth and the primary deficit, and then apply equation (5).
fed = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "federal_budget.csv")
fed = fed[fed.release == "actual (FY2027 Budget)"].set_index("year")
debt_end = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-2.csv").set_index("year").debt_public_gdp_pct
rates = pd.DataFrame({"Y": fed.gdp_billions, "b": debt_end})
rates["B"] = rates.b / 100 * rates.Y                          # debt at the end of the year, billions of dollars
rates["i"] = fed.net_interest * rates.Y / rates.B.shift(1)    # interest paid / debt at the start, percent
rates["g"] = 100 * (rates.Y / rates.Y.shift(1) - 1)
rates["d"] = -fed.balance - fed.net_interest                  # primary deficit, percent of GDP
rates["predicted"] = (1 + rates.i / 100) / (1 + rates.g / 100) * rates.b.shift(1) + rates.d   # equation (5)
rates = rates.loc[1950:2025]
gap = rates.i - rates.g
print(f"(a) i < g in {(gap < 0).sum()} of {len(rates)} years; average i - g {gap.mean():.2f} points")
for start in range(1950, 2030, 10):
    part = rates.loc[start:start + 9]
    print(f"(b) {start}s: i {part.i.mean():.2f}%, g {part.g.mean():.2f}%")
print(f"(c) FY2022: i {rates.i[2022]:.2f}%, g {rates.g[2022]:.2f}%, i - g {gap[2022]:.2f}; rank {int(gap.rank()[2022])} of {len(gap)}")
print(rates.loc[2019:2025, ["i", "g", "d", "b", "predicted"]].round(2))

(a) The effective rate was below nominal growth in 48 of the 76 years, and on average 1.64 points below it. That is the “magic elixir” of the Model overview: most of the time, the United States outgrew its debt.
(b) By decade, \(i\) was far below \(g\) in the 1950s (2.31 against 6.29 percent), the 1960s and the 1970s, when the debt ratio fell from its war peak to 23.2 percent of GDP (FY1974). It was above \(g\) in the 1980s (9.13 against 8.05 percent), the 1990s (6.93 against 5.49) and, narrowly, the 2000s (4.81 against 4.35). In those decades the term \((i-g)\,b\) pushed the ratio up, on top of the deficits of the 1980s. Since 2010 \(i\) is again below \(g\): 2.12 against 3.94 percent in the 2010s, and 2.56 against 6.13 percent in 2020–2025.
(c) In FY2022, \(i = 2.14\) percent and \(g = 10.94\) percent, so \(i - g = -8.81\) points, the second-lowest value since 1950, after FY1951. Inflation surged in 2021–22 (Chapter 8), so nominal GDP grew fast, while most of the debt had been sold earlier at low fixed rates. Unexpected inflation lowered the real value of the debt, as the Model overview predicts: the ratio fell from 96.7 to 94.9 percent although the primary deficit was 3.51 percent of GDP.
(d) Equation (5) predicts the ratio within about 1 point in FY2019 and FY2023–2025, but it misses by 5.28 points in FY2020 (predicted 93.22, actual 98.5), by −6.54 points in FY2021 (103.24 against 96.7) and by 2.36 points in FY2022. In those years the Treasury did not borrow exactly its deficit. It borrowed more than it needed in FY2020 and held the cash at the Federal Reserve, where its balance rose from about 0.3 trillion dollars in September 2019 to 1.7 trillion in September 2020; it spent the cash down to 0.2 trillion by September 2021, and raised it to 0.7 trillion by September 2022 (Federal Reserve Board, H.4.1, U.S. Treasury General Account, week averages, via FRED, WTREGEN). The flow budget constraint holds once we count changes in the government’s cash as a use of funds. Our \(i\) is also approximate: net interest is interest paid minus some interest received.




Modeling problems
Problem 8 (Basic): Can France meet the EU’s debt rule? France’s gross government debt was 113.15 percent of GDP in 2024 (gross_debt.csv). Under the EU’s reformed fiscal rules of 2024, the debt ratio of a country above 90 percent of GDP must fall by at least 1 point of GDP a year on average, in plans that run four to seven years (European Parliament Research Service, 2024). The calculator below starts from France’s 2024 ratio and runs four years of equation (5), with nominal GDP growth fixed at \(g = 3\%\) (an illustrative value).

With an interest rate of \(i = 3\%\), which constant primary balance meets the rule exactly?
If lenders demand \(i = 4\%\) instead, how large must the yearly primary surplus be?



Hint

The slider sets the primary deficit \(d\); a negative value is a surplus. Move it until the title shows an average change of −1.00 point a year, or as close as the slider allows. Before you move it, use equation (6) to predict the answer to (a).


b_france = gross[(gross.country == "France") & (gross.year == 2024)].gross_debt.iloc[0]


def eu_debt_rule(i=3.0, g=3.0, d=0.0):
    """Equation (5) for four years from France's 2024 debt ratio, with a constant primary deficit d."""
    path = [b_france] + debt_ratio_path(b_france, i / 100, g / 100, [d] * 4)
    rule = []
    for t in range(5):
        rule.append(b_france - t)                # the EU minimum: 1 point of GDP less each year
    average = round((path[-1] - b_france) / 4, 2) + 0.0
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(2024, 2029)), y=rule, mode="lines", name="EU rule: −1 point a year",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(2024, 2029)), y=path, mode="lines+markers", name="Debt ratio",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Average change {average:+.2f} points a year: {path[-1]:.2f}% of GDP in 2028",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", tickvals=[2024, 2025, 2026, 2027, 2028]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Gross debt (% of GDP)", range=[90, 130]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(eu_debt_rule,
         i=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=2.0, max=5.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate i (%)", style=WIDE),
         g=fixed(3.0),
         d=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-4.0, max=1.0, step=0.1, description="primary deficit d (% of GDP)",
                       style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the debt-ratio tools of the Model overview, equations (5) and (6), adapted from the discussion of the debt-GDP ratio in Chapter 18 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here



Solution

(a) With \(i = g\), the term \(\frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b\) of equation (6) is zero, so the ratio changes by exactly the primary deficit: \(b_t - b_{t-1} = d_t\). A primary surplus of 1.0 percent of GDP (\(d = -1.0\)) meets the rule exactly, and the slider confirms it: an average change of −1.00 point a year, to 109.15 percent of GDP in 2028.
(b) With \(i = 4\%\), interest adds \(\frac{0.04 - 0.03}{1.03} \times 113.15 = 1.10\) points to the ratio in the first year, so the surplus must cover that as well: about \(1 + 1.10 = 2.1\) percent of GDP. On the slider, \(d = -2.1\) gives an average change of −1.02 point a year, and \(d = -2.0\) only −0.91. The exact constant surplus is 2.08 percent of GDP (a little less than 2.10, because the debt, and with it the interest effect, falls along the way):
for d in [-2.0, -2.08, -2.1]:
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_france, 0.04, 0.03, [d] * 4)
    print(f"d = {d}: debt in 2028 {path[-1]:.2f}%, average change {(path[-1] - b_france) / 4:.3f} points a year")
One point more interest costs France about 1.1 points of GDP of extra surplus every year, because its debt is larger than its GDP. A rise in the interest rate makes the EU rule much harder to meet.

Problem 9 (Intermediate): Growth or austerity? A hypothetical country pays an interest rate of 4 percent on its debt, its nominal GDP grows by 3 percent a year, and its primary budget is balanced. Its government can choose one of two reforms, each kept for 20 years:

Plan A (austerity): a primary surplus of 1 percent of GDP every year (\(d = -1\)), with growth unchanged;
Plan B (growth): reforms that raise nominal growth to 4 percent a year, with a balanced primary budget (\(d = 0\)).


The debt starts at 100 percent of GDP. Which plan leaves the lower debt ratio after 20 years?
Repeat for a starting ratio of 50 percent and of 150 percent of GDP.
Find the starting ratio at which the two plans tie. Explain the result with equation (6), and use equation (8) to show why the tie is exact.



Hint

Plan A is g = 3, d = -1; Plan B is g = 4, d = 0. Compare the two “after 20 years” numbers in the title. For (c), compare what each plan subtracts from the change in the ratio in the first year, using equation (6): one of the two effects grows with the debt, the other does not.


def growth_or_austerity(b0=100.0, g=3.0, d=0.0):
    """Equation (5) for 20 years with i = 4%: the debt ratio with growth g and a constant primary deficit d."""
    path = [b0] + debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, g / 100, [d] * 20)
    no_reform = [b0] + debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.03, [0.0] * 20)
    end = round(path[-1], 1) + 0.0               # + 0.0 prints a tiny negative number as 0.0, not -0.0
    low, high = 0, 150
    if b0 > 100:
        high = 300                               # a second, fixed scale for high debts
    if min(path) < 10:
        low = -50                                # room below zero: the government may end up owning more than it owes
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(21)), y=no_reform, mode="lines", name="No reform (g = 3%, d = 0)",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(range(21)), y=path, mode="lines", name="This plan",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"After 20 years: {end:.1f}% of GDP (no reform: {no_reform[-1]:.1f}%)",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Years from now", range=[0, 20]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Debt (% of GDP)", range=[low, high]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(growth_or_austerity,
         b0=FloatSlider(value=100.0, min=20.0, max=200.0, step=1.0, description="starting debt b0", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=3.0, max=5.0, step=0.5, description="nominal growth g (%)", style=WIDE),
         d=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=1.0, step=0.5, description="primary deficit d", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the debt-ratio tools of the Model overview, equations (5) to (8), adapted from the discussion of growth and the debt-GDP ratio in Chapter 18 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Starting from 100 percent, with no reform the ratio rises to 121.3 percent after 20 years. Plan A ends at 99.4 percent and Plan B at 100.0 percent: austerity wins, but only just.
(b) From 50 percent, Plan A ends at 38.7 and Plan B at 50.0 percent: austerity wins clearly. From 150 percent, Plan A ends at 160.0 and Plan B at 150.0 percent: now growth wins, and austerity does not even stop the ratio from rising.
for b0 in [50, 100, 103, 150]:
    plan_a = debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.03, [-1.0] * 20)[-1]
    plan_b = debt_ratio_path(b0, 0.04, 0.04, [0.0] * 20)[-1]
    print(f"start {b0}%: Plan A {plan_a:.1f}%, Plan B {plan_b:.1f}%")
(c) The two plans tie at a starting ratio of 103 percent of GDP. By equation (6), Plan A lowers the change in the ratio by 1 point a year, whatever the debt. Plan B removes the interest-minus-growth term \(\frac{i-g}{1+g}\,b = \frac{0.01}{1.03}\,b\), which is proportional to the debt: it is worth \(0.0097\,b\) points, so more than 1 point when \(b > 103\). Growth works on the whole stock of debt; a surplus is a fixed amount.
The tie is exact, by equation (8). Under Plan B, \(i = g\) and \(d = 0\), so the ratio stays at \(b_0\). Under Plan A, the steady state is
\[b^* = \frac{1+g}{g-i}\,d = \frac{1.03}{0.03 - 0.04} \times (-1) = 103,\]
and equation (8), \(b_{20} = b^* + \left(\frac{1.04}{1.03}\right)^{20}(b_0 - b^*)\), keeps the ratio at \(b^*\) when it starts there. Since \(i > g\) under Plan A, \(b^*\) is the tipping point of the Model overview: below 103 percent the ratio falls further and further below \(b^*\), above it the ratio rises without limit. In this example, for highly indebted countries such as Italy (135.3 percent of GDP in 2024 in our data) or Japan, a lasting rise in growth is worth more than a surplus of the same size.

Problem 10 (Challenge): Health costs and the debt in 2056. CBO’s projections of Figs. 6 and 7 assume a path for Medicare and Medicaid, which reach 8.1 percent of GDP in FY2056. Health costs are hard to forecast. Suppose the cost per recipient grows by extra points a year faster (or slower, if negative) than CBO assumes, from FY2026 on. By equation (11), the health share then grows by extra points a year faster too, and the extra spending adds to CBO’s primary deficits. The calculator draws the debt ratio (with nominal growth \(g = 4\%\)) next to CBO’s path with \(i = g = 4\%\).

With \(i = 4\%\), what are health spending and the debt ratio in FY2056 if costs grow 1 point a year faster than CBO assumes? Compare the effect on the debt with that of an interest rate one point above growth (\(i = 5\%\)) and CBO’s health path.
Congress wants the FY2056 debt ratio below 150 percent of GDP (\(i = 4\%\)). What is the smallest slowdown of health costs, on the slider, that achieves it?
Could cost control alone bring the FY2056 ratio back to its FY2025 level of 99.5 percent? Try the largest slowdown on the slider, and explain what you find with the primary deficits of Fig. 6.



Hint

Read the title: it shows the FY2056 debt ratio and the health share. For (a), set the extra cost growth to 1, then set it back to 0 and move the interest rate to 5. For (c), compare the health share in FY2056 at the largest slowdown with its FY2025 level in Fig. 7 (6.0 percent of GDP), and remember that CBO projects primary deficits even without any rise in health spending.


cbo_health = components[components.projection == 1].medicare_medicaid.tolist()   # FY2026-2056, % of GDP
cbo_path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, 0.04, 0.04, cbo_deficits)                     # CBO's deficits, i = g = 4%


def health_and_debt(extra=0.0, i=4.0, g=4.0):
    """Equations (11) and (5): the debt ratio when health costs grow `extra` points a year faster than CBO's."""
    deficits = []
    for t in range(len(cbo_deficits)):
        share = cbo_health[t] * (1 + extra / 100) ** (t + 1)        # after the loop: the FY2056 share
        deficits.append(cbo_deficits[t] + share - cbo_health[t])
    path = debt_ratio_path(b_2025, i / 100, g / 100, deficits)
    fig = go.Figure()
    years = [2025] + cbo.year.tolist()           # start the lines at the FY2025 ratio
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=[b_2025] + cbo_path, mode="lines", name="CBO, i = g = 4%",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=[b_2025] + path, mode="lines", name="This scenario",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"FY2056: debt {path[-1]:.1f}% of GDP, Medicare and Medicaid {share:.1f}% of GDP",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Fiscal year", range=[2025, 2057]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Debt held by the public (% of GDP)", range=[0, 400],
                                 tickvals=[50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(health_and_debt,
         extra=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="extra cost growth", style=WIDE),
         i=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=3.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate i (%)", style=WIDE),
         g=fixed(4.0));

Source. The debt projection of Fig. 6 above, with the health spending of Fig. 7 and equation (11), adapted from the discussion of Figs. 18.6 and 18.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

Equation (11) says the health share grows at \(g_{N_r/N} + (g_c - g_y)\). Adding extra points to \(g_c\) multiplies CBO’s share in year \(t\) after FY2025 by \((1 + \text{extra}/100)^t\). With \(i = g\), equation (5) simply adds up the primary deficits, so every extra point of health spending stays in the debt ratio.
for extra, i in [(0.0, 4.0), (1.0, 4.0), (0.0, 5.0), (-0.25, 4.0), (-0.5, 4.0), (-2.0, 4.0)]:
    fig = health_and_debt(extra, i)
    print(f"extra {extra:+.2f}, i = {i}%:", fig.layout.title.text)
debt_cbo = health_and_debt(0.0, 4.0).data[1].y[-1]     # the FY2056 end of the blue line, unrounded
print(f"Extra FY2056 debt: health costs +1 point {health_and_debt(1.0, 4.0).data[1].y[-1] - debt_cbo:.1f}, "
      f"i = 5% {health_and_debt(0.0, 5.0).data[1].y[-1] - debt_cbo:.1f} points of GDP")
(a) With CBO’s path and \(i = 4\%\), the FY2056 ratio is 164.2 percent of GDP, with health spending at 8.1 percent. If costs grow 1 point a year faster, health spending reaches 11.0 percent of GDP in FY2056 (\(8.085 \times 1.01^{31}\)) and the debt 205.3 percent: 41.1 points more. An interest rate one point above growth, with CBO’s health path, gives 208.8 percent, 44.7 points more. (The last line of the code subtracts the unrounded ratios, so a gap can differ by 0.1 from the difference of the rounded titles.) One point of extra health-cost growth weighs about as much as one point of \(i - g\), because both compound year after year.
(b) A slowdown of 0.25 point a year leaves the ratio at 155.2 percent; a slowdown of 0.5 point a year brings it to 146.6 percent, below 150. Health spending is then 6.9 percent of GDP in FY2056 instead of 8.1.
(c) No. Even a slowdown of 2 points a year, which pushes health spending down to 4.3 percent of GDP in FY2056, below its FY2025 level of 6.0 percent, leaves the debt at 103.4 percent of GDP, after a peak of 116.5 percent. Cost control works slowly: the slowdown saves only 0.12 point of GDP in FY2026 and builds up year after year, while CBO’s primary deficits, about 2 percent of GDP a year (Fig. 6), start right away. Health is the part of the budget that grows, but closing the gap quickly also needs higher revenue or lower spending elsewhere, the two “possible solutions” of the chapter.

title: 19. International Trade
text:
Learning goals
The United States buys more from the rest of the world than it sells to it, and it has done so every year since 1976. Is that a problem? This chapter looks at the facts of trade and at a few small examples that explain why countries trade at all. By the end of it you will be able to:

title: 19. International Trade
19. International Trade
text:
19.1 Model overview
Picture Islandia, the small island country we have followed through the book, and its large trading partner across the water, Mainland. Islanders sell fish to Mainland and buy many goods they do not make, and in some years they buy more than they sell. How does Islandia pay for the gap, and why trade at all with a partner that is better at almost everything? This section answers with a few accounting rules and four small trade models, with Islandia in view throughout.






NoteThe big idea



The question. Why do countries trade, and what does it mean when a country buys more from abroad than it sells?
The answer in one sentence. A trade deficit is borrowing from abroad, which must be repaid in present value, and trade pays off because each country can specialize in its comparative advantage.
What goes in and what comes out. The accounting takes spending, taxes, the return \(\bar{r}\) and the growth rate \(\bar{g}\), and gives back the trade balance, the saving–investment gap and the foreign debt. The trade models take endowments, productivities and labor forces, and give back prices, wages, who makes what and who consumes how much.

19.1.1 The trade balance and the national income identity

Definitions

Exports \(EX\) are goods and services made at home and bought by buyers in other countries: the fish that Islandia sells on Mainland. Imports \(IM\) go the other way: goods and services made abroad and bought at home, whether by households, firms or the government.
The trade balance, or net exports, is \(NX \equiv EX - IM\). When it is positive, the country runs a trade surplus; when it is negative, a trade deficit.
The share of GDP of a flow \(X\) is \(100 \times X/Y\) (Appendix C.2). Shares let us draw a tiny and a huge economy, or the year 1950 and the year 2025, on one axis.
The national income identity divides production among its uses: \(Y = C + I + G + NX\). Why net exports, and not exports alone? The spending \(C + I + G\) also buys goods made abroad, which are no part of domestic production, so imports come out. Goods made at home and shipped abroad are part of production, but no domestic buyer spends on them, so exports go in. That gives \(Y = (C + I + G) + EX - IM\).



Solving the identity
Step 1: net exports as production minus domestic spending. Take \(C + I + G\) away from both sides of the identity:
\[NX = Y - (C + I + G).\]
The sum \(C + I + G\) is all that households, firms and the government use at home. Economists call it domestic absorption. The equation splits into two cases:
\[NX < 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; C + I + G > Y, \qquad\qquad NX > 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; C + I + G < Y.\]






TipIn words



In a deficit year, islanders use more goods than they make. The extra goods come from Mainland, which takes a promise of payment in return. To keep that promise, Islandia must later make more than it uses, and the inequality turns around.


Step 2: the same identity in shares of GDP. Divide each term by \(Y\):
\[\frac{NX}{Y} = \frac{Y}{Y} - \frac{C}{Y} - \frac{I}{Y} - \frac{G}{Y}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad nx = 1 - c - i - g.\]
The Penn World Table gives the shares \(c\), \(i\) and \(g\), but not \(nx\), so this formula is how we compute the trade balances of Figs. 3 and 4. Shares of \(c = 0.55\), \(i = 0.25\) and \(g = 0.18\), for instance, sum to \(0.98\), and the remaining 2 percent of GDP is a surplus.






ImportantKey result: the trade balance identity



\[NX = Y - (C + I + G) \tag{1}\]
\[nx = 1 - c - i - g \tag{2}\]
The trade balance is production minus domestic use, in levels (1) or in shares of GDP (2).
Islandia in numbers. Take the economy of Check 1 in Model in code: \(Y = 100\), \(C = 70\), \(I = 20\) and \(G = 15\). Then \(NX = 100 - 105 = -5\), a trade deficit of 5 percent of GDP.


Step 3: the world as a whole. Divide the world into two regions, the United States (US) and the rest of the world (RoW). Whatever the United States imports, the rest of the world exports, and the other way round: \(IM_{US} = EX_{RoW}\) and \(EX_{US} = IM_{RoW}\). So
\[NX_{US} = EX_{US} - IM_{US} = IM_{RoW} - EX_{RoW} = -NX_{RoW}.\]
Nobody outside the world buys from it, so all countries’ trade balances add up to zero. To see which countries finance the U.S. deficit, we must measure everything against one GDP. Multiply and divide by the GDP \(Y_j\) of country \(j\):
\[\frac{NX_j}{Y_{US}} = \frac{NX_j}{Y_j}\times\frac{Y_j}{Y_{US}}.\]
That is the second bar of Fig. 3. An economy three quarters as large as the United States, with a surplus of 2 percent of its own GDP, covers \(2 \times 0.75 = 1.5\) percent of U.S. GDP.


What the identity predicts
An identity says nothing about cause and effect. It only says which numbers can go together. Holding output \(Y\) fixed:







A change in …
effect on the trade balance




\(C\), \(I\) or \(G\) up by 1
\(NX\) down by 1

\(nx\) down by 1 point


U.S. deficit up by 1 point of U.S. GDP

Each effect is one for one, since the identity is just a sum. The direction of cause stays open: a boom in spending at home can create a deficit, and easy credit from abroad can also fuel a boom in spending. The models below, and the data sections, help us judge which story fits.

A trade deficit means a country uses more goods than it makes, and the missing goods arrive from abroad on credit.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Islandia produces \(Y = 100\), with \(C = 70\), \(I = 20\) and \(G = 15\). What is its trade balance, as a share of GDP? What would it be if the government cut its purchases to \(G = 10\), with everything else unchanged?


Answer

By equation (1), \(NX = 100 - (70 + 20 + 15) = -5\): a deficit of 5 percent of GDP. With \(G = 10\), domestic uses add up to exactly 100, so \(NX = 0\) and trade is balanced.

2. Islandia’s deficit grows by 1 point of GDP. Can we conclude from the identity that islanders began to overspend?


Answer

No. Equation (2) says only that \(c + i + g\) rose by 1 point. It does not say why: islanders may have chosen to spend more, or cheap loans from Mainland may have pulled spending up. The identity holds in both stories.






19.1.2 Saving, investment and the trade balance

Definitions

Private saving is income after taxes, minus consumption: \(Y - T - C\). As in Chapter 18, \(T\) stands for taxes net of transfers.
Government saving is the budget surplus \(T - G\) (for Islandia, the surplus of the Islandia Treasury). It turns negative when the government runs a deficit.
Foreign saving is \(IM - EX = -NX\): the goods the rest of the world sends us in excess of what we send back. That excess is a loan to us.
Domestic saving is the sum of the first two: \(S \equiv (Y - T - C) + (T - G)\).



Solving the identity
Step 1. Solve the national income identity for investment: \(I = Y - C - G - NX\).
Step 2. Take taxes away and add them back, which leaves the value unchanged: \(I = (Y - T - C) + (T - G) - NX\).
Step 3. Replace \(-NX\) by \(IM - EX\):
\[I = \underbrace{(Y - T - C)}_{\text{private saving}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{government saving}} + \underbrace{(IM - EX)}_{\text{foreign saving}}.\]
Each unit of investment has one of three sources of funds: households, the government or foreigners.
Step 4. Inside domestic saving the taxes cancel: \(S = (Y - T - C) + (T - G) = Y - C - G\). So the equation of Step 1 is \(I = S - NX\). Move \(NX\) to the left and \(I\) to the right, and the trade balance appears as the gap between saving and investment.






ImportantKey result: saving, investment and the trade balance



\[I = (Y - T - C) + (T - G) + (IM - EX) \tag{3}\]
\[NX = S - I \tag{4}\]
Investment is paid for by private, government and foreign saving (3). The trade balance equals the net capital outflow \(S - I\), the net amount a country lends to the rest of the world (4).
Islandia in numbers. Add taxes \(T = 12\) to the economy above. Private saving is \(100 - 12 - 70 = 18\), government saving is \(12 - 15 = -3\), and foreign saving is 5. Together they pay for \(I = 20\). Domestic saving is \(S = 15\), so \(S - I = -5\), the same as \(NX\).








TipIn words: one deal, two sides



Equation (4) tells one story twice. On the goods side, Islandia receives more from Mainland than it ships, \(NX < 0\). On the money side, islanders save less than they invest, \(S < I\), and Mainland lends them the gap in exchange for bonds, shares or money. A deficit and foreign borrowing are the same deal.


Step 5: the twin deficits. Break domestic saving into its two parts:
\[NX = \underbrace{(Y - T - C - I)}_{\text{private saving minus investment}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{government saving}}.\]
Suppose private saving and investment move roughly together, so that the first term stays near zero. Then the trade balance tracks the budget balance: a budget deficit goes with a trade deficit of about the same size. These are the twin deficits of Fig. 5.


What the identity predicts
Equation (4) is true every year, but it does not say which term gives way. The table lists the cases, each for a change of 1 point of GDP:

And when the U.S. budget deficits were large, in the 1980s and the 2000s, they came mostly with larger trade deficits, not with lower investment (Fig. 5).

Investment is financed by households, the government or foreigners, and a trade deficit is simply the foreigners’ share.

Answer

By Step 5, \(NX = (18 - 20) + (12 - 17) = -2 - 5 = -7\). The trade deficit grows from 5 to 7 percent of GDP, one for one with the budget deficit: the twin deficits.

2. Islanders build many new boats, and yet Islandia runs a trade surplus. Is that a contradiction?


Answer

No. By equation (4), \(NX = S - I\). High investment and a surplus go together whenever saving is higher still. The extra saving is then lent to Mainland. The fast-growing economies of Fig. 4 show exactly this pattern.






19.1.3 Net foreign assets and the intertemporal budget constraint

Definitions

A country’s net foreign assets \(F_t\) are what its residents own abroad, minus what foreigners own in the country, at the end of year \(t\). In the data this is the net international investment position (Fig. 6). If \(F_t < 0\), then \(-F_t\) is the net foreign debt: what Islandia owes Mainland, net.
The current account is the trade balance plus the net income on foreign assets: \(CA_t \equiv NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1}\), with \(\bar{r}\) the return on those assets. (Remittances and aid also enter the data; we leave them out.) The textbook’s trade examples set this income to zero, so there the current account and the trade balance coincide.



Solving the model
Step 1: assets pile up the current account. A current account surplus is a new loan to the rest of the world, so the stock of foreign assets rises by that amount:
\[F_t - F_{t-1} = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} + NX_t.\]
This is a difference equation (Appendix C.10). When \(\bar{r} = 0\), as in the island example below and the dotted line of Fig. 6, it reduces to \(F_t = F_{t-1} + NX_t\). Then \(F_t = F_0 + NX_1 + NX_2 + \dots + NX_t\): today’s stock is the first stock plus every trade balance since.
Step 2: the budget constraint over many years. Divide both sides by \((1 + \bar{r})^t\), and note that \((1 + \bar{r})/(1 + \bar{r})^t = 1/(1 + \bar{r})^{t-1}\):
\[\frac{F_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = \frac{F_{t-1}}{(1 + \bar{r})^{t-1}} + \frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t}.\]
Write this line once for each year \(t = 1, 2, \dots, T\), and add up all the lines. Every term \(F_t/(1+\bar{r})^t\) with \(t\) between 1 and \(T - 1\) shows up once on each side and cancels. Only the first and the last stock remain:
\[\frac{F_T}{(1 + \bar{r})^T} = F_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t}.\]
Lenders do not let a debt grow forever without being repaid, and no country ships goods to the world forever without ever cashing its claims. So, far enough ahead, the final stock is worth zero today, \(F_T/(1 + \bar{r})^T = 0\), and the trade balances must cover the starting stock.






ImportantKey result: foreign assets and the budget constraint



\[F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} + NX_t \tag{5}\]
\[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = -F_0 \tag{6}\]
Equation (5) moves foreign assets from year to year. Equation (6) is the intertemporal budget constraint: in present value, future trade balances must repay the starting debt.


The left-hand side of (6) is a sum of present values (Appendix C.12). It is the same algebra as the government’s budget constraint in Chapter 18, applied now to a whole country.






TipIn words



If Islandia starts owing Mainland nothing, \(F_0 = 0\), its trade balances must be worth zero in present value: each deficit today needs later surpluses of equal present value. If it starts in debt, \(F_0 < 0\), it must run surpluses on average.


Step 3: foreign debt as a share of GDP. Let GDP grow at the rate \(\bar{g}\), so that \(Y_t = (1 + \bar{g})Y_{t-1}\), and define \(f_t \equiv F_t/Y_t\). Dividing equation (5) by \(Y_t\) gives
\[f_t = \frac{(1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1}}{(1 + \bar{g})Y_{t-1}} + \frac{NX_t}{Y_t} = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx_t.\]
When GDP grows faster than the return, \(\bar{g} > \bar{r}\), the coefficient on \(f_{t-1}\) is less than one. With a constant trade balance \(nx\), the ratio then comes to rest. At rest \(f_t = f_{t-1} = f^*\), so \(f^* - \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}f^* = nx\), that is \(f^*\,\frac{\bar{g} - \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = nx\). Solving for \(f^*\):






ImportantKey result: the long-run foreign debt ratio



\[f^* = \frac{(1 + \bar{g})\,nx}{\bar{g} - \bar{r}} \tag{7}\]
A steady deficit leads to a stable debt ratio, as long as GDP grows faster than the return on the debt.
Islandia in numbers. \(F\) and \(Y\) are both in money, so \(\bar{g}\) is the growth of nominal GDP. If Islandia runs a deficit of 3 percent of GDP every year, \(nx = -0.03\), while nominal GDP grows at \(\bar{g} = 0.04\) and \(\bar{r} = 0\), then \(f^* = 1.04 \times (-0.03)/0.04 = -0.78\): a net foreign debt of 78 percent of GDP.


The U.S. debt in Fig. 6, about 70 percent of GDP, is of the same order.


What the model predicts

Deficits are loans, and they accumulate. By equation (5), the foreign debt is roughly the sum of past current account deficits. Fig. 6 checks this. It also reveals a second source of change in the data: foreign assets gain or lose value as stock prices and the dollar move.
Over time, trade must balance in present value. By equation (6), deficits cannot last forever. A deficit is a promise of surpluses to come, not goods for free.

1. Islandia keeps its deficit at 3 percent of GDP with \(\bar{r} = 0\), but its nominal GDP now grows at 5 percent a year instead of 4. Where does its foreign debt ratio settle?


Answer

By equation (7), \(f^* = 1.05 \times (-0.03)/0.05 = -0.63\): a net foreign debt of 63 percent of GDP, down from 78 percent. The same yearly deficit is spread over an economy that grows faster.

2. Islandia owes Mainland money, and the return \(\bar{r}\) is positive. Last year its trade was balanced, yet its foreign debt grew. How can that be?

19.1.4 Gains from exchange: two islands, two goods

Assumptions

Two islands have equal populations. Everyone eats bananas and fish, and only in equal amounts: one meal is one banana together with one fish.
Nobody produces anything. Every year, each person on island 1 gets 200 bananas and 800 fish, and each person on island 2 gets the opposite, 800 bananas and 200 fish.
The islands may swap goods. Since the setup is symmetric, the swap is one fish for one banana.



Solving the model
Without trade, a person on island 1 can make only \(\min(200, 800) = 200\) meals, and the other 600 fish are useless. Now let island 1 give \(q\) fish for \(q\) bananas. It ends with \(200 + q\) bananas and \(800 - q\) fish. Meals need equal amounts, so
\[200 + q = 800 - q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2q = 600 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q = 300.\]
Everyone on both islands ends with 500 bananas and 500 fish.






ImportantKey result: the gains from exchange



With endowments \((a, b)\) on one island and \((b, a)\) on the other, the swap is
\[q = \frac{b - a}{2},\]
and everyone ends with \((a + b)/2\) of each good. Meals per person rise from \(\min(a, b)\) to \((a + b)/2\).
The two islands in numbers. With \(a = 200\) and \(b = 800\), the islands swap 300 fish for 300 bananas, and meals per person rise from 200 to 500.








TipIn words



Picture Islandia as island 1: its fishers land more fish than islanders can eat, while bananas are scarce. A fish is worth little at home and a lot on the other island. The swap moves each good to the people who value it most, and both islands gain without one more fish caught.




What the model predicts

Both islands are better off. Meals per person go from 200 to 500 on each island, and nothing extra is produced. The whole gain comes from sending each good to the people who value it more at the margin.
Trade here is balanced. Each island ships as much as it receives every year, so \(NX = 0\). The next block shows where deficits and surpluses come from.
Trade between countries is like trade between people. Inside a country, people specialize and buy most of what they use from others. Trade across borders takes the same idea one step further.


Swapping goods can make everyone better off even when nothing more is produced.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Suppose each person on island 1 receives 300 bananas and 700 fish, and each person on island 2 receives 700 bananas and 300 fish. How much do the islands swap, and how many meals does each person get with and without trade?


Answer

By the Key result, \(q = (700 - 300)/2 = 200\). Everyone ends with 500 bananas and 500 fish, so meals rise from 300 to 500 per person.

2. No new good is made. Where, then, does the gain come from?


Answer

From moving goods to where they are worth more. On island 1 an extra fish adds no meal, but on island 2 it completes a meal. The swap uses goods that were idle before. Each island ships as much as it receives, so trade stays balanced, \(NX = 0\).






19.1.5 Trade across time: Oddtopia and Eventopia

Assumptions

The only good is wheat, and wheat cannot be kept from one year to the next.
Oddtopia harvests 100 bushels in odd years and none in even years. Eventopia harvests in the opposite years.
People like a smooth path of consumption better than one that jumps up and down. With diminishing marginal utility, the last bushel eaten in a rich year is worth less than the first bushel in a poor year (consumption smoothing, as in Chapter 16).
Nobody invests and there is no government, \(I = G = 0\). A bushel lent this year comes back as one bushel next year, so \(\bar{r} = 0\). Neither island starts with foreign assets, \(F_0 = 0\).



Solving the model
Step 1: the trade balance. With \(I = G = 0\), equation (1) reads \(NX_t = Y_t - C_t\): the harvest minus what is eaten.
Step 2: consumption. Together the islands harvest 100 bushels each year. Wheat cannot be stored, so all 100 bushels are eaten in the year they grow. The smoothest way to share a constant total, the same in every year, is 50 bushels per island: \(C_t = 50\).
Step 3: the trade balances. Oddtopia’s trade balance is \(NX_t = 100 - 50 = +50\) in odd years and \(NX_t = 0 - 50 = -50\) in even years. Eventopia’s is the mirror image. So the two balances sum to zero every year, just as Step 3 of the first block says they must.
Step 4: the assets. Equation (5) with \(\bar{r} = 0\) and \(F_0 = 0\) gives Oddtopia’s net foreign assets: \(F_1 = 50\), \(F_2 = 50 - 50 = 0\), \(F_3 = 50\), and so on. After each good harvest Oddtopia holds a claim of 50 bushels on Eventopia, and the claim is repaid a year later. Eventopia’s assets run \(-50, 0, -50, \dots\)
Step 5: the budget constraint. With \(\bar{r} = 0\) and \(F_0 = 0\), equation (6) requires the trade balances to sum to zero. Over every pair of years they do: \(+50 - 50 = 0\).






ImportantKey result: trade as lending across time



Each island eats \(C_t = 50\) bushels every year. Oddtopia’s trade balance alternates between \(+50\) and \(-50\), and its net foreign assets between 50 and 0. Eventopia mirrors it, and every two years each island’s balances sum to zero, as equation (6) requires.








TipIn words



Islandia’s catch has good and bad seasons too. In a good season it ships fish to Mainland and keeps the claims; in a bad one it cashes them and runs a deficit. That deficit is no sign of trouble: it keeps islanders fed when the nets come back empty.




What the model predicts

Sharing risk. Each island eats 50 bushels a year, although its own harvest jumps between 0 and 100. Without trade, it would alternate between feast and famine.
A deficit can raise welfare. Each island has a deficit in exactly the years when its harvest fails. The deficit is a loan that keeps it fed.
Balanced on average. Each island’s average trade balance is zero, as equation (6) requires. Today’s deficit is the other side of tomorrow’s surplus.
A guide to the data. By the same logic, a country should borrow, and so run deficits, when its income is low for a while, when it expects to grow faster than the rest of the world, or when it has good projects to invest in. Fig. 4 asks whether countries that grow fast really do borrow.


A deficit can be a loan that smooths consumption, and over time it is balanced by later surpluses.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Suppose Oddtopia harvests 80 bushels in odd years and 20 in even years, and Eventopia the reverse. What does each island eat, and what are Oddtopia’s trade balance and foreign assets in years 1 and 2?


Answer

The world still harvests 100 bushels a year, so each island eats 50. By Step 1, Oddtopia’s trade balance is \(80 - 50 = +30\) in year 1 and \(20 - 50 = -30\) in year 2. By equation (5) with \(\bar{r} = 0\), its assets are \(F_1 = 30\) and \(F_2 = 0\).

2. In an even year, Oddtopia runs a large trade deficit. Is that bad news?


Answer

No. The deficit is the repayment of last year’s loan by Eventopia, in wheat, and it lets Oddtopia eat 50 bushels in a year with no harvest. Over any two years its trade balances add up to zero, as equation (6) requires.






19.1.6 Comparative advantage: the North and the South

Assumptions

Two countries, the North (\(n\)) and the South (\(s\)), make and consume two goods: apples and computers. Labor is the only input. Each worker supplies one unit of labor for a wage \(w\), and the wage is all of the worker’s income.
In country \(j\) there are \(L_j\) workers, and each can make either \(x_j\) apples or \(z_j\) computers. We use the textbook’s numbers throughout this notebook:

Inside its own country, a worker can move freely between the two sectors, but nobody crosses the border (the migration block below lifts this rule).
Everybody spends half of income on apples and half on computers. Apples are the unit of account (the numéraire): an apple costs 1, and a computer costs \(p\) apples. Let \(c_A\) and \(c_C\) be the apples and computers that one person consumes. The two spending shares then give

\[\frac{1 \times c_A}{w} = \frac{1}{2} \;\;\text{and}\;\; \frac{p \times c_C}{w} = \frac{1}{2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad c_A = \frac{w}{2}, \qquad c_C = \frac{w}{2p}. \tag{8}\]
The North makes more of both goods per worker, \(x_n > x_s\) and \(z_n > z_s\): it has an absolute advantage in both. But its edge is far larger in computers, \(z_n/z_s = 16/2 = 8\), than in apples, \(x_n/x_s = 160/100 = 1.6\). Cross-multiplying, \(z_n/z_s > x_n/x_s\) is the same as \(x_s/z_s > x_n/z_n\). To make one computer, the North gives up \(160/16 = 10\) apples and the South \(100/2 = 50\). Computers cost relatively less to make in the North, so the North has a comparative advantage in computers, and the South in apples.


Solving the model: autarky
In autarky, neither country trades.
Step 1: the wage. A worker who grows apples makes \(x\) of them, at a price of 1 each, so the wage is \(w = x\).
Step 2: the price of a computer. A worker who makes computers makes \(z\) of them and earns \(p\,z\) apples. People want both goods, so both sectors need workers, and so both must pay the same wage: \(p\,z = x\). If computers paid more, all workers would leave the orchards; if they paid less, nobody would make computers. The price of a computer is therefore \(p = x/z\), its opportunity cost: the apples given up to make it (Appendix C.9 on solving such conditions).
Step 3: consumption. Put \(w = x\) and \(p = x/z\) into equation (8): \(c_A = x/2\) and \(c_C = \dfrac{x/2}{x/z} = \dfrac{z}{2}\).
Step 4: who works where. The \(L_A\) apple growers produce \(L_A\,x\) apples, and the \(L\) people eat \(L\,x/2\). Equating the two gives \(L_A = L/2\): half of the workers grow apples, and half make computers.






ImportantKey result: autarky



\[w = x, \qquad p = \frac{x}{z} \tag{9}\]
Each person consumes \(c_A = x/2\) apples and \(c_C = z/2\) computers, and half of the workers are in each sector.
The North and the South in numbers. The North has \(w = 160\) and \(p = 10\), and each person consumes 80 apples and 8 computers. The South has \(w = 100\) and \(p = 50\), and each person consumes 50 apples and 1 computer.


In total, the North makes \(50 \times 160 = 8{,}000\) apples and \(50 \times 16 = 800\) computers, and the South makes \(200 \times 100 = 20{,}000\) apples and \(200 \times 2 = 400\) computers.


Solving the model: free trade
Step 1: arbitrage. In autarky a computer costs 10 apples in the North but 50 in the South. A trader could buy computers in the North and resell them in the South at a profit (arbitrage). Under free trade such gaps vanish, and there is a single world price \(p\).
Step 2: a guess. Suppose each country makes only the good of its comparative advantage: the North only computers, the South only apples. World output is then \(L_n z_n = 1{,}600\) computers and \(L_s x_s = 40{,}000\) apples.
Step 3: the world price. World income in apples is the value of all output, \(L_s x_s + p\,L_n z_n\). Half of it buys computers, and in equilibrium the computers bought are the computers made:
\[p\,L_n z_n = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(L_s x_s + p\,L_n z_n\right)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tfrac{1}{2}\,p\,L_n z_n = \tfrac{1}{2}\,L_s x_s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n}.\]
Because people spend equal shares on the two goods, world apples and world computers must be worth the same in total. The price of a computer is therefore world apples divided by world computers: \(40{,}000/1{,}600 = 25\) apples.
Step 4: wages. A southern worker still grows 100 apples, so \(w_s = x_s = 100\). A northern worker makes 16 computers worth 25 apples each, so \(w_n = p\,z_n = 400\) apples. With the formula for \(p\), \(w_n = L_s x_s/L_n\).
Step 5: consumption. Equation (8) gives, in the North, \(c_A = 400/2 = 200\) and \(c_C = 400/(2 \times 25) = 8\); in the South, \(c_A = 100/2 = 50\) and \(c_C = 100/(2 \times 25) = 2\).
Step 6: check the guess. Northern workers keep making computers only if computers pay at least as much as apples, \(p\,z_n \ge x_n\), or \(p \ge x_n/z_n\). Southern workers keep growing apples only if \(x_s \ge p\,z_s\), or \(p \le x_s/z_s\). With strict inequalities, both countries specialize completely when the world price sits strictly between the two autarky prices.






ImportantKey result: free trade



\[p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n} \tag{10}\]
\[\frac{x_s}{z_s} \;>\; p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n} \;>\; \frac{x_n}{z_n} \tag{11}\]
The world price (10) is the ratio of world apples to world computers. Complete specialization requires it to lie between the two autarky prices (11).
The North and the South in numbers. \(p = 40{,}000/1{,}600 = 25\) apples, and \(50 > 25 > 10\), so the guess is right. The northern wage is 400 apples and the southern wage 100.


If, say, the South were large enough to push \(p\) above 50, some southern workers would also make computers, and the South would keep its autarky price.






TipIn words: why Islandia trades with a stronger partner



Suppose Mainland is better than Islandia at both fishing and making machines. Trade still pays for both, because what counts is what each side gives up. If Islandia is a little worse at fishing but much worse at machines, a machine costs it many fish at home, and buying it from Mainland is cheaper.




What the model predicts
Both countries gain, for any numbers that satisfy (11). Compare each item of consumption under autarky and free trade:










autarky
free trade

\(x_n/2 = 80\)
\(p\,z_n/2 = 200\)

Each country gets more of the good it imports, and no less of the good it makes. What drives trade is comparative advantage: the North gains although it is better at everything. World output grows too, from \(28{,}000\) apples and \(1{,}200\) computers in autarky to \(40{,}000\) apples and \(1{,}600\) computers.
Comparative statics. Take logs of the free-trade results (Appendix C.4), for instance \(\ln p = \ln L_s + \ln x_s - \ln L_n - \ln z_n\), and each coefficient is an elasticity. They are valid as long as condition (11) holds:











A 1% rise in …
\(p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n}\)
\(w_n\), North apples \(= \frac{L_s x_s}{2L_n}\)
North computers \(= \frac{z_n}{2}\)
South apples \(= \frac{x_s}{2}\)
South computers \(= \frac{L_n z_n}{2L_s}\)

\(L_n\) (northern workers)
\(-1\%\)
