When the North gets better at making computers, computers become cheaper everywhere. The northern wage in apples stays put, because each computer now buys fewer apples, and the South gains just as many computers as the North. Prices spread productivity gains across borders. With \(z_n = 20\), for example, the world price drops to \(40{,}000/2{,}000 = 20\) apples, and condition (11) still holds, \(50 > 20 > 8\).

Trade follows comparative advantage, so even a country that is better at everything gains from it.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. The North’s computer productivity rises to \(z_n = 20\), and nothing else changes. Find the world price, the northern wage, and what one person consumes in each country.


Answer

By equation (10), \(p = 40{,}000/(100 \times 20) = 20\) apples, and condition (11) still holds, \(50 > 20 > 8\). The northern wage is \(w_n = 20 \times 20 = 400\) apples, unchanged. By equation (8), a northerner consumes 200 apples and \(400/40 = 10\) computers, and a southerner 50 apples and \(100/40 = 2.5\) computers. Both countries get 25 percent more computers.

2. The South is less productive than the North in both goods. Why does it still gain from trade?


Answer

Because what matters is the opportunity cost. A computer costs the South 50 apples at home (equation 9), but only 25 apples on the world market (equation 10). By growing apples and buying computers, each southerner gets 2 computers instead of 1, with the same 50 apples.






19.1.7 Free migration: moving workers instead of goods

Assumptions
Keep the North–South model, but now let workers cross the border. Technology stays put: in the North, any worker makes \(x_n\) apples or \(z_n\) computers, wherever he or she was born. Production has constant returns, so output per worker does not depend on how many workers a country has.


Solving the model
Step 1: who moves. Under free trade a computer costs the same everywhere, so a higher wage in apples means a higher real wage. The northern wage, 400 apples, is four times the southern wage of 100 apples (in autarky it is 160 against 100). Southern workers keep moving while any gap is left. The North is more productive in both goods, so a worker makes more of either good there, and in the end the South is empty.
Step 2: the new world economy. The world now looks like the North in autarky, with \(L_n + L_s = 500\) workers. By equation (9), \(w = x_n = 160\) and \(p = x_n/z_n = 10\). By equation (8), each person eats \(c_A = 80\) apples and has \(c_C = 8\) computers.
Step 3: production. Half of the 500 workers make each good: \(250 \times 160 = 40{,}000\) apples and \(250 \times 16 = 4{,}000\) computers.






ImportantKey result: free migration



All workers end up in the North, which then works like a closed economy with \(L_n + L_s\) workers. By equations (8) and (9),
\[w = x_n, \qquad p = \frac{x_n}{z_n}, \qquad c_A = \frac{x_n}{2}, \qquad c_C = \frac{z_n}{2}.\]
The North and the South in numbers. Everyone earns 160 apples, a computer costs 10 apples, and each person has 80 apples and 8 computers. The world makes 40,000 apples and 4,000 computers.








TipIn words



Moving goods lets each country use its own technology where it is relatively best. Moving people lets every worker use the best technology in the world. If Mainland’s workshops beat Islandia’s at everything, islanders who moved there would make more of every good, and they would keep most of the gain.




What the model predicts

Migration follows absolute advantage, while trade in goods follows comparative advantage. Workers go where productivity is highest, full stop.
The world produces more than under free trade: the same 40,000 apples, but 4,000 computers instead of 1,600.
The gains go to the migrants. What one worker consumes under each arrangement:











autarky
free trade
free migration




a worker born in the North
80 apples, 8 computers
200 apples, 8 computers
80 apples, 8 computers


a worker born in the South
50 apples, 1 computer
50 apples, 2 computers
80 apples, 8 computers



Northern workers are back at their autarky bundle: with constant returns, the newcomers leave their productivity unchanged. So northerners like free trade better than free migration.

The North could be compensated. Going from free trade to free migration, each of the 100 northerners loses 120 apples, 12,000 apples in all. Each of the 400 migrants gains 30 apples and 6 computers, 12,000 apples and 2,400 computers in all. The gains exceed the losses. If each migrant handed 30 apples to the North, every northerner would be back at the free-trade bundle of 200 apples and 8 computers, and every migrant would still have 50 apples and 8 computers: four times the computers of free trade.
Moving labor or moving capital. The production and Solow models (Chapter 4, Chapter 5) showed that poor countries are poor mainly because of low total factor productivity, and much less because they lack capital. Sending capital to an economy with low productivity leaves that problem where it is. Letting workers move to where productivity is high goes to the root of it, which is why the potential gains from migration are so large.
The costs of trade. In the model, northern apple growers turn into computer makers overnight, and nobody loses. In real life, changing jobs takes time and new skills, so trade makes winners and losers inside each country. Since the winners gain more than the losers lose, the winners could in principle compensate the losers, for instance through retraining and a social safety net.


Free migration raises world output the most, but the gains go to the migrants unless they share them.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Under free migration, how many apples must each of the 400 migrants hand to the North so that each of the 100 northerners is back at the free-trade bundle of 200 apples?


Answer

Each northerner has 80 apples and needs 120 more, so the North needs \(100 \times 120 = 12{,}000\) apples. Shared among 400 migrants, that is \(12{,}000/400 = 30\) apples each. Each migrant keeps 50 apples and 8 computers, still more than under free trade.

2. Why does free migration raise the world’s computer output from 1,600 to 4,000, while free trade does not?


Answer

Under free trade, the South’s 400 workers grow apples with their own technology. Under free migration, they work with the North’s technology, which makes 16 computers per worker instead of 2. Migration follows absolute advantage, so every worker uses the best technology, and the world’s output of computers rises.









NoteRecap




A deficit means using more than you make: \(NX = Y - (C + I + G)\) (the basic facts, Fig. 3).
A deficit is borrowing: \(NX = S - I\) (Fig. 4), and budget deficits can bring twin deficits.
Deficits pile up into a foreign debt (5), are repaid in present value (6), and settle at a stable ratio to GDP when \(\bar{g} > \bar{r}\) (7) (foreign debt).
Trade moves goods to where they are worth most, and shares risk (Oddtopia and Eventopia).
Comparative advantage: under free trade the world price lies between the autarky prices, and both countries gain (the North and the South).
Free migration follows absolute advantage, raises world output most, and the gains go to the migrants (free migration).

title: 19. International Trade
text:
19.2 Model in code
Now we turn the accounting rules and the trade models into Python. The section has three parts: the setup (folded, because it is the same in every chapter), the model as functions, and numerical checks that also recompute the textbook’s tables. Run its cells once, in order. Every later section of the notebook reuses them.

19.2.1 Setup
Run the setup cells once, before anything else. They load the Python libraries, give every chart the same look, store the address of the chapter’s data and define the helpers that only the book website needs. You can use the notebook without reading them; open the box if you are curious.






NoteShow the setup code





The first cell loads the libraries and sets the look of the charts. Its comments explain each step.

# @title Setup: libraries, chart colors and the data location
# Text after a "#" is a comment: Python ignores it, it is there for human readers.

# Step 1: load the libraries. `import` loads a library, a toolbox written by
# other people, and `as np` gives it a short nickname, so the code stays short.
import numpy as np                    # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                   # data tables
import plotly.express as px           # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go     # charts built piece by piece
import plotly.io as pio               # settings shared by every chart
# sliders, buttons and menus for the interactive figures
from ipywidgets import interact, IntSlider, FloatSlider, ToggleButtons, Dropdown, SelectMultiple, fixed

# Step 2: one light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
# the same chart size in Colab and on the website
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full widget labels

# Step 3, Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets.
# `try` runs the indented lines; if the import fails (we are not in Colab),
# `except` skips them.
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# Step 4: the data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch19/"

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider. The next helper builds those versions. Run it and move on.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure
        name        : the argument the slider moves
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

Every figure of this chapter can also show other countries. On the website, the many-country versions get a menu of country groups, built by two more helpers.

# @title Helpers for the many-country website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
# Step 1: two fixed groups of countries for the menus
G7 = ["U.S.", "Japan", "Germany", "France", "United Kingdom", "Italy", "Canada"]
EMERGING = ["China", "India", "Brazil", "Russia", "Mexico", "Indonesia", "Türkiye", "South Africa",
            "Saudi Arabia", "Argentina"]


def country_groups(regions, book):
    """The menu groups: the textbook's countries, the G7, large emerging economies, the World Bank regions.

    Arguments
        regions : a table with one row per country and the columns country and region
        book    : the countries the textbook shows
    Returns
        a dictionary from each group's name to its list of countries
    """
    # Step 2: the three fixed groups first, then one group per region, A to Z
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Large emerging": EMERGING}
    for region in sorted(regions.region.unique()):
        # the countries whose region is this one
        groups[region] = list(regions[regions.region == region].country)
    return groups


def group_menu(fig, groups, start, title):
    """Show one group of countries at a time, chosen from a menu above the chart.

    A trace belongs to the country named before ', ' in its legendgroup. Each group gets a y range that covers
    its values; in groups of more than 15 countries it leaves out extreme outliers (double-click the chart to
    show them).

    Arguments
        fig    : a Plotly figure with the traces of every country
        groups : the menu groups, from country_groups
        start  : the group shown first
        title  : the chart's title
    Returns
        the same figure, with the menu
    """
    # Step 3: the country of each trace
    owners = [t.legendgroup.split(", ")[0] for t in fig.data]
    # Step 4: one menu entry per group: its traces and a y range that fits them
    buttons = []
    for name, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in members for o in owners]   # the traces of this group
        # all their y values, without the missing ones (or a single 0 if none)
        ys = np.concatenate([np.asarray(t.y, dtype=float) for t, v in zip(fig.data, visible) if v]
                            or [np.zeros(1)])
        ys = ys[np.isfinite(ys)] if np.isfinite(ys).any() else np.zeros(1)
        lo, hi = ys.min(), ys.max()
        # large groups: leave out extreme outliers
        if len(set(o for o, v in zip(owners, visible) if v)) > 15:
            q5, q95 = np.percentile(ys, [5, 95])
            lo, hi = max(lo, q5 - 0.3 * (q95 - q5)), min(hi, q95 + 0.3 * (q95 - q5))
        pad = 0.06 * (hi - lo) + 0.5                # a little room above and below
        buttons.append(dict(label=name, method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": visible},
                                  {"yaxis.range": [lo - pad, hi + pad], "yaxis.autorange": False}]))
    # Step 5: start with the group `start`, and put the menu above the chart
    first = list(groups).index(start)
    for t, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[first]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        t.visible = v
    # the title, the start group's y range and the menu at the top left
    fig.update_layout(title=title, yaxis_range=buttons[first]["args"][1]["yaxis.range"], yaxis_tickvals=None,
                      margin=dict(t=115), updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=first, direction="down",
                                                             x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])
    return fig

The last helper is like slider_figure, but with a drop-down menu instead of a slider.

# @title Helper for the website versions with a menu of countries (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def menu_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Like slider_figure, but with a drop-down menu; each choice also sets its own y-axis range.

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure
        name        : the argument the menu sets
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a menu that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value, and copy every trace into one figure
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[values.index(start)].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (values[i] == start)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 2: one menu entry per value: its traces, title and y range
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        # the version's own y range, or Plotly's automatic one if it has none
        rng = f.layout.yaxis.range
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "yaxis.autorange": rng is None,
                  "yaxis.range": list(rng) if rng is not None else None}
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    # Step 3: the menu at the top left, starting at the value `start`
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=115), updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start),
                                                            direction="down", x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left",
                                                            yanchor="bottom")])
    return fig






19.2.2 The model as functions
We write each accounting rule and each trade model as a Python function: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives back a result. Each function’s description names the equation it computes, and the figure sections reuse them.

The accounting rules
The first five functions are the trade balance and the national income identity, equations (1) and (2), plus two ways to express a variable as a share of GDP.

# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses, and
# `return` gives back the result. The text in triple quotes describes it.
# The same function works for single numbers and for whole columns of a data
# table, because pandas does arithmetic on every row at once.
def share_of_gdp(x, gdp):
    """Any variable as a percent of GDP, as in Fig. 1.

    Fig. 1:  100 x / Y

    Arguments
        x   : the variable, e.g. exports EX or the trade balance NX
        gdp : GDP, Y
    Returns
        x as a percent of GDP
    """
    return 100 * x / gdp


def net_exports(exports, imports):
    """The trade balance (net exports).

    Fig. 2:  NX = EX - IM

    Arguments
        exports : exports, EX
        imports : imports, IM
    Returns
        net exports, NX (negative for a trade deficit)
    """
    return exports - imports


def net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G):
    """The national income identity solved for net exports.

    Equation (1):  NX = Y - (C + I + G)

    Arguments
        Y : output, GDP
        C, I, G : consumption, investment and government purchases
    Returns
        net exports, NX: what is produced minus what is used at home
    """
    return Y - (C + I + G)


def trade_balance_share(c, i, g):
    """Net exports as a percent of GDP, from the GDP shares of C, I and G.

    Equation (2):  100 nx = 100 (1 - c - i - g)

    Arguments
        c, i, g : C, I and G as fractions of GDP
    Returns
        net exports as a percent of GDP
    """
    # equation (1) with Y = 1, so that NX is already a share of GDP
    return 100 * net_exports_from_uses(1, c, i, g)


def share_of_us_gdp(share, gdp, gdp_us):
    """Rescale a share of a country's own GDP to a share of U.S. GDP.

    Fig. 3, second bar:  share * Y / Y_US

    Arguments
        share  : a variable as a percent of the country's own GDP
        gdp    : the country's GDP
        gdp_us : U.S. GDP, in the same units
    Returns
        the same variable as a percent of U.S. GDP
    """
    return share * gdp / gdp_us

Four more functions handle saving and the data over time: two forms of equation (4), an average over a window of years, and the sum of past flows, which turns yearly trade balances into a stock of foreign assets or debt (equation 5 with \(\bar{r} = 0\)).

def domestic_saving(I, NX):
    """Domestic saving, S = Y - C - G, from investment and the trade balance.

    Equation (4) solved for S:  S = I + NX

    Arguments
        I  : investment
        NX : net exports
    Returns
        domestic saving, S
    """
    return I + NX


def net_capital_outflow(S, I):
    """The trade balance as saving minus investment.

    Equation (4):  NX = S - I

    Arguments
        S : domestic saving
        I : investment
    Returns
        net exports, NX: what the country lends abroad (borrows, if negative)
    """
    return S - I


def period_average(data, start, end):
    """The simple average over the years start to end, as in Fig. 4.

    Fig. 4:  the average of each column over a window of years

    Arguments
        data       : a table whose rows are years
        start, end : the first and the last year of the window
    Returns
        one average per column
    """
    # `data.loc[start:end]` keeps the rows from start to end, both included,
    # and `.mean()` averages them, one average per column
    return data.loc[start:end].mean()


def accumulate(start_value, flows):
    """Net foreign assets with no interest: the starting value plus each year's trade balance.

    Equation (5) with r-bar = 0:  F_t = F_(t-1) + NX_t

    Arguments
        start_value : net foreign assets before the first year, F_0
        flows       : the trade balances NX_t, one row per year
    Returns
        net foreign assets F_t at the end of each year
    """
    # `.cumsum()` is the cumulative sum: row by row, the sum of all values so far
    return start_value + flows.cumsum()

The long-run debt ratio of equation (7) is the last accounting function.

def debt_ratio_steady_state(nx, g, r=0.0):
    """Long-run net foreign assets as a share of GDP, f*.

    Equation (7):  f* = (1 + g) nx / (g - r)

    Arguments
        nx : the trade balance as a fraction of GDP (negative for a deficit)
        g  : the growth rate of nominal GDP, g-bar
        r  : the return on foreign assets, r-bar (0 unless we pass another value)
    Returns
        long-run net foreign assets as a fraction of GDP, f*
    """
    # `r=0.0` gives r a default value, used whenever we do not pass one
    return (1 + g) * nx / (g - r)



The North and the South
Two functions solve the comparative-advantage model. autarky follows Steps 1 to 4 of the autarky solution: the wage and price of equation (9), and consumption from equation (8).

def autarky(x, z, L):
    """Table 19.3: a closed economy whose L workers each make x apples or z computers.

    Equations (9) and (8):  w = x,  p = x / z,  c_A = w / 2,  c_C = w / (2 p)

    Arguments
        x : apples per worker
        z : computers per worker
        L : the number of workers
    Returns
        the economy's row of Table 19.3: wage, price, consumption and production
    """
    # the wage in apples: what a worker makes in the apple sector (equation 9)
    w = x
    # the price of a computer: both sectors must pay the same wage (equation 9)
    p = x / z
    # `pd.Series({...})` builds a list of numbers with labels from a dictionary
    # of label: value pairs
    return pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w,
                      "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                      "Apples per person": w / 2,          # equation (8), apples cost 1
                      "Computers per person": w / 2 / p,   # equation (8)
                      "Workers making apples (%)": 50,
                      "Workers making computers (%)": 50,
                      "Apples produced": L / 2 * x,
                      "Computers produced": L / 2 * z})

free_trade follows Steps 2 to 5 of the free-trade solution: complete specialization, the world price of equation (10), and the wages and consumption from equation (8).

def free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s):
    """Table 19.4: the North makes only computers, the South only apples, and they trade.

    Equations (10) and (8):  p = L_s x_s / (L_n z_n),  w_n = z_n p,  w_s = x_s

    Arguments
        x_n, z_n, L_n : apples or computers per worker, and workers, in the North
        x_s, z_s, L_s : the same for the South
    Returns
        Table 19.4: a table with one column per country
    """
    # Step 1: world production, with each country fully specialized
    computers = L_n * z_n                      # world production of computers
    apples = L_s * x_s                         # world production of apples
    # Step 2: the world price and the wages
    # equation (10): half of world spending goes to each good
    p = apples / computers
    w_n, w_s = z_n * p, x_s                    # wages in apples
    # Step 3: each country's column, as in autarky
    north = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_n, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_n / 2, "Computers per person": w_n / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 0, "Workers making computers (%)": 100,
                       "Apples produced": 0, "Computers produced": computers})
    south = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_s, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_s / 2, "Computers per person": w_s / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 100, "Workers making computers (%)": 0,
                       "Apples produced": apples, "Computers produced": 0})
    # `pd.DataFrame({...})` builds a table from a dictionary of columns
    return pd.DataFrame({"North": north, "South": south})




19.2.3 Checking the key results
The formulas came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, one Key result at a time, and recompute the textbook’s tables for the trade examples.

Checking the accounting
Check 1: equations (1) to (4). An economy produces 100, consumes 70, invests 20, its government buys 15 and collects 12 in taxes. Each identity must give the same trade balance.

# Step 1: output, consumption, investment, government purchases and taxes
Y, C, I, G, T = 100, 70, 20, 15, 12
# Step 2: equation (1). An f-string, f"... {value:.0f}", puts a value into
# the text; ":.0f" means no decimals and ":.1f" one decimal.
NX = net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G)
print(f"Equation (1): NX = {Y} - ({C} + {I} + {G}) = {NX}, or {share_of_gdp(NX, Y):.0f}% of GDP")
# equation (2), from the shares c = C/Y, i = I/Y and g = G/Y
print(f"Equation (2): 100 (1 - c - i - g) = {trade_balance_share(C / Y, I / Y, G / Y):.1f}% of GDP")
# Step 3: equation (3), the three kinds of saving add up to investment
private, government, foreign = Y - T - C, T - G, -NX
print(f"Equation (3): private {private} + government {government} + foreign {foreign} "
      f"= {private + government + foreign}, and I = {I}")
# Step 4: equation (4), with domestic saving = private + government saving
S = private + government
print(f"Equation (4): S - I = {S} - {I} = {net_capital_outflow(S, I)}, the same as NX = {NX}")
print(f"... and back again: S = I + NX = {domestic_saving(I, NX)}")
# Step 5: the economy uses more than it makes
print(f"Domestic uses C + I + G = {C + I + G} > Y = {Y}: a trade deficit")

Equation (1): NX = 100 - (70 + 20 + 15) = -5, or -5% of GDP
Equation (2): 100 (1 - c - i - g) = -5.0% of GDP
Equation (3): private 18 + government -3 + foreign 5 = 20, and I = 20
Equation (4): S - I = 15 - 20 = -5, the same as NX = -5
... and back again: S = I + NX = 15
Domestic uses C + I + G = 105 > Y = 100: a trade deficit


Check 2: the world adds up to zero. The United States runs a deficit of 3 (in goods) and the rest of the world, three times as large, runs the matching surplus.

# Step 1: two economies, the rest of the world three times as large
gdp_us, gdp_row = 100, 300
NX_us = -3
NX_row = -NX_us                         # every U.S. import is a rest-of-world export
# Step 2: the surplus as a share of its own GDP and of U.S. GDP (Fig. 3)
row_share = share_of_gdp(NX_row, gdp_row)
print(f"World trade balance: {NX_us + NX_row}")
print(f"Rest of the world: a surplus of {row_share:.0f}% of its own GDP, "
      f"or {share_of_us_gdp(row_share, gdp_row, gdp_us):.0f}% of U.S. GDP")

World trade balance: 0
Rest of the world: a surplus of 1% of its own GDP, or 3% of U.S. GDP


Check 3: the intertemporal budget constraint. A country with no foreign assets borrows 50 in year 1 and repays the loan with 5 percent interest in year 2. Equation (5) should bring its assets back to zero, and the present value of its two trade balances should be zero, as equation (6) says.

# Step 1: the loan; a list in square brackets holds the two trade balances
r = 0.05
trade_balance = [-50, 50 * (1 + r)]     # borrow 50, then repay 50 plus interest
F = 0.0                                 # no foreign assets at the start
present_value = 0.0
# Step 2: one pass per year. `range(1, 3)` counts 1, 2, so the `for` loop runs
# its indented lines twice. A list is numbered from 0, so `trade_balance[t - 1]`
# is the trade balance of year t. `x = x + ...` replaces the old value of x
# with the new one, and `**` means "to the power of".
for t in range(1, 3):
    F = (1 + r) * F + trade_balance[t - 1]                     # equation (5)
    present_value = present_value + trade_balance[t - 1] / (1 + r) ** t
    print(f"Year {t}: NX = {trade_balance[t - 1]:+.1f}, F = {F:+.2f}")
# Step 3: equation (6) with F_0 = 0
print(f"Present value of the trade balances = {present_value:.6f}   (equation 6: -F0 = 0)")

Year 1: NX = -50.0, F = -50.00
Year 2: NX = +52.5, F = +0.00
Present value of the trade balances = 0.000000   (equation 6: -F0 = 0)


Check 4: the long-run debt ratio. We apply the ratio form of equation (5) year after year with a constant deficit of 3 percent of GDP, and compare where it ends with the formula of equation (7).

# For three pairs of the growth rate g and the return r, apply equation (5)
# divided by GDP for 1,000 years; ":.0%" shows a share as a percentage
for g, r in [(0.04, 0.0), (0.05, 0.0), (0.04, 0.02)]:
    f = 0.0                                          # start with no foreign assets
    for year in range(1000):
        f = (1 + r) / (1 + g) * f + (-0.03)          # equation (5) divided by GDP
    # the end point of the simulation next to equation (7)
    print(f"g = {g:.0%}, r = {r:.0%}: simulated f = {100 * f:.1f}% of GDP, "
          f"formula = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, g, r):.1f}%")

g = 4%, r = 0%: simulated f = -78.0% of GDP, formula = -78.0%
g = 5%, r = 0%: simulated f = -63.0% of GDP, formula = -63.0%
g = 4%, r = 2%: simulated f = -156.0% of GDP, formula = -156.0%




Gains from exchange: the banana-and-fish islands
Check 5: the gains from exchange. Each island swaps half of the gap between its fish and its bananas, one for one, and the number of complete meals (one banana and one fish) per person should rise.

# Step 1: what each island has, per person
bananas_1, fish_1 = 200, 800                     # island 1, per person
bananas_2, fish_2 = 800, 200                     # island 2, per person
# the fish that island 1 swaps for bananas, one for one
q = (fish_1 - bananas_1) / 2
# Step 2: what each island eats after the swap
print(f"Island 1 swaps {q:.0f} fish for {q:.0f} bananas")
print(f"Island 1 eats {bananas_1 + q:.0f} bananas and {fish_1 - q:.0f} fish; "
      f"island 2 eats {bananas_2 - q:.0f} bananas and {fish_2 + q:.0f} fish")
# Step 3: `min(a, b)` is the smaller of two numbers: the number of complete meals
print(f"Meals per person on island 1: {min(bananas_1, fish_1)} without trade, "
      f"{min(bananas_1 + q, fish_1 - q):.0f} with trade")

Island 1 swaps 300 fish for 300 bananas
Island 1 eats 500 bananas and 500 fish; island 2 eats 500 bananas and 500 fish
Meals per person on island 1: 200 without trade, 500 with trade




Trade across time: Oddtopia and Eventopia (Table 19.1)
With no investment and no government, equation (1) gives \(NX = Y - C\), the harvest minus what is eaten. The sum of past trade balances (equation 5 with \(\bar{r} = 0\)) is what the other island owes. The next cell builds Table 19.1.

# Step 1: the harvests of the two islands, one row per year
wheat = pd.DataFrame({"year": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
                      "Oddtopia harvest": [100, 0, 100, 0, 100, 0],
                      "Eventopia harvest": [0, 100, 0, 100, 0, 100]})
# Step 2: the `for` loop repeats the indented lines for each island in the list;
# `island + " harvest"` glues two pieces of text into a column name
for island in ["Oddtopia", "Eventopia"]:
    # each island eats half of the world harvest, every year
    wheat[island + " consumption"] = 50
    # equation (1) with I = G = 0: NX = Y - C
    wheat[island + " trade balance"] = net_exports_from_uses(wheat[island + " harvest"],
                                                             wheat[island + " consumption"], 0, 0)
    # equation (5) with r = 0: the sum of past trade balances
    wheat[island + " is owed"] = accumulate(0, wheat[island + " trade balance"])
# Step 3: `.T` turns the table on its side, so that the years become columns,
# as in the textbook
wheat.set_index("year").T

# Step 1: compare with the textbook. `==` compares the two row by row, giving
# True or False, and `.all()` is True only when every row is True.
book_balance = [50, -50, 50, -50, 50, -50]      # Oddtopia's row of Table 19.1
same = (wheat["Oddtopia trade balance"] == book_balance).all()
print(f"Oddtopia's trade balance equals Table 19.1: {same}")
# Step 2: the world's trade balance in every year
world = wheat["Oddtopia trade balance"] + wheat["Eventopia trade balance"]
print(f"The two trade balances add to zero in every year: {(world == 0).all()}")

for island in ["Oddtopia", "Eventopia"]:

          f"consumption always {wheat[island + ' consumption'].iloc[0]}")

Comparative advantage: the North and the South (Tables 19.2 to 19.5)
The productivities of Table 19.2 come first. The North is better at making both goods, but much more so at making computers.

# Table 19.2: apples or computers per worker, and the number of workers
x_n, z_n, L_n = 160, 16, 100        # North
x_s, z_s, L_s = 100, 2, 400         # South
# absolute advantage: how many times more productive the North is
print(f"North / South productivity: apples {x_n / x_s:.1f} times, computers {z_n / z_s:.0f} times")
# comparative advantage: the cost of a computer in apples
print(f"Apples given up for one computer: North {x_n / z_n:.0f}, South {x_s / z_s:.0f}")

Autarky. We compute Table 19.3 with autarky and put the textbook’s numbers next to it.

table_19_3 = pd.DataFrame({"North": autarky(x_n, z_n, L_n), "South": autarky(x_s, z_s, L_s)})
# Step 2: the textbook's numbers, in the same rows
book_19_3 = pd.DataFrame({"North": [160, 10, 80, 8, 50, 50, 8000, 800],
                          "South": [100, 50, 50, 1, 50, 50, 20000, 400]}, index=table_19_3.index)
# Step 3: `pd.concat([...], axis=1, keys=[...])` places the two tables next to

pd.concat([table_19_3, book_19_3], axis=1, keys=["Notebook", "Textbook"])

Check 7: free trade is an equilibrium. Both world markets clear, and condition (11) holds, so complete specialization really is the outcome.

# Step 1: world demand = consumption per person times the number of people;
# ":,.0f" shows no decimals and a comma between thousands
demand_computers = (table_19_4.loc["Computers per person"] * [L_n, L_s]).sum()
demand_apples = (table_19_4.loc["Apples per person"] * [L_n, L_s]).sum()

      f"{x_n / z_n:.0f}: {x_s / z_s > p_world > x_n / z_n}")

print(f"World output: {table_19_3.loc['Apples produced'].sum():,.0f} apples and "
      f"{table_19_3.loc['Computers produced'].sum():,.0f} computers under autarky, "
      f"{table_19_4.loc['Apples produced'].sum():,.0f} and {table_19_4.loc['Computers produced'].sum():,.0f} with trade")

# Step 2: the rows and countries to compare, as (row, country) pairs
items = [("Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"), ("Wage, w (apples)", "North"),
         ("Apples per person", "North"), ("Computers per person", "North"),
         ("Apples per person", "South"), ("Computers per person", "South")]
# Step 3: the percent change of each; `row, country = item` unpacks a pair
for item in items:
    row, country = item
    change = better.loc[row, country] / table_19_4.loc[row, country] - 1
    print(f"{country}, {row}: {100 * change:+.2f}%")

Free migration (Table 19.5)

Check 9: compensating the North. Each migrant hands 30 apples to the North. Northerners should get back their free-trade bundle, migrants should still beat theirs, and the world’s apples and computers should be enough for all.

      f"{migration['Apples produced']:,.0f}")

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, a color for every economy
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses.

    As far as the palette allows: when no color is free, the country gets the least
    used one, searched from the end of the palette.

    Arguments
        names  : the countries to color
        groups : the lists of countries shown together (the menu views)
        fixed  : {country: color} for the textbook countries, or None
    Returns
        a dictionary {country: color}
    """
    # start from a copy of the fixed colors (or an empty dictionary)
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue                    # `continue` skips to the next country
        # Step 1: `score` gives every color a cost (lower is better): 1 for each
        # country that already uses it anywhere
        score = {}
        for color in PALETTE:
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)
        # Step 2: 10 for each country of a large group that uses it (Europe has
        # more countries than there are colors), and 100 for each one of a group
        # small enough to avoid any clash. `a if test else b` gives a when the
        # test is True and b otherwise; `colors.get(other)` is None for a country
        # without a color yet
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        # Step 3: `min(PALETTE, key=score.get)` picks the color with the lowest
        # cost (the first one on ties)
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)
        # no free color: the least used one, searching from the end of the list
        # (`PALETTE[::-1]` is the list in reverse order), so that the leftovers
        # take the last, rarely used colors
        if score[best] >= 10:
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors


# The color of every economy; the U.S. keeps the book's blue
COLORS = group_colors(
    regions.country,
    country_groups(regions, ["U.S."]).values(),
    {"U.S.": BLUE},

# @title Drawing code: Figs. 1 to 6, the textbook's axis range when the data fit
def fit_range(values, book_range):
    """The textbook's axis range if every value fits in it, otherwise None.

    With None, Plotly chooses a range that shows every value.

    Arguments
        values     : the values drawn on the axis
        book_range : [lowest, highest], the textbook's range
    Returns
        book_range, or None
    """
    # every value between the lowest and the highest end of the textbook's range
    if values.min() >= book_range[0] and values.max() <= book_range[1]:
        return book_range
    # some value would fall off the chart: let Plotly choose
    return None


The figure draws Fig. 19.1 for any list of economies. First the data: trade_shares_data keeps the rows of the chosen economies and computes exports plus imports, the openness of each economy, in its latest year. The title of the figure reports it.

# The flows that the buttons of the figure can show
FLOWS = {
    "Exports and imports": ["Exports", "Imports"],
    "Exports": ["Exports"],
    "Imports": ["Imports"],
}


def trade_shares_data(countries, flow):
    """The data of Fig. 1 for any economies, and the openness of each.

    Openness: exports + imports, percent of GDP, in each economy's latest year.

    Arguments
        countries : the economies to show
        flow      : a key of FLOWS, the flows to show
    Returns
        rows     : the chosen economies' rows of `world`
        long     : the flows to draw, one row per economy, year and flow
        openness : each economy's exports + imports in its latest year
    """
    # Step 1: `.isin(countries)` is True for the rows whose economy is in the
    # list; `.rename(columns={...})` gives the columns readable names
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)].rename(
        columns={"exports": "Exports", "imports": "Imports"}
    )
    # Step 2: `.melt(...)` stacks the export and import columns into one column
    # `share`, with a new column `flow` that says which is which
    long = rows.melt(
        id_vars=["country", "year"],
        value_vars=FLOWS[flow],
        var_name="flow",
        value_name="share",
    )
    # Step 3: `.groupby("country").last()` keeps each economy's last row with
    # both flows; openness is exports + imports in that year
    last = rows.dropna(subset=["Exports", "Imports"]).groupby("country").last()
    openness = last.Exports + last.Imports
    return rows, long, openness

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1 for any economies
def trade_shares_world(countries=("U.S.",), flow="Exports and imports"):
    """Exports and imports, percent of GDP (World Bank WDI), for any economies.

    Draws Fig. 1 (inspired by Fig. 19.1 in Jones) for any list of economies.

    Arguments
        countries : the economies to show
        flow      : "Exports and imports", "Exports" or "Imports"
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (trade_shares_data)
    rows, long, openness = trade_shares_data(countries, flow)
    if len(rows) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Choose at least one economy"))

    # Step 2: the title names two economies and counts the rest.
    # `", ".join(names)` glues a list of texts together
    names = []
    for name in openness.index[:2]:
        names.append(f"{name} {openness[name]:.0f}%")
    more = f" + {len(openness) - 2} more" if len(openness) > 2 else ""

    # Step 3: one line per economy and flow: `line_dash="flow"` draws exports
    # solid and imports dashed, and `color_discrete_map=COLORS` gives each
    # economy its own color, in Colab and on the website
    fig = px.line(
        long,
        x="year",
        y="share",
        color="country",
        line_dash="flow",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        labels={"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "flow": "Flow"},
        title="Latest exports + imports, % of GDP: " + ", ".join(names) + more,
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)

    # Step 4: the axes: the textbook's range when the data fit in it
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(long.share.dropna(), [2, 18.5]))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")

The Oddtopia example says that the trade balance must average zero over a long period. balance_window computes the average trade balance over a window of years, using our period_average, and counts the deficit years in it. The figure shades that window and reports both numbers.

def balance_window(start, end):
    """The average U.S. trade balance over a window of years, and its deficit years.

    Fig. 2:  the average of 100 NX / Y from start to end (period_average)

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year of the window
    Returns
        start, end : the same two years, in order (start <= end)
        avg        : the average trade balance, percent of GDP
        deficits   : the number of years with a deficit, NX < 0
    """
    # `min(a, b)` and `max(a, b)` give the smaller and the larger of two numbers,
    # so the window stays valid even if the two sliders cross
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)
    avg = period_average(us.trade_balance, start, end)
    # `(series < 0).sum()` counts the deficit years, because each True counts as 1
    deficits = (us.trade_balance.loc[start:end] < 0).sum()
    return start, end, avg, deficits

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, the U.S. trade balance
def trade_balance_chart(start=1976, end=2025):
    """The U.S. trade balance (percent of GDP), with its average from start to end.

    Draws Fig. 2 (inspired by Fig. 19.2 in Jones).

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year of the shaded window
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (balance_window)
    start, end, avg, deficits = balance_window(start, end)

    # Step 2: the trade balance, year by year; the title reports the window
    fig = px.line(
        us.reset_index(),
        x="year",
        y="trade_balance",
        color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
        labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"},
        title=(
            f"{start}–{end}: average trade balance {avg:+.2f}% of GDP, "
            f"deficits in {deficits} of {end - start + 1} years"
        ),
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)

    # Step 3: the zero line; `add_vrect` shades the window between two x values,
    # and `add_shape(type="line", ...)` draws the dotted average as one segment
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_shape(
        type="line",
        x0=start,
        x1=end,
        y0=avg,
        y1=avg,
        line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dot"),
    )

    # Step 4: what the two sides of zero mean
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=1990,
        y=1.6,
        text="Above zero: exports > imports",
        showarrow=False,
        font=dict(size=13),
    )
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=1965,
        y=-4.5,
        text="Below zero: imports > exports",
        showarrow=False,
        font=dict(size=13),
    )

    # Step 5: the textbook's axes, with no tick label in the corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1948, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-6.5, 2.5], tickvals=[-5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2])
    return fig

From 1950 to 1975 the United States usually had a small surplus (the dotted average line is above zero for that window). After 1975 the pattern reversed: there has not been a single surplus year since.

Over the whole period 1950–2025 the average is still negative, about −1.5 percent of GDP. Trade has not balanced yet: according to the Oddtopia example, the rest of the world expects future U.S. surpluses.

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2, the dotted average line of each economy
def add_average(fig, series, name, start, end):
    """Draw the average of a yearly series from start to end as a dotted segment.

    The dotted lines of Fig. 2 for any economies; period_average gives the average.

    Arguments
        fig        : the Plotly figure to draw on
        series     : a yearly series, with the years as labels
        name       : the economy, for its color and its legend group
        start, end : the first and the last year of the window
    Returns
        the average (NaN when the window has no data)
    """
    avg = period_average(series, start, end)
    # NaN (no data in the window) is not equal to itself
    if avg == avg:
        # `go.Scatter(..., mode="lines")` with two points draws one straight
        # segment. `legendgroup=name` ties it to the economy's line, so that a
        # click on the legend hides both, and `showlegend=False` keeps it out of
        # the legend
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=[start, end],
                y=[avg, avg],
                mode="lines",
                name=name + ", average",
                legendgroup=name,
                showlegend=False,
                line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=3, dash="dot"),
            )
        )
    return avg

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2 for any economies
def trade_balance_world(countries=("U.S.",), start=1976, end=2024):
    """The trade balance (percent of GDP, WDI) and its average from start to end.

    Draws Fig. 2 (inspired by Fig. 19.2 in Jones) for any economies.

    Arguments
        countries  : the economies to show
        start, end : the first and the last year of the averages
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the window, in order even if the sliders cross, and the chosen rows
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)]

    # Step 2: one line per economy, in its own color
    fig = px.line(
        rows,
        x="year",
        y="trade_balance",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"},
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)

    # Step 3: each economy's dotted average (add_average), and its text for the
    # title
    names = []
    for name in sorted(set(rows.country)):
        series = rows[rows.country == name].set_index("year").trade_balance
        avg = add_average(fig, series, name, start, end)
        if avg == avg:
            # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
            names.append(f"{name} {round(avg, 1) + 0.0:+.1f}%")
        else:
            names.append(f"{name}: no data")

    # Step 4: the title names two economies and counts the rest
    more = f" + {len(names) - 2} more" if len(names) > 2 else ""
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Average trade balance {start}–{end}: " + ", ".join(names[:2]) + more,
        legend_title_text="",
    )

    # Step 5: the zero line, the shaded window and the axes
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(rows.trade_balance.dropna(), [-6.5, 2.5]))
    return fig

The second bar of the textbook’s figure shows each country’s trade balance as a share of U.S. GDP, so the bars of different countries can be added up and compared with the U.S. deficit: we multiply the share of own GDP by the country’s GDP and divide by U.S. GDP.
You can add any country to the figure. book_order keeps the textbook’s countries first and says which chosen countries have no data (PWT 10.01 has only the nine textbook countries).

# The textbook's five countries of Fig. 3, in its order
FIG3 = ["U.S.", "Japan", "China", "France", "Germany"]


def book_order(countries, book, available):
    """The chosen countries with data, the textbook's first, and those without data.

    The textbook's countries come in its order, then the others from A to Z.

    Arguments
        countries : the chosen countries
        book      : the textbook's countries, in its order
        available : the countries that have data
    Returns
        order   : the chosen countries with data
        missing : the chosen countries without data
    """
    order, missing = [], []
    for name in list(book) + sorted(countries):
        # each chosen country once
        if name in countries and name not in order and name not in missing:
            if name in available:
                order.append(name)
            else:
                missing.append(name)
    # a function can `return` two results at once; the caller unpacks them into
    # two names: `order, missing = book_order(...)`
    return order, missing

The two bars of each country are the economics of Fig. 3: its trade balance as a share of its own GDP, and the same balance as a share of U.S. GDP, from share_of_us_gdp. world_balance_data computes them for one year and one version of the table.

def world_balance_data(year, vintage, countries):
    """The two bars of Fig. 3 for each chosen country, in one year.

    Fig. 3:  100 NX / Y, and the same as a share of U.S. GDP, 100 NX / Y_US

    Arguments
        year      : the year
        vintage   : "PWT 11.0" or "PWT 10.01", the version of the table
        countries : the chosen countries
    Returns
        year    : the year shown (PWT 10.01 ends in 2019)
        bars    : one row per country: the trade balance as a percent of its own
                  GDP and as a percent of U.S. GDP
        missing : the chosen countries without data
    """
    # Step 1: the table of that version, and the year (PWT 10.01 ends in 2019)
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    year = min(year, source[source.vintage == vintage].year.max())
    rows = source[(source.year == year) & (source.vintage == vintage)]
    rows = rows.set_index("country")
    # Step 2: the chosen countries with data, the textbook's first
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG3, rows.index)
    one = rows.loc[order]
    # Step 3: the two bars: a share of own GDP, and a share of U.S. GDP
    bars = pd.DataFrame({
        "Share of own GDP": one.trade_balance,
        "Share of U.S. GDP": share_of_us_gdp(
            one.trade_balance, one.cgdpo, rows.loc["U.S.", "cgdpo"]
        ),
    })
    return year, bars, missing



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, the title
def world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing):
    """The title of Fig. 3: the U.S. deficit and the largest surplus.

    The surplus in percent of U.S. GDP; a note instead when a chosen country has no
    data.

    Arguments
        year    : the year shown
        vintage : the version of the Penn World Table
        bars    : the two bars of each country (world_balance_data)
        missing : the chosen countries without data
    Returns
        the title, a text
    """
    # Step 1: a note when some chosen country has no data, or none is chosen
    if missing:
        return f"{year}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])
    if len(bars) == 0:
        return "Choose at least one country"
    # Step 2: the year and the U.S. deficit, in percent of U.S. GDP
    text = f"{year} ({vintage}): "
    if "U.S." in bars.index:
        text += f"U.S. deficit {-bars.loc['U.S.', 'Share of own GDP']:.1f}% of GDP; "
    # the country with the largest balance in percent of U.S. GDP; + 0.0 turns
    # -0.0 into 0.0
    top = bars["Share of U.S. GDP"].idxmax()
    value = round(bars.loc[top, "Share of U.S. GDP"], 2) + 0.0
    # Step 3: a surplus if the largest balance is positive, else a deficit
    if value > 0:
        return text + f"largest surplus {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"
    return text + f"smallest deficit {top}, {value:.2f}% of U.S. GDP"




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, the trade balance around the world
def world_balance_chart(year=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG3):
    """The trade balance as a share of own GDP and of U.S. GDP, in one year.

    Draws Fig. 3 (inspired by Fig. 19.3 in Jones).

    Arguments
        year      : the year
        vintage   : "PWT 11.0" or "PWT 10.01", the version of the table
        countries : the countries to show
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the two bars of each country (world_balance_data)
    year, bars, missing = world_balance_data(year, vintage, countries)

    # Step 2: `.melt(id_vars="country")` turns the two measure columns into rows,
    # one row per country and measure: the long shape that `px.bar` needs
    long = bars.reset_index().melt(
        id_vars="country",
        var_name="Measure",
        value_name="Percent",
    )

    # Step 3: with `color="Measure"` and `barmode="group"`, the two bars of each
    # country stand side by side
    fig = px.bar(
        long,
        x="country",
        y="Percent",
        color="Measure",
        barmode="group",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map={"Share of own GDP": BLUE, "Share of U.S. GDP": GREEN},
        labels={"country": "", "Percent": "Percent"},
        title=world_title(year, vintage, bars, missing),
    )
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)

    # Step 4: the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    book = fit_range(long.Percent, [-9, 12.5])
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(
            range=book,
            tickvals=[-8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12],
        )
    fig.update_layout(
        legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", title="")
    )
    return fig

The world as a whole cannot run a deficit, so the surpluses of a few large economies (China, Germany, the Netherlands, the oil exporters) must offset many deficits. In the PWT data they do not offset them exactly: measured in U.S. GDP, the balances of all 185 economies add up to +3.9 percent in 2023, a reminder that trade statistics have errors.
Hover over a small island economy: some PWT balances are extreme, beyond −60 percent of GDP, because their consumption and investment shares are very large and poorly measured. The color scale stops at ±20 percent so that these few values do not wash out the rest of the map.

19.4 Trade and growth around the world
Should fast-growing countries borrow from abroad to invest? Here we check whether the fastest growers really run trade deficits.

Fig. 4: The trade balance in rapidly growing countries
Goal. Test whether fast-growing countries borrow from abroad, as consumption smoothing predicts.
A country that expects to be much richer tomorrow should borrow today, like a student who expects a high income later: it should run trade deficits. The textbook checks this for five fast-growing economies. Each bar is the simple average of the yearly trade balance over a window of years. We first make a table with one row per year and one column per country, so that period_average gives one average per country.

# The textbook's five fast-growing economies, and their rows of both PWT versions
FIG4 = ["China", "India", "Singapore", "Ireland", "S. Korea"]
fast = pwt[pwt.country.isin(FIG4)]


def fast_growers_data(start, end, vintage, countries):
    """The bars of Fig. 4: each economy's average trade balance over a window.

    Fig. 4:  the average of 100 NX / Y from start to end (period_average)

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year of the window
        vintage    : "PWT 11.0" or "PWT 10.01", the version of the table
        countries  : the chosen economies
    Returns
        end     : the last year used (PWT 10.01 ends in 2019)
        avg     : each economy's average trade balance, percent of own GDP
        missing : the chosen economies without data
    """
    # Step 1: one row per year and one column per country, with `.pivot(...)`
    source = pwt_world if vintage == "PWT 11.0" else pwt
    wide = source[source.vintage == vintage].pivot(
        index="year",
        columns="country",
        values="trade_balance",
    )
    end = min(end, wide.index.max())                 # PWT 10.01 ends in 2019
    # Step 2: the chosen economies, the textbook's first: `wide[order]` keeps
    # their columns in that order, and period_average gives one average each
    order, missing = book_order(countries, FIG4, wide.columns)
    avg = period_average(wide[order], start, end)
    return end, avg, missing



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, the trade balance in rapidly growing countries
def fast_growers_chart(start=2000, end=2023, vintage="PWT 11.0", countries=FIG4):
    """The average trade balance (percent of own GDP) of fast-growing economies.

    Draws Fig. 4 (inspired by Fig. 19.4 in Jones), for the textbook's five or any
    chosen economies.

    Arguments
        start, end : the first and the last year of the averages
        vintage    : "PWT 11.0" or "PWT 10.01", the version of the table
        countries  : the economies to show
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the averages (fast_growers_data), and the title
    end, avg, missing = fast_growers_data(start, end, vintage, countries)
    bars = avg.rename("average").reset_index()
    title = (
        f"{start}–{end} ({vintage}): {(avg > 0).sum()} of {len(avg)} economies "
        "ran trade surpluses on average"
    )
    if missing:
        title = f"{start}–{end}: no {vintage} data for " + ", ".join(missing[:3])

    # Step 2: one bar per economy; `text_auto=".1f"` writes each bar's value, with
    # one decimal, on the bar
    fig = px.bar(
        bars,
        x="country",
        y="average",
        text_auto=".1f",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN],
        labels={"country": "", "average": "Percent of own GDP"},
        title=title,
    )
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)

    # Step 3: the textbook's range, unless a bar does not fit
    book = fit_range(avg.dropna(), [-5, 30])
    if book:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=book, tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30])
    return fig

What to notice.

With one exception, India, these fast-growing economies run trade surpluses, not deficits. They lend to the rest of the world instead of borrowing from it.
This is the opposite of what consumption smoothing (the permanent-income idea of Chapter 16) predicts. The textbook suggests that the causality may run the other way: countries that push their firms to export may grow faster.
Singapore’s and Ireland’s averages are very sensitive to the window. Move the first year back to 1990: Singapore’s average falls from 19.3 to 10.6 percent. The next subsection shows why.


Look at your data: an average can hide big swings
We draw the yearly balances behind the averages, in PWT 11.0, and find the lowest and the highest of them.

Two series behave strangely. Singapore’s balance jumps from −33 percent of GDP in 1993 to +15 percent in 1998. Singapore is a trading hub: in the Penn World Table its exports and its imports were each about two to three times its GDP in the mid-1990s, so its trade balance is a small difference between two huge numbers, and a small error in either one moves it a lot. Ireland’s balance swings from 32 percent of GDP in 2018 to 7 percent in 2019 and 50 percent in 2022: large multinational firms book much of their production and profits in Ireland, which moves its GDP and trade statistics far more than Irish living standards. Neither country’s data are “wrong”, but a single average hides all this, and it changes a lot with the choice of years. That is why the figure lets you choose the window.

Beyond the textbook’s five: do fast-growing economies borrow?
The textbook picked five fast-growing economies. A fairer test uses every economy: does faster growth go with smaller trade balances (borrowing), as consumption smoothing predicts? We measure growth of real GDP per person, rgdpna / pop, from 2000 to 2023, and the average trade balance over the same years.

def growth_rate(y, start, end):
    """The average annual growth rate between two years, in percent.

    The growth formula of Chapter 3:  100 ln(y_end / y_start) / (end - start)

    Arguments
        y          : a table whose rows are years (here one column per economy)
        start, end : the first and the last year
    Returns
        the average annual growth rate of each column, in percent
    """
    # `np.log` is the natural logarithm; the formula works on every column of the
    # wide table at once
    return 100 * np.log(y.loc[end] / y.loc[start]) / (end - start)


# Step 1: real GDP per person, then one row per year and one column per economy

balance = pwt_world.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="trade_balance")

# Step 2: growth and the average trade balance, 2000-2023, in one table;
# `.dropna()` drops the economies that miss either one
growers = pd.DataFrame({
    "growth": growth_rate(income, 2000, 2023),
    "trade_balance": period_average(balance, 2000, 2023),

What to notice.

Across all economies the fitted line slopes down: economies that grew faster ran smaller trade balances on average, as consumption smoothing predicts. But the link is weak (a correlation of about −0.2), and many fast growers sit on both sides of zero.

19.5 The twin deficits
The identity \(NX = S - I\) links the trade balance to saving. This section compares the U.S. budget deficit, investment and the trade deficit over time.

Fig. 5: U.S. investment, budget deficit, and trade deficit
Goal. See the twin deficits: large budget deficits that come with large trade deficits.
Equation (4) says \(NX = S - I\): a country that saves less than it invests must borrow the difference abroad. When the government runs a larger budget deficit, government saving \(T - G\) falls, and so does domestic saving \(S\). Either investment falls too, or foreigners fill the gap and the trade deficit grows. The file has the three series of the textbook’s figure, as percent of GDP.

The trade deficit is minus the trade balance, so \(NX = -\)(trade deficit). With our function domestic_saving we add a fourth line, domestic saving \(S = I + NX\). The gap between saving and investment is then exactly the trade deficit.

# Step 1: readable column names, which then appear in the legend;
# `.rename(columns={...})` renames the columns

# Step 2: domestic saving S = I + NX, equation (4), with NX = -(trade deficit)

The menu chooses an episode with a rising budget deficit. episode_change computes how much each line changed between the first and the last year of the episode, and the title of the figure reports it.

# The episodes of the menu, each with its first and last year
EPISODES = {
    "1980s: 1979 to 1986": (1979, 1986),
    "2000s: 2000 to 2006": (2000, 2006),
    "Great Recession: 2007 to 2010": (2007, 2010),
    "Covid-19: 2019 to 2021": (2019, 2021),
}
# the four lines of the figure
LINES = ["Investment", "Budget deficit", "Trade deficit", "Domestic saving, S = I + NX"]


def episode_change(episode):
    """The change of each line of Fig. 5 over one episode, in points of GDP.

    Fig. 5:  the value in the last year minus the value in the first year

    Arguments
        episode : a key of EPISODES
    Returns
        start, end : the first and the last year of the episode
        change     : the change of each column of `named`, in points of GDP
    """
    start, end = EPISODES[episode]
    # `named.loc[end] - named.loc[start]` subtracts two rows, column by column
    change = named.loc[end] - named.loc[start]
    return start, end, change



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, U.S. investment, budget deficit and trade deficit
def twin_deficits_chart(episode="1980s: 1979 to 1986"):
    """Investment, the budget deficit and the trade deficit, percent of GDP.

    Draws Fig. 5 (inspired by Fig. 19.5 in Jones), with one episode shaded.

    Arguments
        episode : a key of EPISODES, the episode to shade
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the changes over the episode (episode_change)
    start, end, change = episode_change(episode)

    # Step 2: the four lines; the title reports the changes
    fig = px.line(
        named.reset_index(),
        x="year",
        y=LINES,
        color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, BLUE, GREEN, GRAY],
        labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP"},
        title=(
            f"{start}→{end}: budget deficit {change['Budget deficit']:+.1f}, "
            f"trade deficit {change['Trade deficit']:+.1f}, "
            f"investment {change['Investment']:+.1f} points"
        ),
    )
    # thick lines, and domestic saving thinner and dotted
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name=LINES[3]), line_width=2, line_dash="dot")

    # Step 3: the zero line, the shaded episode and the axes
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.2, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1958, 2027])
    # room above the lines for the legend
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-5, 28], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25])
    fig.update_layout(
        legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"),
        legend_title_text="",
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

From 1979 to 1986 the budget deficit rose by 2.9 points of GDP and the trade deficit by 2.0 points; investment fell by 2.0 points, but it stayed high by historical standards. Foreign saving paid for part of the government’s borrowing: the first episode of twin deficits.
From 2000 to 2006 the pattern repeats: the budget deficit rose by 3.2 points and the trade deficit by 2.0 points, while investment hardly changed (−0.3).
In the Great Recession the twins split: the budget deficit soared, investment collapsed, and the trade deficit fell. In the Covid-19 years the budget deficit jumped by more than 7 points, the trade deficit rose by less than 1 point, and investment barely moved. Compared with the 1970s, the 1980s had higher budget deficits (4.0 against 3.5 percent of GDP) and much higher trade deficits (1.75 against 0.18), with no fall in investment (18.5 against 18.0). Domestic saving has drifted down, from about 17 percent of GDP in the 1960s and 1970s to 13–15 percent since 2000, and the trade deficit has filled the gap.


Beyond the United States: twin deficits in other countries
Did large budget deficits come with large trade deficits elsewhere too? The file twin_deficits_world.csv has the three lines of Fig. 19.5 for most economies, as percent of GDP, from 1980 to 2025:

investment: gross capital formation (World Bank WDI NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS). It includes government investment, so it is higher than the private investment of Fig. 5;
budget_deficit: minus the net lending of the general government, federal plus state and local (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026, GGXCNL_NGDP; the last year or two are IMF estimates). For the United States the IMF series starts only in 2001;
trade_deficit: minus the WDI trade balance of Figs. 1 and 2.

The trade deficits agree within 0.1 point, but total investment is about 4 points higher than private investment, and the general-government deficit is about 1 point higher than the federal one. twin_deficits_data keeps the three lines of one economy and computes the correlation of its two deficits, a number between −1 and +1 that is positive when they rise and fall together. The figure draws the lines, and its title reports the correlation.

# Step 1: readable names for the three lines
WORLD_LINES = {
    "investment": "Investment",
    "budget_deficit": "Budget deficit",
    "trade_deficit": "Trade deficit",
}
# Step 2: the economies with both deficits in at least 5 years, for the menu
counts = twin_world.dropna(subset=["budget_deficit", "trade_deficit"])
counts = counts.groupby("country").year.count()
TWIN_COUNTRIES = sorted(counts[counts >= 5].index)


def twin_deficits_data(country):
    """The three lines of Fig. 5 for one economy, and the correlation of its deficits.

    Fig. 5:  r = the correlation of the budget and the trade deficit

    Arguments
        country : the economy
    Returns
        one  : its rows of `twin_world`, with readable column names
        both : the rows of the years with both deficits
        r    : the correlation of the two deficits, rounded to two decimals
    """
    # Step 1: the economy's rows, and the years that have both deficits
    one = twin_world[twin_world.country == country].rename(columns=WORLD_LINES)
    both = one.dropna(subset=["Budget deficit", "Trade deficit"])
    # Step 2: the correlation of the two columns; + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
    r = round(both["Budget deficit"].corr(both["Trade deficit"]), 2) + 0.0
    return one, both, r



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5 for any economy
def twin_deficits_world(country="U.S."):
    """Investment, the budget deficit and the trade deficit, percent of GDP.

    Draws Fig. 5 (inspired by Fig. 19.5 in Jones) for any economy.

    Arguments
        country : the economy
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data and the correlation (twin_deficits_data)
    one, both, r = twin_deficits_data(country)

    # Step 2: the three lines; the title reports the correlation
    fig = px.line(
        one,
        x="year",
        y=list(WORLD_LINES.values()),
        color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, BLUE, GREEN],
        labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP"},
        title=(
            f"{country}, {both.year.min()}–{both.year.max()}: correlation of the "
            f"budget and trade deficits {r:+.2f}"
        ),
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)

    # Step 3: the axes. `.stack()` puts all the columns of a table into one long
    # column, so that fit_range sees every value of the three lines
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1975, 2027])         # 1980 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(
        range=fit_range(one[list(WORLD_LINES.values())].stack(), [-5, 28])
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0, y=-0.15, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"),
        legend_title_text="",
    )
    return fig

19.6 Net foreign assets and foreign debt
Years of trade deficits add up to a debt to the rest of the world. We measure that debt for the United States and for every other economy.

Fig. 6: Net international investment position of the United States
Goal. Follow how decades of trade deficits turned the United States from a lender into a debtor.
The net international investment position (NIIP) is what U.S. residents own abroad (foreign shares, bonds, factories) minus what foreigners own in the United States, at the end of each year. When it is negative, it is the net foreign debt. Each year’s trade deficit is new borrowing, so the position should fall by about the size of the deficit. With our function accumulate, we start from the 1976 position and add the trade balance of every later year, as in the Oddtopia table. We also compare the current data with the same series as published in July 2023, which the textbook used.

    "As published in July 2023 (the textbook)": share_of_gdp(

    "1976 position + sum of later trade balances": share_of_gdp(

What to notice.

Until 1988 the United States was a net creditor: it owned more abroad than foreigners owned in the United States. Since 1989 it has been a net debtor, and its net foreign debt has grown to about 70 percent of GDP.
The dotted line adds up the trade balances since 1976. It has the same downward trend: the foreign debt is, roughly, the sum of past trade deficits. But the gap between the two lines is large in some years (37 points of GDP in 2010), because the position also changes when asset prices and the dollar move, and with the income earned on foreign assets. Until 2020 these effects kept the debt below the summed deficits; in 2021 and since 2023 it is above them.
The textbook’s data (dashed) show a trough of about −80 percent in 2021. BEA has since revised the series: the current data are 9 to 16 points of GDP less negative for 2020–2022, and the deepest point is now 2024.


Key numbers: the foreign debt
The textbook says that the United States was a net creditor “up until the late 1980s” and that its net foreign debt “exceeded 60 percent of GDP in 2022”.

# Step 1: the last year as a net creditor, and 2022 in both vintages

)

)

    f"sum of trade balances {summed / 1000:+.1f} trillion"

In the textbook’s vintage the net foreign debt was 63.5 percent of GDP in 2022, as the text says. In the current data it is 54.6 percent for 2022, because BEA has revised the position upward by 1.9 to 3.4 trillion dollars for 2020–2022. The statement still holds for the most recent years: the debt is above 60 percent of GDP in 2021 and in 2023–2025. Over the whole period, trade deficits of 18.0 trillion dollars came with a fall of 22.0 trillion in the investment position.


Beyond the United States: creditors and debtors around the world
The BEA measures only the U.S. position. For other countries, economists use the External Wealth of Nations database of Philip Lane and Gian Maria Milesi-Ferretti (Brookings, release of February 2026), which collects and completes the official investment positions of about 200 economies. niip_world_data keeps the rows of the chosen economies and finds each one’s latest position, which the title of the figure reports.

def niip_world_data(countries):
    """The data of Fig. 6 for any economies, and the latest position of each.

    The net international investment position: foreign assets minus foreign
    liabilities, percent of GDP (External Wealth of Nations).

    Arguments
        countries : the economies to show
    Returns
        rows   : the chosen economies' rows of `niip_world`
        latest : each economy's position in its latest year, percent of GDP
    """
    rows = niip_world[niip_world.country.isin(countries)]
    # each economy's last row: its latest year
    latest = rows.groupby("country").last().niip
    return rows, latest

    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(rows.niip, [-100, 30]))
