title: 19. International Trade
text:
19.7 Concluding remarks

Trade has become much more important: U.S. exports and imports have risen from about 4 percent of GDP each in 1950 to 11 and 14 percent. Since 1976 imports have exceeded exports every year, and the trade deficit reached 5.7 percent of GDP in 2006.
The national income identity shows what a deficit means. With \(NX < 0\), a country uses more than it produces (equation 1), and it invests more than it saves, \(NX = S - I\) (equation 4). The deficit is borrowing from the rest of the world, and past deficits add up to the net foreign debt (equation 5), about 70 percent of U.S. GDP today. In present value, trade has to balance over time (equation 6), and a steady deficit leads to a stable debt ratio only if GDP grows faster than the return on the debt (equation 7).
Trade can make everyone better off: across time it shares risks (Oddtopia and Eventopia), and across goods it lets countries specialize by comparative advantage. In the North–South model the world price of equation (10) lies between the two autarky prices of equation (9), condition (11), and each country gains in the good it imports. Free migration follows absolute advantage and raises world output even more.
The data hold surprises: the textbook’s fast-growing economies run surpluses, not deficits, and the large U.S. budget deficits of the 1980s and 2000s came with large trade deficits (the twin deficits). Looking beyond the textbook’s countries changes both stories: across all economies, faster growth goes with slightly smaller trade balances, and the twin deficits are clear in some countries (Germany, Greece) but not in others.
The data also teach care: the textbook’s “2019” bars are 2017 data, revisions changed the recent U.S. foreign debt by up to 16 points of GDP, and two sources for the same country can differ by vintage and definition.
The next chapter, exchange rates and international finance, brings trade into the short-run model and asks how the exchange rate adjusts.

title: 19. International Trade
text:
Practice problems
These problems let you use the chapter’s tools in three ways: conceptual problems apply the identities and the trade models to real cases, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data, and modeling problems use small calculators built on the Model overview to answer policy questions. On average Japan earned about 3.1 percent of GDP a year from abroad, more than enough to pay for its trade deficits. (The data’s current account also counts transfers such as aid and remittances, which the model leaves out, so these gaps are the income from foreign assets plus net transfers.)
(b) Divide the income by the assets at the start of the year:
\[\bar{r} \approx \frac{\bar{r}F_{2010}}{F_{2010}} = \frac{2.74}{54.7} = 0.050,\]
a return of about 5 percent a year. That is high for a safe investment. The reason is that the income is earned on gross positions, which are much larger than the net one: if what Japan owns abroad earns more than what it owes foreigners costs, the return on the net position looks high.
(c) Equation (5) says \(F_t - F_{t-1} = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} = CA_t\): net foreign assets grow by the current account, not by the trade balance. From 2011 to 2015 Japan’s trade balances add up to \(-0.64 - 1.63 - 2.38 - 2.55 - 0.54 = -7.74\) percent of a year’s GDP, but its current accounts add up to \(2.1 + 0.9 + 0.9 + 0.7 + 3.0 = 7.6\) percent, so its claims on the rest of the world kept growing. The data show a rise of \(61.1 - 54.7 = 6.4\) points; the rest of the difference comes from changes in asset prices, in the yen and in GDP. A creditor can run trade deficits for as long as they are smaller than its income from abroad. A debtor is in the opposite position: its interest payments make its current account weaker than its trade balance.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Norway’s oil fund and the spend-only-the-return rule. Norway puts its government’s oil and gas revenue into the Government Pension Fund Global, which invests abroad. A fiscal rule says that, over time, the government may spend only the fund’s expected real return, now estimated at 3 percent a year, and never its capital. At the end of 2025 the fund was worth about NOK 21,300 billion, almost four times Norway’s GDP (norskpetroleum.no, run by Norway’s Ministry of Energy and its Offshore Directorate). In our data, Norway’s net foreign assets were 358 percent of GDP at the end of 2024 (the file of Fig. 6), and its trade surplus averaged 12.2 percent of GDP from 2000 to 2024 (the file of Fig. 2).
Take a stylized Norway whose foreign assets \(F\) earn a real return of \(\bar{r} = 0.03\).

Suppose that, once the oil runs out, Norway runs a trade deficit equal to the return on its assets in every year, \(NX_t = -\bar{r}F_{t-1}\). Show with equation (5) that its foreign assets then never change. What is its current account?
Show that this plan satisfies the intertemporal budget constraint, equation (6), for a creditor with \(F_0 > 0\), as the horizon \(T\) goes to infinity. You may use \(\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} 1/(1+\bar{r})^t = 1/\bar{r}\).
Now measure the assets relative to GDP, \(f = F/Y = 3.58\). With no growth of GDP, how large a trade deficit, in percent of GDP, does the rule allow? With real GDP growth of \(\bar{g} = 0.02\), which constant trade balance keeps \(f\) at 3.58? Why does growth lower the deficit that Norway can afford?



Hint

For (a), put the trade balance into \(F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} + NX_t\). For (b), take the constant \(\bar{r}F_0\) out of the sum. For (c), use the ratio form of equation (5) from the Model overview, \(f_t = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx_t\), set \(f_t = f_{t-1}\) and solve for \(nx\). A real return together with real growth is fine here: the ratio \(F/Y\) is the same in real and in nominal terms.

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Substitute \(NX_t = -\bar{r}F_{t-1}\) into equation (5):
\[F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} - \bar{r}F_{t-1} = F_{t-1}.\]
The assets stay at \(F_0\) forever. The current account is \(CA_t = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} = -\bar{r}F_{t-1} +
\bar{r}F_{t-1} = 0\): the return pays for the extra imports, and nothing is added to or taken from the fund.
(b) With \(NX_t = -\bar{r}F_0\) in every year,
\[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = -\bar{r}F_0\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1 + \bar{r})^t}
= -\bar{r}F_0 \times \frac{1}{\bar{r}} = -F_0,\]
which is equation (6). The end term of the derivation also vanishes, as it must: \(F_T/(1 + \bar{r})^T =
F_0/(1 + \bar{r})^T\) goes to zero as \(T\) grows. For a creditor, equation (6) reads the other way round than for a debtor: the present value of its trade balances is negative, so it can run trade deficits forever.
(c) With no growth, \(nx = -\bar{r}f = -0.03 \times 3.58 = -0.107\): a deficit of 10.7 percent of GDP in every year. With growth, setting \(f_t = f_{t-1} = f\) gives
\[f = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f + nx \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
nx = f\left(1 - \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\right) = -\frac{(\bar{r} - \bar{g})\,f}{1 + \bar{g}}
= -\frac{0.01 \times 3.58}{1.02} = -0.035.\]
The rule now allows a deficit of only 3.5 percent of GDP. The return is worth \(0.03 \times 3.58/1.02 = 0.105\), or 10.5 percent of this year’s GDP, but \(0.02 \times 3.58/1.02 = 0.070\), or 7.0 points of it, must be invested abroad again, so that the fund keeps up with a growing economy. Today Norway is still far from that stage: it runs trade surpluses (12.2 percent of GDP on average since 2000), because each year it turns more oil and gas into foreign assets.

Customs duties collected rose from 84 billion dollars in 2024 to 269 billion in 2025, or from 0.284 to 0.871 percent of GDP (BEA, Customs duties (B235RC1Q027SBEA), via FRED, annual averages of the quarterly data). Write the trade balance as in Step 5 of the saving–investment block, \(NX = (Y - T - C - I) + (T - G)\). Suppose the extra customs revenue had raised government saving \(T - G\) one for one, while private saving and investment stayed the same. By how much would the trade deficit have fallen?
Now use the table. By how much did private saving minus investment, \(Y - T - C - I\), change from 2024 to 2025, according to the identity? What does that imply for private saving itself? (The budget deficit here is the federal one, so treat state and local governments as part of the private term.)
Many economists argue that a tariff can lower the trade deficit only if it raises national saving or lowers investment. Explain this argument with equation (4). Give two reasons why private saving might fall when tariffs rise. Is one year of data enough to judge the policy?



Hint

For (a), the change in customs revenue, in points of GDP, goes one for one into \(NX\). For (b), solve the identity for the private term, \(Y - T - C - I = NX - (T - G) = \text{budget deficit} - \text{trade deficit}\), compute it for both years, and add back the change in investment. For (c), think about who pays a tariff and how they react, and recall that \(NX = EX - IM\): if \(S - I\) does not move, what must happen to exports when imports fall?

Your answer:


Solution

(a) Customs duties rose by \(0.871 - 0.284 = 0.587\), about 0.59 points of GDP. With the private term fixed, \(\Delta NX = \Delta(T - G) = +0.59\), so the trade deficit would have fallen from 3.00 to about 2.41 percent of GDP.
(b) The private term is the budget deficit minus the trade deficit:
\[2024:\; 6.474 - 3.000 = 3.474, \qquad 2025:\; 5.761 - 2.985 = 2.776, \qquad \text{change} = -0.698.\]
Private saving minus investment fell by about 0.70 points of GDP. Investment changed by \(18.007 - 18.060 = -0.053\), so private saving itself fell by about \(0.698 + 0.053 = 0.75\) points. In 2025 the federal government saved more (its deficit fell by 0.71 points, in part thanks to the tariffs), the private sector saved less by about the same amount, and the trade deficit hardly moved.
(c) Equation (4), \(NX = S - I\), holds whatever the tariff. Tariffs make imports dearer and may reduce them, but if national saving and investment do not change, net exports cannot change either: exports must then fall by about as much as imports. Possible channels are retaliation by other countries, a stronger dollar (Chapter 20), and imported parts that make U.S. exports dearer. Two reasons why private saving may fall:

A tariff is a tax, paid by importers and, through higher prices, by households. If households keep their consumption smooth (Chapter 16), they pay it by saving less, and the rise in government saving is then offset one for one.
Firms that absorb part of the tariff earn smaller profits, so business saving falls.

One year is not enough to judge. Many things change at once, and the timing of trade was distorted: in the first quarter of 2025, net exports fell to −1,215 billion dollars at an annual rate, from −944 billion in the last quarter of 2024 (BEA, Net exports of goods and services (NETEXP), via FRED), a jump that suggests importers bought ahead of the tariffs. A fair test compares several years with what saving and investment would have done without the tariffs.

Problem 4 (Basic): Mexico’s opening after NAFTA. The North American Free Trade Agreement between Canada, Mexico and the United States entered into force on January 1, 1994, and its tariff cuts were phased in until 2008 (Office of the U.S. Trade Representative). Use the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, exports and imports of goods and services in percent of GDP, in the file wdi_trade.csv of Fig. 1.

Compute Mexico’s openness, exports plus imports in percent of GDP, in 1993 and in 2024. By what factor did it grow?
In which year was Mexico’s openness highest, and how high was it?
Compute the openness of Canada and of the United States in 1993 and in 2024. Which of the three economies is the most open today?



Hint

Read the file with trade = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv") and keep one country with trade[trade.country == "Mexico"].set_index("year"). The sum of its exports and imports columns is a Series with the years as labels: .loc[[1993, 2024]] picks two years, and .idxmax() gives the year of the largest value. A loop over ["Canada", "U.S."] repeats the steps for the other two.

Solution

Add the two shares, pick the years, and repeat for the neighbors:
trade = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")
mexico = trade[trade.country == "Mexico"].set_index("year")
open_mexico = mexico.exports + mexico.imports
print(open_mexico.loc[[1993, 2024]].round(1).to_dict())
print(f"Growth factor: {open_mexico[2024] / open_mexico[1993]:.1f}")
print(f"Highest: {open_mexico.max():.1f}% of GDP in {open_mexico.idxmax()}")
for name in ["Canada", "U.S."]:
    one = trade[trade.country == name].set_index("year")
    print(name, (one.exports + one.imports).loc[[1993, 2024]].round(1).to_dict())
It prints {1993: 26.2, 2024: 75.4}, a growth factor of 2.9, a peak of 88.8 percent of GDP in 2022, then Canada {1993: 58.2, 2024: 65.1} and U.S. {1993: 20.0, 2024: 25.0}.
Mexico’s openness almost tripled, and Mexico is now the most open of the three economies. Canada was already open in 1993 (it had had a free trade agreement with the United States since 1989, as the USTR page explains), and the United States remains one of the least open economies in the world. A word of caution: Mexico’s openness jumped by 14.5 points from 1994 to 1995 (from 29.15 to 43.67 percent of GDP), far faster than tariff cuts phased in over 14 years could explain. Other forces move these shares too, such as the exchange rate (Chapter 20). The data show that Mexico opened up after NAFTA; by themselves they do not tell how much of the opening NAFTA caused.

open_2023 = trade[trade.year == 2023].copy()

print(f"Correlation with log population: {log_open.corr(np.log(merged['pop'])):.2f}")

print(f"Median openness: {largest.openness.median():.1f}% for the 15 most populous, {merged.openness.median():.1f}% for all")

It prints 156 economies, correlations of −0.18 with log GDP and −0.50 with log population, and medians of 41.3 percent for the 15 most populous economies against 79.0 percent for all of them. In the list, every large economy but one has an openness between 20.6 percent (Ethiopia) and 86.7 percent (DR Congo); the United States, at 24.9 percent, is the second lowest.
The claim holds, and it holds much more clearly for population than for GDP. GDP mixes two things: the number of people, which sets how much trade can take place inside the borders, and income per person, which has little to do with that. Several small, rich economies are trading hubs with extreme openness, such as Singapore (about 324 percent) and Ireland (about 240 percent) in 2023, and they blur the link between GDP and openness. The big exception among the 15 is Vietnam: with 100.4 million people, its openness is 165.0 percent, because its exports alone were 86.7 percent of GDP. Size makes trade less likely to be large, but it does not rule it out.

Modeling problems
Problem 7 (Basic): Paying for a hurricane. A hypothetical island economy is hit by a hurricane. To rebuild, it runs trade deficits of 5 percent of GDP for 3 years, borrowing abroad at the interest rate \(\bar{r}\), and then repays with equal trade surpluses over the next 10 years. It has no foreign assets before the storm, \(F_0 = 0\), and its GDP stays constant, so everything can be measured in percent of GDP. The calculator below applies equation (5) year by year and picks the surplus that satisfies equation (6). Answer with its sliders.

If the loans are free of interest, \(\bar{r} = 0\), how large must each surplus be? Check it with equation (6).
If the island borrows at a market rate of 4 percent, how large is each surplus, and how large is the debt when the rebuilding ends?
A development bank offers a loan at 1 percent instead. How much smaller is each year’s surplus than at 4 percent, and how much less does the island hand over in total during the 10 years?



Hint

Read the title of the calculator for each interest rate. To check by hand: with \(\bar{r} = 0\), equation (6) says that the trade balances add up to zero. With \(\bar{r} > 0\), find the debt after the 3 years of deficits with equation (5), then pick the surplus \(S\) whose present value over 10 years equals that debt: \(S\sum_{j=1}^{10} 1/(1+\bar{r})^j = \text{debt}\).


def repayment_plan(deficit=5.0, years=3, r=0.0, repay_years=10):
    """Equations (5) and (6): trade deficits for some years, then equal surpluses that repay the debt (% of GDP)."""
    pv = 0.0
    for j in range(1, repay_years + 1):
        pv = pv + 1 / (1 + r / 100) ** j                       # present value of 1 a year (Appendix C.12)
    F, flows, assets = 0.0, [], []
    for t in range(1, years + repay_years + 1):
        nx = -deficit if t <= years else -assets[years - 1] / pv   # equation (6): the surpluses repay the debt
        F = (1 + r / 100) * F + nx                             # equation (5)
        flows.append(nx)
        assets.append(F)
    year = list(range(1, years + repay_years + 1))
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=year, y=flows, name="Trade balance, NX", marker_color=TEAL))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=year, y=assets, mode="lines+markers", name="Net foreign assets, F",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Surplus needed: {flows[-1]:.2f}% of GDP a year; peak debt {-assets[years - 1]:.1f}% of GDP",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Years after the storm", range=[0.3, 15.7]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Percent of GDP", range=[-60, 12]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.03, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))
    return fig


interact(repayment_plan,
         deficit=FloatSlider(value=5.0, min=1.0, max=10.0, step=1.0, description="deficit, % of GDP", style=WIDE),
         years=IntSlider(value=3, min=1, max=5, step=1, description="years of deficits", style=WIDE),
         r=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="interest rate r, %", style=WIDE),
         repay_years=fixed(10));

Source. A calculator built on the accounting for net foreign assets in the Model overview, equations (5) and (6), adapted from the discussion of trade across time in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Solution

(a) With \(\bar{r} = 0\) the island owes \(3 \times 5 = 15\) percent of GDP after the rebuilding, and equation (6) with \(F_0 = 0\) says that the trade balances must add up to zero: \(3 \times (-5) + 10\,S = 0\), so \(S = 1.5\) percent of GDP a year. The calculator’s title reads “Surplus needed: 1.50% of GDP a year; peak debt 15.0% of GDP”.
(b) With interest, the debt grows during the rebuilding. By equation (5), the debt after 3 years is
\[5\,(1.04)^2 + 5\,(1.04) + 5 = 15.61\]
percent of GDP. The surplus must have a present value equal to that debt: \(S \times 8.111 = 15.61\), where \(8.111 = \sum_{j=1}^{10} 1/1.04^j\), so \(S = 1.92\) percent of GDP a year.
(c) At 1 percent the debt is 15.15 percent of GDP and the surplus 1.60 percent a year, 0.32 points less than at 4 percent. Over 10 years the island hands over 16.00 percent of a year’s GDP instead of 19.24 percent: the cheaper loan saves it about 3.2 percent of a year’s output. The code below confirms the numbers:
for rate in [0.0, 0.04, 0.01]:
    debt, pv = 0.0, 0.0
    for k in range(3):
        debt = (1 + rate) * debt + 5                     # equation (5), for the debt
    for j in range(1, 11):
        pv = pv + 1 / (1 + rate) ** j
    surplus = debt / pv                                  # equation (6)
    print(f"r = {rate:.0%}: debt {debt:.2f}% of GDP, surplus {surplus:.2f}% a year, {10 * surplus:.2f}% in total")
print(repayment_plan(5.0, 3, 4.0, 10).layout.title.text)
It prints r = 0%: debt 15.00% of GDP, surplus 1.50% a year, 15.00% in total, then 15.61, 1.92 and 19.24 for 4 percent, 15.15, 1.60 and 16.00 for 1 percent, and the calculator’s title for 4 percent. The lesson of equation (6) is that every deficit is repaid by later surpluses; the interest rate decides how large they must be.

Problem 8 (Intermediate): How much foreign debt can the United States carry? The net foreign debt of the United States was 70.9 percent of GDP at the end of 2025 (Fig. 6), and its trade deficit has been about 3 percent of GDP for years. The calculator starts from the 2025 position and applies the ratio form of equation (5), \(f_t = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx\), for 100 years with a constant trade balance. The dashed line is the long-run ratio \(f^*\) of equation (7). Here \(\bar{g}\) is the growth rate of nominal GDP and \(\bar{r}\) the net return that foreigners earn on the debt. Answer with the sliders.

With \(nx = -3\), \(\bar{g} = 4\) and \(\bar{r} = 0\) percent, does the debt ratio rise or fall from its 2025 level, and where does it settle? Which constant trade balance would hold the ratio at its 2025 level?
A policy committee wants the net foreign debt never to exceed 100 percent of GDP in the long run, even if foreigners earn a net return of 2 percent on it while nominal GDP grows at 4 percent. What is the largest steady trade deficit that meets this goal? Find it roughly with the sliders, then exactly with equation (7).
Suppose instead that nominal growth slows to 3 percent, the return is 2 percent, and the deficit stays at 3 percent of GDP. Where does the ratio head, and in which year does the debt pass 100 percent of GDP? Why does a small change in \(\bar{g} - \bar{r}\) matter so much?



Hint

The title shows \(f^*\) and the year in which the debt passes 100 percent of GDP. For the trade balance that holds a ratio \(f\), solve equation (7) for \(nx\): \(nx = f\,(\bar{g} - \bar{r})/(1 + \bar{g})\). For (c), compare the factor \(\frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\) in the cases, and look at the denominator of equation (7).


def debt_projection(nx=-3.0, g=4.0, r=0.0):
    """Equations (5) and (7): U.S. net foreign assets (% of GDP) if the trade balance stays at nx after 2025."""
    history = share_of_gdp(us.niip, us.gdp).dropna()                   # the BEA data of Fig. 6
    f_star = round(100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(nx / 100, g / 100, r / 100), 1) + 0.0    # equation (7)
    passed = "never above 100% of GDP" if f_star >= -100 else "above 100% of GDP only after 2125"
    ratio, path, years = history.iloc[-1] / 100, [], list(range(history.index[-1] + 1, 2126))
    for year in years:
        ratio = (1 + r / 100) / (1 + g / 100) * ratio + nx / 100       # equation (5) divided by GDP
        path.append(100 * ratio)
        if ratio < -1 and passed.endswith("2125"):
            passed = f"above 100% of GDP from {year}"
    low = -200 if min(path + [f_star]) > -190 else -700                 # a wider axis only for very large debts
    fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=history.index, y=history, mode="lines", name="BEA data", line=dict(color=GRAY, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=path, mode="lines", name="Projection", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1900, 2200], y=[f_star, f_star], mode="lines", name="Long run, f*",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_hline(y=-100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Long run: f* = {f_star:.1f}% of GDP; net foreign debt {passed}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[1970, 2130]), yaxis=dict(title="Percent of GDP", range=[low, 20]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))
    return fig


interact(debt_projection,
         nx=FloatSlider(value=-3.0, min=-6.0, max=0.0, step=0.5, description="trade balance nx, % of GDP", style=WIDE),
         g=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=3.0, max=7.0, step=0.5, description="nominal GDP growth g, %", style=WIDE),
         r=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="return on the debt r, %", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the foreign-debt dynamics of the Model overview, equations (5) and (7), and the BEA data of Fig. 6, adapted from the discussion of foreign debt in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) The title reads \(f^* = -78.0\) percent: the debt ratio keeps rising, but slowly, from 70.9 percent toward 78.0 percent of GDP (it is still at 75.3 percent in 2050). Solving equation (7) for the trade balance that holds today’s ratio,
\[nx = f\,\frac{\bar{g} - \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = -0.709 \times \frac{0.04}{1.04} = -0.0273,\]
a deficit of about 2.7 percent of GDP keeps the net foreign debt at its 2025 level. The current deficit is only a little larger.
(b) With \(\bar{r} = 2\), the slider shows \(f^* = -104.0\) percent at \(nx = -2.0\) and \(-78.0\) percent at \(nx = -1.5\). Exactly, with \(f^* = -1\):
\[nx = -1 \times \frac{0.04 - 0.02}{1.04} = -0.0192.\]
The deficit must not exceed 1.92 percent of GDP, about two thirds of today’s deficit. A positive return on the debt adds interest to the borrowing, so the same debt ceiling allows a smaller trade deficit.
(c) Equation (7) gives \(f^* = 1.03 \times (-0.03)/(0.03 - 0.02) = -3.09\): the debt heads toward 309 percent of GDP, and the calculator shows it passing 100 percent of GDP in 2039. The long-run ratio of equation (7) has \(\bar{g} - \bar{r}\) in its denominator: with the same deficit of 3 percent, \(f^*\) is \(-156\) percent when \(\bar{g} = 4\) and \(\bar{r} = 2\), so halving the gap from 2 points to 1 point roughly doubles the debt. The factor \(\frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = 1.02/1.03 = 0.990\) is also close to one, so the ratio drifts for a very long time before it settles. If \(\bar{r}\) reached \(\bar{g}\), no stable ratio would exist, and equation (6) says that such a path cannot last. The code below confirms the numbers:
f_2025 = share_of_gdp(us.niip, us.gdp).dropna().iloc[-1] / 100
print(f"(a) f* = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, 0.04):.1f}%; the balance that holds {100 * f_2025:.1f}% "
      f"is {100 * f_2025 * 0.04 / 1.04:.2f}% of GDP")
nx_max = -1.0 * (0.04 - 0.02) / (1 + 0.04)               # equation (7) solved for nx, with f* = -1
print(f"(b) largest deficit {-100 * nx_max:.2f}% of GDP; check: f* = "
      f"{100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(nx_max, 0.04, 0.02):.1f}%")
ratio, crossing = f_2025, 0
for year in range(2026, 2126):
    ratio = 1.02 / 1.03 * ratio - 0.03                     # equation (5) divided by GDP
    if ratio < -1 and crossing == 0:
        crossing = year
print(f"(c) f* = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, 0.03, 0.02):.1f}%; the debt passes 100% of GDP in {crossing}")
It prints (a) f* = -78.0%; the balance that holds -70.9% is -2.73% of GDP, then a largest deficit of 1.92 percent (with \(f^* = -100.0\)), and \(f^* = -309.0\) percent with a crossing in 2039.

Problem 9 (Challenge): When the South grows. In the North–South model of the Model overview, let the South’s workforce \(L_s\) grow while all the other numbers stay the same. Think of a large economy with many workers joining world trade, as China did when it entered the World Trade Organization in 2001 (WTO). The calculator compares consumption per person under free trade with autarky (autarky = 100) for each good and each country; the numbers on the green bars are the amounts per person. Answer with its slider.

Move \(L_s\) from 400 to 600. What happens to the world price of a computer, to apples per person in the North and to computers per person in the South?
Use equations (10) and (11) to find the range of \(L_s\) for which complete specialization is the outcome, given the other numbers. What happens to the South’s gain from trade at the upper end of the range?
A northern politician says that the South’s growth hurts the North; a southern politician says that a bigger South is better for southern workers. Who is right in this model? Show that the South’s total consumption of computers does not depend on \(L_s\), and explain why in words.



Hint

Equation (10) gives the world price as a function of \(L_s\). Put it into each inequality of condition (11) and solve each one for \(L_s\). For (c), multiply the South’s computers per person, \(x_s/(2p)\), by the number of southern workers, and think about what an apple buys on the world market.


def south_grows(L_s=400):
    """Equations (8) to (11): consumption per person with free trade, relative to autarky, for any size of the South."""
    closed = pd.DataFrame({"North": autarky(x_n, z_n, L_n), "South": autarky(x_s, z_s, L_s)})
    trade = free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s)
    p = trade.loc["Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"]
    labels, index, text = [], [], []
    for country in ["North", "South"]:
        for good in ["Apples", "Computers"]:
            amount = trade.loc[good + " per person", country]
            labels.append(f"{country}: {good.lower()}")
            index.append(100 * amount / closed.loc[good + " per person", country])
            text.append(f"{amount:.0f}" if good == "Apples" else f"{amount:.2f}")     # the amount per person
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=labels, y=[100, 100, 100, 100], name="Autarky", marker_color=GRAY))
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=labels, y=index, name="Free trade", marker_color=GREEN, text=text, textposition="outside"))
    note = f"between the autarky prices {x_n / z_n:.0f} and {x_s / z_s:.0f}"             # condition (11)
    if p >= x_s / z_s:
        note = "the South's gain from trade is gone"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"L_s = {L_s}: a computer costs {p:.1f} apples, {note}", barmode="group",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Consumption per person, autarky = 100", range=[0, 600]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.98, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
    return fig


interact(south_grows, L_s=IntSlider(value=400, min=200, max=800, step=50, description="southern workers L_s", style=WIDE));

Source. A calculator built on the autarky and free_trade functions of “Model in code”, adapted from the apple-and-computer example in Chapter 19 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:


Solution

(a) From \(L_s = 400\) to \(600\) the world price of a computer rises from 25.0 to 37.5 apples. Northern workers eat 300 apples instead of 200 (the bar goes from 250 to 375), and still have 8 computers. Southern workers still eat 50 apples, but have 1.33 computers instead of 2.00.
(b) By equation (10), \(p = L_s x_s/(L_n z_n) = 100\,L_s/1{,}600 = L_s/16\). Condition (11) has two parts:
\[\frac{x_s}{z_s} > p \;\Longleftrightarrow\; 50 > \frac{L_s}{16} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; L_s < \frac{L_n z_n}{z_s} = 800,
\qquad
p > \frac{x_n}{z_n} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \frac{L_s}{16} > 10 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; L_s > \frac{L_n x_n}{x_s} = 160.\]
So the North makes only computers and the South only apples for \(160 < L_s < 800\). As \(L_s\) approaches 800, the world price rises to 50 apples, the South’s own autarky price, and southern computers per person fall to \(x_s/(2p) = 100/100 = 1\), the autarky level: the South’s gain from trade disappears. With an even larger South, southern workers would also make computers, the price would stay at 50, and all the gains from trade would go to the North.
(c) In this model the northern politician is wrong: each northerner’s apples, \(L_s x_s/(2L_n)\), rise with \(L_s\), and computers stay at \(z_n/2 = 8\). The southern politician is wrong too: a bigger South is worse for each southern worker. Apples stay at \(x_s/2 = 50\), but computers per person, \(L_n z_n/(2L_s)\), fall as \(L_s\) grows, so each worker’s gain from trade shrinks, although nobody falls below the autarky bundle. The South’s total computers are
\[L_s \times \frac{x_s}{2p} = L_s \times \frac{L_n z_n}{2L_s} = \frac{L_n z_n}{2} = 800,\]
half of the world’s computers, whatever the size of the South. The extra southern workers make more apples, but each apple buys fewer computers on the world market, in the same proportion: the price of what the South sells falls relative to the price of what it buys. The South gets more apples, but no more computers. (In reality, as the free-migration block of the Model overview notes, switching jobs is costly, so northern workers in the industries that compete with imports can lose even when the North as a whole gains.) The code below confirms the numbers:
for workers in [400, 600, 800]:
    world_trade = free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, workers)
    p = world_trade.loc["Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"]
    north_apples = world_trade.loc["Apples per person", "North"]
    south_computers = world_trade.loc["Computers per person", "South"]
    print(f"L_s = {workers}: p = {p:.1f}, North apples {north_apples:.0f}, South computers {south_computers:.2f} "
          f"each and {workers * south_computers:.0f} in total")
print(f"Complete specialization for {L_n * x_n / x_s:.0f} < L_s < {L_n * z_n / z_s:.0f}")
It prints L_s = 400: p = 25.0, North apples 200, South computers 2.00 each and 800 in total, then 37.5, 300, 1.33 and 800 for 600 workers, 50.0, 400, 1.00 and 800 for 800 workers, and the range 160 < L_s < 800.

Learning goals
Chapter 19 studied trade between countries. This chapter adds the price at which their currencies trade, the exchange rate, and asks what moves it in the long run and in the short run. By the end of it you will be able to:

title: 20. Exchange Rates and International Finance
text:
20.1 Model overview
Picture Islandia again, with its own money: paper Islandia dollars, which only the Bank of Islandia may print. Mainland, across the water, pays in its own money, which we call the euro (so that the units read as in the book’s examples). Harbor Boatworks sells some of its boats in Mainland, and islanders buy boats and other goods from Mainland, so every deal needs a price at which dollars trade for euros: the exchange rate. What decides that price over decades, and why can it jump overnight when the Bank of Islandia changes its interest rate? We follow Islandia through seven small models to find out.






NoteThe big idea



The question. What sets the price of Islandia’s money in terms of Mainland’s money, over decades and from one week to the next, and how does that price feed back into output and inflation at home?
The answer in one sentence. In the long run the exchange rate follows the two price levels (purchasing power parity), while in the short run, with sticky prices, it follows the gap between the two interest rates (uncovered interest parity), and through net exports it flattens the IS curve and turns Mainland’s interest rate into a demand shock for Islandia.
What goes in and what comes out. We choose the money, velocity and output of both countries, the productivity of their sectors, the two interest rates and what investors expect, and the parameters of the short-run model. The model gives back the nominal and real exchange rates and their growth rates, the interest rate a fixed exchange rate requires, and Islandia’s output and inflation after a shock from abroad.
Road map.

Exchange rates in the long run: the law of one price and PPP: the long-run exchange rate, in levels and in growth rates.
Why real exchange rates drift: the Balassa-Samuelson effect: why fast-growing countries look expensive.
Exchange rates in the short run: uncovered interest parity: why the exchange rate jumps with interest rates.
Fixed exchange rates and the policy trilemma: what a peg costs.
The open-economy IS curve: trade joins investment in the short-run model.
The open economy in the AS/AD model: a rise in Mainland’s interest rate, period by period.
The arithmetic of the euro crisis: interest bills, spreads and wages inside a currency union.
Model in code: the key results as Python functions, checked with numbers.

Notation. A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number set outside the model, such as \(\bar{b}_{nx}\); letters without a bar are endogenous variables. As in the book, a bar over a price or an exchange rate, such as \(\bar{E}\), marks instead its long-run value. A superscript \(w\) (“world”) marks Mainland.

Meaning

\(P, P^w\)

20.1.1 Exchange rates in the long run: the law of one price and PPP

Assumptions
1. The exchange rate. \(E\) is the nominal exchange rate: the number of euros that one dollar buys, for example 0.92. It is the price of Islandia’s money. When \(E\) goes up, a dollar fetches more euros and the dollar appreciates. When \(E\) goes down, the dollar depreciates.
2. Arbitrage in goods. Suppose a fishing net were cheaper in Islandia than in Mainland, once both prices are put in euros. Traders would buy nets in Islandia, ship them across and sell them in Mainland. Their buying lifts the Islandia price and their selling lowers the Mainland price, until the gap closes. In the long run this leaves the law of one price. With \(P\) the net’s price in Islandia (in dollars) and \(P^w\) its price in Mainland (in euros):






ImportantKey result: the law of one price



\[EP = P^w. \tag{1}\]
The left side converts the dollar price into euros: euros per dollar times dollars per net gives euros per net, the unit of the right side. Shipping costs, tariffs and taxes can keep the two sides apart, but only by about the size of those frictions.
Islandia in numbers. At \(E = 0.92\), a net that costs 100 dollars in Islandia must cost 92 euros in Mainland.


3. Price levels come from money. Apply equation (1) to the whole basket of goods of each country, so that \(P\) and \(P^w\) become the two price levels. In the long run each one follows from the quantity theory of money (Chapter 8): \(M_tV_t = P_tY_t\), with constant velocity \(\bar{V}\) and output at potential \(\bar{Y}\). So \(\bar{P} = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}\) in Islandia and, in the same way, \(\bar{P}^w = \bar{M}^w\bar{V}^w/\bar{Y}^w\) in Mainland.


Solving the model
Step 1: the long-run nominal exchange rate. Once the quantity theory has fixed both price levels, \(E\) is the only thing in equation (1) that can still adjust. Dividing both sides by \(\bar{P}\) gives \(\bar{E} = \bar{P}^w/\bar{P}\).
Step 2: money and the exchange rate. Replace each price level with its quantity-theory value:
\[\bar{E} = \frac{\bar{M}^w\bar{V}^w/\bar{Y}^w}{\bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}} = \frac{\bar{M}^w}{\bar{M}}\times\frac{\bar{V}^w}{\bar{V}}\times\frac{\bar{Y}}{\bar{Y}^w}.\]
Logs turn the products into sums (Appendix C.4):
\[\ln\bar{E} = (\ln\bar{M}^w - \ln\bar{M}) + (\ln\bar{V}^w - \ln\bar{V}) + (\ln\bar{Y} - \ln\bar{Y}^w).\]
Every coefficient is \(+1\) or \(-1\), so every elasticity has size one. If the Bank of Islandia doubled the number of dollars, Islandia’s prices would double and each dollar would buy half as many euros. In the long run, the exchange rate is the relative price of two stacks of paper money.
Step 3: pricing goods instead of money. The real exchange rate asks how many Mainland goods one Islandia good is worth:
\[RER \equiv \frac{EP}{P^w}, \qquad \text{in units}\quad \frac{\text{euros}}{\text{dollar}}\times\frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{Islandia good}}\times\frac{\text{Mainland good}}{\text{euros}} = \frac{\text{Mainland goods}}{\text{Islandia good}}.\]
The nominal rate is the price at which two monies trade; the real rate is the price at which two countries’ goods trade. By equation (1), \(EP\) and \(P^w\) are equal in the long run, so the long-run real exchange rate is \(\bar{E}\bar{P}/\bar{P}^w = 1\).






ImportantKey result: the long-run exchange rates



\[\bar{E} = \frac{\bar{P}^w}{\bar{P}} \tag{2}\]
\[\overline{RER} = \frac{\bar{E}\bar{P}}{\bar{P}^w} = 1 \tag{3}\]
The two price levels, and so the two money supplies, set the nominal rate; the real rate is pinned at one.
Islandia in numbers. If Islandia’s basket costs 100 dollars and Mainland’s costs 92 euros, \(\bar{E} = 92/100 = 0.92\) euros per dollar, and \(\overline{RER} = 0.92 \times 100/92 = 1\).








TipIn words



A dollar is worth what it buys. If 100 dollars buy the same basket in Islandia as 92 euros buy in Mainland, then 100 dollars and 92 euros are the same amount of purchasing power, and one dollar is worth 0.92 euros.


Step 4: purchasing power parity in growth rates. Equation (2) is also known as purchasing power parity (PPP). To see how it moves through time, take logs, \(\ln\bar{E}_t = \ln\bar{P}^w_t - \ln\bar{P}_t\), and subtract the same equation for the year before. The change in a log is close to a growth rate (Appendix C.5), and the growth rate of a price level is inflation:
\[\underbrace{\ln\bar{E}_t - \ln\bar{E}_{t-1}}_{\approx\, g_E} = \underbrace{(\ln\bar{P}^w_t - \ln\bar{P}^w_{t-1})}_{\approx\,\pi^w} - \underbrace{(\ln\bar{P}_t - \ln\bar{P}_{t-1})}_{\approx\,\pi}.\]
So \(g_E \approx \pi^w - \pi\): the growth rule for a ratio, \(g_{X/Z} = g_X - g_Z\). The exact yearly version is \(\bar{E}_t/\bar{E}_{t-1} = (1+\pi^w)/(1+\pi)\). With the quantity theory and constant velocities, inflation equals money growth minus output growth, \(\pi = g_M - g_Y\) (Chapter 8), so the same rule also reads \(g_E \approx (g_{M^w} - g_{Y^w}) - (g_M - g_Y)\).
Step 5: the real exchange rate in growth rates. Apply the same log steps to the definition of step 3. A product grows at the sum of the growth rates, and a ratio at their difference, so \(g_{RER} \approx g_E + \pi - \pi^w\). When PPP holds, the right side is zero and the real rate stays at one. When the real rate does move, either the nominal rate moved by more than the inflation gap, or prices moved while the nominal rate stood still. Fig. 3 uses this formula to build Japan’s real exchange rate from the data.






ImportantKey result: PPP in growth rates



\[g_E \approx \pi^w - \pi \tag{4}\]
\[g_{RER} \approx g_E + \pi - \pi^w \tag{5}\]
The money of the country with faster inflation loses value, at a yearly rate equal to the inflation gap, and that loss leaves the real exchange rate where it was.
Islandia in numbers. If Islandia’s prices rise by 4 percent a year and Mainland’s by 2 percent, the dollar loses about 2 percent a year against the euro. After 25 years it buys \((1.02/1.04)^{25} \approx 0.62\) times as many euros as at the start: about 38 percent fewer.








TipIn words: inflation and the exchange rate



Each year Islandia’s prices outrun Mainland’s, a dollar buys a little less at home compared with what a euro buys in Mainland. The exchange market simply records this: the dollar slides by the inflation gap.



In the long run a currency is worth what it buys, so the country with faster inflation sees its money lose value.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Start from \(\bar{E} = 0.92\) euros per dollar. Mainland doubles its money supply, and nothing else changes. What are the new long-run nominal and real exchange rates?


Answer

Mainland’s prices double, so by equation (2) \(\bar{E}\) doubles too, to \(2 \times 0.92 = 1.84\) euros per dollar: the elasticity of \(\bar{E}\) with respect to \(\bar{M}^w\) is \(+1\) (step 2). The real exchange rate stays at one, by equation (3).

2. Islandia’s inflation falls to 3 percent a year while Mainland’s rises to 5 percent. Does the dollar appreciate or depreciate, and by how much a year? What happens to the real exchange rate?


Answer

By equation (4), \(g_E \approx 5 - 3 = 2\) percent a year: the dollar appreciates. By equation (5), \(g_{RER} \approx 2 + 3 - 5 = 0\), so the real exchange rate does not change.





What the model predicts








A permanent 1% rise in …
changes \(\bar{E}\) (euros per dollar) by
because




Islandia’s money \(\bar{M}\)
\(-1\%\)
Islandia’s prices rise 1%


Mainland’s money \(\bar{M}^w\)
\(+1\%\)
Mainland’s prices rise 1%


Islandia’s output \(\bar{Y}\)
\(+1\%\)
Islandia’s prices fall 1%


Islandia’s velocity \(\bar{V}\)
\(-1\%\)
Islandia’s prices rise 1%


any of them
\(0\) for \(\overline{RER}\)
the long-run real exchange rate is always one




Higher inflation, weaker money. For the dollar to lose value against the yen for decades, as in Fig. 1, U.S. inflation must have stayed above Japan’s (equation 4). Fig. 2 puts this to the test.
The level of the nominal rate means nothing by itself. If Islandia swapped 1,000 old dollars for one new dollar, \(\bar{E}\) would rise a thousandfold, while the real exchange rate and every real variable would stay put: the classical dichotomy of the long run.
The law holds only roughly. It needs goods that can be shipped. The next block shows how goods that cannot be shipped let real exchange rates drift.


Money moves the nominal exchange rate one for one in the long run, and leaves the real exchange rate at one.




20.1.2 Why real exchange rates drift: the Balassa-Samuelson effect
This block turns the book’s verbal account of the Balassa-Samuelson effect into a small model, with our own notation.

Assumptions

Each country has a traded sector and a nontraded sector. In Islandia, Harbor Boatworks builds boats that sell in Mainland too; the island’s barbers and cafés serve only islanders. Output per worker is \(A_T\) in the traded sector and \(A_N\) in the nontraded one, and \(A^w_T\) and \(A^w_N\) in Mainland.
Workers can switch sectors within their own country, so both sectors pay one wage \(W\). With competitive firms, the wage equals the value of what a worker makes: \(W = P_TA_T = P_NA_N\).
The law of one price, equation (1), holds only for traded goods: \(EP_T = P^w_T\).
The price level averages the two prices, with weight \(\theta\) on traded goods: \(P = P_T^{\theta}P_N^{1-\theta}\), and likewise in Mainland.



Solving the model
Step 1: the price of nontraded goods. Divide \(P_TA_T = P_NA_N\) by \(A_N\):
\[P_N = P_T\,\frac{A_T}{A_N}.\]
A haircut costs more where the barber could have earned more building boats.
Step 2: the price level. Put \(P_N\) into the price level and use the exponent rule \(x^{\theta}x^{1-\theta} = x\) (Appendix C.3):
\[P = P_T^{\theta}\left(P_T\frac{A_T}{A_N}\right)^{1-\theta} = P_T^{\theta}P_T^{1-\theta}\left(\frac{A_T}{A_N}\right)^{1-\theta} = P_T\left(\frac{A_T}{A_N}\right)^{1-\theta}.\]
Step 3: the real exchange rate. Write the same expression for Mainland and form \(EP/P^w\). The traded-goods factor \(EP_T/P^w_T\) equals one by assumption 3, so only the productivity terms survive:
\[RER = \frac{EP_T}{P^w_T}\times\left(\frac{A_T/A_N}{A^w_T/A^w_N}\right)^{1-\theta}.\]






ImportantKey result: the Balassa-Samuelson real exchange rate



\[RER = \left(\frac{A_T/A_N}{A^w_T/A^w_N}\right)^{1-\theta} \tag{6}\]
In growth rates, by the rules for powers and ratios, \(g_{RER} = (1-\theta)\left[(g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}) - (g_{A^w_T} - g_{A^w_N})\right]\).
Islandia in numbers. With \(\theta = 1/2\), if Harbor Boatworks becomes twice as productive while everything else stays the same, \(RER = 2^{1/2} \approx 1.41\): Islandia’s goods become about 41 percent dearer than Mainland’s.








TipIn words



Better boatbuilding raises what a worker can earn at Harbor Boatworks, and barbers and cooks must be paid the same to stay. Boats cannot get dearer, because they compete with Mainland’s boats. Haircuts and meals do, because their wage bill grows while their productivity does not. So Islandia’s price level, and with it its real exchange rate, rises.




What the model predicts

Fast-growing economies appreciate in real terms. With \(\theta = 1/2\), a country whose traded-sector productivity grows 3 points a year faster than the other’s (relative to services) sees its real exchange rate rise by about \(1.5\%\) a year, a factor of \(1.015^{24} \approx 1.43\) over 24 years. Japan’s real exchange rate climbed in this way while it caught up, until 1995 (Fig. 3).
Rich countries look expensive. At any moment, rich countries have a high \(A_T/A_N\), so their services and their price levels are high. A Big Mac contains the cook’s wage and the restaurant’s rent, so it should cost more in rich countries; the Big Mac section after Fig. 3 tests this.
No money is involved. The effect runs through relative productivities, so it can last for decades while the law of one price holds for every traded good.


Productivity gains in traded goods raise wages everywhere, so services, and the whole price level, become dearer.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. For a decade, Harbor Boatworks’ productivity grows 4 points a year faster than that of Islandia’s cafés, while Mainland’s two sectors grow at the same pace. With \(\theta = 1/2\), how fast does Islandia’s real exchange rate rise?


Answer

By the growth form of equation (6), \(g_{RER} = 0.5 \times (4 - 0) = 2\) percent a year.

2. Does this real appreciation mean that boats now cost more in Islandia than in Mainland?


Answer

No. Assumption 3 keeps \(EP_T = P^w_T\): boats still obey equation (1). Islandia’s real exchange rate climbs only because nontraded goods, which cannot be shipped, get dearer in Islandia (equation 6).






20.1.3 Exchange rates in the short run: uncovered interest parity
The book argues in words that a higher interest rate makes a currency stronger. This block writes that argument as an equation, uncovered interest parity (UIP), a standard tool of international finance.

Assumptions

Sticky prices. Over a few weeks or months, \(P\) and \(P^w\) barely move, as with the sticky inflation of the short-run model.
Free financial flows. Investors can hold Islandia’s bonds, which pay the nominal interest rate \(i_t\) in dollars and is set by the Bank of Islandia, or Mainland’s bonds, which pay \(i^w\) in euros. They look only at the expected return and ignore risk.
An anchor for the future. Investors expect next year’s exchange rate to be \(E^e_{t+1}\). PPP, equation (2), pins down the long run, so we hold this expectation fixed when an interest rate changes.



Solving the model
Step 1: two ways to invest a dollar. Kept in Islandia, one dollar becomes \(1 + i_t\) dollars after a year. Sent to Mainland, it is first changed into \(E_t\) euros, which grow to \(E_t(1+i^w)\), and these are changed back at the expected rate \(E^e_{t+1}\), giving \(E_t(1+i^w)/E^e_{t+1}\) dollars. If one route paid more, money would pour into it until the two expected returns were equal: \(1 + i_t = (1+i^w)\,E_t/E^e_{t+1}\).
Step 2: solve for today’s exchange rate. Multiply both sides by \(E^e_{t+1}\) and divide by \(1+i^w\):
\[E_t = E^e_{t+1}\times\frac{1+i_t}{1+i^w}.\]
Take logs and use \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) for small \(x\) (Appendix C.6): \(\ln E_t \approx \ln E^e_{t+1} + (i_t - i^w)\). If the interest gap is expected to last \(n\) years before the exchange rate returns to its anchor \(E^e_{t+n}\), repeating the step \(n\) times gives \(E_t = E^e_{t+n}\left[(1+i_t)/(1+i^w)\right]^n\), and in logs \(\ln E_t \approx \ln E^e_{t+n} + n\,(i_t - i^w)\).






ImportantKey result: uncovered interest parity



\[1 + i_t = (1+i^w)\,\frac{E_t}{E^e_{t+1}} \tag{7}\]
\[\ln E_t \approx \ln E^e_{t+n} + n\,(i_t - i^w) \tag{8}\]
A 1-point rise in Islandia’s interest rate, with \(i^w\) and the anchor unchanged, makes the dollar jump today by about \(n\) percent. The trilemma model of Fig. 7 uses a jump of 5 percent per point, a gap expected to last about 5 years.
Islandia in numbers. Both rates start at 5 percent and the anchor is 0.92 euros per dollar. The Bank of Islandia raises \(i_t\) to 6 percent. If the gap lasts a year, \(E_t = 0.92 \times 1.06/1.05 \approx 0.9288\), a jump of about 1 percent. If it lasts five years, \((1.06/1.05)^5 \approx 1.048\): a jump of about 4.8 percent.


Step 3: what happens after the jump. Rearrange equation (7) as \(E^e_{t+1}/E_t = (1+i^w)/(1+i_t)\). In logs, the expected growth rate of \(E\) is \(g^e_E \approx i^w - i_t\). When Islandia’s bonds pay more, the dollar must be expected to lose value from then on, by exactly the interest gap, so that dollars are no better to hold than euros.






TipIn words: jump, then slide



The Bank of Islandia raises its rate, and investors everywhere want dollar bonds. They bid up the dollar until it is so dear that it can only be expected to fall back. That is the only way to have both: the dollar jumps at once, then slides back to its anchor.


Step 4: what sticky prices do to the real rate. With sticky prices, \(\pi\) and \(\pi^w\) are close to zero over a few weeks, so equation (5) gives \(g_{RER} \approx g_E\): every surprise move in \(E\) is also a move in the real exchange rate. With sticky inflation, a higher nominal rate \(i_t\) also means a higher real rate \(R_t = i_t - \pi^e_t\) (the Fisher equation), so the same chain starts from the real interest rate:
\[\uparrow R_t \;\Rightarrow\; \uparrow E_t \;\Rightarrow\; \uparrow \frac{E_tP}{P^w}.\]


What the model predicts

1. Mainland’s central bank raises \(i^w\) by 1 point, and investors expect the gap to last 3 years. The Bank of Islandia does not move. Roughly what happens to the dollar today?


Answer

By equation (8), \(\ln E_t\) changes by about \(n\,(i_t - i^w) = 3 \times (-1) = -3\), so the dollar falls by about 3 percent today.

2. After the Bank of Islandia raises its rate, why must investors expect the dollar to depreciate?


Answer

Equation (7) says that both bonds must have the same expected return in dollars. Islandia’s bonds now pay more interest, so the euro route must make up the difference through an expected rise in the euro: \(g^e_E \approx i^w - i_t < 0\) (step 3).






20.1.4 Fixed exchange rates and the policy trilemma

Assumptions

The Bank of Islandia promises to trade dollars for euros at a fixed rate \(E_{fix}\), and holds foreign exchange reserves, a stock of euros, to keep that promise.
Investors trust the promise, so they expect the rate to stay put: \(E^e_{t+1} = E_t = E_{fix}\).
Money flows freely across the water, so uncovered interest parity, equation (7), holds.



Solving the model
Step 1: the interest rate is no longer free. Put \(E_t = E^e_{t+1}\) into equation (7). The ratio \(E_t/E^e_{t+1}\) becomes one, so \(1 + i_t = 1 + i^w\).






ImportantKey result: a credible peg ties the interest rate



\[i_t = i^w \tag{9}\]
With a trusted peg and open financial markets, the Bank of Islandia must copy Mainland’s interest rate, whatever is happening on the island.
Islandia in numbers. If Mainland’s rate is 5 percent, so is Islandia’s.








TipIn words



If the dollar paid less interest than the euro while trading at a guaranteed rate, nobody would hold dollars; if it paid more, everybody would. Only an equal rate keeps money still. So once the Bank of Islandia has fixed the price of the dollar, Mainland’s central bank in effect sets Islandia’s interest rate.


Step 2: prices are no longer free either. In the long run, equation (2) with \(\bar{E} = E_{fix}\) gives \(\bar{P} = \bar{P}^w/E_{fix}\): Islandia’s price level must move one for one with Mainland’s. Equation (4) with \(g_E = 0\) gives \(\pi = \pi^w\), and by the quantity theory, Islandia’s money growth must match Mainland’s (adjusted for output growth). That is how a peg can import a trusted central bank, and also why it breaks when a government needs to print money to pay its bills (Chapter 8).
Step 3: the gold standard is a law of one price for gold. Under the gold standard each country fixed the price of an ounce of gold in its own money: \(P^{gold}\) dollars in the United States, \(P^{gold,w}\) pounds in Britain. Apply equation (2) to gold alone: \(E = P^{gold,w}/P^{gold}\) pounds per dollar. Fig. 6 computes this gold parity.
Step 4: a peg that markets doubt. Suppose investors start to fear a devaluation and expect \(E^e_{t+1}\) below \(E_{fix}\). Solve equation (7) for the interest rate:
\[1 + i_t = (1+i^w)\,\frac{E_{fix}}{E^e_{t+1}}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad i_t \approx i^w + \text{expected percent depreciation}.\]
With \(i^w = 5\) percent and an expected devaluation of 10 percent, holding dollars requires \(i_t = 1.05/0.90 - 1 \approx 16.7\) percent. If the Bank of Islandia stops short of that, investors swap their dollars for its reserves; when the reserves run out, the peg breaks. Mexico in 1994, Asia in 1997 and Argentina in 2002 went through this (Fig. 8).


What the model predicts
UIP ties together three things: the exchange rate, the domestic interest rate, and the freedom of money to cross borders. Fix any two and the third follows. This is the policy trilemma of Fig. 7:

1. Islandia pegs to the euro. Mainland’s rate is 3 percent, and markets start to expect the dollar to lose 5 percent. What interest rate must the Bank of Islandia set to keep investors holding dollars?


Answer

By equation (7) with \(E_{fix}/E^e_{t+1} = 1/0.95\), \(i_t = 1.03/0.95 - 1 \approx 8.4\) percent. The rough rule, \(3 + 5 = 8\) percent, is a little too low, because a 5 percent fall is not a very small change.

2. A recession hits Islandia, but not Mainland. Can the Bank of Islandia cut its rate while it keeps both the peg and free financial flows?


Answer

No. With the peg and free flows, equation (9) forces \(i_t = i^w\). To cut its rate it must give up one of the two: let the dollar float, or restrict trading in the currency. That is the trilemma.






20.1.5 The open-economy IS curve

Assumptions

Net exports and the real exchange rate. When Islandia’s goods are dear compared with Mainland’s (a high real exchange rate), Harbor Boatworks sells fewer boats abroad and islanders buy more Mainland goods, so net exports \(NX \equiv EX - IM\) are low.
The exchange-rate channel. By the UIP block, the real exchange rate rises when Islandia’s real interest rate \(R_t\) rises, and falls when Mainland’s real rate \(\bar{R}^w\) rises. Together with assumption 1, net exports as a share of potential output fall with the gap between the two real rates, as in the box below. Here \(\bar{a}_{nx}\) is the medium-run trade balance and \(\bar{b}_{nx} > 0\) measures how strongly trade reacts to the gap. With \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0\) we are back in the closed-economy IS curve of Chapter 11.
The rest of the IS curve is unchanged (Chapter 11): \(C_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_c\), \(G_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_g\), \(I_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_i - \bar{b}_i(R_t - \bar{r})\), where \(\bar{r}\) is the marginal product of capital; and all output is spent, \(Y_t = C_t + I_t + G_t + NX_t\). Short-run output is \(\tilde{Y}_t \equiv (Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)/\bar{Y}_t\).







ImportantKey result: net exports



\[\frac{NX_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}\,(R_t - \bar{R}^w) \tag{10}\]
A higher real rate in Islandia strengthens the dollar and cuts net exports; a higher real rate in Mainland does the opposite.




Solving the model
Step 1: add and subtract \(\bar{r}\). Investment depends on \(R_t - \bar{r}\), but net exports on \(R_t - \bar{R}^w\). Write \(R_t - \bar{R}^w = (R_t - \bar{r}) - (\bar{R}^w - \bar{r})\) and multiply out:
\[\frac{NX_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}(R_t - \bar{r}) + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}).\]
Nothing has really changed, since the two \(\bar{r}\) terms cancel. But now trade reacts to the same gap as investment, plus a term that only Mainland can move.
Step 2: divide spending by potential output. Divide \(Y_t = C_t + I_t + G_t + NX_t\) by \(\bar{Y}_t\) and put in each share:
\[\frac{Y_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_c + \left[\bar{a}_i - \bar{b}_i(R_t - \bar{r})\right] + \bar{a}_g + \left[\bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}(R_t - \bar{r}) + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r})\right].\]
Step 3: collect terms. Subtract 1 from both sides, since \(\tilde{Y}_t = Y_t/\bar{Y}_t - 1\), and group the constants and the \((R_t - \bar{r})\) terms.






ImportantKey result: the open-economy IS curve



\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}), \qquad
\bar{a} \equiv \bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{nx} - 1 + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}), \qquad
\bar{b} \equiv \bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx}. \tag{11}\]
The curve has the same form as in a closed economy, so every tool of the short-run model still works. Only the two parameters mean more: \(\bar{b}\) adds the trade channel to the investment channel, and \(\bar{a}\) now holds a demand shock from Mainland.
Islandia in numbers. With \(\bar{b}_i = 1\) and \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), \(\bar{b} = 2\). A rise in \(R_t\) from \(\bar{r} = 5\) to 6 percent lowers output by 2 percent, against 1 percent with no trade channel (Fig. 4).








TipIn words: why trade reacts like investment



Islanders’ saving can build boats at home or be lent to Mainland: \(S = I + NX\) (Chapter 19). When the Bank of Islandia raises the real rate, both uses lose at once. Harbor Boatworks invests less because borrowing costs more, and the stronger dollar makes its boats harder to sell abroad.


Step 4: the slope. Solve equation (11) for the interest rate: \(R_t - \bar{r} = (\bar{a} - \tilde{Y}_t)/\bar{b}\). With the output gap on the horizontal axis, the IS curve has slope \(-1/\bar{b}\), so a larger \(\bar{b}\) makes it flatter.

1. With \(\bar{b}_i = 1\) and \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), Mainland’s real rate rises from 5 to 8 percent, while the Bank of Islandia keeps \(R_t = \bar{r} = 5\) percent. How large is Islandia’s demand shock, and what is short-run output?


Answer

By equation (11), \(\bar{a}\) rises by \(\bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}) = 1 \times (8 - 5) = 3\). With \(R_t = \bar{r}\), \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} = 3\) percent: a boom driven by a weaker dollar and higher net exports.

Answer

Now \(\bar{b} = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5\), smaller than 2, so the IS curve (slope \(-1/\bar{b}\)) is steeper. A 1-point rise in \(R_t\) lowers output by 1.5 percent instead of 2 (equation 11).






20.1.6 The open economy in the AS/AD model

Assumptions

The open-economy IS curve, equation (11).
The policy rule of Chapter 13: the Bank of Islandia sets the real interest rate above \(\bar{r}\) when inflation is above its target, \(R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\).
The Phillips curve with adaptive expectations (Chapter 12), read as an AS curve: \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\).



Solving the model
Step 1: the AD curve. Put the policy rule into the IS curve: \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r}) = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\).
Step 2: where AD meets AS. Put the AS curve into the AD curve and solve for \(\tilde{Y}_t\):
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t - \bar{\pi})
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\tilde{Y}_t(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}).\]
Dividing by \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}\) gives output, and the AS curve then gives inflation.






ImportantKey result: the open-economy AD curve and the short-run equilibrium



\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \tag{12}\]
\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}, \qquad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t \tag{13}\]
The AD curve has slope \(-1/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\), so the trade channel, by raising \(\bar{b}\), makes it flatter.
Islandia in numbers. With \(\bar{b} = 2\), \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), \(\bar{b}\bar{m} = 1\) and the denominator is 2. Mainland’s real rate 2 points above \(\bar{r}\) gives \(\bar{a} = 1 \times 2 = 2\), so in the first period \(\tilde{Y}_1 = 2/2 = 1\) percent and \(\pi_1 = 2 + 1 = 3\) percent.


Step 3: the dynamics. Call \(x_t \equiv \pi_t - \bar{\pi}\) the inflation gap. Equation (13) in the AS curve gives \(x_t = x_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t = \left(x_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\bar{a}\right)/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\). While \(\bar{a}\) stays constant, this difference equation (Appendix C.10) has the resting point \(x^* = \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\), where output is back at potential, and the distance to it shrinks by the same factor every period:
\[x_t - x^* = \frac{x_{t-1} - x^*}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.\]
Step 4: a rise in Mainland’s interest rate. In Fig. 5, Mainland’s real rate sits 2 points above \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent in periods 1 to 9. By equation (11) that is a demand shock \(\bar{a} = \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}) = 2\) for Islandia. With the numbers in the box:

period 1: \(\tilde{Y}_1 = 1\) percent and \(\pi_1 = 3\) percent;
periods 2 to 9: the resting point is \(x^* = 2/1 = 2\), so inflation heads for 4 percent, and the remaining gap halves each period (\(\pi_2 = 3.5\), output \(0.5\) percent);
period 10: the shock ends, so \(\bar{a} = 0\) and the resting point is back at \(x^* = 0\). With \(\pi_9 \approx 4\), \(\tilde{Y}_{10} = (0 - 1 \times 2)/2 \approx -1\) percent: a recession, after which inflation halves its gap to 2 percent each period.







TipIn words: a shock from across the water



Mainland tightens, investors move toward euros, and the dollar weakens. Harbor Boatworks’ boats become cheap abroad, so Islandia booms and inflation rises. The Bank of Islandia leans against it, and the boom fades. When Mainland’s rate comes back down, the dollar recovers, net exports fall, and the inflation that built up now has to be squeezed out with a recession.




What the model predicts

Monetary policy travels across borders. Tighter money in Mainland weakens the dollar, raises Islandia’s net exports and acts like any positive demand shock: a boom, then higher inflation, then a recession once Mainland’s rate returns to normal. A recession in Mainland pushes the other way, by lowering \(\bar{a}_{nx}\), so the net effect of Mainland’s tightening can have either sign.
A larger \(\bar{b}\) makes the AD curve flatter. For a given demand shock, output moves less on impact (the denominator \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}\) is larger), because the Bank’s rate moves now work through trade as well as investment.

1. Mainland’s real rate rises by only 1 point above \(\bar{r}\), with the baseline \(\bar{b}_i = \bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), \(\bar{m} = 1/2\), \(\bar{\nu} = 1\) and \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent. What are output and inflation in the first period?


Answer

Now \(\bar{a} = 1 \times 1 = 1\). Equation (13) with \(\pi_0 = \bar{\pi}\) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = 1/2 = 0.5\) percent, and \(\pi_1 = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5\) percent.

2. In the long run, where do Islandia’s output and inflation settle while Mainland’s rate stays high, and why?


Answer

Output returns to potential and inflation settles at \(\bar{\pi} + x^* = 2 + 2 = 4\) percent (step 3). At that inflation rate the Bank’s higher real rate exactly offsets the boost from Mainland, so the AD curve gives \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) (equation 12).






20.1.7 The arithmetic of the euro crisis
The euro section of the chapter has no formal model, but three short pieces of arithmetic sit behind its figures. To tell them as a story, suppose Islandia gives up its dollar and shares Mainland’s euro, and the Islandia Treasury borrows by selling bonds to islanders and to lenders on Mainland.

Definitions

Sovereign debt \(D\) is the government’s debt; \(D/Y\) is the debt-GDP ratio, and \(i\) is the nominal interest rate the government pays on it.
A bond’s default probability \(p\) is the chance that the government does not repay it.
The unit labor cost is the wage cost of one unit of output: the nominal wage \(W\) divided by real output per worker \(Y/L\), \(ULC \equiv W/(Y/L)\).



Solving the model
Step 1: the interest bill. The Treasury pays \(i \times D\) in interest each year. Divide by \(Y\): interest in percent of GDP is \(i \times (D/Y)\). With debt equal to 100 percent of GDP, each point on the interest rate costs one point of GDP a year: a rate that climbs from 2 to 6 percent lifts the bill from 2 to 6 percent of GDP.
Step 2: why yields converged and then split (Fig. 9). A lender who cares only about the expected return must earn as much on a risky bond as on a safe one, the Mainland bond with rate \(i^{safe}\). If the Treasury’s bond pays \(1 + i\) with probability \(1 - p\) and nothing otherwise, then \((1 - p)(1 + i) = 1 + i^{safe}\). Solve for \(i\), and use the approximation of Appendix C.6 for small \(p\) and \(i\).
Step 3: competitiveness in a currency union (Fig. 13). The unit labor cost is a ratio, so by the growth rule for a ratio its growth rate is wage growth minus productivity growth.






ImportantKey result: spreads and unit labor costs



\[i = \frac{1 + i^{safe}}{1 - p} - 1 \;\approx\; i^{safe} + p \tag{14}\]
\[g_{ULC} = g_W - g_{Y/L} \tag{15}\]
The spread over the safe bond is roughly the default probability.
Islandia in numbers. With a safe rate of 2 percent and a default probability of 3 percent, the Treasury pays \(1.02/0.97 - 1 \approx 5.15\) percent, a spread of about 3 points. If Islandia’s wages grow 4 percent a year and its productivity 1 percent, while both grow 1.5 percent in Mainland, Islandia’s real exchange rate rises by about 3 percent a year: \(1.03^{10} \approx 1.34\) over a decade.


Before the euro, spreads also held the expected inflation gap (by the Fisher equation, \(i = R + \pi^e\)). One currency removed that part, so yields converged; after 2008, fear of default opened the spreads again. Inside the union the nominal exchange rate between Islandia and Mainland is fixed at one, so their real exchange rate is the ratio of their price levels. If firms set prices as a fixed markup over unit labor cost, equation (5) with \(g_E = 0\) gives \(g_{RER} = g_{ULC} - g^w_{ULC}\), the gap between the two growth rates of equation (15).






TipIn words



Sharing Mainland’s money takes away the inflation premium, so Islandia borrows cheaply at first. But it also takes away the exchange rate as a shock absorber. If islanders’ wages race ahead of their productivity, Harbor Boatworks’ boats get dearer abroad, and there is no dollar left to fall and set prices right.




What the model predicts

Crises can feed themselves. At high debt, a rise in the feared default probability \(p\) raises \(i\) by equation (14), which raises the interest bill, which makes default more likely. Investors’ fears can come true because they hold them. A central bank that promises to buy the bonds lowers \(p\) and can stop the spiral.
No exchange rate to fall back on. A country with its own money can win back competitiveness by letting \(E\) fall. Inside a monetary union \(g_E = 0\), so the real exchange rate can fall only if wages grow more slowly than productivity at home (equation 15), or faster abroad. That is slow and painful, and it helps explain the high unemployment of southern Europe.


Inside a currency union, competitiveness can be regained only through wages and productivity, which is slow and painful.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. The Treasury’s debt is 100 percent of GDP. Investors’ feared default probability rises from 1 to 4 percent, with a safe rate of 2 percent. Using the approximation in equation (14), by how much does the yearly interest bill rise, in percent of GDP?


Answer

By equation (14) the rate rises from about \(2 + 1 = 3\) to \(2 + 4 = 6\) percent. At a debt of 100 percent of GDP the bill is \(i \times D/Y\), so it rises from 3 to 6 percent of GDP: 3 points more each year (step 1).

2. In the union, Islandia’s wages grow 2 percent a year and its productivity 2 percent, while in Mainland wages grow 3 percent and productivity 1 percent. Does Islandia gain or lose competitiveness?


Answer

By equation (15), \(g_{ULC} = 2 - 2 = 0\) in Islandia and \(3 - 1 = 2\) percent in Mainland. Islandia’s real exchange rate falls by about 2 percent a year: its goods get cheaper relative to Mainland’s, so it gains competitiveness.









NoteRecap




In the long run, PPP: the exchange rate equals the ratio of the price levels, \(\bar{E} = \bar{P}^w/\bar{P}\), and the money with faster inflation loses value, \(g_E \approx \pi^w - \pi\) (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2).
Real exchange rates drift when traded-goods productivity grows faster in one country, the Balassa-Samuelson effect (Fig. 3).
In the short run, UIP: with sticky prices, a higher interest rate at home makes the currency, and the real exchange rate, jump up.
The trilemma: a credible peg with free flows forces \(i_t = i^w\), so a country keeps only two of three goals (Fig. 7, Fig. 8).
The open-economy IS and AD curves are flatter, \(\bar{b} = \bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx}\), and a rise in foreign interest rates is a demand shock at home (Fig. 4 and Fig. 5).
Inside a currency union, spreads track default risk, \(i \approx i^{safe} + p\), and competitiveness moves with unit labor costs (Fig. 9, Fig. 13).
