20.2 Model in code
Now we turn the Key results into Python. The section has four parts: the setup (folded, because it is the same in every chapter), the model as functions, numerical checks of the Key results, and the drawing and data tools that the figures use (folded too). Run its cells once, in order. Every later section of the notebook reuses them.

20.2.1 Setup
Run the setup cells once, before anything else. They load the Python libraries, give every chart the same look, store the address of the chapter’s data and define the helpers that only the book website needs. You can use the notebook without reading them; open the box if you are curious.






NoteShow the setup code





The first cell loads the libraries and sets the look of the charts. Its comments explain each step.

# @title Setup: libraries, chart colors and the data location
# Text after a "#" is a comment: Python ignores it, it is there for human readers.

# Step 1: load the libraries. `import` loads a library, a toolbox written by
# other people, and `as np` gives it a short nickname, so the code stays short.
import numpy as np                              # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                             # data tables
import plotly.express as px                     # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go               # charts built piece by piece
import plotly.io as pio                         # settings shared by every chart
# sliders, buttons and lists for the interactive figures
from ipywidgets import interact, FloatSlider, IntSlider, ToggleButtons, Dropdown, SelectMultiple, fixed

# Step 2: one light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
# the same chart size in Colab and on the website
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full slider labels

# Step 3, Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets.
# `try` runs the indented lines; if the import fails (we are not in Colab),
# `except` skips them.
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# Step 4: the data files of this chapter live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/ch20/"

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider. The next helper builds those versions. Run it and move on.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. the one of Fig. 4
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "b_nx"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

The data figures can show many countries. On the website they use the helpers below: a legend you can click, a slider that changes the data of every line at once, and a menu of country groups.

# @title Helpers for the many-country website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def compact(y):
    """Round to 4 significant digits, so that the saved figure stays small.

    Arguments
        y : the values of one line (None or NaN for a gap)
    Returns
        the rounded values as a list, with None for every gap
    """
    # `v != v` is True only for NaN, the code for a missing value
    return [None if v is None or v != v else float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in y]


def slim(trace):
    """Make a line smaller: rounded y values, and one hover label for the whole line.

    The hover label comes from the trace name instead of one text per point.

    Arguments
        trace : one line of a Plotly figure
    Returns
        the same line, smaller
    """
    # Step 1: round the y values
    trace.y = compact(trace.y)
    # Step 2: if each point's hover text is just the line's name, use the name once
    if trace.hovertext is not None and len(trace.hovertext) > 0 and trace.hovertext[0] == trace.name:
        trace.hovertext = None
        trace.hovertemplate = trace.hovertemplate.replace("%{hovertext}", "%{fullData.name}")
    return trace


def legend_only(fig, keep):
    """Show the traces named in keep; list the others in the legend only, so a click adds them.

    Arguments
        fig  : a Plotly figure with one trace per country
        keep : the names of the traces drawn at the start
    Returns
        the same figure, with smaller traces
    """
    for trace in fig.data:
        # drawn, or "legendonly": listed in the legend, a click away
        trace.visible = True if trace.name in keep else "legendonly"
        slim(trace)
    return fig


def data_slider(make_figure, name, values, start, title, label=None, **fixed):
    """A slider whose steps replace the y data of every line, so that legend clicks are kept.

    Lines are matched by name, and lines missing at the start value are added empty.

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "base"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        title       : the title, a text with {} where the slider value goes
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
        fixed       : further arguments, passed to make_figure unchanged
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with a slider
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = {v: make_figure(**{name: v}, **fixed) for v in values}
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[start].layout)
    # Step 2: one line per name; a line missing at the start value is added empty
    for v in [start] + list(values):
        for t in figures[v].data:
            if t.name not in [u.name for u in fig.data]:
                t.y = t.y if v == start else [None] * len(t.y)
                fig.add_trace(slim(t))
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: the new y data of every line, the new title
    steps = []
    for v in values:
        ys = {t.name: compact(t.y) for t in figures[v].data}
        new_y = [ys.get(t.name, [None] * len(t.y)) for t in fig.data]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(v),
                          args=[{"y": new_y}, {"title.text": title.format(v)}]))
    fig.update_layout(title=title.format(start), sliders=[dict(
        active=values.index(start), steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60), currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig


# @title Helper: groups of countries for the website menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
# Step 1: two groups of countries that the data files do not list
G7 = ["Canada", "France", "Germany", "Italy", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States"]
EMERGING = ["Argentina", "Brazil", "China", "India", "Indonesia", "Mexico", "Russia", "Saudi Arabia",
            "South Africa", "Türkiye"]


def country_groups(names, book, book_label, regions=True):
    """The groups of the website menus, for the countries that have data.

    The groups are the textbook's countries, the G7, the euro area, the large emerging economies
    and the World Bank regions. It uses `country_info`, read in the drawing and data tools.

    Arguments
        names      : the countries that have data
        book       : the textbook's countries
        book_label : the menu's name for them, e.g. "Textbook: Japan"
        regions    : True to add one group per World Bank region
    Returns
        a dictionary {group name: list of countries}, without empty groups
    """
    # Step 2: the countries with data, and the euro members among them
    info = country_info[country_info.country.isin(names)]
    euro = list(info[info.euro_since.notna() | (info.country == "Euro area")].country)
    groups = {book_label: list(book), "G7": [c for c in G7 if c in set(names)], "Euro area": euro,
              "Large emerging economies": [c for c in EMERGING if c in set(names)]}
    # Step 3: one group per World Bank region
    if regions:
        for region in sorted(info.region.unique()):
            if region != "Euro area":
                groups[region] = list(info[info.region == region].country)
    # leave out the empty groups
    return {k: v for k, v in groups.items() if v}


# @title Helper: a figure with a menu of country groups (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def menu_figure(make_figure, options, categories=False):
    """Precompute make_figure for every menu option and join the figures with a dropdown menu.

    With categories=True (bar charts) each option also sets the order and the range of the x-axis.

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure
        options     : maps each menu label to a list of countries, or to a dict of keyword arguments
        categories  : True for bar charts, with one bar per country
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a menu that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every menu option
    labels = list(options)
    figures = [make_figure(**options[g]) if isinstance(options[g], dict) else make_figure(tuple(options[g]))
               for g in labels]
    # Step 2: copy every line into one figure; only the first option's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[0].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == 0)
            fig.add_trace(slim(trace))
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one menu button per option: its lines, title, axes, shapes and notes
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title.text": f.layout.title.text, "yaxis.type": f.layout.yaxis.type or "linear",
                  "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range, "yaxis.tickvals": f.layout.yaxis.tickvals,
                  "yaxis.autorange": f.layout.yaxis.range is None,
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes],
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations]}
        # a bar chart also gets the order of its bars and the range of its x-axis
        if categories:
            names = list(dict.fromkeys(x for t in f.data for x in t.x))
            layout.update({"xaxis.categoryorder": "array", "xaxis.categoryarray": names,
                           "xaxis.range": [-0.5, len(names) - 0.5]})
            # the first option is the one shown at the start
            if i == 0:
                fig.update_xaxes(categoryorder="array", categoryarray=names, range=[-0.5, len(names) - 0.5])
        buttons.append(dict(label=labels[i], method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    # Step 4: the menu sits above the plot, at the left
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=110), updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=0, x=0, y=1.02,
                                                            xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])
    return fig






20.2.2 The model as functions
Now the Key results become Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes. In the code, Islandia plays the part of the book’s United States and Mainland that of the rest of the world.
One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers. Both model diagrams of this notebook start from one illustrative set of parameters, which the worked numbers above also use:

marginal product of capital \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent, as in Chapter 11’s example, and no demand shock at home, \(\bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{nx} = 1\);
interest sensitivities \(\bar{b}_i = 1\) and \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), so the total \(\bar{b} = 2\) is the value of Chapters 11 and 13, split half and half between investment and trade;
inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, policy response \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and Phillips-curve slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), as in Chapter 13;
the foreign shock of Fig. 5: the foreign real interest rate is 2 points above \(\bar{r}\), at 7 percent, in periods 1 to 9 and back at \(\bar{r}\) afterwards.

The first cell stores this baseline. Then it writes the first pieces of the model as functions: the long-run exchange rate, equation (2), the real exchange rate, equation (3), net exports, equation (10), and the part of the demand shock that comes from abroad.

# Step 1: the baseline. Names in capital letters, such as `R_BAR`, are constants:
# we set them once and never change them.
# marginal product of capital r-bar (%), interest sensitivities b_i and b_nx
R_BAR, B_I, B_NX = 5.0, 1.0, 1.0
# inflation target pi-bar (%), policy response m-bar, Phillips-curve slope nu-bar
PI_BAR, M_BAR, NU_BAR = 2.0, 0.5, 1.0
# the foreign rate minus r-bar in periods 1 to A_LAST; T_MAX periods are simulated
RW_GAP, A_LAST, T_MAX = 2.0, 9, 20


# Step 2: the functions. `def` creates a function, a named recipe: its inputs
# are the arguments in parentheses, and `return` gives back the result.
def long_run_exchange_rate(P_w, P):
    """The long-run nominal exchange rate, E-bar.

    Equation (2):  E = P_w / P   (foreign currency per dollar)

    Arguments
        P_w : the foreign price level (Mainland's), in foreign currency per basket
        P   : the U.S. price level (Islandia's), in dollars per basket
    Returns
        the long-run exchange rate E, in foreign currency per dollar
    """
    # the exchange rate at which a basket costs the same in both countries
    return P_w / P


def real_exchange_rate(E, P, P_w):
    """The real exchange rate: the foreign goods needed to buy one U.S. good.

    Equation (3):  RER = E P / P_w

    Arguments
        E   : the nominal exchange rate, foreign currency per dollar
        P   : the U.S. price level, in dollars
        P_w : the foreign price level, in foreign currency
    Returns
        the real exchange rate, RER (1 when the law of one price holds)
    """
    return E * P / P_w


# `R_w=R_BAR` gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one;
# `b_nx=B_NX` does the same for the interest sensitivity of net exports.
def net_exports(R, R_w=R_BAR, a_nx=0.0, b_nx=B_NX):
    """Net exports, in percent of potential output.

    Equation (10):  NX/Y = a_nx - b_nx (R - R_w)

    Arguments
        R    : the U.S. real interest rate (%)
        R_w  : the foreign real interest rate, R-bar^w (%), r-bar unless we pass another value
        a_nx : the net-exports shock, a-bar_nx (% of potential output)
        b_nx : the interest sensitivity of net exports, b-bar_nx
    Returns
        net exports NX/Y, in percent of potential output
    """
    # a higher U.S. rate than abroad makes the dollar dearer and lowers net exports
    return a_nx - b_nx * (R - R_w)


def foreign_shock(R_w, b_nx=B_NX, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """The part of the demand shock a-bar that comes from abroad.

    Equation (11), its foreign term:  b_nx (R_w - r_bar)

    Arguments
        R_w   : the foreign real interest rate (%)
        b_nx  : the interest sensitivity of net exports, b-bar_nx
        r_bar : the marginal product of capital, r-bar (%)
    Returns
        the shock to a-bar, in percent of potential output
    """
    return b_nx * (R_w - r_bar)

The next four functions are the short-run model: the open-economy IS curve, equation (11), the AD and AS curves, and the point where they cross, equation (13).

def is_curve(R, a=0.0, b_i=B_I, b_nx=B_NX, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """The open-economy IS curve: short-run output for a given real interest rate.

    Equation (11):  Y~ = a - (b_i + b_nx) (R - r_bar), in percent

    Arguments
        R     : the U.S. real interest rate (%)
        a     : the demand shock, a-bar (0 in the baseline)
        b_i   : the interest sensitivity of investment, b-bar_i
        b_nx  : the interest sensitivity of net exports, b-bar_nx
        r_bar : the marginal product of capital, r-bar (%)
    Returns
        short-run output Y~, in percent
    """
    # trade adds b_nx to the slope, so the open-economy IS curve is flatter
    return a - (b_i + b_nx) * (R - r_bar)


def ad_output(pi, a=0.0, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX):
    """The AD curve with the open-economy b: short-run output for a given inflation rate.

    Equation (12):  Y~ = a - b m (pi - pi_bar)

    Arguments
        pi : inflation (%)
        a  : the demand shock, a-bar
        m  : the policy response, m-bar
        b  : the interest sensitivity of spending, b-bar = b_i + b_nx
    Returns
        short-run output Y~, in percent
    """
    return a - b * m * (pi - PI_BAR)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS curve of Chapter 13: inflation for a given short-run output.

    Equation (13), second part:  pi = pi_e + nu Y~

    Arguments
        Y    : short-run output Y~ (%)
        pi_e : expected inflation, last period's inflation (%)
        nu   : the Phillips-curve slope, nu-bar
    Returns
        inflation pi (%)
    """
    return pi_e + nu * Y


def solve_asad(pi_e, a=0.0, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Short-run output and inflation in one period, where the AD and AS curves cross.

    Equation (13):  Y~ = (a - b m (pi_e - pi_bar)) / (1 + b m nu),  pi = pi_e + nu Y~

    Arguments
        pi_e : expected inflation, last period's inflation (%)
        a    : the demand shock, a-bar
        m    : the policy response, m-bar
        b    : the interest sensitivity of spending, b-bar = b_i + b_nx
        nu   : the Phillips-curve slope, nu-bar
    Returns
        two numbers: short-run output Y~ and inflation pi
    """
    # Step 1: output where the two curves cross
    Y = (a - b * m * (pi_e - PI_BAR)) / (1 + b * m * nu)
    # Step 2: inflation from the AS curve; `return Y, ...` gives back two results
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu)

Two more functions take the long-run model one step further. The quantity theory gives each country’s price level, and bs_price_level builds a price level from the prices of traded and nontraded goods, the starting point of equation (6).

def quantity_price(M, V, Y):
    """The long-run price level of the quantity theory, which leads to equation (2).

    The quantity theory:  P = M V / Y

    Arguments
        M : the money supply, M-bar
        V : the velocity of money, V-bar
        Y : real output, Y-bar
    Returns
        the price level P
    """
    return M * V / Y


def bs_price_level(P_T, A_T, A_N, theta=0.5):
    """The price level of the Balassa-Samuelson model, behind equation (6).

    P = P_T^theta P_N^(1-theta), with P_N from equal wages: P_T A_T = P_N A_N

    Arguments
        P_T   : the price of traded goods
        A_T   : productivity in traded goods
        A_N   : productivity in nontraded goods
        theta : the weight of traded goods in the price level
    Returns
        the price level P
    """
    # Step 1: a worker's output in the traded sector is worth P_T A_T: the wage
    wage = P_T * A_T
    # Step 2: the same wage is paid in the nontraded sector
    P_N = wage / A_N
    # Step 3: the price level weights traded and nontraded prices by theta and 1 - theta
    return P_T ** theta * P_N ** (1 - theta)

Uncovered interest parity, equation (7), gives today’s exchange rate from the expected one and the two interest rates. Solved for the interest rate instead, it gives the rate that defends a peg.

def uip_exchange_rate(E_anchor, i, i_w, years=1):
    """Today's exchange rate from uncovered interest parity.

    Equation (7), applied `years` times:  E = E_anchor ((1 + i) / (1 + i_w))^years

    Arguments
        E_anchor : the exchange rate investors expect at the end, E^e
        i, i_w   : the U.S. and the foreign interest rate (%)
        years    : how many years the gap between them lasts
    Returns
        today's exchange rate E
    """
    # the rates are in percent, so i / 100 is the rate as a share
    return E_anchor * ((1 + i / 100) / (1 + i_w / 100)) ** years


def defend_peg_rate(i_w, expected_fall):
    """The interest rate that keeps uncovered interest parity when the peg may fall.

    Equation (7), solved for i, with E fixed today and expected to fall by `expected_fall` %

    Arguments
        i_w           : the foreign interest rate (%)
        expected_fall : the devaluation markets expect (%)
    Returns
        the interest rate i that defends the peg (%)
    """
    E_ratio = 1 / (1 - expected_fall / 100)              # E_fix / E_expected
    # equation (7): 1 + i = (1 + i_w) E_fix / E_expected
    return 100 * ((1 + i_w / 100) * E_ratio - 1)

Fig. 5 follows the economy period by period. Each period, firms expect last period’s inflation, and the economy jumps to the point where that period’s AD and AS curves cross. simulate repeats this step; shock_list builds the list of demand shocks, one value per period.

def shock_list(size, last=A_LAST):
    """The demand shocks of Fig. 5, one value per period.

    The shock has the given size in periods 1, ..., last and is zero afterwards, for T_MAX periods.

    Arguments
        size : the size of the shock, a-bar
        last : the last period of the shock
    Returns
        a list of T_MAX shocks
    """
    # `values = []` starts an empty list, and `values.append(x)` adds x at its end.
    # `for t in range(1, T_MAX + 1)` repeats the indented lines for t = 1, ..., 20.
    values = []
    for t in range(1, T_MAX + 1):
        if t <= last:
            values.append(size)
        else:
            values.append(0.0)
    return values


def simulate(a_list, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS/AD model, solved period by period.

    Equation (13) in every period; period 0 is the steady state (Y~ = 0, pi = pi_bar).

    Arguments
        a_list : the demand shock of each period (from shock_list)
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        b      : the interest sensitivity of spending, b-bar = b_i + b_nx
        nu     : the Phillips-curve slope, nu-bar
    Returns
        a table with one row per period: the shock, expected inflation, output and inflation
    """
    # Step 1: period 0. `dict(period=0, Y=0.0)` is a dictionary, a set of named
    # values, and `rows` is a list of them, one per period.
    rows = [dict(period=0, a=0.0, pi_e=PI_BAR, Y=0.0, pi=PI_BAR)]
    # Step 2: each period, solve equation (13)
    for t in range(1, len(a_list) + 1):
        # adaptive expectations: `rows[-1]["pi"]` is the value named "pi" in the
        # last element of the list, last period's inflation
        pi_e = rows[-1]["pi"]
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a_list[t - 1], m, b, nu)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, a=a_list[t - 1], pi_e=pi_e, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    # Step 3: `pd.DataFrame(rows)` turns the list of dictionaries into a table,
    # one row per dictionary
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

20.2.4 Drawing and data tools
The figures share a few tools: three draw the model diagrams, and the others read the list of countries, color them and write the titles of the data figures. In Colab, choose countries from a list (hold Ctrl, or Cmd on a Mac, to choose several); on the website, click the legend or pick a group in the menu.






NoteShow the drawing and data tools





Both model diagrams use the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

add_curve draws a curve and writes its name at its last point inside the axes, as the textbook does;
add_point marks a point with a dot, a letter and dashed guides to the axes;
add_arrow draws an arrow between two points.


# @title Drawing tools: curves, points and arrows
def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, x_range, y_range, dash="solid"):
    """Draw one curve and write its label at its last point inside the axes.

    No label is written if label is "". A label such as "AS<sub>8</sub>" uses HTML to write AS with a
    subscript 8.

    Arguments
        fig              : the figure to draw on
        x, y             : the points of the curve (arrays)
        label            : the curve's name, e.g. "IS"
        color            : its color, e.g. TEAL
        x_range, y_range : the two axes, each as [lowest, highest]
        dash             : "solid" or "dash"
    """
    # Step 1: the curve, without a legend entry
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    # Step 2: the points inside both axes. `(x >= 0) & (y <= 8)` is True where both
    # conditions hold, and `x[inside]` keeps the values where `inside` is True.
    inside = (x >= x_range[0]) & (x <= x_range[1]) & (y >= y_range[0]) & (y <= y_range[1])
    # Step 3: the label at the last point inside; `[-1]` takes the last of them
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        fig.add_annotation(x=x[inside][-1], y=y[inside][-1], text=label, showarrow=False,
                           xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_point(fig, x, y, label, x0, y0, guides=True):
    """Mark the point (x, y) with a dot and a label, and dashed guides to the axes.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        x, y   : the point
        label  : its letter, e.g. "B"
        x0, y0 : where the axes start, so the guides end there
        guides : True to draw the dashed lines to the axes
    """
    # Step 1: the dashed guides, from the vertical axis to the point and down
    if guides:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x0, x, x], y=[y, y, y0], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")))
    # Step 2: the dot and its letter
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition="top right",
                             name=label, showlegend=False, textfont=dict(size=16),
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, color="black"):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1), in axis units.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        x0, y0 : where the arrow starts
        x1, y1 : where it points
        color  : its color
    """
    # nothing if the two points almost coincide. `add_annotation` with `axref="x"`
    # and `ayref="y"` draws an arrow from (`ax`, `ay`) to (`x`, `y`) in axis units.
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y", text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor=color)

Five small tools are shared by the data figures:

group_colors gives every country a fixed color, so a line keeps its color when you add or remove others. The textbook’s countries keep the textbook’s colors, and the countries of one menu group (the G7, a region, …) never share a color, as far as Plotly’s 44 dark enough colors allow;
ratio_ticks chooses round tick values for a ratio-scale axis that spans less than a factor of 10 (Plotly’s own ticks crowd there; over wider spans we let Plotly choose);
missing_note adds a note to a title when a chosen country has no data;
high_low names the countries with the highest and the lowest value, for the titles;
book_order puts the textbook’s countries first in a bar chart.

The colors come from a palette of Plotly’s colors, without the pale ones.

# @title Color tool: a palette of 44 colors
# Step 1: the colors that are too pale on a white background
LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]
# Step 2: `px.colors.qualitative.Dark24` and `.Alphabet` are lists of colors that
# Plotly provides, 24 + 26 colors; we keep 44 of them
PALETTE = []
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if color not in LIGHT and color != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(color)
# Step 3: Dark24's medium blue goes last: it is close to the book's navy
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")

group_colors walks through the countries one by one and gives each the cheapest color.

# @title Color tool: a color for every country
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    Arguments
        names  : every country to color
        groups : the lists of countries shown together (the menu views)
        fixed  : {country: color} for the textbook's countries (None for no fixed colors)
    Returns
        a dictionary {country: color}
    """
    # Step 1: start from the fixed colors, and color the other countries A to Z
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue
        # Step 2: `score` gives every color a cost, lower is better: 1 for each country
        # that already uses it, 10 for each one in a large group (Europe has more
        # countries than there are colors) and 100 for each one in a group small enough
        # to avoid any clash
        score = {}
        for color in PALETTE:
            # 1 per country using it anywhere
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                # `a if test else b` gives a when the test is True, b otherwise
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        # Step 3: `min(PALETTE, key=score.get)` picks the color with the lowest cost
        # (the first one on ties)
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)
        # no free color: `PALETTE[::-1]`, the list in reverse order, starts the search
        # from the end of the list, so the leftovers take the last, rarely used colors
        if score[best] >= 10:
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors

ratio_ticks tries the round numbers 1, 1.2, 1.5, …, 9 times every power of 10, and keeps those on the axis.

# @title Drawing tool: round ticks for a ratio-scale axis
def ratio_ticks(low, high):
    """Round tick values between low and high for a ratio-scale axis.

    Arguments
        low, high : the two ends of the axis
    Returns
        a list of tick values, or None (Plotly's own ticks) beyond a factor of 10
    """
    # Step 1: over a factor of 10 or more, Plotly's own ticks are fine
    if high / low >= 10:
        return None
    # Step 2: every round number between low and high
    ticks = []
    for power in range(-3, 6):
        for step in [1, 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]:
            if low <= step * 10 ** power <= high:
                ticks.append(round(step * 10 ** power, 6))
    return ticks

missing_note writes the names of the chosen countries without data in a second, smaller title line.

# @title Drawing tool: a note on the countries without data
def missing_note(wanted, found):
    """A second, smaller title line naming the chosen countries that have no data.

    Arguments
        wanted : the chosen countries
        found  : the countries that have data
    Returns
        the extra title line, or '' if all have data
    """
    # Step 1: the chosen countries without data
    missing = []
    for name in wanted:
        if name not in set(found):
            missing.append(name)
    # Step 2: the note. In a Plotly title, `<br>` starts a new line and
    # `<sup>...</sup>` writes smaller text.
    if len(missing) == 0:
        return ""
    if len(missing) > 3:
        return f"<br><sup>no data for {len(missing)} of the chosen countries</sup>"
    # `", ".join(missing)` glues the names into one text, with ", " between them
    return "<br><sup>no data: " + ", ".join(missing) + "</sup>"

The last two tools write the titles and the order of the bar charts. The cell ends by trying the tools on a few examples.

# @title Drawing tools: the highest and lowest values, and the order of the bars
def high_low(values, fmt=".0f"):
    """The countries with the highest and the lowest value, for the titles: 'A 12, B 3'.

    Arguments
        values : one value per country (a pandas Series with the countries as index)
        fmt    : the format code of the numbers, e.g. ".1f" for one decimal
    Returns
        the text, with one name only for one country
    """
    # In f"{value:{fmt}}" the format itself is a variable: fmt=".0f" shows no
    # decimals, ".1f" one. `idxmax()` gives the country with the highest value.
    text = f"{values.idxmax()} {values.max():{fmt}}"
    if len(values) > 1:
        text = text + f", {values.idxmin()} {values.min():{fmt}}"
    return text


def book_order(countries, book):
    """The textbook's countries in the textbook's order, then the others alphabetically.

    Arguments
        countries : the countries of a bar chart
        book      : the textbook's countries, in the textbook's order
    Returns
        the list of countries in that order
    """
    # Step 1: the textbook's countries first
    order = []
    for name in book:
        if name in countries:
            order.append(name)
    # Step 2: then the others, A to Z
    for name in sorted(countries):
        if name not in order:
            order.append(name)
    return order

dollar_index_data computes the index of each chosen currency and the title of the chart. The drawing code then draws one line per currency.

def dollar_index_data(countries, base):
    """The price of a dollar in each chosen currency, as an index (Fig. 1).

    index = 100 x (currency per dollar) / (its average in the base year)

    Arguments
        countries : the countries (or currency areas) to show
        base      : the base year, in which every index is 100
    Returns
        picked : one row per currency and month, with the index in the column "index"
        title  : the chart's title: the highest and the lowest latest index, and the
                 currencies that have no data in the base year
    """
    # Step 1: the chosen currencies. `isin(countries)` is True in the rows whose
    # country is in the list
    picked = fx_all[fx_all.country.isin(countries)].copy()
    # Step 2: each currency's average in the base year: `groupby("country").mean()`
    # averages the base-year months of each country
    level = picked[picked.year == base].groupby("country").per_usd.mean()
    # Step 3: the index. `.map(level)` looks up that average for every row
    picked["index"] = (100 * picked.per_usd / picked.country.map(level)).round(1)
    # a currency with no data in the base year gets NaN, and `dropna` removes it
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["index"])
    # Step 4: the title names the highest and the lowest latest index (`high_low`)
    latest = picked.groupby("country")["index"].last()     # each currency's last month
    title = f"No data in {base} for these currencies"
    if len(latest) > 0:
        title = f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100), latest: " + high_low(latest)
    # `missing_note` adds the chosen currencies without data in the base year
    return picked, title + missing_note(countries, level.index)

def dollar_index(countries=("Japan", "Euro area"), base=1999, scale="linear"):
    """The price of a dollar in any currencies, as an index (100 in the base year).

    Draws Fig. 1 for any currency (inspired by Fig. 20.1 in Jones).

    Arguments
        countries : the countries (or currency areas) to show
        base      : the base year, in which every index is 100
        scale     : "linear", or "ratio" for a ratio (log) scale
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (dollar_index_data)
    picked, title = dollar_index_data(countries, base)
    # Step 2: one line per currency, in its fixed color; `log_y=True` draws a ratio
    # scale, on which equal distances are equal percentage changes
    fig = px.line(
        picked,
        x="date",
        y="index",
        color="label",
        hover_name="label",
        color_discrete_map=FX_COLORS,
        log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
        title=title,
        labels={"date": "Year", "index": f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100)"},
    )
    # Step 3: the dotted line at 100, the base year's price of a dollar.
    # `add_hline` draws a horizontal line across the whole figure
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    # round tick values on the ratio scale (`ratio_ticks`)
    if scale == "ratio" and len(picked) > 0:
        fig.update_yaxes(
            tickvals=ratio_ticks(picked["index"].min(), picked["index"].max())
        )
    # the axis starts in 1965, so that no tick label sits in the corner
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", xaxis_range=["1965-01-01", "2027-06-01"])
    return fig

# control and draws the figure again every time you change one: `SelectMultiple` is

inflation_data picks the chosen countries and computes their mean inflation for the title; the drawing code, inflation_chart, then draws the textbook’s figure for any list of countries. Hyperinflations reach thousands of percent, so the vertical axis stops at 100 percent, and the title says so when a line is cut.

def inflation_data(countries):
    """Inflation of the chosen countries, and the title of Fig. 2.

    The title reports the highest and the lowest mean inflation over 1971-2024.

    Arguments
        countries : the countries to show
    Returns
        picked : one row per country and year, inflation in percent
        title  : the chart's title, with the mean inflation rates
    """
    # Step 1: the chosen countries
    picked = inflation_all[inflation_all.country.isin(countries)]
    # Step 2: each country's mean inflation over 1971-2024
    span = picked[(picked.year >= 1971) & (picked.year <= 2024)]
    means = span.groupby("country").inflation.mean()
    # Step 3: the title names the highest and the lowest mean
    title = "No inflation data for these countries"
    if len(means) > 0:
        title = "Mean inflation 1971–2024 (%): " + high_low(means, ".1f")
    # a hyperinflation: the axis stops at 100 percent, and the title says so
    if len(picked) > 0 and picked.inflation.max() > 100:
        title = title + "; axis cut at 100"
    return picked, title + missing_note(countries, means.index)

def inflation_chart(countries=("United States", "Japan")):
    """Consumer-price inflation of any countries, percent per year.

    Draws Fig. 2 (inspired by Fig. 20.2 in Jones) for any list of countries.

    Arguments
        countries : the countries to show
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (inflation_data)
    picked, title = inflation_data(countries)
    # Step 2: the top of the axis: at least 25 percent, at most 100
    top = 25.0
    if len(picked) > 0:
        top = min(max(25.0, 1.05 * picked.inflation.max()), 100.0)
    # Step 3: one line per country; `color_discrete_map` fixes each country's color
    fig = px.line(
        picked,
        x="year",
        y="inflation",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS,
        title=title,
        labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation (percent per year)"},
    )
    # the dashed line at zero: below it, prices fall
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    # Step 4: the bottom of the axis, at least 3 points below zero.
    # `a if c else b` is a when c is true, and b otherwise
    bottom = min(-3.0, picked.inflation.min() - 1) if len(picked) > 0 else -3.0
    # the axis starts in 1955, so that 1960 is not a tick label in the corner
    fig.update_layout(
        yaxis_range=[bottom, top],
        xaxis_range=[1955, 2026],
        legend_title_text="",
    )
    return fig

def big_mac_table(release="2022-07-01"):
    """Table 20.1: Big Mac prices in local currency and in dollars, for one release.

    The dollar price is the local price divided by the exchange rate; vs_US_percent
    compares it with the U.S. dollar price.

    Arguments
        release : the date of the release, e.g. "2022-07-01"
    Returns
        a table with one row per economy of Table 20.1
    """
    # Step 1: one release. `set_index("country")` uses the country names as row
    # labels, and `.loc[BOOK_ROWS]` picks the rows in the order of the list
    table = big_mac[big_mac.release == release].set_index("country").loc[BOOK_ROWS]
    # Step 2: dearer (+) or cheaper (-) than in the U.S., in percent. A new column
    # is created simply by assigning to it
    us_price = table.loc["United States", "dollar_price"]
    table["vs_US_percent"] = 100 * (table.dollar_price / us_price - 1)
    columns = ["local_price", "currency", "ex_rate", "dollar_price", "vs_US_percent"]
    return table[columns].round(2)

Goal. See that the real exchange rate can move for decades, and learn one reason why: the Balassa-Samuelson effect.

We can also build the real exchange rate ourselves, from the data of Figs. 1 and 2. Inflation tells us how fast the price level grows each year, so multiplying the growth factors \(1 + \pi_t/100\) year after year gives the price level.

# Step 1: yen per dollar, yearly average. `fx.date.dt.year` takes the year out of
# each date, and `groupby("year").yen_per_usd.mean()` averages the 12 months
fx["year"] = fx.date.dt.year
yen = fx.groupby("year").yen_per_usd.mean()

# Step 2: the consumer price levels, 1971 = 1. `.cumprod()` is the cumulative
# product: it multiplies the growth factors year after year, P_t = P_t-1 (1 + pi_t/100)
prices = inflation[inflation.year >= 1971].set_index("year")
growth_us = 1 + prices.inflation_us / 100
growth_jp = 1 + prices.inflation_jpn / 100
P_us = growth_us.cumprod() / growth_us.loc[1971]
P_jp = growth_jp.cumprod() / growth_jp.loc[1971]

# Step 3: the dollar price of Japanese goods relative to U.S. goods, (P_Japan / E) /
# P_US. Dividing two pandas series lines up their rows by year automatically
estimate = (P_jp / yen) / P_us
estimate = (100 * estimate / estimate.loc[1971]).dropna()  # index, 1971 = 100
estimate.loc[[1971, 1995, 2023, 2024]].round(1)

Key numbers: the law of one price, 1971–1995
If the law of one price had held, the yen-dollar rate would have changed each year only by the inflation gap. We apply the growth factors of 1972–1995 to the 1971 rate.

# Step 1: the factor by which the law of one price moves the yen-dollar rate from
# 1971 to 1995: the product of the yearly factors (1 + pi_Japan/100) / (1 + pi_US/100).
# `.prod()` multiplies all the values of a series, here the 24 yearly factors
years = inflation[(inflation.year >= 1972) & (inflation.year <= 1995)]
ratio = ((1 + years.inflation_jpn / 100) / (1 + years.inflation_us / 100)).prod()
# Step 2: the 1995 rate that the law of one price predicts, and the actual one
print(f"Yen per dollar, 1971 average:                     {yen[1971]:.0f}")
print(f"1995 rate predicted by the law of one price:      {yen[1971] * ratio:.0f}")
print(f"Actual 1995 average:                              {yen[1995]:.0f}")

The Balassa-Samuelson effect in the Big Mac data
The explanation is that only traded goods obey the law of one price. Haircuts and restaurant meals cannot be shipped, and their prices follow local wages. As an economy grows, wages rise, nontraded goods become dearer, and the real exchange rate appreciates. So richer countries should have dearer Big Macs (the burger includes the work of the staff and the rent of the restaurant). We check this with the latest Big Mac release and GDP per person.

rer_data computes the chosen measure for the chosen countries, and the title of the chart.

def rer_data(countries, measure):
    """The real exchange rate of the chosen countries, and the title of the chart.

    The index divides each country's rer by its 1971 value; the level is rer x 100
    (the U.S. = 100 in every year).

    Arguments
        countries : the countries to show
        measure   : "index, 1971 = 100" or "level, U.S. = 100"
    Returns
        picked : one row per country and year, with the measure in the column "value"
        title  : the chart's title, with the highest and the lowest value in 2023
    """
    # Step 1: the chosen countries, and the measure
    picked = rer_all[rer_all.country.isin(countries)].copy()
    if measure == "index, 1971 = 100":
        # each country's 1971 value, looked up for every row with `.map(start)`
        start = picked[picked.year == 1971].set_index("country").rer
        picked["value"] = (100 * picked.rer / picked.country.map(start)).round(1)
        picked = picked[picked.year >= 1971]
    else:
        picked["value"] = (100 * picked.rer).round(1)    # the U.S. = 100 in every year
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["value"])
    # Step 2: the title names the highest and the lowest value in 2023
    last = picked[picked.year == 2023].set_index("country").value
    title = "No data for these countries"
    if len(last) > 0:
        title = "Real exchange rate in 2023: " + high_low(last)
    return picked, title + missing_note(countries, picked.country.unique())

Each country gets a fixed color. The website menu shows each group’s countries with data in 1971 (the index needs a 1971 value), so these smaller groups must not share colors either.

Germany (index 163) and Switzerland (262) followed Japan up until 1995: their currencies gained against the dollar much faster than their inflation fell below U.S. inflation. By 2023 Japan (91) and Germany (87) were back below their 1971 level, while Switzerland stayed at 150.
Switch to the level: in 2023 GDP cost about as much in Switzerland as in the U.S. (101), 69 percent of the U.S. price in Japan, 52 percent in China and 25 percent in India. Poorer countries have lower price levels, as the Balassa-Samuelson effect predicts.
Look at your data: Bermuda’s price level in 2000 is more than 1,000 times the U.S. one, an obvious error in the table. Check a surprising number before you build on it.

In the short run, the exchange rate is set in the market for currencies, and that market is enormous. The textbook compares the daily trade in foreign exchange, more than 5 trillion dollars, with GDP.

section: 20.4 The open economy in the short-run model
text:
20.4 The open economy in the short-run model
Now prices are sticky and the exchange rate reacts to interest rates. These two model figures show how this flattens the IS curve and turns a rise in foreign interest rates into a demand shock.

Fig. 4: Increasing interest rates and the IS curve
Goal. See why the IS curve is flatter in an open economy: a higher interest rate lowers net exports as well as investment.
The central bank raises the real interest rate from \(\bar{r}\) to \(R'\). The economy moves along the IS curve from \(A\) to \(B\). Two forces lower output:
\[\uparrow R \;\Rightarrow\; \downarrow \frac{I}{\bar{Y}} \quad\text{and}\quad
\uparrow R \Rightarrow \uparrow E \Rightarrow \uparrow \frac{EP}{P^w} \Rightarrow \downarrow \frac{NX}{\bar{Y}}.\]
From the IS curve, equation (11), \(\tilde{Y}' = -(\bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx})(R' - \bar{r})\). The dashed gray line is the IS curve without the trade channel (\(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0\)), the closed economy of Chapter 11.
First we compute the numbers the figure reports. tightening_point finds output at the new interest rate, point \(B\), and splits its fall into the investment and the net-export channel.

def tightening_point(R_new, b_nx, b_i):
    """Output after the central bank raises R, and its two channels (Fig. 4).

    Equation (11) with a = 0:  Y~' = -(b_i + b_nx) (R' - r-bar)

    Arguments
        R_new : the new real interest rate, R' (%)
        b_nx  : the interest sensitivity of net exports, b-bar_nx
        b_i   : the interest sensitivity of investment, b-bar_i
    Returns
        Y_new  : short-run output at R', point B (%)
        invest : the fall through investment, -b_i (R' - r-bar)
        trade  : the fall through net exports, -b_nx (R' - r-bar)
    """
    # point B on the open-economy IS curve, equation (11)
    Y_new = is_curve(R_new, b_i=b_i, b_nx=b_nx)
    # the two channels; + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0, so the title never shows "-0.0"
    invest = -b_i * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0
    trade = -b_nx * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0
    return Y_new, invest, trade



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, increasing interest rates and the IS curve
# Step 1: the real interest rates at which we draw the IS curves.
# `np.linspace(9, 2, 141)` gives 141 evenly spaced values from 9 down to 2
R_LINE = np.linspace(9, 2, 141)              # high to low: the label goes at R = 2
R_UP = np.linspace(2, 9, 141)                # low to high: the label goes at the top
X_IS, R_AXIS = [-11, 5], [2, 9]              # fixed axes: you see the curve turn


def tightening(R_new=6.0, b_nx=B_NX, b_i=B_I):
    """The IS curve when the central bank raises R from r-bar to R_new.

    Draws Fig. 4 (adapted from Fig. 20.4 in Jones): the economy moves along the IS
    curve from A to B. The dashed gray line is the IS curve without trade.

    Arguments
        R_new : the new real interest rate, R' (%)
        b_nx  : the interest sensitivity of net exports, b-bar_nx
        b_i   : the interest sensitivity of investment, b-bar_i
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (tightening_point)
    Y_new, invest, trade = tightening_point(R_new, b_nx, b_i)
    # Step 2: the IS curve without trade (dashed gray), then the open-economy one
    fig = go.Figure()
    if b_nx > 0:
        closed = is_curve(R_UP, b_i=b_i, b_nx=0.0)
        add_curve(fig, closed, R_UP, "IS without trade", GRAY, X_IS, R_AXIS, "dash")
    open_is = is_curve(R_LINE, b_i=b_i, b_nx=b_nx)
    add_curve(fig, open_is, R_LINE, "IS", BLUE, X_IS, R_AXIS)
    # Step 3: point A, and point B unless the rate does not change (B is then A)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", X_IS[0], R_AXIS[0])
    if R_new != R_BAR:
        add_point(fig, Y_new, R_new, "B", X_IS[0], R_AXIS[0])
    # Step 4: the interest rate rises (arrow on the left) ...
    add_arrow(fig, X_IS[0] + 0.6, R_BAR, X_IS[0] + 0.6, R_new)
    # ... and output falls (arrow at the bottom)
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, R_AXIS[0] + 0.3, Y_new, R_AXIS[0] + 0.3)
    # Step 5: the title reports the new output and its two channels
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"R′ = {R_new:.1f}%  →  Ỹ′ = {Y_new + 0.0:.1f}%   "
            f"(investment {invest:.1f}, net exports {trade:.1f})"
        ),
        xaxis=dict(
            title="Short-run output, Ỹ (percent)",
            range=X_IS,
            tickvals=list(range(-10, 5, 2)),
            zeroline=False,
        ),
        yaxis=dict(
            title="Real interest rate, R (percent)",
            range=R_AXIS,
            tickvals=list(range(3, 9)),
            zeroline=False,
        ),
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

With the baseline, raising \(R\) from 5 to 6 percent lowers output by 2 percent: 1 point through investment and 1 point through net exports. Without trade, output would fall by only 1 percent.
Raise \(\bar{b}_{nx}\): the IS curve turns flatter and point \(B\) moves left. The more net exports react to the exchange rate, the more powerful monetary policy is.
Nothing else changes: the curve still passes through \(A\), because at \(R = \bar{r}\) there is no gap to react to.

Fig. 5: An increase in foreign interest rates
Goal. Follow the international transmission of monetary policy: the European Central Bank raises its interest rate, and the U.S. economy booms, then slumps.
When the foreign real interest rate rises to \(\bar{R}^w = 7\) percent, 2 points above \(\bar{r}\), investors move from dollars to euros, the dollar depreciates, U.S. goods become cheap and U.S. net exports rise. In the IS curve, equation (11), this is a positive demand shock, \(\bar{a} = \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}) = 2\), so the AD curve shifts out to AD₁. Then the familiar dynamics of Chapter 13 take over:

period 1: the economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\), with output and inflation above normal;
periods 2–9: inflation rises, the Fed raises U.S. interest rates, and the economy climbs AD₁ toward \(C\) (period 8 in the textbook), with output back at potential but inflation above target;
period 10: the foreign rate falls back to \(\bar{r}\), the shock ends, AD shifts back, and the economy drops to a recession at \(D\); it then slides down AD back to \(A\).

The function draws period t: the original AS curve, the AS curve of period t, both AD curves (the one that holds in period t in full color), the path so far with the textbook’s letters, and the path still to come in gray.
First we compute the path that the figure draws. foreign_shock_path turns the foreign interest rate into a demand shock, equation (11), and simulates the economy period by period.

def foreign_shock_path(gap, b_nx, m):
    """The economy's path when the foreign real interest rate rises (Fig. 5).

    Equation (11): a-bar = b_nx (R_w - r-bar) in periods 1 to A_LAST, then
    equation (13) in every period (simulate)

    Arguments
        gap  : the foreign rate minus r-bar, R_w - r-bar (points)
        b_nx : the interest sensitivity of net exports, b-bar_nx
        m    : the policy response, m-bar
    Returns
        a    : the demand shock from abroad, a-bar
        b    : the interest sensitivity of spending, b-bar = b_i + b_nx
        path : one row per period: shock, expected inflation, output Y and inflation pi
    """
    # Step 1: equation (11): the demand shock from abroad
    a = foreign_shock(R_BAR + gap, b_nx)
    # Step 2: trade makes spending more sensitive to the interest rate
    b = B_I + b_nx
    # Step 3: the AS/AD model, period by period
    path = simulate(shock_list(a), m, b)
    return a, b, path



Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, the AS and AD curves
# Step 1: where we draw the curves, the fixed axes, and the textbook's letters
Y_LINE = np.linspace(-6, 6, 121)                # output levels for the AS curves
PI_LINE = np.linspace(12, -4, 161)              # inflation, high to low, for AD
X_AD, PI_AXIS = [-3.5, 3.5], [-0.5, 7.5]        # fixed axes
LETTERS = {0: "A", 1: "B", 8: "C", 10: "D"}     # the textbook's letters, by period
FADED = "rgba(22,82,140,0.35)"                  # light blue: the AD curve not in force


def add_asad_curves(fig, a, pi_e, t, m, b):
    """Draw the AS curves (original and period t) and the AD curves of Fig. 5.

    The AD curve that holds in period t is drawn in full color, the other one faded.

    Arguments
        fig  : the figure to draw on
        a    : the demand shock from abroad, a-bar
        pi_e : expected inflation in period t (%)
        t    : the period shown
        m    : the policy response, m-bar
        b    : the interest sensitivity of spending, b-bar
    """
    # Step 1: the original AS curve, and the AS curve of period t unless it is the
    # same line; its label only when the two lines are far enough apart
    add_curve(fig, Y_LINE, as_inflation(Y_LINE, PI_BAR), "AS", TEAL, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    if abs(pi_e - PI_BAR) > 0.05:
        label = f"AS<sub>{t}</sub>" if abs(pi_e - PI_BAR) > 0.6 else ""
        add_curve(fig, Y_LINE, as_inflation(Y_LINE, pi_e), label, TEAL, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    # Step 2: the original AD curve, faded while the shock lasts (periods 1 to A_LAST)
    shock_on = 1 <= t <= A_LAST
    ad_label = f"AD = AD<sub>{t}</sub>" if t > A_LAST else "AD"
    ad_line = ad_output(PI_LINE, 0.0, m, b)
    ad_color = FADED if shock_on else BLUE
    add_curve(fig, ad_line, PI_LINE, ad_label, ad_color, X_AD, PI_AXIS)
    # Step 3: the shifted curve AD1, in full color while the shock lasts; no label
    # when it would sit on top of AD's
    if a != 0:
        label = "AD<sub>1</sub>" if abs(a) > 0.8 and abs(a / (b * m)) > 0.6 else ""
        ad1_line = ad_output(PI_LINE, a, m, b)
        ad1_color = BLUE if shock_on else FADED
        add_curve(fig, ad1_line, PI_LINE, label, ad1_color, X_AD, PI_AXIS)




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, the path of the economy
def add_path(fig, path, t):
    """Draw the economy's path up to period t, and the rest of the path in gray.

    Draws the path of Fig. 5: dots, arrows and the textbook's letters up to period t.

    Arguments
        fig  : the figure to draw on
        path : the simulated path (from simulate), one row per period
        t    : the period shown
    """
    # Step 1: the path still to come: gray dots on a dotted line
    future = path[path.period >= t]
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=future.Y,
            y=future.pi,
            mode="lines+markers",
            showlegend=False,
            hoverinfo="skip",
            line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dot"),
            marker=dict(color=GRAY, size=5),
        )
    )
    # Step 2: an arrow from each period to the next, up to period t
    for s in range(1, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s])
    # Step 3: the dots and the textbook's letters. A letter is left out when its
    # point lies within 0.3 points of output and 0.6 points of inflation of a point
    # that already has one (a small shock or a strong policy keeps B, C, D near A)
    written = []                                # the points that already carry a letter
    for s in range(t + 1):
        if s in LETTERS:
            letter = LETTERS[s]
            # `for x, y in written:` goes through a list of pairs and unpacks each
            # pair into x and y
            for x, y in written:
                if abs(path.Y[s] - x) < 0.3 and abs(path.pi[s] - y) < 0.6:
                    letter = ""                 # too close to a letter already written
            add_point(
                fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], letter, X_AD[0], PI_AXIS[0], guides=False
            )
            if letter != "":
                written.append((path.Y[s], path.pi[s]))




Show the drawing code
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, an increase in foreign interest rates
def foreign_rate_shock(gap=RW_GAP, t=10, b_nx=B_NX, m=M_BAR):
    """The AS/AD diagram in period t after the foreign real interest rate rises.

    Draws Fig. 5 (adapted from Fig. 20.5 in Jones): the foreign rate is gap points
    above r-bar in periods 1-9, and the economy moves from A to B, C and D.

    Arguments
        gap  : the foreign rate minus r-bar, R_w - r-bar (points)
        t    : the period shown
        b_nx : the interest sensitivity of net exports, b-bar_nx
        m    : the policy response, m-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (foreign_shock_path). `path.loc[t]` is the
    # row of period t, and `now.pi` its value in the column pi
    a, b, path = foreign_shock_path(gap, b_nx, m)
    now = path.loc[t]
    # Step 2: the curves, then the path
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_asad_curves(fig, a, now.pi_e, t, m, b)
    add_path(fig, path, t)
    # Step 3: the title reports inflation and output in period t, and the shock
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0:+.2f}%   "
            f"(Rʷ − r̄ = {gap:.1f}, so ā = {a:.2f} in periods 1–{A_LAST})"
        ),
        xaxis=dict(
            title="Output, Ỹ (percent)",
            range=X_AD,
            tickvals=list(range(-3, 4)),
            zeroline=False,
        ),
        yaxis=dict(
            title="Inflation, π (percent)",
            range=PI_AXIS,
            tickvals=list(range(0, 8)),
            zeroline=False,
        ),
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

At \(B\) (period 1) output is 1 percent above potential and inflation 3 percent: half of the shock goes into output, half into inflation, because \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\) as in Chapter 13.
At \(C\) output is back at potential, but inflation is close to \(\bar{\pi} + \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m}) = 4\) percent. The AS curves of periods 8, 9 and 10 are almost the same line, which is why the textbook draws \(C\) and \(D\) on one curve, AS₈.
When the shock ends, the economy pays for the boom with a recession at \(D\): output 1 percent below potential.
The U.S. did nothing, yet its economy boomed and slumped: a change in interest rates abroad is a demand shock at home.

text:
20.5 Exchange-rate regimes and the policy trilemma
Countries have chosen very different ways to manage their currencies, from the gold standard to free floating. This section follows that history and the trade-off behind every choice, including what happens when a fixed rate breaks.

Fig. 6: The U.K.-U.S. exchange rate
Goal. Read two centuries of exchange-rate history in one line: the gold standard, Bretton Woods and floating rates.
Under the gold standard each country fixed the price of an ounce of gold in its currency. From 1834 the United States paid about 20.67 dollars an ounce and the United Kingdom 4.25 pounds, so a dollar was worth \(4.25/20.67 \approx 0.206\) pounds. Under Bretton Woods (1944 to the early 1970s) other currencies were pegged to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at 35 dollars an ounce. Since 1973 the major currencies float.

What to notice.

For most of the 19th century the line is flat at the gold parity. The exception is the Civil War: the U.S. left gold, and in 1864 the dollar fell to 0.100 pounds, half its value.
Bretton Woods shows up as long flat steps: 0.357 pounds (2.80 dollars per pound) in the 1950s and 1960s, 0.417 (2.40 dollars) after the pound’s devaluation in 1967.
Since 1973 the line moves a lot every year. And over the two centuries the dollar appreciated, from 0.22 pounds in 1791 to 0.76 in 2025, as the U.S. economy overtook the British one.


Key numbers: how stable is each regime?
We measure stability by the typical yearly change of the exchange rate: the standard deviation of its percent changes.

# Step 1: the gold parity, from the two gold prices
print(f"Gold parity: 4.25 / 20.67 = {4.25 / 20.67:.4f} pounds per dollar")
# Step 2: the three regimes. A dictionary maps each name to a pair of years
REGIMES = {
    "Gold standard, 1880–1913": (1880, 1913),
    "Bretton Woods, 1951–1966": (1951, 1966),
    "Floating rates, 1974–2025": (1974, 2025),
}
# Step 3: the yearly changes. `.pct_change()` computes the percent change from one
# row (year) to the next
rate = uk.set_index("year").gbp_per_usd
changes = 100 * rate.pct_change()
# Step 4: each regime's average and typical yearly change: `.std()` is the standard
# deviation, the typical size of the changes. `first, last = REGIMES[name]` unpacks
# the pair of years
for name in REGIMES:
    first, last = REGIMES[name]
    print(f"{name}: average {rate.loc[first:last].mean():.3f} pounds per dollar, "
          f"typical yearly change {changes.loc[first:last].std():.2f}%")

Gold parity: 4.25 / 20.67 = 0.2056 pounds per dollar
Gold standard, 1880–1913: average 0.206 pounds per dollar, typical yearly change 0.26%

The units differ by factors of trillions, so we show an index (base year = 100) on a ratio scale. The dotted lines mark 1914 (the gold standard breaks down), 1945 (the end of the war; Bretton Woods follows) and 1973 (floating).
history_data computes the index of each chosen country and the title of the chart.

def history_data(countries, base):
    """The price of a dollar in 17 currencies since 1870, as an index (Fig. 6).

    index = 100 x (currency per dollar) / (its value in the base year)

    Arguments
        countries : the countries to show
        base      : the base year, in which every index is 100
    Returns
        picked : one row per country and year, with the index in the column "index"
        title  : the chart's title, with the highest and the lowest index in 2020
    """
    # Step 1: the chosen countries, and each one's rate in the base year
    picked = fx_hist[fx_hist.country.isin(countries)].copy()
    start = picked[picked.year == base].set_index("country").per_usd
    # Step 2: the index; a country with no rate in the base year drops out
    picked["index"] = 100 * picked.per_usd / picked.country.map(start)
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["index"])
    # Step 3: the title names the highest and the lowest index in 2020
    last = picked[picked.year == 2020].set_index("country")["index"]
    title = f"No data in {base} for these countries"
    if len(last) > 0:
        title = f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100) in 2020: " + high_low(last, ".3g")
    return picked, title + missing_note(countries, start.index)

Fig. 7: The policy trilemma in open economies
Goal. See why an open economy can have at most two of three good things: a stable exchange rate, its own monetary policy, and free flows of international finance.
The textbook draws the policy trilemma as a triangle: the three goals are its corners, and each side is a regime that achieves the two goals at its ends and gives up the one opposite. Here the triangle is live. A small model from the chapter computes what happens when the foreign central bank (say, the Fed) raises its interest rate by \(\Delta i^w\), while your economy needs its own interest rate to change by \(\Delta i^{need}\):

with free financial flows, the exchange rate moves with the interest gap (uncovered interest parity, equation 8: \(\uparrow i \Rightarrow \uparrow E\)), \(\%\Delta E = \eta\,(\Delta i - \Delta i^w)\), with an illustrative \(\eta = 5\) percent per point;
floating exchange rate: the central bank sets \(\Delta i = \Delta i^{need}\), and the exchange rate moves;
currency board (or monetary union): to keep \(E\) fixed, the interest rate must follow abroad, \(\Delta i = \Delta i^w\);
capital controls: the central bank sets \(\Delta i = \Delta i^{need}\) and keeps \(E\) fixed, because it rations the trade in its currency, so money cannot flow freely.


# Step 1: the slope of uncovered interest parity, and the goal each regime gives up
ETA = 5.0          # percent change of E per point of interest gap (illustrative)
# the goal each regime gives up: the corner opposite its side of the triangle
LOST = {
    "floating exchange rate": "stable exchange rate",
    "currency board": "monetary autonomy",
    "capital controls": "free financial flows",
}


def trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need):
    """The policy trilemma as a model: what each regime does with its interest rate.

    Floating: di = di_need, %dE = ETA (di - di_w). Currency board: di = di_w, dE = 0.
    Capital controls: di = di_need, dE = 0.

    Arguments
        regime   : "floating exchange rate", "currency board" or "capital controls"
        di_world : the rise of the foreign interest rate, delta i^w (points)
        di_need  : the change in the interest rate the economy needs (points)
    Returns
        di   : the change in the domestic interest rate (points)
        dE   : the percent change in the exchange rate E
        lost : the goal the regime gives up
    """
    # Step 1: the interest rate
    if regime == "currency board":
        di = di_world                   # the peg forces the rate to follow abroad
    else:
        di = di_need                    # floating or capital controls: it chooses
    # Step 2: the exchange rate
    if regime == "floating exchange rate":
        dE = ETA * (di - di_world)      # free capital flows move the exchange rate
    else:
        dE = 0.0                        # fixed by the peg, or by rationing
    return di, dE + 0.0, LOST[regime]

def draw_sides(fig, regime):

    Draws the sides of Fig. 7, each with its label along it.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        regime : "floating exchange rate", "currency board" or "capital controls"

    )

# @title Drawing code: Fig. 7, the corners of the triangle
def draw_triangle(fig, regime):
    """Draw the trilemma triangle for one regime.

    Draws the triangle of Fig. 7: the chosen side thick and green (draw_sides), and
    the goal it gives up marked with a gray cross.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        regime : "floating exchange rate", "currency board" or "capital controls"
    """
    # Step 1: the triangle and its sides
    draw_sides(fig, regime)
    # Step 2: each corner: a green dot for a goal kept, a gray cross for the one lost
    for goal in CORNERS:
        kept = goal != LOST[regime]
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=[CORNERS[goal][0]],
                y=[CORNERS[goal][1]],
                mode="markers",
                name=goal,
                showlegend=False,
                marker=dict(
                    size=20,
                    color=GREEN if kept else GRAY,
                    symbol="circle" if kept else "x",
                ),
            )
        )
        # its label. `xanchor="right"` makes a text end at its point instead of
        # being centered on it
        x, y, xanchor, yanchor, text = CORNER_TEXT[goal]
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=x,
            y=y,
            text=text,
            xanchor=xanchor,
            yanchor=yanchor,
            showarrow=False,
            font=dict(size=14, color="black" if kept else GRAY),
        )

def trilemma(regime="floating exchange rate", di_world=1.0, di_need=0.0):
    """The policy trilemma: the regime's side of the triangle, and its outcome.

    Draws Fig. 7 (adapted from Fig. 20.7 in Jones). The foreign rate rises by
    di_world, and the economy needs its own rate to change by di_need.

    Arguments
        regime   : "floating exchange rate", "currency board" or "capital controls"
        di_world : the rise of the foreign interest rate, delta i^w (points)
        di_need  : the change in the interest rate the economy needs (points)
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the outcome of the regime (trilemma_outcome)
    di, dE, lost = trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need)
    flows = "blocked" if regime == "capital controls" else "free"
    # Step 2: the triangle
    fig = go.Figure()
    draw_triangle(fig, regime)
    # Step 3: the readout in a box at the top right, an annotation with a border
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=2.72,
        y=1.97,
        xanchor="right",
        yanchor="top",
        showarrow=False,
        align="left",
        font=dict(size=13, color=BLUE),
        bordercolor=BLUE,
        borderpad=6,
        bgcolor="white",
        text=(
            f"Interest rate: {di:+.1f} pt<br>Exchange rate: {dE:+.1f}%<br>"
            f"Capital flows: {flows}"
        ),
    )
    # Step 4: `visible=False` hides the axes, and the small margin lets the triangle
    # fill the figure
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[-0.75, 2.75])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[-0.38, 2.0])
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"{regime.capitalize()}: Δi = {di:+.1f}, %ΔE = {dE:+.1f}; lost: {lost}",
        margin=dict(l=30, r=30, t=60, b=30),
    )
    return fig

crisis_data computes the index of each chosen currency and finds the deepest fall for the title.

# The textbook's four crises: the countries shown at the start
BOOK_CRISIS = ("Argentina", "South Korea", "Mexico", "Indonesia")


def crisis_data(countries, base):
    """The dollar value of each chosen currency, as an index (Fig. 8).

    index = 100 x (currency per dollar in the base year) / (currency per dollar),
    with end-of-year rates: a fall to 40 means the currency buys 40% of its dollars

    Arguments
        countries : the countries to show
        base      : the base year, in which every index is 100
    Returns
        picked : one row per country and year, with the index in the column "index"
        title  : the chart's title, with the deepest fall among the chosen currencies
    """
    # Step 1: the chosen countries, and each one's rate at the end of the base year
    picked = fx_crisis[fx_crisis.country.isin(countries)].copy()
    start = picked[picked.year == base].set_index("country").per_usd_eop
    # Step 2: the index; a country without a rate in the base year drops out
    picked["index"] = 100 * picked.country.map(start) / picked.per_usd_eop
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["index"])
    # Step 3: the deepest fall among the chosen currencies, for the title
    low = picked.sort_values("index").head(1)
    title = f"No data at the end of {base} for these countries"
    if len(low) > 0:
        title = (f"Currencies vs the dollar ({base} = 100): "
                 f"lowest {low.country.iloc[0]}, "
                 f"{low['index'].iloc[0]:.3g} in {low.year.iloc[0]}")
    return picked, title + missing_note(countries, start.index)

def crisis_chart(countries=BOOK_CRISIS, base=1991, scale="linear"):
    """The dollar value of any currencies, index = 100 at the end of the base year.

    Draws Fig. 8 for any countries (inspired by Fig. 20.8 in Jones).

    Arguments
        countries : the countries to show
        base      : the base year, in which every index is 100
        scale     : "linear", or "ratio" for a ratio (log) scale
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (crisis_data)
    picked, title = crisis_data(countries, base)
    # Step 2: one line with dots per country, and a dotted line at the base year
    fig = px.line(
        picked,
        x="year",
        y="index",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        markers=True,
        color_discrete_map=CRISIS_COLORS,
        log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
        range_x=[1987.5, 2025.5],
        title=title,
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "index": f"Dollar value of the currency ({base} = 100)",
        },
    )
    fig.add_vline(x=base, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    # Step 3: the vertical axis: from 0 to at least 120 on the linear scale, round
    # tick values on the ratio scale
    if scale == "linear":
        y_range = [0, 120]
        if len(picked) > 0:
            y_range = [0, max(120, 1.05 * picked["index"].max())]
        fig.update_yaxes(range=y_range)
    elif len(picked) > 0:
        fig.update_yaxes(
            tickvals=ratio_ticks(picked["index"].min(), picked["index"].max())
        )
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig

Fig. 9: 10-year government bond yields in Europe
Goal. See the euro crisis in its most useful single graph: interest rates on government debt in Germany, Italy and Spain.
Before the euro, Italian and Spanish bonds paid much more than German ones, mostly because inflation was higher there. With one currency and one central bank, investors expected similar inflation, and the yields converged. After the global financial crisis they diverged again, this time because investors feared a default on sovereign debt.
