title: C. Math Review for Macroeconomics
text:
C.4 Notation, functions and equations
Goal. Read the equations of the book with confidence, and let SymPy turn them into numbers and charts.
Economic models are written with a few conventions. Once you know them, an equation reads like a sentence.








Symbol
Meaning
Example in the book




a bar, as in \(\bar{s}\)
a parameter: a value the model takes as given
the investment rate \(\bar{s}\) (Chapter 5)


a subscript \(t\), as in \(K_t\)
the value in period \(t\) (usually a year)
capital \(K_t\)


\(\Delta x_{t+1} \equiv x_{t+1}-x_t\)
the change from one period to the next
\(\Delta K_{t+1}\), equation (5.3)


\(g_x\)
the growth rate of \(x\)
\(g_Y\), equation (6.14)


a star, as in \(k^*\)
a steady state or equilibrium value
\(k^*\), equation (5.8)


a tilde, as in \(\tilde{Y}_t\)
short-run output: the percent gap between GDP and potential GDP
equation (9.2)


\(\equiv\)
“is defined as”
\(\tilde{Y}_t \equiv (Y_t-\bar{Y}_t)/\bar{Y}_t\)


\(\pi\)
the inflation rate (not 3.14159…)
Chapter 8


\(\sum_{t=0}^{T}\)
the sum over periods 0 to \(T\)
present values, Chapter 7



A function links an input to an output. The IS curve of Chapter 11 is a function: it says how short-run output \(\tilde{Y}_t\) (in percent) depends on the real interest rate \(R_t\) (also in percent):
\[\tilde{Y}_t=\bar{a}-\bar{b}\,(R_t-\bar{r}). \qquad (11.14)\]
Here \(\bar{a}\) is an aggregate demand shock, \(\bar{b}\) says how strongly spending reacts to the interest rate, and \(\bar{r}\) is the long-run real interest rate. Let us write it in SymPy and ask: which interest rate brings output back to potential (\(\tilde{Y}_t=0\))?

Python note. SymPy shows a symbol named "abar" as \(\bar{a}\) and "Ytilde" as \(\tilde{Y}\). .subs(...) substitutes: it replaces a symbol with a number or another formula. A dictionary such as {abar: 1} replaces several symbols at once.


Y_tilde, R, abar, bbar, rbar = sp.symbols("Ytilde R abar bbar rbar")
IS = sp.Eq(Y_tilde, abar - bbar * (R - rbar))     # equation (11.14)
IS

\(\displaystyle \tilde{Y} = \bar{a} - \bar{b} \left(R - \bar{r}\right)\)



R_closes_gap = sp.solve(IS.subs(Y_tilde, 0), R)[0]   # set output to potential and solve for R
R_closes_gap

\(\displaystyle \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}} + \bar{r}\)


The formula says: raise the interest rate above \(\bar{r}\) by \(\bar{a}/\bar{b}\). With a positive demand shock of \(\bar{a}=1\) percent, \(\bar{b}=0.5\) and \(\bar{r}=2\) percent (our own illustrative numbers):

IS_values = {abar: 1, bbar: 0.5, rbar: 2}
print(f"Real interest rate that closes the gap: {float(R_closes_gap.subs(IS_values)):.1f} percent")

Real interest rate that closes the gap: 4.0 percent


sp.lambdify turns a SymPy formula into an ordinary Python function that works on NumPy arrays. That is how we go from algebra to a chart.

IS_formula = sp.solve(IS, Y_tilde)[0].subs(IS_values)    # output as a formula of R
IS_function = sp.lambdify(R, IS_formula)                 # now a Python function of R
R_grid = np.linspace(0, 8, 81)
is_fig = go.Figure()
is_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=IS_function(R_grid), y=R_grid, mode="lines", name="IS curve",
                            line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
is_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0], y=[float(R_closes_gap.subs(IS_values))], mode="markers", name="output at potential",
                            marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=12)))
is_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1], y=[2], mode="markers", name="R at its long-run value",
                            marker=dict(color=GRAY, size=12)))
is_fig.update_layout(title="With a demand shock of 1 percent, a real rate of 4 percent closes the gap",
                     xaxis=dict(title="short-run output, Ỹ (percent)", range=[-3, 3], tickvals=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]),
                     yaxis=dict(title="real interest rate, R (percent)", range=[0, 8]),
                     legend=dict(x=0.99, xanchor="right", y=0.98))
is_fig




                                
                                            




Source. Illustration of the IS curve, equation (11.14) in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The book draws the IS curve with output on the horizontal axis and the interest rate on the vertical axis, so we plot x=IS_function(R_grid), y=R_grid.
SymPy gave the general answer \(\bar{r}+\bar{a}/\bar{b}\); the numbers came last. Working with letters first shows which parameters matter.

Your turn. Suppose spending reacts twice as strongly to the interest rate (\(\bar{b}=1\)). Which real interest rate now closes the gap? Answer with R_closes_gap.subs(...).


Hint

Copy IS_values, change bbar to 1, and substitute the new dictionary. A larger \(\bar{b}\) means a smaller rise in \(R\) is enough.

text:
C.5 Percentages, ratios and index numbers
Goal. Compute percent changes, rebase an index, turn nominal values into real ones, and annualize monthly or quarterly changes.
The percent change of a variable from \(x_0\) to \(x_1\) is \(100 \times (x_1-x_0)/x_0\). Be careful with rates that are already in percent, such as the unemployment rate. When it rises from 4 to 5 percent, it rises by 1 percentage point, but by 25 percent.

u_before, u_after = 4.0, 5.0           # unemployment rate, percent
print("Change:", u_after - u_before, "percentage point")
print("Change:", 100 * (u_after - u_before) / u_before, "percent")

Change: 1.0 percentage point
Change: 25.0 percent


A ratio divides one variable by another, often to remove the size of the economy. Public debt of 30 trillion dollars means little on its own; debt of 100 percent of GDP is easy to compare over time and across countries (Chapter 18).

C.5.1 Index numbers and inflation
A price index measures the price level relative to a base period. The U.S. consumer price index (CPI) has the base 1982–84 = 100. To rebase it to another year, divide by the value in that year and multiply by 100.

cpi = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_cpi.csv")
cpi_2025 = cpi.loc[cpi["year"] == 2025, "cpi"].iloc[0]
cpi["cpi_2025"] = 100 * cpi["cpi"] / cpi_2025           # now 2025 = 100
cpi["inflation"] = 100 * cpi["cpi"].pct_change()        # percent change from the year before

The rebased index answers questions such as “what would 100 dollars of 1913 buy today?”

C.5.2 Nominal and real values
Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP at the prices of a base year. Their ratio is the GDP deflator, a price index for everything the economy produces (Chapter 2):
\[\text{deflator}_t = 100 \times \frac{\text{nominal GDP}_t}{\text{real GDP}_t}.\]

nipa = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "nipa_annual.csv", usecols=["year", "gdp", "real_gdp", "population"])
nipa["deflator"] = 100 * nipa["gdp"] / nipa["real_gdp"]    # 2017 = 100, because real GDP is in 2017 dollars

C.5.3 Annualizing
Monthly and quarterly changes are usually reported at an annual rate: the change that would result if the same monthly (or quarterly) change went on for a whole year. Because changes compound, a monthly change \(m\) becomes \((1+m)^{12}-1\) a year, which is a bit more than \(12 \times m\).

monthly = 0.3                                          # prices rise 0.3 percent in one month
annual = 100 * ((1 + monthly / 100) ** 12 - 1)
print(f"{monthly}% a month is {annual:.2f}% at an annual rate (12 x {monthly} = {12 * monthly:.1f})")
quarterly = 0.5                                        # real GDP grows 0.5 percent in one quarter
print(f"{quarterly}% a quarter is {100 * ((1 + quarterly / 100) ** 4 - 1):.2f}% at an annual rate")

0.3% a month is 3.66% at an annual rate (12 x 0.3 = 3.6)
0.5% a quarter is 2.02% at an annual rate


What to notice.

The chart shows the deflation of 1921 and of the early 1930s, and the bursts of inflation around 1917–1920, in 1947, around 1980 and in 2022.
Rebasing changes the levels of an index but not its percent changes: inflation is the same whatever the base year.
The deflator in 2017 equals 100 because the real GDP series is measured in 2017 dollars.

title: C. Math Review for Macroeconomics
text:
C.6 Exponents and exponential growth
Goal. See how compound growth works, and why small differences in growth rates become large differences in income.
An exponent says how many times a number is multiplied by itself: \(x^3 = x \cdot x \cdot x\). The rules you need are few:



Rule
Example




\(x^a \cdot x^b = x^{a+b}\)
\(K^{1/3}K^{2/3}=K\)


\((x^a)^b = x^{ab}\)
\((k^{1/3})^{3/2}=k^{1/2}\)


\(x^{-a}=1/x^a\)
\(K^{-2/3}=1/K^{2/3}\)


\(x^{1/n}=\sqrt[n]{x}\)
\(k^{1/3}\) is the cube root of \(k\)


\((xy)^a=x^a y^a\)
\((AK)^{1/3}=A^{1/3}K^{1/3}\)



If income per person grows at a constant rate \(\bar{g}\) each year, then after one year it is \(y_0(1+\bar{g})\), after two years \(y_0(1+\bar{g})^2\), and after \(t\) years
\[y_t=y_0\,(1+\bar{g})^t. \qquad (3.7)\]
This is exponential growth: income grows by the same percent each year, so it grows by more and more dollars.

def income_path(g, years):
    """Equation (3.7): income y_t = (1 + g)^t for t = 0, ..., years, with g in percent and y_0 = 1."""
    t = np.arange(0, years + 1)
    return (1 + g / 100) ** t

for rate in [1, 2, 3]:
    print(f"{rate}% a year for 100 years multiplies income by {income_path(rate, 100)[-1]:.1f}")

1% a year for 100 years multiplies income by 2.7
2% a year for 100 years multiplies income by 7.2
3% a year for 100 years multiplies income by 19.2


In more advanced work, growth is often written in continuous time: \(y_t=y_0e^{gt}\), where \(e \approx 2.718\) is Euler’s number. For small growth rates the two versions are close (Section C.6 explains why).

print(f"(1.02)^100 = {1.02 ** 100:.2f}   versus   e^(0.02 x 100) = {math.exp(0.02 * 100):.2f}")

(1.02)^100 = 7.24   versus   e^(0.02 x 100) = 7.39



C.6.1 The Rule of 70

text:
C.7 Logarithms
Goal. Use logarithms to undo exponents, to turn multiplication into addition, and to read charts on a ratio scale.
The natural logarithm \(\ln x\) is the power to which \(e\) must be raised to get \(x\): if \(x=e^{z}\), then \(\ln x=z\). So the logarithm undoes the exponential: \(\ln e^{z}=z\) and \(e^{\ln x}=x\). (The base-10 logarithm, \(\log_{10}\), works the same way with 10 instead of \(e\): \(\log_{10}1000=3\).) Logs are defined only for positive numbers. Their rules are the reason economists love them:








Rule
In words
Used for




\(\ln(xy)=\ln x+\ln y\)
the log of a product is the sum of the logs
growth of GDP = growth of GDP per person + growth of population


\(\ln(x/y)=\ln x-\ln y\)
the log of a ratio is the difference of the logs
growth of a ratio such as \(Y/L\)


\(\ln(x^a)=a\ln x\)
an exponent comes down as a factor
growth of \(K^{1/3}\)


\(\ln 1=0\)





SymPy knows these rules. sp.expand_log applies them; the symbols must be declared positive, because logs of negative numbers are not defined.

x, y, a = sp.symbols("x y a", positive=True)
print(sp.expand_log(sp.log(x * y)))
print(sp.expand_log(sp.log(x / y)))
print(sp.expand_log(sp.log(x ** a)))
print(sp.expand_log(sp.log(sp.symbols("Abar", positive=True) * sp.symbols("K", positive=True) ** sp.Rational(1, 3))))

log(x) + log(y)
log(x) - log(y)
a*log(x)
log(Abar) + log(K)/3


NumPy computes logs of numbers: np.log is the natural log and np.log10 the base-10 log. A quick numerical check of the rules:

print(np.log(3 * 5), np.log(3) + np.log(5))       # the same number
print(np.log(2 ** 10), 10 * np.log(2))            # the same number
print(np.log10(1000), np.exp(np.log(42)))         # 3, and 42 back again

2.70805020110221 2.70805020110221
6.931471805599453 6.931471805599453
3.0 42.00000000000001


Log differences are (almost) percent changes. When income rises from 100 to 103, it rises by 3 percent, and \(100 \times (\ln 103-\ln 100)=2.96\). Economists call \(100 \times \Delta\ln x\) a change in log points. For changes of a few percent, log points and percent are nearly the same number (Section C.6).

C.7.1 The ratio scale
On a ratio scale (or log scale), equal distances on the vertical axis mean equal ratios: from 5,000 to 10,000 dollars is as far as from 40,000 to 80,000. Taking logs of (3.7) gives \(\ln y_t=\ln y_0+t\ln(1+\bar{g})\), a straight line in \(t\) with slope \(\ln(1+\bar{g})\). So a series that grows at a constant rate is a straight line on a ratio scale, and the slope of the line shows the growth rate (Chapter 3).

C.8 Growth rates and the growth rules
Goal. Compute growth rates in three ways, and use the three growth rules of Chapter 3 to find the growth of products, ratios and powers.
There are three common ways to measure growth:








Measure
Formula
In pandas




growth from one year to the next
\(g_t=(y_t-y_{t-1})/y_{t-1}\)
100 * y.pct_change()


log difference
\(\ln y_t-\ln y_{t-1}\)
100 * np.log(y).diff()


average annual growth over \(T\) years
\(\bar{g}=(y_T/y_0)^{1/T}-1\), equation (3.9)
as in Section C.4




gdp_pc["growth"] = 100 * gdp_pc["gdppc"].pct_change()           # percent
gdp_pc["log_growth"] = 100 * np.log(gdp_pc["gdppc"]).diff()      # log points
print(f"Average annual growth, equation (3.9):     {avg_growth:.2f}%")
print(f"Simple mean of the yearly growth rates:    {gdp_pc['growth'].mean():.2f}%")
print(f"Mean of the yearly log differences:        {gdp_pc['log_growth'].mean():.2f} log points")

Average annual growth, equation (3.9):     1.88%
Simple mean of the yearly growth rates:    1.99%
Mean of the yearly log differences:        1.86 log points


Why is the simple mean of the yearly rates higher than the average annual growth rate? Because ups and downs do not cancel out in percent: a fall of 50 percent followed by a rise of 50 percent leaves you at \(0.5 \times 1.5 = 0.75\), not where you started, even though the mean of \(-50\) and \(+50\) is zero. When you want the growth rate that takes \(y_0\) to \(y_T\), use (3.9). The mean log difference is the continuous-time version of (3.9).

C.8.1 The growth rules
If \(x\) grows at rate \(g_x\) and \(y\) at rate \(g_y\), Chapter 3 gives three rules:

Product: \(z=x \times y \;\Rightarrow\; g_z \approx g_x+g_y\).
Ratio: \(z=x/y \;\Rightarrow\; g_z \approx g_x-g_y\).
Power: \(z=x^a \;\Rightarrow\; g_z \approx a \times g_x\).

Why “approximately”? Over one year, \(1+g_z=(1+g_x)(1+g_y)=1+g_x+g_y+g_x g_y\). The last term is the product of two small numbers (0.02 × 0.03 = 0.0006), so we drop it. SymPy shows the exact result:

g_x, g_y = sp.symbols("g_x g_y")
print("Product, exact:", sp.expand((1 + g_x) * (1 + g_y) - 1))
print("With 2% and 3%:", sp.expand((1 + g_x) * (1 + g_y) - 1).subs({g_x: 0.02, g_y: 0.03}))

Product, exact: g_x*g_y + g_x + g_y
With 2% and 3%: 0.0506000000000000


In continuous time the rules are exact (Section C.11 proves them with derivatives).
The famous example. Apply the rules to the production function \(Y_t=A_tK_t^{1/3}L_t^{2/3}\): the product rule adds the pieces, and the power rule multiplies each growth rate by its exponent,
\[g_Y=g_A+\tfrac{1}{3}g_K+\tfrac{2}{3}g_L. \qquad (6.14)\]

def output_growth(g_A, g_K, g_L):
    """Growth rules applied to Y = A K^(1/3) L^(2/3), equation (6.14); rates in percent."""
    return g_A + g_K / 3 + 2 * g_L / 3

print("Output growth with g_A = 1, g_K = 3, g_L = 1:", round(output_growth(1, 3, 1), 2), "percent")
print("GDP per worker grows at", round(output_growth(1, 3, 1) - 1, 2), "percent (ratio rule: g_Y - g_L)")

Output growth with g_A = 1, g_K = 3, g_L = 1: 2.67 percent
GDP per worker grows at 1.67 percent (ratio rule: g_Y - g_L)


The same rules give the quantity theory of money in growth rates (Chapter 8): from \(MV=PY\) (8.1), \(g_M+g_V=g_P+g_Y\) (8.3). With a constant velocity, inflation is money growth minus output growth (8.4): 7 percent money growth and 3 percent output growth give about 4 percent inflation.


C.8.2 The rules in the data
Nominal GDP is real GDP times the deflator (divided by 100), so by the product rule, nominal GDP growth ≈ real GDP growth + inflation. Let us check it with the U.S. national accounts.

C.9 Approximations
Goal. Know the few approximations the book uses, where they come from, and when they break down.
Economists often replace an exact formula with a simpler one that is almost right for small numbers. Four approximations do most of the work:








Approximation
Good when
Used for




\(\ln(1+x) \approx x\)
\(x\) is small
log differences ≈ percent changes; the output gap


\((1+a)(1+b) \approx 1+a+b\)
\(a\) and \(b\) are small
the growth rules (C.5)


\((1+a)/(1+b) \approx 1+a-b\)
\(a\) and \(b\) are small
the Fisher equation \(R \approx i-\pi\) (Chapter 8)


\(f(x) \approx f(x_0)+f'(x_0)(x-x_0)\)
\(x\) is close to \(x_0\)
linearizing a model around its steady state (C.10)



The last line is the general idea, the first-order Taylor approximation: near a point \(x_0\), any smooth function looks like a straight line through \(f(x_0)\) with slope \(f'(x_0)\) (the derivative, Section C.7). The others are special cases. SymPy’s series gives the approximation to any order:

x = sp.symbols("x")
sp.series(sp.log(1 + x), x, 0, 4)    # ln(1 + x) near x = 0, up to x^3

\(\displaystyle x - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{x^{3}}{3} + O\left(x^{4}\right)\)


So \(\ln(1+x)=x-x^2/2+x^3/3-\dots\). For \(x=0.02\) the second term is only \(0.0002\).
Where the Rule of 70 comes from. The exact doubling time is \(\ln 2/\ln(1+g)\). Its series in \(g\):

g = sp.symbols("g", positive=True)
sp.series(sp.log(2) / sp.log(1 + g), g, 0, 2)

\(\displaystyle \frac{\log{\left(2 \right)}}{g} + \frac{\log{\left(2 \right)}}{2} - \frac{g \log{\left(2 \right)}}{12} + O\left(g^{2}\right)\)


With \(g\) in percent (\(g=G/100\)), the first two terms are \(69.3/G+0.35\). At \(G=2\) this is \(34.66+0.35=35.0\), exactly \(70/2\). So “70” is \(100\ln 2 \approx 69.3\), rounded up to absorb the second term at the growth rates that matter for income.

def approximation_chart(x0=0.05):
    """The curve ln(1 + x), the straight line x, and the error at x0."""
    x0 = round(x0, 2) + 0.0                             # a slider step can give -2e-17 instead of 0
    x_grid = np.linspace(-0.5, 1.05, 311)
    exact, error = math.log(1 + x0), x0 - math.log(1 + x0)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x_grid, y=np.log(1 + x_grid), mode="lines", name="exact: ln(1 + x)", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x_grid, y=x_grid, mode="lines", name="approximation: x", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x0, x0], y=[exact, x0], mode="lines+markers", name="error",

    fig.update_layout(title=f"x = {x0:.2f}: ln(1 + x) = {exact:.4f}; the error is {error:.4f}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="x", range=[-0.5, 1.05]), yaxis=dict(title="value", range=[-0.8, 1.1]),

Exactly, \(1+\pi=(1+g_M)/(1+g_Y)=2/1.02\). The approximation gives \(100-2=98\) percent.

C.10 Derivatives and marginal thinking
Goal. Compute derivatives by hand, with SymPy and numerically, and use them for marginal products, elasticities and returns to scale.
The derivative \(f'(x)\), also written \(df/dx\), is the slope of a function at a point: how much \(f\) changes per unit change in \(x\), for a very small change. Economists say “marginal”: the marginal product of capital (MPK) is the extra output from one more unit of capital. The rules you need:








Function
Derivative
Example




\(x^n\)
\(n\,x^{n-1}\)
\(\frac{d}{dk}k^{1/3}=\tfrac{1}{3}k^{-2/3}\)


\(\ln x\)
\(1/x\)
\(\frac{d}{dc}\ln c=1/c\) (marginal utility, Chapter 16)


\(e^{ax}\)
\(a\,e^{ax}\)



\(c \cdot f(x)\)
\(c \cdot f'(x)\)
constants stay


\(f(g(x))\)
\(f'(g(x))\,g'(x)\)
the chain rule



A function of several inputs, such as \(Y=F(K,L)\), has a partial derivative for each input: change one, hold the others fixed. It is written \(\partial Y/\partial K\).

Abar, K, L = sp.symbols("Abar K L", positive=True)
Y = Abar * K ** sp.Rational(1, 3) * L ** sp.Rational(2, 3)      # equation (4.1)
MPK = sp.diff(Y, K)                                             # partial derivative with respect to K
MPL = sp.diff(Y, L)
MPK

\(\displaystyle \frac{\bar{A} L^{\frac{2}{3}}}{3 K^{\frac{2}{3}}}\)



Python note. sp.Rational(1, 3) is the exact fraction 1/3. Writing 1/3 would give the decimal 0.3333…, and SymPy could no longer simplify exactly. sp.diff(Y, K) differentiates Y with respect to K, treating every other symbol as a constant.

Chapter 4 writes these as shares of the average product: \(MPK=\tfrac{1}{3}\,Y/K\) (4.3) and \(MPL=\tfrac{2}{3}\,Y/L\) (4.4). SymPy confirms both: the differences simplify to zero.

print("MPK - (1/3) Y/K =", sp.simplify(MPK - Y / (3 * K)))
print("MPL - (2/3) Y/L =", sp.simplify(MPL - 2 * Y / (3 * L)))
print("Second derivative in K:", sp.simplify(sp.diff(Y, K, 2)), "(negative: diminishing returns)")

MPK - (1/3) Y/K = 0
MPL - (2/3) Y/L = 0
Second derivative in K: -2*Abar*L**(2/3)/(9*K**(5/3)) (negative: diminishing returns)



C.10.1 Elasticities and returns to scale
An elasticity is a ratio of percent changes: the elasticity of \(Y\) with respect to \(K\) is \((\partial Y/\partial K)\cdot(K/Y)\), the percent change in output for a 1 percent change in capital. In a Cobb-Douglas function, each exponent is an elasticity. Constant returns to scale means that doubling all inputs doubles output: \(F(\lambda K,\lambda L)=\lambda F(K,L)\).

lam = sp.symbols("lambda", positive=True)
print("Elasticity of Y with respect to K:", sp.simplify(MPK * K / Y))
print("Elasticity of Y with respect to L:", sp.simplify(MPL * L / Y))
print("F(λK, λL) / F(K, L) =", sp.simplify(Y.subs({K: lam * K, L: lam * L}, simultaneous=True) / Y))
print("K·MPK + L·MPL - Y =", sp.simplify(K * MPK + L * MPL - Y))

Elasticity of Y with respect to K: 1/3
Elasticity of Y with respect to L: 2/3
F(λK, λL) / F(K, L) = lambda
K·MPK + L·MPL - Y = 0


The last line is the reason factor shares add up to one in Chapter 4: when firms pay \(r=MPK\) and \(w=MPL\), capital gets \(rK/Y=1/3\) of output and labor gets \(wL/Y=2/3\), and together they exhaust output (4.5)–(4.6).


C.10.2 Numerical derivatives
When a function has no formula, or the formula is messy, we can approximate the slope with a small step \(h\): \(f'(x) \approx [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h\). NumPy’s np.gradient does this for a whole grid at once.

def y_per_person(k):
    """Output per person y = k^(1/3), equation (5.6) with A = 1."""
    return k ** (1 / 3)

k0 = 8.0
for h in [1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001]:
    print(f"h = {h:<6}: slope = {(y_per_person(k0 + h) - y_per_person(k0)) / h:.5f}")
print(f"exact      : slope = {(1 / 3) * k0 ** (-2 / 3):.5f}")
k_grid = np.linspace(1, 20, 191)                    # steps of 0.1
slopes = np.gradient(y_per_person(k_grid), k_grid)
print(f"np.gradient at k = 8: {slopes[70]:.5f}")

h = 1     : slope = 0.08008
h = 0.1   : slope = 0.08299
h = 0.01  : slope = 0.08330
h = 0.001 : slope = 0.08333
exact      : slope = 0.08333
np.gradient at k = 8: 0.08334



tangent_fig = go.Figure()
k_axis = np.linspace(0, 20, 401)
tangent_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k_axis, y=y_per_person(k_axis), mode="lines", name="y = k^(1/3)",
                                 line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
for k_point, color in [(1.0, TEAL), (8.0, GREEN)]:
    slope = (1 / 3) * k_point ** (-2 / 3)
    k_near = np.linspace(max(k_point - 4, 0), k_point + 4, 50)
    tangent_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k_near, y=y_per_person(k_point) + slope * (k_near - k_point), mode="lines",
                                     name=f"slope at k = {k_point:.0f}: {slope:.3f}", line=dict(color=color, width=2, dash="dash")))
    tangent_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[k_point], y=[y_per_person(k_point)], mode="markers", showlegend=False,
                                     marker=dict(color=color, size=11)))
tangent_fig.update_layout(title="Diminishing returns: the marginal product falls from 0.333 at k = 1 to 0.083 at k = 8",
                          xaxis=dict(title="capital per person, k", range=[0, 20], tickvals=[5, 10, 15, 20]),
                          yaxis=dict(title="output per person, y", range=[0, 3.2]),
                          legend=dict(x=0.99, xanchor="right", y=0.02, yanchor="bottom"))
tangent_fig




                                
                                            




Source. Illustration of the production function (5.6) and its marginal product, as in Chapters 4 and 5 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The dashed lines touch the curve at one point each: they are the tangents, and their slopes are the derivatives. The curve gets flatter as \(k\) rises: each extra unit of capital adds less output.
The numerical slope approaches the exact one as \(h\) shrinks. With \(h=0.001\) they agree to five decimals.

Create c = sp.symbols("c", positive=True) and use sp.diff(sp.log(c), c) and sp.diff(sp.sqrt(c), c). The second derivative, sp.diff(..., c, 2), tells you whether the slope falls.

text:
C.11 Optimization
Goal. Find the best choice of a firm and of a household: set the derivative to zero, and check the answer with a numerical optimizer.
At the top of a hill the ground is flat. So when a function has a maximum at \(x^*\), its slope there is zero: \(f'(x^*)=0\). This is the first-order condition. (To be sure it is a maximum and not a minimum, the slope must fall as you pass through \(x^*\): the second derivative is negative.)

C.11.1 A firm chooses how many workers to hire
A firm with a fixed capital stock \(\bar{K}=8\) and productivity \(\bar{A}=1\) pays the wage \(w\) per worker. It chooses labor \(L\) to maximize profit (compare (4.2)): \(\Pi(L)=\bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}L^{2/3}-wL\). The first-order condition says: hire until the marginal product of labor equals the wage, \(MPL=w\).

L, w = sp.symbols("L w", positive=True)
profit = 1 * 8 ** sp.Rational(1, 3) * L ** sp.Rational(2, 3) - w * L     # A = 1, K = 8
first_order_condition = sp.Eq(sp.diff(profit, L), 0)                      # MPL - w = 0
L_star = sp.solve(first_order_condition, L)[0]
L_star

\(\displaystyle \frac{64}{27 w^{3}}\)



print("Workers hired when w = 2/3:", L_star.subs(w, sp.Rational(2, 3)))
print("Second derivative at that point:", sp.diff(profit, L, 2).subs({w: sp.Rational(2, 3), L: 8}))

Workers hired when w = 2/3: 8
Second derivative at that point: -1/36


SciPy finds the same answer numerically. Its optimizers minimize, so we give it minus the profit.

def minus_profit(L):
    """Minus the firm's profit with A = 1, K = 8 and w = 2/3 (SciPy minimizes)."""
    return -(8 ** (1 / 3) * L ** (2 / 3) - (2 / 3) * L)

best_L = optimize.minimize_scalar(minus_profit, bounds=(0.1, 50), method="bounded")
print(f"minimize_scalar: L* = {best_L.x:.4f}, profit = {-best_L.fun:.4f}")

minimize_scalar: L* = 8.0000, profit = 2.6667




C.11.2 A household chooses consumption today and tomorrow
In Chapter 16 a household lives two periods, values consumption with \(U=\ln c_{\text{today}}+\beta\ln c_{\text{future}}\), and faces the budget constraint \(c_{\text{today}}+c_{\text{future}}/(1+R)=\bar{X}\), where \(\bar{X}\) is its lifetime wealth (16.5). There are two ways to solve such a problem.
Substitution. Use the constraint to write \(c_{\text{future}}=(1+R)(\bar{X}-c_{\text{today}})\), put it into \(U\), and set the derivative with respect to \(c_{\text{today}}\) to zero.

c_today, c_future, R, beta, X = sp.symbols("c_today c_future R beta X", positive=True)
U = sp.log(c_today) + beta * sp.log((1 + R) * (X - c_today))
c_today_star = sp.solve(sp.diff(U, c_today), c_today)[0]
c_today_star

\(\displaystyle \frac{X}{\beta + 1}\)


With \(\beta=1\) this is \(\bar{X}/2\), equation (16.9): the household consumes half of its lifetime wealth today.
The Lagrangian. Add the constraint, multiplied by a new variable \(\mu\) (the Lagrange multiplier), to the objective, and set the derivative with respect to every variable to zero. This method works even when you cannot substitute easily.

mu = sp.symbols("mu")                           # the Lagrange multiplier
lagrangian = sp.log(c_today) + beta * sp.log(c_future) + mu * (X - c_today - c_future / (1 + R))
conditions = [sp.diff(lagrangian, c_today), sp.diff(lagrangian, c_future), sp.diff(lagrangian, mu)]
solution = sp.solve(conditions, [c_today, c_future, mu], dict=True)[0]
print("c_today  =", solution[c_today])
print("c_future =", solution[c_future])
print("c_future / c_today =", sp.simplify(solution[c_future] / solution[c_today]), " (the Euler equation, 16.8)")

c_today  = X/(beta + 1)
c_future = X*beta*(R + 1)/(beta + 1)
c_future / c_today = beta*(R + 1)  (the Euler equation, 16.8)


The ratio \(c_{\text{future}}/c_{\text{today}}=\beta(1+R)\) is the Euler equation with log utility: patience (\(\beta\)) and a high interest rate (\(R\)) tilt consumption toward the future.

X_value, beta_value, R_value = 100, 0.96, 0.05            # our own illustrative numbers
c_grid = np.linspace(5, 95, 181)
utility = np.log(c_grid) + beta_value * np.log((1 + R_value) * (X_value - c_grid))
c_best = X_value / (1 + beta_value)
utility_fig = go.Figure()
utility_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=c_grid, y=utility, mode="lines", name="lifetime utility", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
u_best = np.log(c_best) + beta_value * np.log((1 + R_value) * (X_value - c_best))
utility_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[c_best - 15, c_best + 15], y=[u_best, u_best], mode="lines", name="slope zero",
                                 line=dict(color=TEAL, dash="dash")))
utility_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[c_best], y=[u_best], mode="markers", name="the best choice", marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=12)))
utility_fig.update_layout(title=f"With X = 100, β = 0.96 and R = 5%, utility is highest at c_today = {c_best:.1f}",
                          xaxis=dict(title="consumption today", range=[0, 100], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100]),
                          yaxis=dict(title="lifetime utility", range=[5.6, 8.1]), legend=dict(x=0.02, y=0.02, yanchor="bottom"))
utility_fig




                                
                                            




Source. Illustration of the household’s problem, equation (16.5) in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The curve is flat at its peak, where the tangent is horizontal. That is the first-order condition at work.
The household consumes a little more than half today (\(100/1.96=51.0\)): with \(\beta=0.96\) it is slightly impatient, and the 5 percent interest rate is not quite enough to make up for it.

Your turn. Check the household’s answer with SciPy: use optimize.minimize_scalar on minus the utility along the budget line, with \(\bar{X}=100\), \(\beta=0.96\) and \(R=0.05\), searching between 1 and 99.

Write a function of c that returns -(np.log(c) + 0.96 * np.log(1.05 * (100 - c))), then call optimize.minimize_scalar(your_function, bounds=(1, 99), method="bounded") and print .x.

C.12 Solving equations and systems
Goal. Solve a system of linear equations with NumPy and SymPy, and a nonlinear equation with SymPy and SciPy.

C.12.1 A linear system: the short-run model
The short-run model of Chapters 11–13 has three equations and three unknowns: output \(\tilde{Y}_t\), the real interest rate \(R_t\) and inflation \(\pi_t\).
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{IS:}\quad & \tilde{Y}_t=\bar{a}-\bar{b}(R_t-\bar{r}) & (11.14)\\
\text{MP rule:}\quad & R_t-\bar{r}=\bar{m}(\pi_t-\bar{\pi}) & (13.1)\\
\text{AS:}\quad & \pi_t=\pi_{t-1}+\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t+\bar{o} & (13.2)
\end{aligned}\]
Move all unknowns to the left and all numbers to the right, and the system has the matrix form \(Mz=c\):
\[\begin{pmatrix}1 & \bar{b} & 0\\ 0 & 1 & -\bar{m}\\ -\bar{\nu} & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{Y}_t\\ R_t\\ \pi_t\end{pmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix}\bar{a}+\bar{b}\bar{r}\\ \bar{r}-\bar{m}\bar{\pi}\\ \pi_{t-1}+\bar{o}\end{pmatrix}.\]
We take our own illustrative numbers: a negative demand shock \(\bar{a}=-2\), \(\bar{b}=\bar{m}=\bar{\nu}=0.5\), \(\bar{r}=\bar{\pi}=2\), last year’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}=2\) and no price shock, \(\bar{o}=0\).

Python note. np.array([[...], [...]]) builds a matrix row by row. np.linalg.solve(M, c) solves \(Mz=c\) for the vector \(z\).


a_, b_, m_, nu_, r_, pibar_, pi_last, o_ = -2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 2, 2, 2, 0
M = np.array([[1, b_, 0],
              [0, 1, -m_],
              [-nu_, 0, 1]])
c = np.array([a_ + b_ * r_, r_ - m_ * pibar_, pi_last + o_])
Y_short, R_short, pi_short = np.linalg.solve(M, c)
print(f"Output gap {Y_short:.3f}%, real rate {R_short:.3f}%, inflation {pi_short:.3f}%")

Output gap -1.778%, real rate 1.556%, inflation 1.111%


SymPy solves the same system with letters, which shows how the answer depends on each parameter:

Yt, Rt, pit = sp.symbols("Ytilde R_t pi_t")
abar, bbar, mbar, nubar, rbar, pibar, obar = sp.symbols("abar bbar mbar nubar rbar pibar obar")
pi_prev = sp.Symbol(r"\pi_{t-1}")          # a symbol may carry its own LaTeX name
short_run = [sp.Eq(Yt, abar - bbar * (Rt - rbar)),
             sp.Eq(Rt - rbar, mbar * (pit - pibar)),
             sp.Eq(pit, pi_prev + nubar * Yt + obar)]
short_run_solution = sp.solve(short_run, [Yt, Rt, pit], dict=True)[0]
sp.simplify(short_run_solution[Yt])

\(\displaystyle \frac{- \pi_{t-1} \bar{b} \bar{m} + \bar{a} - \bar{b} \bar{m} \bar{o} + \bar{b} \bar{m} \bar{\pi}}{\bar{b} \bar{m} \bar{\nu} + 1}\)


The formula says: output falls with a negative demand shock \(\bar{a}\) and with inflation inherited from last year above target, and the factor \(1/(1+\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\) shows how the monetary policy rule softens the shock.


C.12.2 A nonlinear equation: the Solow steady state
In the Solow model (Chapter 5), capital per person stops changing when investment equals depreciation: \(\bar{s}\bar{A}k^{1/3}=\bar{d}k\). With \(\bar{s}=0.4\), \(\bar{d}=0.1\) and \(\bar{A}=1\):

k = sp.symbols("k", positive=True)
steady_state_equation = sp.Eq(sp.Rational(2, 5) * k ** sp.Rational(1, 3), sp.Rational(1, 10) * k)
print("SymPy:", sp.solve(steady_state_equation, k))
print("Formula (5.8):", (0.4 * 1 / 0.1) ** (3 / 2))

SymPy: [8]
Formula (5.8): 8.0



def net_investment(k):
    """Investment minus depreciation per person, s A k^(1/3) - d k, with s = 0.4, A = 1, d = 0.1."""
    return 0.4 * k ** (1 / 3) - 0.1 * k

print("brentq:", optimize.brentq(net_investment, 1, 100))     # one sign change between 1 and 100
print("fsolve:", optimize.fsolve(net_investment, 5)[0])       # starts at k = 5 and walks to the root

brentq: 8.0
fsolve: 7.999999999999998



Python note. brentq needs an interval where the function changes sign, and it always finds a root inside it. fsolve needs only a starting guess, and it also solves systems of equations, but it can end at a different root (here \(k=0\) is a root too) if the guess is poor.


k_line = np.linspace(0, 20, 401)
solow_fig = go.Figure()
solow_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k_line, y=0.4 * k_line ** (1 / 3), mode="lines", name="investment, s·y",
                               line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
solow_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k_line, y=0.1 * k_line, mode="lines", name="depreciation, d·k",
                               line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
solow_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[8], y=[0.8], mode="markers", name="steady state k* = 8", marker=dict(color=GREEN, size=12)))
solow_fig.update_layout(title="The steady state solves s·A·k^(1/3) = d·k: k* = 8 when s = 0.4, d = 0.1, A = 1",
                        xaxis=dict(title="capital per person, k", range=[0, 20], tickvals=[5, 10, 15, 20]),
                        yaxis=dict(title="investment and depreciation", range=[0, 1.25]),
                        legend=dict(x=0.02, y=0.98))
solow_fig




                                
                                            




Source. Adapted from Fig. 5.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

NumPy and SymPy agree: the demand shock opens a negative output gap of about 1.8 percent, inflation falls below target and the central bank cuts the real rate below \(\bar{r}\).
The Solow equation has two roots, \(k=0\) and \(k^*=8\). SymPy, told that \(k\) is positive, reports only \(k^*=8\); brentq finds it because we started the interval at 1, away from zero.

text:
C.13 Difference equations: how macro variables move over time
Goal. Find the steady state of a difference equation, decide whether it is stable, and simulate the path of capital, unemployment, inflation and public debt.
A difference equation says how a variable today depends on its own value in the period before. Many key equations of the book are difference equations: capital accumulation \(\Delta k_{t+1}=\bar{s}y_t-\bar{d}k_t\) (5.7), the “bathtub” model of unemployment (Chapter 7), the Phillips curve \(\pi_t=\pi_{t-1}+\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\) (12.5), and the government budget constraint \(B_{t+1}=(1+i)B_t+G_t-T_t\) (18.2). The simplest form is first-order and linear:
\[x_{t+1}=a\,x_t+b.\]

Its steady state is the value that repeats itself: \(x^*=a\,x^*+b\), so \(x^*=b/(1-a)\) when \(a \neq 1\).
Its solution is \(x_t=x^*+a^t(x_0-x^*)\): the gap to the steady state is multiplied by \(a\) each period.
So the steady state is stable when \(|a|<1\): the gap shrinks to zero. With \(0<a<1\) the path approaches \(x^*\) smoothly; with \(-1<a<0\) it jumps from one side to the other. When \(|a|>1\) the gap explodes.
The half-life, the number of periods it takes to close half of the gap, is \(\ln 0.5/\ln|a|\).

SymPy finds the steady state and the whole solution (rsolve solves recurrences, another name for difference equations):

x = sp.Function("x")
t, a, b, x0 = sp.symbols("t a b x_0")
x_star = sp.symbols("x_star")
print("Steady state:", sp.solve(sp.Eq(x_star, a * x_star + b), x_star))
sp.rsolve(x(t + 1) - a * x(t) - b, x(t), {x(0): x0})

Steady state: [-b/(a - 1)]


\(\displaystyle \frac{a^{t} \left(a x_{0} + b - x_{0}\right)}{a - 1} - \frac{b}{a - 1}\)


With a loop, Python simulates any difference equation, linear or not:

def simulate_linear(a, b, x0, periods):
    """Iterate x_{t+1} = a x_t + b for the given number of periods, starting from x0."""
    path = [x0]
    for period in range(periods):
        path.append(a * path[-1] + b)
    return np.array(path)

path = simulate_linear(0.8, 1.0, 0.0, 10)
formula = 5 + 0.8 ** np.arange(0, 11) * (0.0 - 5)      # x* + a^t (x_0 - x*), with x* = 1 / (1 - 0.8) = 5
print(path.round(3))
print("Largest difference from the formula:", np.abs(path - formula).max())

[0.    1.    1.8   2.44  2.952 3.362 3.689 3.951 4.161 4.329 4.463]
Largest difference from the formula: 1.7763568394002505e-15



C.13.1 Interactive: stability and speed
Move \(a\) and \(b\) and watch the path from \(x_0=0\). In Colab both sliders are live. On the website the slider moves \(a\) with \(b=1-a\), so the steady state stays at \(x^*=1\) and you see only the speed of the approach and the zigzag of a negative \(a\).

def difference_chart(a=0.8, b=1.0):
    """The path of x_{t+1} = a x_t + b from x_0 = 0, with its steady state x* = b / (1 - a)."""
    a = round(a, 2) + 0.0                               # a slider step can give 2e-16 instead of 0
    path = simulate_linear(a, b, 0.0, 30)
    x_star = b / (1 - a)
    top = 45.0
    for candidate in [2.5, 5.0, 12.0, 25.0, 45.0]:       # widen the axis in steps, only when needed
        if max(path.max(), x_star) * 1.05 <= candidate:
            top = candidate
            break
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[-5, 40], y=[x_star, x_star], mode="lines", name=f"steady state x* = {x_star:.2f}",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=np.arange(0, 31), y=path, mode="lines+markers", name="path of x",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), marker=dict(size=6)))
    if a == 0:
        speed = "x reaches x* after one period"
    else:
        speed = f"half of the gap closes every {math.log(0.5) / math.log(abs(a)):.1f} periods"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"a = {a:.2f}: x* = {x_star:.2f}; {speed}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="period, t", range=[0, 30], tickvals=[5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30]), yaxis=dict(title="x", range=[-0.04 * top, top]),
                      legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0, y=1.02, yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig

C.13.2 Example 1: the bathtub model of unemployment
Each month a fraction \(\bar{s}\) of the employed lose their job and a fraction \(\bar{f}\) of the unemployed find one (Chapter 7). With the labor force normalized to 1, the unemployment rate follows \(u_{t+1}=u_t+\bar{s}(1-u_t)-\bar{f}u_t=(1-\bar{s}-\bar{f})\,u_t+\bar{s}\). That is our linear form with \(a=1-\bar{s}-\bar{f}\) and \(b=\bar{s}\), so the steady state is \(u^*=\bar{s}/(\bar{s}+\bar{f})\) (7.4). With the book’s monthly values \(\bar{s}=0.01\) and \(\bar{f}=0.20\):

s_job, f_job = 0.01, 0.20
u_path = simulate_linear(1 - s_job - f_job, s_job, 0.10, 12)          # start at 10 percent unemployment
print(f"Natural rate u* = {100 * s_job / (s_job + f_job):.2f}%")
print("Unemployment, months 0-12 (%):", (100 * u_path).round(2))
print(f"Half-life: {math.log(0.5) / math.log(1 - s_job - f_job):.1f} months")

Natural rate u* = 4.76%
Unemployment, months 0-12 (%): [10.    8.9   8.03  7.34  6.8   6.37  6.04  5.77  5.56  5.39  5.26  5.15
  5.07]
Half-life: 2.9 months




C.13.3 Example 2: the Solow model, a nonlinear difference equation
Capital per person follows \(k_{t+1}=k_t+\bar{s}\bar{A}k_t^{1/3}-\bar{d}k_t\) (5.7). This is not linear, but near the steady state it behaves like a linear equation whose \(a\) is the slope of the right-hand side at \(k^*\) (the Taylor approximation of Section C.6). SymPy computes that slope:

k, s_, d_ = sp.symbols("k s d", positive=True)
next_k = k + s_ * k ** sp.Rational(1, 3) - d_ * k                      # A = 1
k_star_formula = (s_ / d_) ** sp.Rational(3, 2)                        # equation (5.8)
slope_at_steady_state = sp.simplify(sp.diff(next_k, k).subs(k, k_star_formula))
slope_at_steady_state

\(\displaystyle 1 - \frac{2 d}{3}\)


The slope is \(1-\tfrac{2}{3}\bar{d}\). With \(\bar{d}=0.1\) it is about 0.933, so the gap to the steady state halves roughly every 10 years. A simulation from \(k_0=4\) confirms it:

k_values = [4.0]
for year in range(40):
    k_values.append(k_values[-1] + 0.4 * k_values[-1] ** (1 / 3) - 0.1 * k_values[-1])
k_values = np.array(k_values)
half_closed = np.argmax(8 - k_values <= 0.5 * (8 - 4.0))               # first year with half the gap closed
print(f"Linear approximation: half-life {math.log(0.5) / math.log(1 - 2 * 0.1 / 3):.1f} years")
print(f"Simulation: half of the gap is closed after {half_closed} years (k = {k_values[half_closed]:.2f})")

Linear approximation: half-life 10.0 years
Simulation: half of the gap is closed after 11 years (k = 6.00)




C.13.4 Example 3: disinflation with the Phillips curve
Combine the Phillips curve \(\pi_t=\pi_{t-1}+\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\) (12.5) with the aggregate demand curve \(\tilde{Y}_t=-\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t-\bar{\pi})\) (13.3, with \(\bar{a}=0\)). Solving the two for \(\pi_t\) gives a linear difference equation in inflation:

pi_t, nubar, bbar, mbar, pibar = sp.symbols("pi_t nubar bbar mbar pibar")
pi_prev = sp.Symbol(r"\pi_{t-1}")
inflation_next = sp.solve(sp.Eq(pi_t, pi_prev - nubar * bbar * mbar * (pi_t - pibar)), pi_t)[0]
sp.collect(sp.expand(inflation_next), pi_prev)

\(\displaystyle \frac{\pi_{t-1}}{\bar{b} \bar{m} \bar{\nu} + 1} + \frac{\bar{b} \bar{m} \bar{\nu} \bar{\pi}}{\bar{b} \bar{m} \bar{\nu} + 1}\)


The coefficient on \(\pi_{t-1}\) is \(a=1/(1+\bar{\nu}\bar{b}\bar{m})\), between 0 and 1, so inflation falls smoothly to the target \(\bar{\pi}\). With \(\bar{\nu}=\bar{b}=\bar{m}=0.5\), \(\bar{\pi}=2\) and inflation starting at 6 percent:

a_pi = 1 / (1 + 0.5 * 0.5 * 0.5)
inflation_path = simulate_linear(a_pi, (1 - a_pi) * 2, 6.0, 10)      # b = (1 - a) x pi_bar keeps x* = pi_bar
print(f"a = {a_pi:.3f}; inflation over 10 years (%):", inflation_path.round(2))

a = 0.889; inflation over 10 years (%): [6.   5.56 5.16 4.81 4.5  4.22 3.97 3.75 3.56 3.39 3.23]




C.13.5 Example 4: the public debt ratio
The government budget constraint (18.2) says \(B_{t+1}=(1+i)B_t+D_t\), where \(B\) is the debt, \(i\) the nominal interest rate and \(D_t=G_t-T_t\) the primary deficit (spending other than interest, minus taxes). Divide both sides by next year’s GDP, \(Y_{t+1}=(1+g)Y_t\), where \(g\) is the growth rate of nominal GDP. With \(b_t=B_t/Y_t\) and \(d=D_t/Y_t\):
\[b_{t+1}=\frac{1+i}{1+g}\,b_t+\frac{d}{1+g}.\]
This is our linear form with \(a=(1+i)/(1+g)\). When the economy grows faster than the interest rate (\(g>i\)), \(a<1\) and the ratio settles at \(b^*=d/(g-i)\). When \(i>g\), \(a>1\) and the ratio keeps rising unless the government runs primary surpluses. The chart starts from the actual U.S. debt ratio of 2025.

debt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig18-2.csv")

debt_2025 = debt.loc[debt["year"] == 2025, "debt_public_gdp_pct"].iloc[0]
print(f"Federal debt held by the public, FY2025: {debt_2025:.1f}% of GDP")
debt.tail(3)

def debt_chart(i=3.5, g=4.0, d=2.5):
    """The debt ratio b_{t+1} = (1 + i)/(1 + g) b_t + d/(1 + g) from 2025 to 2055 (from equation 18.2)."""
    path = simulate_linear((1 + i / 100) / (1 + g / 100), d / (1 + g / 100), debt_2025, 30)
    top = 2000.0
    for candidate in [200.0, 400.0, 1000.0, 2000.0]:          # widen the axis in steps, only when needed
        if path.max() * 1.05 <= candidate:
            top = candidate
            break
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=debt["year"], y=debt["debt_public_gdp_pct"], mode="lines", name="actual, 1940–2025",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=np.arange(2025, 2056), y=path, mode="lines", name="simulation, 2025–2055",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    if g > i:
        ending = f"steady state {round(100 * d / (g - i)) + 0}%"    # b* = d / (g - i), with rates in percent
    else:
        ending = "no stable steady state (i ≥ g)"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"i = {i:.1f}%, g = {g:.1f}%, d = {d:.1f}%: {round(path[-1]) + 0}% of GDP in 2055; {ending}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="", range=[1940, 2055], tickvals=[1950, 1970, 1990, 2010, 2030, 2050]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="debt held by the public (% of GDP)", range=[-50 if path.min() < 0 else 0, top]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.02, y=0.98))
    return fig

What to notice.

In the difference-equation chart, a value of \(a\) close to 1 means a slow approach and a large steady state; a negative \(a\) makes the path zigzag around \(x^*\).
The bathtub model converges in a few months, the Solow model in decades: the half-life tells you which equations describe the short run and which the long run.
In the debt chart, the gap between \(g\) and \(i\) matters as much as the deficit. With \(g\) only half a point above \(i\), a primary deficit of 2.5 percent of GDP has a steady state of 500 percent: the ratio keeps rising for decades. Set \(i\) above \(g\) and even a balanced primary budget (\(d=0\)) makes the ratio grow.

text:
C.14 Continuous time and differential equations
Goal. Read the continuous-time notation of more advanced books, prove the growth rules, and solve a differential equation with SymPy and SciPy.
The book counts time in periods \(t=0,1,2,\dots\), but many advanced books let time flow continuously. Then the change \(\Delta x_{t+1}\) becomes the time derivative \(\dot{x}\equiv dx/dt\), and the growth rate becomes \(\dot{x}/x\). A neat fact: the growth rate is the time derivative of the log, \(\dot{x}/x=d\ln x/dt\) (by the chain rule, since \(d\ln x/dx=1/x\)). With it, the growth rules of Section C.5 become exact:

t = sp.symbols("t")
x_t = sp.Function("x", positive=True)(t)
y_t = sp.Function("y", positive=True)(t)
a = sp.symbols("a")

def growth_rate(z):
    """The continuous-time growth rate of z(t): the time derivative of its log."""
    return sp.simplify(sp.diff(sp.expand_log(sp.log(z), force=True), t))

print("product:", growth_rate(x_t * y_t))
print("ratio:  ", growth_rate(x_t / y_t))
print("power:  ", growth_rate(x_t ** a))

product: Derivative(y(t), t)/y(t) + Derivative(x(t), t)/x(t)
ratio:   -Derivative(y(t), t)/y(t) + Derivative(x(t), t)/x(t)
power:   a*Derivative(x(t), t)/x(t)


Derivative(x(t), t)/x(t) is \(\dot{x}/x=g_x\): the growth of a product is the sum of the growth rates, with no term dropped.
A differential equation links a variable to its own time derivative. The simplest one is constant growth, \(\dot{y}=g\,y\). sp.dsolve solves it:

y = sp.Function("y")
g, y0 = sp.symbols("g y_0", positive=True)
sp.dsolve(sp.Eq(y(t).diff(t), g * y(t)), y(t), ics={y(0): y0})

\(\displaystyle y{\left(t \right)} = y_{0} e^{g t}\)


That is the continuous version of (3.7): \(y_t=y_0e^{gt}\).

C.14.1 The Solow model in continuous time
In continuous time, capital accumulation reads \(\dot{k}=\bar{s}\bar{A}k^{1/3}-\bar{d}k\). Most differential equations of this kind are solved numerically. integrate.solve_ivp (“solve an initial value problem”) takes a function that returns \(\dot{k}\), the time span and the starting value, and returns the path.

def k_dot(t, k):
    """Continuous-time Solow model: dk/dt = s A k^(1/3) - d k with s = 0.4, A = 1, d = 0.1."""
    return 0.4 * k ** (1 / 3) - 0.1 * k

years_solow = np.arange(0, 61)
continuous = integrate.solve_ivp(k_dot, t_span=(0, 60), y0=[1.0], t_eval=years_solow)
discrete = [1.0]
for year in range(60):
    discrete.append(discrete[-1] + 0.4 * discrete[-1] ** (1 / 3) - 0.1 * discrete[-1])
print(f"Year 20: discrete k = {discrete[20]:.2f}, continuous k = {continuous.y[0][20]:.2f}")

Year 20: discrete k = 5.80, continuous k = 5.75



time_fig = go.Figure()
time_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years_solow, y=discrete, mode="lines+markers", name="discrete time (one step a year)",
                              line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2), marker=dict(size=5)))
time_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years_solow, y=continuous.y[0], mode="lines", name="continuous time (solve_ivp)",
                              line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
time_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, 60], y=[8, 8], mode="lines", name="steady state k* = 8", line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")))
time_fig.update_layout(title=f"Both versions approach k* = 8; in year 20, k = {discrete[20]:.2f} (discrete) and "
                             f"{continuous.y[0][20]:.2f} (continuous)",
                       xaxis=dict(title="years", range=[0, 60]), yaxis=dict(title="capital per person, k", range=[0, 9], tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8]),
                       legend=dict(x=0.99, xanchor="right", y=0.02, yanchor="bottom"))
time_fig




                                
                                            




Source. Illustration of the Solow model’s capital accumulation equation (5.7) in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., and of its continuous-time version.
What to notice.

The two paths are close and reach the same steady state: the choice between discrete and continuous time is mostly one of convenience.
The discrete path runs slightly ahead after the first few years. It adds a whole year of net investment at the rate of the start of the year; in continuous time that rate is updated at every instant, and it falls as diminishing returns set in.

Your turn. Solve the continuous-time Solow model with an investment rate of \(\bar{s}=0.3\). What is the new steady state, and how far is \(k\) from it after 20 years?


Hint

Copy k_dot under a new name with 0.3 instead of 0.4, and call integrate.solve_ivp again. The steady state is \((0.3/0.1)^{3/2}\approx 5.2\).

C.15 Present value and discounting
Goal. Value payments that arrive in the future, with the formulas of Chapters 7, 16 and 17, and with Python.
A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because a dollar today can be saved at the interest rate \(R\). So the present discounted value (pdv) of a payment \(X\) that arrives in \(T\) years is
\[pdv=\frac{X}{(1+R)^T}. \qquad (7.6)\]
The pdv of a stream of payments is the sum of the pdv of each payment (7.10). For a stream of equal payments, the sum is a geometric series, which has a closed form (7.12):
\[1+a+a^2+\dots+a^n=\frac{1-a^{n+1}}{1-a}.\]
SymPy proves it, and also sums the series to infinity:

a = sp.symbols("a", positive=True)
n, j = sp.symbols("n j", integer=True, nonnegative=True)
R = sp.symbols("R", positive=True)
print("Finite sum:  ", sp.summation(a ** j, (j, 0, n)))
print("Perpetuity:  ", sp.simplify(sp.summation(1 / (1 + R) ** j, (j, 0, sp.oo))), " (payments of 1 from today on)")

Finite sum:   Piecewise((n + 1, Eq(a, 1)), ((1 - a**(n + 1))/(1 - a), True))
Perpetuity:   (R + 1)/R  (payments of 1 from today on)



Python note. sp.summation(term, (j, 0, n)) adds up term for j from 0 to n; sp.oo (two letters o) is infinity. A Piecewise result lists answers for different cases: here, the special case \(a=1\), where all terms equal 1.


C.15.1 Human capital: the value of a working life
Chapter 7 values a working life of 45 years with an income of 100,000 dollars a year, discounted at \(R=3\) percent (7.15). We recompute the book’s 2.53 million dollars (7.16) with the formula and with a NumPy sum:

R_value, years_working, wage = 0.03, 45, 100_000
by_formula = wage * (1 - (1 / (1 + R_value)) ** years_working) / (1 - 1 / (1 + R_value))   # (7.15)
by_sum = np.sum(wage / (1 + R_value) ** np.arange(0, years_working))                     # payments in years 0-44
print(f"Formula: {by_formula:,.0f} dollars;  sum of 45 discounted payments: {by_sum:,.0f} dollars")

Formula: 2,525,427 dollars;  sum of 45 discounted payments: 2,525,427 dollars




C.15.2 Interactive: the present value of a stream
Twenty yearly payments of 100, the first one today (the stream of equation 7.11). The light bars are the payments; the dark bars are what each one is worth today.

def pv_chart(R=5.0):
    """Present values of 20 yearly payments of 100, the first one today (equation 7.11), at R percent."""
    years_pv = np.arange(0, 20)
    values = 100 / (1 + R / 100) ** years_pv
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=years_pv, y=np.full(20, 100.0), name="payment", marker_color="#d5dde6"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=years_pv, y=values, name="present value", marker_color=TEAL))
    fig.update_layout(barmode="overlay", title=f"R = {R:.1f}%: the 20 payments of 100 are worth {values.sum():,.0f} today",
                      xaxis=dict(title="year of the payment", range=[-0.6, 19.6]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="value", range=[0, 110]), legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0, y=1.02, yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig

slider_figure(pv_chart, "R", [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0, 10.0, 15.0], start=5.0, label="interest rate R (%)")

C.15.3 Bonds, stocks and investment projects
Bond prices. A bond that pays 100 dollars in 10 years is worth \(100/(1+i)^{10}\) today. When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, which is why rate hikes hurt bondholders (Chapters 12 and 14).

for i_bond in [0.02, 0.04, 0.06]:
    print(f"i = {100 * i_bond:.0f}%: a 10-year bond paying 100 costs {100 / (1 + i_bond) ** 10:.1f} today")

i = 2%: a 10-year bond paying 100 costs 82.0 today
i = 4%: a 10-year bond paying 100 costs 67.6 today
i = 6%: a 10-year bond paying 100 costs 55.8 today


Stocks. A stock pays a dividend that grows at rate \(g\). Its pdv is a growing perpetuity: summing \(D(1+g)^j/(1+R)^{j}\) gives \(P=D(1+R)/(R-g)\) when the first dividend is paid today, or \(P=D/(R-g)\) when it is paid a year from now. Chapter 17 reaches the same form from an arbitrage argument (17.16): the price is the dividend divided by the interest rate minus the capital gain. Turned around, the dividend yield \(D/P\) equals \(R-g\). If firms paid out all their earnings, the earnings yield \(E/P\), the inverse of the price-earnings ratio, would be \(R-g\): a low earnings yield means investors accept a low \(R\) or expect fast growth (17.17).

cape = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig17-3.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
cape["earnings_yield"] = 100 / cape["cape"]                  # percent: earnings per 100 dollars of stock
latest = cape.iloc[-1]
yield_fig = px.line(cape, x="date", y="earnings_yield",
                    labels={"date": "", "earnings_yield": "earnings yield, 1/CAPE (percent)"},
                    title=f"U.S. earnings yield: {latest['earnings_yield']:.1f}% in {latest['date']:%B %Y}, "
                          f"versus {cape['earnings_yield'].mean():.1f}% on average since 1881")
yield_fig.add_hline(y=cape["earnings_yield"].mean(), line_color=GRAY, line_dash="dash")
yield_fig




                                
                                            




Sources. Data: Robert Shiller, Online Data (ie_data.xls), cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio of the S&P composite. Prepared file: data/appC/fig17-3.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 17.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
Investment projects. A project costs 100 today and pays 12 a year for 10 years. Its net present value (NPV) is the pdv of the payments minus the cost; it is worth doing when the NPV is positive. The internal rate of return (IRR) is the interest rate at which the NPV is zero, which brentq finds:

def npv(rate):
    """Net present value of a project that costs 100 today and pays 12 a year in years 1-10."""
    return -100 + np.sum(12 / (1 + rate) ** np.arange(1, 11))

print(f"NPV at 3%: {npv(0.03):.2f};  NPV at 5%: {npv(0.05):.2f}")
print(f"Internal rate of return: {100 * optimize.brentq(npv, 0.0001, 0.5):.2f}%")

NPV at 3%: 2.36;  NPV at 5%: -7.34
Internal rate of return: 3.46%


What to notice.

At \(R=0\) the 20 payments are worth 2,000; at 5 percent about 1,300; at 15 percent about 720. Distant payments lose the most value.
The earnings yield moves inversely with stock prices: it was high around 1920, in 1932 and in the early 1980s, when stocks were cheap, and it was low around 2000, in 2021 and again now.
The project pays if the interest rate is below its internal rate of return of about 3.5 percent. This is the logic of Chapter 17: higher interest rates make fewer investment projects worthwhile.

Your turn. Recompute the value of the working life of Chapter 7 when wages grow 1 percent a year. The payment in year \(j\) is then \(100{,}000 \times 1.01^j\).


Hint

Multiply each payment by 1.01 ** np.arange(0, 45) before discounting. The value rises to about 3.0 million dollars: wage growth works like a lower interest rate, about \(R-g\).

C.16 Describing macro data: averages, volatility, trends and cycles
Goal. Summarize a series with a few numbers, measure how two series move together, and separate a long-run trend from short-run fluctuations.

C.16.1 Averages and volatility
The mean is the average, the median the middle value, and the standard deviation measures how much a series moves around its mean, its volatility. pandas computes them all with .describe().

growth_stats = nipa[nipa["year"] >= 1930][["year", "g_real"]]
print(growth_stats["g_real"].describe().round(2))
early = growth_stats[growth_stats["year"].between(1950, 1984)]["g_real"]
late = growth_stats[growth_stats["year"].between(1985, 2025)]["g_real"]

Real GDP growth became much less volatile after the mid-1980s, a change economists call the Great Moderation (Chapter 13 discusses one explanation, better monetary policy), though the 2008–2009 and 2020 recessions interrupted it.


C.16.2 Correlation: the Phillips curve in the data
The correlation coefficient measures how closely two series move together, from \(-1\) (exactly opposite) to \(+1\) (exactly together). The Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi_t=\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\) (12.6) predicts that inflation rises when output is above potential. A least-squares line fitted through the points estimates the slope \(\bar{\nu}\).

gap_inflation = potential[["year", "gap_percent"]].merge(cpi[["year", "inflation"]], on="year")
gap_inflation["change_in_inflation"] = gap_inflation["inflation"].diff()
gap_inflation = gap_inflation[gap_inflation["year"] >= 1950]
correlation = gap_inflation["gap_percent"].corr(gap_inflation["change_in_inflation"])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(gap_inflation["gap_percent"], gap_inflation["change_in_inflation"], 1)
print(f"Correlation: {correlation:.2f};  fitted slope ν = {slope:.2f}")

Correlation: 0.37;  fitted slope ν = 0.34



Python note. .merge(other, on="year") joins two tables row by row on the year. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits a straight line \(y=\text{slope}\cdot x+\text{intercept}\) by least squares and returns the two numbers.


phillips_fig = px.scatter(gap_inflation, x="gap_percent", y="change_in_inflation", hover_name="year",
                          trendline="ols", trendline_color_override=TEAL,
                          labels={"gap_percent": "short-run output, Ỹ (percent)",
                                  "change_in_inflation": "change in CPI inflation (points)"},

C.16.3 Trend and cycle
Chapter 9 splits GDP into a long-run trend (potential output \(\bar{Y}_t\)) and short-run fluctuations (\(\tilde{Y}_t\)). Potential output cannot be observed, so it has to be estimated. Two simple statistical methods:

A straight line through the logs. Fit \(\ln y_t=\alpha+\beta t\). The slope \(\beta\) is the trend growth rate (in log points), and the distance to the line is the cycle.
The Hodrick–Prescott (HP) filter. It draws a smooth curve through the data, trading off closeness to the data against smoothness. The parameter \(\lambda\) sets the smoothness; 100 is a common choice for annual data. It lives in statsmodels, a statistics library that comes with Colab.


trend_slope, trend_intercept = np.polyfit(gdp_pc["year"], np.log(gdp_pc["gdppc"]), 1)
print(f"Trend growth of U.S. GDP per person, 1870-2025: {100 * trend_slope:.2f} log points a year")

from statsmodels.tsa.filters.hp_filter import hpfilter      # imported here, where we first use it
postwar = potential[potential["year"] >= 1950].copy()
cycle, trend = hpfilter(np.log(postwar["gdp_actual"]), lamb=100)
postwar["gap_hp"] = 100 * cycle                              # percent deviation from the HP trend
print(f"Correlation of the HP gap with the CBO gap: {postwar['gap_hp'].corr(postwar['gap_log']):.2f}")

Trend growth of U.S. GDP per person, 1870-2025: 1.95 log points a year
Correlation of the HP gap with the CBO gap: 0.80



gaps_long = postwar.melt(id_vars="year", value_vars=["gap_log", "gap_hp"], var_name="method", value_name="gap")
gaps_long["method"] = gaps_long["method"].map({"gap_log": "CBO potential output", "gap_hp": "HP filter (λ = 100)"})
gaps_fig = px.line(gaps_long, x="year", y="gap", color="method",
                   labels={"year": "", "gap": "output gap (percent of trend)"},
                   title="Two estimates of the U.S. output gap move together, but differ in size")
gaps_fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
gaps_fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", legend=dict(x=0.99, xanchor="right", y=0.02, yanchor="bottom"))
gaps_fig




                                
                                            




Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPCA), via FRED; Congressional Budget Office, Real Potential Gross Domestic Product (GDPPOT), via FRED. Prepared file: data/appC/fig9-2.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 9.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

The fitted trend, about 2 log points a year, is close to the average growth rate of Section C.4.
The points of the Phillips-curve scatter are widely spread, so the correlation is positive but far from 1: other forces, such as oil prices and expectations, also move inflation (Chapters 12 and 13).
The HP gap and the CBO gap rise and fall together, but the HP trend follows the data more closely, so its gaps are smaller and it sees less of a slump after 2008. Every estimate of potential output is a model, not a fact.

Your turn. Recompute the HP gap with a much smoother trend, \(\lambda=6{,}400\), and with a very flexible one, \(\lambda=10\). How does the volatility of the gap (its standard deviation) change?


Hint

Call hpfilter(np.log(postwar["gdp_actual"]), lamb=6400) and compute (100 * cycle).std() for each value of \(\lambda\). A smoother trend (larger \(\lambda\)) leaves more of the movement to the cycle.

title: C. Math Review for Macroeconomics
text:
C.18 Concluding remarks

Most of the math in macroeconomics is about growth and change: percent changes, compound growth, logs, growth rates and the growth rules, and the approximations that make them simple. They work well for the small rates of normal times and break down in high inflation.
Derivatives give marginal products, elasticities and the first-order conditions of firms and households. Systems of equations give equilibria, and difference equations describe how capital, unemployment, inflation and public debt move from one year to the next; their stability depends on whether \(|a|<1\).
Present value turns streams of future payments into one number today: the value of a working life, a bond, a stock or an investment project.
Python offers three complementary ways to do this math: NumPy computes, SymPy does the algebra and calculus with letters, and SciPy solves, optimizes and simulates when there is no formula.
Every chapter of this book uses these tools. When an equation in a chapter looks hard, come back to the section of this appendix that covers it, and try it in code.

title: D. Growth and Development Accounting
text:
Learning goals
Two simple questions sit behind much of growth economics. Why did an economy grow as fast as it did? And why is one economy so much richer than another? Growth accounting answers the first question, and development accounting answers the second. Both split output into a part explained by measured inputs (physical capital, workers, hours, schooling) and a part that is left over, total factor productivity (TFP). This appendix applies both methods to the Penn World Table, for any economies you choose. By the end of it you will be able to:
The appendix builds on the production model of Chapter 4, which does a first development accounting exercise with physical capital only, and on the growth accounting of Chapter 6, which uses U.S. data. The growth rules it uses are reviewed in Appendix C.5.

title: D. Growth and Development Accounting
text:
D.2 Two questions, two methods
Both methods start from the same production function, the one of Chapters 4 to 6:
\[
Y = A K^{\alpha} L^{1-\alpha}, \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1. \tag{1}
\]
Output \(Y\) is made with physical capital \(K\) and labour \(L\), and \(A\) is total factor productivity: how efficiently the economy turns its inputs into output. The exponent \(\alpha\) is the capital share. We can measure \(Y\), \(K\) and \(L\) in national data, but not \(A\). Both methods therefore find \(A\) the same way: as the part of output that the measured inputs do not explain, the residual.









Growth accounting
Development accounting




Question
Why did this economy grow?
Why is this economy poorer than the United States?


Compares
one economy with itself, year after year
many economies with each other, in one year


Works with
growth rates of total GDP, capital and labour
levels of output per worker, capital and schooling


Main result
contributions of capital, labour and TFP to GDP growth, in percentage points
the share of the income gap due to TFP, physical capital and human capital


Sections
D.4 to D.7
D.8 to D.11



Both methods are accounting, not explanation. They tell us where growth and income differences appear in equation (1), not why an economy invested more, schooled its workers longer, or used its inputs more efficiently. The models of Chapters 5 and 6 answer those questions.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

D.4 The Penn World Table
The Penn World Table (PWT) is a database of national accounts for 185 economies since 1950, built at the Groningen Growth and Development Centre of the University of Groningen (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015). It is the standard source for growth and development accounting, for two reasons:

it makes output comparable across countries: GDP is converted with purchasing power parities (PPPs), so a dollar buys the same basket of goods everywhere, as Chapter 3 explains;
it provides the inputs of the production function: capital stocks built from past investment, the number of workers, their hours, and an index of their schooling.

We use version 11.0, released in 2025, which covers 1950 to 2023 with prices of 2021. These are the variables we need:

title: D. Growth and Development Accounting
text:
D.5 Growth accounting: the theory

Assumptions

Output is produced with the Cobb–Douglas production function (1), \(Y_t = A_t K_t^{\alpha} L_t^{1-\alpha}\), in every year \(t\).
The capital share \(\alpha\) is the same in every economy and every year. Following the Growth Atlas and Hall and Jones (1999), we use \(\alpha = 0.33\), about one third.
Output \(Y_t\) is real GDP (rgdpna), capital \(K_t\) is the real capital stock (rnna), and labour \(L_t\) is one of three measures: persons engaged (emp), total hours (emp × avh), or quality-adjusted hours (emp × avh × hc).



Deriving the equation
Take natural logs of equation (1). The log of a product is the sum of the logs, and the log of a power is the exponent times the log:
\[
\ln Y_t = \ln A_t + \alpha \ln K_t + (1-\alpha) \ln L_t .
\]
The same equation holds a year earlier, at \(t-1\). Subtract the two:
\[
\ln Y_t - \ln Y_{t-1} = (\ln A_t - \ln A_{t-1}) + \alpha (\ln K_t - \ln K_{t-1}) + (1-\alpha)(\ln L_t - \ln L_{t-1}).
\]
The change in the log of a variable is, approximately, its growth rate: \(\ln X_t - \ln X_{t-1} \approx
\Delta X / X\). Writing \(g_X\) for the growth rate of \(X\) gives the growth accounting equation:
\[
g_Y = \underbrace{\alpha\, g_K}_{\text{capital}} + \underbrace{(1-\alpha)\, g_L}_{\text{labour}} + \underbrace{g_A}_{\text{TFP}} . \tag{2}
\]
GDP growth is the sum of three contributions: the growth of capital weighted by its share \(\alpha\), the growth of labour weighted by its share \(1-\alpha\), and the growth of TFP.


The residual
We observe \(g_Y\), \(g_K\) and \(g_L\), but not \(g_A\). So we turn equation (2) around:
\[
g_A = g_Y - \alpha\, g_K - (1-\alpha)\, g_L . \tag{3}
\]
TFP growth is whatever GDP growth the inputs cannot explain: the Solow residual. Because it is computed this way, the three contributions always add up to GDP growth exactly, even though equation (2) holds only approximately for growth rates. Like the Growth Atlas, we use simple yearly growth rates, \(g_X = 100 \times (X_t / X_{t-1} - 1)\), in percent, so each contribution is in percentage points.
Intuition. With \(\alpha = 0.33\), a 3 percent rise in the capital stock adds about 1 percentage point to GDP growth, and a 3 percent rise in labour adds about 2 points. Whatever growth is left is credited to TFP.
What the residual contains. Over long periods, TFP growth reflects new ideas (Chapter 6), better organization, and the movement of workers to more productive jobs. In a single year it also absorbs anything the inputs miss: changes in hours or skills when labour is counted in persons, how intensively machines are used in booms and recessions, commodity price swings, wars, and measurement error. Treat a large residual in a single year with care.

D.6.1 A function for any economy and any labour measure
Steps 1 to 3 become one function. It works on many economies at once: groupby("iso3") makes pct_change compute growth rates within each economy, so the first year of one economy is never compared with the last year of another.

LABOUR = {"persons": "Persons engaged", "hours": "Total hours", "quality": "Quality-adjusted hours"}
LABOUR_MENU = [("Persons engaged", "persons"), ("Total hours", "hours"), ("Quality-adjusted hours", "quality")]

def growth_accounting(alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Equations (2) and (3) for every economy: contributions to GDP growth, in percentage points."""
    d = pwt.sort_values(["iso3", "year"]).copy()
    d["L"] = d["emp"]
    if labour in ("hours", "quality"):
        d["L"] = d["L"] * d["avh"]
    if labour == "quality":
        d["L"] = d["L"] * d["hc"]
    growth = d.groupby("iso3")[["rgdpna", "rnna", "L"]].pct_change(fill_method=None) * 100
    d["gdp"] = growth["rgdpna"]
    d["capital"] = alpha * growth["rnna"]
    d["labour"] = (1 - alpha) * growth["L"]
    d["tfp"] = d["gdp"] - d["capital"] - d["labour"]
    d = d[(d["year"] >= START) & (d["year"] <= END)]
    return d[["iso3", "country", "year", "gdp", "capital", "labour", "tfp"]].dropna()

print(ga["iso3"].nunique(), "economies,", len(ga), "economy-years")

Fig. 3: The growth accounting of one economy
Goal. Draw the decomposition year by year: stacked bars for the three contributions, and a line for GDP growth. The bars of each year add up to the line.

PARTS = [("capital", "Capital, αg_K", BLUE), ("labour", "Labour, (1−α)g_L", GREEN), ("tfp", "TFP, g_A", RUST)]

def add_decomposition(fig, d, row=None, col=None, legend=True):
    """Add the three contribution bars and the GDP growth line of one economy to a figure."""
    for column, label, color in PARTS:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=d["year"], y=d[column], name=label, marker_color=color,
                             legendgroup=column, showlegend=legend), row=row, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=d["year"], y=d["gdp"], mode="lines+markers", name="GDP growth, g_Y",
                             line=dict(color="black", width=2), marker=dict(size=4),
                             legendgroup="gdp", showlegend=legend), row=row, col=col)
    return fig

def decomposition_figure(code="USA", alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Fig. 3: contributions to GDP growth in one economy, equation (2)."""
    d = growth_accounting(alpha, labour)
    d = d[d["iso3"] == code]
    fig = add_decomposition(go.Figure(), d)
    fig.update_layout(barmode="relative", title=f"{NAMES[code]}: where GDP growth came from, {START}-{END}",
                      xaxis_title="Year", yaxis_title="Percentage points", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15))
    return fig

Python note. barmode="relative" stacks positive bars upwards and negative bars downwards from zero, so a year with a negative contribution still reads correctly. legendgroup ties the bars of one kind together, which matters when the same legend serves several panels (Fig. 4).

What to notice.

In 2020 the pandemic cut U.S. employment, so the labour contribution fell to about −3.7 percentage points, while TFP rose. Workers who kept their jobs were, on average, more productive, and output per worker held up: a classic composition effect that the residual absorbs.
TFP contributions swing much more from year to year than capital contributions, because the capital stock changes slowly while output moves with the business cycle.

Fig. 4: Contributions to GDP growth, economy by economy
Goal. Compare the growth accounting of several economies side by side, and test how it changes with the capital share \(\alpha\) and the measure of labour.
Some economies lack hours or human capital in some years. A small helper writes their codes under the title, so a missing panel is never a mystery.

def no_data_note(codes, d):
    """A small second title line naming the chosen economies that have no data in d."""
    missing = []
    for code in codes:
        if code not in set(d["iso3"]):
            missing.append(code)
    if len(missing) == 0:
        return ""
    return "<br><sup>No data: " + ", ".join(missing) + "</sup>"


def growth_panels(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES), alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Fig. 4: one growth accounting panel per chosen economy, equation (2)."""
    d = growth_accounting(alpha, labour)
    codes = list(codes)[:9]                         # at most nine panels
    if len(codes) == 0:
        codes = ["USA"]                             # nothing chosen: show the United States
    rows = (len(codes) + 2) // 3
    titles = []
    for code in codes:
        titles.append(NAMES[code][:28])
    fig = make_subplots(rows=rows, cols=3, shared_yaxes=True, vertical_spacing=0.12, subplot_titles=titles)
    for i, code in enumerate(codes):
        add_decomposition(fig, d[d["iso3"] == code], row=i // 3 + 1, col=i % 3 + 1, legend=(i == 0))
    note = no_data_note(codes, d)
    fig.update_layout(barmode="relative", height=300 + 260 * rows, legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.08),
                      title=f"Contributions to GDP growth, α = {alpha:.2f}, labour = {LABOUR[labour]}{note}")
    shown = d[d["iso3"].isin(codes)][["gdp", "capital", "labour", "tfp"]]
    if shown.abs().max().max() < 20:                # one fixed scale, unless a year is far outside it
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[-20, 20])
    return fig

text:
D.8 Averages over periods and decades
Yearly numbers are noisy. Over longer periods, business-cycle swings cancel out and the residual reflects long-run productivity growth more closely.

Fig. 5: Average contributions over a period
Goal. Compare average contributions across your economies over a period you choose.

def period_averages(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES), start=START, end=END, alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Average contributions to GDP growth over start-end, one row per economy."""
    d = growth_accounting(alpha, labour)
    d = d[d["iso3"].isin(codes) & (d["year"] >= start) & (d["year"] <= end)]
    return d.groupby("country")[["gdp", "capital", "labour", "tfp"]].mean().sort_values("gdp")

def average_figure(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES), start=START, end=END, alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Fig. 5: stacked average contributions, with average GDP growth as a diamond."""
    avg = period_averages(codes, start, end, alpha, labour).reset_index()
    avg["gdp"] = avg["gdp"].round(4)
    fig = go.Figure()
    for column, label, color in PARTS:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=avg["country"], y=avg[column], name=label, marker_color=color))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=avg["country"], y=avg["gdp"], mode="markers", name="GDP growth, g_Y",
                             marker=dict(color="black", symbol="diamond", size=12)))
    fig.update_layout(barmode="relative", title=f"Average contributions to GDP growth, {start}-{end}",
                      yaxis_title="Percentage points a year")
    parts = avg[["capital", "labour", "tfp"]]
    if parts.clip(lower=0).sum(axis=1).max() < 12 and parts.clip(upper=0).sum(axis=1).min() > -4:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[-4, 12])            # one fixed scale, so periods are easy to compare
    return fig
