Fig. 6: Unconditional and conditional convergence
Goal. See conditional convergence in a chart. Panel A plots growth against initial income, with no controls. Panels B and C plot the same relation after removing the part of both variables that the controls explain.
How do we “remove” the controls? Regress growth on the controls and keep the residual, the part they do not explain; do the same for initial income; then plot one residual against the other. The slope of that cloud is exactly the coefficient on initial income in the multiple regression: this is the Frisch–Waugh theorem. We add back each variable’s mean, so the axes keep their units.

def partial_out(d, column, controls):
    """The part of a column that the controls do not explain, plus its mean (Frisch-Waugh)."""
    if len(controls) == 0:
        return d[column]
    fit = smf.ols(column + " ~ " + " + ".join(controls), data=d).fit()
    return fit.resid + d[column].mean()

PANELS = [("A: no controls", []), ("B: saving, population", ["ln_s", "ln_ngd"]),
          ("C: and schooling", ["ln_s", "ln_ngd", "ln_school"])]
d = sample(mrw, "Intermediate").dropna(subset=["growth", "ln_ngd", "ln_school"])
x = partial_out(d, "ln_y60", PANELS[2][1])
y = partial_out(d, "growth", PANELS[2][1])
print(f"slope of panel C: {np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0]:.4f}; "
      f"coefficient in the regression: {conditional_h[1].params['ln_y60']:.4f}")

slope of panel C: -0.3660; coefficient in the regression: -0.3660



Python note. " + ".join(controls) glues a list of names into one string, "ln_s + ln_ngd", to build a formula. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits a straight line and returns its slope and intercept.


def convergence_figure(name="Intermediate"):
    """Fig. 6: growth against initial income, without and with controls, one MRW sample."""
    d = sample(mrw, name).dropna(subset=["growth", "ln_ngd", "ln_school"])
    panels, titles = [], []
    for label, controls in PANELS:
        x = partial_out(d, "ln_y60", controls)
        y = partial_out(d, "growth", controls)
        slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
        panels.append((x, y, slope, intercept))
        titles.append(f"{label}<br>slope {round(slope, 2) + 0.0:.2f}")     # + 0.0 avoids printing -0.00
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=3, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.04, subplot_titles=titles)
    for col, (x, y, slope, intercept) in enumerate(panels, start=1):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="markers", text=d["country"], hovertemplate="%{text}",
                                 marker=dict(color=[BLUE, TEAL, GREEN][col - 1], size=7), showlegend=False),
                      row=1, col=col)
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[5.5, 10.5], y=[intercept + slope * 5.5, intercept + slope * 10.5], mode="lines",
                                 line=dict(color="black", dash="dash"), hoverinfo="skip", showlegend=False),
                      row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[5.5, 10.5], title="Log income, 1960")
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-0.9, 1.9])
    fig.update_yaxes(title="Log growth, 1960–1985", col=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{name} sample: poor countries catch up only once the controls are in",
                      margin=dict(t=120))
    return fig

Panel A has no downward slope: the poorest countries of 1960 did not grow faster than the richest.
Panels B and C slope down clearly. Among countries with the same saving and population growth (B), and also the same schooling (C), the poorer ones grew faster.
In the OECD sample all three panels slope down: these countries have similar steady states, so unconditional and conditional convergence look alike.

Hint

The horizontal axis of panel C is the part of log income in 1960 that saving, population growth and schooling do not explain. A narrower spread means they explain much of it: countries that were poor in 1960 were mostly poor because their steady states were low. text:
F.13 Simulation: catch-up between two countries

Fig. 7: Conditional and unconditional convergence in the model
Goal. See why the model predicts conditional, not unconditional, convergence, with two countries that share the same technology.
A rich country invests the baseline rates, \(\bar{s}_K=0.20\) and \(\bar{s}_H=0.10\), and sits on its balanced growth path. A poor country starts at a fraction of the rich country’s income and invests a share of the rich country’s rates, in both kinds of capital. Both have \(\alpha=\beta=1/3\), so the poor country’s steady state is that share squared times the rich country’s (the elasticities of Section F.6 add up to 2). The chart follows income per worker for 100 years, relative to the rich country’s in year 0, on a ratio scale.

def catch_up_figure(rates=1.0, start=0.1):
    """Fig. 7: income per worker of a rich and a poor country; equations (5) and (6)."""
    t = np.arange(101)
    k_rich, h_rich, y_rich = steady_state()
    scale = start ** (1 / (2 / 3))                    # alpha + beta = 2/3
    k, h, y = simulate(0.20 * rates, 0.10 * rates, k_rich * scale, h_rich * scale, years=100)
    poor = y / y_rich * np.exp(0.02 * t)              # technology grows at g = 0.02 in both countries
    rich = np.exp(0.02 * t)
    path = steady_state(0.20 * rates, 0.10 * rates)[2] / y_rich * np.exp(0.02 * t)
    g_poor = 100 * math.log(poor[25] / poor[0]) / 25
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=rich, mode="lines", name="Rich country", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=poor, mode="lines", name="Poor country", line=dict(color=RUST, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=path, mode="lines", name="Poor country's own balanced growth path",
                             line=dict(color=RUST, dash="dot")))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Growth in the first 25 years: poor {g_poor:.1f}%, rich 2.0% a year",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Years", range=[0, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Income per worker (rich country in year 0 = 1)", type="log",
                                 range=[np.log10(0.02), np.log10(10)], tickvals=[0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, xanchor="right", y=0.02, yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig

                           style=WIDE),

                           style=WIDE));

Source. Model: the augmented Solow model, equations (5) and (6) of this appendix, with \(\alpha=\beta=1/3\), \(\bar{n}=0.01\), \(\bar{g}=0.02\) and \(\bar{d}=0.03\) in both countries. Adapted from the transition dynamics of Chapter 5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.
What to notice.

With the same investment rates (the slider at 1.0), the poor country grows much faster than the rich one and closes the gap: unconditional and conditional convergence are the same thing.
With half the rich country’s rates, its own path is a quarter of the rich country’s. It still grows faster at first, while it catches up with its own path, then settles a fixed distance below.
With rates below about a third of the rich country’s, its steady state lies below where it starts, and it grows slower than the rich country: a poor country that falls further behind, as many did in panel A of Fig. 6. This is exactly what conditional convergence allows.

Your turn. With the poor country’s starting income at 0.1 of the rich country’s, what share of the rich country’s investment rates makes it grow at exactly 2 percent a year, neither catching up nor falling behind?


Hint

It grows at the rich country’s rate when it starts on its own balanced growth path: when its steady state, the share squared times the rich one, equals its starting income. Solve \(\text{share}^2=0.1\): \(\text{share}=\sqrt{0.1}\approx0.32\). Check with catch_up_figure(rates=0.32).

What to notice.

Investment rates agree much less. PWT 11.0 measures investment at current PPP prices, where MRW used constant prices, and the price of machines relative to other goods is much higher in poor countries. So by today’s measure many poor countries invested a larger share than MRW thought.



F.14.3 The regressions again
pwt_estimates runs, for one window, one sample and one measure of human capital, the restricted regressions of this appendix on the same set of countries: the textbook levels regression, the augmented levels regression (equation (7) with school, or equation (8) with the hc index) and the augmented convergence regression (equation (11)). It returns the implied α, β and λ and the fit. A sample with fewer than 15 economies is skipped.

HUMAN = {"ln_school": "School enrollment, eq. (7)", "ln_hc": "PWT hc index, eq. (8)"}
PWT_SAMPLES = {"MRW non-oil": "mrw_non_oil", "MRW intermediate": "mrw_intermediate", "MRW OECD": "mrw_oecd",
               "Full sample": "full"}
LABELS["ln_y0"] = "ln(initial income)"

def pwt_estimates(window, name, human):
    """Implied alpha, beta and λ in PWT 11.0, for one window, sample and measure of human capital."""
    d = pwt[(pwt["window"] == window) & (pwt[PWT_SAMPLES[name]] == 1)].dropna(subset=[human])
    row = {"window": window, "sample": name, "human capital": HUMAN[human], "N": len(d)}
    if len(d) < 15:
        return row
    terms = "ln_s_ngd + ln_school_ngd" if human == "ln_school" else "ln_s_ngd + ln_hc"
    textbook = smf.ols("ln_y ~ ln_s_ngd", data=d).fit()
    levels = smf.ols("ln_y ~ " + terms, data=d).fit()
    growth = smf.ols("growth ~ ln_y0 + " + terms, data=d).fit()
    c_K, c_H = levels.params[terms.split(" + ")[0]], levels.params[terms.split(" + ")[1]]
    if human == "ln_school":
        alpha, beta = implied_shares(c_K, c_H)
    else:
        alpha = c_K / (1 + c_K)                       # equation (8): c_K = alpha/(1-alpha), c_H = beta/(1-alpha)
        beta = c_H * (1 - alpha)
    row.update({"alpha, textbook": implied_shares(textbook.params["ln_s_ngd"])[0],
                "alpha": alpha, "beta": beta, "R², textbook": textbook.rsquared_adj,
                "R², augmented": levels.rsquared_adj,
                "speed (%)": 100 * implied_speed(growth.params["ln_y0"], int(window[-4:]) - int(window[:4]))[0]})
    return row


rows = []
for window in ["1960-1985", "1990-2023"]:
    for name in PWT_SAMPLES:
        for human in HUMAN:
            rows.append(pwt_estimates(window, name, human))
estimates = pd.DataFrame(rows)

What to notice.

The textbook puzzle is still there, and larger. In 1990–2023 the textbook regression implies α of about 0.7 in every sample outside the OECD (the column alpha, textbook of the table), even higher than MRW’s 0.6. Saving and population growth still matter far more than a capital share of one third allows.
With MRW’s schooling measure, β is remarkably stable. In 1990–2023 the implied β is 0.25 to 0.27 in the non-oil, intermediate and full samples, next to MRW’s 0.28. The implied α, about 0.47, is higher than MRW’s 0.31. In 1960–1985, with enrollment only for 43 to 60 economies, β is again 0.27 to 0.30 and α is lower.
With the hc index, β is far too large. The coefficient on ln(h) is about 2.5 in the full samples, so the implied β is 1.2 to 1.9, above \(1-\alpha\): impossible in the model. The log of the index varies little across countries (a standard deviation of about 0.3, against 1.2 for log income), so the regression needs a large coefficient to match income gaps with it. This is the measurement problem that Section F.14 discusses.
The fit holds up. With either measure, the augmented model explains 72 to 84 percent of the variation in log income outside the OECD in 1990–2023, close to MRW’s 78 percent.
So does the speed of convergence. Outside the OECD, every window, sample and measure gives λ between 1.2 and 2.2 percent a year, around MRW’s 1.4 percent and the model’s 2 percent.
Within the OECD, nothing fits in 1990–2023: the adjusted \(R^2\) is near zero or negative. Rich countries have become too similar in saving, schooling and population growth for these variables to explain their remaining differences.

title: F. Augmented Solow Growth Model
text:
F.15 Go further

Is saving really unrelated to \(A(0)\)? The regressions assume that \(\bar{s}_K\) and \(\bar{n}\) are unrelated to the country’s technology and institutions. But a country with good institutions may both invest more and use its capital better, which would bias the coefficients up. Panel-data studies, such as Islam (1995), let each country have its own \(A(0)\) and find faster convergence and a smaller role for capital.
Better measures of human capital. SCHOOL measures the flow into secondary school, and the hc index the years of schooling, not what students learn. Hanushek and Woessmann (2012) use test scores and find that cognitive skills matter far more for growth than years in school.
How much is left for technology? Klenow and Rodríguez-Clare (1997) argue that MRW’s SCHOOL varies much more across countries than years of schooling do, which overstates the role of human capital. With better measures, differences in productivity explain about half of income differences, as the development accounting of Appendix D finds.
Is growth exogenous? Bernanke and Gürkaynak (2001) re-run MRW on later data and find that the levels results hold up, but that long-run growth rates are correlated with saving, which the Solow model, with its exogenous \(\bar{g}\), cannot explain. Chapter 6 turns to the models of ideas that can.

title: F. Augmented Solow Growth Model
text:
F.16 Concluding remarks

The textbook Solow model, equation (3), predicts the signs of the effects of saving and population growth on income, and they explain about 59 percent of income differences across countries in 1985. But the size of the effects implies a capital share of about 0.6, twice capital’s share of income.
The augmented model, equation (7), adds human capital. With \(\alpha=\beta=1/3\) it doubles the elasticity of income to saving (Fig. 2), and in MRW’s data it fits with α and β of about 0.3 each and explains almost 80 percent of income differences.
The model predicts conditional, not unconditional, convergence, at the speed of equation (9): about 2 percent a year with human capital, half the textbook speed (Figs. 5 and 7). MRW’s growth regressions, turned into speeds with equation (12), find 1.4 to 2.1 percent a year.
With PWT 11.0 and the WDI, for 1990–2023 and many more countries, the main results survive: a large textbook α, a β near 0.27 with MRW’s schooling measure, a fit of about three quarters and a speed of 1.3 to 2 percent. How we measure human capital matters, and PWT’s hc index gives implausibly large shares.
The model takes the investment rates, schooling and population growth as given, and leaves the technology term \(A(0)\) unexplained. Chapter 6 turns to the ideas behind technology, and Appendix D measures how much of income differences it accounts for.

title: G. Growth and Institutions
text:
Learning goals
Rich countries have more capital and more schooling than poor ones. But Chapter 4 and Appendix D showed that most of the gap comes from total factor productivity (TFP): rich countries also use their capital and their workers much better. Why? A leading answer is institutions, the rules that decide whether people can keep what they build, sign contracts that courts enforce, and invest without fear that a ruler will take it away. Countries with good institutions are clearly richer. The hard question is whether the institutions cause the prosperity, or only go together with it. In a famous paper, Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001), “AJR” from now on, proposed a way to answer it, with a clever use of history and a tool from econometrics called instrumental variables (IV). This appendix rebuilds their argument and runs their regressions on their data. By the end of it you will be able to:
This appendix builds on my tutorial Do Institutions Cause Prosperity? An IV Tutorial in Python, which goes further into the robustness checks of AJR (Section G.11 lists them).

title: G. Growth and Institutions
text:
G.1 Why institutions?
Economists distinguish two kinds of causes of income differences. The proximate causes are the ones the production model of Chapter 4 measures: capital per worker, schooling, and TFP. But they only push the question back. Why do some countries invest so little, school their children so little, and use what they have so badly? The fundamental causes are the answers to that question. Three are discussed most: geography (climate, disease, soils, access to the sea), culture (values and beliefs), and institutions.
The economic historian Douglass North called institutions “the rules of the game in a society”. Good economic institutions protect property, enforce contracts, and give a broad part of the population the chance to invest and innovate. Bad ones let a small elite take what others produce. Two examples make the case vivid. North and South Korea share their history, culture and geography, but not their institutions since 1945; the satellite photograph of the Korean peninsula at night, discussed in Chapter 4, shows the result. And Botswana, which kept secure property rights and stable rules after independence, grew faster than almost any country in the world for three decades, while many of its neighbors stagnated.
Examples are not proof. Across all countries, a better measure of institutions goes with higher income (Fig. 2 shows it). But the correlation alone cannot tell us which way the arrow points. Rich countries can afford good courts. And something else, such as a healthy climate, may give a country both good institutions and high income. AJR’s idea was to find a piece of history that changed the institutions of some countries and not others, for reasons that have nothing to do with their income today. Section G.3 shows why such a piece of history, an instrument, solves the problem, and Sections G.7 and G.8 put AJR’s choice to work.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def button_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for each value; one button per value.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this
    precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = i == first
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {
            "title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
            "yaxis": f.layout.yaxis.to_plotly_json(),
            "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
            "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes],
        }
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        buttons.append(
            dict(
                label=str(values[i]),
                method="update",
                args=[{"visible": visible}, layout],
            )
        )
    fig.update_layout(
        updatemenus=[
            dict(
                type="buttons",
                direction="right",
                buttons=buttons,
                active=first,
                x=0,
                y=1.02,
                xanchor="left",

            )
        ],
        margin=dict(t=130),

    return fig



G.2.1 Tools for regressions
We run the same few kinds of regression many times. Four short functions do the work. ols_fit runs OLS with pyfixest. Like AJR, it uses robust standard errors (called HC1), which stay valid when the spread of the errors differs from country to country. coef_table puts several OLS regressions side by side.

def ols_fit(formula, data):
    """OLS with robust (HC1) standard errors; rows with a missing value are dropped."""
    return pf.feols(formula, data=data, vcov="HC1")


def coef_table(models, names, term="avexpr"):
    """One row per regression: the coefficient on term, its standard error and N."""
    rows = []
    for model, name in zip(models, names):
        rows.append(
            {
                "regression": name,
                "coefficient": model.coef()[term],
                "std. error": model.se()[term],
                "countries": len(model.resid()),
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("regression").round(3)


Python note. pf.feols("logpgp95 ~ avexpr", data=d) reads like the regression equation: the variable on the left of ~ is explained by the variables on the right, and a constant is added automatically. The fitted model answers questions through its methods: .coef() gives the coefficients, .se() their standard errors and .resid() the residuals, one per country used. Each is a pandas Series indexed by the variable names, so model.coef()["avexpr"] is the coefficient on avexpr.

iv_fit runs the IV regression of AJR with linearmodels: log income on institutions, with institutions instrumented by log settler mortality, plus any control variables. add_line draws a fitted line on a chart, and first_stage_F reads off the test of the instrument that Section G.8 explains.

def iv_fit(data, controls=()):
    """2SLS of logpgp95 on avexpr, instrumented by logem4 (linearmodels)."""
    controls = list(controls)
    d = data.dropna(subset=["logpgp95", "avexpr", "logem4"] + controls)
    exog = d[controls].assign(const=1.0)  # the controls and a constant
    return IV2SLS(d["logpgp95"], exog, d[["avexpr"]], d[["logem4"]]).fit(
        cov_type="robust"
    )


def add_line(fig, x, y, name="OLS line"):
    """Add a dashed black line through the points (x, y) to a figure."""
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=name, line=dict(color="black", dash="dash"))
    )


def first_stage_F(result):
    """The robust F statistic of the first stage: how strongly Z moves institutions."""
    return float(result.first_stage.diagnostics.loc["avexpr", "f.stat"])


Python note. IV2SLS(y, exog, endog, instruments) takes four pieces: the outcome, the exogenous variables (the constant and the controls), the endogenous variable that needs an instrument, and the instruments. linearmodels does not add a constant by itself, so .assign(const=1.0) adds a column of ones. cov_type="robust" asks for robust standard errors.

title: G. Growth and Institutions
text:
G.3 Model overview
Picture Islandia again, but this time not alone. It sits in an archipelago of many island countries that make the same goods with the same kind of boats and tools. On some islands a boat builder can be sure that the boat she builds stays hers. On others a chief can seize it, and the courts do nothing. Islanders on the secure islands build more boats and try new ways to fish; on the insecure ones they do neither. This section turns that story into the models of Chapters 4 and 5, derives the regression that AJR estimate, and shows why running it the simple way can mislead.






NoteThe big idea



The question. Do better institutions cause higher income, and by how much?
The answer in one sentence. In the growth models, institutions raise income through productivity and investment, which gives a straight line between log income and institutions. A simple regression gets its slope wrong whenever institutions are tied to other causes of income or measured with error, but an instrument, a force that moved institutions and nothing else, recovers it as a ratio of two slopes.
What goes in and what comes out. We choose how strongly institutions raise productivity and investment. The model gives back the effect of institutions on long-run income, the slope that OLS finds, and the slope that IV finds.
Road map.

Section G.3.1, institutions in the growth model: the assumptions, the solution, and what the model predicts.
Section G.3.2, why a simple regression can mislead: omitted variables, reverse causality and measurement error.
Section G.3.3, an instrument: the first stage, the reduced form, and the IV estimate.
Section G.3.4, the model in code: the key results as Python functions, checked with numbers.

Notation. A bar over a letter marks a parameter. Subscript \(i\) is an island (or, in the data, a country).








Symbol
Meaning
Type




\(y_i\)

\(\bar{A}_i\), \(\bar{s}_i\)

depend on institutions


\(R_i\)

\(\bar{\phi}\), \(\bar{\psi}\)

G.3.1 Institutions in the growth model

Assumptions
1. Production. Each island makes output with capital and workers, with the production function of Chapter 4. Per worker it reads
\[y_i = \bar{A}_i k_i^{1/3}.\]
2. Capital accumulation. Each island invests a share \(\bar{s}_i\) of output, and capital wears out at the rate \(\bar{d}\), the same everywhere. As in Chapter 5, capital per worker settles where investment just covers depreciation, and steady-state output per worker is
\[y_i^* = \bar{A}_i^{3/2}\left(\frac{\bar{s}_i}{\bar{d}}\right)^{1/2}.\]
3. Institutions raise productivity and investment. An island with more secure property uses its tools and workers better and invests more. We write both effects in logs, with \(R_i\) the security of property:
\[\ln \bar{A}_i = a_0 + \bar{\phi}R_i + \varepsilon_i^A, \qquad \ln \bar{s}_i = s_0 + \bar{\psi}R_i + \varepsilon_i^s.\]
The terms \(\varepsilon_i^A\) and \(\varepsilon_i^s\) hold everything else that makes an island productive or thrifty: its soil, its harbors, its climate, its luck.

Institutions matter twice: they decide how well an island uses its tools, and how many tools it builds.



Solving the model
Step 1: take logs. The log of a product is the sum of the logs, and the log of a power is the exponent times the log (Appendix C):
\[\ln y_i^* = \tfrac{3}{2}\ln \bar{A}_i + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln \bar{s}_i - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln \bar{d}.\]
Step 2: put in the two rules of assumption 3. Collect the terms that are the same on every island into a constant \(\mu\), the terms with \(R_i\), and the rest:
\[\ln y_i^* = \underbrace{\tfrac{3}{2}a_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}s_0 - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln \bar{d}}_{\mu}
+ \underbrace{\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\bar{\phi} + \tfrac{1}{2}\bar{\psi}\right)}_{\beta}R_i
+ \underbrace{\tfrac{3}{2}\varepsilon_i^A + \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_i^s}_{u_i}.\]






ImportantKey result: institutions and income



\[\ln y_i = \mu + \beta R_i + u_i \tag{1}\]
\[\beta = \tfrac{3}{2}\bar{\phi} + \tfrac{1}{2}\bar{\psi} \tag{2}\]
Equation (1) is the regression that AJR estimate, with log GDP per person for \(\ln y_i\). Equation (2) says what its slope means: the total long-run effect of institutions, through productivity (weighted by \(3/2\)) and through investment (weighted by \(1/2\)).
Islandia in numbers. In this appendix’s baseline, \(\bar{\phi} = \bar{\psi} = 0.5\), so \(\beta = 0.75 + 0.25 = 1\). One more point of secure property raises log income by 1, which multiplies income by \(e^1 \approx 2.7\).








TipIn words



Productivity gets the larger weight for the same reason as in Chapter 5: better productivity raises output directly, and the extra output is partly invested, which raises capital and output again. A higher investment rate works only through capital, and diminishing returns damp it.




What the model predicts
Comparing two islands. Write equation (1) for two islands and subtract. The constant cancels:
\[\ln y_1 - \ln y_2 = \beta\,(R_1 - R_2) + (u_1 - u_2).\]
With \(\beta = 1\), an island whose institutions score 2 points higher is, other things equal, \(e^2 \approx 7.4\) times as rich. Institutions that differ by a few points can explain income gaps of the size we see between rich and poor countries.
A line through the cloud. If we plot \(\ln y_i\) against \(R_i\) for many islands, equation (1) says the points scatter around a straight line with slope \(\beta\). The scatter comes from \(u_i\): the islands differ in many ways besides their institutions.

In the model, log income is a straight line in institutions, and the slope is the effect we are after.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. Suppose institutions raise productivity (\(\bar{\phi} = 0.5\)) but do not change the investment rate (\(\bar{\psi} = 0\)). What is \(\beta\)?


Answer

Equation (2) gives \(\beta = \tfrac{3}{2}\times 0.5 + 0 = 0.75\). Institutions still matter a lot, through productivity alone.

2. Two islands differ by 1 point in \(R\), and \(\beta = 1\). Is the richer island exactly \(e \approx 2.7\) times as rich?


Answer

Only on average. The gap is \(\beta(R_1-R_2) + (u_1-u_2)\), and the second term can be positive or negative: the islands also differ in soil, harbors and luck.






G.3.2 Why a simple regression can mislead

The OLS slope
The obvious way to estimate \(\beta\) is to fit a line through the cloud of countries by OLS. The OLS slope is the covariance of log income with institutions divided by the variance of institutions. Put equation (1) into the covariance, and use \(\text{Cov}(R, R) = \text{Var}(R)\):
\[\widehat{b}_{OLS} = \frac{\text{Cov}(\ln y, R)}{\text{Var}(R)}
= \frac{\text{Cov}(\mu + \beta R + u,\, R)}{\text{Var}(R)}
= \beta + \frac{\text{Cov}(R, u)}{\text{Var}(R)}. \tag{3}\]
OLS finds \(\beta\) only when institutions are unrelated to everything else in \(u\). A regressor that is related to the error term is called endogenous. There are three reasons why institutions may be endogenous.


Three reasons for a bias
Omitted variables. Suppose a healthy climate makes an island productive (it is in \(u\)) and also lets its people build good institutions. Then \(\text{Cov}(R, u) > 0\), and OLS gives the climate’s credit to the institutions: the slope is too steep.
Reverse causality. Suppose income also shapes institutions, because rich islands can pay for honest judges. Then a lucky year, a high \(u_i\), raises income and through it \(R_i\). Again \(\text{Cov}(R, u) > 0\), and OLS is too steep.
Measurement error. We never see the true security of property, only an index \(\tilde{R}_i = R_i + m_i\), built from the judgment of experts, with an error \(m_i\) that is unrelated to everything else. Regress log income on the index instead of the truth. The numerator becomes \(\text{Cov}(\ln y, \tilde{R}) = \beta\,\text{Var}(R)\), the denominator \(\text{Var}(\tilde{R}) = \text{Var}(R) + \text{Var}(m)\), so
\[\widehat{b}_{OLS} = \beta\,\frac{\text{Var}(R)}{\text{Var}(R) + \text{Var}(m)}. \tag{4}\]
The fraction is below one: noise in the index flattens the line. This is called attenuation bias.






TipIn words



The first two biases make OLS too large, the third makes it too small. Which one wins is an empirical question, and the answer in Section G.9 is a surprise: OLS turns out to be too small.



OLS measures how institutions and income move together, which is the causal effect only when nothing else moves with them.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. The noise in the index has half the variance of the true institutions, and \(\beta = 1\). Where does OLS end up?


Answer

Equation (4) gives \(1 \times 1/(1 + 0.5) = 2/3 \approx 0.67\): a third of the effect is lost.

2. Why does collecting more countries not fix any of the three biases?


Answer

Equations (3) and (4) do not depend on the number of countries. More data make the OLS slope more precise, but precisely wrong: it settles on \(\beta\) plus the bias, not on \(\beta\).






G.3.3 An instrument

Assumptions
Long ago, sailors explored the archipelago. On some islands deadly fevers killed most newcomers, so the sailors did not stay. They set up a few trading posts with harsh rules, built to ship goods away, and left. On the healthy islands they settled with their families and wrote rules that protected their own property. The rules outlived the sailors. Let \(Z_i\) be how deadly the fevers were. Two assumptions make \(Z_i\) an instrument:

Relevance. The fevers changed institutions. In the first stage, \[R_i = \pi_0 + \pi Z_i + v_i, \qquad \pi \neq 0. \tag{5}\]
Exclusion. The old fevers have no other path to income today: they are not in \(u_i\), so \(\text{Cov}(Z, u) = 0\). In particular, the fevers that killed sailors long ago do not make today’s islanders less productive, except through the rules they left behind.

Relevance can be checked in the data. Exclusion cannot: it is an argument about history, and Section G.10 weighs it.


Solving the model
Step 1: the reduced form. Put the first stage (5) into equation (1):
\[\ln y_i = \mu + \beta(\pi_0 + \pi Z_i + v_i) + u_i = (\mu + \beta\pi_0) + \beta\pi\,Z_i + (\beta v_i + u_i).\]
So log income is a straight line in \(Z_i\) too, the reduced form, with slope \(\rho = \beta\pi\).
Step 2: divide. The first-stage slope \(\pi\) says how much the fevers moved institutions; the reduced-form slope \(\rho\) says how much they moved income. If the fevers reach income only through institutions, the second is the first times \(\beta\), so \(\beta\) is their ratio. Each slope is a covariance with \(Z\) divided by \(\text{Var}(Z)\), which cancels:






ImportantKey result: the IV estimate



\[\rho = \beta\pi \tag{6}\]
\[\widehat{b}_{IV} = \frac{\widehat{\rho}}{\widehat{\pi}} = \frac{\text{Cov}(\ln y, Z)}{\text{Cov}(\tilde{R}, Z)} \tag{7}\]
The IV estimate is the reduced-form slope divided by the first-stage slope. It uses only the part of the differences in institutions that the instrument created.


Step 3: why measurement error does no harm. In equation (7) the index \(\tilde{R} = R + m\) appears only in a covariance with \(Z\). The noise \(m\) is unrelated to the old fevers, so \(\text{Cov}(\tilde{R}, Z) = \text{Cov}(R, Z)\), and the IV estimate is not flattened. This is one reason IV and OLS can differ.
Step 4: two stages give the same number. The name two-stage least squares describes another way to compute (7). First regress \(\tilde{R}\) on \(Z\) and keep the fitted values \(\widehat{R}_i = \widehat{\pi}_0 +
\widehat{\pi}Z_i\). Then regress \(\ln y\) on \(\widehat{R}\) by OLS. Since \(\text{Cov}(\ln y, \widehat{R}) =
\widehat{\pi}\,\text{Cov}(\ln y, Z)\) and \(\text{Var}(\widehat{R}) = \widehat{\pi}^2\,\text{Var}(Z)\), the slope of the second stage is \(\widehat{\rho}/\widehat{\pi}\) again.






TipIn words



An instrument is like a natural experiment. History “assigned” deadly fevers to some islands and not others, and the fevers changed their rules. Comparing the incomes of fever and healthy islands, and scaling by how much their rules differ, gives the effect of the rules, with the climate, the luck and the noise in the index all left out.




What the model predicts
A weak instrument amplifies small problems. Suppose exclusion fails a little, \(\text{Cov}(Z, u) \neq 0\). Put equation (1) into the numerator of (7):
\[\widehat{b}_{IV} = \beta + \frac{\text{Cov}(Z, u)}{\text{Cov}(R, Z)}. \tag{8}\]
The bias is a small number divided by \(\text{Cov}(R, Z)\). If the instrument moves institutions only a little, the denominator is small, and a small violation, or plain bad luck in a sample of 64 countries, becomes a large error. That is why Section G.8 tests how strong the instrument is.
A local effect. If institutions matter more in some countries than in others, the IV estimate averages the effect over the countries whose institutions the instrument actually moved: the former colonies whose rules were set by how deadly they were for settlers. It is a local average treatment effect (LATE), not a statement about every country in the world.

IV trades one strong assumption, exclusion, for the many weak ones that OLS needs, and it is only as good as that assumption and the strength of the instrument.







NoteCheck your understanding



1. The fevers lower institutions by 0.6 points per unit (\(\pi = -0.6\)) and lower log income by 0.57 per unit (\(\rho = -0.57\)). What is the IV estimate?


Answer

Equation (7): \(-0.57/-0.6 = 0.95\). Both slopes are negative, so the ratio is positive: better institutions raise income.

2. Suppose the old fevers still make islanders sick today, and sick workers produce less. Which assumption fails, and in which direction does the IV estimate move?


Answer

Exclusion fails: the fevers now also sit in \(u\), lowering income, so \(\text{Cov}(Z, u) < 0\). The first stage is negative too, \(\text{Cov}(R, Z) < 0\), so the ratio in (8) is positive: the IV estimate is too large. Part of the health effect is counted as an effect of institutions.









NoteRecap




The model gives a line: \(\ln y_i = \mu + \beta R_i + u_i\), with \(\beta = \tfrac{3}{2}\bar{\phi} + \tfrac{1}{2}\bar{\psi}\), the effect of institutions through productivity and investment.
OLS can mislead: omitted variables and reverse causality push it up, measurement error pulls it down (equations 3 and 4; the simulation of Fig. 1).
An instrument must move institutions (relevance) and have no other path to income (exclusion).
The IV estimate is the reduced-form slope over the first-stage slope (equation 7; Figs. 3 and 4), and two-stage least squares computes the same number.
Weak instruments turn small violations into large errors (equation 8), and the IV estimate is a local effect.






G.3.4 The model in code
Now we turn the key results into Python and check them with numbers. First equation (2), for Islandia’s baseline.

PHI, PSI = 0.5, 0.5  # effects of institutions on ln A and on ln s


def total_effect(phi, psi):
    """Equation (2): the long-run effect of institutions on log income per worker."""
    return 1.5 * phi + 0.5 * psi


BETA = total_effect(PHI, PSI)
print(f"beta = {BETA:.2f}: one more point multiplies income by {np.exp(BETA):.2f}")
print(f"two islands 2 points apart: one is {np.exp(2 * BETA):.1f} times as rich")

beta = 1.00: one more point multiplies income by 2.72
two islands 2 points apart: one is 7.4 times as rich


Next, an archipelago we can build ourselves. simulate_islands draws n islands that follow equations (1) and (5): an instrument fever, an omitted factor other (say, a healthy climate) that raises both institutions and income, the true institutions R, an index R_obs measured with noise, and log income ln_y. Three arguments set the three problems: confound (how strongly the omitted factor shapes institutions), noise (the measurement error) and strength (how strongly the fevers moved institutions).

def simulate_islands(n, beta=1.0, confound=0.5, noise=1.0, strength=0.6, seed=0):
    """An archipelago of n islands that follows equations (1) and (5): a data table."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    fever = rng.normal(size=n)  # the instrument Z
    other = rng.normal(size=n)  # an omitted factor, part of u
    R = 5 - strength * fever + confound * other + rng.normal(scale=0.8, size=n)
    ln_y = 2 + beta * R + 0.5 * other + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=n)  # equation (1)
    R_obs = R + rng.normal(scale=noise, size=n)  # the measured index
    return pd.DataFrame({"fever": fever, "R": R, "R_obs": R_obs, "ln_y": ln_y})


def ols_slope(y, x):
    """The OLS slope Cov(y, x) / Var(x), as in equation (3)."""
    return np.cov(x, y)[0, 1] / np.var(x, ddof=1)


def iv_slope(y, x, z):
    """Equation (7): the IV slope Cov(y, z) / Cov(x, z)."""
    return np.cov(z, y)[0, 1] / np.cov(z, x)[0, 1]


def ols_limit(beta=1.0, confound=0.5, noise=1.0, strength=0.6):
    """Where OLS ends up in a huge archipelago: equations (3) and (4).

    The numbers are those of simulate_islands.
    """
    var_R = strength**2 + confound**2 + 0.8**2  # variance of the true institutions
    return (beta * var_R + 0.5 * confound) / (var_R + noise**2)


Python note. np.random.default_rng(seed) makes a random number generator; the same seed always gives the same numbers, so your results match the book’s. rng.normal(size=n) draws n numbers from a standard normal distribution. np.cov(x, y) returns a 2 by 2 table of covariances, and [0, 1] picks the covariance of x with y.

Now the checks. In an archipelago of 200,000 islands, sampling noise is tiny, so the estimates should land on the formulas.

big = simulate_islands(200_000)
pi_hat = ols_slope(big["R_obs"], big["fever"])  # first stage, equation (5)
rho_hat = ols_slope(big["ln_y"], big["fever"])  # reduced form
print(
    f"OLS slope {ols_slope(big['ln_y'], big['R_obs']):.3f}   "
    f"formula {ols_limit():.3f}   true beta {BETA}"
)
print(f"IV slope  {iv_slope(big['ln_y'], big['R_obs'], big['fever']):.3f}")
print(f"ratio rho/pi = {rho_hat:.3f} / {pi_hat:.3f} = {rho_hat / pi_hat:.3f}   (eq. 7)")

# Two-stage least squares by hand: regress ln_y on the fitted values of the first stage
R_hat = big["R_obs"].mean() + pi_hat * (big["fever"] - big["fever"].mean())
print(f"second stage slope {ols_slope(big['ln_y'], R_hat):.3f}   (the same number)")

OLS slope 0.668   formula 0.667   true beta 1.0
IV slope  1.003
ratio rho/pi = -0.605 / -0.604 = 1.003   (eq. 7)
second stage slope 1.003   (the same number)


What to notice. OLS lands on about 0.67, as the formula predicts, a third below the true effect of 1: in the baseline the measurement error, which flattens the line, outweighs the omitted factor, which steepens it. The IV slope, the ratio of the two slopes and the second stage of two-stage least squares all give the same number, close to 1.

title: G. Growth and Institutions
section: G.4 Simulation: when OLS fails and IV works
text:
G.4 Simulation: when OLS fails and IV works
AJR have 64 countries, not 200,000. With so few, every estimate also has sampling noise: a different set of 64 countries would give a different number. A simulation shows both problems at once. We build 1,000 archipelagos of 64 islands each, run OLS and IV in each, and look at the spread of the 1,000 estimates.

Fig. 1: OLS and IV estimates in 1,000 simulated archipelagos
Goal. See when OLS misses the true effect, and when IV finds it.

def sampling_estimates(confound=0.5, noise=1.0, strength=0.6, reps=1000, n=64):
    """OLS and IV estimates from reps archipelagos of n islands (true effect: BETA)."""
    ols_est, iv_est = [], []
    for r in range(reps):
        d = simulate_islands(n, BETA, confound, noise, strength, seed=r)
        ols_est.append(ols_slope(d["ln_y"], d["R_obs"]))
        iv_est.append(iv_slope(d["ln_y"], d["R_obs"], d["fever"]))
    return np.array(ols_est), np.array(iv_est)

simulation_figure draws the two histograms, a dashed line at the true effect, and reports in the title where each histogram is centered (its median).

def simulation_figure(confound=0.5, noise=1.0, strength=0.6):
    """Fig. 1: histograms of the OLS and IV estimates from 1,000 archipelagos."""
    ols_est, iv_est = sampling_estimates(confound, noise, strength)
    off = np.mean((iv_est < -1) | (iv_est > 3)) * 100  # IV estimates outside the chart
    bins = dict(start=-1, end=3, size=0.05)  # bars 0.05 wide
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Histogram(x=ols_est, xbins=bins, name="OLS", marker_color=RUST, opacity=0.6)
    )
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Histogram(
            x=iv_est, xbins=bins, name="IV (2SLS)", marker_color=BLUE, opacity=0.6
        )
    )
    fig.add_vline(
        x=BETA,
        line=dict(color="black", dash="dash"),
        annotation_text="true effect",
        annotation_position="top right",
    )
    title = f"OLS centers on {np.median(ols_est):.2f}, IV on {np.median(iv_est):.2f}"
    if off >= 1:
        title += f" ({off:.0f}% of the IV estimates are off the chart)"
    fig.update_layout(
        title=title,
        barmode="overlay",
        legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.2),
        xaxis=dict(
            title="Estimated effect of institutions on log income",
            range=[-1, 3],
            tickvals=[-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3],
        ),
        yaxis=dict(title="Number of archipelagos", range=[0, 450]),
    )
    return fig

SCENARIOS = {
    "Omitted factor only": dict(confound=0.5, noise=0.0, strength=0.6),
    "Measurement error only": dict(confound=0.0, noise=1.0, strength=0.6),

    """Fig. 1 for one of the four scenarios."""
    return simulation_figure(**SCENARIOS[scenario])


button_figure(scenario_figure, "scenario", list(SCENARIOS), start="Both (baseline)")





                                
                                            




Source. Simulation with simulate_islands (Section G.3.4): 1,000 archipelagos of 64 islands, true effect of institutions \(\beta = 1\).
What to notice.

Omitted factor only: OLS is centered above the true effect. The healthy climate raises both institutions and income, and OLS gives the climate’s credit to the institutions. IV stays centered on 1.
Measurement error only: OLS is centered below the true effect, the attenuation of equation (4). IV again stays on 1.
In both cases the OLS histogram is narrow: OLS is precise, but precisely wrong. The IV histogram is wider: IV pays for its honesty with more sampling noise.
Weak instrument: with strength 0.15 the IV histogram spreads out widely, some estimates fall off the chart, and its center slides toward OLS. A weak instrument gives no reliable answer in a sample of 64.

Your turn. In Colab, set the omitted factor to \(-0.5\) (the factor now weakens institutions while it still raises income) and the measurement error to 0. Which way does OLS miss now? Check your answer with ols_limit.


Hint

ols_limit(confound=-0.5, noise=0) gives about 0.8: with a negative confound, \(\text{Cov}(R, u) < 0\) in equation (3), so OLS is too small even without any measurement error. The IV histogram does not move.

        labels={
            "avexpr": "Protection against expropriation, 1985–1995 (0 to 10)",
            "gdp": "GDP per person, 1995 (PPP dollars)",
            "group": "",
        },
        title=f"{len(d)} countries: one more point goes with {b:.2f} more log income",

    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000])

title: G. Growth and Institutions
text:
G.7 The instrument: settler mortality
AJR’s instrument is the island story of Section G.3.3 with real history. Where European settlers faced high death rates, from malaria and yellow fever, they did not settle. Instead they set up extractive states, built to move gold, rubber or slaves to Europe, with few protections for anyone else. Where settlers could survive, as in North America, Australia and New Zealand, they settled in large numbers and demanded the rights they had at home. Those early institutions persisted after independence. AJR summarize the argument as a chain:
\[\text{settler mortality} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{settlements} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{early institutions}
\;\Rightarrow\; \text{current institutions} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{current income}.\]
The first stage, equation (5), tests the first links of the chain: does log settler mortality predict the expropriation risk of 1985–1995? The reduced form tests the whole chain: does it predict income in 1995? The two charts below show both, for the 64 former colonies.

Fig. 3: The first stage: settler mortality and institutions
Goal. Check relevance: did settler mortality move institutions?
The horizontal axis is on a ratio scale, so the slope is the change in institutions for a 1 log point (about 2.7-fold) rise in mortality. The menu drops groups of countries, to see whether the slope depends on a few of them. The neo-Europes are the four settler colonies with the lowest mortality and the best institutions: the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

NEO_EUROPES = ["USA", "CAN", "AUS", "NZL"]
SUBSAMPLES = [
    "All 64",
    "Without the neo-Europes",
    "Without Africa",
    "Without the Americas",
    "Without Asia",
]
COLORS = {"Africa": BLUE, "Americas": TEAL, "Asia": GREEN, "Australia, Malta, NZ": RUST}
MORTALITY_TICKS = [5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 3000]
# countries labeled on the charts (the others show their name when you hover over them)
LABELED = ["AUS", "NZL", "USA", "SGP", "HKG", "MLT", "CHL", "IND", "PAK", "ETH", "TZA",
           "GAB", "GMB", "NGA", "MLI", "SLE", "NER", "ZAR", "HTI", "BGD", "ZAF"]


def subsample(name):
    """The rows of the base sample that one menu choice keeps."""
    if name == "Without the neo-Europes":
        return base[~base["code"].isin(NEO_EUROPES)]
    if name.startswith("Without"):
        continent = name.replace("Without the ", "").replace("Without ", "")
        return base[base["continent"] != continent]
    return base


def sample_name(name, d):
    """The menu choice with its number of countries, for the chart titles."""
    return "64 former colonies" if name == "All 64" else f"{name} ({len(d)})"

add_highlight marks one country with an arrow, if it is in the data shown.

def add_highlight(fig, d, y, highlight):
    """Mark the country named highlight with an arrow (nothing if it is not in d)."""
    if highlight not in list(d["country"]):
        return
    row = d[d["country"] == highlight].iloc[0]
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=np.log10(row["extmort4"]),
        y=row[y],
        text=highlight,
        showarrow=True,
        arrowhead=2,
        ax=40,
        ay=-40,
        font=dict(color=RUST, size=13),
    )

mortality_scatter draws both charts of this section: the countries, colored by region, with the codes of some of them, and the OLS line through them. The highlight argument marks one country with an arrow.

def mortality_scatter(d, y, y_label, title, highlight):
    """A scatter of y against settler mortality (ratio scale), with the OLS line.

    Colored by region; the countries in LABELED show their codes.
    """
    fit = ols_fit(f"{y} ~ logem4", d)
    d = d.assign(label=np.where(d["code"].isin(LABELED), d["iso3"], ""))
    fig = px.scatter(
        d,
        x="extmort4",
        y=y,
        color="region",
        text="label",
        hover_name="country",
        log_x=True,
        hover_data={"label": False},
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        range_x=[4, 4000],
        labels={
            "extmort4": "Settler mortality (deaths per 1,000 a year, ratio scale)",
            y: y_label,
            "region": "",
        },
        title=title,
    )
    fig.update_traces(textposition="top center", textfont_size=9, marker_size=8)
    m = np.linspace(np.log(6), np.log(3500), 50)
    add_line(fig, np.exp(m), fit.coef()["Intercept"] + fit.coef()["logem4"] * m)
    add_highlight(fig, d, y, highlight)
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=MORTALITY_TICKS)
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.2), height=540)
    return fig


Python note. On a ratio-scale axis (log_x=True), px.scatter takes the data and range_x in deaths per 1,000, as they are. But an annotation added afterwards is placed in powers of ten, so a point at 200 deaths sits at \(\log_{10}(200) \approx 2.3\). That is why the annotation, and only the annotation, uses np.log10.

title: G. Growth and Institutions
text:
G.8 The 2SLS estimate
Now the headline result of AJR, column 1 of their Table 4. We compute it three ways: by hand in two stages, with pyfixest and with linearmodels. Then we test the instrument and the need for it.

G.8.1 Two stages by hand
The first stage regresses institutions on the instrument and keeps the fitted values. The second regresses income on the fitted values.

stage1 = ols_fit("avexpr ~ logem4", base)
by_hand = base.assign(
    avexpr_hat=stage1.predict()
)  # the part of institutions the instrument predicts
stage2 = ols_fit("logpgp95 ~ avexpr_hat", by_hand)
print(
    f"first stage:  avexpr = {stage1.coef()['Intercept']:.3f} "
    f"+ ({stage1.coef()['logem4']:.3f}) x logem4"
)
print(
    f"second stage: logpgp95 = {stage2.coef()['Intercept']:.3f} "
    f"+ {stage2.coef()['avexpr_hat']:.3f} x avexpr_hat"
    f"   (standard error {stage2.se()['avexpr_hat']:.3f})"
)

first stage:  avexpr = 9.341 + (-0.607) x logem4
second stage: logpgp95 = 1.910 + 0.944 x avexpr_hat   (standard error 0.120)


The coefficient, 0.944, is the right one. Its standard error is not: the second stage treats the fitted values as if they were data, and forgets that they were estimated in the first stage. The IV commands below compute the standard error correctly.


G.8.2 With pyfixest and linearmodels
pyfixest writes an IV regression as a formula in three parts: the outcome, the exogenous variables (1, just a constant here), and after a second | the endogenous variable with its instrument, avexpr ~ logem4.

What to notice.

The 2SLS estimate is 0.94, the number of AJR’s Table 4. Both libraries agree on it to every decimal.
Their standard errors differ slightly, 0.179 and 0.176, because they make slightly different small-sample corrections. Both give a confidence interval of about 0.6 to 1.3, which does not include the OLS estimate.
IV is about 80 percent larger than OLS (0.94 against 0.52). Section G.9 asks why.



G.8.3 Is the instrument strong enough?
Equation (8) showed that a weak instrument turns small problems into large errors. The standard check is the first-stage F statistic: the test that the instrument’s coefficient in the first stage is zero. A common rule of thumb (Staiger and Stock 1997) asks for an F above 10. Stock and Yogo (2005) give a stricter threshold, 16.38, for an instrument whose IV tests are at most a little distorted.

print(f"first-stage F (robust, linearmodels):          {first_stage_F(iv_lm):.2f}")
r2 = iv_lm.first_stage.diagnostics.loc["avexpr", "rsquared"]
print(f"first-stage R-squared:                          {r2:.2f}")
iv_pf.IV_Diag()  # pyfixest computes its IV tests and stores them in the model
print(f"effective F (Olea and Pflueger 2013, pyfixest): {iv_pf._eff_F:.2f}")

first-stage F (robust, linearmodels):          16.85
first-stage R-squared:                          0.27
effective F (Olea and Pflueger 2013, pyfixest): 16.32


The F statistic is about 16 to 17, depending on the small-sample correction: above the rule of thumb of 10, and right at the Stock–Yogo threshold. The instrument is strong enough, but not by a wide margin. With controls that are themselves related to mortality, the F statistic falls, as Fig. 5 shows.


G.8.4 Is IV needed? The Wu–Hausman test
If institutions were not endogenous, OLS and IV would estimate the same thing, and OLS, being more precise, would be better. The Wu–Hausman test asks whether the gap between them is too large to be chance.

wh = iv_lm.wu_hausman()
print(f"Wu-Hausman test: statistic {wh.stat:.2f}, p-value {wh.pval:.6f}")

Wu-Hausman test: statistic 24.22, p-value 0.000007


The p-value is far below 0.01: the gap between OLS and IV is not chance. The data reject that OLS and IV estimate the same thing, so institutions are endogenous, as Section G.3 warned, and IV is needed. (The test assumes that the instrument itself is valid: it compares OLS with IV, not IV with the truth.)
Your turn. pyfixest and linearmodels gave standard errors of 0.179 and 0.176. Refit the linearmodels regression with cov_type="unadjusted", the textbook standard errors that assume the same spread of errors in every country. Is the standard error larger or smaller?


Hint

Use IV2SLS(base["logpgp95"], base[[]].assign(const=1.0), base[["avexpr"]], base[["logem4"]]).fit(cov_type="unadjusted") and read .std_errors["avexpr"]. It is smaller, about 0.154: in these data the spread of the errors differs across countries, and the robust standard error allows for it. The point estimate is the same 0.944. Libraries agree on estimates and differ on corrections, so always say which standard errors you report.

def estimates_trace(e, method, color, controls):
    """The estimates of one method (OLS or IV) with their 95% intervals."""
    opacity = []  # the chosen row in full color, the others faded
    for c in e["controls"]:
        opacity.append(1.0 if c == controls else 0.25)
    return go.Scatter(
        x=e[method],
        y=e["controls"],
        mode="markers",
        name=method,
        marker=dict(color=color, size=12, opacity=opacity),
        error_x=dict(
            type="data",
            symmetric=False,
            color=color,
            array=e[method + " high"] - e[method],
            arrayminus=e[method] - e[method + " low"],
        ),
    )

estimates_figure draws the two sets of estimates and writes the chosen row’s numbers in the title.

def estimates_figure(controls="None"):

What to notice.

IV is above OLS with every set of controls: about 1 against 0.4 to 0.5. The controls barely move the IV estimate.
But the IV intervals widen as controls are added, and the first-stage F statistic falls from about 17 to about 3. Latitude and the continents are related to mortality, so they absorb part of what the instrument does. With all controls, the instrument is weak, and the wide interval should be read, not the point estimate.

Your turn. Add a fifth set of controls: the share of Europeans in the population in 1900, euro1900. Does the IV estimate change? What happens to the first-stage F, and why might it?


Hint

The estimate barely moves (0.99), but the F statistic drops to about 5, because the share of Europeans in 1900 is one of the links of AJR’s chain: settlers settled where mortality was low. G.9.1 What the coefficient means
An estimate of 0.94 means that one more point of protection against expropriation raises log income by 0.94, so income by \(e^{0.94} - 1 \approx 156\) percent. AJR’s own example compares Nigeria and Chile:

nga = base.loc[base["code"] == "NGA", "avexpr"].iloc[0]
chl = base.loc[base["code"] == "CHL", "avexpr"].iloc[0]
beta_iv = iv_lm.params["avexpr"]
gap = beta_iv * (chl - nga)
print(
    f"institutions: Nigeria {nga:.2f}, Chile {chl:.2f}, a gap of {chl - nga:.2f} points"
)
print(f"IV:  log income gap {gap:.2f}, a factor of {np.exp(gap):.1f}")
ols_gap = ols_models[1].coef()["avexpr"] * (chl - nga)
print(f"OLS: log income gap {ols_gap:.2f}, a factor of {np.exp(ols_gap):.1f}")

institutions: Nigeria 5.55, Chile 7.82, a gap of 2.27 points
IV:  log income gap 2.15, a factor of 8.6
OLS: log income gap 1.19, a factor of 3.3


If Nigeria had Chile’s institutions, the IV estimate predicts that it would be about 8 to 9 times as rich, close to the actual gap between the two countries. OLS would predict a factor of about 3.
Why is IV larger than OLS? Section G.3 gave two biases that push OLS up (omitted variables and reverse causality) and one that pulls it down (measurement error). IV is larger, so the downward pull must be the stronger. AJR argue that the index of expropriation risk is a noisy measure of the institutions that matter, which are broader and older than an investor rating of 1985–1995. The simulation of Fig. 1 showed exactly this pattern in the scenario “Measurement error only”.
A second reason is the local nature of the IV estimate (Section G.3.3): it is the effect for the former colonies whose institutions were shaped by settler mortality. If institutions matter more for them than for the average country, IV is larger than an OLS slope that averages over all.

title: G. Growth and Institutions
text:
G.10 Discussion and limits
AJR’s paper changed how economists think about growth. It also started a long debate. Four questions are at its center.
Is exclusion credible? The key assumption is that settler mortality affects income today only through institutions. The most serious doubt is disease: the malaria that killed settlers still makes workers sick today, and it might lower income directly. AJR control for malaria and life expectancy today and find a smaller, but still large, effect of institutions (about 0.6 to 0.7, in their Table 7). But today’s health is also partly an outcome of institutions, so controlling for it may hide part of their effect. Others argue that settlers brought human capital, their skills and schooling, not only institutions (Glaeser and coauthors 2004). Then mortality would affect income through schooling too, and the IV estimate would mix the two effects.
Are the mortality data reliable? Albouy (2012) went back to AJR’s sources. He found that 36 of the 64 countries in the base sample are assigned mortality rates from other countries, often neighbors, and that rates from very different groups, soldiers in barracks, soldiers on campaign, laborers and bishops, are combined. When he corrects for these problems, the first stage weakens, and the IV estimates become fragile. AJR (2012) reply that limiting the influence of the outliers, such as capping mortality at 250, leaves their results intact. The debate is a lesson for every data project: an instrument is only as good as the data it is built from.
What does the coefficient mean for policy? The IV estimate is a local effect of institutions that were set long ago by history. It does not tell a government how to raise its expropriation score, or how fast income would respond. Reforms change institutions in ways that history did not, and they can fail.
What does it mean for the growth models? In the model of Section G.3, institutions work through productivity and investment. AJR’s estimate is large enough to account for a big share of the income differences across former colonies, and so for much of the TFP gap that Chapter 4 and Appendix D measure. Institutions are a candidate answer to the question the production model leaves open: why some countries use their capital and workers so much better than others. Hall and Jones (1999), with the author of our textbook, reached a similar conclusion with a different instrument: what they called social infrastructure explains much of the differences in output per worker.

title: G. Growth and Institutions
text:
G.11 Go further
The tutorial behind this appendix, Do Institutions Cause Prosperity? An IV Tutorial in Python, reproduces the rest of AJR’s paper with the same tools. It comes with slides, a web app and a Stata version. There you can:

Add colonial, legal and religious controls (AJR’s Table 5): the identity of the colonizer, French legal origin and religion. The IV estimate stays between about 0.9 and 1.3.
Add geography (Table 6): temperature, humidity, soils, natural resources, being landlocked and ethnic fractionalization. The estimate stays between about 0.7 and 1.4, but the first stage often becomes weak.
Add health (Table 7): malaria, life expectancy and infant mortality today. This is the one place where the estimate falls, to about 0.55 to 0.7, and where the first stage is weakest.
Test overidentification (Table 8): with more instruments than endogenous variables (for example settler mortality together with the share of Europeans in 1900), the Hansen J (or Sargan) test checks whether the instruments agree. They do, but agreeing witnesses can share the same mistake.
Stress-test exclusion yourself. Pick a variable you think could break exclusion, add it to iv_fit as a control, and ask whether it is a cause of mortality (a real threat) or a result of institutions (a “bad control”).
Instrument two variables at once. In Table 7, AJR instrument both institutions and malaria with four instruments. pyfixest does not allow two endogenous variables; linearmodels’ IV2SLS does, and reports the Hansen J test (.sargan). Why can the test be computed here, but not with one instrument?

The original data and programs are in Daron Acemoglu’s data archive. The documentation of pyfixest and linearmodels has many more IV examples.

title: G. Growth and Institutions
text:
G.12 Concluding remarks

In the production and Solow models, institutions raise income through productivity and investment, which gives a straight line between log income and institutions, equation (1). Its slope, equation (2), is the effect we want.
OLS finds the slope only if institutions are unrelated to everything else that moves income. Omitted variables and reverse causality push it up, measurement error pulls it down (equations 3 and 4; Fig. 1).
An instrument that moves institutions and has no other path to income recovers the slope as the ratio of the reduced form to the first stage, equation (7). Two-stage least squares computes the same number. A weak instrument makes the answer unreliable (equation 8).
With settler mortality as the instrument, AJR’s 64 former colonies give an IV estimate of 0.94 (Figs. 3 and 4), 80 percent above OLS, with a first-stage F of about 17 and a Wu–Hausman test that rejects that OLS is enough. The estimate survives the controls of Fig. 5, but the instrument weakens with them.
The result rests on the exclusion restriction and on old, partly borrowed mortality data. It is a local effect of history-made institutions, and the debate about disease, human capital and data quality is not settled. But it is strong evidence that institutions are a fundamental cause of the TFP differences that Chapter 4 and Appendix D measure.

title: H. DSGE Modeling with Python
section: H.2 What a DSGE model is, and what estimating one means
text:
H.2 What a DSGE model is, and what estimating one means
Each word of the name says something about the model.

Dynamic. Decisions link the periods. Households save today to consume tomorrow, firms invest today to produce tomorrow, and what people expect about the future changes what they do today.
Stochastic. Random shocks hit the economy: to productivity, to preferences, to the costs of firms, to monetary policy. The shocks are what make the economy fluctuate; without them it would sit in its steady state.
General equilibrium. All markets clear at once, and every household’s and firm’s plans are consistent with each other and with the resource constraint of the economy.


H.2.1 The ingredients
A DSGE model is a list of equations. Most of them come from one of five ingredients:

Optimizing households and firms. The Euler equation for consumption (Chapter 16), the demand for capital (Chapter 17) and price setting by firms are first-order conditions of optimization problems.
Expectations. Today’s choices depend on what people expect tomorrow. DSGE models assume rational expectations: people’s forecasts are the model’s own forecasts, so they make no systematic mistakes.
Constraints and market clearing. Output is consumed or invested; the capital stock carries over from one period to the next.
Shocks. Each shock follows a simple random process, usually an AR(1): \(z_t=\rho z_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\).
Policy rules. The central bank follows a rule for the interest rate, like the rule of Chapter 13.

To solve the model is to find decision rules: formulas that give every variable today as a function of the past (the state of the economy) and of today’s shocks. With the decision rules we can simulate the economy for any sequence of shocks.


H.2.2 From equations to numbers: the workflow








Step
What happens
In this appendix




1. Write
equations, variables, shocks and parameters go into a model file
H.5, H.6


2. Calibrate
choose parameter values from long-run facts and other studies
H.6–H.8


3. Steady state
find the values that the model settles at when no shocks hit
H.8


4. Solve
find the decision rules (linear models) or the whole path (nonlinear models)
H.4, H.7, H.8


5. Simulate
impulse responses, scenarios, contribution charts
H.6–H.8


6. Take to data
write the solution in state-space form; the Kalman filter gives the likelihood
H.9–H.11


7. Estimate
choose the parameters that make the data most likely, with or without priors
H.10–H.12





H.2.3 Calibration versus estimation
There are two ways to choose the parameters. Calibration, the approach of the real business cycle school (Chapter 15), takes each value from outside evidence: the capital share from the national accounts, the discount factor from average interest rates. Estimation lets the model’s own time series pick the values: the parameters that make the observed data most likely win (maximum likelihood). Bayesian estimation combines the two: outside evidence enters as a prior distribution for each parameter, and the data update it. Most central banks estimate their DSGE models this way (Smets and Wouters, 2007; Del Negro et al., 2013).


H.2.4 The toolboxes
Economists rarely code solvers from scratch. Three toolboxes dominate: Dynare (free, runs on MATLAB or the free Octave), IRIS (free, runs on MATLAB) and TROLL (commercial). MATLAB itself is commercial software. A Python package removes the license cost and connects DSGE modeling to the data tools of Appendices A and B. That is the gap Snowdrop wants to fill.

title: H. DSGE Modeling with Python
text:
H.3 The Snowdrop paper
The paper is Goumilevski, A., and Otterson, J. (2025), “Snowdrop: Python Package for DSGE Modeling,” Journal of Open Source Software 10(112), 8197 (doi:10.21105/joss.08197). The code is on GitHub at gumilevskij/Framework. Both authors work at the International Monetary Fund. The Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS) publishes short papers about research software: the paper is a summary, and the software itself goes through peer review (installation, documentation, tests). The details are in the package’s 56-page User Guide and its notes on numerical algorithms, which come with the code.

H.3.1 Why Snowdrop exists
The paper’s statement of need makes four points:

DSGE models are a basic tool of central banks for monetary policy and forecasting (it cites work at the IMF, the ECB, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Japanese Ministry of Finance).
Python, for all its scientific libraries, lacked an integrated DSGE toolbox.
Each existing toolbox has a strength: Dynare is easy to use but handles only stationary models, so users must rewrite growing variables as ratios; IRIS handles non-stationary models; TROLL solves very large systems. But all of them are commercial or run on commercial software.
Snowdrop is free (GNU General Public License) and handles a wide range of models. Benchmarked against Dynare and IRIS on models with several hundred equations, it runs about as fast and needs less memory.



H.3.2 What the package does








Feature
In Snowdrop
Where you meet it




Model files
human-readable YAML; also Python scripts, Dynare, IRIS and Sirius XML files
H.5–H.8, H.11


Nonlinear models
perfect-foresight paths by Newton’s method: the stacked ABLR method and the forward–backward LBJ method (Juillard et al., 1998)
H.4, H.7, H.8


Linear models
Binder–Pesaran, Anderson–Moore, and two generalized Schur methods that reproduce Dynare and IRIS
H.8, H.11


Time-varying parameters
a parameter can follow a path
H.5


Estimation
maximum likelihood, and a Bayesian version with priors
H.11, H.12


Sampling
Markov chain Monte Carlo: the emcee ensemble sampler of Goodman and Weare, and adaptive Metropolis–Hastings
H.13


Filters
Kalman (several versions), unscented Kalman, particle, Hodrick–Prescott, band-pass
H.9–H.11


Output
plots, contribution charts, Excel and SQLite files
throughout



It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, on CPUs and, through the CuPy library, on GPUs.


H.3.3 The paper’s three examples

A monetary policy model with four equations: a Phillips curve, a real interest rate, a policy rule and an IS curve. The paper prints its model file and, in its Fig. 1, the forecast of inflation, the real and nominal interest rates and the output gap after a 2 percent output shock in period 1 and a 3 percentage point revision of the policy rate in period 4, split into the contribution of each term. Section H.7 replicates Fig. 1.
Ireland’s (2004) New Keynesian model, estimated on U.S. data. Sections H.11 and H.12 estimate it.
The Eichenbaum–Rebelo–Trabandt (2020) model of the macroeconomics of epidemics, with two strains of a virus, sticky- and flexible-price economies linked by a Taylor rule, and 64 equations. It is highly nonlinear, and Snowdrop solves it by a homotopy: it moves the parameters step by step from an easy case to the real one. The paper’s Figs. 2 and 3 forecast infections, deaths and the economy for 2020–2022. This model is too big for an introduction; Section H.13 tells you where its files are.



H.3.4 How the paper runs a model
The paper gives three steps: write or edit a YAML model file, open the test script tests/test_toy_models.py and set fname to the file’s name, then run the script. In a notebook we do the same with two functions: importModel reads the file, and run solves and simulates the model.


H.3.5 Reading research software with care
A short paper cannot document everything, and research code changes faster than its documentation. As we go, we will meet a few places where the paper, the User Guide and the code disagree, or where a function needs help. None of them is serious, but each one teaches the habit that matters most in computational economics: check every result. Compare it with a case you can solve by hand, look at the residuals of the equations, and try more than one starting point. The appendix shows how.

H.4 Setup

H.4.1 Installing Snowdrop
Snowdrop is not part of Colab, so we install it. One detail matters. The package asks for old versions of NumPy (1.26) and SciPy (1.11), which do not exist for Colab’s Python 3.13: a plain install would fail. Everything this appendix uses runs on Colab’s own, newer NumPy and SciPy, so we install Snowdrop without its version requirements (--no-deps), together with the three small libraries it needs and Colab lacks: particles (probability distributions), ruamel.yaml (it reads YAML files; Snowdrop needs version 0.17.21) and that library’s C helper. We install a fixed version of Snowdrop: the GitHub commit of 3 October 2026, which corrected the standard errors of estimated parameters. The install takes about 20 seconds. pip then prints a note that you may need to restart the kernel; you do not, because the install changes nothing that Colab has already loaded.

Python note. %pip install is a notebook command, not Python: it installs packages into the computer that runs the notebook. -q keeps it quiet, and --no-deps installs exactly the packages named, nothing else. A GitHub address ending in .tar.gz is a compressed copy of the code at one commit.


# Snowdrop at the commit of 3 October 2026, without its old NumPy/SciPy pins, plus three small libraries
%pip install -q --no-deps "https://github.com/gumilevskij/Framework/archive/47a63b2b780e1876898229c09f7f1e8644462692.tar.gz"
%pip install -q --no-deps particles==0.4 "ruamel.yaml==0.17.21" ruamel.yaml.clib

Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.
Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.




H.4.2 Libraries and the work folder
Snowdrop writes files next to each model file it reads (a cache of the parsed model) and into an output folder. We keep all of that in one work folder, dsge. Two lines need a word of explanation. Snowdrop first tries the GPU library CuPy; we tell Python that CuPy is not available, so Snowdrop always uses the CPU. And importing Snowdrop moves Python into Snowdrop’s own folder, so we move back to ours right after.

BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY, ORANGE, RUST = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3", "#e0a33b", "#c4651a"
SERIES = [BLUE, "#5aa0d8", TEAL, GREEN, ORANGE, "#b04a5a", "#8e5ea2", GRAY, RUST, "#0b4f47"]
INK, GRID, AXIS, TOTAL, NAVY = "#2a3f5f", "#e3e9f1", "#b8c4d2", "#1b2733", "#06253e"
DARK = {"#16528c": "#5eb1f2", "#008070": "#3dd6c4", "#7fb23a": "#a6d85b", "#8a96a3": "#97a9bd",
        "#5aa0d8": "#a9d3f7", "#0b4f47": "#22a08d", "#e0a33b": "#f2c14e", "#c4651a": "#f08c4a",
        "#b04a5a": "#f07a8c", "#8e5ea2": "#c39be0", INK: "#d8e3ee", TOTAL: "#e6edf5",
        "#000000": "#e6edf5", "#ffffff": NAVY}

def _lin(v): return v / 12.92 if v <= 0.04045 else ((v + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4
def _gam(v): return min(1.0, max(0.0, 12.92 * v if v <= 0.0031308 else 1.055 * v ** (1 / 2.4) - 0.055))
def oklab(rgb):
    r, g, b = (_lin(x) for x in rgb[:3])
    l, m, s = [(u * r + v * g + w * b) ** (1 / 3) for u, v, w in ((0.4122214708, 0.5363325363, 0.0514459929),
               (0.2119034982, 0.6806995451, 0.1073969566), (0.0883024619, 0.2817188376, 0.6299787005))]
    return (0.2104542553 * l + 0.7936177850 * m - 0.0040720468 * s,
            1.9779984951 * l - 2.4285922050 * m + 0.4505937099 * s,
            0.0259040371 * l + 0.7827717662 * m - 0.8086757660 * s)
def from_oklab(L, A, B):
    for k in np.arange(1.0, -0.01, -0.05):                     # lower the chroma until the color fits sRGB
        a, b = A * k, B * k
        l, m, s = (L + 0.3963377774 * a + 0.2158037573 * b) ** 3, (L - 0.1055613458 * a - 0.0638541728 * b) ** 3, \
                  (L - 0.0894841775 * a - 1.2914855480 * b) ** 3
        rgb = (4.0767416621 * l - 3.3077115913 * m + 0.2309699292 * s, -1.2684380046 * l + 2.6097574011 * m
               - 0.3413193965 * s, -0.0041960863 * l - 0.7034186147 * m + 1.7076147010 * s)
        if k < 0.05 or all(-0.002 < v < 1.002 for v in rgb):
            return tuple(_gam(v) for v in rgb)
NAVY_LAB = oklab(to_rgba(NAVY))
def dark_color(c, role="ink"):
    """The dark-theme version of a color: the same rules as the website's Plotly charts."""
    r, g, b, a = to_rgba(c)
    if a == 0:
        return (r, g, b, a)
    L, A, B = oklab((r, g, b)); chroma = math.hypot(A, B); hexc = to_hex((r, g, b))
    if role == "rule" and chroma >= 0.035: role = "ink"
    if role == "ink" and hexc in DARK:
        return to_rgba(DARK[hexc], a * 0.85 if a < 1 else 1)
    if chroma < 0.035 or (role != "ink" and L > 0.6):          # neutrals: swap light and dark
        hi, lo = (0.78 if role == "rule" else 0.93), (NAVY_LAB[0] + 0.08 if role == "ink" and L < 0.985 else NAVY_LAB[0])
        L2 = hi - (hi - lo) * L; f = max(0.0, (1 - L2) / (1 - NAVY_LAB[0]))
        A, B = A * 0.6 + NAVY_LAB[1] * f, B * 0.6 + NAVY_LAB[2] * f
    else:
        L2 = 0.66 + L * 0.175 if (role == "ink" and L < 0.8) else L   # lift dark ink above the navy
    return (*from_oklab(L2, A, B), a * 0.85 if (role == "ink" and a < 1) else a)
