# @title Helper code: restyle a chart (Snowdrop's colors to the book's; light to dark)
def recolor(fig, fn):
    """Apply fn(color, role) to every color of a matplotlib figure; role is paper, rule or ink."""
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(fn(fig.patch.get_facecolor(), "paper"))
    for t in fig.texts: t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
    for ax in fig.axes:
        ax.set_facecolor(fn(ax.get_facecolor(), "paper"))
        for sp in ax.spines.values(): sp.set_edgecolor(fn(sp.get_edgecolor(), "rule"))
        for axis in (ax.xaxis, ax.yaxis):
            for gl in axis.get_gridlines(): gl.set_color(fn(gl.get_color(), "rule"))
            for lab in axis.get_ticklabels(which="both"): lab.set_color(fn(lab.get_color(), "ink"))
            axis.label.set_color(fn(axis.label.get_color(), "ink"))
            axis.set_tick_params(which="both", color=fn(AXIS, "rule"))
        for t in [ax.title, ax._left_title, ax._right_title] + ax.texts: t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
        for ln in ax.lines:
            role = "rule" if ln.get_gid() == "rule" else "ink"
            ln.set_color(fn(ln.get_color(), role))
            ln.set_markerfacecolor(fn(ln.get_markerfacecolor(), role)); ln.set_markeredgecolor(fn(ln.get_markeredgecolor(), role))
        for p in ax.patches:
            p.set_facecolor(fn(p.get_facecolor(), "ink")); p.set_edgecolor(fn(p.get_edgecolor(), "ink"))
        for col in ax.collections:
            col.set_facecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in col.get_facecolors()])
            col.set_edgecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in col.get_edgecolors()])
        leg = ax.get_legend()
        if leg is not None:
            leg.get_frame().set_facecolor(fn(leg.get_frame().get_facecolor(), "paper"))
            leg.get_frame().set_edgecolor(fn(leg.get_frame().get_edgecolor(), "rule"))
            for t in leg.get_texts(): t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
            for h in leg.legend_handles:
                if isinstance(h, matplotlib.lines.Line2D):
                    h.set_color(fn(h.get_color(), "ink"))
                    h.set_markerfacecolor(fn(h.get_markerfacecolor(), "ink")); h.set_markeredgecolor(fn(h.get_markeredgecolor(), "ink"))
                elif isinstance(h, matplotlib.collections.Collection):
                    h.set_facecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in h.get_facecolors()])
                    h.set_edgecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in h.get_edgecolors()])
                elif isinstance(h, matplotlib.patches.Patch):
                    h.set_facecolor(fn(h.get_facecolor(), "ink")); h.set_edgecolor(fn(h.get_edgecolor(), "ink"))

# @title Helper code: Snowdrop's colors to the book's colors
def to_book_colors(fig):
    """Snowdrop's colors -> the book's: black lines stay dark, red data dots become rust, others follow SERIES."""
    seen = {}
    def book(c, role):
        r, g, b, a = to_rgba(c); L, A, B = oklab((r, g, b)); chroma = math.hypot(A, B)
        if role == "paper": return to_rgba("white")
        if role == "rule": return to_rgba(GRID if L > 0.7 else AXIS)
        if chroma < 0.035: return to_rgba(TOTAL if L < 0.3 else (INK if L < 0.6 else "white"), a)
        if r > 0.9 and g < 0.15 and b < 0.15: return to_rgba(RUST, a)
        key = to_hex((r, g, b))
        if key not in seen: seen[key] = SERIES[len(seen) % len(SERIES)]
        return to_rgba(seen[key], a)
    recolor(fig, book)
    for ax in fig.axes:
        ax.grid(True, color=GRID, linewidth=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        for p in ax.patches: p.set_edgecolor("white"); p.set_linewidth(0.6)
        leg = ax.get_legend()
        if leg is not None:
            for h in leg.legend_handles:
                if isinstance(h, matplotlib.patches.Patch): h.set_edgecolor("white")

           "axes.spines.right": False, "xtick.color": INK, "ytick.color": INK, "text.color": INK,
           "axes.titlesize": 13, "axes.titleweight": "normal", "axes.labelsize": 11, "legend.frameon": False,
           "axes.prop_cycle": matplotlib.cycler(color=SERIES), "lines.linewidth": 2.2, "font.size": 11}

def book_figure(rows=1, cols=1, width=8.6, height=4.6):
    """A new matplotlib figure in the book's style (Snowdrop's plots change the global style, so reset it)."""
    plt.rcdefaults(); plt.rcParams.update(BOOK_RC)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(rows, cols, figsize=(width, height), squeeze=False)
    return fig, (axes[0, 0] if rows * cols == 1 else axes.ravel())

def _png(fig):
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format="png", dpi=110, facecolor=fig.get_facecolor(), bbox_inches="tight")
    return base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode()

def show(fig, alt, snowdrop=False):
    """Show a chart twice, light and dark; the website picks the one that matches its theme."""
    if snowdrop:
        to_book_colors(fig)
    light = _png(fig)
    recolor(fig, dark_color)
    dark = _png(fig)
    plt.close(fig)
    alt = alt.replace('"', "'")
    display(HTML(f'<div class="book-mpl"><img class="book-mpl-light" alt="{alt}" src="data:image/png;base64,{light}">'
                 f'<img class="book-mpl-dark" alt="{alt}" style="display:none" src="data:image/png;base64,{dark}"></div>'))




Show the helper code
# @title Helper code: run Snowdrop quietly, change model values, read its estimation tables
import snowdrop.src.numeric.estimation.estimate as sd_estimate
os.chdir(WORK)                                    # this import also moves Python into Snowdrop's folder
ANSI = re.compile(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*m")              # Snowdrop prints colored text; we strip the colors

def quietly(function, *args, **kwargs):
    """Call a Snowdrop function and keep its printout; return (result, text)."""
    buf = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
        result = function(*args, **kwargs)
    return result, ANSI.sub("", buf.getvalue())

def load_model(file, verbose=False, **options):
    """Read a model file with importModel; print Snowdrop's report only if verbose."""
    model, text = quietly(driver.importModel, fname=os.path.join(WORK, file), **options)
    if verbose:
        print(text.strip())
    return model

def simulate(model, **options):
    """Solve and simulate a model with run(); return a table, one row per period, one column per variable."""
    (y, dates), text = quietly(driver.run, model=model, Plot=False, **options)
    y = np.asarray(y)
    return pd.DataFrame(y[:len(dates)], index=dates, columns=model.symbols["variables"])

def set_values(model, kind, values):
    """Change parameters or starting values: kind is 'parameters' or 'variables', values a dict name -> number."""
    names = model.symbols[kind]
    new = np.array(model.calibration[kind], dtype=float)  # Snowdrop's arrays are read-only: change a copy
    for name, value in values.items():
        new[names.index(name)] = value
    model.calibration[kind] = new

def estimate(model, **options):
    """Run Snowdrop's estimate() quietly; print its results table and return it as a DataFrame, with the output."""
    sd_estimate.est_shocks_names.clear()          # Snowdrop keeps a list here between runs; start afresh
    out, text = quietly(driver.estimate, model=model, Output=False, Plot=False, **options)
    start = text.find("Estimation\n+")
    print(text[text.rfind("\n", 0, start - 30) + 1: text.find("Estimation time")].strip())
    rows = re.findall(r"\|\s*(\w+)\s*\|\s*([-0-9.e]+)\s*\|\s*([-0-9.e]+)\s*\|\s*([-0-9.e]+)\s*\|", text)
    table = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["parameter", "start", "estimate", "std. error"]).set_index("parameter")
    table = table.astype(float)
    table.attrs["log value"] = float(re.findall(r"function value: ([-0-9.]+)", text)[-1])
    return table, out

section: H.5 Rational expectations from small pieces
text:
H.5 Rational expectations from small pieces
Before Snowdrop does it for us, let us solve the smallest possible model with expectations by hand. It shows what “solving a DSGE model” means, and why a solution exists and is unique.

H.5.1 A model with one equation
Take the New Keynesian Phillips curve of Ireland’s model in Section H.11, stripped to its core:
\[x_t = a\,\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}] + b\,z_t, \qquad (H.1)\]
\[z_t = \rho\, z_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t. \qquad (H.2)\]
Read \(x_t\) as inflation and \(z_t\) as a cost shock that fades at rate \(\rho\). Inflation today depends on the shock today and on the inflation that people expect for tomorrow; \(a\) is close to 1 (it is the discount factor of price setters), and \(b\) is the slope of the curve. The problem is that tomorrow’s inflation depends on the day after, and so on forever: today’s inflation depends on all expected future shocks.
Guess and verify. Since only \(z_t\) moves the economy, guess that inflation is proportional to it: \(x_t=\phi\,z_t\). Then \(\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}]=\phi\,\mathbb{E}_t[z_{t+1}]=\phi\rho z_t\), and equation (H.1) becomes \(\phi z_t = a\phi\rho z_t + b z_t\). This holds for every \(z_t\) only if
\[\phi = \frac{b}{1-a\rho}. \qquad (H.3)\]
The guess works, and (H.3) is the decision rule. A shock that lasts longer (larger \(\rho\)) moves inflation more, because price setters expect it to raise their costs for longer.
We use teaching values: \(a=0.9\), \(b=0.14\) and \(\rho=0.8\), so that \(\phi=0.5\). A shock of 1 hits in period 1, and after that the economy is left alone. With no more shocks, the expectation of tomorrow is simply tomorrow, so we can check (H.1) period by period.

a, b, rho = 0.9, 0.14, 0.8           # discount factor, slope, persistence of the cost shock
phi = b / (1 - a * rho)              # equation (H.3)
T = 30
z = np.zeros(T + 1)                  # periods 0, 1, ..., 30
z[1] = 1.0                           # a cost shock of 1 in period 1
for t in range(2, T + 1):
    z[t] = rho * z[t - 1]            # equation (H.2) with no new shocks
x = phi * z                          # the decision rule

residual = x[1:T] - a * x[2:T + 1] - b * z[1:T]  # equation (H.1), period by period
print(f"phi = b / (1 - a rho) = {phi:.3f}")
print(f"largest error in equation (H.1): {np.abs(residual).max():.1e}")

phi = b / (1 - a rho) = 0.500
largest error in equation (H.1): 5.6e-17



fig, ax = book_figure()
ax.plot(range(T + 1), z, color=GRAY, linestyle="--", label="cost shock $z_t$")
ax.plot(range(T + 1), x, color=BLUE, marker="o", markersize=4, label="inflation $x_t = \\phi z_t$")
ax.set_title("A cost shock and the inflation it causes")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, T + 1, 5))
ax.set_xlabel("period")
ax.legend()
show(fig, "Inflation follows the cost shock at half its size and fades at the same rate")




What to notice. Inflation jumps in period 1 and then fades at the rate of the shock, always at half its size (\(\phi=0.5\)). Nothing else moves inflation: the decision rule has turned a forward-looking equation into a simple formula.


H.5.2 Why the solution is unique: stable and unstable paths
The decision rule is not the only path that satisfies (H.1) each period. Write the equation forward: \(x_{t+1}=(x_t-b\,z_t)/a\). Suppose inflation starts a little off the rule, by a gap \(d_1=x_1-\phi z_1\). Subtracting the rule from both sides gives
\[d_{t+1} = \frac{1}{a}\,d_t. \qquad (H.4)\]
Because \(a<1\), the factor \(1/a\) is larger than 1: any gap explodes. Of all the paths that satisfy (H.1), only the one with no gap stays bounded. Inflation is a jump variable: nothing ties it to the past, so it jumps in period 1 to the one value that keeps the economy on the stable path. This is the Blanchard–Kahn condition in its simplest form. A linear model has a unique stable solution when the number of unstable roots (here \(1/a>1\)) equals the number of jump variables (here one: \(x_t\)). Snowdrop counts both for every model it solves (Section H.5).

fig, ax = book_figure()
gaps = [-0.1, -0.05, 0.0, 0.05, 0.1]          # how far inflation starts from the decision rule
for d in gaps:
    path = np.zeros(T + 1)
    path[1] = phi * z[1] + d
    for t in range(1, T):
        path[t + 1] = (path[t] - b * z[t]) / a  # equation (H.1) solved for next period's inflation
    if d == 0:
        ax.plot(range(1, T + 1), path[1:], color=BLUE, linewidth=3, label="the decision rule (gap 0)")
    else:
        ax.plot(range(1, T + 1), path[1:], color=GRAY, linewidth=1.3)
ax.plot([], [], color=GRAY, linewidth=1.3, label="starting gaps of ±0.05 and ±0.1")
ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 2.0)
ax.set_title("Only one path stays bounded: every other path explodes")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, T + 1, 5))
ax.set_xlabel("period")
ax.set_ylabel("inflation $x_t$")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
show(fig, "Paths of inflation that start off the decision rule explode; only the rule stays bounded")
print(f"Unstable root 1/a = {1 / a:.3f} > 1, one jump variable: a unique stable solution.")




Unstable root 1/a = 1.111 > 1, one jump variable: a unique stable solution.




H.5.3 Perfect foresight: the whole path as one system of equations
There is a second way to solve the model, and it is the one Snowdrop uses for nonlinear models. Look at all the periods at once. Equation (H.1) for periods \(1, 2, \dots, T\) gives \(T\) equations in the \(T\) unknowns \(x_1,\dots,x_T\), if we add a terminal condition: far in the future the economy is back at its steady state, \(x_{T+1}=0\). Solve the \(T\) equations together and you have the whole path.
Newton’s method solves such systems. Start from a guess for the path, compute the residuals (how far each equation is from holding), and correct the guess with the matrix of derivatives (the Jacobian \(J\)): \(x \leftarrow x - J^{-1}\,\text{residuals}(x)\). For a linear model one step is enough; a nonlinear model needs a few. Snowdrop’s ABLR method stacks all periods into one large sparse system like this one, and its LBJ method solves the same system period by period, forward and then backward.

Python note. rho ** np.arange(80) gives \(1, \rho, \rho^2, \dots\): the shock in periods 1 to 80. np.append(x[1:], 0.0) shifts the path one period ahead and adds the terminal value \(x_{T+1}=0\). np.eye(T) is the identity matrix and np.eye(T, k=1) has ones just above the diagonal, so J @ x gives \(x_t - a\,x_{t+1}\) for every \(t\). np.linalg.solve(J, r) computes \(J^{-1}r\).


T_long = 80                                     # a long horizon, so that x_81 = 0 does no harm
z_long = rho ** np.arange(T_long)               # the cost shock in periods 1, ..., 80

def residuals(x_path):
    """Equation (H.1) for t = 1, ..., 80, with the terminal condition x_81 = 0."""
    x_next = np.append(x_path[1:], 0.0)
    return x_path - a * x_next - b * z_long

J = np.eye(T_long) - a * np.eye(T_long, k=1)    # the Jacobian of the residuals
guess = np.zeros(T_long)                        # start from "nothing happens"
for step in range(1, 4):
    guess = guess - np.linalg.solve(J, residuals(guess))
    print(f"Newton step {step}: largest residual {np.abs(residuals(guess)).max():.1e}")

print(f"Largest gap to the decision rule in periods 1-{T}: {np.abs(guess[:T] - x[1:T + 1]).max():.1e}")

Newton step 1: largest residual 2.8e-17
Newton step 2: largest residual 2.8e-17
Newton step 3: largest residual 2.8e-17
Largest gap to the decision rule in periods 1-30: 4.1e-11


What to notice. Newton’s method converges in one step, because the model is linear; the later steps change nothing. Its path matches the decision rule. The terminal condition \(x_{81}=0\) is slightly wrong (the rule gives \(0.5\times0.8^{80}\)), but 80 periods later that error no longer matters. With a short horizon it would: this is why Snowdrop simulates models over many periods.
Your turn. Set \(a=1.1\). What is the unstable root \(1/a\) now? Run the cell with the five starting gaps again: do the other paths still explode? What does this mean for the uniqueness of the solution?


Show the answer

With \(a=1.1\) the root is \(1/a\approx 0.91<1\): there is no unstable root but still one jump variable, so the Blanchard–Kahn condition fails. Every gap now shrinks, so every starting value of inflation gives a bounded path. The model has many stable solutions (it is indeterminate): it cannot tell us what inflation will be. Expectations alone can then move the economy (economists call these sunspots). In New Keynesian models, a central bank that raises the interest rate by more than one for one with inflation (the Taylor principle of Chapter 13) rules this out.
a = 1.1
phi = b / (1 - a * rho)       # the decision rule changes too
print(f"1/a = {1 / a:.3f}, phi = {phi:.3f}")   # then rerun the cell that draws the five paths
Set a = 0.9 and phi = b / (1 - a * rho) again before you go on.

H.6 Anatomy of a Snowdrop model file

H.6.1 YAML in five minutes
Snowdrop’s model files are written in YAML, a plain-text format for structured data. Four rules cover almost everything:

key: value pairs, one per line;
nesting by indentation with spaces (never tabs);
lists either in brackets, [x, z], or one item per line starting with -;
# starts a comment.

Python reads YAML into dictionaries and lists. Here is a tiny example:

import yaml
text = """
name: A tiny example          # the model's name
symbols:
   variables: [x, z]
   parameters: [a, b, rho]
calibration:
   a: 0.9
   b: 0.14
"""
print(yaml.safe_load(text))

{'name': 'A tiny example', 'symbols': {'variables': ['x', 'z'], 'parameters': ['a', 'b', 'rho']}, 'calibration': {'a': 0.9, 'b': 0.14}}




H.6.2 The blocks of a model file
Here is the model file of the paper’s monetary policy model, as it comes with Snowdrop. (Its name, JLMP98, points to Juillard, Laxton, McAdam and Pioro, 1998, the paper behind Snowdrop’s LBJ method.)

print(open("JLMP98.yaml").read())

# For details, please see https://link.springer.com/article/10.1057/imfsp.2008.11

symbols:
   variables: [PDOT,RR,RS,Y]
   exogenous: [exo]
   shocks: [ey,err,ers,epdot]
   parameters: [g,p_pdot1,p_pdot2,p_pdot3,p_rs1,p_y1,p_y2,p_y3]

equations:
      - PDOT = p_pdot1*PDOT(+1) + (1-p_pdot1)*PDOT(-1) + p_pdot2*(g^2/(g-Y) - g) + p_pdot3*(g^2/(g-Y(-1)) - g) + epdot
      - RR = RS - p_pdot1*PDOT(+1) - (1-p_pdot1)*PDOT(-1) + err
      - RS = p_rs1*PDOT + Y + ers + exo 
      - Y = p_y1*Y(-1) - p_y2*RR - p_y3*RR(-1) + ey

# steady_state:

   PDOT: "Inflation"
   PDOT(-1): "Lag of Inflation"

Block
What it holds




name
a description of the model


symbols
the names of the variables (endogenous), the exogenous variables (paths given from outside), the shocks and the parameters


equations
one equation per line, left side = right side; one equation per endogenous variable


calibration
parameter values, and starting values of the variables

readable names for charts, also for leads and lags such as PDOT(-1)

Models that are estimated have four more blocks: measurement_variables, measurement_shocks, measurement_equations and estimated_parameters. We meet them in Section H.11.


H.6.3 Timing, shocks and exogenous variables

PDOT(-1) is last period’s value (a lag), and PDOT(+1) (or PDOT(1)) is the value people expect for next period (a lead). An equation with a lead is forward-looking.
Shocks are listed under symbols: shocks. options: periods: [1] and shock_values: [0.02] mean “in period 1, the shocks take these values”, in the order of the shock list: here the first shock, ey, equals 0.02. Values not given are zero.
Exogenous variables follow a path set from outside, period by period (H.7 uses one for the policy-rate revision).
A parameter can change over time: in calibration, p_pdot1: [0.4, 0.5, 0.6] would mean 0.4 in period 1, 0.5 in period 2 and 0.6 from period 3 on.



H.6.4 From file to model object
importModel reads the file, checks its syntax, and writes Python functions for the equations and their derivatives. Its report lists the equations; the number in front of each one is its residual at the starting values. A residual of 0.000 means the starting values satisfy that equation, which is a quick check that you start from a steady state.

jlmp = load_model("JLMP98.yaml", verbose=True)

Finally, Snowdrop can count the roots of the linearized model, as we did by hand in Section H.4. The model has one forward-looking variable, inflation PDOT(+1), so it needs exactly one root larger than 1 in absolute value.

roots, text = quietly(driver.findEigenValues, model=jlmp)
roots = np.sort(np.abs(roots))
print("Absolute values of the roots:", np.round(roots, 3))
print("Roots larger than 1:", int(np.sum(roots > 1)), "| forward-looking variables: 1")

Absolute values of the roots: [0.    0.015 0.015 0.995 1.42 ]
Roots larger than 1: 1 | forward-looking variables: 1


The model has one unstable root and one jump variable: the Blanchard–Kahn condition holds, and the model has a unique stable solution.

text:
H.7 Your first model file: the AS/AD model of Chapter 13
The best first model is one you already know. Chapter 13 combines an AD curve (the IS curve plus the central bank’s rule \(R_t-\bar{r}=\bar{m}(\pi_t-\bar{\pi})\)) with an AS curve (the Phillips curve with adaptive expectations):
\[\tilde{Y}_t=\bar{a}_t-\bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t-\bar{\pi}), \qquad (H.5)\]
\[\pi_t=\pi_{t-1}+\bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t+\bar{o}_t. \qquad (H.6)\]
\(\tilde{Y}_t\) is the output gap and \(\pi_t\) inflation, both in percent. The demand shock \(\bar{a}_t\) and the inflation shock \(\bar{o}_t\) move the economy away from its steady state, where output is at potential and inflation equals the target \(\bar{\pi}\). We use Chapter 13’s baseline: \(\bar{\pi}=2\), \(\bar{m}=0.5\), \(\bar{b}=2\) and \(\bar{\nu}=1\). The model has no expected future values, only the past (\(\pi_{t-1}\)), so it is not a DSGE model, but it is written, solved and simulated with exactly the same tools.

H.7.1 Writing the model file
The notebook command %%writefile saves the rest of a cell as a file. One name needs care: \(\pi\) is a built-in constant (3.14159…) in the algebra library that Snowdrop uses, so a variable called pi would clash with it. We call inflation infl.

%%writefile asad.yaml
name: The AS/AD model of Chapter 13

symbols:
   variables: [Ytil, infl]           # output gap and inflation, in percent
   shocks: [a, o]                    # demand shock and inflation shock
   parameters: [b, m, nu, infl_bar]  # IS slope, policy response, Phillips slope, inflation target

equations:
   - Ytil = a - b*m*(infl - infl_bar)        # the AD curve (H.5)
   - infl = infl(-1) + nu*Ytil + o           # the AS curve (H.6)

calibration:
   b: 2.0
   m: 0.5
   nu: 1.0
   infl_bar: 2.0
   Ytil: 0.0                         # starting values: the steady state
   infl: 2.0

labels:
   Ytil: "Output gap, %"
   infl: "Inflation, %"

options:
   T: 20
   periods: [1]
   shock_values: [[0.0, 2.0]]        # Event 1: an inflation shock o = 2 in period 1

Writing asad.yaml

            var_labels=asad.symbols["variables_labels"], header="Event 1: an inflation shock",
            sizes=(1, 2), figsize=(10, 4), show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "Snowdrop's chart of the inflation shock: inflation jumps to 3 percent and output falls 1 percent", snowdrop=True)






H.7.3 Snowdrop and Chapter 13 agree
Chapter 13 solved the model period by period with a formula: given last period’s inflation, equations (H.5) and (H.6) are two linear equations in this period’s \(\tilde{Y}_t\) and \(\pi_t\), with the solution \(\tilde{Y}_t=[\bar{a}_t-\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1}+\bar{o}_t-\bar{\pi})]/(1+\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\). Here is that solution again, to check Snowdrop against it.

def ch13_path(a_list, o_list, infl_start=2.0, infl_bar=2.0, b=2.0, m=0.5, nu=1.0):
    """Chapter 13's solution of (H.5)-(H.6), one period at a time; period 0 is the starting point."""
    rows = [(0.0, infl_start)]
    for t in range(len(a_list)):
        infl_prev = rows[-1][1]
        Y = (a_list[t] - b * m * (infl_prev + o_list[t] - infl_bar)) / (1 + b * m * nu)
        rows.append((Y, infl_prev + nu * Y + o_list[t]))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Ytil", "infl"])

no_shock = [0.0] * 20
check1 = ch13_path(no_shock, [2.0] + [0.0] * 19)
gap = event1.to_numpy() - check1.iloc[:len(event1)].to_numpy()   # same periods
print(f"Largest difference between Snowdrop and Chapter 13: {np.abs(gap).max():.1e}")

Largest difference between Snowdrop and Chapter 13: 0.0e+00



Python note. [0.0] * 20 repeats the list: twenty zeros. [2.0] + [0.0] * 19 joins two lists: a shock of 2 in period 1 and zeros afterwards.

The central bank lowers its inflation target from 4 to 2 percent. We start the economy at the old steady state, with inflation at 4 percent, and use the new target of 2 percent from period 1 on. No shock hits.

The demand shock first raises output and inflation; as inflation rises, the central bank’s rule raises the real interest rate and pulls output back to potential, with inflation stuck near 4 percent. text:
H.8 The paper’s example: a monetary policy model with expectations

H.8.1 The model, read as economics
The paper’s model has four equations. In the file, PDOT is inflation \(\pi_t\), Y the output gap \(y_t\), RS the central bank’s interest rate \(i_t\) and RR the real interest rate \(r_t\). All four are deviations from the steady state, in decimals (0.01 is one percentage point). With the paper’s names for the parameters:
\[\pi_t = p_1\,\pi_{t+1} + (1-p_1)\,\pi_{t-1} + p_2\Big(\frac{g^2}{g-y_t}-g\Big) + p_3\Big(\frac{g^2}{g-y_{t-1}}-g\Big) + \varepsilon^{\pi}_t, \qquad (H.7)\]
\[r_t = i_t - p_1\,\pi_{t+1} - (1-p_1)\,\pi_{t-1} + \varepsilon^{r}_t, \qquad (H.8)\]
\[i_t = p_4\,\pi_t + y_t + \varepsilon^{i}_t + \text{exo}_t, \qquad (H.9)\]
\[y_t = p_5\,y_{t-1} - p_6\,r_t - p_7\,r_{t-1} + \varepsilon^{y}_t. \qquad (H.10)\]

(H.7) is a Phillips curve that mixes expected inflation (weight \(p_1=0.414\)) and past inflation. The output gap enters through \(g^2/(g-y)-g\), which is close to \(y\) when the gap is small but rises ever faster as \(y\) approaches \(g=0.049\): an economy near full capacity sees inflation accelerate. Booms raise inflation by more than slumps of the same size lower it. Such a convex Phillips curve was a feature of the IMF’s models of the 1990s.
(H.8) defines the real interest rate: the policy rate minus the inflation people expect (Chapters 8 and 12).
(H.9) is the policy rule: the rate rises by \(p_4=3\) points for each point of inflation and one for one with the output gap. \(\text{exo}_t\) is a deliberate change of policy, set from outside.
(H.10) is an IS curve with lags: a higher real interest rate, now or last period, lowers the output gap (Chapters 11 and 12).

Because inflation and the real rate depend on expected inflation, the model is forward-looking; because of the convex term, it is nonlinear.

g = 0.049
y_gap = np.linspace(-0.04, 0.03, 141)
fig, ax = book_figure()
ax.plot(100 * y_gap, 100 * y_gap, color=GRAY, linestyle="--", label="a linear Phillips curve: $y$")
ax.plot(100 * y_gap, 100 * (g**2 / (g - y_gap) - g), color=BLUE, label="the paper's term: $g^2/(g-y)-g$")
ax.set_title("The output gap enters the Phillips curve in a convex way")
ax.set_xlabel("output gap $y$, percent")
ax.set_ylabel("effect on inflation, before $p_2$")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
show(fig, "The convex term equals the gap near zero but rises much faster for large positive gaps")

H.8.3 Solving with Newton’s method
Snowdrop solves nonlinear models along the whole path, as in Section H.4: it stacks the four equations for every period and applies Newton’s method until the residuals vanish. First the output shock alone, with both of Snowdrop’s methods. quietly keeps Snowdrop’s report, and we print its last lines.

paths = {}
for method in ["LBJ", "ABLR"]:
    jlmp = load_model("JLMP98.yaml", Solver=method)
    jlmp.options["periods"] = [1]
    jlmp.options["shock_values"] = [0.02]             # ey = 0.02: a 2 percent output shock in period 1
    (y, dates), text = quietly(driver.run, model=jlmp, Plot=False)
    paths[method] = np.asarray(y)
    print(method, "|", " | ".join(text.strip().splitlines()[-2:]))

print(f"Largest difference between the two methods: {np.abs(paths['LBJ'] - paths['ABLR']).max():.1e}")

In period 1 the output shock opens a positive output gap, and the output gap term pushes inflation up; so does the lead of inflation, because people expect the boom to raise inflation next period too. text:
H.9 A real business cycle model

H.9.1 The model
Chapter 15 described real business cycle (RBC) models: an economy without frictions, hit by productivity shocks. Snowdrop’s RBC.yaml is the simplest one with a household that chooses how much to save. Labor is fixed at one.
\[\frac{1}{C_t}=\beta\,\frac{1+r_t}{C_{t+1}} \qquad (H.11)\]
\[Y_t = C_t + K_t-(1-\delta)K_{t-1} \qquad (H.12)\]
\[Y_t = K_{t-1}^{\gamma}\,A_t^{1-\gamma} \qquad (H.13)\]
\[\gamma\,\frac{Y_{t+1}}{K_t}=r_t+\delta \qquad (H.14)\]
\[\log A_t=\rho\log A_{t-1}+(1-\rho)\log a+\varepsilon_t \qquad (H.15)\]

(H.11) is the Euler equation of Chapter 16 with log utility: the household gives up a unit of consumption today if the return \(1+r_t\), discounted by \(\beta\), makes up for it.
(H.12) is the resource constraint: output is consumed or invested, and investment \(K_t-(1-\delta)K_{t-1}\) builds the capital stock, which depreciates at rate \(\delta\) (Chapter 17).
(H.13) is the production function of Chapter 4, with labor-augmenting technology \(A_t\).
(H.14) says that capital is rented until its marginal product equals its user cost \(r_t+\delta\) (Chapter 17). Capital chosen in period \(t\) produces in \(t+1\).
(H.15) is the technology shock, an AR(1) in logs around the level \(a\).

The calibration is \(\beta=0.99\), \(\gamma=0.5\), \(\delta=0.03\), \(\rho=0.8\) and \(a=0.1\), with one period a quarter.

H.9.2 The steady state by hand
In the steady state nothing changes, so (H.11) gives \(1=\beta(1+r)\), (H.14) gives the capital–output ratio, and (H.13) and (H.12) give output and consumption:
\[r^*=\frac{1}{\beta}-1,\qquad \frac{K^*}{Y^*}=\frac{\gamma}{r^*+\delta},\qquad Y^*=a\Big(\frac{K^*}{Y^*}\Big)^{\gamma/(1-\gamma)},\qquad C^*=Y^*-\delta K^*. \qquad (H.16)\]
The third formula comes from writing (H.13) as \(Y=(K/Y)^{\gamma/(1-\gamma)}A\) with \(A=a\).

r_star = 1 / beta - 1
KY = gamma / (r_star + delta)
Y_star = a_level * KY ** (gamma / (1 - gamma))
K_star = KY * Y_star
C_star = Y_star - delta * K_star

ax.set_ylabel("percent deviation from the steady state")
ax.legend()
show(fig, "Output jumps with technology; consumption rises little but stays up; capital builds up slowly")




What to notice. Output jumps with technology, by about half as much (the exponent \(1-\gamma=0.5\) in (H.13)). Consumption rises only a little: the household knows the shock is temporary and smooths consumption (Chapter 16). The rest of the extra output is invested, so capital builds up for several years, and it keeps output and consumption above their steady state after technology has returned to normal. The interest rate rises with the marginal product of capital and then falls below its steady state while the extra capital is run down.


H.9.4 How nonlinear is the model?
The RBC model is nonlinear: (H.13) has a power, (H.11) a ratio. Linear solution methods, like Klein’s and Dynare’s first-order perturbation, replace the model by a straight-line approximation around the steady state. A linear model responds in proportion to the shock: twice the shock, twice the response. We can test how far the RBC model is from that. We simulate technology shocks \(\varepsilon_1\) of 0.01, 0.1, 0.3 and −0.3 (in logs, so roughly 1, 10, 30 and −30 percent) and scale each response of output to a shock of 1 percent.

fig, ax = book_figure()
sizes = [0.01, 0.1, 0.3, -0.3]
colors = [GRAY, BLUE, TEAL, RUST]
for k in range(len(sizes)):
    rbc = load_model("RBC.yaml")
    set_values(rbc, "variables", steady)
    rbc.options["shock_values"] = [[sizes[k]]]
    path = simulate(rbc)
    per_unit = 100 * (path["Y"] / Y_star - 1) / (100 * sizes[k])   # % response per 1% shock
    ax.plot(per_unit.index[:41], per_unit.iloc[:41], color=colors[k], label=f"shock of {100 * sizes[k]:+.0f}%")
ax.set_title("Output response per 1 percent of shock, for four shock sizes")
ax.set_xlabel("quarters after the shock")
ax.set_ylabel("percent per percent of shock")
ax.legend()
show(fig, "The responses to small shocks coincide; large positive and negative shocks give different responses per unit")




What to notice. For small shocks the scaled responses lie on top of each other, so a linear solution would be accurate. For shocks of ±30 percent they come apart: per unit of shock, a large positive shock raises output by more than a large negative one lowers it. Technology enters in logs, so \(\varepsilon=0.3\) raises \(A\) by 35 percent (\(e^{0.3}-1\)), while \(\varepsilon=-0.3\) lowers it by only 26 percent. Normal business cycles are small, so linear methods serve well for estimation (Sections H.11 and H.12). Big events (a pandemic, a financial crisis) are where nonlinear methods like Snowdrop’s earn their keep.


H.9.5 Random shocks: one model, many histories
So far one shock hit, once. In RBC1.yaml, two shocks hit every period: the technology shock and a shock to output in (H.13). They are drawn from a normal distribution (!MvNormal) for ten different histories (Npaths). The file gives the shocks means of −0.05 and 0.05; we set both to zero, so that the shocks only add noise around the steady state.

text = open("RBC1.yaml").read().replace("mean: [-0.05,0.05]", "mean: [0.0, 0.0]")
open("RBC1_zero.yaml", "w").write(text)
print(text[text.find("options"):])

options:
    T : 51    
    Npaths : 10
    distribution: !MvNormal
        mean: [0.0, 0.0]
        cov: [[std^2, cov],[cov, std^2]]




Python note. np.random.seed(2026) fixes the random numbers, so that the same histories come out every time the notebook runs. A stochastic run returns an array with three dimensions: path, period and variable.

One more setting matters. By default, Snowdrop solves each history as one perfect-foresight path: it imposes all the random shocks at once, as if households knew in period 1 every shock still to come. In a stochastic simulation the shocks must be surprises. anticipate=False makes Snowdrop solve the model period by period and reveal each shock only when it hits. This takes a few seconds longer.

rbc1 = load_model("RBC1_zero.yaml", anticipate=False)
set_values(rbc1, "variables", steady)
np.random.seed(2026)
(y, dates), text = quietly(driver.run, model=rbc1, Plot=False, anticipate=False)
print("Shape of the result (paths, periods, variables):", np.shape(y))
figs = plot(path_to_dir=WORK, data=np.asarray(y), variable_names=rbc1.symbols["variables"], Npaths=10,
            var_labels=rbc_labels, header="Ten histories of the RBC model with random shocks", sizes=(2, 3), figsize=(12, 6.5),
            show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "Ten simulated histories of output, consumption, capital, the interest rate and technology", snowdrop=True)

Shape of the result (paths, periods, variables): (10, 53, 5)





What to notice. The same model, the same parameters and the same distribution of shocks produce ten different histories. This is how DSGE models see the business cycle: a stable economy constantly hit by small random shocks. Consumption is much smoother than output in every history, and capital moves slowly around its steady state. (Run the cell without anticipate=False and you will see what goes wrong when households know the future: consumption jumps once in period 1 and then drifts, and capital wanders far from its steady state.) Estimation (Sections H.11 and H.12) asks the reverse question: given one observed history, which parameters make it most likely?
Your turn. Make technology shocks more persistent, \(\rho=0.95\), and draw the impulse responses again. How does the response of consumption change, and why?

A more persistent shock raises income for longer, so it is closer to a permanent rise in income: consumption jumps by more on impact (the permanent income idea of Chapter 16), and the household invests less of each extra unit of output.

H.10 From model to data: state space and the Kalman filter

H.10.1 The solved model is a state-space model
Once a linear model is solved, its decision rules say how the variables today depend on the variables yesterday and on today’s shocks. Stack the variables into a vector \(s_t\), the state:
\[s_t = T\,s_{t-1} + R\,\varepsilon_t \qquad \text{(transition equation)}\]
\[y_t = Z\,s_t + u_t \qquad \text{(measurement equation)}\]
The first line is the model. The second says which combinations of the state we observe in the data, \(y_t\), perhaps with measurement errors \(u_t\). In Ireland’s model of Section H.11 the state has seven variables and the data three. The output gap, the preference shock and the cost-push shock are never observed. The Kalman filter does two jobs at once: it infers the unobserved states from the data, period by period, and it computes the likelihood of the data, the number that estimation maximizes. We build it for the smallest case first.


H.10.2 A Kalman filter for one variable
The state is an AR(1), and we observe it with noise:
\[s_t=\rho\,s_{t-1}+e_t,\quad e_t\sim N(0,\sigma_e^2), \qquad (H.17)\]
\[y_t=s_t+u_t,\quad u_t\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2). \qquad (H.18)\]
Think of \(s_t\) as the true output gap and \(y_t\) as a noisy first estimate of it. We simulate 200 periods with \(\rho=0.9\) and \(\sigma_e=\sigma_u=1\), so we know the truth and can see how well the filter recovers it.

Python note. np.random.default_rng(2026) creates a random number generator with a fixed seed, so the numbers are the same every time; rng.normal() draws one number from the standard normal distribution.


rho_true, sig_e, sig_u = 0.9, 1.0, 1.0
T_data = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
s_true = np.zeros(T_data)
y_obs = np.zeros(T_data)
s_prev = 0.0
for t in range(T_data):
    s_true[t] = rho_true * s_prev + sig_e * rng.normal()    # equation (H.17)
    y_obs[t] = s_true[t] + sig_u * rng.normal()             # equation (H.18)
    s_prev = s_true[t]
print(f"Standard deviation of the state: {s_true.std():.2f}, of the data: {y_obs.std():.2f}")

Standard deviation of the state: 2.00, of the data: 2.25


Each period the filter does three things. Write \(\hat{s}_{t|t-1}\) for the best guess of the state before seeing \(y_t\), \(\hat{s}_{t|t}\) for the guess after, and \(P\) for the variance (the uncertainty) of each guess.

Predict the state with the model: \(\hat{s}_{t|t-1}=\rho\,\hat{s}_{t-1|t-1}\) and \(P_{t|t-1}=\rho^2P_{t-1|t-1}+\sigma_e^2\). (H.19)
Compare with the data: the forecast error is \(v_t=y_t-\hat{s}_{t|t-1}\), with variance \(F_t=P_{t|t-1}+\sigma_u^2\). (H.20)
Update: move the guess toward the data by the Kalman gain \(K_t=P_{t|t-1}/F_t\): \(\hat{s}_{t|t}=\hat{s}_{t|t-1}+K_tv_t\) and \(P_{t|t}=(1-K_t)P_{t|t-1}\). (H.21)

The gain weighs the two sources of information: when the model’s prediction is uncertain (\(P\) large) the filter trusts the data; when the data are noisy (\(\sigma_u\) large) it trusts the model. Before the first observation we use the long-run variance of the state, \(\sigma_e^2/(1-\rho^2)\); Snowdrop calls this choice Prior="Equilibrium".
The likelihood comes for free. If the model is right, each forecast error \(v_t\) is normal with mean 0 and variance \(F_t\). The probability of the whole sample is the product of these normal densities, so its logarithm is a sum:
\[\log L=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big(\log 2\pi+\log F_t+\frac{v_t^2}{F_t}\Big). \qquad (H.22)\]

def kalman_filter(y, rho, sig_e, sig_u):
    """Equations (H.19)-(H.21) for the model (H.17)-(H.18); returns the filtered states and log L of (H.22)."""
    s_hat = 0.0                                    # the state's mean before any data
    P = sig_e**2 / (1 - rho**2)                    # and its long-run variance
    filtered = np.zeros(len(y))
    loglik = 0.0
    for t in range(len(y)):
        s_pred = rho * s_hat                       # 1. predict
        P_pred = rho**2 * P + sig_e**2
        v = y[t] - s_pred                          # 2. compare: forecast error and its variance
        F = P_pred + sig_u**2
        K = P_pred / F                             # 3. update with the Kalman gain
        s_hat = s_pred + K * v
        P = (1 - K) * P_pred
        filtered[t] = s_hat
        loglik = loglik - 0.5 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.log(F) + v**2 / F)
    return filtered, loglik

filtered, loglik = kalman_filter(y_obs, rho_true, sig_e, sig_u)
print(f"Log-likelihood at the true parameters: {loglik:.2f}")
print(f"Typical error: data {np.std(y_obs - s_true):.2f}, filtered state {np.std(filtered - s_true):.2f}")

Log-likelihood at the true parameters: -381.78
Typical error: data 1.07, filtered state 0.76



fig, ax = book_figure()
periods = np.arange(1, 81)
ax.plot(periods, y_obs[:80], color=GRAY, linestyle="none", marker="o", markersize=3.5, label="data $y_t$")
ax.plot(periods, s_true[:80], color=TEAL, linewidth=1.6, label="true state $s_t$")
ax.plot(periods, filtered[:80], color=BLUE, linewidth=2.4, label="filtered state $\\hat{s}_{t|t}$")
ax.set_title("The Kalman filter recovers the state from noisy data (first 80 periods)")
ax.set_xlabel("period")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
show(fig, "The filtered state follows the true state much more closely than the noisy data do")




What to notice. The data jump around the true state; the filtered state follows the truth much more closely, because it combines each new observation with what the model predicted. The filter’s error is smaller than the error of the raw data.
The same filter with matrices. For a model with many variables, the scalars become matrices: \(P_{t|t-1}=TP_{t-1|t-1}T'+RQR'\), \(F_t=ZP_{t|t-1}Z'+H\) and \(K_t=P_{t|t-1}Z'F_t^{-1}\), where \(Q\) and \(H\) hold the variances of the shocks and of the measurement errors. The log-likelihood has the same form, with \(\log\det F_t\) and \(v_t'F_t^{-1}v_t\). Snowdrop’s Durbin_Koopman filter does this, in a version that is fast and numerically careful (Durbin and Koopman, 2012).

Show the answer

With noisy data the filter trusts the model more: the Kalman gain falls from about 0.6 to about 0.23, so each new observation moves the estimate less. The filtered state becomes smoother and reacts to the data more slowly.

filtered_noisy, ll = kalman_filter(y_noisy, rho_true, sig_e, sig_u)
P = sig_e**2 / (1 - rho_true**2)
for t in range(T_data):                       # the gain does not depend on the data, only on the variances
    P_pred = rho_true**2 * P + sig_e**2
    K = P_pred / (P_pred + sig_u**2)
    P = (1 - K) * P_pred
print(f"Kalman gain with sig_u = 3: {K:.2f}")
sig_u = 1.0                                   # back to the baseline

H.11 Maximum likelihood from small pieces

H.11.1 The likelihood of one parameter
Pretend we do not know \(\rho\). Every value of \(\rho\) gives a value of the log-likelihood (H.22): how probable the observed data would be if \(\rho\) were the truth. The maximum likelihood estimate is the value that makes the data most probable. With one parameter we can simply try a grid of values.

rho_grid = np.linspace(0.5, 0.99, 99)
loglik_grid = np.zeros(len(rho_grid))
for k in range(len(rho_grid)):
    filtered_k, loglik_grid[k] = kalman_filter(y_obs, rho_grid[k], sig_e, sig_u)
rho_best = rho_grid[np.argmax(loglik_grid)]

fig, ax = book_figure()
ax.plot(rho_grid, loglik_grid, color=BLUE)
ax.axvline(rho_true, color=GRAY, linestyle="--", label=f"true value {rho_true}")
ax.axvline(rho_best, color=RUST, label=f"maximum at {rho_best:.3f}")
ax.set_ylim(loglik_grid.max() - 40, loglik_grid.max() + 4)
ax.set_title("The log-likelihood of the persistence parameter")
ax.set_xlabel("$\\rho$")
ax.set_ylabel("log-likelihood")
ax.legend(loc="lower center")
show(fig, "The log-likelihood is highest near the true persistence of 0.9")






H.11.2 Curvature and the standard error
How sure can we be? If the log-likelihood falls steeply on both sides of its peak, values far from the peak are much less likely, and the estimate is precise. If it is flat, many values fit the data almost as well. The curvature at the peak, the second derivative, measures this, and the standard error of the estimate is \(1/\sqrt{-\text{curvature}}\). We compute the second derivative numerically, from three nearby points. Snowdrop does exactly this for all its parameters at once.

def negative_loglik_rho(rho):
    """Minus the log-likelihood (H.22) as a function of rho alone (the two sigmas stay at their true values)."""
    filtered_k, ll = kalman_filter(y_obs, rho, sig_e, sig_u)
    return -ll

result = optimize.minimize_scalar(negative_loglik_rho, bounds=(0.01, 0.999), method="bounded")
rho_hat = result.x
h = 1e-4
curvature = -(negative_loglik_rho(rho_hat + h) - 2 * negative_loglik_rho(rho_hat)
              + negative_loglik_rho(rho_hat - h)) / h**2
se = 1 / np.sqrt(-curvature)
print(f"Estimate {rho_hat:.4f}, standard error {se:.4f}")
print(f"95 percent interval: {rho_hat - 1.96 * se:.3f} to {rho_hat + 1.96 * se:.3f} (true value {rho_true})")

Estimate 0.8512, standard error 0.0376
95 percent interval: 0.778 to 0.925 (true value 0.9)




H.11.3 All parameters at once, with a numerical optimizer
In practice we estimate all parameters together. A numerical optimizer searches for the maximum, here SciPy’s L-BFGS-B, the method Snowdrop uses. It accepts bounds: \(\rho\) must lie between 0 and 1, and standard deviations must be positive. The matrix of second derivatives (the Hessian) then gives the standard errors: they are the square roots of the diagonal of the inverse of minus the Hessian.

Python note. optimize.minimize finds the minimum of a function, so we give it minus the log-likelihood. x0 is the starting point, bounds one (lower, upper) pair per parameter, and result.x the solution.


def negative_loglik(theta):
    """Minus the log-likelihood (H.22) of theta = (rho, sig_e, sig_u)."""
    filtered_k, ll = kalman_filter(y_obs, theta[0], theta[1], theta[2])
    return -ll

result = optimize.minimize(negative_loglik, x0=[0.5, 0.5, 0.5], method="L-BFGS-B",
                           bounds=[(0.01, 0.999), (0.01, 10.0), (0.01, 10.0)])

def hessian(f, x, h=1e-4):
    """The matrix of second derivatives of f at x, by central differences."""
    n = len(x)
    H = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            e_i, e_j = np.eye(n)[i] * h, np.eye(n)[j] * h
            H[i, j] = (f(x + e_i + e_j) - f(x + e_i - e_j) - f(x - e_i + e_j) + f(x - e_i - e_j)) / (4 * h * h)
    return H

std_errors = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(hessian(negative_loglik, result.x))))
pd.DataFrame({"true": [rho_true, sig_e, sig_u], "estimate": result.x, "std. error": std_errors},
             index=["rho", "sigma_e", "sigma_u"]).round(3)

What to notice. The optimizer started far from the truth (0.5 for every parameter) and found the peak of the likelihood. (Since negative_loglik is minus the log-likelihood, its Hessian is already “minus the curvature”.) The estimates are within about two standard errors of the true values, but they are not very close, and the standard error of \(\sigma_u\) is almost as large as the estimate. With 200 observations the data cannot tell well how much of the movement in \(y_t\) comes from shocks to the state and how much from noise in the measurement. This is a first taste of weak identification, which we will meet again in Ireland’s model. That is the whole of maximum likelihood estimation: write the model in state-space form, compute the likelihood with the Kalman filter, and let an optimizer find its peak. Snowdrop does the same for a model with seven variables and twelve parameters.

H.12 Estimating Ireland (2004) by maximum likelihood

H.12.1 The model
Ireland (2004) asked how much technology shocks, the heart of real business cycle theory, matter once a New Keynesian model gives other shocks a chance. His model has four shocks and seven equations. All variables are deviations from the steady state, quarterly, in decimals:
\[a_t=\rho_a\,a_{t-1}+\varepsilon_{at} \qquad (H.23)\]
\[e_t=\rho_e\,e_{t-1}+\varepsilon_{et} \qquad (H.24)\]
\[x_t=\alpha_x\,x_{t-1}+(1-\alpha_x)\,\mathbb{E}_tx_{t+1}-(r_t-\mathbb{E}_t\pi_{t+1})+(1-\omega)(1-\rho_a)\,a_t \qquad (H.25)\]
\[\pi_t=\beta\,[\alpha_\pi\,\pi_{t-1}+(1-\alpha_\pi)\,\mathbb{E}_t\pi_{t+1}]+\psi\,x_t-e_t \qquad (H.26)\]
\[x_t=y_t-\omega\,a_t \qquad (H.27)\]
\[g_t=y_t-y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_{zt} \qquad (H.28)\]
\[r_t-r_{t-1}=\rho_\pi\,\pi_t+\rho_g\,g_t+\rho_x\,x_t+\varepsilon_{rt} \qquad (H.29)\]

(H.23) and (H.24) are the preference shock \(a_t\) and the cost-push shock \(e_t\), both AR(1).
(H.25) is the IS curve: the output gap \(x_t\) depends on the expected gap and the real interest rate, as in Chapters 11 and 12, with a preference shock that raises demand. \(\alpha_x\) adds a backward-looking element.
(H.26) is the New Keynesian Phillips curve of Section H.4, with a backward-looking weight \(\alpha_\pi\).
(H.27) defines the output gap as output minus its efficient level, which moves with the preference shock.
(H.28) is output growth \(g_t\); \(\varepsilon_{zt}\) is the technology shock. It changes the level of output permanently, so it shows up in growth.
(H.29) is the monetary policy rule, written in changes of the interest rate: the Fed raises the rate when inflation, output growth or the output gap are high (Chapter 13).

We observe three variables: output growth, inflation and the interest rate. Following Ireland, there are no measurement errors, so \(g^{obs}_t=g_t\), \(\pi^{obs}_t=\pi_t\) and \(r^{obs}_t=r_t\). The discount factor \(\beta=0.99\) and the slope \(\psi=0.1\) are fixed; the other twelve parameters (eight coefficients and four shock standard deviations) are estimated.


H.12.2 The data
Snowdrop’s file holds Ireland’s U.S. data from 1948Q1 to 2002Q4: per-capita real GDP growth, inflation of the GDP deflator, and the three-month Treasury bill rate, all as quarterly rates. Ireland’s own sample ends one quarter later, in 2003Q1. The columns obs_g, obs_pie and obs_r are deviations from the sample means, which is what the model needs; obsg, obspie and obsr are the raw rates.

H.12.4 A first run
We read the model with four settings. Solver="Klein" solves the linear model with the generalized Schur method (the method of IRIS). Filter="Durbin_Koopman" is the filter; Snowdrop’s estimation works only with this filter or "Non_Diffuse_Filter". Smoother="Durbin_Koopman" lets Snowdrop also compute the smoothed variables that we plot below. Prior="Equilibrium" starts the filter from the long-run variance of the state, as in Section H.9. (In this option, “prior” means the filter’s starting point, not the priors of Section H.12.) Then estimate(..., estimate_ML=True) maximizes the likelihood, starting from the second column of estimated_parameters. This takes about one minute here, and about two minutes in Colab.

What to notice. Started from Ireland’s values, the search stays there: our estimates reproduce his Table 1 almost to the last digit, and most standard errors are close to his. Two exceptions are worth understanding:

\(\alpha_\pi\) sits at its lower bound of zero, and its standard error is reported as 0. That number is meaningless. Standard errors come from the curvature of the likelihood, which is computed by stepping a little to each side of the estimate; at a bound one side is off limits, so the calculation breaks down. Ireland reports a standard error of 0.07 for his estimate of zero, computed in a different way.
Some standard errors, such as those of \(\sigma_a\) and \(\rho_a\), differ from Ireland’s by a third or more. Numerical second derivatives are sensitive to the step size, and Ireland’s sample has one more quarter.



H.12.7 Why the two runs differ: a flat likelihood
Compare the two log-likelihoods printed above. When the first run ends lower, its optimizer simply stopped too early. But it can also happen that the first run reaches the same log-likelihood with very different values of \(\omega\) and \(\alpha_x\) (our test run in Colab did: \(\omega\approx0.16\) instead of 0.06, with the same log-likelihood to two decimals). Then the likelihood has a flat ridge: many combinations of these parameters fit the data equally well, and the data cannot tell them apart. Ireland’s large standard errors for \(\omega\) (0.063 for an estimate of 0.062) and \(\alpha_x\) say the same thing. Economists call such parameters weakly identified.
Three habits follow:

Start the search from several places, including published estimates, and keep the run with the highest log-likelihood.
Read the standard errors: a parameter whose standard error is as large as its estimate is barely identified; do not build conclusions on it.
Know your software. Snowdrop computes the filter’s starting variance (Prior="Equilibrium") once, from the starting values, before the search begins. So the likelihood itself depends a little on where you start, one more reason to start near the answer.

Bayesian estimation, next, is the other standard remedy: a prior adds curvature exactly where the likelihood is flat.


H.12.8 What the estimated model says
estimate also returns the smoothed values of all seven variables: the filter’s best estimate of each one in each quarter, using the whole sample. Snowdrop’s plot shows them, with the data as dots. With no measurement errors, the three observed series are matched exactly; the interesting panels are the variables we never observe.

smoothed = np.asarray(out_ml[0])[1]                 # [0] holds the filtered values, [1] the smoothed ones
dates = list(out_ml[1])
measured = data[["obs_g", "obs_pie", "obs_r"]]
labels = {"y": "Output", "x": "Output gap", "r": "Interest rate", "g": "Output growth", "pie": "Inflation",
          "a": "Preference shock", "e": "Cost-push shock"}
figs = plot(path_to_dir=WORK, data=smoothed[1:], variable_names=ireland.symbols["variables"], meas_values=measured,
            meas_variables=list(measured.columns), output_variables=["g", "pie", "r", "x", "a", "e"],
            var_labels=labels, rng=dates, rng_meas=list(measured.index), sizes=(3, 2), figsize=(12, 9),
            header="Ireland (2004) estimated: data (dots) and smoothed variables", show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "The smoothed output gap, preference shock and cost-push shock over 1948-2002, with the observed "
     "series", snowdrop=True)




What to notice. The model reads the 1970s and the Volcker disinflation of 1979–1982 through the shocks. The cost-push shock falls sharply in 1974 and again in 1979–1980; it enters the Phillips curve (H.26) with a minus sign, so these dips are inflationary cost shocks, the two oil shocks. The output gap is deeply negative in the early 1980s, when the Fed raised interest rates to bring inflation down, while a large positive preference shock (strong demand) pushed the other way. In Ireland’s own decomposition of the forecast errors (his Table 2), technology shocks explain about a quarter of the variance of output growth, monetary policy shocks more than a third, and preference and cost-push shocks the rest: real business cycle theory is part of the story, not all of it.
The estimates themselves describe the U.S. economy:

The policy rule responds strongly to inflation (\(\rho_\pi\approx0.36\)) and output growth (\(\rho_g\approx0.25\)) and little to the output gap (\(\rho_x\approx0.03\)). Because the rule is written in changes, these responses accumulate over time.
The preference and cost-push shocks are very persistent (\(\rho_a\) and \(\rho_e\) near 0.95).
The backward-looking weights \(\alpha_x\) and \(\alpha_\pi\) are small: the data prefer the purely forward-looking IS and Phillips curves.

text:
H.13 Bayesian estimation: priors and the posterior mode

H.13.1 Bayes’ rule with one parameter
Bayesian estimation treats parameters as uncertain and describes what we know about them with probability distributions. Before seeing the data, the prior \(p(\theta)\) sums up outside evidence. The data enter through the likelihood \(p(y\mid\theta)\). Bayes’ rule combines the two into the posterior:
\[p(\theta\mid y)\;\propto\;p(y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta),\qquad\text{so}\qquad \log p(\theta\mid y)=\log L(\theta)+\log p(\theta)+\text{constant}. \qquad (H.30)\]
The posterior mode is the value of \(\theta\) that maximizes the posterior: the maximum likelihood problem with one extra term, the log of the prior. Back to the AR(1) of Section H.9. Suppose we have only 40 observations, and an economist who believes shocks fade fast: her prior for \(\rho\) is a beta distribution with mean 0.5 and standard deviation 0.15.

Python note. A beta distribution lives between 0 and 1, which suits a persistence parameter. Its two shape parameters follow from the mean \(m\) and standard deviation \(s\): with \(k=m(1-m)/s^2-1\), they are \(mk\) and \((1-m)k\). stats.beta.logpdf(x, a, b) is the log of its density.


y_short = y_obs[:40]
m_prior, s_prior = 0.5, 0.15
k = m_prior * (1 - m_prior) / s_prior**2 - 1
a_prior, b_prior = m_prior * k, (1 - m_prior) * k

rho_grid = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 197)
log_prior = stats.beta.logpdf(rho_grid, a_prior, b_prior)
log_lik = np.zeros(len(rho_grid))
for j in range(len(rho_grid)):
    filtered_j, log_lik[j] = kalman_filter(y_short, rho_grid[j], sig_e, sig_u)
log_post = log_lik + log_prior                       # equation (H.30)

def density(log_values):
    """Turn log values on the grid into a density that integrates to one."""
    values = np.exp(log_values - log_values.max())
    return values / (values.sum() * (rho_grid[1] - rho_grid[0]))

print(f"Prior mean {m_prior}, maximum likelihood {rho_grid[log_lik.argmax()]:.3f}, "
      f"posterior mode {rho_grid[log_post.argmax()]:.3f}")

Prior mean 0.5, maximum likelihood 0.815, posterior mode 0.740



fig, ax = book_figure()
ax.plot(rho_grid, density(log_prior), color=GRAY, linestyle="--", label="prior")
ax.plot(rho_grid, density(log_lik), color=TEAL, label="likelihood (scaled)")
ax.plot(rho_grid, density(log_post), color=BLUE, linewidth=3, label="posterior")
ax.axvline(rho_true, color=AXIS, linewidth=1, gid="rule")
ax.set_title("Prior, likelihood and posterior of the persistence parameter (40 observations)")
ax.set_xlabel("$\\rho$ (the thin line is the true value, 0.9)")
ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
show(fig, "The posterior lies between the prior and the likelihood, closer to the more precise of the two")




What to notice. The posterior is a compromise between the prior and the likelihood, and it leans toward whichever is more precise. With 40 observations the likelihood is narrower than the prior, so the data win most of the argument, but the prior still pulls the posterior mode down from the maximum likelihood estimate. With more data the likelihood narrows further and the prior matters less. Where the likelihood is flat, as for \(\omega\) in Ireland’s model, the prior decides.


H.13.2 The posterior mode of Ireland’s model, with the file’s priors
The last three entries of each line of estimated_parameters are the prior: its distribution, mean and standard deviation. Snowdrop’s file uses normal priors throughout. estimate_Posterior=True maximizes the log-likelihood plus the log of the priors. We start from the same values as the maximum likelihood run.

# @title Helper code: prior densities and the prior-versus-estimates charts
from snowdrop.src.utils.distributions import pdf, getHyperParameters

def prior_density(prior, x):
    """Snowdrop's prior density of one parameter at the points x, as estimate() evaluates it."""
    distribution = prior["distribution"]
    pars = np.array(prior["parameters"], dtype=float)
    if not distribution.endswith("_hp"):
        pars[3], pars[4] = getHyperParameters(distr=distribution, mean=pars[3], std=pars[4])
    values = np.zeros(len(x))
    for i in range(len(x)):
        values[i] = pdf(distribution, x[i], pars)[0]
    return values

def prior_panels(priors, estimates, title):
    """One panel per parameter: the prior density and vertical lines for the estimates {label: Series}."""
    fig, axes = book_figure(3, 4, width=13, height=8.4)
    styles = [("--", RUST), ("-", BLUE), ("-", TEAL)]
    for k in range(len(names)):
        name, ax = names[k], axes[k]
        lower, upper, mean, sd = [float(v) for v in priors[name]["parameters"][1:5]]
        values = [float(est[name]) for est in estimates.values()]
        lo = max(lower, min(mean - 3 * sd, min(values) * 0.7))
        hi = min(upper, max(mean + 3 * sd, max(values) * 1.3), 5 * max(max(values), mean))
        x = np.linspace(lo, hi, 300)
        ax.fill_between(x, prior_density(priors[name], x), color=GRAY, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0)
        j = 0
        for label, est in estimates.items():
            ax.axvline(float(est[name]), linestyle=styles[j][0], color=styles[j][1], label=label)
            j += 1
        ax.set_title(greek[name] + "  (" + priors[name]["distribution"].replace("_pdf", "") + ")", fontsize=11)
        ax.set_yticks([])
        ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8)
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.6)
    fig.suptitle(title, y=1.02)
    return fig

H.13.3 A conventional set of priors
Normal priors are an odd choice for most of these parameters. A normal distribution puts probability on negative values and, for the persistence parameters, on values above one, which the model rules out (the bounds then cut the distribution off). Some of the file’s priors are also very tight or very loose. The prior for \(\alpha_\pi\) has mean 0.000005 and standard deviation 0.000001: it nails \(\alpha_\pi\) at zero before any data are seen. The prior for \(\sigma_a\) has mean 0.03 and standard deviation 1.8, which is flat over every plausible value.

Snowdrop takes the mean and standard deviation and computes each distribution’s own parameters. For the beta distribution this is the formula above; a gamma with mean \(m\) and standard deviation \(s\) has shape \(m^2/s^2\) and scale \(s^2/m\). In this version of Snowdrop, the other two inverse-gamma variants (inv_gamma_pdf and inv_gamma2_pdf) do not turn the mean and standard deviation into the right parameters, so check any prior you use by plotting it, as we do below. What to notice.

Where the data are informative, the three columns agree and the posterior is much narrower than the prior. The policy responses \(\rho_\pi\) and \(\rho_g\) barely move. For the shock standard deviations and the persistence parameters, the posterior standard error is a fifth of the prior standard deviation or less.
Where the likelihood is flat, the prior decides. For \(\alpha_x\) the posterior is hardly narrower than the prior (the ratio is close to one): the data say almost nothing about it. The file’s tight normal prior around 0.2 pulls \(\omega\) from 0.06 up to about 0.15. The conventional beta prior has the same mean but is five times wider, and \(\omega\) lands at about 0.09, between the prior and the maximum likelihood estimate. For \(\alpha_\pi\) the conventional prior pulls the estimate off its bound of zero, where the file’s prior had nailed it.
A prior on one parameter moves others. When the file’s prior pushes \(\omega\) up, the standard deviation of the preference shocks \(\sigma_a\) falls from about 0.040 to 0.026 at the same time. Both shape how preference shocks enter the model, so the data pin down a combination of them rather than each one alone.

This is what Bayesian estimation offers: where the data are silent, the answer is the prior, and you can see it. It is also its danger: a prior chosen without care can decide a result that looks like a finding from the data. Always report the priors, and compare the posterior with them.
Your turn. Suppose you believe the Fed responds more strongly to inflation. Give \(\rho_\pi\) a tight gamma prior with mean 0.5 and standard deviation 0.05 and estimate the posterior mode again. Does \(\rho_\pi\) move? What happens to the posterior standard error, and to the other parameters?

The tight prior pulls \(\rho_\pi\) up from about 0.35 to about 0.41: halfway to the prior mean of 0.5, because the likelihood pushes back. Its posterior standard error, about 0.03, is smaller than both the prior’s 0.05 and the 0.04 of the conventional run: prior and data now both carry information about \(\rho_\pi\). Other parameters adjust a little; for example, the response to output growth \(\rho_g\) rises. The estimation takes about two minutes in Colab.

title: H. DSGE Modeling with Python
text:
H.14 Going further

H.14.1 Sampling the whole posterior
The posterior mode is one number per parameter. Bayesian studies usually report the whole posterior distribution, drawn by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Snowdrop offers the affine-invariant ensemble sampler of Goodman and Weare (2010), through the emcee library, and adaptive Metropolis–Hastings samplers from pymcmcstat. Choose one when you read the model, importModel(..., SamplingMethod="emcee"), then call driver.estimate(model=..., sample=True, Ndraws=..., Niter=..., burn=...). With Plot=True, Snowdrop draws the prior and posterior densities and a corner plot of the draws. Serious runs take hours, not minutes, and you must check that the chains have converged. Herbst and Schorfheide (2016) explain how.


H.14.2 The Kalman smoother and historical decompositions
Section H.11 plotted the smoothed variables. The same output holds the smoothed shocks: the fourth element of what estimate returns has one column per structural shock and one row per quarter. With them you can rebuild history shock by shock and ask, for example, how much of the 1980–82 recession monetary policy shocks explain. Snowdrop’s kalman_filter function runs the filter and smoother without estimating, and plotDecomposition (with isKF=True) is the place to start for the contribution charts.


H.14.3 The paper’s epidemic model, and the Smets–Wouters model
The folder supplements/models/COVID19 of the package (in SUPP) holds the paper’s third example, ert_model.yaml (Eichenbaum, Rebelo and Trabandt), with its data in supplements/data/COVID19 and the code that runs it in snowdrop/src/epidemic/ert.py. The same folder has sw_model.yaml, a replication of the Smets and Wouters (2007) model whose estimated responses appear in Chapter 15, and gsw_model.yaml, the Galí–Smets–Wouters model applied to the COVID-19 lockdowns. These are large models; read their files first, then simulate them with the tools of Sections H.6 to H.8.


H.14.4 Your own data
Ireland’s sample ends in 2002. To re-estimate the model on today’s data, download the four series with the tools of Appendix B: real GDP, population, the GDP deflator and the three-month Treasury bill rate (FRED: GDPC1, CNP16OV, GDPDEF, TB3MS). Average the monthly series by quarter. Compute quarterly per-capita output growth and inflation (log differences) and the quarterly interest rate (the annual rate divided by 400), subtract each series’ mean, and save a CSV file with a Date column and the columns obs_g, obs_pie and obs_r. Change range and filter_range in the model file and pass the new file as measurement_file_path. Two warnings: from 2009 to 2015 the interest rate was stuck at zero, which a linear policy rule cannot describe, and the pandemic quarters of 2020 are huge outliers.


H.14.5 Other model files and other tools
importModel also reads Dynare (.mod) and IRIS model files: supplements/models/MPAF holds the IMF’s basic Quarterly Projection Model both as model.mod and as model.yaml. The package’s User Guide (supplements/docs/UserGuide.pdf) lists every option of the model files and functions, and supplements/docs/NumericalAlgorithms.pdf describes the solvers and filters. Other open-source Python projects for DSGE models exist too, for example dolo and pydsge.

text:
H.15 Concluding remarks

A DSGE model is a set of equations from optimizing households and firms, market clearing, policy rules and random shocks. Solving it means finding decision rules (or, for a nonlinear model, a whole path) that satisfy every equation in every period; the Blanchard–Kahn condition tells whether a unique stable solution exists.
Snowdrop, a free Python package from the IMF, writes models as plain YAML files and solves them with Newton’s method (nonlinear models) or generalized Schur methods (linear models). With it we reproduced Chapter 13’s AS/AD model exactly, replicated Fig. 1 of the Snowdrop paper, and simulated a real business cycle model with one shock and with many random ones.
To take a model to data, write its solution in state-space form; the Kalman filter infers the unobserved states and gives the likelihood. Maximum likelihood finds the parameters that make the data most probable; the curvature of the likelihood gives their standard errors.
Estimating Ireland’s (2004) model reproduced his published estimates, but only after we restarted the search from a second point: DSGE likelihoods are often flat in some directions, and an optimizer can stop early. Bayesian estimation adds priors, which decide exactly where the data are silent; always report them and compare the posterior with them.
The habit that runs through the appendix is to check every result: against a case you can solve by hand, against the residuals of the equations, against a second starting point, against the published numbers. Research software is powerful, and like any tool it is only as reliable as the checks you run on it.

import math, base64, matplotlib, matplotlib.collections, matplotlib.patches
from matplotlib.colors import to_rgba, to_hex
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY, ORANGE, RUST = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3", "#e0a33b", "#c4651a"
SERIES = [BLUE, "#5aa0d8", TEAL, GREEN, ORANGE, "#b04a5a", "#8e5ea2", GRAY, RUST, "#0b4f47"]
INK, GRID, AXIS, TOTAL, NAVY = "#2a3f5f", "#e3e9f1", "#b8c4d2", "#1b2733", "#06253e"
DARK = {"#16528c": "#5eb1f2", "#008070": "#3dd6c4", "#7fb23a": "#a6d85b", "#8a96a3": "#97a9bd",
        "#5aa0d8": "#a9d3f7", "#0b4f47": "#22a08d", "#e0a33b": "#f2c14e", "#c4651a": "#f08c4a",
        "#b04a5a": "#f07a8c", "#8e5ea2": "#c39be0", INK: "#d8e3ee", TOTAL: "#e6edf5",
        "#000000": "#e6edf5", "#ffffff": NAVY}

def _lin(v): return v / 12.92 if v <= 0.04045 else ((v + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4
def _gam(v): return min(1.0, max(0.0, 12.92 * v if v <= 0.0031308 else 1.055 * v ** (1 / 2.4) - 0.055))
def oklab(rgb):
    r, g, b = (_lin(x) for x in rgb[:3])
    l, m, s = [(u * r + v * g + w * b) ** (1 / 3) for u, v, w in ((0.4122214708, 0.5363325363, 0.0514459929),
               (0.2119034982, 0.6806995451, 0.1073969566), (0.0883024619, 0.2817188376, 0.6299787005))]
    return (0.2104542553 * l + 0.7936177850 * m - 0.0040720468 * s,
            1.9779984951 * l - 2.4285922050 * m + 0.4505937099 * s,
            0.0259040371 * l + 0.7827717662 * m - 0.8086757660 * s)
def from_oklab(L, A, B):
    for k in np.arange(1.0, -0.01, -0.05):                     # lower the chroma until the color fits sRGB
        a, b = A * k, B * k
        l, m, s = (L + 0.3963377774 * a + 0.2158037573 * b) ** 3, (L - 0.1055613458 * a - 0.0638541728 * b) ** 3, \
                  (L - 0.0894841775 * a - 1.2914855480 * b) ** 3
        rgb = (4.0767416621 * l - 3.3077115913 * m + 0.2309699292 * s, -1.2684380046 * l + 2.6097574011 * m
               - 0.3413193965 * s, -0.0041960863 * l - 0.7034186147 * m + 1.7076147010 * s)
        if k < 0.05 or all(-0.002 < v < 1.002 for v in rgb):
            return tuple(_gam(v) for v in rgb)
NAVY_LAB = oklab(to_rgba(NAVY))
def dark_color(c, role="ink"):
    """The dark-theme version of a color: the same rules as the website's Plotly charts."""
    r, g, b, a = to_rgba(c)
    if a == 0:
        return (r, g, b, a)
    L, A, B = oklab((r, g, b)); chroma = math.hypot(A, B); hexc = to_hex((r, g, b))
    if role == "rule" and chroma >= 0.035: role = "ink"
    if role == "ink" and hexc in DARK:
        return to_rgba(DARK[hexc], a * 0.85 if a < 1 else 1)
    if chroma < 0.035 or (role != "ink" and L > 0.6):          # neutrals: swap light and dark
        hi, lo = (0.78 if role == "rule" else 0.93), (NAVY_LAB[0] + 0.08 if role == "ink" and L < 0.985 else NAVY_LAB[0])
        L2 = hi - (hi - lo) * L; f = max(0.0, (1 - L2) / (1 - NAVY_LAB[0]))
        A, B = A * 0.6 + NAVY_LAB[1] * f, B * 0.6 + NAVY_LAB[2] * f
    else:
        L2 = 0.66 + L * 0.175 if (role == "ink" and L < 0.8) else L   # lift dark ink above the navy
    return (*from_oklab(L2, A, B), a * 0.85 if (role == "ink" and a < 1) else a)

# @title Helper code: restyle a chart (Snowdrop's colors to the book's; light to dark)
def recolor(fig, fn):
    """Apply fn(color, role) to every color of a matplotlib figure; role is paper, rule or ink."""
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(fn(fig.patch.get_facecolor(), "paper"))
    for t in fig.texts: t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
    for ax in fig.axes:
        ax.set_facecolor(fn(ax.get_facecolor(), "paper"))
        for sp in ax.spines.values(): sp.set_edgecolor(fn(sp.get_edgecolor(), "rule"))
        for axis in (ax.xaxis, ax.yaxis):
            for gl in axis.get_gridlines(): gl.set_color(fn(gl.get_color(), "rule"))
            for lab in axis.get_ticklabels(which="both"): lab.set_color(fn(lab.get_color(), "ink"))
            axis.label.set_color(fn(axis.label.get_color(), "ink"))
            axis.set_tick_params(which="both", color=fn(AXIS, "rule"))
        for t in [ax.title, ax._left_title, ax._right_title] + ax.texts: t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
        for ln in ax.lines:
            role = "rule" if ln.get_gid() == "rule" else "ink"
            ln.set_color(fn(ln.get_color(), role))
            ln.set_markerfacecolor(fn(ln.get_markerfacecolor(), role)); ln.set_markeredgecolor(fn(ln.get_markeredgecolor(), role))
        for p in ax.patches:
            p.set_facecolor(fn(p.get_facecolor(), "ink")); p.set_edgecolor(fn(p.get_edgecolor(), "ink"))
        for col in ax.collections:
            col.set_facecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in col.get_facecolors()])
            col.set_edgecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in col.get_edgecolors()])
        leg = ax.get_legend()
        if leg is not None:
            leg.get_frame().set_facecolor(fn(leg.get_frame().get_facecolor(), "paper"))
            leg.get_frame().set_edgecolor(fn(leg.get_frame().get_edgecolor(), "rule"))
            for t in leg.get_texts(): t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
            for h in leg.legend_handles:
                if isinstance(h, matplotlib.lines.Line2D):
                    h.set_color(fn(h.get_color(), "ink"))
                    h.set_markerfacecolor(fn(h.get_markerfacecolor(), "ink")); h.set_markeredgecolor(fn(h.get_markeredgecolor(), "ink"))
                elif isinstance(h, matplotlib.collections.Collection):
                    h.set_facecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in h.get_facecolors()])
                    h.set_edgecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in h.get_edgecolors()])
                elif isinstance(h, matplotlib.patches.Patch):
                    h.set_facecolor(fn(h.get_facecolor(), "ink")); h.set_edgecolor(fn(h.get_edgecolor(), "ink"))

# @title Helper code: Snowdrop's colors to the book's colors
def to_book_colors(fig):
    """Snowdrop's colors -> the book's: black lines stay dark, red data dots become rust, others follow SERIES."""
    seen = {}
    def book(c, role):
        r, g, b, a = to_rgba(c); L, A, B = oklab((r, g, b)); chroma = math.hypot(A, B)
        if role == "paper": return to_rgba("white")
        if role == "rule": return to_rgba(GRID if L > 0.7 else AXIS)
        if chroma < 0.035: return to_rgba(TOTAL if L < 0.3 else (INK if L < 0.6 else "white"), a)
        if r > 0.9 and g < 0.15 and b < 0.15: return to_rgba(RUST, a)
        key = to_hex((r, g, b))
        if key not in seen: seen[key] = SERIES[len(seen) % len(SERIES)]
        return to_rgba(seen[key], a)
    recolor(fig, book)
    for ax in fig.axes:
        ax.grid(True, color=GRID, linewidth=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        for p in ax.patches: p.set_edgecolor("white"); p.set_linewidth(0.6)
        leg = ax.get_legend()
        if leg is not None:
            for h in leg.legend_handles:
                if isinstance(h, matplotlib.patches.Patch): h.set_edgecolor("white")

def book_figure(rows=1, cols=1, width=8.6, height=4.6):
    """A new matplotlib figure in the book's style (Snowdrop's plots change the global style, so reset it)."""
    plt.rcdefaults(); plt.rcParams.update(BOOK_RC)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(rows, cols, figsize=(width, height), squeeze=False)
    return fig, (axes[0, 0] if rows * cols == 1 else axes.ravel())

def _png(fig):
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format="png", dpi=110, facecolor=fig.get_facecolor(), bbox_inches="tight")
    return base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode()

def show(fig, alt, snowdrop=False):
    """Show a chart twice, light and dark; the website picks the one that matches its theme."""
    if snowdrop:
        to_book_colors(fig)
    light = _png(fig)
    recolor(fig, dark_color)
    dark = _png(fig)
    plt.close(fig)
    alt = alt.replace('"', "'")
    display(HTML(f'<div class="book-mpl"><img class="book-mpl-light" alt="{alt}" src="data:image/png;base64,{light}">'
                 f'<img class="book-mpl-dark" alt="{alt}" style="display:none" src="data:image/png;base64,{dark}"></div>'))

# @title Helper code: run Snowdrop quietly
ANSI = re.compile(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*m")              # Snowdrop prints colored text; we strip the colors

def quietly(function, *args, **kwargs):
    """Call a Snowdrop function and keep its printout; return (result, text)."""
    buf = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
        result = function(*args, **kwargs)
    return result, ANSI.sub("", buf.getvalue())

text:
I.4 The model, equation by equation
The model file writes the model in log-linear form. Every variable is a percent deviation from the economy’s balanced growth path (Chapter 5): \(y_t = 0.5\) means that GDP is 0.5 percent above its trend in quarter \(t\). Inflation \(\pi_t\) and the interest rate \(r_t\) are deviations in percentage points per quarter; we multiply them by 4 to report annual rates, as the textbook does. \(E_t x_{t+1}\) is what people expect, in quarter \(t\), for \(x\) next quarter; as in Appendix H, expectations are rational: they are the model’s own forecasts.
Log-linear equations are what you get when you take the first-order conditions of households and firms (Chapter 15’s labor supply and labor demand are two of them) and approximate them around the growth path with the rules of Appendix C.5. Each equation is a weighted average of a few variables, and the weights are combinations of the deep parameters. We read them in five blocks, each with its line in the model file (file names in code font).

I.4.1 The parameters
The deep parameters, with Smets and Wouters’ estimates (the posterior mode) and the names that the file uses:
