Some parameters are fixed rather than estimated: depreciation \(\delta = 0.025\) per quarter (ctou), the steady-state wage markup \(\lambda_w = 1.5\) (clandaw), government purchases at 18 percent of GDP (cg), and the curvature of the goods and labor markets \(\varepsilon_p = \varepsilon_w = 10\) (curvp, curvw). Two combinations appear in many equations: the growth-adjusted discount factor \(\bar{\beta}\gamma\), where \(\bar{\beta} = \beta\gamma^{-\sigma_c}\) (cbetabar), and the steady-state ratios of consumption, investment and capital costs to GDP, \(c_y\), \(i_y\) and \(z_y\) (ccy, ciy, crkky).


I.4.2 Demand: the resource constraint, consumption and investment
The resource constraint. GDP is used for consumption, investment, government purchases and the cost of using capital more intensively:
\[y_t = c_y\,c_t + i_y\,i_t + z_y\,z_t + \varepsilon^g_t \tag{I.1}\]
This is the national income identity \(Y = C + I + G\) of Chapter 2, in percent deviations: each component counts with its share of GDP (\(c_y \approx 0.65\), \(i_y \approx 0.17\)). The spending shock \(\varepsilon^g_t\) is measured in percent of GDP. File: y = ccy*c+ciy*inve+g + crkky*zcap.
The consumption Euler equation. Households choose consumption today versus tomorrow (Chapter 16):
\[c_t = c_1\,c_{t-1} + (1-c_1)\,E_t c_{t+1} + c_2\,(l_t - E_t l_{t+1}) - c_3\,(r_t - E_t\pi_{t+1} + \varepsilon^b_t) \tag{I.2}\]
with \(c_1 = \dfrac{h/\gamma}{1+h/\gamma}\) and \(c_3 = \dfrac{1-h/\gamma}{\sigma_c(1+h/\gamma)}\).

Without habits (\(h = 0\)), \(c_1 = 0\) and the equation is the permanent-income Euler equation: consumption today equals expected consumption tomorrow, less a term in the real interest rate \(r_t - E_t\pi_{t+1}\). A higher real rate makes saving more attractive, so people consume less today.
With habits, \(c_1 > 0\): consumption today also leans on consumption last quarter. Consumption becomes sluggish and hump-shaped, and it reacts less to the interest rate (\(c_3\) falls as \(h\) rises).
\(\varepsilon^b_t\) is the risk premium: a wedge between the federal funds rate \(r_t\) and the rate at which households save and borrow. It is the financial friction of textbook Fig. 15.13.
The \(c_2\) term links consumption and hours. It appears because utility does not separate consumption and work when \(\sigma_c \neq 1\); it is small.

File: c = (chabb/cgamma)/(1+chabb/cgamma)*c(-1) + (1/(1+chabb/cgamma))*c(+1) + ...*(lab-lab(+1)) - (1-chabb/cgamma)/(csigma*(1+chabb/cgamma))*(r-pinf(+1)) + b. Note that the file writes the risk premium as \(b_t = -c_3\,\varepsilon^b_t\), a rescaled version, with a plus sign (Section I.4).
The investment Euler equation. Firms change investment gradually, because large changes are costly:
\[i_t = \frac{1}{1+\bar{\beta}\gamma}\left(i_{t-1} + \bar{\beta}\gamma\,E_t i_{t+1} + \frac{1}{\gamma^2\varphi}\,q_t\right) + \varepsilon^i_t \tag{I.3}\]
Investment rises with \(q_t\), the value of installed capital (Tobin’s \(q\), Chapter 17). The larger the adjustment cost \(\varphi\), the less it reacts. \(\varepsilon^i_t\) is the investment-specific shock: a change in how efficiently investment goods become capital. File: inve = (1/(1+cbetabar*cgamma))*(inve(-1) + cbetabar*cgamma*inve(1)+(1/(cgamma**2*csadjcost))*pk) + qs.
The value of capital. Owning a unit of capital pays its rental rate \(r^k\) and its resale value next quarter; holding a bond pays the real interest rate. Arbitrage between the two gives
\[q_t = -(r_t - E_t\pi_{t+1} + \varepsilon^b_t) + q_1\,E_t r^k_{t+1} + (1-q_1)\,E_t q_{t+1} \tag{I.4}\]
with \(q_1 = r^k_*/(r^k_* + 1 - \delta)\), the share of the rental rate in the return on capital. A higher real interest rate, or risk premium, lowers the value of capital, and through (I.3) investment. This is the investment channel of monetary policy in the IS curve of Chapter 11. File: pk = -r+pinf(1) + (1/c3)*b + (crk/(crk+(1-ctou)))*rk(1) + ((1-ctou)/(crk+(1-ctou)))*pk(1).


I.4.3 Supply: production and capital
The production function. A Cobb–Douglas function of capital services and hours, as in Chapters 4 and 15:
\[y_t = \Phi\left(\alpha\,k^s_t + (1-\alpha)\,l_t + \varepsilon^a_t\right) \tag{I.5}\]
\(\varepsilon^a_t\) is TFP (Chapter 15’s \(\bar{A}\), in percent). \(\Phi > 1\) because firms pay fixed costs: output must cover them, so a 1 percent rise in inputs raises output by more than 1 percent. File: y = cfc*(calfa*k+(1-calfa)*lab +a).
Capital services and capacity utilization. The capital that firms use is the installed stock times how intensively they run it: \(k^s_t = k_{t-1} + z_t\). Firms run capital harder when renting it pays more, \(z_t = \frac{1-\psi}{\psi}\,r^k_t\); a \(\psi\) close to 1 makes utilization expensive to change. Utilization lets output respond to shocks before the capital stock does. Files: k = kp(-1)+zcap and zcap = (1/(czcap/(1-czcap)))*rk.
Capital accumulation.
\[k_t = (1-i_k)\,k_{t-1} + i_k\,i_t + i_k\,(1+\bar{\beta}\gamma)\,\gamma^2\varphi\,\varepsilon^i_t \tag{I.6}\]
with \(i_k = 1-(1-\delta)/\gamma\), the investment–capital ratio. It is the law of motion of capital of the Solow model (Chapter 5) in percent deviations. The last term adds the investment-specific shock. Here the file differs from the paper: it leaves out the factor \((1+\bar{\beta}\gamma)\) (Section I.4). File: kp = (1-cikbar)*kp(-1)+cikbar*inve + cikbar*cgamma**2*csadjcost*qs.
The demand for capital. Firms minimize costs, so the ratio of what they spend on capital and on labor is fixed: \(r^k_t = w_t + l_t - k^s_t\). File: rk = w+lab-k.


I.4.4 Prices: the New Keynesian Phillips curve
Firms set prices as a markup over marginal cost. With Cobb–Douglas production, marginal cost is a weighted average of the rental rate and the real wage, less TFP:
\[mc_t = \alpha\,r^k_t + (1-\alpha)\,w_t - \varepsilon^a_t \tag{I.7}\]
Each quarter a firm can reset its price with probability \(1-\xi_p\). A firm that resets looks ahead, because its price may be stuck for a while, and a firm that cannot reset raises its price with past inflation (indexation \(\iota_p\)). Together these give the New Keynesian Phillips curve:
\[\pi_t = \frac{1}{1+\bar{\beta}\gamma\iota_p}\left(\bar{\beta}\gamma\,E_t\pi_{t+1} + \iota_p\,\pi_{t-1} + \kappa_p\,mc_t\right) + \varepsilon^p_t,
\qquad \kappa_p = \frac{(1-\xi_p)(1-\bar{\beta}\gamma\xi_p)}{\xi_p\left((\Phi-1)\varepsilon_p + 1\right)} \tag{I.8}\]
Compare it with the Phillips curve of Chapter 13, \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\): inflation depends on past inflation (here through indexation), on a measure of how hard the economy is running (here marginal cost), on a shock (here the price markup shock \(\varepsilon^p\)), and also on expected inflation. The slope \(\kappa_p\) is small when prices are sticky (\(\xi_p\) close to 1): marginal cost then moves prices only slowly. Files: mc = calfa*rk+(1-calfa)*w - a and pinf = (1/(1+cbetabar*cgamma*cindp))*(cbetabar*cgamma*pinf(1) + cindp*pinf(-1) + kappa_p*mc) + spinf.


I.4.5 Wages: the wage Phillips curve
Households supply labor through unions that set wages as a markup over the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) between consumption and leisure. The MRS is the wage at which a household is just willing to work one more hour; it is the labor supply curve of Chapter 15:
\[mrs_t = \sigma_l\,l_t + \frac{1}{1-h/\gamma}\left(c_t - \frac{h}{\gamma}\,c_{t-1}\right) \tag{I.9}\]
More hours make leisure more valuable (\(\sigma_l l_t\)), and more consumption makes extra income less valuable: as in Chapter 15, labor supply shifts in when consumption rises. When wages are sticky (Calvo probability \(1-\xi_w\) of resetting, indexation \(\iota_w\)), the real wage closes the gap to the MRS only slowly:
\[w_t = w_1\,w_{t-1} + (1-w_1)\left(E_t w_{t+1} + E_t\pi_{t+1}\right) - w_2\,\pi_t + w_3\,\pi_{t-1} + \kappa_w\,(mrs_t - w_t) + \varepsilon^w_t \tag{I.10}\]
with \(w_1 = 1/(1+\bar{\beta}\gamma)\), \(w_2 = (1+\bar{\beta}\gamma\iota_w)/(1+\bar{\beta}\gamma)\), \(w_3 = \iota_w/(1+\bar{\beta}\gamma)\) and \(\kappa_w = \dfrac{(1-\xi_w)(1-\bar{\beta}\gamma\xi_w)}{(1+\bar{\beta}\gamma)\,\xi_w\left((\lambda_w-1)\varepsilon_w+1\right)}\).
Read it as Chapter 15’s sticky wage: the nominal wage moves slowly, so the real wage falls when inflation rises (\(-w_2\pi_t\)), and the labor market is off its labor supply curve (\(mrs_t \neq w_t\)) for a while. With \(\xi_w \to 0\), \(\kappa_w\) becomes very large and the real wage stays on the labor supply curve. \(\varepsilon^w\) is the wage markup shock. File: w = (1/(1+cbetabar*cgamma))*w(-1) + ... + kappa_w*(csigl*lab + (1/(1-chabb/cgamma))*c - ((chabb/cgamma)/(1-chabb/cgamma))*c(-1) - w) + sw.


I.4.6 Policy: a Taylor rule with an output gap
The central bank sets the interest rate with a Taylor rule (Chapter 12), with three changes:
\[r_t = \rho\,r_{t-1} + (1-\rho)\left(r_\pi\,\pi_t + r_y\,(y_t - y^p_t)\right) + r_{\Delta y}\left[(y_t - y^p_t) - (y_{t-1} - y^p_{t-1})\right] + \varepsilon^r_t \tag{I.11}\]

Smoothing (\(\rho\)): the rate moves partway toward its target each quarter.
The output gap compares GDP with \(y^p_t\), potential output, defined as the GDP of the same economy with flexible prices and wages. That is the meaning of potential output in Chapter 9, made precise.
The rule also responds to the change in the output gap.

\(\varepsilon^r_t\) is the monetary policy shock: a rate change that the rule does not explain. File: r = crpi*(1-crr)*pinf + cry*(1-crr)*(y-yf) + crdy*(y-yf-y(-1)+yf(-1)) + crr*r(-1) + ms.
The flexible-price economy. To compute \(y^p_t\), the file contains a second copy of the real side of the model: equations (I.1)–(I.6) for variables with an f at the end (yf, cf, labf, wf, …), with marginal cost fixed (\(\alpha r^k + (1-\alpha) w = \varepsilon^a\)), the real wage equal to the MRS, and a real interest rate rrf in place of \(r_t - E_t\pi_{t+1}\). Both economies face the same shocks. The flexible economy still has habits, adjustment costs and variable utilization: it removes the nominal frictions only. That makes it a ready-made experiment, which we use in Section I.11.


I.4.7 Shocks
Each of the seven shocks follows an AR(1) process, the process of Chapter 15’s equation (1):
\[\varepsilon^x_t = \rho_x\,\varepsilon^x_{t-1} + \eta^x_t \tag{I.12}\]
where \(\eta^x_t\) is a surprise, and \(\rho_x\) sets how long the shock lasts. Three details:

the spending process also moves with TFP surprises: \(\varepsilon^g_t = \rho_g\varepsilon^g_{t-1} + \eta^g_t + \rho_{ga}\eta^a_t\) (in the data, net exports, which the model counts in \(G\), move with productivity);
the two markup shocks have a moving-average term: \(\varepsilon^p_t = \rho_p\varepsilon^p_{t-1} + \eta^p_t - \mu_p\eta^p_{t-1}\), and the same for wages. This lets a markup surprise fade quickly;
the estimates: TFP is persistent (\(\rho_a = 0.96\)), and so are government purchases (\(\rho_g = 0.98\)); the monetary policy shock (\(\rho_r = 0.13\)) and the risk premium (\(\rho_b = 0.18\)) die out fast.

The file has 37 equations in all: 13 for the sticky economy (it plugs the wage markup into the wage equation, so the paper’s 14 equations become 13 lines), 11 for the flexible copy, 9 for the shock processes and 4 that define growth rates. Snowdrop solves them all at once.

# The estimates of Smets and Wouters (2007, Table 1): the posterior mode, in the file's names.
# Values from the mode file of the published replication (usmodel_mode.mat), rounded to 4 decimals.
SW_MODE = {
    "csadjcost": 5.4882, "csigma": 1.3952, "chabb": 0.7124, "cprobw": 0.7375, "csigl": 1.9199,
    "cprobp": 0.6563, "cindw": 0.5920, "cindp": 0.2284, "czcap": 0.5472, "cfc": 1.6150,
    "crpi": 2.0295, "crr": 0.8153, "cry": 0.0847, "crdy": 0.2229,
    "constepinf": 0.8180, "constebeta": 0.1607, "constelab": -0.1031, "ctrend": 0.4320, "calfa": 0.1928,
    # shock processes: persistence, moving-average terms, and the effect of TFP surprises on spending
    "crhoa": 0.9588, "crhob": 0.1824, "crhog": 0.9762, "crhoqs": 0.7096, "crhoms": 0.1271,
    "crhopinf": 0.9038, "crhow": 0.9719, "cmap": 0.7449, "cmaw": 0.8881, "cgy": 0.5261,
}
# The estimated standard deviations of the seven surprises (percent; inflation and the rate per quarter)
SW_SD = {"ea": 0.4518, "eb": 0.2425, "eg": 0.5200, "eqs": 0.4501, "em": 0.2398, "epinf": 0.1411, "ew": 0.2444}

# Two combinations that we will meet again: the habit weight c1 and the interest-rate weight c3 of (I.2)
gamma = 1 + SW_MODE["ctrend"] / 100
h, sigma_c = SW_MODE["chabb"], SW_MODE["csigma"]
c1 = (h / gamma) / (1 + h / gamma)
c3 = (1 - h / gamma) / (sigma_c * (1 + h / gamma))
print(f"gamma = {gamma:.4f}: trend growth of {4 * (gamma - 1) * 100:.2f} percent a year")
print(f"c1 = {c1:.3f}: weight of last quarter's consumption in (I.2)")
print(f"c3 = {c3:.3f}: response of consumption to a 1-point rise in the quarterly real rate")
print(f"Half-life of a TFP shock: {np.log(0.5) / np.log(SW_MODE['crhoa']):.1f} quarters")

What to notice. With habits, consumption reacts to the real interest rate with a coefficient of only about 0.12: a 1 point rise in the quarterly real rate (4 points at an annual rate) lowers consumption by 0.12 percent on impact, before the effects that build up through expected future consumption. The TFP shock loses half its size in about 16 quarters: exactly the “4 years” of Chapter 15 (equation 1 there).
Your turn. How much does the habit parameter matter for these two numbers? Compute \(c_1\) and \(c_3\) for \(h = 0\) (no habits) and for \(h = 0.9\). Which value of \(h\) makes consumption react most to the interest rate?


Show the answer

for h_try in [0.0, 0.71, 0.9]:
    c1_try = (h_try / gamma) / (1 + h_try / gamma)
    c3_try = (1 - h_try / gamma) / (sigma_c * (1 + h_try / gamma))
    print(f"h = {h_try}: c1 = {c1_try:.3f}, c3 = {c3_try:.3f}")
With \(h = 0\), \(c_1 = 0\) and \(c_3 = 1/\sigma_c \approx 0.72\): consumption reacts six times more to the interest rate than at the estimate. With \(h = 0.9\), \(c_1 \approx 0.47\) and \(c_3 \approx 0.04\): consumption is very sluggish. Strong habits make consumption smooth and slow, which is what Smets and Wouters find in the data.

I.5 Reading the model file with care
A model file from a package is research software: someone wrote it for one project and shared it. Before we trust it, we read it (Appendix H.2 makes the same point). Here is its header, which its authors wrote for that purpose.

text = open(os.path.join(WORK, "sw_model.yaml"), newline="").read()
print("Line endings: Windows (\\r\\n)" if "\r\n" in text else "Line endings: Unix (\\n)")
text = text.replace("\r\n", "\n")                     # use one kind of line ending
print("\n".join(text.splitlines()[:44]))

Line endings: Windows (\r\n)
name: Smets and Wouters Model.
 
#   This file provides replication files for 
#   Smets, Frank and Wouters, Rafael (2007): "Shocks and Frictions in US Business Cycles: A Bayesian
#   DSGE Approach", American Economic Review, 97(3), 586-606, that are compatible with Dynare 4.5 onwards
#  
#   To replicate the full results, you have to get back to the original replication files available at
#   https:#www.aeaweb.org/articles.php?doi=10.1257/aer.97.3.586 and include the respective estimation commands and mode-files.
#  
#   Notes:
#    - The consumption Euler equation in the paper, equation (2), premultiplies the risk premium process \varepsilon_t**b,
#        denoted by b in this code, by the coefficient c_3. In the code this prefactor is omitted by setting the 
#        coefficient to 1. As a consequence, b in this code actually is b:=c_3 #  \varepsilon_t**b. As a consequence, in 
#        the arbitrage equation for the value of capital in the paper, equation (4), the term 1 #  \varepsilon_t**b
#        is replaced by 1/c_3 #  b, which is equal to \varepsilon_t**b given the above redefinition. This rescaling also explains why the 
#        standard deviation of the risk premium shock in the AR(1)-process for b has a different standard deviation than reported
#        in the paper. However, the results are unaffected by this scaling factor (except for the fact that the posterior distribution
#        reported in the paper cannot be directly translated to the present mod-file due to parameter correlation in the posterior.  
#    - As pointed out in Del Negro/Schorfheide (2012): "Notes on New-Keynesian Models"
#        in the code implementation of equation (8) for both the flex price and the sticky price/wage economy, 
#        there is a (1+cbetabar #  cgamma) missing in the i_2 in front of q_t (denoted qs in the code). 
#        Equation (8) in the paper reads:  
#            (1-(1-delta)/gamma) #  (1+beta #  gamma**(1-sigma)) #  gamma**2 #  varphi
#        which translates to the code snippet:
#            (1-(1-ctou)/cgamma)*(1+cbetabar*cgamma)*cgamma**2*csadjcost
#        But the code implements
#            (1-(1-ctou)/cgamma)*cgamma**2*csadjcost
#        which corresponds to an equation reading
#            (1-(1-delta)/gamma)*gamma**2*varphi
#    - Chib/Ramamurthy (2010): "Tailored randomized block MCMC methods with application to DSGE models", Journal of Econometrics, 155, pp. 19-38
#        have pointed out that the mode reported in the original Smets/Wouters (2007) paper is not actually the mode. \bar \pi (constepinf) is estimated lower
#        while \bar \l (constelab) is higher.
#    - Note that at the prior mean, [cmap,crhopinf] and [cmaw,crhow] are pairwise collinear. Thus, running identification at the prior
#        mean will return a warning. But this is only a local issue. These parameters are only indistinguishable at the prior mean, but not 
#        at different points.
#    - In the prior Table 1A in the paper, the 
#            - habit parameter $\lambda$ is erroneously labeled h
#            - the fixed cost parameter $\phi_p$ is labeled $\Phi$ 
#    - Table 1B claims that $\rho_{ga}$ follows a beta prior with B(0.5,0.2**2), but the code shows that it actually
#        follows a normal distribution with N(0.5,0.25**2)
#  
#   This file was originally written by Frank Smets and Rafeal Wouters and has been updated by Johannes Pfeifer. 
 



The header says four things:

The file follows the published replication files of Smets and Wouters (2007), updated by Johannes Pfeifer.
The risk premium is rescaled: the file’s b is \(c_3\) times the paper’s \(\varepsilon^b\). Our equation (I.2) shows why: in the paper the premium enters consumption multiplied by \(c_3\); the file writes \(c_3\varepsilon^b\) as one variable. The file also flips its sign: it subtracts \(c_3(r_t - E_t\pi_{t+1})\) and adds b, so b equals \(-c_3\varepsilon^b\), and a rise in the risk premium is a negative b.
Equation (8) of the paper, our (I.6), is coded without the factor \((1+\bar{\beta}\gamma)\) in front of the investment shock, as Del Negro and Schorfheide (2012) noticed. The published code has the same slip, and so the published estimates were computed with it.
Some prior distributions in the paper’s tables differ from those in the code.

Reading the rest of the file finds four more things to know.

I.5.1 What the file changes, and what it leaves out

table["differs"] = (table["in the file"] - table["Smets-Wouters estimate"]).abs() > 0.005
print(f"{table['differs'].sum()} of {len(table)} values differ from the published estimates")

Python note. yaml.safe_load(text) turns a YAML file into a Python dictionary: one key per block (symbols, calibration, equations, …). cal.get(k) returns the value of key k, or None if it is missing. pd.to_numeric turns the column into numbers, and .abs() > 0.005 flags the rows that differ.

Every value differs. The file is the starting point of the COVID-19 project in its folder, not a copy of the paper: its authors switched off the two markup processes (crhopinf, crhow, cmap and cmaw are 0) and the persistence of the monetary shock (crhoms is 0), and set many other parameters to other values. The other things to know:

The time preference is set twice. constebeta (0.742) should give the discount factor \(\beta = 1/(1 + 0.742/100) = 0.9926\), but the file sets cbeta: 0.9995 separately; the line that would link them is a comment.
The growth rates are not deviations. The starting values of the four growth rates (dy, dc, dinve, dw) are set to the trend growth rate, although in the model’s own equations they are deviations from it, so their steady state is 0. Snowdrop’s report then shows residuals of 0.398 for those four equations.
The estimation block does not load. The block estimated_parameters has a different layout from the one Snowdrop expects (it lacks the starting-value column, and one prior is misspelled BETA_PD), so importModel stops with could not convert string to float: 'inv_gamma_pdf'. We do not estimate, so we leave the block out.

I.5.2 Our corrected copy
We write our own copy of the file, sw_ours.yaml, from the dictionary, with five changes: the published estimates, \(\beta\) linked to constebeta, growth rates that start at 0, no estimation block, and the factor \((1+\bar{\beta}\gamma)\) restored in the capital equations of both economies. The function write_sw does this for any set of parameter values, so that we can change them later; load_sw writes the file and reads it with Snowdrop.

FIX = [("cikbar*cgamma**2*csadjcost*qs", "cikbar*(1+cbetabar*cgamma)*cgamma**2*csadjcost*qs"),        # sticky economy
       ("(cikbar)*(cgamma**2*csadjcost)*qs", "(cikbar)*(1+cbetabar*cgamma)*(cgamma**2*csadjcost)*qs")]  # flexible economy

def write_sw(values=None, fixed=True, file="sw_ours.yaml"):
    """Write a Smets-Wouters model file: the published estimates, changed by `values`; return its path."""
    d = yaml.safe_load(text)
    d.pop("estimated_parameters")                      # not used, and Snowdrop cannot read it
    d["calibration"].update(SW_MODE)                   # the published estimates
    d["calibration"]["cbeta"] = "1/(1+constebeta/100)" # the discount factor follows constebeta
    for name in ["dy", "dc", "dinve", "dw"]:
        d["calibration"][name] = 0                     # deviations start at 0
    d["calibration"].update(values or {})              # our own changes, if any
    if fixed:                                          # restore the factor (1 + beta*gamma) of equation (I.6)
        eqs = "\n".join(d["equations"])
        for old, new in FIX:
            assert eqs.count(old) == 1, old            # stop if the file is not what we expect
            eqs = eqs.replace(old, new)
        d["equations"] = eqs.split("\n")
    path = os.path.join(WORK, file)
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        yaml.safe_dump(d, f, sort_keys=False, width=10_000)
    return path

def load_sw(values=None, fixed=True, solver="AndersonMoore", file="sw_ours.yaml"):
    """Write the model file and read it with Snowdrop (the linear solver is chosen here)."""
    model, report = quietly(driver.importModel, fname=write_sw(values, fixed, file), Solver=solver)
    return model

sw = load_sw()
P = dict(zip(sw.symbols["parameters"], sw.calibration["parameters"]))
print(f"{len(sw.symbols['variables'])} variables, {len(sw.symbols['shocks'])} shocks, "
      f"{len(sw.symbols['parameters'])} parameters")
print("Derived values:", {k: round(P[k], 4) for k in ["cbetabar", "ccy", "ciy", "crkky", "cikbar"]})

37 variables, 7 shocks, 41 parameters
Derived values: {'cbetabar': np.float64(0.9924), 'ccy': np.float64(0.6469), 'ciy': np.float64(0.1731), 'crkky': np.float64(0.1928), 'cikbar': np.float64(0.0292)}



Python note. d.pop("estimated_parameters") removes a key from a dictionary; .update(...) adds or replaces several keys at once. assert condition, message stops the program with the message if the condition is false: a cheap way to make sure that a text replacement really happened, exactly once. values or {} uses an empty dictionary when values is None.

What to notice. Snowdrop computes the derived values from the deep parameters when it reads the file: the consumption share \(c_y\) is 0.65 and the investment share \(i_y\) is 0.17, close to U.S. data. This is why we change parameters by writing a new file rather than by changing them in a model already read: the derived values would otherwise keep their old values.

text:
I.6 Solving the model and the impulse response function
Solving a linear rational-expectations model means finding its decision rules: every variable today as a linear function of the state (last quarter’s variables) and today’s shocks, with the Blanchard–Kahn condition of Appendix H.4 checking that there is exactly one stable solution. Snowdrop has several solvers for linear models. We choose Anderson and Moore’s (Solver="AndersonMoore"), for a reason that this section shows.

I.6.1 An impulse response, in the textbook’s units
Our function irf gives one shock in quarter 1 and returns the response of the main variables over the following quarters, in the units of Chapter 15: percent deviations for GDP, consumption, investment, hours and the real wage, and percentage points at an annual rate for inflation and the interest rate.

NAMES = {"y": "GDP", "c": "consumption", "inve": "investment", "lab": "hours", "w": "real wage",
         "pinf": "inflation", "r": "interest rate", "zcap": "utilization", "kp": "capital",
         "yf": "flexible-price GDP", "labf": "flexible-price hours"}
ANNUAL = ["pinf", "r"]                                  # quarterly rates: multiply by 4

def irf(model, shock, size, T=40):
    """Response to a shock of `size` in quarter 1, for T quarters, in the textbook's units."""
    shocks = model.symbols["shocks"]
    values = [0.0] * len(shocks)
    values[shocks.index(shock)] = size
    model.options["periods"] = [1]                     # the shock hits in period 1 only
    model.options["shock_values"] = [values]
    (y, dates), report = quietly(driver.run, model=model, Plot=False)
    table = pd.DataFrame(np.asarray(y)[1:T + 1], columns=model.symbols["variables"])
    for name in ANNUAL:
        table[name] = 4 * table[name]
    table = table[list(NAMES)].rename(columns=NAMES)
    table.index = range(1, T + 1)                       # quarter 1 is the quarter of the shock
    table.index.name = "quarter"
    return table

I.6.2 Checking the solution
Appendix H’s habit is to check every result. Snowdrop’s checkSolution puts a simulated path back into every equation and returns the residuals: for a correct solution they are zero, up to rounding.

def max_residual(model, shock, size):
    """The largest equation residual along a simulated path."""
    shocks = model.symbols["shocks"]
    values = [0.0] * len(shocks); values[shocks.index(shock)] = size
    model.options["periods"] = [1]; model.options["shock_values"] = [values]
    (y, dates), report = quietly(driver.run, model=model, Plot=False)
    errors = checkSolution(model, periods=model.options["periods"], y=np.asarray(y))
    return float(np.max(np.abs(np.asarray(errors))))

}, index=["Anderson-Moore", "Klein"])

Klein’s solver, the one we used for Ireland’s model in Appendix H, returns a solution that leaves residuals of about 0.02 in this model, and its consumption response is a tenth of the correct one. text:
I.7 A monetary policy shock
Textbook Figs. 15.9 and 15.10 show what happens after a temporary rise of 1 percentage point in the federal funds rate. In the model the rate is quarterly, so a rise of 1 percentage point at an annual rate is a shock \(\eta^r = 0.25\) to the Taylor rule (I.11). The shock is close to Smets and Wouters’ estimated typical size, 0.24 (SW_SD["em"]).

Fig. 1: The response of GDP to a monetary policy shock

fig, ax = book_figure(width=8.0, height=4.4)
gdp = mp["GDP"].iloc[:20]
ax.plot(gdp.index, gdp, color=BLUE)
ax.axhline(0, color=AXIS, linewidth=1, linestyle="--", gid="rule")
low = gdp.idxmin()
ax.plot([1, low], [gdp[1], gdp[low]], "o", color=BLUE)
ax.annotate(f"quarter 1: {gdp[1]:.2f}", (1, gdp[1]), xytext=(2.2, gdp[1] - 0.02), color=INK)
ax.annotate(f"largest fall, quarter {low}: {gdp[low]:.2f}", (low, gdp[low]), xytext=(low + 1.2, gdp[low] - 0.02), color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(0, 20.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.45, 0.05); ax.set_xticks([1, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20])
ax.set_title(f"After a 1-point rise in the funds rate, GDP falls most in quarter {low}, by {abs(gdp[low]):.2f} percent")

What to notice. The numbers match the textbook’s: GDP falls 0.2 percent at once and about 0.35 percent at the trough, a year after the shock. The delayed peak is what Chapter 15’s adjustment-cost rule produced (its equation (1) with partial adjustment), and here it has three sources: habits slow consumption, adjustment costs slow investment, and the interest rate stays high for several quarters because the Taylor rule smooths it.


Fig. 2: The dynamic effects of a monetary policy shock
Textbook Fig. 15.10 adds consumption, hours and inflation. We write a function for these four-panel charts, which we use for every shock from now on. runs is a list of impulse responses; the first is drawn as a solid line, the others are dashed comparisons.

PANELS = [("GDP", "GDP"), ("consumption", "Consumption"), ("hours", "Hours worked"), ("inflation", "Inflation")]

def four_panels(runs, title, alt, T=20, panels=PANELS, legend=True):
    """Draw 2x2 impulse responses. runs: list of (label, table, color, linestyle)."""
    many = legend and len(runs) > 1
    fig, axes = book_figure(2, 2, width=10.0, height=7.0 if many else 6.6)
    for ax, (column, name) in zip(axes, panels):
        for label, table, color, style in runs:
            ax.plot(table.index[:T], table[column].iloc[:T], color=color, linestyle=style, label=label)
        ax.axhline(0, color=AXIS, linewidth=1, linestyle="--", gid="rule")
        low, high = ax.get_ylim()                       # keep the zero line off the edges
        pad = 0.08 * (high - low)
        ax.set_ylim(min(low, -pad), max(high, pad))
        ax.set_title(name)
        ax.set_xlim(0, T + 0.5)
        ax.set_ylabel("percentage points, annual rate" if column in ("inflation", "interest rate")
                      else "percent change", fontsize=9.5)
    for ax in axes[2:]:
        ax.set_xlabel("quarters after the shock")
    fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=13, color=INK)
    if many:                                            # one legend, in a strip under the title
        fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.92])
        strip = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.905, 1.0, 0.04])
        strip.axis("off")
        strip.legend(*axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="center", ncol=min(len(runs), 4), fontsize=9.5)
    else:
        fig.tight_layout()
    show(fig, alt)

four_panels([("monetary policy shock", mp, BLUE, "-")],
            "A 1-point rise in the funds rate lowers GDP, consumption, hours and inflation",
            "Four impulse responses to a monetary policy shock: GDP, consumption and hours fall, with a trough "
            "after about a year; inflation falls by about 0.2 points")




Source. Adapted from Fig. 15.10 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., based on Smets and Wouters (2007); computed with the model file of the Snowdrop package and the published estimates.

Python note. zip(axes, panels) walks through two lists side by side: the first chart with the first panel, and so on. A tuple such as (label, table, color, style) in a for statement unpacks the four parts of each run.

print(f"Largest fall: GDP {peak['GDP']:.2f}%, consumption {peak['consumption']:.2f}%, "
      f"hours {peak['hours']:.2f}%, inflation {peak['inflation']:.2f} points")
print(f"Quarters in which inflation is below -0.15 points: {(mp['inflation'] < -0.15).sum()}")

      f"{mp['interest rate'][3]:.2f} in quarter 3")

Largest fall: GDP -0.35%, consumption -0.35%, hours -0.23%, inflation -0.20 points
Quarters in which inflation is below -0.15 points: 6
The funds rate itself rises by 0.75 points in quarter 1, 0.33 in quarter 3


What to notice. As in the textbook, consumption falls almost exactly as much as GDP, hours fall less (part of the fall in output comes from lower capacity utilization), and inflation falls by up to 0.2 points and stays below \(-0.15\) for a year and a half (the textbook says about two years). The funds rate itself rises by only 0.75 points: the rule responds at once to the lower inflation and output, and offsets part of the shock.
Jones (2024) explains the large consumption response by the investment adjustment costs. Section I.11 tests this and finds that, in this model, the habits matter more.

The largest fall is almost twice as large, about \(-0.65\) percent, still in quarter 4: a tightening that people expect to last longer raises long-term real rates more, and the Euler equations (I.2) and (I.4) look at the whole future path of rates. This is also why central banks care about forward guidance (Chapter 13).

I.8 A TFP shock
Textbook Fig. 15.11 shows a rise of 1 percent in TFP: a surprise \(\eta^a = 1\) in (I.12), which then decays at the rate \(\rho_a = 0.96\). Because the spending process moves with TFP surprises, government purchases rise too, by \(\rho_{ga} = 0.53\) percent of GDP.

Consumption: 0.19% at once, largest 0.81%
Hours: -0.63% at once; first above zero in quarter 6
Inflation: -0.48 points at once


What to notice. Each pattern that Jones (2024) describes is here, with the same sizes:

GDP rises by about 1.5 percent at its peak, more than the 1 percent rise in TFP, because capital accumulates as in the Solow model (investment rises by almost 3 percent at its peak).
Consumption rises by about half as much: households smooth it.
Hours fall by more than half a percent at first, and turn positive only in the sixth quarter.
Inflation falls by about half a point: higher TFP lowers marginal cost (I.7), and demand rises only slowly.



Fig. 4: Ten years after a TFP shock
The TFP shock is persistent, so five years do not show the end of the story. Over ten years, with capital and investment added:

long_panels = [("GDP", "GDP"), ("consumption", "Consumption"), ("investment", "Investment"), ("capital", "Capital stock")]
four_panels([("TFP shock", tfp, BLUE, "-")],
            "Over ten years, capital builds up and keeps GDP high while TFP returns to normal",
            "Impulse responses to a TFP shock over 40 quarters: GDP, consumption, investment and the capital stock",
            T=40, panels=long_panels)




Source. Computed with the model file of the Snowdrop package and the estimates of Smets and Wouters (2007); related to Chapter 15 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed..
What to notice. Investment responds most, peaking at almost 3 percent after two years, and the capital stock builds up slowly and peaks only after about seven years. After ten years TFP is back to a fifth of its first rise (\(0.96^{40} \approx 0.19\)), but capital is still well above its trend, and it keeps GDP and consumption up. This is the Solow model’s transition dynamics (Chapter 5) inside a business-cycle model.
Your turn. Make the TFP shock almost permanent: crhoa = 0.99. Do hours still fall at first? Why might they?


Show the answer

tfp_perm = irf(load_sw({"crhoa": 0.99}), "ea", 1.0)
tfp_perm[["GDP", "consumption", "hours"]].iloc[[0, 3, 7, 19]].round(2)
Yes: hours still fall by almost 0.6 percent at first, and they stay close to zero for years. A lasting rise in TFP makes households richer, so they want to consume more and work less (the wealth effect on labor supply of Chapter 15); and with habits, adjustment costs and sticky prices, demand still rises only slowly, so firms need fewer workers to produce it. Consumption now rises much more, since the gain in income is more permanent.

I.9 A rise in government purchases
Textbook Fig. 15.12 shows a temporary rise in government purchases of 1 percent. In the model, \(\varepsilon^g\) is in percent of GDP, and the textbook’s numbers (GDP rises by about 1 percent, a multiplier of about 1) match a surprise \(\eta^g = 1\): purchases rise by 1 percent of GDP, about 5.5 percent of purchases themselves.

Fig. 5: The dynamic effects of a rise in government purchases

gov = irf(sw, "eg", 1.0)
four_panels([("government purchases shock", gov, BLUE, "-")],
            "Purchases of 1 percent of GDP raise GDP and hours and crowd out consumption",
            "Four impulse responses to a government purchases shock: GDP rises about 1 percent and hours about "
            "0.65 percent; consumption falls slowly to about -0.5 percent; inflation barely moves")




Source. Adapted from Fig. 15.12 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., based on Smets and Wouters (2007); computed with the model file of the Snowdrop package and the published estimates.
The multiplier is the change in GDP per unit of extra purchases (Chapter 11). Both are in percent of GDP here, so the impact multiplier is the GDP response in quarter 1. The cumulative multiplier adds up the responses of GDP and of purchases over several quarters.

g_path = SW_MODE["crhog"] ** np.arange(40)             # purchases: 1, rho_g, rho_g^2, ... percent of GDP
for quarters in [1, 4, 8, 20]:
    cumulative = gov["GDP"].iloc[:quarters].sum() / g_path[:quarters].sum()
    print(f"Multiplier over {quarters:2d} quarters: {cumulative:.2f}")
print(f"Consumption: {gov['consumption'][1]:.2f}% at once, {gov['consumption'].iloc[:20].min():.2f}% at its lowest")
print(f"Inflation: at most {gov['inflation'].iloc[:20].abs().max():.2f} points")

Multiplier over  4 quarters: 0.80
Multiplier over  8 quarters: 0.68
Multiplier over 20 quarters: 0.52
Consumption: -0.11% at once, -0.50% at its lowest
Inflation: at most 0.13 points


What to notice. The impact multiplier is about 0.94, close to the textbook’s “around 1”, and it falls over time as private spending is crowded out: consumption falls steadily (the wealth effect of future taxes of Chapter 15, Fig. 5), and investment falls with the higher real interest rate. Hours rise, because the poorer households supply more labor. Inflation barely moves: the extra output comes mostly from more work, not from prices.
Your turn. Make the spending rise short-lived: crhog = 0.5. What happens to the impact multiplier, and to consumption? Use the idea of Chapter 16: what matters for consumption is lifetime wealth.

gov_short[["GDP", "consumption", "hours"]].iloc[[0, 1, 3, 7]].round(2)
A short-lived rise costs little in lifetime taxes, so the wealth effect is small: consumption no longer falls, it even rises a little with the extra income from work, and the impact multiplier rises to about 1.1. Persistent spending crowds out more private spending.

What to notice. Both markup shocks are the inflation shocks \(\bar{o}\) of Chapter 13: inflation rises and, because the Taylor rule raises the interest rate, GDP and hours fall. The price markup shock is short and sharp: inflation jumps by about 1 point and is back to normal within two years, and the real wage falls because prices rise faster than wages. The wage markup shock raises the real wage, lasts much longer (\(\rho_w = 0.97\)), and lowers GDP and hours for many years. In Smets and Wouters’ variance decompositions, the markup shocks explain most of the movements of inflation, and the wage markup shock a large part of the movements of output at long horizons.

text:
I.12 Which frictions matter? Experiments
Chapter 15 explained each pattern with one friction: sticky prices for the fall in hours after a TFP shock, sticky wages for the fall in the real wage after a monetary expansion, investment adjustment costs for the large fall in consumption after a monetary tightening. In a model with all frictions at once, we can test these explanations: we change one parameter, solve the model again, and compare. The function experiment does this for a list of values.

def experiment(parameter, values, shock, size):
    """Impulse responses to one shock for several values of one parameter; returns a list of runs."""
    colors, runs = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY], []
    for j, value in enumerate(values):
        model = load_sw({parameter: value}, file="sw_experiment.yaml")
        label = f"{parameter} = {value}" + (" (estimate)" if abs(value - SW_MODE[parameter]) < 0.01 else "")
        runs.append((label, irf(model, shock, size), colors[j], "-" if j == 0 else "--"))
    return runs

def peaks(runs, columns, T=20):
    """The largest response (in absolute value) of each column within T quarters, for each run."""
    rows = {}
    for label, table, color, style in runs:
        part = table[columns].iloc[:T]
        rows[label] = [part[c][part[c].abs().idxmax()] for c in columns]
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, index=[f"largest {c}" for c in columns]).T.round(2)


Python note. enumerate(values) gives each value together with its position j, which we use to pick a color. part[c].abs().idxmax() is the quarter in which the response is largest in absolute value, so that peaks reports falls as negative numbers and rises as positive ones.


Fig. 9: Sticky prices and the fall in hours after a TFP shock
The textbook explains the fall in hours after a TFP shock by sticky prices: demand rises slowly, and firms with higher productivity need fewer workers to meet it. If that is the whole story, hours should rise when prices are flexible. We lower the Calvo parameter \(\xi_p\) from its estimate, 0.66 (prices last about three quarters on average, \(1/(1-\xi_p)\)), to 0.1, and add the model’s own flexible economy, which has flexible prices and wages.

            "Impulse responses to a TFP shock for four values of the Calvo price parameter: GDP rises faster and "
            "inflation falls more when prices are less sticky; hours fall at first in every case", panels=panels)

What to notice. Only when the nominal and the real frictions are weak does the fall in hours almost vanish: hours fall by about 0.15 percent in the first quarter and rise from the second. The textbook’s simple labor market, with no habits and no adjustment costs, is close to this last case. Which frictions are strong in the real economy is exactly what estimation decides, and the estimated frictions make hours fall. Whether they do in the data is, as the textbook says, still debated.


Fig. 10: Sticky wages and the real wage after a monetary shock
Chapter 15 showed that with sticky nominal wages, a monetary shock moves the real wage against employment. We vary the Calvo parameter of wages \(\xi_w\).

What to notice. At the estimate, a tightening lowers the real wage only a little, and slowly: nominal wages are sticky, and so are prices. With more flexible wages, the real wage falls more, which makes marginal cost (I.7) and inflation fall more, and GDP and hours a little less. More flexible wages make the economy adjust through prices rather than quantities. In this model prices are sticky too, so the real wage falls with employment, unlike the sticky-wage-only case of Chapter 15, Fig. 7: both nominal frictions together decide its sign.


Fig. 11: Habits, investment costs and consumption after a monetary shock

What to notice. The adjustment cost changes the response of investment a lot (it falls about twice as much with \(\varphi = 2\) as at the estimate), but the largest fall in consumption hardly changes. The habit parameter changes the consumption response: with \(h = 0.1\), consumption falls by about 0.6 percent at once, against 0.2 at the estimate, and its trough comes at once instead of after a year. So in this model, habits shape the consumption response, and adjustment costs the investment response. Consumption falls about as much as GDP because GDP falls less: investment, held back by its adjustment costs, falls only about 0.6 percent, and capacity utilization absorbs part of the shock.

What to notice. Smoothing does most of the work. With \(\rho = 0.82\), a surprise keeps the funds rate high for about a year, and it is the expected path of rates, not one quarter’s rate, that moves consumption and investment through (I.2)–(I.4). Without smoothing, the rate is back to normal in the next quarter and GDP falls by only about 0.05 percent. A stronger response to inflation (\(r_\pi = 3\)) makes the fall in inflation and GDP smaller: people know that the bank will push inflation back hard, so it moves less in the first place.
Your turn. Combine the two cases of Fig. 9. Which friction, on its own, removes most of the fall in hours after a TFP shock: flexible prices (cprobp = 0.1), weak habits (chabb = 0.1), or low adjustment costs (csadjcost = 2)?


Show the answer

for change in [{"cprobp": 0.1}, {"chabb": 0.1}, {"csadjcost": 2.0}]:
    hours = irf(load_sw(change), "ea", 1.0)["hours"]
    print(change, f"hours in quarter 1: {hours[1]:.2f}%, quarter 4: {hours[4]:.2f}%")
Each change on its own leaves a fall in hours in the first quarter; none removes it. Weak habits do the most (hours fall by about 0.3 percent instead of 0.6), flexible prices less, and low adjustment costs almost nothing. The frictions reinforce each other: demand rises slowly when any of them is strong, so the fall in hours almost disappears only when all are weak.

I.13 The file’s own numbers, and the corrected equation
How much did our two changes to the file matter? We compare four versions for the monetary policy and the investment-specific shocks: the published estimates with and without the corrected equation (I.6), and the file’s own calibration.

def load_file_calibration(fixed):
    """The file as shipped (its own calibration), without the estimation block."""
    d = yaml.safe_load(text); d.pop("estimated_parameters")
    if fixed:
        eqs = "\n".join(d["equations"])
        for old, new in FIX:
            eqs = eqs.replace(old, new)
        d["equations"] = eqs.split("\n")
    path = os.path.join(WORK, "sw_file.yaml")
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        yaml.safe_dump(d, f, sort_keys=False, width=10_000)
    model, report = quietly(driver.importModel, fname=path, Solver="AndersonMoore")
    return model

versions = {"estimates, corrected (I.6)": sw,
            "estimates, as published": load_sw(fixed=False, file="sw_published.yaml"),
            "file's calibration, corrected": load_file_calibration(True)}
rows = {}
for name, model in versions.items():

What to notice. The corrected equation changes only the responses to the investment-specific shock, by a few percent: it multiplies only that shock. The calibration matters much more: with the file’s values, the same monetary shock lowers GDP by almost twice as much. A file with the right equations and the wrong numbers gives confident, wrong answers. Before you use a model file, compare its numbers with the source it claims to follow.

I.14 Go further

I.14.1 Estimating the model
Appendix H.11–H.12 estimated a three-equation model. The same steps estimate this one: the seven observed series, measurement equations (the file’s measurement_equations block links them to the model), priors (Table 1 of the paper, or the file’s estimated_parameters block, rewritten in Snowdrop’s layout) and Snowdrop’s estimate. The data are in the replication files of Smets and Wouters (2007) and in Pfeifer’s collection of Dynare models; the FRED series can be downloaded with the tools of Appendix B. Expect a long computation: 36 parameters and a flat likelihood in some directions.


I.14.2 Where the equations come from
The log-linear equations of Section I.3 are derived in Smets and Wouters (2007, Section I and the online appendix) and, step by step, in Galí (2015, for the simpler New Keynesian model) and in the notes of Del Negro and Schorfheide (2012). Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (2005) explain why each friction is there: they choose them to match the responses of the U.S. economy to a monetary policy shock estimated without a model.

title: I. The DSGE Model of Smets and Wouters
text:
I.15 Concluding remarks

The Smets–Wouters model puts the pieces of Chapter 15 together, with habits, investment adjustment costs, variable capacity utilization, sticky prices and wages with indexation, a Taylor rule on the output gap and seven shocks. Its 14 equations are log-linear: each one is a weighted average whose weights come from the deep parameters.
Snowdrop solves it in a fraction of a second, but only one of its linear solvers gives the right answer for this model: checking the residuals found the problem.
With the published estimates, the model reproduces the textbook’s responses to a monetary policy shock, a TFP shock and a rise in government purchases, almost number for number. The financial friction shock matches once its units are understood.
Experiments show that the frictions work together. The fall in hours after a TFP shock comes from sticky prices and from real frictions; habits shape the response of consumption to monetary policy, and adjustment costs that of investment; interest-rate smoothing carries most of the effect of a policy surprise.
Research files must be read with care. The model file differs from the paper in its numbers, in one equation and in the units of one shock, and each difference changes the answers.
